649] It is said: Indeed, this treatise is not intended to demonstrate the primacy of the individual word-meanings; rather, it is devoted entirely to [establishing] their status as subsidiaries (*śeṣatā*) to the sacrifice.

The meaning is that, according to the *prāya* view, by means of words such as "clarified butter" (*ājya*) and so forth, the sacrifice which has clarified butter and the like as its instrumental means is indicated through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Now, even on this view, since all [subsidiaries] would have subsidiariness (*śeṣatva*) by being directly for the sake of the mandate (*niyoga*), just like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, it would not be possible— on the alternative view— to distinguish between subsidiary and principal elements, such as the *prayāja* and the *āgneya* sacrifice, because all subsidiaries would [be equally related] to their own sentences...
Because it is subordinate to the purpose of the application of the vessels. The answer is: we shall state the refutation of this objection when examining the authority of *prakaraṇa* (context).

Here, however, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is based on the impossibility of any other function; for it has been stated that [the grinding] is connected by the phrase "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām*). If another function, such as the preparation of rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), were resorted to, then it would not be connected with the phrase "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

This is because rice and the like are understood to be effects (*kārya*) by virtue of their own independence. However, the intermediate apūrva, which is the effect of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, is not understood as an effect in its own right. Rather, since momentary sacrifices cannot logically function as auxiliary members (*aṅga*), intermediate apūrvas are postulated here for the sake of establishing that status; yet they are not perceived as independent. Therefore, the *niyoga* (the mandate) is indeed characterized in this manner, just like the *prayāja* offerings and the rest.

All [the actions] are connected with all [the substances]. How then is there the accusative case in the words *vrīhīn* (rice grains) and *ājyam* (clarified butter)? In this view, it will be just like the case of the groats (*saktu*); the meaning is that there is a transposition of the case endings. Or, as in the expression *gāṃ dadāti* ("he gives a cow"), the accusative is used for an object that is not intended (*anīpsita-karman*). On this point, the Bhāṣya says: "But the ritual acts such as threshing are [known] through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)."
"Their connection with rice and so forth is enjoined by the sentence"—

this [statement] is consistent only with this very prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because it accepts that they are subordinate actions (*guṇakarman*); it is not [consistent] with the definition of the non-difference of the injunction (*niyoga*).

However, this is consistent with the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). Demonstrating that, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), there is no injunction by the Vedic text itself, he says: "Therefore, it was stated that ritual items such as threshing are enjoined by the text. The meaning is that verbal roots denoting action (bhāvārtha) have a connection with the mandate (niyoga) through the text.

Therefore, this is the meaning of the commentary: "they are enjoined," that is, they are connected with the injunction (*vidhi*). The statement, "their connection with rice and so forth is by means of the sentence," means that rice and the other materials are connected to the *niyoga* (the mandate) through their entry into the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). This, indeed, is the commentary regarding threshing and the like.

He states that the connection with rice and other materials occurs through the sentence (*vākya*). Thinking that it follows from this that threshing and the like are merely subordinate (*śeṣatā*) to the rice and so forth, [the author] has explained it thus. The literal meaning of the *bhāṣya* is that these actions, such as threshing, are connected to the rice and other materials by the sentence itself precisely because they are subordinate; it does not mean that the accomplishment of the mandate (*niyoga*) belongs to the rice and other materials which are the primary elements. Why? Because [the mandate] is not indeed a substance (*dravya*)—

The injunction has its limit in itself, because it is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). For two things cannot be accomplished by a single sentence, as that would contradict the understanding of it being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). Nor do rice grains (*vrīhi*) deserve to be connected with the injunction as something to be accomplished in the same way as heaven (*svarga*), because they are not mutually compatible. Indeed, they are not construed as qualifiers of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya-viśeṣaṇa*). Nor [can they be so construed] for the sake of supporting the status of being accomplished as understood from the accusative case ending.

It is not even possible to conceive of [the object] as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). This is because, precisely due to its being indicated by the accusative case, it is that which possesses the fruit produced by the action;

thus, it cannot be the fruit of the injunction (*niyoga*). For when something, while being a qualification of the person to be enjoined, is intended to be the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it cannot be the fruit of the action.

If it were the fruit of the action, it would be impossible for one who desires that fruit to have a connection with the injunction. For if the injunction were the cause of that [fruit], [the injunction would be dependent on the fruit].

In that case, for one who desires that [result], the connection with the injunction (*niyoga*) would occur precisely through the desire for that result. Otherwise, if the connection with the desire for that result were not intended, it would be connected merely as a substance. Furthermore, if the injunction were the fruit, the status of the ritual action as having a fruit would be untenable; for that alone is the fruit of the action which is produced directly from the action without requiring an intermediary, because actions have fruits that reside in the factors of action (*kāraka*). By this same reasoning, [the objection regarding] the consecration (*adhāna*)...

The claim that [the fire] is for the sake of the fire and thus falls within the scope of an injunction has already been refuted. How then is it that, in the case of the *āśrayis* (substances), even the refinement of the substance (*dravya-saṃskāra*) is intended to be expressed?

It is because this is directly perceived, and not because it is the fruit of the action. Therefore, it is well said that "all [substances] serve all purposes," just like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.

[Page 651] By virtue of being enjoined through the context (*prakaraṇa*). What is this that becomes the "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*)? He thinks that this Bhāṣya says this because the unseen assistance will be directed toward the substance (*dravyaniṣṭha*). The answer is: the unseen, the *apūrva*, and the injunction (*niyoga*)—these are one and the same.

This was stated by him in the passage "having produced the apūrva. Herein is the summary of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): since the removal of husks and chaff can be established even independently of a specific qualification for ritual performance (adhikāra), when that [removal] is the purpose, it is impossible for acts such as threshing to enter into the qualification for performance.

For the sake of establishing entry into that [final apūrva], it is better to resort to its similarity with the *prayāja* offerings and the like. Since the intermediate *apūrva* of the *prayāja* and other such rites is indeed an action (*kārya*) that stands in need of a qualification (*adhikāra*), its entry into that qualification is logical for the purpose of serving that end.

As for the fruit (*phala*), however, it would exist only when separated from the verbal meaning, because the word’s meaning is [only] concomitant with the ritual action (*ceṣṭā*). To this, it is replied: let there be a universal applicability (*sarvārthatā*).

If there were a contradiction of the *niyoga* (injunction) regarding the purpose of the action, there would be a problem; however, no such contradiction exists here. How is it that no contradiction exists? Or how would a contradiction exist? It has been stated that this is because the removal of the husks and chaff is a different kind of action (*kāryāntara*). One action is not connected with another action in the way that heaven (*svarga*) is connected with cattle (*paśu*). Thus, the *niyoga* is the action [of the injunction], while the removal of the husks and chaff is...

"What is it?"—this is a contradiction. He states the answer: "It has been said that you are ignorant of the objects and the things to be enjoined. This is the underlying intention here: First of all, a substance is understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) through its connection with an accusative case in acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*). And that which already possesses another thing to be accomplished cannot be the object (*viṣaya*) of an injunction (*niyoga*), because a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) is impossible when there is a connection with two mutually incompatible things to be accomplished.

(1) G. There is no contradiction with the result (*kāryavirodha*), nor should it be stated that this very [result] is a qualification of the person to be exhorted (*niyojyaviśeṣaṇa*), because [the result] is qualified by a category of entity that has not become a factor of action (*akārakabhūtapadārtha*).

Because [the person] is the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*). But what is the reasoning for [the claim that] one who is qualified by a category of entity that is not an agent (*akāraka*) is the one to be enjoined?

It is said: whatever is related to an action is an agent (*kāraka*). And that is of two kinds: some are to be accomplished by the action, and some are not. Of these, the former is the object (*karman*), and the second consists of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth; neither of these two can serve as a qualification of the one to be enjoined. For in both cases...

Qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*) occurs either by way of an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*) or by being the object of a desire (*kāmanā-viṣayatā*). In this regard, it cannot first be by way of an essential relation, because such a relation is not established prior to the relationship characterized as that between the mandate (*niyoga*) and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Nor is it established by being the object of a desire in the case of the instrumental factors (*karaṇa*) and so forth; for it is impossible for them to be accomplished by an *apūrva* produced by an action. Furthermore, the instrumental factors and the ritual act itself do not constitute a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) precisely because they are not things to be accomplished [by the mandate].

The qualification [of the person] is that which, being accomplished by the mandate (*niyoga*), qualifies the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) because it is what is desired, and not anything else. Therefore, he who asserts that subsidiary acts (*guṇakarma*) are the objects of the mandate does not understand either the nature of the object or the nature of the person to be enjoined. Commencing to explain this very point, he asks: "How is he ignorant? The answer is: "He is ignorant in this way: for the so-called 'object'..."

The connection with the qualification is expressed as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice. For that which is fit for connection with the qualification is the subject matter (*viṣaya*). And that alone is fit for connection with the qualification where the mandate (*niyoga*) is perceived as the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Nevertheless, one might ask: what is its purpose? To this he says: the very accomplishment of the mandate is the purpose of that subject matter, even when a visible result is possible, as in the case of "one desiring cattle [should perform the ritual] with the *godohana* vessel."

"One should enjoin" [the sacrifice]. Because there is a contradiction in the co-occurrence of two objects to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in a single locus, another object to be accomplished cannot be included. Now, one might object: "In this case too, the 'animals' are another object to be accomplished. To this he says: "But surely, even here the purpose is the accomplishment of the fruit, not the accomplishment of the injunction (*niyoga*.

The reply is: "We shall explain in the sixth book that the accomplishment of the fruit is for the sake of accomplishing the injunction; therefore, even here, the accomplishment of the injunction alone is the purpose. Since...

And thus, the accomplishment of the fruit is for the sake of the accomplishment of the injunction; for this very reason, Jaimini also [holds that] ritual acts are for the sake of the fruit. (1) *Kāmādhikāra*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya. (2) G. *sādhyam*. (3) G. *adhikārapadasaṃ* [p.

This is what is meant: the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhyabhūta*), and that [meaning] is accomplished through the accomplishment of its object. Furthermore, only one who understands the meaning of the injunction as something to be accomplished in relation to himself engages in the performance of that object. And a person desiring a result (*kāmī*) would not, by virtue of his desire alone, think "this is my duty" (*mamedaṃ kāryam*) with respect to an injunction whose means does not accomplish what he desires.

Thus, because it must conform to the status of being a cognizer (*boddhṛ*), the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) itself assumes the role of a causal condition (*nimittabhāva*) for the production of the fruit, in order to obtain a person capable of accomplishing the object that serves as the cause for its own establishment.

Therefore, the accomplishment of the fruit is for the sake of the fulfillment of the mandate (*niyoga*); hence, that which is called "fruit" is not a separate, independent purpose. [The person who is] to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
Now, who is this? We shall explain in the sixth [book] that he is one characterized by categories of entities that are non-agents (*akāraka*). This has already been described previously:

[the author], intending to show that the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) cannot be other than the agent (*kartṛ*), and that the agent may indeed be characterized by categories of entities that are agents, asks—"But who is this? The answer is: "The one entitled (*adhikṛta*) to the ritual action, by the force of the reasoning to be stated."

The meaning is that he is one who has become a master over actions. Again, with that same intention, he asks a question containing an objection: "What is this 'authorized' (adhikṛta)? He states it in a single passage: "But surely only the agent is authorized; there is no such thing as someone else called 'authorized'. The answer is: "Just as the agent does not have authorization, we shall also explain in the sixth [book] that the status of being an agent belongs to the authorized person. If these two were indeed so—
[Objection: Even though the two eyes are to be employed upon their respective objects, what does this have to do with the statement, "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*)? [Response:

The answer is that even when there is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to a substance for the sake of another action, there is no contradiction with the injunction (*niyoga*); this is what follows.
(1) The very non-establishment of the mandate; (2) the purpose of the establishment of the mandate; (3) the contradiction of the mandate.

This is the intended meaning: if even that which has another task were to possess the status of being an object [of the mandate], then [the status of being an object would apply to] that which resides in a substance...

Even if the task (kārya) were understood, since the mandate (niyoga) is heard only in its own sentence and thus lacks entry into the mandate contained in another's sentence, it would not touch upon that [other] task; consequently, the task residing in the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth would be incompatible with it, resulting in a contradiction between two tasks. However, according to the aforementioned definition of the object (*viṣaya*), because no other thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is seen, there is an absence of objectivity; and due to this lack of an object, the cognition of the mandate by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth cannot arise.

Since there is no injunction (*niyoga*) within its own sentence, for the sake of establishing a connection with an injunction—namely, for the purpose of entering into an injunction contained in another sentence—the refinement of the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth, which exist in a state of connection with that [injunction], is perceived as being dependent upon it. Thus, because it enters into that causal operation (*kārya*), this [refinement] does not bring about any contradiction even with respect to another causal operation. However, in the absence of the aforementioned definition of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the aforementioned definition of the object (*viṣaya*) itself does not obtain, even in the case of a single [sentence].

Since the fruit of the action can also be construed as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) within the sentence, the aforementioned definition of the *niyojya* indeed serves a purpose. To the question, "How then does there occur an entry into the injunction (*niyoga*) contained in another sentence? he replies: because of the contact with the rice (*vrīhi*), which is the object (*viṣaya*) constituting the primary meaning of the sentence "He sprinkles the rice" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), there arises the cognition of another injunction in the aspect of what is to be done (*kāryāṃśa*), just as in the case of the *samit* and other subsidiary rites.

The rice grains (*vrīhi*), which constitute the primary object regarding the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), are touched [by the injunction] for the sake of that specific application (*niyoga*). Therefore, since it is possible for them to enter into the application by way of the rice grains, no other distinct application is understood to reside within its own sentence, just as in the case of the *samid* and other offerings in relation to the portion of the task (*kāryāṃśa*) and the portion of the qualification (*adhikārāṃśa*).

In order to clarify his intention, he states [the objection] preceded by a challenge: "But has it not been said that there is another effect? And if there is another effect, there must be the understanding of another injunction, as in the case of the *some* sacrifices. The reply is: "True, if there were the understanding of another effect.

Why is it not another effect? Because the production of rice grains implies the primary injunction of qualification (*adhikāraniyoga*), just as the accomplishment of heaven [implies the primary injunction]."
It is not another effect. Just as the attainment of heaven, which is brought about by the mandate (*niyoga*), is not another effect [of the mandate], so too is the production of rice-grains.
(1) G. *vidhyarthā* (2) G. *yadi kāryāntaraṃ syāt*, then there would be the necessity of another mandate.

Therefore, this very mandate of qualification (*adhikāraniyoga*) is what is to be accomplished by means of the purification of the rice grains, as in the injunction "he sprinkles the rice grains," just like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. However, there is this distinction from the *prayāja* offerings and the rest: whereas those function through a visible effect, this functions directly as the effect of the mandate itself.

The same applies to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Initially, the *prayāja* and other such rites are understood as being devoid of their own specific qualification (*adhikāra*), yet they are perceived as the task (*kārya*) of an injunction possessing a qualification. However, it has been stated that subsequently there occurs a reflection upon the task inherent within them. Thus, it has been explained that there is no contradiction even in the case of another task.
Now, since entry [into the primary injunction] is impossible without another task, he states that another task must necessarily be admitted: "And not..."

Only a door can function as an obstacle; specifically, even for those things directly perceived as being connected to the injunction, a door characterized by the assistance of the instrument must be postulated. However, the distinction here is that this [door] is already established. We shall explain later, in the investigation of the nature of the means of proof known as *prakaraṇa* (context), how the accomplishment of the primary procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is impossible without the postulation of such a door.

By this it is said: even though [the *japa*] is equal to the *prayāja* offerings and others, since a medium (*dvāra*) must necessarily be postulated, why is the visible medium (*dṛṣṭadvāra*) abandoned?

This is what was stated: "Because there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*), it does not serve all purposes. The meaning is that when a visible cause for the connection is possible, another cause cannot establish itself. But surely, the application (*viniyoga*) follows from the purpose (*kārya*), not the purpose from the application?

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: with respect to application (*viniyoga*), there is the task (*kārya*), but the application does not depend on the task; therefore, according to the application, this is understood to be merely a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the rice-grains (*vrīhi*). Otherwise, the word "rice-grain" would have to function through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean "that which is a subsidiary means for the *apūrva*. Consequently, how could there be entry into another task?

(1) Regarding the response "It has been seen": this has already been refuted on the grounds that it pertains to the subject matter observed in other treatises (*śāstrāntara*). That which has been observed by another treatise—

Because it is connected with the task (*kārya*), it is the object of application (*viniyoga*); by the statement "another [element] is applied to that," this is refuted—namely, that an independent substance does not become a subordinate (*śeṣin*). Precisely because that which is understood from another scriptural injunction becomes the subordinate, for that very reason the cause is characterized by difference or non-difference. And this has been explained. Therefore, it is well said: "But the fruit [is attained] together."

Regarding the phrase "ceṣṭayet" (one should cause to act): one might think that the sūtra implies the acceptance of the effect (*kārya*) by mere sight, but considering that this is untenable, he explains: the meaning is that the injunction (*niyoga*) conforms to the effect. The meaning is that even the intermediate effect conforms to—that is, depends upon—the injunction. Therefore, it is established that "those [words] which are heard in a particular context [belong there]. Consequently, it is well said: "But the fruit must be performed in that very [context]."

"And the substance [is for all purposes] because of its connection with the origin. Here, the author of the Bhāṣya raises a doubt: "Is it that whatever can be done by these [implements], for each of those purposes, whatever is connected with which [implement], is for that [purpose] alone? He states the doubt that serves as the reason for this: "This is considered: the injunctions of bringing near, such as 'the wooden sword (sphya) and the potsherds (kapāla),' are without distinction due to their connection [with the general context]. Context—

And because there is no distinction: are they understood as being for all purposes, or are they restricted by such rules as "he digs with a wooden sword" (*sphyena uddhanti*)? The meaning of this is as follows: regarding these injunctions of proximity (*sannidhāpana-vidhi*), which are injunctions merely for establishing a connection with a primary mandate (*niyoga*), are they restricted, or rather, even without being restricted, are they themselves employed in every ritual function? What, then, is the correct position?
"They are not subsumed. Why? Because of incapacity—that is, because of the incapacity to subsume. How is there incapacity? The answer is:
for when there is proximity, due to the unity of the injunction and because only the means are permitted, it can only be said that they have a perceptible means (*dṛṣṭadvārakatva*).

Because they serve as counteragents to what is to be postulated, and not even by way of a specific visible result. The meaning of this is as follows: first, by the force of the injunction of procurement (*sannidhāpana-vidhi*), these [implements] such as the wooden sword (*sphya*) are understood as being for the sake of the mandate (*niyoga*) itself, independent of any specific purpose. In that regard, when there is an expectation as to "by what means," the mandate accepts only a visible means, not an invisible one; furthermore, even though it is visible, it does not accept a specific visible means that is not sanctioned by the mandate.

And it is not the meaning of the treatise. Therefore, the determination is based on capacity. To this, it is replied: this would be so if the injunction (*niyoga*) were merely followed by way of a door. But why is it not so? He says: for the injunction conforms to the relationship. If the injunction did not conform to the relationship, and if the door were something unrelated to the injunction, then the door alone would be [the basis] in the injunction.

The application (*niyoga*), however, must follow the relationship [between the elements]. For it has been stated that the scripture of application (*viniyoga-śāstra*) has as its object that which is already established by another scripture. Indeed, the application pertains to that very subject which is made related through the injunction of another scripture; it does not pertain to anything else. Thus, the application follows the relationship. Now, even if this is so, let there be no application where there is no relationship; but where a relationship exists, there must be application everywhere.
To this he says: "It may be so. Therefore, the rules of proximity (*sannidhāpana*) cannot be considered opponents to the rule of connection (*saṃbandhavidhi*), because they are rooted in it.

For once the connection with the principal (*śeṣin*) has been established by the rule of connection, the specific application (*viniyoga*) occurs subsequently through the rules of proximity. Thus, it is established here as well that "those [subsidiaries] which are heard in relation to a particular [principal] belong to it," just as in the case of that which brings about the proximity of the principal.

The injunction for bringing together is not an opponent to the injunction for connection; likewise, the injunction "one digs with the wooden sword" (sphyenoddhanti) cannot be its opponent, because there is no distinction. Thus, the established rule applies here as well, and it is not limited solely to acts such as threshing.

Regarding the unity of purpose: it has been stated that those injunctions concerning purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) and substances (*dravya*) which are heard in a particular context belong to that very context alone. Now, the question is considered regarding a subordinate quality (*guṇa*): do those [qualities] which are heard in a particular place belong only there, or are they to be inserted into the entire context? By this, he states the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*). The application of purificatory acts through direct statement (*śruti*) has been explained; immediately following that, the application of substances through syntactical connection (*vākya*) [is now discussed].

The application (*viniyoga*) has been stated; and since the application of qualities is accomplished through the application of substances, that [application of qualities] is considered immediately thereafter. Desiring to introduce the doubt regarding the absence of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says: "But surely, because words denote objects as already connected, it is not possible for them to express qualities in isolation. Objects are denoted by words as being connected; therefore, qualities are [denoted] only as connected with substances."

The meaning is that qualities are denoted by their respective words, and being thus [denoted], they are indeed capable of attaining the status of being the means for accomplishing an action. He states an illustration: "Just as [in the case of] 'one should sacrifice' (*ālabheta*), there is no expression of form alone; and just as in the case of 'one should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu' (*vāyavyaṃ śvetamālabheta*), it cannot be said that there is an expression of quality alone—otherwise, that too would be an example here. He refutes [this objection]: "True."

Where the persistence (*anvaya*) of that which has not relinquished its substance is observed—such as in the case of something incorporeal—that is not the example here. However, where there is the persistence of a word denoting a quality alone with the intention of relinquishing the substance—as in "the whiteness of the cloth"—there arises a doubt:

even though a case-ending denoting a grammatical relation (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is present, does the word denoting the quality connect with the action (*kriyā*), or does it connect only with the substance?

r659] This is precisely the doubt here: whether, by virtue of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*), the quality of redness (*āruṇimā*) is enjoined for the act of purchase (*kraya*) alone, or whether, having split the sentence, it is connected to the context (*prakaraṇa*).
"It is prescribed with respect to substances that have been fixed [in place].

But surely, in this sentence, its status as a word denoting a quality alone (*kevalaguṇavacanatā*) is not perceived at all. For in that case—such as "the white of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*)—because it is indicated by the genitive case and because the relationship between the substance and that [quality] is understood, it is appropriate for the word "white" (*śukla*) to denote the quality alone.

The word must be construed [with the action]. For if the word "white" (śukla) were not related to a substance, it would not be construed solely with a quality. However, when there is a relation to a substance, because one substance lacks a relation to another substance, it is construed solely with the quality.

In this case, however, because of the mention of a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) in the phrase "by means of the red one" (*aruṇayā*), there is an understanding of a connection to an action, and not an understanding of a connection to a substance. Thus, it is not [the case that it applies to all substances].

[The word denotes] the state of being accompanied solely by a quality (*guṇa*). He states another argument: "And because of the cognition of that [quality], and because of the cognition of its connection with the action; for a mere quality is incapable of performing an action. It is logical that only that which has not abandoned its substance (*dravya*) is connected [with the action], as in the case of 'one should sacrifice a white [animal]' (*śvetam ālabheta*). He refutes this: "It is said: the cognition of the connection with a substance alone is not the reason for its denoting a mere quality. What then?"

The non-perception of another substance is also a reason [for its being a word denoting a quality]. For if another substance were also perceived there, then there would not be a state of denoting a quality alone, as in the case of "the white part of the cloth. Therefore, just like the non-mention of a substance already employed, the non-mention of another substance is also a reason for its being a word denoting a quality alone. But how is it that there is no perception of another substance here? To this he says: "For if there were the perception of another substance..."
Just as in the case of "the white part of the cloth," there would be no relationship between quality and the possessor of the quality. If this were so, what would follow regarding the word *aruṇayā*?
[It would follow that it denotes] a substance (*dravyatva*), just like [the word *paṭa*].

This follows: for here too, no other substance is understood by the term *ekahāyanī*. Since there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), and because the purchase (*kraya*) is already occupied by the *ekahāyanī*, there is no room for the entry of another substance. Therefore, since the substance is denoted by the word *ekahāyanī*, the word *aruṇā* cannot denote a quality attached to a different substance. And as for its attachment to the *ekahāyanī*, [it is not possible].

The connection with purchase will be demonstrated later. Therefore, it is established that in a sentence where the substance is expressed by another word, there is only a connection with the quality alone. Consequently, a doubt arises. Since this doubt is justified—given that the quality must be connected with a substance—is the sentence to be split and the quality inserted into the context (*prakaraṇa*), or is it to be inserted into the substances already contained within that context?
Or rather, because of the indication by the instrumental case-ending, it refers only to the act of purchasing. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya says: "But surely this is not a word denoting a quality.

He raises an objection to that: "How so? Thus, since the status of the word *aruṇā* as denoting a quality is established by the principle stated in the Bhāṣya—characterized by its conformity to the presence and absence of the connection with a quality—the [objection] states: "But surely this is not a word denoting a quality; what then? It is a word denoting a substance."

Thus, how is this objection justified? It is said: because of the employment of the feminine gender and because the feminine gender resides in a substance (*dravya*), there is no inherence of gender in qualities (*guṇa*). [Objection: But will the gender not inhere in the substance implied [by the quality]? To this he says: "And because gender belongs to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). That is to say, when a nominal stem occurs in the feminine, the feminine suffix is applied; thus, gender belongs precisely to the meaning of the nominal stem.

Even though gender is denotable by the suffix (*pratyaya*), since gender is related only to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), gender is indeed dependent upon the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In this regard:

He asks: "Is there no observation [of the rule] such as 'aruṇā' and so forth for the proponent of the theory of implication (ākṣepavādī)? Does the proponent of implication not see that a feminine suffix occurs even from a word denoting a quality alone? For what reason does he desire that it denote a substance even from the observation of that [quality] alone? The meaning is this: It is not that there is no such observation; indeed, there is. However, the intention is that it is not the case in instances such as "aruṇayā" (with the red one). It is precisely the thing to be expressed [that is denoted].

Because of its being seen [in the Vedic text]. How, then, is there a refutation by means of the mention of *aruṇā* (the red one) and so forth? [The answer is: because in the case of *aruṇā* and others, there is grammatical correctness (*sādhutā*) in their usage. How is it that the word *aruṇā* is a sign (*liṅga*) [of gender], thereby refuting its status as a denotation of a substance? The reply is: the intention is that once its status as a quality-denoter (*guṇavacana*) is firmly established, it will function as a sign (*liṅga*) for the sake of a stronger reason. "Now, if [it is not connected] with the verb *krīṇāti* (he buys)..."

What is the intention of one who says, "It shall be connected; it will be linked with the word *ekahāyanī* in that very same sentence, and there will be no split in the sentence"? Having read this commentary (*bhāṣya*), he raises an objection. And this is the intention behind the objection:

Since it expresses only a quality (*kevalaguṇavacana*), how can there be any suspicion of a connection with a substance? He provides the answer: this is the intended meaning. When there is a connection of both [the quality and the substance] with the action, then, because other substances are excluded by the inclusion of the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), the word *aruṇā* expresses only a quality. However, when there is no connection of redness (*aruṇiman*) with the action, then, because qualities are dependent upon substances, [it follows that it must refer to a substance].
Since substances are the substrata for qualities, who indeed can obstruct the connection between a quality and a substance?

Thus, it is considered logical that there is a connection with the purchase by way of being dependent, just as in the case of "a blue lotus. To this, the reply is: [the suffix] from the nominal stem...
(1) G. na (2) G. āśrayatvena.

Just as only a quality is perceived, yet through its connection with another word, there is a syntactic relation (*anvaya*) that does not abandon the substance; furthermore, gender (*liṅga*) is stronger than sentence-meaning (*vākya*). Therefore, there is no connection with the substance. He objects that gender is stronger than sentence-meaning by asking: "What is this?"

"Syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than indicative power (*liṅga*). For it was in the section on *śruti* and *liṅga* that the relative strength and weakness were discussed regarding "being for the sake of this" (*aidamarthya*), which is defined as subordination (*śeṣatva*) characterized by being for the sake of another. However, no discussion of relative strength or weakness was made regarding "connection" (*anvaya-yoga*), even when there is a connection such as between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka*), or quality and the possessor of quality (*guṇa-guṇin*). It is replied: When there is a connection and another connection is understood, by what means would the relative strength or weakness be precluded? Even if [the relationship of] being for the sake of this...

Thus the relative strength and weakness has been stated; nevertheless, by the same logic, who can prevent that [relative strength] even in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? The word *ca* (and) has the sense of the word *api* (also). And we have already stated the relative strength and weakness.
Regarding this, the Bhāṣya says: "From its form, the word *aruṇā* denotes a quality (*guṇavacanatā*)."
Thus he says. That is untenable.

Because [the word] has as its referent a substance already associated [with qualities], it does not denote a quality alone; with this doubt in mind, he demonstrates the meaning of the Bhāṣya: since a substance is introduced by another word and because of the connection with an action, the fact that the two words are associated solely with a quality cannot be sublated by the sentence.

First of all, the word *aruṇā* (red) does not serve the purpose of connecting a quality with a substance within the context of the action (*kriyā*), because the substance is already provided by another word. Nor does it serve the purpose of connecting a quality with the substance alone, because there is no basis for establishing a mutual relationship between two words when they are both connected to the action.

Therefore, the word *aruṇā* is connected solely with the quality; it is with this very intention that the Bhāṣya states that the word *aruṇā* is a "denoter of a quality" (*guṇavacana*) on account of its form.

Thus it has been said. To this, the following reply is now given: considering that if [the universal] were connected with action, there would be a lack of connection due to its being formless (*amūrta*), it is better to have a connection with substance (*dravya*). Even when there is a connection with substance, the connection with action is not entirely abandoned; for, in the case of a connection with substance—(1) P.
686 (2) G. *dravyānvayitve hi*—its own substance [is involved].
Because it is established in this very way. And this must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, even the connection with the context would not exist.
For in a context, there is a connection either with an action or with a substance. First of all, it is not connected with an action.

This has been stated because [the word] is formless (*amūrta*). Now, if [the word] were not connected even with a substance (*dravya*) on the basis of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), then alas, a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) would be admitted. And it has been said that this property of lacking syntactic connection, characterized by non-denotation, is not observed in the world within the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) regarding the denotative word. Therefore, for the sake of favoring the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatā*), [the connection must be sought] in that very sentence.

The acceptance of a relation between substances is logical; for precisely because there would otherwise be the consequence of a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*), there is connection by means of the inferential mark (*liṅga*). For this very reason, connection is observed even in cases such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*). Otherwise, how could there be a connection for words like "blue lotus," which are devoid of case-endings denoting a relation? The word *vā* has the sense of *iva*; the meaning is: "How, indeed, could there be a connection?"
Just as in the expression "the ocean is a great being," by this passage the commentary beginning with "To this it is said" and ending with "there is no split in the sentence" has been explained.

The commentary is accepted as being explained by the phrase "not indeed so" (*naitadeva*). It is true that even a relationship characterized by grammatical case-inflection (*vaibhaktika*) exists if it is without opposition; however, this one is opposed.

By means of the instrumental case. For the instrumental case is not applicable when there is a relation with a substance; therefore, its syntactic connection must be in accordance with the instrumental case.
It must be so construed; it cannot, however, be construed merely in accordance with the literal expression. Therefore, a relationship [of the quality] like that of "blue lotus" is not tenable.

To this, it is replied: if the meaning of the instrumental case were contradictory to the connection of the substance with the quality of redness (aruṇimā), which is the meaning of the nominal stem...

It might be argued that this would be so if there were no connection with a substance; however, since that [connection] is the sense of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyārtha*), it is not contradictory because it is already established.

Therefore, there is no fault in the fact that [the quality] is connected with the *ekahāyanī* cow as long as it has not yet been so connected. Consequently, the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "We do not say that it is not a factor of action" (*na brūmo na kārakam*) implies that "there is no split in the sentence" (*nāsti vākyabhedaḥ*).
Thus far has been explained. This would be so if the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) were not for another purpose;

however, she is indeed for another purpose. Furthermore, a mutual connection between two things intended for different purposes is not possible. For what purpose, then, is the one-year-old cow? We say: for the purpose of purchase (*kraya*). But what is the reason that, when the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) is equal, [the connection] is with the quality (*guṇa*) and the action (*kriyā*) rather than [with each other]?

The one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is mentioned solely for the purpose of purchase, and not for the purpose of establishing a connection with a quality. Regarding this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* reads the *Bhāṣya* passage—"Even though it has been stated, it is questioned again"—in order to raise an objection, and then raises that objection: "If it has already been stated, why is it questioned again?"

"It is appropriate" [if the connection with the purchase were established] through the application of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyāvibhakti*), because of the statement "of the redness" (*āruṇyasya*). Since this [redness] has already been stated to be for the purpose of the purchase due to its connection with the third case-ending in relation to the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), why is it asked again: "How is it that the one-year-old cow is indeed for the purpose of the purchase?

The answer is: even for something intended for another purpose, there may be a connection with another; this is for the sake of demonstrating a contradiction, and for that very reason, the subsequent answer also begins with the third case-ending.
(1) P. 687 (2) G. Therefore, there is no fault;

because of the connection, it serves the purpose of purchase. When this has been asked, and the answer has been given by the force of the instrumental case itself, how could something else, even if it has another purpose, be [connected] by another?

The meaning is that this question and answer are intended to address the following doubt: "There is no contradiction in the relationship [between two things] because of their proximity. This is not a fault, for even when one thing is intended for another purpose, it may still be connected with something else. For indeed, that which possesses expectancy can fulfill the expectancy of another proximate element—even if that other is intended for a different purpose—since there is no difference in their proximity. Therefore, the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) would fulfill the requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*) for the redness (*āruṇya*), which itself possesses expectancy.

It is indeed capable [of connection], but not merely by virtue of being related to that for whose sake it exists. Therefore, although the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) is connected with redness (*aruṇimā*) due to proximity, nevertheless, since she exists solely for the purpose of purchase, she is not [connected] as such; thus, redness is not connected with the act of purchase alone, but rather with all *ekahāyanīs* occurring within the context (*prakaraṇa*).

But surely, proximity (*sannidhāna*) is no different even for that which is related to it, and there is a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the other; therefore, the connection occurs precisely through its being related to that [other]. This would be so if proximity were indeed indistinct; however, in this case, the proximity is for the sake of another purpose. And proximity intended for another purpose does not require [the presence of] something else for the sake of accomplishing its own purpose. The answer is as follows:

Because the denotation must necessarily follow [the word] and because no other [denotation] is present, one sets aside its connection with another meaning and accepts merely its proximity; this has been demonstrated in the case of the *rātrisatra* and similar rites. Its meaning is as follows: (1) R. *saṃbandhaḥ*; (2) G. *tatsaṃbandhasyāpi*; (3) G. *apahāya*; (4) G. *aruṇā*.
The utterance of the word "aruṇimā" (redness) must necessarily be pronounced with a view toward bringing about some concomitance; therefore, there must necessarily be such a concomitance.

In that regard, when the question arises as to with what [the *ekahāyanī*] is connected, by virtue of proximity (*sannidhāna*), it is connected specifically for the purpose of purchase. Having abandoned its connection to any other purpose, likewise, in the case of the *rātrisatra*, although "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is connected as a matter of praise, it is nevertheless grasped as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) due to proximity. The reply is: what has been said is correct; however, in this case, due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), the proximity is not for any other purpose, because of the injunction of entitlement (*adhikāravidhi*).

Therefore, the redness that has been grasped is connected only with all those substances belonging to it; thus, because of the syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), such a connection is proper, since we understand it to belong to the prescriptive injunction (*adhikāravidhi*) which has no other purpose. Consequently, it is established that the application is to everything within the context (*prakaraṇa*). Herein lies the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): it is logical that even though the generic form (*ākṛti*) is incorporeal, [it is nevertheless determined...]

The status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) with respect to an action belongs to a substance by virtue of its being the cause of that action; however, the status of being a means for a quality (*guṇa*) is not possible in any way. [Objection:

But surely there is utility for a quality even in the act of taking up [a substance], for it cannot be said that something is taken up without being delimited [by a quality]; and since such non-delimitation is not possible without a quality, [the quality must serve as a means]. [Response: That is incorrect. Just as [a substance] is [taken up] even in the absence of the application of a quality...

If it is argued that "just as a ritual application is accomplished by taking up any substance whatsoever, why should it not be accomplished here as well? Thus, there is no lack of a means of accomplishment," we introduce the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): this being the position, we reply:

"When there is a unity of purpose. To this, it is stated: the quality of redness (*āruṇimā*) enters into the act of purchase itself. How so? Because of the perception of its connection with that [purchase].

From the third [point]: Now, it was argued that because [the word] denotes a quality alone, it cannot be connected with an action. That was poorly stated. How was it poorly stated? It was poorly stated in this way: for whatever kind of instrumentality for an action is observed in the world...

The case-endings of such a [word] bring about a relationship [between the quality and the substance]. Furthermore, a quality brings about an action by way of being a qualifier of a substance, because it is impossible for that which is unqualified to function as a cause. Herein lies the intended meaning: due to its connection with the purchase (*kraya*), the redness (*āruṇya*) is employed in that very context, and its status as a means of the purchase is possible because the redness is employed as a qualifier of the substance.

For it is enjoined in this manner: "The purchase must be performed with that in which redness (āruṇya) inheres. And its employment is not possible unless it is qualified by redness. Nor can an action be accomplished by means of something that has not been employed; thus, the status of redness as an instrument of the action is established, and its application to the purchase is proven. To explain this very point, he begins the objection: "But surely this performance consists of a substance that has not [yet] been employed..."

It has been stated that [the agenthood] is like saying "the whiteness of the cloth. Therefore, it was said that there is no status as a means (*sādhanabhāva*); that is indeed correctly stated. However, the connection with action cannot be denied on the grounds that the substance is not explicitly mentioned, because all means of action (*sādhana*) possess a connection with action by virtue of depending upon their own specific operations (*vyāpāra*). Nor is there a loss of operation simply because the substance is not explicitly mentioned; such is the nature of operation.
Thus, it cannot be said that [the quality] does not exist.

Now, one might object: "In a ritual action where a substance is the means (*sādhana*), how can a quality serve as the means? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And since the factors of action (*kārakas*) are connected with the action by depending upon their own respective operations, they do not depend upon the operations of other factors. The meaning of this is as follows: not...

There is no contradiction in [the view] that a quality (*guṇa*) is a means (*sādhana*) with respect to an action, just as substance (*dravya*) and so forth are. Now, one might object: "Just as in the case of the word *śveta* ('white'), there is the apprehension of a substance, such is not the case here; how then can there be the status of being a means? To this he replies: "Nor is there, for the denotation, any abandonment or apprehension residing in another object—that is, residing in a substance. Even if the denotation does abandon or apprehend another object, nevertheless, the status of being a means is not contradicted.
Thus he concludes: "Therefore, because their functions are distinct, the connection with the purchase is logically established only by means of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).

Precisely because the application (*viniyoga*) occurs through the medium of the substance, there is no option (*vikalpa*); rather, the action exists for the purpose of connecting with the substance that serves a specific purpose."

The primacy [of the action] was stated with reference to the red one-year-old cow (*aruṇaikahāyanī*) for the purpose of ensuring its connection with another substance possessing a purpose, namely that which is called *soma*.

However, when that [action] is primary, there is no completion of the sentence (*vākyaparisamāpti*) with each individual [subordinate element]. For it is not the case that the principal is taught in relation to the subordinate;
rather, the subordinate is taught in relation to the principal. Thus, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) with respect to each subordinate element.

Therefore, because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), it is established that since substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) share a single function (*aikakarmya*), [the number] is restricted. "That which is joined with oneness [belongs] to one, because of its connection with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Now, an objection is raised: "But this inquiry is indeed irrelevant; for here, a ritual application (*viniyoga*) of oneness based on direct scriptural statement is not even suspected. Anticipating this, he says: "The ritual application of substances, qualities, and purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) has already been stated."

Now, the consideration regarding the object to be applied (*viniyojya-viṣaya*) is undertaken. The meaning of this is as follows: once the application (*viniyoga*) of substances and so forth has been considered, in order to consider the specific details of that very application, the consideration concerning the object of the thing to be applied—that is, the principal (*śeṣin*)—is undertaken. [The question is:

does the application extend up to the principal characterized by the intended number, or not? Therefore, there is both a connection to the chapter (*adhyāya-saṅgati*) and an intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*).
But from where does this doubt arise? To this he says: For it is heard thus: "He cleanses the cup.
Because of the hearing of the singular number (1), because [the cleansing] is for the sake of the door (2), and because [it is not] for the sake of the substance (3). (4) G. R. omit; G. R. add *na*.

There is a doubt regarding the object to be applied (*viniyojya-viṣaya*). To the question "What kind of doubt is this?", he says: "In this regard, the doubt is as follows: Is the singularity and so forth a qualifier of the *śeṣin* (the principal) by virtue of its being a *śeṣin*?"

Is it that [the qualifier] is taken into account as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*)—as in the case of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) and so forth—or is it not taken into account? But how can there be a doubt in this matter?

The questioner states his own intention in a single sentence: "It is indeed appropriate that 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) is the division. How is it appropriate? Because the remainder is being taken up (*upādīyamāna*), its qualifier is useful for that—that is, useful for the taking up—since that which is not delimited cannot be taken up.

Furthermore, it is logical that the *śeṣin* (the principal), whose status as a remnant of a sacrifice has already been determined in another ritual act such as a *homa*, should be connected with its own subordinate elements (*śeṣa*). Since the *śeṣin* is enjoined by another scriptural injunction, we see no room for doubt. Because the *śeṣins* have their requirements already known through another ritual act, they are not to be further prescribed; thus, since even their specific qualifications are not required, any suspicion of needing to pay special heed to them is indeed improper. Having thus refuted the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author proceeds].

Supporting this, he says: It is stated that everything—whether something is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣitatva*) or not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatva*), and so forth—is determined by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

Because the singularity of the animal is not something to be adopted for its own sake, it is intended to be expressed. Why? Because of the scriptural statement. If the scriptural statement were not respected, why would duality or plurality not be adopted as a limiting factor? They are not accepted [as such]. Therefore, even in the case of the principal element (*śeṣin*), it is just as follows...

Just as the scriptural statement regarding Brahman is respected, so too must the scriptural statement regarding oneness be respected, since there is no distinction between them. This has been stated: "Oneness is joined [to the subject] because of its connection with a direct scriptural statement. As for the claim that there is no requirement [for oneness], that is incorrect; let it be understood that the requirement arises precisely through the force of the scriptural statement, just as in the case of the "red-clad" (Buddhist) ascetics. For it is by the mere fact of scriptural mention that the number is accepted; it does not depend upon being something to be actively sought or adopted.
(1) G. It is taken up from this very source: "One should establish the sacred fires."

Thus, from the Vedic scripture, the plurality of the fires is established in the context of their installation; and likewise, from the statement "he cuts the sacrificial post," the singularity of the post is established.

"Or rather, because it is a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) common to all, the characteristic is indeed non-distinct. To this it is replied: "This is not so; for [the rule] 'the refinement (*saṃskāra*) belongs to one' applies. Refinement is, by definition, fitness for another operation. Only that for which refinement—characterized as fitness for another operation—is possible, attains the status of being related to that refinement, namely, the status of being the primary object (*śeṣitā*). However, for that which lacks another operation—

The refinement characterized by fitness does not occur because there is no other operation; therefore, that [object] is not fit for refinement. This is explained by the fact that the word "that" (tat), ending in the masculine gender, does not refer to any other operation. By this, the following is stated:
since only the act of grasping is connected with another operation, the refinement belongs to that alone. To reveal this very point by means of an objection, he says: "But surely..."

This [substance], being already endowed with number, is rendered fit for connection with another operation by means of grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*). With the intention that "number has no connection with another operation," he asks: "Why? The answer is:

because another operation belongs to number and gender as subordinate elements (*śeṣa*) to the material cause (*upādāna*). And in whatever state it exists—possessing the intended gender and number—it [performs] its own operation.

The connection of that which has become a subordinate element (śeṣabhūta) with the very same kind of consecration (saṃskāra) is for the sake of the ritual effect, because the purpose of the consecration is the effect. Furthermore, in the sentences concerning the cups for Indra-Vāyu and others, the cups joined with the singular number alone are heard as being subordinate elements. Therefore, because of its connection with the ritual effect, singularity [is significant].

It is incorrect to say that singularity is not intended because it is subordinate to the consecration (*saṃskāra*). Nor is the mere cup (*graha*) the subordinate element. This is the meaning: one should not suspect that as many cups as there are, all combined together, constitute the subordinate elements for another purpose, such that the consecration would apply only when all are combined. Why? Because each individual one is employed [in the ritual]. But [one might object]: what of that which has already been employed?

Number and other such qualities attain the status of being subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to the cup (*graha*) that is being taken up (*upādāna*). Just as there is primacy (*prādhānya*) in the state of being subsidiary, so too is there primacy in the state of being the principal (*śeṣibhāva*). The meaning of this is as follows: it is agreed by both parties that number and the rest are indeed subsidiary to the cup which has been employed (*viniyukta*) for the act of taking it up. Therefore, just as in the state of being subsidiary—by virtue of relying on the state of being taken up—the cup possesses primacy with respect to number and the rest, so too [is it here].

Even though it is subordinate (*śeṣabhāva*) and even though it is connected with a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), it would possess primacy (*prādhānya*). The meaning is that its primacy with respect to number and so forth would exist precisely by virtue of being taken up [as an object]. The reply is: Let there be primacy; there is no contradiction whatsoever. However, we say that just as it attains the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatā*) without abandoning number and so forth, so too does it attain the status of being the object of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāryatā*) by virtue of being taken up for the sake of the preparation. By being taken up for the sake of the preparation...

"Let it be otherwise; there is no contradiction for us. The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) replies: "To this it is said: It is true that the refinement (saṃskāra) belongs only to that which is subordinate (śeṣabhūta); nevertheless, number and the other qualities are not connected with that refinement. Why? Because in all cases, the connection with another word-meaning belongs only to the principal (pradhāna), as in the expression 'bring the king's man. For in that case, the purpose is the king's [man]."

It appears merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Likewise here, too, substance alone is primary; that which is other than it—namely, genus (*jāti*) and so forth—is the indicator. Furthermore, there is no connection with the ritual action (*kārya*), nor a connection with the injunction (*vidheya*), for genus and the rest are indicators of the substance; thus, they have a connection with the preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*).
The meaning is that it does not exist. Therefore, this was said: "For the defining characteristic is non-distinct. To the question, "In what way is it non-distinct? he says:
"For oneness and so forth do not possess the capacity to exclude other perceptions when they themselves are of a different character. Why is there no such capacity? He says:
"For a related entity excludes another related entity, just as redness excludes non-redness. And this is not the case in the state of being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇatva*)."

There is no relationship between oneness and so forth and the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*). Therefore, how could they exclude a second [object] and the rest? But was it not said that it is not merely being related that is the cause for relating to another thing, but rather that which is related as a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*)?
What then? The answer is: "being presented by direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth. And here, the principal (*śeṣin*) qualified by oneness is presented by direct statement. And how...

It can be said that regarding a matter where the Veda is the authoritative means of knowledge, unity is intended to be expressed. Furthermore, being the subject of an enunciation (*uddiśyamānatva*) or being the object of an injunction (*vidhīyamānatva*) does not contradict the direct statement (*śruti*). It is not the case that being the subject of an enunciation is not heard [in the text]. The mention of "being enjoined" is merely for the sake of argument. For if the direct statement were sublated, then because the direct statement regarding the cup (*graha*) would also be sublated, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) would not apply to the cup either.

It might be so. Now, if the intention is that the qualification of that which is being designated is not intended to be expressed, then the reason for this very point must be described in this section; yet it has been stated that such a reason does not exist. It is replied: this reason does exist. [p. r673]

That which is mentioned as having a purpose becomes primary; that which is mentioned as having a purpose becomes primary. And the connection belongs to the primary with the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), not to the primary with subordinate elements (*guṇa*). Why? Because the subordinate elements have the status of being remnants of the mention [of the primary], based on the mention of the primary. Otherwise, they would not have the status of being remnants of the mention, but would instead have the status of being remnants of the application (*viniyoga*).

It may be so. But what, then, are these *guṇas* (qualifiers)? The answer is: they are number and the rest, which are denoted by case-endings (*vibhakti*) and pertain to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). How is there the status of being a *guṇa* for the meanings of the case-endings? Because they serve as delimiters (*avacchedaka*) with respect to the meaning of the nominal stem; for the meaning of the case-ending delimits the meaning of the nominal stem, and by virtue of being a delimiter, it stands in a subordinate relationship (*upādāna-śeṣatā*) [to that meaning]. Therefore, it is established that [the meaning of the case-ending is a *guṇa*].

The denoted objects, such as number and so forth, possess the status of being subordinate (*guṇatva*) with respect to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Furthermore, there is no connection between subordinate elements themselves, because all of them are related to a primary element (*pradhāna*); and this refinement (*saṃskāra*) is indeed a subordinate element. As it has been said: "And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another."

Thus, it follows that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself—the primary object—is what connects with the ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), as well as with number and so forth; it is not, however, the case that number and the like connect directly with the refinement. This has been stated regarding number and the rest, assuming they are denoted by the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

Even if, on the other hand, this object—namely the genus (*jāti*) and so forth—is indeed denoted by the nominal stem and is the thing to be employed [in the rite], nevertheless, without being specifically indicated—

Pride (*māna*) is not at all able to attain predominance with respect to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). Why? Because it would not even be that which is intended as the object of reference. The answer is: for that which is called "intended as the object of reference" (*uddeśa*) pertains to a thing delimited by its function, not to a mere category of entity (*padārtha*).

Of that which is cut off: the meaning expressed by a word is not merely as much as is denoted by it; what then? It is that substance which is connected with the function, for both substance and [the categories such as] genus (*jāti*) are connected with the function. Indeed, the utility of genus and the others lies in their being the substrata (*upādāna*) for things connected with the function, and not in the function itself. Therefore, it is substance alone that is to be indicated by genus and the other categories. Why is this so? He says: "For without a particular substance... [the function cannot be realized].

The result culminates in a specific effect. The meaning is that the accomplishment of an action does not occur apart from a substance (*dravya*). Therefore, the connection of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth—which are intended [as qualifiers]—is solely by way of characterizing the substance that is connected to the effect; it is not, however, by way of being a *kāraka*, an object (*karman*), or something to be refined (*saṃskārya*).
But if this is the case, even though [the genus] is being taken up [as a qualifier], since no specific effect is understood for it, and since the substance is what is connected to the effect...

Consequently, it would follow that universals (*jāti*) and the like are merely secondary indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*). However, the Mīmāṃsakas do not maintain that the universal alone is the constituent part (*aṅga*). The reply is: you are ignorant of the relationship between the denoted (*upātta*) and the indicated (*upādeya*). For the thing being pointed out (*uddiśyamāna-padārtha*) is characterized by the substance already denoted; the thing being pointed out indicates the substance denoted as fit for the ritual action. Therefore, in that context, there is a cognition of the substance.
Furthermore, what does the *vidheya* (the thing to be enjoined) indicate? For it is not uttered for the purpose of bringing to mind a category (*padārtha*) that is connected with the action.

How, then, does it enter into a specific substance (*dravyaviśeṣa*)? To this he says: Precisely because it is enjoined, it implies its own substratum—the substance—for the sake of accomplishing the action;
it does not merely indicate it. Therefore, since in an enunciation (*uddeśa*) that which is being enunciated functions as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), there arises a cognition of the substance.

(1) With respect to the subject (*uddeśya*); (2) G. [states]: "It is the substance itself that is characterized (*lakṣyate*), for it is perceived as being connected with other functions, and not rather a cognition directed toward the denoted object related to itself. Because:"

The reference is to that which is delimited by the mere action (*kāryamātra*); therefore, only the mere action is required as the delimiter, not the singularity and so forth expressed by direct statement (*śruti*). To the question, "Why is singularity not required? he says: "In that case, being already included (*upāttatā*) is the cause for the cognition of a distinction; however, that which is to be enjoined (*upādeya*) must be understood as qualified by the direct statement itself, and not from any other source. Therefore, in that context, it is appropriate—

The distinction lies in the term "expectancy" (*apekṣā*). This very reason has been stated [in the previous passage]: that when something is being enunciated, its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). This does not mean, however, that the enunciation itself is unintended; for [if it were], there would be no comprehension of what has been employed [in the text]. Therefore, the argument that even the mention of the "cup" (*graha*) need not be intended is refuted. Furthermore, the reason—that the qualification is not intended because it has been employed—is of the form already stated.

By this it is meant that number follows the substrate (*anvaya*) by virtue of being its residual property (*upādānaśeṣatva*) and because of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). However, in the case of that which has already been taken up (*upātta*), since there is no further substrate, its status as a residual property is absent from the very outset. Therefore, due to the lack of an object, there is no requirement for number at all. What then can be said of [sentences such as] "one should establish the fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*) or "one cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*)? Here too, because the fires and the sacrificial post are intended objects (*uddeśya*), they are not intended to be qualified [by number].

[The opponent] thinks that the number [of fires] becomes intended [to be significant]. The answer is: "The number is intended. Why? Because here this very sentence is the injunctive statement (*upādānavākya*). Therefore, since it is not known from any other source, the number is required [by the injunction]. [Objection: But surely the word *agni* (fire) is the designator (*uddeśaka*), and the fires are the primary entities, not the number; therefore, how can there be an intention [to signify the number]? The answer is: True, as follows...

The venerable one says: "However, there are two kinds of reference (uddeśa): that of what is mentioned and that of what is not mentioned. 'He cleanses the cups' is an instance of reference to what is mentioned; in the sentences concerning the Aindravāyava and other cups, the cleansing is enjoined with reference to the cups already mentioned, and thus it is a reference to what is mentioned. In some places, he also says:

Because [entities] such as the *vanīyaka* (the one who desires to marry) are not mentioned [in the injunction], and since that which is not mentioned is what is referred to (*uddiśyate*), how can this be? This objection arises from the view that both restatement (*anuvāda*) and reference (*uddeśa*) possess the same form. The answer is: reference is said to concern that which is to be enjoined; the meaning is that whatever something is enjoined upon, that is what is referred to. Being mentioned or not being mentioned is not the cause for reference. Therefore, by means of another source of knowledge—

A qualifying attribute that is mentioned as a mere reference (*uddiśyamāna*) is one whose specific quality is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). On the other hand, when something is mentioned as a reference while its qualifying attribute remains unknown, it must be understood as being qualified by that very attribute through the force of the scriptural statement (*śruti*), just like the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Therefore, it is rightly said by the authoritative tradition: "In the case of the subject matter where [the word] *graha* is employed as a reference—as in the phrase 'he wipes the cup' (*grahaṃ samārṣṭi*)—the qualifying attribute is not intended to be significant. Now, as for the word *graha*...

"He cleanses" (*saṃmārṣṭi*): this is the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*), which is a kāraka-case. Grammarians (*śābdāḥ*) maintain that a kāraka exists for the sake of an action (*kriyārtha*). Herein lies the intention: this is the second case-ending, a kāraka, and a kāraka exists for the sake of an action. And whatever exists for the sake of something else must be adopted (*upādeya*) for the sake of accomplishing that [action]. And whatever is to be adopted possesses an expectancy for a delimiting factor (*avacchedakākāṅkṣā*). Now, [one might object: what if the delimiting factor is already known?

It is true that it does not require another delimitant (*avacchedaka*) provided that the delimitant were already known in relation to the act of wiping (*saṃmārga*). However, since the status of being a delimitant is not known here, the number cannot be a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) of the act of taking up (*upādāna*). He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "But surely, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs in the sense of that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*); and that which is most desired is not for the sake of the action, but rather the action itself is for its sake; therefore, [the number] belongs to the most desired object through the action."

"Because there is no further appropriation, there is no remainder of appropriation. But the proponent says: "True, but that is the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyāvibhakti*) for a factor of action (*kāraka*);
therefore, because it is a factor of action, there is appropriation with respect to the activity. He himself states this in a single passage: "But surely this is contradictory:
(1) 'non-appropriation' and (2) 'the definition is not distinct'."

"And the *kāraka* that is most desired. Therefore, in the ultimate sense, the meaning is simply the status of being a *kāraka*. However, it is implied (*ārtha*) that even a *kāraka* possesses a connection with the fruit of the action. The proponent asks: "How is this contradictory? The opponent, having raised an alternative view, replies:

He refutes [the opponent's position]: What is this so-called "most desired" (*īpsitatama*)? If it means that which, from which the accomplishment of the action arises—that being the "most desired" for the sake of that action—then there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that every *kāraka* would be an object (*karman*). Consequently, the specific designation of "this is the object" and "this is the instrument" (*karaṇa*) would be useless, since all *kārakas* would incur the status of being the object. Alternatively, if it means that which is reached by the action...

By study, the Veda is produced—just as rice is produced by cooking; it is refined—just as grains of rice are refined by sprinkling; it is transformed—just as clarified butter (*ājya*) is transformed by melting. We shall explain in the eighth [chapter] that clarified butter is not produced by melting; rather, because it possesses fragrance, the earthly substance of clarified butter is solid by nature and merely becomes liquid through contact with fire. That is called its "action" (*karman*). Thus...

For one who speaks thus, fourfold action is intended, because the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) and the object to be modified (*vikārya*) are distinct. He refutes this: "In that case, the *kāraka* would not be a *kāraka*"—the meaning is that it would not be the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) by virtue of its state of being reached (*prāpti*) and so forth. Why? Because qualities such as reaching and the like depend upon the completion of the action; once the action has been accomplished, the result of the action is subsequently produced. For the result [depends] on the cause...

[The result] arises.
