There is a fixed sequence of priority between cause and effect; for when the operation has reached its conclusion and is accomplished, the result arises, and not while the action is still being brought about by the result. Therefore, [the result] does not possess the status of a *kāraka*. The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) replies: "To this it is said: this is not contradictory; qualities such as reaching (*prāpti*) reside both in the *kāraka* and not in the *kāraka*. When they reside in the *kāraka*..."

(1) G. "But even so, it exists"; (2) R. "for the sake of the accomplishment of the action"; (3) G. "that which, in a particular factor (*aṃśa*), has the state of attainment (*āpti*) and so forth is the *kāraka* [agent/cause] therein—this is the meaning.

In that case, the agent itself (*kāraka*) is the fruit; then the quality (*guṇa*), such as attainment (*prāpti*) and so forth, is twofold. Otherwise, there would be only a single uniform nature. The opponent asks: "What is this [statement] that 'the agent itself is the fruit'? The answer: For when the agent itself—by undergoing some modification—is intended as the object to be pervaded (*vyāpya*), produced (*utpādya*), refined (*saṃskārya*), or transformed (*vikārya*), then that very [agent] is called the fruit. That very...

By assuming a particular state, a factor (*kāraka*) receives the designation of "that which is most desired" (*īpsitatama*), whether for the sake of accomplishing an action or for the sake of accomplishing a result. Whatever is a *kāraka* serves both to accomplish the action and to accomplish the result; that very same factor receives the designation of "most desired" through the occurrence of some modification. Therefore, it is not contradictory to say that a *kāraka* is "that which is most desired. How is it not contradictory? For it exists [as such].

An agent (kāraka) does not inherently reside in its fruit, just as an instrument (karaṇa) and so forth do not; likewise, while a fruit such as heaven exists, it does not inherently reside in the agent. Therefore, it was stated that "the most desired agent" (*īpsitatamaṃ kārakam*) is the object (*karman*), so that whatever agent is inherent in the fruit may be designated as such. By this, the objection that the specific definition is redundant has been refuted. Now, one might ask: is not heaven and so forth also an agent?

"The fruit of the action resides in the agent precisely because of its inherence [in him]," as stated in the rule: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer" (*śāstraphalaṃ prayoktari*). To this, the reply is: "Inherence of the fruit [in the agent] does not exist by virtue of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action); rather, this is the operation defined by 'eligibility' (*adhikāra*), which was explained under the section on eligibility. [Objection: "If that is so, how then is the rule of the venerable Pāṇini, 'When the fruit of the action is intended for the agent' (*kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*), to be understood?"
(1) It was stated, "G. says 'na'";
the meaning of this is also determined in that very place. Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore, although [it is said] 'he cleanses the cup'..."

Although the act of sweeping (*saṃmārga*) indeed brings about the grasping (*graha*), nevertheless, the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyāvibhakti*) expressive of that [grasping] portion does not denote the "most desired object" (*īpsitatamatva*)—that is to say, it does not denote the resultant portion (*phalāṃśa*). This means that it denotes what is to be produced by the action (*kriyāniṣpādya*). By this, the following is stated:

singularity is heard in respect to a certain portion, yet that subsidiary element (*aṅga*) is not something to be taken up (*upādeya*); and that which is to be taken up is not the one in respect to which the case-ending occurs. Therefore, according to the scriptural text (*śruti*)...

Thus, it is established that there is a comprehension of distinction. Therefore, it is settled that the *saṃskāra* (grammatical refinement) has as its object that which is already expressed (*upātta*). Now, an objection is raised: "Is this observation not inconsistent? For the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs even for that which is not most desired (*anīpsitatama*), as in 'he gives a cow to the teacher' (*upādhyāyāya gāṃ dadāti*). What follows from this? This follows from it: through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the status of] a *kāraka* (participant in action) [is determined].

It denotes the factor (kāraka), not the portion of the result (phalāṃśa). Likewise, the word "graham" also expresses the factor itself. Consequently, it cannot be said that the singularity [of the cup] is unintended, because it is heard precisely in its status as something to be enjoined (upādeya). If the accusative case denotes the factor, then how can the cleansing (saṃmārga) be for the sake of the cup? The meaning is that its being for the sake of that [cup] is improper due to a lack of evidence (pramāṇābhāva).

The answer: Because it serves a purpose, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) of the cups has that [the Soma] as its objective; this is just as the *paśupuroḍāśa* cake is for the sake of the deities Agni and Soma. To this, it is replied: the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) expresses the state of being most desired (*īpsitatamatva*). As for the rule "and that which is not desired but is connected with the action," its meaning is that it is established solely by the action itself. The sense of this is: first, the accusative expresses the factor of the result (*phalāṃśa*); likewise, that which is connected [with the action]...
Since it is stated that the same applies here as well, [the term] denotes precisely that portion of the result produced by the action; this much is the distinction:
the mention and expression of a single [element] is solely by way of its connection with another action, as in “one threshes the rice.”

Thus, rice-grains (*vrīhayaḥ*) are taken up as being connected with the injunction (*niyoga*); in that very context lies their status as the most desired (*īpsitatamatā*). It is not so for one [other] thing; for example, in the expression "he gives a cow" (*gāṃ dadāti*), the cow is not taken up as being connected with another action. And that [cow], while not being the most desired, is still connected with the fruit produced by the action. Likewise, even that which is the least desired (*anīpsitatamam*) is [connected] with the action—so it is said.

There is no distinction in the connection with the fruit to be produced (*janya-phala-yogitva*). One must understand that the second case (*dvitīyā*) also denotes only that much: the state of being most desired (*īpsitatamatva*) on the part of the rice-grains (*vrīhīṇām*) by virtue of its being the effect (*kāryataḥ*). Thus, in both instances, the second case retains its primary meaning; therefore, it is stated that the second case does not denote a factor of action (*kāraka-aṃśa*). If, even in the rule *tathā-yuktaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.50), the second case does not denote a factor of action, then in that case—

In the expression "he gives a cow" (*gāṃ dadāti*), there is no intention to convey the number. The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) raises and then refutes this doubt: "Let it be so," he says, "but no; for that would entail the necessity of postulating another purpose. For as long as another purpose for the cow has not been established, it cannot be said that the number is unintended, because [the cow], having its number unknown, requires a limiting factor (*avacchedaka*). A partial proponent of the final conclusion (rāddhāntaikadeśin) asks: "Why?"
No other purpose is accepted. The reply is: because there is a lack of evidence; there is no evidence for the postulation of an action (*kārya*).

But surely the accusative case-ending itself is the evidence for the postulation of an action? True, the accusative is evidence, but it provides a specific [object] when there is a requirement for an action; it is not, however, capable of making known that the meaning expressed by the word ending in the accusative is necessarily an action.

Like flour and so forth. Why, then, is it not capable? He says: case-endings (*vibhakti*) terminate in their specific application (*viniyoga*); their power is exhausted merely by establishing a mutual relationship, and they do not terminate in the action itself. Now, one might ask: "What is the need for postulating another purpose? Let the injunction (*niyoga*) itself be the thing to be accomplished within this very sentence. To this he replies: "There is no injunction devoid of a qualification (*adhikāra*)," because [the injunction] must be in proximity to that which possesses a fruit (*phala*).

We shall explain this point later. Furthermore, since the cow is seen here to be the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), no other object to be accomplished, such as entitlement (*adhikāra*), can be admitted. Nor is there an injunction (*niyoga*) without entitlement. Therefore, this postulation also does not exist. If, in that case—

There is another goal to be accomplished, yet there is no entitlement (adhikāra) therein; how then is there a connection with entitlement for the injunctions regarding purificatory rites (saṃskāra)? To this he says: "The injunctions regarding purificatory rites, however, have been explained in the [sūtra] 'teṣāmarthena'.
Just as, despite their having other effects, they enter into the sphere of entitlement, so too [is it here].

Regarding the phrase "for their sake," it has already been stated there. The proponent (rāddhāntin) offers a rebuttal: "We consider that you have raised this objection even though it has already been answered; we suspect it is due to the fault of forgetfulness. Therefore, this is now being reminded: this predominance (*prādhānya*) lacks a specified object (*anupātta-viṣaya*);

like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the intendedness (*vivakṣitatva*) of the number remains [unestablished]. By means of this distinction, there is a connection with one action and a lack of connection with other actions.
On account of the basis characterized by being the most desired (*īpsitatama*) or not the most desired (*anīpsitatama*), the Blessed Pāṇini composed another rule, namely *akathitaṃ*.

Here too, the phrase "likewise [the case is] so" (*tathā yuktam*) is understood to carry over. Therefore, it is established that the use of the second case (*dvitīyā*) does not deviate from denoting predominance (*prādhānya*), that is, the state of being the recipient of the fruit produced by the action. However, when the object is already apprehended through another means of knowledge, its qualification is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*).

Siddham. "One should state the singularity [required] for the planets and so forth; one should not prohibit the second and so on," says the Bhāṣya. That is untenable. Just as the singular number, enjoining the singularity residing in the animal, excludes the meanings of the second and so forth, so it is here as well.

To the question "Why should this not be so?", he says: "But because the Vedic text regarding 'graha' has [already] taken its object, for in that case, singularity and so forth are qualifiers of what is to be taken (*upādeya*).
Here, however, it has been stated that the very fact of being "taken" (*upāttatā*) is the cause for the cognition of the specific [quality]. This meaning has already been explained.
Now, what is the intention behind the statement “it enumerates”? It is thought that an enumeration (parisaṃkhyā) is vitiated by three defects; this is the intended meaning.

The singular number would then be unconnected [to the action]. And it has been stated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* that there is no denotation of something unconnected. Therefore, one might think that an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) is preferable. This is not so. It is true that the denotation of the singular number would result in being unconnected; however, an exclusion is not possible because [the connection] has not yet been established. Only when the connection between the cup and the cleansing is already established can there be an exclusion of others.

An injunction (niyoga) has no force regarding that which is already attained through passion, such as eating, as in the case of the rule "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten. However, regarding what is not so attained, the scriptural text (śruti), such as "the white [horse]," is not capable of excluding crows and the like. Nor is there a lack of syntactic connection (ananvitābhidhāna), for that too—

The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: just as in the case of the dog’s eating, where the attainment [of the object] is understood, so too here there is no *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) regarding the second and subsequent [dogs].

Now, it might be argued that while it is appropriate for the dog and so forth because of its lack of connection [to others], singularity (*ekatvam*)—when many are being employed—is not obtained even in the alternative view, because a number remains fixed only by excluding other numbers; therefore, the charge of expressing something unconnected (*ananvitābhidhānam*) is difficult to avoid.

This has been answered by the author of the Bhāṣya when he stated: “The sole purpose of the case-ending is not merely its utterance. But how does this answer the objection regarding the non-connection (*ananvaya*) of number? It is answered in this way: even though there is no connection with number, we observe usage in the mere sense of the object (*karma*), as in the example, “A Brāhmaṇa is not to be killed. If it is argued that here too [the action] is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*):
(1) It is possible; (2) by which [means]; (3) P. 723 [p.

"If it is argued that even here we intend a connection with negation (*saṅkhyānanvaya*), [we reply: no, for when [the word] is connected with 'non-existence' (*avadha*) in the sense of a negation (*nañ-artha*), there is singularity..."

It is capable of being understood from another source, because its engagement [in the action] is known from elsewhere. The meaning of this is as follows: for when "killing" (vadha) is connected with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and is thus prohibited, it must be admitted that it has already been engaged in elsewhere. Consequently, since it is not something to be enjoined (*anupādeya*), number cannot be subordinate to it as an object of injunction;

therefore, it is simply not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣā*). Thus, it should be understood that the expression of singularity is appropriate only in the case of a mere property (*dharmamātra*). On this point, the Bhāṣya says: "This..."
"And there is another fault.

This is its meaning: even if the connection with the apprehension of oneness is enjoined, it is not possible to restrict the oneness of the cup (*graha*) regarding the act of cleansing (*sammārjana*), because the cleansing is not differentiated by virtue of being the object [of the injunction]. Thus, this [argument] appears to be untenable.

Since it is logical to describe how, upon hearing of oneness (*ekatva*), its connection with the action cannot possibly exist in that same manner [as the cup’s], the word "cup" (*graha*) should therefore be understood as having only the unprescribed subject as its referent; thus, the restriction of the cup’s oneness is established as being solely within the scope of the cleansing (*sammārga*). To remove this inconsistency, the author of the *Ṭīkā* quotes the *Bhāṣya* using the phrase "this is another fault" as a marker.

He refutes the objection regarding logical inconsistency: if one resorts to the theory of denoting a single entity (*ekatvānvitābhidhāna*), then the nature of being a "cup" (*grahatva*) would not have its object already established; it would not serve as a qualifier for the cups that are already mentioned. And if the object were not already established, it would follow that there is no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) between the cup and the act of cleansing (*sammārga*). This is because a purification (*saṃskāra*) is unfit to be applied to something that is entering into another action. Furthermore, if there is no such connection, the injunction for cleansing [would be meaningless].

Because it would lack an object and be devoid of a subordinate element (śeṣin), it would be meaningless. Therefore, this [objection] is not a flaw; rather, this is established as the flaw stated in the Bhāṣya: that this is indeed an "enjoined mention" (upāttoddeśa) and not an "un-enjoined mention" (anupāttoddeśa).
[Objection: "Now, suppose the connection between oneness and the cleansing (saṃmārga) were enjoined."

The commentary beginning with these words is untenable; for if a relationship is being enjoined, a relation of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) must necessarily be admitted. In that case, since singularity is the principal factor, the act of cleansing (*sammārga*) is directed toward that singularity.
(1) P. 715 (2) G. For the purpose of refutation (3) P. 715.
[If it were so] enjoined, then the word *graha* (cup) would be syntactically disconnected. Alternatively, since two objects of reference— the cup and its singularity— are heard,

and because a sentence is completed with respect to each object of reference (*pratyuddeśyam*), one [part of the injunction] would establish the connection between the cup and the cleansing, while the other would establish the connection between singularity and the cleansing.

It might be argued that [the number] should be enjoined. That is not so. Since the connection between the cup (*graha*) and the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is not already established, how could the connection between oneness and the cleansing be enjoined? Furthermore, because the cleansing is subordinate (*apradhāna*) and oneness is primary (*pradhāna*), the primary cannot be enjoined with respect to the subordinate. If, on the other hand, the cleansing itself were the primary, even then, one would have to resort to a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the difference in the objects to be designated (*uddeśya*): "cleansing is for the cup" and "oneness is for the cleansing."

It is prescribed [that the singular number is enjoined]. That is untenable, because since oneness is immaterial, it cannot logically serve as a means (*sādhana*) for the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*); furthermore, it lacks the status of being a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*).

Restating this objection, the author provides the following explanation: "If the connection between oneness and cleansing were to be enjoined, there too there would be two possible courses"—by this, he shows that the injunction is neither possible as a connection between a quality and a fruit (*guṇaphala-sambandha*), nor is it like the case of the red cow (*aruṇā*).

This is what is meant: just as in the case of the connection between a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and its result (*phala*), the principal sacrificial fire (*vaitānāgni*) is enjoined as connected with the subordinate act of establishing it (*ādhāna*), so too here, the doubt that the connection of the cleansing (*sammārga*) with singularity (*ekatva*) might likewise be enjoined does not arise; nor does the doubt that, just as the immaterial quality of "redness" (*āruṇya*) serves as a means for the purchase (*kraya*), so too singularity might serve as a means for the cleansing. This [doubt] also does not occur.

"It is possible. How is it impossible? First of all, singularity is not capable of qualifying or characterizing that which is mentioned in its own sentence. Singularity, for its part, is not sufficient to qualify or characterize the *saṃmārga* (the act of cleansing) mentioned in its own sentence.

For when something is connected with the *saṃmārga*, it must be either the primary element (*pradhāna*) or a subordinate quality (*guṇa*); there is no other mode of connection. How is it that there is none?

For it has been stated that the expression of number by case-endings (*vibhakti*) is dependent upon the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Why, then, is a connection with the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) impossible for the singular number, whether as an object (*viṣaya*), a subject of reference (*uddeśya*), or something to be enjoined (*vidheya*)? Because it is dependent on another;
[and] because there is no absence of its being a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*).

Because it is dependent upon the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is no connection with the act of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*). Why, then, does the Commentator not maintain that— since the cup (*graha*) is not mentioned as the primary factor with respect to the cleansing— the singularity possesses a subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) in the cleansing by virtue of its utility for the mention, just like the quality of redness (*aruṇā*)?

It has been stated that [the qualification] is possible. To this, it is replied: even granting [the possibility], it was stated that it is not possible in the case of the *aruṇā* (red cow), because the cup (*graha*) is the primary element (*pradhāna*).
But surely, even in the case of the primary element, the qualification is indeed possible by relying on its status as a causal factor (*kāraka*), which serves as the basis for the qualification.

This is the meaning: even the primacy of the cup and so forth is caused solely by their status as causal factors; it is precisely those cups that have become causal factors which constitute the primary elements.

[They] exist. Therefore, by relying on that state, the singularity of the cup (*graha*) and so forth becomes a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), just like [the quality of] "red" (*aruṇā*). And who has said that a qualification is not possible? Here, however, the impossibility of an injunction itself has been demonstrated because the cup is the primary element (*pradhāna*).

The meaning of this is as follows: if the cup were enjoined with respect to the cleansing (*sammārga*), then, because it would be something to be taken up (*upādeya*), its qualification [would be possible].
It might be so; however, in this case, the cup (*graha*) is not enjoined because it is the primary element. By this passage beginning with "being the primary element" (1), [it is said]:
"But surely, being the primary element..."
The commentary beginning with "mityādi" and ending with "bhidyeta vākyam" has been explained. Now, if it should be argued that,
having characterized the cup (*graha*) and so forth, their connection with oneness is enjoined rather than their connection with the act of cleansing (*sammārga*)— what is the intention behind this?

"The partiality [of the injunction] applies to the cleansing (*saṃmārga*), which is the recurring element (*anvayin*), and not to oneness. The answer is: "Even if devoid of an action, a recurrence of number and so forth is not possible when there is no thing to be enjoined, even if it were otherwise possible. The meaning of this is: when the cleansing is the thing to be enjoined, a recurrence of number and so forth that is devoid of an action is not possible; however, when there is no thing to be enjoined, it may indeed be possible. And not by direct statement (*śruti*).
It has been stated that there is a connection of the unity residing in the cup (*graha*) with the action; the subsequent commentary should also be explained in this manner.
Thus, it would have to be admitted that the study of the *saṃmārga* and other such rites is an error, as long as the study of the *saṃmārga* and others is regarded as an error.

It is not said that, while the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and so forth—which are the objects to be enjoined—is possible, the sentence lacks the capacity to enjoin merely the connection with singularity;
for [the opponent asks]: "If singularity were not intended to be expressed..."

By this commentary, he demonstrates a contradiction with the grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*). The intention is as follows: while it is established by authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) that "the plural number is used for many"—a principle accepted by grammarians (*śābdāḥ*), yet not something we ourselves are here deliberating upon—what will the definition do for the object of description (*lakṣya*) once it has been so established? Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the definition here, for the expression of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not the sole purpose [of the definition]. This has already been explained previously.
Furthermore, the "graha" (cup) is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), while singularity is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). What follows from this being so? This follows:

the case-ending expresses its own meaning—which resides in the meaning of the nominal stem—by means of direct denotation (*śruti*) itself. By this statement in the *Bhāṣya*, he demonstrates that the singularity expressed by the case-ending is dependent—that is, it is dependent upon the meaning of the nominal stem. And that...

This has been explained. Now, as for what was said—that just as in the case of "this [is] for the cattle-herder," where singularity is intended to be expressed, so it is here as well—what is the rebuttal to that? The distinction has already been stated: there is a distinction based on the Vedic text (*śruti*) regarding those things to be employed (*upādeya*), or based on the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the qualities of speech.

If the material cause (*upādāna*) is [determined] by its function (*kāryataḥ*), and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of that which has been taken up (*upātta*) is by way of being the remainder (*śeṣitayā*), then even the scriptural mention of the "cup" (*graha*) would likewise be merely a characteristic of any vessel for holding Soma, because they share a single function. By this, he states the intermediate connection and the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): if the material cause is determined by its function—that is, if there is a taking up of that which has a function—and if it is a characteristic or indicator of that which has been taken up by the word used as the subject (*uddeśaka*).
"Not as something remaining. Therefore, even the scriptural mention of the *graha*, that is, the nominal stem *graha* itself, is intended solely to indicate the vessel for holding the *soma*.

Because the *grahas* and *camasas* have both been taken up [for use], and because cleansing (*sammārjana*) has the single purpose of removing the Soma that remains after being poured out—since its sole function is to clear away the Soma spilled during the Soma sacrifice—and since that purpose is no different for the *grahas* and *camasas*, it is logical that the *camasas* should also be cleansed. This has been demonstrated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "In whichever [vessel] the Soma is being taken up... [and so forth].

By the phrase "it would be sprinkled," and by implication (*sāmarthyataḥ*) when the purpose is accomplished, there is the attainment of a mere injunction for cleansing (*saṃmārga*), just like the instruction regarding a mantra within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*). The meaning of this is as follows: let there be an injunction for the cleansing alone, without any intended connection to the cup (*graha*). And so it is.

And thus there is simplicity of injunction. How, then, is the connection with the doors established? It is by virtue of the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). First, the act of cleansing (*sammārga*) is capable of performing the removal of the Soma-drops; therefore, by means of indicative power (*liṅga*), its application (*viniyoga*) is restricted to that very purpose. Just as a mantra taught within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) is applied through indicative power, so it is here as well. And this has been stated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*): "In the case of cleansing, [it refers to] human effort..."
By such a commentary as this,
the meaning is established.

To this it is replied: through the scriptural statement (*śruti*), there is the cognition of what has been taken up (*upātta*), but the scriptural statement does not arise from the act of taking up. Since the cups (*graha*) and the bowls (*camasa*) are taken up by virtue of their function (*kārya*), for that reason alone the scriptural mention of "cup" (*graha-śruti*) should not be interpreted as referring to all vessels. For the capacity of a function is such that there is an absence of refinement (*saṃskāra*) for that which lacks a function; it does not extend, however, to everything that possesses a function.

[The response is: "The refinement (*saṃskāra*) of everything. But has it not been stated that the sprinkling with Soma and the wiping are equal in their effect, namely, the attainment of a state of purity?

"Therefore, because of the connection with the function (*kārya*), there should be a cleansing (*sammārga*) for all [vessels]. This is true that was said; however, we have stated that it is not capable of overriding the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "For even when something is heard in scripture, if it is indeed a function (*kārya*), why should it not occur even when it is not so heard? The meaning of this is: when the cup (*graha*) is mentioned in scripture, the removal of the soma-juice by pouring it out is precisely what is intended.

[Question: What is the purpose of the cleansing (*sammārga*)? Why does it not occur even when [the purpose] is not explicitly heard in the scripture? For even in that case, there is no difference regarding that effect (*kārya*), and the performance [of the action] is for the sake of that effect. [Answer: No, for the effect is not heard [in the text]. But was it not stated that the effect is indeed heard? The meaning of this is as follows: it is heard in the text, "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*). In that regard, when one considers what the purpose of the cleansing might be with respect to the cups, [it is concluded that] it is the pouring out of the Soma (*somāvaseka*).

The purpose (*prayojana*) is seen to be the removal (*nirharaṇa*), characterized by the attainment of a pure state; therefore, nothing else is postulated. Furthermore, it is not the case that only an action (*kārya*) is heard [in the scripture]. Consequently, an action whose nature is obtained through the force of what is heard is not capable of uprooting the scripture itself. He raises an objection:

"If the action is not respected, then how is there sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) in the case of barley (*yava*)? For the function of sprinkling is the same whether it concerns rice (*vrīhi*) or barley. Therefore...

If it is argued that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is likewise appropriate for barley (*yava*), this is because the underlying logic is not being respected; thus, the deluded opponent asks how there can be sprinkling in the case of barley.

We shall explain in the ninth [book] how that is so: since ritual properties (*dharma*) are prompted by the *apūrva*, the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) functions as an indicator (*lakṣaṇā*) for its specific means of accomplishment; therefore, sprinkling applies even to barley. However, in the present case, because of the difference in the *apūrva* resulting from the repetitions in the cups (*graha*) and the bowls (*camasa*), the situation is not the same.

Even if [the act] were prompted by something unprecedented (*apūrva*), there would be no cleansing (*sammārga*) of the cups (*camasa*), because of the state of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*). As for what was said—that the mere injunction of cleansing results in the attainment [of the desired end]—that is incorrect, because an injunction (*niyoga*) has as its object a specific application (*viniyoga*). Application is a mutual relationship;
that is the object of the injunction here. And that [injunction] is not capable of subverting its own object; otherwise, it would follow that the injunction itself is subverted.

And the object [of the action] is connected with the relationship of the *graha* (cup). This very point has been stated by the Commentator: "When [the singular number] is set aside, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) itself is sublated, namely 'the cup' (*graham*).

The meaning is that the direct Vedic statement regarding the injunction would be sublated. But surely, the connection of the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) with the injunction is established by the direct statement (*śruti*), while [its connection with the specific cup] is by the syntactical context (*vākya*).

Fearing that the word *grahasya* might mean that one should set aside the distant cup (*graha*) and instead enjoin only the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*), he says: "For when there is a specific application (*viniyoga*), [the injunction does not apply to something else].
(1) G. *sādapūrva* (2) P. 726 [p. r689]

There is no contradiction regarding the injunction (*niyoga*), for it enjoins both [the application and the performance], since they consist of related word-meanings; this is the meaning. For whatever distinction exists in the application—that is, in the mutual relationship—such as one being swift and another being delayed, that distinction occurs only when there is a contradiction. But here, because there is an absence of contradiction, remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) is irrelevant; this is established. As for oneness, however, just as...

It does not follow [in that way]; rather, it has been stated that the cup (*graha*) follows because it is being restated as the subject. Herein lies the investigation: should the mention of the cup (*grahaśruti*)—on account of its intermediate function—be taken as indicating any vessel whatsoever for holding the *soma*, just as the mention of rice (*vrīhiśruti*) indicates a specific means of accomplishment on account of the ultimate function? Or should it not? In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that since the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) exists for the sake of a function, [it serves] the intermediate function...
The opponent considers this to be a [mere] connection. The proponent [of the final view] holds that because the intermediate action is rooted in Śruti, it lacks the capacity to sublate that [Śruti];
therefore, in accordance with Śruti, the cleansing (*sammārjana*) applies only to the individual cups.
[This is so] because of the futility [of applying it otherwise], it should apply to their subordinate parts (*aṅga*).

Regarding this commentary, there is a doubt: does the height of seventeen *aratnis* apply to the upper vessel (*ūrdhvapātra*) of the *vājapeya*, or to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of that sacrifice? In this regard, he states the cause for the doubt: in the statement "the sacrificial post of the *vājapeya* is seventeen *aratnis*," is the word "of the *vājapeya*" the qualifier (*uddeśaka*), such that it means "seventeen [aratnis] of the *vājapeya*," or is it "seventeen [aratnis] of the post," such that the word "*vājapeya*" is the qualifier and the word "post" is the qualificand?

This is the intention of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*): if the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) is the term denoting the subject, then the expression "of the Vājapeya" would be a statement of something unconnected;
thus, he considers that its meaning serves to qualify [the sacrifice] by way of an exception (*apavādaka*).

One does not obtain [the result] by means of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), because there is no connection with the *vājapeya* sacrifice. This is the meaning: if the seventeen-cubit length were prescribed for the sacrificial post, then there would be a connection between the *vājapeya* and the sacrificial post; however, such a connection with the sacrificial post is not possible. This is because the *vājapeya* is expressed in the genitive case, and the genitive denotes a relationship, yet no relationship exists between the *vājapeya* and the sacrificial post. And as for the sacrificial post...

Because its connection terminates merely with the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*), there is no connection with the ultimate transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*). Therefore, since the *vājapeya* itself is the object of reference (*uddeśya*), the height of seventeen cubits is enjoined solely for the sake of that [sacrifice]. In that case, when there is a requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*), the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) denotes a tall vessel belonging to the *vājapeya* by virtue of a common quality. Thus he says: "Therefore, [the height] belongs to that which is connected to the *vājapeya*..."

The word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) is to be understood [as connected]. In this way, the meaning of the sentence, consisting of the meanings of the words as they are mutually related, becomes established. To this it is replied:

if the word *vājapeya* were unrelated to the word *yūpa* which possesses a direct syntactical connection (*śrautānvayin*), then this [objection] would indeed hold; but here, even in the connection "the sacrificial post is seventeen cubits long," the word *vājapeya* is indeed related. How so? Because of the connection—

Since the genitive case-ending is seen to have a connection even with a relative (saṃbandhin), as in examples such as "the grandson of Devadatta," the following is the intended meaning: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the word *yūpa* does not bear its literal Vedic sense; however, in this [present] view, it bears its primary meaning. Nor is there a lack of connection for the *vājapeya*, because we observe the connection of the genitive case-ending even in the absence of a direct relationship. This is what is meant: although there is no [direct] connection with it, nevertheless...

The genitive case is not contradicted; even when something has a relationship with another related entity, the use of the genitive occurs in relation to that [entity] as well. Therefore, there is no evidence for the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) being used figuratively; rather, the measurement of seventeen cubits is connected to the sacrificial post itself. The opponent objects: "But what is the purpose here of the phrase 'of the Vājapeya'? For in my view, it serves to provide the object to be qualified (*uddeśya*).
He thinks: "How can this be established? The reply is: "What does it matter to us whether this has been done or not?
For there exists a positive concomitance (*anvaya*). And when the meaning of a sentence possesses a positive concomitance, it becomes connected with some effect; something..."

The fault is that what has already been established as a fact is merely being restated (*anūdyate*). This has been stated as a concession (*abhyupagamya-vāda*); however, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthatas*), even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), both words would be redundant. For, by virtue of the context, the connection with the *vājapeya*, and suitability, the use of the tall vessel is already established.
But [the word "soma"] applies to the agent because of its inherent connection (*samavāya*).

Regarding this commentary, there is a doubt: does the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) find its place only within the *prayāja* offerings, or throughout the entire context? In this regard, he states the cause for the doubt: it is considered whether, in the injunction "he offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmaṃ juhoti*), there exists a connection of one action with another action, or not. If such a connection exists, then the placement is only within the *prayājas*; if, however, it does not exist, then...

By splitting the sentence, the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) applies to the qualified agent (*yogyakartṛ*), and thus it is to be inserted into the entire context. But how does the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) occur, or how does it not? Demonstrating therein how the connection does not occur, he states the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*): "An action cannot be accomplished by another action. To this effect, the venerable Kāśyapa said: "An action is not something to be accomplished by an action."

Thus, according to Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.11, while a quality (*guṇa*) may function as a means (*sādhana*), an action (*karman*) does not. Therefore, whatever agent is mentioned in the context is to be construed with the word "stepping forward" (*abhikrāman*). Since there is no mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the stepping forward and the oblation (*homa*), [they do not form a single] sentence (*vākya*).

By the phrase "having approached, he steps forward," the injunction regarding the ritual action (*karmavidhi*) is established; that is, stepping forward is enjoined for a qualified agent. Now, one might object: surely there is also a connection with the agent who performs the *prayāja* offerings. Therefore, due to the particularity of proximity (*sannidhāna*), the connection must be with the agent of the *prayāja* itself.
(1) P. 729 (2) G. [This connection] indeed exists.

It would be true if "juhoti" (he offers) were expressive; however, since it is not expressive, the status of being the intended object (*uddheśyatva*) for the agent is not possible in that case, just as in the rule "one should not speak untruth. The meaning of this is: if the verbal suffix in "juhoti" were expressive, then...

Since a grammatical usage refers only to the agent currently being expressed, and because the agent who prompts the action is the one present and intended as the object [of the injunction], the application [of the rule] would occur only in that case. However, this [word *ahar*] denotes the day. According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), its purpose is to enjoin the accessory known as the "stepping forward" (*abhikramaṇa*). Therefore, the agent is not the intended object, just as in the case of the injunction "one should not speak untruth. Consequently, due to the lack of distinction in connection and the lack of distinction in context, it belongs to the [entire] context.

"Because of the lack of connection with the agent who stands [in place], there is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*); that is to say, this sentence is distinct from the sentence concerning the *prayāja* offerings. For if the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) were inserted into that very same [sentence], then there would be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunction of the mere action itself. Now, what is the purpose of the word *juhoti*? In the case of a split sentence, the sentence 'stepping forward' is one thing, and 'he offers' (*juhoti*) is another; such, then, is the split of the sentence."

The reply is: "That which is for a certain purpose shall be for that very purpose; what need have we for this reflection? Since it is a restatement (anuvāda) either by way of the principle of repetition (*abhyāsa-nyāya*) in another ritual action, or by way of the principle of the Full-Moon sacrifice section (*paurṇamāsy-adhikaraṇa-nyāya*), such being the position reached, we say:
'But it must be a single sentence because it is expectant, for it is not completed by the preceding.'"
There is no direct connection of the action with another action.

However, through its connection with the agent, such a connection is possible—just as in the case of the "red" (aruṇā) [cow]—where the connection of one action with another action is established by way of the agent's connection, just as the quality of redness is connected to the substance.
But is it not the case that there is no mention of an agent here, as there is a mention of the "one-year-old cow" (ekahāyanī), because the verb "he offers" (juhoti) does not denote [the agent]?

(1) This has been stated. The reply is: we do not say that the agent's status as the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) exists; rather, it is by reason of that [agent] that there is a connection even when the object (*karman*) is the intended object.

We say that there is no contradiction, because that agent is possible in that *prayāja* offering. The meaning of this is as follows: since the word *abhikrāmam* ends in the suffix *ṇamul*, its connection with the verb *juhoti* ("he offers") is understood. And that connection is appropriate if it can be established by some means; and it is established by way of the agent. Furthermore, there is no absence of an agent therein, for precisely because...

Furthermore, the agent here is not mentioned as a medium for the connection, whereas the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) is mentioned; for this very reason, there is a disparity with the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*.

In that *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, both related items—the red color (*aruṇā*) and the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*)—are explicitly mentioned; however, the distinction here is that the agent serves merely as a possible medium for the connection. Now, the author of the *Bhāṣya* states regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Because of the mere knowledge of the connection, [it follows] from the injunction of performance..."

By stating "the establishment of what is to be done" (*kartavyatāsiddhi*), he shows that even in the case of a *prakaraṇa* (contextual supplement), the injunction applies to the action itself by means of the agent who is understood [therein]. Having raised the objection, "How can there be a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) because the agent is not explicitly mentioned?", he says: "As stated by the author of the Bhāṣya, 'From the full comprehension of the mere relationship, from the injunctive statement of performance (*prayogavacana*), and from the reference to the agent (*kartṛvamarśa*), the establishment of what is to be done follows'; in that very case, the status of the agent as the objective (*uddeśyatva*) is not contradicted."

This is the intended meaning: the sense of this passage is that the word *ekavedam* is read within the context [of the *āghāra* sacrifice]; therefore, when seeking syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with another meaning suitable to it, the agent (*kartṛ*) is the one who is capable of establishing the connection. Thus, having referred to the agent, the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) is enjoined. However, in the case of syntactic unity, it is impossible for the agent to be the object of reference (*uddeśya*), because the expression of the connected meaning is already established by the word *juhoti* itself. This is stated in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to demonstrate such a disparity.

If someone should have a doubt as to how the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached, the proponent of the conclusion says to him: "Since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established by mere possibility alone, it is held that there is no purpose for the agent in terms of being the intended object (*uddeśyatā*). Therefore, it is proven that even the object (*karman*) attains the status of being the intended object of the action."
(1) According to R., it is due to the agent; (2) according to G., this is indeed one [sentence], but it is divided because of the intervention of doubt.

Regarding the phrase "he puts on the upper garment" (*upavyayate*), a doubt arises: is the agent of the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses connected with the act of putting on the upper garment, or does this [injunction] find its place within the entire context? This doubt is restated in order to refute it. Now, one might object:
"Indeed, no word denoting a specific subject (*uddeśaka*) is heard here; and that which has no such designated referent is connected by the context alone."

It has been stated that [the connection is established] because there is no distinction in the syntactical connection (*saṃyoga*) and no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*). The meaning of this is as follows: the *upavīta* is mentioned in the context (*prakaraṇa*) without being explicitly connected [to a specific agent].
Furthermore, the *upavīta* consists of a particular arrangement of the garment, and by means of this arrangement of the garment, the agent becomes unconfused regarding the ritual action;

thus, this is taught as a duty of the agent alone. In that case, how can there be a connection of this [duty] with the agent situated within the context, given the absence of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)?

Is there a doubt? It is said: it was stated in the preceding section that connection with a performer who is present, even if not explicitly mentioned, is not contradictory. Likewise here, because the performers of the *sāmidhenī* verses are in proximity, and by the aforementioned principle, since the wearing of the upper garment (*upavyāna*) is known in common worldly practice to serve the purpose of another action, the performer—though not explicitly mentioned—is present and must perform [the act].

It ought to be capable of fulfilling [the requirement]. The meaning of this is as follows: the single word *upavyayate* requires an agent (*kartṛ*) for its syntactic connection (*anvitābhidhāna*). Since it remains incomplete without an agent, it enters into a single-sentence relationship (*ekavākyatā*) with the agent present there who is capable of fulfilling that requirement; thus, the meaning is that the agent who is present is the very one being consecrated by this act. Furthermore, the expectancy for another action—

"It is completed by the *pavyāna* [offering]. However, in the case of the statement "the immediate sequence is not an injunction," because the sense is already complete through the employment of two words, there is no connection based on mere proximity (*ānantarya*) in the theory of denotation of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*). But if this is so, then even the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward), according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the preceding section, would likewise be a property of the agent present in proximity.

[It might be argued that] it would be so; but no, because since it is not expressed as a verb (*anākhyātatvāt*), it is understood as something already established (*siddhavatpratīteḥ*), and thus there is no expectancy for an agent (*kartrākāṅkṣā*). What then?

For the sake of entering into the context, an agent belonging to another action is required as a subordinate element (*śeṣībhūtaḥ*); and by that subordinate element, there is the expression of the connection (*anvitābhidhāna*).

But here, since the requirement for the agent is primary, it is not contradictory for the completion [of the sentence] to occur through that which is proximate, even if it is already present. [Objection: "But surely this context belongs only to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
the Sāmidhenī verses are heard in another context.
What is the meaning of this commentary?

And this is the intention of the questioner: although the *sāmidhenī* verses belong to another context (*prakaraṇa*), nevertheless, because of their proximity, their performer is indeed connected [to them]; thus, it is logical that the wearing of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) should enter into the recitation of the *sāmidhenīs* alone. The answer: We have already explained that there is no distinction of context due to the absence of a word of reference (*uddeśapada*). What is meant is this: because no word of reference is heard, [the rule] is grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*).

The objection to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the suspicion of the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses entering into the context [of the sacrifice] is not tenable, because there would be a connection with an agent who serves as a gateway consistent with that [context].

However, the explanatory passage (*bhāṣya*) providing the resolution states: "It is true that the *sāmidhenīs* are heard in the context of another [rite], nevertheless, they possess their own intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*)."
Thus [it is asked]: what is this so-called intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*)? Why is an intermediate context untenable?
For there is only one context belonging to a governing injunction (*adhikāravidhi*), not also a context for the injunctions of subsidiaries (*aṅgavidhi*). The meaning of this is as follows:

by the word "context" (*prakaraṇa*), the capacity of the mandate (*niyoga*) to grasp [the subsidiary] is expressed, and likewise its power of application (*viniyojakatva*) belongs to that very same [mandate].

The definition [of expectancy] consists in the requirement for a manner of performance (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣatva*). And both of these [expectancies] belong only to the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), because that alone is perceived as something to be performed by persons. For whatever is to be performed, that which is recited in its proximity is intended solely for the sake of that [performance]. This very capacity to grasp belongs only to what is to be performed, and the requirement for a manner of performance belongs only to what is to be performed; thus, [these expectancies do not apply] to those [injunctions] that lack a qualification.

The context (*prakaraṇa*) exists even for the intermediate injunctions (*antarvidhi*). Now, one might ask: "Why is there no lack of a governing authority (*niradhikāratā*)? To this he says: "Because there is no difference from the principal injunction (*pradhānavidhi*).

To the question "How is there no difference? he says: "We shall explain the non-difference of the principal injunctions in the fourth [book]. Furthermore, regarding the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses... (1) 732-9.

Furthermore, an intermediate application (*avāntaraniyoga*) among the preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*) themselves is not possible. Since, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and others, there is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth of the primary injunction itself, how could there be any suspicion of an intermediate context (*prakaraṇa*)? Thus he says: "And because of those injunctions of preparation, for the sake of the purpose... [p. r696]
Thus, the restatement has been demonstrated. Therefore, a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) is not tenable as a means of application by way of being a "grasper" (*grāhaka*);

consequently, mere proximity (*sannidhāna*) remains as the only possibility. The respondent says: It is replied that this very term "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is employed in the sense of proximity alone. How is it understood that it is employed in the sense of proximity? [It is understood] from the statement: "by which, in its proximity... and so forth.

From the statement "the pride," it is understood that the *upavyāna* (wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder), being mentioned in proximity to that— that is, in proximity to the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses— is [a subordinate element] of that [recitation].

This is understood from the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya. For it is appropriate to say that when proximity (*sannidhi*) is the cause of connection, that which is mentioned in proximity [is connected]. Now, one might object: even in the case of *prakaraṇa* (context) as a means of application (*viniyojaka*), the use of the terms "proximity" (*sannidhāna*) and "direct statement" (*śruti*) is indeed possible. Therefore, this [Bhāṣya] is not exclusively indicative of the *liṅga* (indicative power). To this, he replies:

By whom was it said that [the meaning] is not tenable? Rather, it was said that it is not possible. But if this is so, then the status of the *bhāṣya* as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not supported. It is replied: This *bhāṣya* is tenable by way of its primary sense, with the intention of referring to proximity (*sannidhāna*). Nevertheless, if the *prakaraṇa* (context), which is the cause of connection and the factor that applies [a text], were not mentioned here, then the *bhāṣya* would have to be explained in a non-primary sense, as being directed toward that [context].

However, this is not the case; thus, the Bhāṣya itself serves as an indicative mark (liṅga). Furthermore, because a syntactical split (vākyabheda) is heard in the final conclusion (rāddhānta), it shows that in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) there was a single sentence (ekavākyatā). And that single sentence [is established] neither by way of being an applicator (viniyojaka) nor by way of being a grasper (grāhaka), but rather by way of proximity (sannidhāna). Therefore, for this reason also, the word "context" (prakaraṇa) refers precisely to proximity.

And it demonstrates an intervention by way of being the reason for the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*). In that regard, if the context (*prakaraṇa*) were the means of application (*viniyojaka*) according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), then the intention would be precisely an intervention.

If proximity were presented as the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), then this [objection] would not be tenable. However, if proximity were presented as the reason for the prima facie view, then its intervention would constitute a counter-argument. For this reason as well, by the word "context" (*prakaraṇa*), proximity alone is intended.
This is what he says: "Intervention for the sake of another destroys immediate sequence, not application (*viniyoga*); otherwise, indeed, *svāhā*..."

There would also be a non-application of the *kāra* because of its separation by the *samidh* and other verses. Now, if it is thought that because the *nivid* words have another purpose and are connected to a different *grāhaka*, there is a separation even from the *grāhaka*, [the author] refutes this: even by the phrase "of the twelve [verses] of the *ahīna*," there would be a separation of the *grāhaka*; yet that is not the case. Therefore, it is not so.
The *grāhaka* (the receiver) is separated. Furthermore, there is no separation for the *nivit* verses by means of the optional (*kāmya*) rites, because there is no separation from the *grāhaka*.

Consequently, it follows that the *upavyāna* (the upper garment) would serve the purpose of the *nivit* verses; thus, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is not obtained. However, there is no fault in the case of immediate proximity (*ānantarya*) even when there is separation, for even those [the *nivit* verses] are separated by the optional rites. And this being so, if there were a separation by the *nivit* verses...

The optional variants of the *sāmidhenī* verses would then result in the lack of interruption (*avyavadhāna*) among the *sāmidhenīs*; for that which is not itself contiguous cannot bring about an interruption for another. Therefore, if one accepts that they cause an interruption, one must admit that the *sāmidhenīs* possess contiguity.
Consequently, the *upavyāna* would serve the purpose of reciting the *sāmidhenīs*. He refutes this: "True, it would follow—provided that..."

If it were intended here that there is merely an interruption of the verbal sequence, then the subsequent statement—concerned with the connection between the accessory and the result—would not be interrupted;
for that purpose, the *upavyāna* (wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder) would be required. But in this case, what is intended is an interruption of the agent who is in close proximity.
And that interruption of the agent is appropriate because, when the connection between the accessory and the result is being stated, the ritual action itself is interrupted. For where...

When an action is enjoined, it is understood as something to be performed; and since that understanding cannot occur without an agent, the agent is present within the injunction itself. On the other hand, when there is no injunction, because the cognition of performing the action is interrupted, the agent remains remote.
(1) G. kartṛtānu-

[Page 698] But if this is so, does it not follow that there is no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) at all, because when there is a connection between a subsidiary element and a fruit, the ritual act is not enjoined and there is an absence of a proximate agent?

To this he says: "This being the case, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view is as follows: even when there is a connection between a subsidiary element and a fruit, the agent is [understood] from the scriptural mention of the recitation."

The meaning is that the *upavyāna* (the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder) is for the sake of the *sāmidhenī* verses because [the agent] is indeed in close proximity (*sannihita*) through the action; for even by means of an action, the agent is brought into proximity. However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*) maintains that what is not being enjoined does not become proximate. That which is to be restated must be restated exactly as it stands in its own place; it is not brought into proximity again. This is because the restatements (*anuvāda*) are subject to the force of what is being restated. The meaning of this is: indeed, what is called a "restatement" is...

An object presented by another cognition is restated precisely as being presented by that [other] cognition; it does not, however, present the object itself independently on its own. Thus, it is logical that what is being restated (anūdyamāna) is subject to the control of that [other cognition]. On the other hand, what is to be enjoined (vidheya) follows the injunction itself and is therefore brought into proximity by that injunction. Consequently, because there is no difference in their proximity, [the restatement] is to be applied throughout the entire context (*prakaraṇa*).
Thus it is established.
Because qualities are for the sake of another.

I say: Is it not the case that there are three principal acts in one [rite], since there are three principal acts even in the Full Moon sacrifice—namely those known as the Āgneya, the Agnīṣomīya, and the Upāṃśu—and likewise three even in the New Moon sacrifice, consisting of the Āgneya, the Aindrāgna, and the Sānnāyya? And this is due to the difference in the stages of performance.
This was stated while accepting the distinction of the Āgneya sacrifice.

We do not say that there is only one primary act; rather, we say that each individual act is connected with its own *itikartavyatā* (procedural details). What follows from this? There is no connection between two [acts taken together]; there is no connection with the *itikartavyatā* for the two combined, but rather for each one individually.

Because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*) or because it serves as the door for the instrument, there is a connection with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for each individual instrument. Thus, since there is only one *anuvākyā* for a single principal rite (*pradhāna*), the dual number is untenable. When this objection has been raised from the perspective of the Siddhānta, he states the position of the Pūrvapakṣa:
"But surely, even in the case of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, the connection with the procedure is one by one; thus, the untenability of the dual number is equal [for both sides]."

It is true that in this case, because two [substances] arise from the Vedic text (*śruti*), the use of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is not contradictory. The meaning of this is as follows: in the injunction "he performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings," the two *ājyabhāgas* arise as being conjoined with one another through the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa*. Therefore, having observed that state, the mutual conjunction of the two primary elements cannot be set aside; and by means of the word *dvandva*, there is the designation of the *ekaśeṣa*, because it expresses the mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) which constitutes the meaning of the copulative compound.

The meaning is that the designation of *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder formation) is not contradictory because it arises from *ekaśeṣa*. However, in this case, since the primary [action] is inherently singular and each individual *anuvākyā* verse arises separately, there is a contradiction regarding the dual compound (*dvandva*) of the primary actions. Having thus raised the objection, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), while supporting his position, says: "There is no contradiction with duality; for what could a scriptural statement not effect? For in that case, both the duality and the non-correspondence of the mantra [to the reality] would exist."

It has been stated that there would be an intervention [of another rule], because there is no evidence for such an intervention. The meaning of this is as follows: since there is no evidence for an intervention, this injunction applies directly to the primary element (*pradhāna*). For in that case, let there be an injunction of a specific mantra qualified by duality, which constitutes the meaning of the nominal suffix.
Not [the other way around].

Furthermore, there would be the fault of enjoining multiple qualities, because according to the principle of brevity (*samāsanyāya*), the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) as qualified by the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is enjoined by the Vedic text itself.

Therefore, when one *anuvākyā* (invocatory verse) is already established, two are enjoined. But [an objection may be raised]: "If two *anuvākyās* are enjoined for a single principal act, they will be unable to address the deity. To this, the reply is: "There is both a lack of correspondence to the reality [of the deity] and the presence of duality."

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that the mantra will function like [the word] *aindrī*. The author states the final conclusion (rāddhānta): "To this it is replied—we say that what has been stated is incorrect. Why? Because even in that case, the denotation of the word *yūpa* by its own form is not the reason for its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*).
What then? It is the fitness for connection with the auxiliary belonging to the enjoined quality of 'seventeen cubits' as qualified by the hearing of the word *yūpa*."

And it has been stated in that very same place that, since a relationship by way of fitness is possible, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the term *vājapeyasya* with the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
Likewise here as well, there is evidence for the injunction of mantras according to their respective fitness, as well as for their literalness and duality.
However, the sense is that the connection occurs through an intervention in accordance with the fitness of the thing to be enjoined, and not by altering the thing to be enjoined itself.

Therefore, it is established that the injunction of the mantras applies specifically to the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. As for this further comment in the Bhāṣya—"But even if they were to apply to the principal offerings, there would be two invitatory verses (*anuvākyās*), one for the offering to Agni and one for the offering to Agni-Soma"—how is that? Because of the contradiction with the formation of a *dvandva* compound; the formation of a *dvandva* implies a mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) of the two principal elements, and since that [conjunction] is absent here, [the objection does not hold].

The meaning is: "How can this be a commentary, given the contradiction with the dual number? Even assuming there is no contradiction, [the author] shows the contradiction in the opponent's position by means of another argument characterized by the impossibility of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantra.

If the fitness for another operation is the cause of restriction, then here too— in both the spreading of the grass and the announcement of the consecrated one— it is already fully accomplished.

"In this very context of *yogyatā* (fitness), the purpose [of the action] is fully realized. By this, he states the intermediate course of reasoning and the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But the meaning is that hand-washing and rinsing the mouth are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) for the person; and since a purificatory act consists in making one fit for another function, when there is a requirement for another action—as in the previous case—because the enjoined element is fit for a connection with what is proximate, let the injunction of the purificatory act be for the sake of the proximate ritual action alone."

To this it is replied: True, if the capacity [for connection] were restricted to this very point alone. However, if that capacity were likewise capable of governing a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) for the entire context, then indeed it would apply to the whole; but such is not the case. This is because there is no connection between the two verbal roots (*ākhyāta*), as the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* occur when one action is for the sake of another action, and those two suffixes are absent here. Therefore, due to the lack of connection, [the injunction] finds its place within the entire context.
Success!

However, in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), because the action to be performed is restricted to a specific [object], it is logical that there is a requirement for a specific [qualification]. Therefore, in the injunction of the *āgneya* [offering], the fire—

Does a word apply to another object by denoting its own primary meaning? Therefore, this question is improper. Alternatively, if the intention is that even in the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a word for one thing applies to another, then this question is intended to exclude that possibility. Its meaning is as follows: this inquiry regarding the figurative (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*) is for the purpose of distinguishing between secondary indication and the figurative; the figurative was explained in the section on the establishment of that [distinction]. Thus, a word for one thing [applies] through secondary indication to another.
