The definition that "that which exists elsewhere [than its primary sense] is figurative" (gauṇa) applies equally to metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā). Thus, when this inquiry into the figurative and the primary has been made, the nature of the figurative is described so that it may appear distinct from both the primary and the metaphorical. Among these, the distinction from the primary was demonstrated in the *Tatsiddhyadhikaraṇa*; therefore, the purpose of the question and answer here is to provide knowledge of the distinction from the metaphorical. That [distinction] is not established, because...

For he will state the definition of secondary usage (*gauṇatva*) as follows: "People are seen to understand the burning fire from the word 'fire' even while disregarding the cognition of the boy, but they are not seen to understand the boy while disregarding the cognition of the burning fire; the same applies to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as well. For people do not understand the vicinity of the Gaṅgā while disregarding the cognition of the Gaṅgā itself. The meaning of this is that even the purpose of knowing the different types of metaphorical indication is not tenable.

For that very reason which he will state as the definition of the secondary (gauṇa) [meaning] in his answer to the question— the commentary stating: "The primary meaning is independent of other meanings,
whereas the secondary is dependent on another meaning, just as the word 'fire' depends on the cognition of fire when applied to a young boy"—
that same definition applies to metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) as well, since it depends on the cognition of the Gaṅgā.

In this way, from the word "Ganges," there arises the cognition of that which is near the Ganges. Therefore, because the definition is identical [in both cases], this question and answer cannot be stated for the purpose of excluding that [secondary usage], nor even for the purpose of excluding secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) itself. Now, if it is thought that the term "secondary indication" applies only to secondary indication—since in that case the word "nearness" applies only to that which is connected with the Ganges—whereas in the case of a figurative usage (*gauṇa*), the word expressing the quality-bearer (*guṇin*) does not apply [to the primary object]; as in "The boy is fire," where [the word "fire"] applies to the boy who is related to fire...

[This is] because the word "cow" (*go*) is not perceived [there]. Therefore, the question is asked in order to state the distinction between the figurative based on indication (*lākṣaṇika*) and the figurative based on secondary quality (*gauṇa*). That is incorrect; for first, in the case of cognition (*pratīti*), both [the primary and the secondary] are connected [to the sentence meaning]. However, in the case of the action (*kārya*), not even one of them is connected. Even the Ganges is connected only in the case of cognition, not in the case of the action, because it is only that which is proximate which is connected to the action. Likewise, fire (*agni*) is also connected only in the case of cognition, because there is a cognition of something similar to fire. However, in the case of the action, not even one of them is connected.
Therefore, even by this qualification, no distinction is made. Alternatively, an effort is being made to exclude the meaning of the sentence. This is its meaning:

Now, you might think that from the expression "The boy is fire" (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*), the cognition arises that "the boy is similar to fire. And this [cognition] is not based on the word alone, because in common usage, no connection of the word *agni* with something similar to fire is understood. Rather, since this understanding arises from the employment of two words, it is established that it is caused by the sentence (*vākya*). Therefore, for those who hold that the secondary meaning (*gauṇārtha*) is the meaning of the sentence...

They think that for the sake of excluding that [literal sense], the secondary (gauṇa) meaning is understood due to its similarity to its own primary referent; this question is intended to demonstrate the nature of the secondary meaning. [The opponent claims: "A sentence does not function with respect to a different object. The meaning of this is: "The secondary meaning is understood from the sentence alone"—this suspicion is extremely weak. For instance, a sentence certainly does not function with respect to a different object distinct from the word-meanings. If...
If a sentence were to apply to a meaning distinct from the word-meanings (*padārtha*), then this doubt might arise; however, that is not the case. Now, one might object:

"A word-meaning is an object established in its own form alone, whereas the sentence-meaning consists of objects mutually related. Anticipating and removing this doubt that the sentence applies to a distinct meaning, he says: "For the sentence is nothing other than the words themselves which denote [objects] as already related (*anvitābhidhāyin*)."

The meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) consists of word-meanings (*padārtha*) that are mutually related (*anvita*). Each individual word expresses its own meaning as being related to another meaning that is compatible, required by context, and proximate. A sentence is precisely such a collection of words. Since meanings are expressed by words only as they are thus related, the word-meanings themselves constitute the sentence-meaning. Just as there is a single sentence within many words, so too there is a single sentence-meaning within the various word-meanings.

Thus it is stated in the *Vākyārthamātṛkā*: "Why is it that there is only the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*)? To this he says: "And it has been demonstrated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* that there is no such thing as the denotation of the unrelated (*ananvitābhidhāna*); and in the *Vākyārthamātṛkā*, we have already thoroughly examined this. Such being the case, the meaning of the question must be explained and the purpose of the question must be stated. Now...

It might be argued that "the secondary (gauṇa) is that which is understood from a word accompanied by an epithet," "the secondary is that which is poorly established," or "the secondary is that which has a limited scope of usage.
To refute these pseudo-siddhāntas regarding the grounds for being secondary, this question is raised; to that, he says:

"Thus, in the Bhāṣya, [words] accompanied by epithets, those well-established, and those of frequent usage are respectively refuted as grounds for being secondary or as grounds for being primary. Therefore..."

This question, intended for the purpose of refuting that [position], is also not tenable. The meaning of this is as follows: because those reasons are extremely weak, a question for the sake of refuting them is not appropriate; for even from the word "fire" when preceded by the word "boy," no [actual] fire is produced.

A word can be understood as secondary (gauṇa) only so long as it is not described as having a secondary cognition based on its similarity to its own primary meaning. Otherwise, by the principle that a cognition must have a basis, one would simply have to assume that it possesses expressive power [in that sense]; thus, no cognition arises even from a word that is non-expressive when accompanied by a qualifying term. The same should be applied to words that are poorly known or of infrequent usage.

It is said: this is the meaning of the question. For the distinction between word-meanings (*padārtha*) is understood as the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). The ablative case in "from the sentence" (*vākyāt*) is used with the elision of a verbal suffix (*lyablope*); that is, having perceived a sentence that conveys a qualified meaning in the linguistic usage of elders, one understands the distinction of word-meanings as the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. [The sentence-meaning] is of a qualified nature.

The meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is the word-meaning (*padārtha*) functioning as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); it serves as the means for the comprehension [of that sentence-meaning], because a qualified object cannot be comprehended when its qualifier is not perceived. Thus, the division of word-meanings is understood by way of being the instrumental cause [of comprehension]. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: And this division, by virtue of being the instrumental cause, applies to the boy (*māṇavaka*) with respect to the boy, and to the fire (*agni*) with respect to the fire—[as in the case of the word] *agni*...

The word is equal in both cases; that is to say, in both instances, the cause [of the application] is solely through the denotative function (*vācakavṛtti*). He demonstrates this: when it is said, "The boy is fire," the boy and his tawny color are the causes. When it is said, "Fire burns," the burning [substance] and the act of burning are the causes. Therefore, we perceive no distinction such that the causal status of one is literal while that of the other is figurative (*gauṇa*); rather, both are primary (*mukhya*).

And we observe a distinction between the primary and the secondary; that is to say, everything is indeed primary. Now, it may be argued that the cognition of the boy's ruddiness is preceded by the cognition of fire. The meaning of this is as follows: first of all, it is not logical to assume multiple meanings for the word "fire," since the cognition of another object is established solely through the capacity of the word to convey a single meaning. For instance, when fire is cognized from the word "fire," its ruddiness—
[The opponent] establishes [the following]: "Therefore, the cognition regarding the boy is preceded by the cognition of fire. [The author] refutes this: "It cannot be said in this way.
For it has already been stated that the understanding of the causal status [of words] arises from the sentence. Therefore, for one who [seeks to understand] the meaning of the sentence..."

That thing whose status as a cause (*nimittabhāva*) is understood is the word-meaning (*padārtha*). However, in this case, the status of the word "fire" (*agni*) as a cause is not tenable [in its primary sense].
In the expression "The boy is fire" (*agnir māṇavakaḥ*), it is only the tawny color (*piṅgalatā*) that is understood as the cause, just as in the expression "The tawny boy.

The meaning of this is as follows: first of all, the word "fire" does not function as a cause by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*), because it does not inhere in the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthe asamavāyāt*). Nor...

And it is not so in the case of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because [the word "fire"] brings about the cognition of the tawny color as something inherent in the sentence-meaning; for there is no connection between the tawny color residing in the boy and the fire. Indeed, one object brings another to mind through proximity. Even the Ganges, while indicating the bank through indication, indicates only that which is connected to itself. Therefore, there is no causality toward the fire, neither directly nor indirectly.
[This refers] to the meaning of "fire" (*agni*). Therefore, it is established that the word *agni* conveys the state of being tawny (*piṅgalatā*) just like the word *piṅgala*.

Consequently, this question—asking whether "this is secondary" (*gauṇa*) or "this is primary" (*mukhya*)—is difficult to resolve for one who holds such a view. [The term] *gauṇa* means "derived from a quality" (*guṇāt āgataḥ*), formed with the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *tata āgataḥ*. [The term] *mukhya* means "as if [it were the primary object]," formed with the suffix *ya* in the sense of "likeness" (*ivārthe*) according to the rule *śākhādibhyo yaḥ*. But if this is so, how can there be "secondary" status?

It is examined as follows: If the word *agni* (fire), like the word *piṅgala* (tawny), expresses tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) solely through its denotative function (*vācakavṛtti*), then why does it occur there only when accompanied by a prefix (*sopapada*)? For it should occur there even without a prefix; likewise, why is it so little known among common people? And why is its usage so rare? Or rather, both its well-known status and frequent usage should exist without distinction. To this, he says:

Furthermore, it has been shown in the Bhāṣya that this [denotative capacity] does not arise even through adventitious attributes (*upādhi*) such as secondary words (*upapada*). This is the intended meaning:
cognition, being of the nature of an effect, serves as the cause for postulating the denotative capacity in a word by postulating a cause when it cannot otherwise be accounted for.
And it was stated that the perception of the boy’s tawny color in the expression "The boy is fire" cannot be accounted for otherwise. Therefore, there is indeed denotative capacity.

Otherwise, there would be no cognition even from a word accompanied by a qualifier (*sopapada*). For that which is not expressive, both slight conventional usage (*manāk-prasiddhi*) and limited employment (*alpa-prayogatā*) are indeed difficult to establish.
However, if it is expressive, since the restriction of its usage is also beginningless, nothing is untenable.
Now, if the word *agni*—like the word *piṅgala*—denotes only the tawny boy (*māṇavaka*), how then [is the word "fire" used]?

Regarding this, he states the point of similarity: In the expression "the boy is like fire," it is appropriate that there is a similarity to fire, because we observe the use of words such as *iva* in the sense of similarity. However, the sentence-meaning of "the boy is fire" is devoid of the sense of *iva*, just as the sentence-meaning of "the boy is tawny."

Thus, the status of being a cause (nimittabhāva) is equal [in both cases]. The meaning of this is as follows: when it is said, "This boy is like fire," the similarity that is perceived is appropriate because of the hearing of the word *iva*, and because its usage is observed in the sense of similarity. However, in the case of "The boy is fire," since the word *iva* is not employed, the meaning of the sentence is devoid of the sense of *iva*; just as in the case of "The boy is tawny" (*piṅgalo māṇavakaḥ*), there is no perception of similarity.

Because the intended meaning of the sentence is devoid of the sense of "as it were" (iva), therefore the status of being a cause is equal for both that which is considered secondary (gauṇa) and primary (mukhya), by means of the expressive function (vācakavṛtti) alone. Consequently, we consider this section (adhikaraṇa) to be purposeless; for there is no difference between the secondary and the primary as to whether the application (viniyoga) occurs in the secondary sense or only in the primary sense. [Objection: Even though the tawny color (piṅgalatā) is denoted, nevertheless—

Since that [proximity] is understood through comprehension, even similarity (*sādṛśya*), being perceived, is indeed connected within the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Therefore, how can the sentence-meaning be devoid of the sense of "as" (*iva*)? Now, if similarity—even though it is invariably concomitant—does not connect with the sentence-meaning, then how is it that in the cases "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" and "the Garga family in the well," we consider that the nearby location connects with the sentence-meaning due to invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)? That is indeed appropriate there.

It is not the case that the capacity of the word "prativasati" (dwells near) is absent; rather, it is because the concomitance with "nearness" has not been understood—meaning that the concomitance of nearness is not apprehended through inseparable connection—that the capacity of the word "prativasati" does not function. However, the cognition of a tawny youth (*piṅgala-māṇavaka*) from the expression "agnir māṇavakaḥ" (the youth is fire) is by no means untenable. Therefore, even though similarity is already perceived...

It is not connected with the meaning of the sentence. Therefore, let there be *lakṣaṇā* (indication), based on the resort to another intended meaning produced by the force of the relationship. But as for *gauṇatva* (metaphorical usage), there is no evidence whatsoever. If the word "fire" denotes only tawny color (*paiṅgalya*), how then is the cognition of fire in the expression "The boy is fire" explained in common worldly usage? [For] the cognition of fire arises even from tawny color through the word "fire."
(1) Because the meaning of the sentence is empty; (2) because it is indeed inseparable; (3) because of its proximity and concomitance.

It is said that when something is presented [as being] fire, it is indeed perceived with excellence within the fire; thus, the cognition of fire is a cognition of posteriority and so forth. To this, it is replied: this cognition is based solely on the sense of "as if" (iva). Its meaning is as follows: the sense of "as if" is similarity (*sādṛśya*), and this cognition is based precisely upon that. What is meant is this: by the word "fire," fire is conveyed; that cognition [of fire] is another object consisting of similarity.

[The word] establishes [the primary meaning]. Since the cognition of another object is possible even otherwise, the postulation of a further capacity is not tenable. Therefore, that burning which is cognized from the word itself is primary (*mukhya*); however, that which is understood through similarity to the burning conveyed by the word is secondary (*gauṇa*).
But how is it understood that this cognition arises from similarity? From the cognition of such [a thing], namely, the cognition of something similar. If...

To that extent, when the tawny color is understood, the word "fire" is said to denote the tawny color. However, since there is a cognition of something similar to fire, it is postulated that the cognition of another object arises precisely from similarity.
But how is the sense of "as it were" (iva) perceived in the absence of the word *iva*? The answer is: even the word *iva*...

What is the meaning of the phrase *kimitīvārthaḥ*? Its meaning is as follows: just as similarity (*sādṛśya*) is understood when the word *iva* is employed, so too, wherever similarity is to be understood, the word *iva* expresses that very similarity which is already conveyed by the nominal stem (*pratipadika*); it does not, however, denote it independently in the same manner as the word "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) itself does. If it is argued that this is because we observe such usage—namely, that usage exists there—then [the response is as follows]. If you think that usage is found there...

[The opponent argues: "In the case of similarity, the application of the nominal stem is seen by virtue of the word *iva*. But where the word *iva* is not present as an indicator (*dyotaka*), how is the usage understood to signify similarity? He refutes this: "In this case as well, the observation of usage is the same. Because the word 'fire' (*agni*) is applied to a boy (*māṇavaka*), it is determined that its application is based on similarity; otherwise, its application to the boy would be untenable. [The opponent objects: "But surely [the word 'fire'] refers to the tawny color (*paiṅgalya*)..."

It has been stated that once [the word] ‘boy’ is understood, a resemblance to fire is apprehended, just like the word ‘other. The meaning of this is as follows: the word ‘fire’ denotes ruddiness; and when that is understood, there arises an understanding of the resemblance to fire. However, this usage is not primarily intended to convey the resemblance to fire, and thus it is not figurative (gauṇa). [The opponent] refutes this: "This is not tenable, because there would also be the cognition: 'Fire is similar to the boy.'"
(1) That [cognition] would be well-established. Once the boy Piṅgala has been cognized, there would also arise the cognition: "Fire is similar to the boy. For it is thus:

Otherwise, there would arise the cognition that "the boy is like fire" because the boy is like fire, and likewise that "fire is like the boy" because fire is like the boy; yet, as a rule, the understanding occurs only in terms of fire being similar [to the boy]. To this he says: "But here, on the contrary, it is the opposite. If it is argued that fire is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) because of its extreme redness (*piṅgalatva*), [we reply: that by which something is compared is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); [and fire is so called] because of its extreme redness.

If it is argued that fire is compared by means of that [quality] alone, and not that this [fire] is compared by means of anything else, the reply is: there is no authority for such a conception. That which possesses excellence as its quality is alone the object of comparison. Now, even so, let there be the understanding that "fire is similar to the boy"; let the word *agni* (fire) itself denote the state of being tawny (*piṅgalatā*) in that context. To this he says: for the postulation of a cause [for a word's application] follows according to how it is understood.
This is logical, because the understanding of the cause is rooted in that [understanding]. The meaning of this is as follows:

there is no postulation of a cause according to the mere whim of the proponent; rather, it is according to how it is understood, because the apprehension of the causal state is dependent upon the effect characterized by such understanding.
Therefore, even though a contrary meaning—such as "fire is like a boy"—might be possible, nevertheless...
Because it is a well-established counter-example (*prasiddha-pratipakṣa*), it does not establish itself. The established fact is that "the boy is like fire," which serves as its counter-example;

therefore, the statement "fire is like the boy" does not establish itself. For only that which is not a counter-example is a valid instance (*saṃbhava*). Indeed, being a counter-example does not follow merely from the possibility [of the comparison]; for the case of "fire is like the boy" is possible. Therefore, the application of the formal argument (*prayoga*) is established.

By means of these two [criteria], there is the designation of the secondary (gauṇa) and the primary (mukhya). Once the status of being secondary or primary is established, it is appropriate to investigate whether the application of mantras is restricted solely to the primary denotation, or whether it extends to the secondary as well. What, then, is the prima facie position? It is that there is the denotation of both, because there is no distinction between the secondary and the primary, since both are perceived from the word itself; therefore, it is logical that the mantra denotes both.
To this he says: The usage "the fire burns" is observed, as is the usage "the boy is fire. Therefore, there is no decisive criterion for determining that fire is produced from fire.

There is a reason for this. To this it is replied: this is the reason for the determination that has been demonstrated—namely, that there is no secondary designation (gauṇābhidhāna) devoid of a primary designation (mukhyābhidhāna). Therefore, the operation of the word belongs to the primary meaning alone; as for the secondary meaning, the understanding arises from the sense (artha). Let it be that the operation of the word belongs to the primary meaning alone; nevertheless, why is this so? To this he says: "And the mantras assist by means of their direct denotation."

Denotation applies to the primary sense and not to the secondary; therefore, there is no application of the mantra [to the secondary]. If the cognition of the secondary sense does not arise from the word itself, then from what does it arise? This is the meaning of the question. The answer is: "From similarity.

The meaning is that the perceived fire brings to mind its similar counterpart. The proponent of the prima facie view says: "It is true that you have stated that the understanding of the secondary sense arises from similarity."

That [the word's primary meaning] serves as the means [for application], and not by way of the exclusion of the secondary cause (nimitta). Nevertheless, the meaning is that the status of being a cause has not been excluded. Therefore, since the status of being a cause is indistinguishable in both cases, there is an application of the mantras even to the secondary sense. But the proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin) says: "By whom was it said that the status of being a cause is excluded? Since application is possible in the primary sense—which presents itself first—it does not apply to the secondary sense either."

The application (viniyoga) is appropriate in the secondary sense because the purpose is fulfilled through the recitation of the mantra for the grasper and the grasping; this much is stated. However, where application in the primary sense is not possible, there is application even in the secondary sense. If its application in the primary sense is not possible, then its application is in the secondary sense. In that case, there would be no displacement (utkarṣa) of the mantras for the consecration of Pūṣan and others from their context within the section on Pūṣan.

Because of its absence [elsewhere]. For in any other ritual dedicated to Pūṣan, since there is no general connection, application through indicative mark (*liṅga*) would be impossible. He refutes this: by means of this name (*samākhyā*), "the mantra for recitation" (*anumantraṇa-mantra*), those mantras already applied are [designated] precisely as the instrument for general recitation.

Since the relationship is established through the inferential mark (*liṅga*), application (*viniyoga*) is possible for the primary [meaning] itself even when it occurs in another context; thus, there is an "extraction" (*utkarṣa*). He concludes:

therefore, where there is comprehension of the primary [meaning], there the manifestation must be performed by the mantra alone—this is the restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the secondary [meaning].

"There is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)"—all this has been demonstrated by such [arguments] as "for what purpose does it cause the primary [meaning] to be understood? However, because of the scriptural statement, the *aindrī* verse would be used in a way that does not accord with its literal sense:
"One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the *aindrī* verse."

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the invocation of the Gārhapatya fire be performed with a mantra dedicated to Indra, or that of Indra himself? By this, the word *upasthāna* (invocation) found in the statement of the doubt has been explained. But how can there be a doubt when the accusative case-ending is clearly heard in the injunction, "He invokes the Gārhapatya"? The answer is: because the mantra [is applicable] to its primary meaning...

It has been established in the preceding section that [the word] is employed [in its primary sense]. Therefore, it is considered that the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire is not possible [with this word].

But surely, since the primary sense is impossible, it is indeed employed even in a secondary sense. We do not yet know whether such a possibility exists or not. [Objection: "One designates the *gārhapatya*..."
Thus, the Śruti itself provides the clear answer:

"The application [of a mantra] follows its inherent capacity for application. The view is that the accusative case ending occurs when the object is not intended [as the primary goal]. The meaning of this is:
whatever is capable in a particular respect is applied there as a *kāraka* (grammatical factor). This mantra is not capable of denoting the Gārhapatya fire.
r717] Since it is not fit for application in the state of a householder, the accusative case will have an unintended meaning; and thus it is recorded in the Smṛti. So it is.
And it is logical that [the mantra] expresses what is not desired [by the agent]. Furthermore, this very point is its subject matter:

by virtue of what is to be applied (*viniyojya*), that is, by virtue of the capacity of the mantra to be applied, since there is no application to the *gārhapatya* fire, this sūtra results in [the mantra] ending as a mere *kāraka* (grammatical factor). He states another solution: "Alternatively, because it approaches and denotes the *gārhapatya*, the accusative case is justified. Therefore, it is the denotation of Indra [that is intended].

And this is indeed appropriate; for [if it were otherwise], one would have to postulate a non-worldly denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) for the name "Indra. Now, it might be argued: "Even without postulating such a power, there will be a figurative denotation (*gauṇam abhidhānam*); by that means, the application (*viniyoga*) to the Gārhapatya fire is accomplished. He refutes this: "There is no figurative denotation, because figurative denotation occurs only when the usage is already established; conversely, usage does not arise from figurative denotation."

Success! Where the application of a word denoting one thing to another is established by some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there the designation is figurative (*gauṇa*). However, a figurative usage is not to be assumed merely because the word "figurative" exists. Furthermore, in this case, the application of the word "Indra" to the *gārhapatya* fire is not established by anything else; rather, this sentence—"With the *aindrī* [verse], the *gārhapatya* [is to be addressed]"—has as its purpose the instruction that the naming must be performed with this mantra, based on the teaching of what is to be done.

"One worships [the Gārhapatya fire]," it is said; however, this does not mean that the word "Indra" is intended for the Gārhapatya fire. Therefore, because the function of denotation is independent, the application [of the mantra] follows its denotation. To this, it is replied: the denotation of the Gārhapatya fire alone must be performed by the mantra. Why? Because the ritual action must follow the instruction, not the instruction following the action. The meaning of this is: the basis is the instruction.

When the ritual application (*kārya*) is understood from another source, the description of it is not an *upadeśa* (direct injunction); for that which conforms to a ritual application is indeed an *atideśa* (extended application).
The statement, "One worships the *gārhapatya* fire with the *aindrī* verse," is an *upadeśa*. Therefore, by virtue of this *upadeśa*, there is indeed the designation of the *gārhapatya* fire.

[The opponent] thinks [the injunction] is a *kārya* (task). Now, one might raise the objection that there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows, on the grounds that it was stated in the first section of the seventh book (*saptamādye*) that "the instruction is also according to the task" (*yathākāryam upadeśaḥ*). He resolves this: in that [seventh book], the word *kārya* was used in the sense of *viniyoga* (application), and not in the sense of *āpti* (attainment) and so forth; therefore, because the *kārya* [in these two senses] is different, there is no contradiction. In the first section of the seventh book, having accepted *kārya* as the meaning of *niyoga* (mandate), the instruction is shown to be in accordance with that *kārya*.

It has been stated [elsewhere]. Here, however, with reference to an action consisting of attainment (*āpti*), the action is stated according to the instruction (*upadeśa*). But surely, it is precisely the application (*viniyoga*) that is being doubted. For if the instruction itself were certain, then—on the grounds that "the action is to be performed according to the instruction"—the act of attending upon the *gārhapatya* fire would be determined as the task. Yet, the instruction is not certain. If one asks why it is not certain:

Because the accusative case is not seen even in the case of that which is not intended (*anīpsita*). The meaning is that the accusative is seen in the sense of a mere *kāraka* (participant in action). He [the opponent] objects: "What is this 'not intended'? The reply is: "And that which is thus connected is also 'not intended'. The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) says: "In that case, its predominance with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is all the more evident. For if this accusative were [governed] by the rule *tathāyuktaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.50), then [its predominance] would be all the more so with respect to the meaning of the verbal root."

In comparison [to the primary], the state of being the object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) belongs to the *gārhapatya* fire, and its status as the recipient of the fruit produced by the action is expressed by the word "primary" (*prādhānya*). Otherwise, such a connection would not even exist. In the rule *tathāyuktam cānīpsitam*, the term *tathāyukta* refers to that which is connected with the action in the same way that the desired object is connected with the action—namely, by virtue of being a recipient of the fruit of the action—even though it is undesired.

"It is appropriate that the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is used there. In this context, if the connection with the fruit characterized by the worship (*upasthāna*) of the Gārhapatya fire were not admitted, then such a connection would not exist; consequently, the second case-ending would not appear even in that sūtra. Therefore, from the observation of the second case-ending, it is understood that the Gārhapatya fire is a participant in the fruit of the action. As for what was said—that if something unintended is the primary object, then [the use of the second case] is all the more so—that is now addressed.

What is the meaning of "kastarārthaḥ"? Only this much needs to be said there: that it possesses primacy with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The answer is: even that which is not desired (*anīpsita*) is primary. Its meaning is as follows: although there is the state of being undesired, nevertheless here there is primacy; elsewhere, primacy resides in the state of being desired (*īpsitatva*).
Therefore, it is said that its predominance is even greater. Now, it was argued that the power of a word cannot be postulated if it has not been observed.

By this, he says the following: although the status of the Gārhapatya fire as the one to be approached is understood, nevertheless, because of the mantra’s lack of capacity, such an application does not succeed; thus, either there must be a change in the case-ending, or the word "upetya" (having approached) must be supplied as an ellipsis. Here, the proponent of the final view [responds]:

"What is unseen here? It is indeed seen from the verbal statement itself. When this task is understood through the statement, one acts in such a way that it is accomplished by its force. And since this is accomplished through the figurative application (*gauṇatva*) of the word 'Indra,' there is no fault of postulating an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), because it has been stated that the capacity [of the word] is observed precisely through the verbal statement by resorting to figurative application. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "Not from the statement, but from the meaning of the words..."

"Power (śakti) can be understood"—this means that if power were an established entity (*siddharūpā*), the authority of a word, whose sole object is the task to be accomplished (*kārya*), would not be tenable. [Objection: If power is not understood from the word, how then is there power for the sacrifice and so forth in the accomplishment of the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*)? [Reply: Because it is understood through the task; for [the word] denotes [the sacrifice] as connected with the injunction, which is itself of the nature of a task (*kārya*).

Sacrifices and the like are denoted as being the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Since those [means] do not belong to those who lack capacity, their capacity for that end is determined; however, in this case, it is the opposite. If there were a statement here that "it is to be understood," then the observation of an effect would occur, for understanding (*pratipatti*) is indeed an effect. And if it is understood in this way as an effect—namely, if the Gārhapatya fire is [understood] from the word "Indra"—[then the relationship is established].

The statement "it should be understood" would mean "one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Indra verse. However, this other statement, "one addresses the Gārhapatya fire with the Indra verse," expresses the function of the mantra itself, not that of the word; this is the meaning. As for what we have stated—that because the statement is intent upon the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra, it lacks the capacity to establish the function of the word, and thus no power is seen from the statement—this has now been explained.

"Because the relationship [of the word to its meaning] does not have scripture as its cause. Now, one might object: "Let there be no primary power (*śakti*) in the word; in that case, the denotation will be figurative (*gauṇa*). He refutes this: "But it has been stated that a figurative denotation occurs when the actual usage is already established. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "In this case as well, the scripture [is the authority] for the effect..."

"It is established by that; thus there is no distinction. The meaning of this is as follows: by this very fact—that this mantra is subordinate to the act of attending upon the *gārhapatya* fire—the employment of the word "Indra" with reference to the *gārhapatya* is established. Otherwise, how could the *gārhapatya* be denoted by this mantra?

Thus, by implication, there is a secondary (gauṇī) application. Now, an objection is raised: "In the Sūtra, [the phrase] 'or from a quality' (guṇād vā) indicates a secondary application; how then does the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) speak of its etymological nature (yaugikatva) through such statements as 'from the root ind, whose action is sovereignty'? To this he replies: "The mention of a quality in the Sūtra is for the sake of illustration; thinking thus, the Commentator stated 'or from derivation' (yogād vā)."

If it is argued that the invocation is likewise [to be performed with the mantra], one might ask: "How can this be the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa), since it appears that the mantra is enjoined for the invocation itself, given the rule: 'One invokes while thrice striking [the grain] with the words, "O preparer of the oblation, come"!

To this he replies: Here too, because of the statement "one invokes while striking," the meaning is that one should perform the striking with the mantra—based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of "invocation" (*āhvāna*) as "that by which one is invoked" (*āhūyate anena*). Thus, by means of this mantra, one performs the striking.

The meaning is that by performing [the action], he calls out. By this, the intended relationship between the act of threshing (*avaghāta*) and the mantra is established. Now, one might ask: "How does the mantra express the act of threshing? To this, he replies: "The designation will occur either through a secondary quality (*guṇa*) or through a connection (*yoga*). Because of her connection with that quality, the wife is called *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation), and thus the act of threshing is also so designated. Alternatively, the designation occurs through a primary function (*mukhya-vṛtti*) based on the etymological connection (*yoga*), as she is the one who "makes the oblation" (*haviḥ karoti*). Now, one might object...

Since striking with a pestle cannot be called "invoking," he explains how it can be so termed: the statement "he invokes" (*āhvayati*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*); for whoever says "come here" (*ehi*) is indeed invoking. This is the meaning of "invoking": even in the case of a conscious being, the act of the invoker consists solely in the utterance of the word "come here," whether the one being invoked perceives himself as such or not. And since the word "come here" is employed here, therefore he "invokes."

This is a restatement. If the connection between the mantra and the threshing were indeed being enjoined, how then would the word "thrice" be construed? For a thrice-repeated performance cannot be obtained unless it is itself enjoined. If it were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). The answer is: there is no fault, because it is recited in another Vedic branch (*śākhāntara*); [this refers to] the mention [of the mantra] in R. & G., while P. 755 [states] that it is not a fault, and R. mentions its inclusion.

Because it has already been established, this too is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Likewise, in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), the mantra is recited three times; for this reason as well, it is a restatement. It is replied: only "three times" is enjoined (*vidhīyate*), while everything else is restated. The meaning of this is as follows: regarding the invocation...

Furthermore, the connection with the mantra here is such that the mantra itself is obtained for the purpose of summoning by its very form; thus, it is not something to be enjoined. Likewise, in the case of "he summons while threshing," the time of threshing is already established. For it is precisely at the time of the action that the seeking of assistants occurs.

The threefold repetition of the mantra alone, which was not previously established, is here enjoined. Now, one might object: since the word "threefold" is also found in another recension (śākhā), it is already established; however, it is not established as a constant rule because there is no fixed regulation. Why is there no regulation? Because in some places this mantra is recited twice; therefore, there is no fixed rule. Consequently, the statement is for the purpose of establishing a rule, like the act of threshing (avaghāta) and so forth. He concludes: "Therefore, while threshing... and so on.

The meaning is that this is a *lakṣaṇā* (indication), in the sense that time is indicated by means of the act of threshing (*avaghāta*). Now, one might object: "But surely this very point—that there is *lakṣaṇā*—is a flaw in the position of the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*). This is not a flaw, because [the act] is already established through another source. When "three times" is enjoined, then the other word must be explained in such a way that it connects appropriately. In that context, since a connection with the word "threshing" (*avaghnan*) is impossible in its primary sense (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*), resorting to *lakṣaṇā* is not a flaw.
But surely, since the act of threshing has already commenced, the mantra would not apply; nor would the time for summoning the *haviṣkṛt* apply as a constant rule.

Therefore, that [time] too would have to be enjoined, resulting in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). He refutes this: "This is not to be objected to, because the time is obtained from another source.
For it has been stated that the search for assistants occurs precisely at the time of the task. Therefore, there is no application in a figurative sense.

There is a means of valid cognition [for this]. Therefore, the point of inquiry here is as follows: is the word "three" a partial restatement (*pākṣika-anuvāda*) due to the fear of a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding time, or should a figurative indication of time be resorted to by virtue of the force of the threefold repetition which is connected as if it were permanent? The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) says: "It is merely a partial restatement because, in one alternative, there would be a loss of the primary meaning of the word; it is not a figurative indication. The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntī*) says: "[Rather, it refers to] that which is connected as if it were permanent..."

In that case, there would result a contradiction regarding the logical connection (*anvayabādha*). Therefore, it is better to resort to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), for when that is present, there is a constant connection of all the words. Thus, the final conclusion (*rāddhāntita*) was reached by relying on the view of secondary application (*gauṇapakṣa*). However, if this mantra were intended for the act of threshing (*avaghāta*) itself...

The primary meaning [of the word] would apply, and no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would need to be assumed for the act of threshing. Furthermore, it is possible to express threshing by the word *haviṣkṛt* just as one expresses the wife; just as the wife is denoted by the etymological term *haviṣkṛt*, so too is threshing.
Therefore, since the mantra is already applicable to threshing, it is not being enjoined here; rather, only the threefold repetition will be enjoined. This is true.

It is possible [to argue as follows]: however, the invocation would result in a meaning that is not syntactically connected. The word *ehi* ("come") found within the mantra, being of the nature of an invocation, would result in an unconnected meaning. Therefore, by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*), there is no application of that [mantra] alone. Now, if the mantra for threshing (*avaghāta-mantra*) is also enjoined despite not being [otherwise] obtained, he says in response: "And 'three times' would be indefinite. Therefore, it is better to have [the application] through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone. And by that...

The gender is exclusive. Thus, the wife can be designated as "haviṣkṛt" (the preparer of the oblation) by virtue of her connection with the preparation of the oblation; and the similarity of speech [to that term] is predicated of the haviṣkṛt. And that [similarity] exists through her femininity. Furthermore, that [designation] is exclusive to the wife, because the masculine form of the word "avaghāta" (threshing) is observed [in the context].

The same applies to rising and dismissing. But surely this is merely another example; why is it being extended here? For similarity is not possible except through difference. Otherwise, it would simply be that very same thing; yet here there is this difference from the previous section: (1) P. 758 (2) G. the word "strikes" (3) G. [the reason] is inconclusive.

[Page 723] Only "three times" (trih) is enjoined here; everything else is restated. However, in this case, a connection with time must be enjoined, and since such a connection with time was not previously established, it is argued that figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate for enjoining it. Thus, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers this to be a difference from the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*). This is the meaning.

If only "three times" were enjoined, then since everything else would be merely restated (*anūdyamāna*), it would be appropriate to take the term "striking" (*avaghnann*) as a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). However, in this case, the connection with time has not been previously established and must therefore be enjoined; furthermore, it is not proper to employ secondary indication within an injunction (*vidhi*). This is the distinction from the previous section. The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*), however, stated that it is exactly the same because the lack of syntactic connection with the meaning of the *praiṣa* (directive) is equal [to the previous case]. Just as in the previous instance the meaning of the directive was not syntactically connected, so too here—

Here too, because the two acts of rising and releasing are insentient, there is no connection with the meaning of an injunction (*praiṣa*). Now, one might ask: since the primary sense is adopted in an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*), why should the meaning of an injunction not be intended in a mantra? It is said in reply: for in an injunctive sentence, all word-meanings can be connected even through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); however, in a mantra, the meaning of an injunction is in every respect unconnected, and thus its non-intentionality must be accepted.

And regarding the *sūktavāka*: in the example, "He casts the *prastara* grass-bundle with the *sūktavāka*," a doubt is established by showing the illustration as to whether the *sūktavāka* is enjoined as a means for the act of casting (*harati*), or whether it here also serves to indicate time. Because the word *sūktavāka* is heard in its primary sense in the instrumental case (*sūktavākena*), it is understood that the *sūktavāka* is enjoined as an instrument for the act of casting. And of the act of casting...
Since it denotes merely the act of striking, the *sūktavāka* does not enter into the connection as a means of accomplishment; thus, it appears that there is an indication of time (*kālalakṣaṇā*).

What, then, is correct? Just as in the case of "The *agnīdh* should carry forward the fires," because the mantra serves another purpose, there is no application of the mantra at the moment of rising—since the mantra is for the sake of a command (*praiṣa*)—so too, because the *sūktavāka* reveals the deities and there is no connection of a deity with the act of striking, [it cannot be applied there].

The application is appropriate. Furthermore, there is this other distinction: whereas in that case, by the [injunction] "O Agnīdh, spread the fires," the act of rising can be expressed through the etymological derivation of the word *agnīdh* as "one who kindles the fire" (*agni-indhe*), such that the act of rising can be expressed by the term *agnīdh*, it is not so [in the present case].
(1) Jha. 759 (2) G. āhān (3) G. The meaning is that it is intended to be expressed; therefore, intention (*vivakṣā*) is not to be relied upon. (4) G. *haraṇe* [p. r724]

The *sūktavāka* can be designated as a means for the act of offering (*harati*) in some manner or other. Therefore, since it is possible to understand it as an injunction regarding time, it cannot be assumed to be a purposeful ritual act (*arthakarma*). If the *sūktavāka* were enjoined as a means for the act of offering, then—given that the *sūktavāka* reveals the deity and that there would be no syntactic connection between the deity and the act of offering—the act of offering would have to be accepted as being of the nature of a sacrifice (*yāga*).

Consequently, there is a purposeful action (*arthakarmatā*). And since comprehension is possible, the action is not merely a conceptual construction, nor is it a mere instruction. To this, it is replied: this is not a definition of time; rather, this is an instruction regarding a mantra. This is the underlying intention: by the word *sūktavāka*, a specific mantra is denoted directly through primary denotation (*śruti*); whereas time is indicated only figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*). And it is not...

Since a direct denotation (*śruti*) is possible, it is more logical to adopt an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, the mantra itself is enjoined as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Now, it was argued that the mantra serves another purpose and does not denote the act of "taking away" (*harati*). Let it not be the expresser of the act of taking away; it will nonetheless be the expresser of the deity associated with taking away. Even though this mantra cannot directly denote the act of taking away, nevertheless, by means of manifesting the deity who is the instrument of that act— [it serves its purpose].

It will serve as the instrument for the act of taking away (*haraṇa*). But surely this [mantra] denotes the deities of sacrifices already completed; those sacrifices which have been performed—their very deities it expresses through the mantra. Therefore, how can the root *harati* (to take), which denotes an instrument belonging to something else, become expressive of a deity? Furthermore, *harati* is not the same as *yajati* (to sacrifice); "taking" (*haraṇa*) is said to be merely the act of depositing, not the sacrifice itself. And in what is not a sacrifice, a deity cannot be the instrumental means.

Therefore, manifestation is not possible even by way of a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). It is replied: Even if it is a word denoting the deity of the completed sacrifice, the sacrifice will serve as its consecration (*saṃskāra*), just like the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). Just as the animal-cake is for the purpose of recollecting Agni and Soma, so too this sacrifice, because the deity is already established through the previous sacrifice, will be for the purpose of recollecting the deity.
But has it not been stated that this is the root *harati* (to take) and not *yajati* (to sacrifice)? Therefore, since it is not a sacrifice, it cannot have the purpose of consecrating a deity.
He replies: *Harati* is indeed *yajati*, because of its connection with a mantra. For instance, the mantra is enjoined for the act of taking by a clear scriptural statement.
Thus it is understood that, by this reasoning, *harati* itself will become *yajati*. But [an objection is raised]: if this were so, the same figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would result;

and because that [indication] has been observed, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) must be abandoned, since *yajati* would have to be brought to mind through figurative indication by means of the word *harati*, which merely expresses the act of pouring in. [The author] replies: "There is no figurative indication, because when the sacrifice exists, the meaning of *harati* is already established," just as in the case of [the injunction] "one should touch" (*ālabheta*). The meaning of this is as follows: not...

The root *harati* (to offer) indicates the sacrifice; however, this meaning of "offering" is merely restated as something already established when a sacrifice exists, just as the act of "slaying" (*ālabhbha*) is restated in the injunction, "One should slay the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma. But one might object: that case is appropriate because a sacrifice is inferred there through the connection between the material and the deity. Here, however, there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the presentation of a sacrifice. It is replied: [there is such a means] in the statement, "He offers the grass-bundle (*prastara*) with the *sūktavāka*."
The relationship between the *sūktavāka* and the act of carrying (*haraṇa*) is understood; and that relationship is what is enjoined here. Consequently, the meaning established is this:

one should strive in such a way that the relationship between the *sūktavāka* and the carrying is brought about. In that context, when the sacrifice consisting of the oblation (*homa*) is being performed by means of the *sūktavāka* through the medium of manifesting the deities, there exists between the *sūktavāka* and the carrying a relationship characterized as that of action and instrument (*kriyā-kāraka*).

The connection [is as follows]: Even when a sacrifice consisting of an oblation (*homa*) is being performed, the act of throwing [the material] into the fire (*prakṣepa*) serves as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Furthermore, since a sacrifice consisting of an oblation can be performed by means of a mantra while designating a deity, there exists a relationship of the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) through a mediated succession. Therefore, just as a sacrifice is obtained by implication through the injunction of the connection between the substance and the deity, so too here a sacrifice is obtained through the injunction of the connection with the employment of the mantra. By that very [means], in this case—

The formulation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): Since it is untenable for the *sūktavāka* to be the means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) in the act of taking away (*haraṇa*), the sacrifice consisting of the oblation (*homātmaka-yāga*) must be indicated (*lakṣayitavya*) by the act of throwing (*praharaṇa*). However, that is not proper, because it would entail the fault of indicating (*lakṣaṇā*) the primary meaning of the verbal root (*ākhyātārtha*). It would be better if only the time were indicated by the *sūktavāka*; such is the prima facie view. The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that the sacrifice need not be indicated by the act of taking away, since [the connection] is established through the injunction itself.

Let it be assumed that sacrifice (*yāga*) consists of the oblation (*homa*); for if this is so, all words will indeed possess their Vedic (*śrauta*) meanings. And in this context, when it is said that the act of sacrificing (*yajati*) itself consists of the act of taking away (*harati*), this should be understood as a figurative usage (*upacāra*). For "taking away" is indeed "deposition" (*prakṣepa*), yet sacrifice is not essentially of the nature of deposition. In reality, however, within the sacrifice consisting of an oblation, the term "takes away" functions as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and is thus implied by the sense. And so:
If [the sacrifice] exists, the mantra—"This oblation has been enjoyed, they have increased [the life-span]; this sacrificer desires long life"—will have its meaning established.

Otherwise, that which has already occurred (*vṛtta*) would have to be indicated by the present tense (*āna*). For according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the oblation that has already occurred is what must be celebrated by the *sūktavāka*.

In that case, the use of the word *idam* (this), which denotes something present, would not be appropriate. However, according to the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), since the oblation called the *prastara* is being referred to as currently existing, the indication by *idam* is logical. Furthermore, the expression "he desires" (*āśāste*) is a reference to what has already occurred (*bhūta-nirdeśa*) under the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), whereas [under the conclusion] it refers to the *sūktavāka* as part of another ritual action.

Because of the connection, the benediction (*āśis*) is said to pertain only to the action already performed; in that case, a reference to the present tense would not be appropriate. In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, the benediction pertaining to another action is expressed precisely by means of the present tense, so nothing is inappropriate. He concludes: "Therefore, it is well and beautifully said that 'to sacrifice' (*yajati*) is 'to take away' (*harati*). And this should be understood as the figurative discourse (*upacāra-vāda*) of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*).

Regarding what was stated—that when a disposal (*pratipatti*) is possible, it is not right to perform a purposeful ritual act (*arthakarma*)—the author of the *Bhāṣya* replied that there will be no contradiction, just as in the case of the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering. Just as in the *Sviṣṭakṛt*, the substance is disposed of and the deities are remembered as being worshipped, so too here the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is disposed of and the deities are remembered as being worshipped; thus, even while the sacrifice is taking place, there is no contradiction in the phrase "the *prastara*."
And because the second [offering] and the instrument [of the offering] have the object to be offered as their primary element;
for there is an instruction regarding the whole. It has been established, based on the scriptural statement, that the root *hṛ* (to take) is the sacrifice and that the *sūktavāka* is the mantra.
Now this is being considered: is there an application of the entire *sūktavāka* at both the full moon and the new moon sacrifices?

"Or rather, [it is] by the division of the words denoting deities. By this, he states the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) and restates the doubt in order to raise an objection on the grounds that there is no prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). For only when the application of the *sūktavāka* to the act of striking (*praharaṇa*) is established by means of the sentence can there be a suspicion of a prima facie position; otherwise, it would not. He states the objection: "But surely this inquiry is not tenable, for it has been established that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) due to the unity of purpose (*arthakatva*); and here, the primary [element]..."

In this case, since the words denoting deities are recited in close conjunction (*praśliṣṭapaṭhita*), neither syntactic unity (*ekatva*) nor the state of having an expectancy when separated (*vibhajyamānasākāṅkṣatva*) is possible.

Therefore, these sentences are distinct; and when there is a singular-number designation for distinct [entities], how can the performance of the whole be suspected? The meaning of this is as follows: it has been stated that those mantras recited in close conjunction constitute a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) because they have a single meaning and are syntactically expectant (*sākāṅkṣatva*) when divided. However, in this case, there is neither a single meaning for the words denoting the principal deities, nor is there syntactic expectancy upon division.

Therefore, these sentences are indeed distinct. When sentences are distinct, a word ending in the singular number effects the application of only one sentence, not of all of them, because that would contradict the singular number; just as by the word *paśunā* (with an animal), only one animal is taken. Consequently, the suspicion that the entire mantra is to be employed is untenable. This is just as in the case of the injunction *āgneyyā āgnīdhram upatiṣṭhate* (he worships the Āgnīdhra fire-altar with an Āgneyī verse); when "Āgneyī" is stated there, it does not refer to the whole [Ṛgveda].

The doubt arises that the verses dedicated to Agni (*āgneyyaḥ*) should be employed [in both rites]. Furthermore, it is an established principle that when a primary sense is possible, there is no application in a secondary sense.

If the entire mantra were to be applied in both places, then the words denoting both deities would have to bear a secondary meaning in both instances. Moreover, once a mantra has fulfilled its purpose through application in the primary sense alone, there is no further application in a secondary sense.

This has also been established in the *Gauṇa-mukhya-adhikaraṇa*. Therefore, it is proper that the application (*viniyoga*) be made only after distinguishing [the primary from the secondary]. It is replied: as you have said, however, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains this. He holds that the word "sūktavāka" occurs in the singular number (*ekavacana*) with reference to a collection of sentences (*vākya-samūha*).
Likewise here, in the expression "by the sūktavāka," this singular number refers precisely to the collection. Consequently, it is the collection itself that is intended here.

The instrument (*karaṇa*). Its meaning is as follows: while the *sūktavāka* is being recited—that is, while the entire mantra is being recited—there is indeed a common designation among students, teachers, and listeners in the world. And that [designation] is intended with reference to the mantra as a single, indivisible sentence; otherwise, there would be the contingency of using the plural number. Therefore, because we observe the use of the singular number, we understand that the word *sūktavāka* refers to the collection [of mantras] itself. And thus...
In the case of the injunction "He casts the *prastara* grass-bundle with the *sūktavāka*," since the entire collection is enjoined here as well, the whole must be employed in both instances.

But surely, it is not possible for a collection to have a single referent; the meaning is that words denoting distinct deities cannot possess a single referent. He provides the rebuttal: "It is postulated on the basis of scriptural statement, as in the case of the final *prayāja* offering. This section is intended to dispel the following doubt: "Just as words denoting deities possess a single unified meaning, so too here [in the case of the *sūktavāka*], such unity may be assumed on the basis of the scriptural statement. There is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the application of the *sūktavāka* as a collective whole. Why? Because the use of the singular number in the expression "the *sūktavāka* exists" is justifiable even otherwise. This is the meaning.

The word *sūktavāka* refers to a single sentence, because it is said that "by this [sentence] a hymn (*sūkta*) is spoken"; for it is by means of a sentence that a hymn is expressed, not by a collection of sentences.
Therefore, the *sūktavāka* is indeed a single sentence. These sentences are distinct; consequently, because of the hearing of the singular number, there is no application of the entire collection.
How then is the expression "the *sūktavāka* occurs" justified? It is justified because the singular number applies to the whole as a unified unit.

For since the reciters designate it with a single name, it is appropriate to call it a *sūktavāka*; indeed, all of them speak of it as one single hymn (*sūkta*). Therefore, because of that unity, by relying on its nature as a single functional whole, the use of the singular number even when referring to many [parts] is not contradictory—just as the use of the singular number in "word" (*pada*) or "sentence" (*vākya*), which is based on a single function despite consisting of many syllables or words.

Furthermore, in this case, regarding the statement "one casts the prastara-bundle with the *sūktavāka*," it is not possible to assume syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) by overriding the indicative power (*liṅga*), because the application [of the mantra] is already established through that indicative power. For if one were to maintain that this single sentence is applied to the casting of the prastara-bundle, then one would have to assume a single meaning for words expressing different deities by overriding their respective inherent capacities (*svasāmarthya*). And that is untenable.

Since application is possible even according to the gender [of the deity], therefore, because no distinction is apprehended through the utterance of the *sūktavāka* for all [deities], the act is accomplished by whichever *sūktavāka* is used when the throwing is performed; as it is said: "One throws the *prastara* with the *sūktavāka*. Thus—

[This concerns] the performance [of the ritual] as impelled [by the injunction]. This is the meaning.

Because of indicative mark (*liṅga*), order (*krama*), and name (*samākhyāna*). Consequently, the application of the mantra extends as far as the ritual action dedicated to Indra-Agni (*aindrāgna-karma*). But is it not the case that *liṅga* alone is never the sole applicator?

This will be explained in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): for if *liṅga* (indicative power) were the sole factor that enjoins [a ritual application], then it would enjoin [an element] everywhere, independent of both *krama* (order) and *samākhyā* (name). r730] Furthermore, the consideration of their relative strength (*balābala*) has not yet been stated, nor has it been explained how they function as applicators (*viniyojaka*). Therefore, it is not appropriate to commence this section (*adhikaraṇa*) at this time.

To this it is replied: This is not at all a consideration of relative strength. If it were a consideration of relative strength, then the aforementioned defect would indeed apply. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) must be that "indicative power" (*liṅga*) is the means of application; however, this prima facie view is not tenable, because it is impossible for mere capacity alone to function as the means of application. In the *Balābala-sūtra*, regarding the passage "In the case of a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*)...", this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises from a confusion caused by the sequential order [of the terms]. Because they are enumerated as being of equal status, someone might have this doubt: that an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is independent, just like a direct statement (*śruti*) and the others.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: when a general connection—of the form "this mantra should be used for this [rite]"—has been determined by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the indicative power (*liṅga*) serves as the factor that specifically assigns [the mantra] to a particular subsidiary (*śeṣin*). And just as indicative power is not the sole factor that effects such assignment, so too...

We shall explain this more thoroughly in the section on *śruti-liṅga*. And the author of the treatise, acting as a commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), says: "Since indicative power (*liṅga*) is dependent [on other factors] for its application, it is therefore applied in conjunction with order (*krama*) and in conjunction with name (*samākhyā*).
Now, one might object: even from name alone, the present example is established. For instance, the optional *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses—

[Objection: There is the application of the first-read pair to the ritual action. [Reply: This is not so. An-...
By this same logic, there is no application of the second [verse] to the second [rite]. Likewise, this meaning is obtained from the sequence of the indicative power (*liṅga*);

for when there is a connection by sequence, the application to the function of the *yājyā* is established through the indicative power. Nor should one suspect an application to the function of the *sāmidhenī*s, because these verses are dedicated to Indra-Agni (*aindrāgna*), whereas the *sāmidhenī*s are dedicated to Agni (*āgneya*). Therefore, for what purpose is the sequence of the indicative power [invoked]?

Regarding the phrase "from the name" (*samākhyānāt*): one might object that since both "from the indicative mark and order" (*liṅgakramāt*) and "from the name" (*samākhyānāt*) have been stated together, it would have been sufficient to state only one; anticipating this doubt, he says: "The purpose of combining both means of proof has been stated in the Bhāṣya. For example, if only 'from the indicative mark and order' were stated, then [the mantra] would apply to the *sāmidhenī* function of the pair belonging to the *āgneya* [offering] even in the *pāthikṛtīya* rite."

"There would be an application [of the mantra]. For instance, that pair [of mantras], being sufficient for the function of the *yājyā* in the *pāthikṛtīya* rite dedicated to the deity Agni, might also be used for the function of the *sāmidhenī* verses; however, since the *sāmidhenīs* must belong to Agni, it must be stated that "the application should be only to the function of the *yājyā*" because of the name (*samākhyāna*). But if this is so, then let that alone be the case; what is the use of the phrase "because of indicative power and order" (*liṅgakramāt*)?

It is said: By the designation "the section of optional *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses," there would be an application [of those verses] to the function of the *yājyā*. However, once the function of the *yājyā* has been fulfilled, their application to the function of the *sāmidhenī* verses is established through indicative power (*liṅga*) and sequence (*krama*). Since the designation is to be respected merely as the cause for the connection with the optional sacrifice, it is settled that wherever the designation conforms to the indicative power and the sequence, [that is the case].

By virtue of that [indication], the application according to gender and order is possible. However, where the name (samākhyā) contradicts the application by indication and order, it is described as being concerned merely with a general relationship by virtue of that [name].
And regarding the context (adhikāra), the Bhāṣya here says: "Is one to worship with those [verses] mentioned in the context which possess the [required] indicative marks, or..."

Or rather, those mantras with such indicative marks (*liṅga*) should be brought from the *Daśatayī* collection itself. In that case, the mention of the *Daśatayī* is not for the purpose of abandoning the subject at hand;
[this is so] because of the absence of a *yājyā* verse.

However, thinking that [the opponent] intends to include [all verses] because they are subject to misconception, [the author], raising a doubt, says: "In cases such as 'one worships the Āgnīdhra altar with an Āgneyī verse,' regarding these indications by gender (liṅga), should all verses possessing that gender be taken, or should only those belonging to the context (prakṛta) be taken?

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), considering that the capacity to denote the contextual [verses] for what is being enjoined is not possible, [advocates] the inclusion of all verses possessing that gender.

He says: "What, then, is the reasoning [behind] the claim that the capacity to express the subject matter (*prakṛta*) is not possible for that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*)? To this he replies: For the term denoting the subject (*uddeśyapada*) depends upon what is already under discussion (*prakṛta*), but it does not likewise serve to present the meaning of the thing to be enjoined. Why is this? Because being a subject (*uddeśyatva*) consists in having a purposeful meaning (*prayojanavadarthatā*). That which possesses a purpose is a "purposeful meaning" (*prayojanavān arthaḥ*); the state of being such is its "nature" (*tattā*), which is its purposiveness.

The meaning is that a specific instance (*viśeṣa*) is what becomes the intended object (*uddeśya*). Nor does a universal (*sāmānya*) possess purposefulness; for example, the universal "rice" and so forth do not possess purposefulness because purposefulness has as its object only that which is specifically apprehended.

Only that specific instance which is apprehended is the object of purposefulness; the meaning is that only it possesses purposefulness. [Objection: Let it be so; nevertheless, the universal itself must indeed possess purposefulness.

Because of its specific application (*viniyoga*), and because that which has been applied is what is taken up (*upādāna*). Thus he says: "But surely it is the universal (*sāmānya*) alone that is taken up. He refutes this: "The taking up of the unlimited (*aparimita*) is not possible. For the universal is unlimited; and an unlimited object cannot be taken up. Therefore, it is by way of definition (*lakṣaṇatayā*) alone that the universal is employed there [to indicate] the particular (*viśeṣa*) that has been taken up."

In that context, when there is an application [of a term] where something is intended to be designated (*uddeśya*), it is a universal (*sāmānya*) by its very nature as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatayā*). As stated in the *Grahādhikaraṇa*, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), moreover, is understood from the word itself as being accompanied by a measure and number, because it is not understood from any other source; [this applies] only to that which is [already] mentioned as "belonging to Agni" (*āgneyī*), and not to anything additional.
There is no contradiction whatsoever in its application as well. Therefore, why should a word expressing a general meaning be restricted to a specific instance?
Consequently, all mantra-sets that possess the indicative mark (*liṅga*), whether relevant to the context or not, are to be enjoined. How then is it that the Commentator...

"One should bring [verses] from the *Daśatayīs*," he says. But surely it should be stated exactly as follows: "as many as possess the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that is to be enjoined. To this he replies:
Is one to worship with those verses currently under discussion which possess the indicative mark, or should one bring from the *Daśatayīs* those verses that likewise possess such a mark?

The mention of the *Daśatayīs* is not intended as an alternative to the current topic. The mention of the *Daśatayīs* is not for the purpose of abandoning the current topic, but rather—[to address] the contradiction—...

Because they have been so declared, that very point has been stated. This is what is meant in the Bhāṣya: "Is it that all those possessing the [required] characteristic (*liṅga*) are to be taken, or only those under discussion that possess such characteristics? Here, the Bhāṣya says: "For the instruction of what is of this kind, once already instructed, is not logical.
That is incorrect; for the *ṛc* verses are instructed there in various places, and when there is a difference in the injunctions of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*), how can it be illogical?
With this intention, he asks: "Is it not improper that what has already been taught should be taught again? The answer is:

"Indeed, its distinction lies precisely in the fact that it is taught as 'this' and 'that'; moreover, it has been stated that such [repetition] is not a constituent part of the injunction. The meaning of this is as follows:

by one who maintains that there is an application (*viniyoga*) only of those things already under discussion, it must be said that they are enjoined as qualified by the teaching (*upadeśa*). If, by means of the teaching...

When specific [details] are enjoined, then the state of being the subject matter (*prakṛtatā*) is obtained. Moreover, this instruction is not a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that which is to be enjoined; it has been stated that this instruction does not exist to indicate the thing to be enjoined, but rather to enjoin it itself. Regarding the fact that the state of being the subject matter is equal due to being expressed (*abhidhāna*), he says: "Furthermore, the state of being the subject matter is equal because of being expressed. On this point, the Bhāṣya states: "When there is a conflict, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*)."

r734] Nor is it the case that there is no contradiction between these two; for that [assertion] is untenable, since a contradiction indeed exists here: for by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is an application (*viniyoga*) even of those things not under discussion.

It occurs to [the opponent]: "But by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), their application (*viniyoga*) is not possible. With this intention, he asks: "What is the underlying motive? Since the meaning of the *liṅga* (the gender marker) is indeed supported, there is no contradiction. therefore, there is a contradiction. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "It is said: 'By this, the possession of gender [is indicated],' and so forth.
That is untenable. It is not...
