This is a fault.
The Bhāṣya states, "Furthermore, in the case of the manifestation of the mantra in the *Dāśatayī*," and so forth. That appears to be untenable because:

Anticipating the objection that even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), when a specific mantra instance from the *Daśataya* collection is adopted, the cognition of the mantra under discussion is not at all sublated—since the prima facie position is established on the grounds that all instances possessing those indicative marks (*liṅga*) are to be taken—the author explains: "But in the case of a mantra instance from the *Daśataya*... He considers that once the meaning indicated by the mark (*liṅga*) has been fully realized in the very mantra under discussion, there is no evidence for sublation of that which is under discussion. It appears so. In that case, if even a mantra-form occurring in the *Daśatayī* were to be accepted, the understanding that "only the mantra-form under discussion should be accepted" would be contradicted; and such a contradiction would be without any basis in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). He raises this objection: "If the meaning of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is fully realized, what is this 'falsity'?

If the meaning of the indicative mark were abandoned, then there would be falsity in the cognition produced by that indicative mark; however, when the subject at hand is grasped, the meaning of the indicative mark is indeed fully realized.

He provides the resolution: "The intention is this: this word is not for the purpose of a general application, as in the case of [the injunction] 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice' (*svargakāmo yajeta*)."
It can be said that the purpose of the treatise is concluded even though other applications remain possible. The meaning of this is as follows:

this word *āgneyī* is not intended for a general application—that is, it does not mean "let the general property of possessing the [Agni] mark be applied here. What then? Its purpose is rather this: "let there be an application of that specific mantra-individual which possesses such a mark."

Furthermore, just as the scriptural meaning of "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (svargakāmo yajeta)—though it is applicable to the performance by other persons—is not said to be exhausted merely because it has been indicated by someone [specific], since it must pervade all who desire heaven; so too this [indication] must pervade all mantras containing the indicative mark (liṅga). "The falsity of the object of the mantra's application. Thus, a general summary has been presented. The meaning is that, by virtue of the context, the general [principle] is summarized specifically within the mantra under discussion. "This very [point]" refers to the Bhāṣya.
Its meaning is as follows: "The state of possessing an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not the primary meaning of a word. He establishes this as follows:

"We do not understand this very point," [they say], because in the case of words ending in *taddhita* suffixes, the meaning of the derivative suffix (*pratyaya*) is primary; thus, that which possesses the suffix (*tadvat*) is not the subordinate member (*aṅga*).

It is considered thus: under the governing rule *sāsya devatā* ("that is its deity"), the secondary suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *agnerḍhaka*. Furthermore, it does not possess the capacity to express a different meaning. And since the application of its verbal meaning has been understood, and the mantra is that meaning, therefore the mantra is the subordinate factor (*aṅga*), not the possession of that quality. Consequently, this scriptural injunction—"One should worship the Āgnīdhra fire-altar with an *āgneyī* [verse]"—is neither for the purpose of bringing back what was previously mentioned, nor for the purpose of applying what was previously mentioned. [Objection: "But was it not said that there is another function?"

The commentary beginning with "the instruction of what has already been introduced" appears redundant, since this same point has already been stated previously. If it is argued that it is presented here in order to resolve even what was previously stated, that is not so, because no resolution is seen. If it is further argued that a resolution has been provided by the passage beginning with "it is stated immediately thereafter," that is also not the case; for the objection regarding the instruction of what has already been instructed is not resolved merely by the mention of the term "possessing the characteristic" (*liṅgin*).

It follows [that the statement is] purposeless. Having raised this objection, he says: "But has this not already been stated? Since that which is under discussion is taught for another purpose, it will not be taught for a different purpose. This presentation is intended to avoid the charge of teaching what has already been taught. Thinking that there is no resolution because no resolution has been given, he asks: "Why? It has been shown that this is because only that which possesses the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) is grasped. The meaning of this is as follows:

The Bhāṣya demonstrates that this is an avoidance of the charge of "teaching what has already been taught" (upadiṣṭopadeśa) because of the inclusion of mantras characterized by their indicative marks (liṅga). But how is it avoided?

To this he says: "In this case, being 'already taught' is not the reason. For if being "already taught" were the reason for the inclusion of a mantra, then the application (viniyoga) would have to be stated in the very form in which it was already taught; and that is not logical, due to the contradiction between what has already been applied and what is being applied again.

Furthermore, when the application [of a mantra] occurs through an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that does not depend on anything subsequent to the instructional context (*upadeśa*), then nothing is faulty.

Now, one might object: "In that case, there would be a sublation of the primary context (*prakṛtabādha*); since the primary elements themselves must be accepted by the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), this very understanding would be sublated.

The reply is: let there be a sublation of the primary context because of the explicit statement; it is no fault. Even though there is a sublation of the primary context by the force of the direct Vedic text (*śruti*), it is still not a fault.
Furthermore, neither the indicative mark nor the context should be favored.

Such is the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Its meaning is as follows: the performance [of the mantra] is not for the sake of favoring the context (*prakaraṇa*); rather, because the subject under discussion possesses a fruit, and all individual instances of the mantra become fruitful through their application (*viniyoga*), there is the inclusion of all of them. He explains the meaning of this commentary: "Moreover, neither indicative power (*liṅga*) nor context (*prakaraṇa*)..."

As for what was stated—that the summary of the meaning of the treatise is not for the sake of favoring [others] because they are not to be favored—this is incorrect, since there is no summary of the treatise anywhere for the sake of favoring [others], as in the case of those who desire heaven (*svargakāma*) and so forth;

or rather, it is designated by that [name] due to both the context (*prakaraṇa*) and logical consistency (*upapatti*). To this, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) replies: even in the present case, [the person] is indeed the object of the injunction.

Thinking that the cognition—the cognition of application—is by no means impossible, but rather certainly possible, he stated that there must be the inclusion of the very subject under discussion. The meaning of this is as follows: if the cognition of the thing to be enjoined regarding the subject matter were not possible due to the contradiction between what has already been applied and what is being applied, then, for the sake of avoiding the sublation caused by such an application of what has already been applied, the mantra would be applied by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*). However, since...

Even when [the word] is employed in its primary sense (*prakṛta*), the suffix denoting the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is consistent; therefore, since there is no evidence for abandoning the primary sense, only the primary sense is to be accepted. Now, one might object: "If it is an instruction (*upadeśa*) by virtue of being taught, then only the primary sense is grasped. And if it is an instruction by virtue of being taught, the fault of the contradiction between what has already been employed and what is being employed (*viniyuktaviniyoga-virodha*) is unavoidable. With this intention, he asks: "How? (katham).

The reply is as follows: For being the object of a purpose belongs only to that which possesses a purpose. Where there is the status of being the object, there the thing is grasped precisely in the form in which it has been taught. But here, because it is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), its connection with another function does not assist [the primary injunction]. Therefore, since it is adopted in a form independent of its application to another function, there is no contradiction between what has already been applied and what is being applied, even in the case of those things already under discussion. Thus he says:

r738] — Furthermore, the fact that something is the subject under discussion (*prakṛtatva*) does not at all obstruct the application of the suffix denoting the subject (*prakṛtapratyaya*) even to that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Regarding the [section on] Indicative Power (liṅga), Order (krama), and Name (samākhyā): this is now considered—just as Indicative Power was concluded by virtue of being the subject at hand, does Name also conclude its application based solely on its own cause, or is there an application according to Indicative Power?

The designation (*samākhyā*) restricts the indicative mark (*liṅga*), and thus the entire [formula] is enjoined for the act of eating alone. The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) view here follows the very same reasoning as the previous section. Even though the indicative power (*liṅga*) brings about a connection with eating, it is set aside by the name (*samākhyā*). Thus it is established that because they form a single syntactical unit with the act of eating, they constitute a single mantra.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is not so, because there is no drawing out (*agrahaṇa*). For it is by the act of drawing out that the connection of the substance with a deity is effected.

Because it possesses the quality [of being a Veda], the word *ṛk* is indeed a restatement of the Veda; it denotes the Veda through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The meaning of this is as follows: for you, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), who maintain that the word *ṛk* occurring in the conclusion is explained through secondary indication by virtue of the opening statement, this intention is inferred: namely, that this word "Veda" does not apply to the *ṛc*s. And this is untenable; for how could the word "Veda" not apply to the *ṛc*s?

As long as it functions, it indeed continues to function; therefore, because there is no contradiction, the word "Veda" will apply specifically to the *Ṛg* [mantras]. The answer is: "By whom is it said that it is not so? However, it is not so by way of being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), unlike the enjoining [text] (*vidhāyaka*). The meaning of this is as follows: this word "Veda" is etymological (*yaugika*), derived from "it causes one to know" (*vedayati*). In that regard, the status of being a Veda belongs independently to the enjoining sentence, whereas for the collection of mantras to be enjoined, their status as Veda depends upon their application (*viniyoga*) to a purpose.

The status of being an instrument of illumination is not the same for the word "Veda" when it functions dependently versus independently, as is the case with the injunction (*vidhi*) and the mantra-injunction (*mantra-vidhi*). Therefore, by the word "Veda" occurring in the opening [passage], the injunction itself is expressed in its independent sense. Consequently, because the word *ṛk* must be consistent with the word "Veda"—which denotes an injunction in the opening passage—the word *ṛk* also refers exclusively to the injunction; thus, this is a characteristic of the injunction governing eligibility (*adhikāra-vidhi*). And this word *ṛk* is indeed observed [to be used in such a sense].
"In the Veda, [it is said]: 'O God, you move through the sky at dawn with the Ṛks. By this, he shows that this figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) is not entirely unknown.
Why is this so? Because the words "Ṛk" and so forth appear in the Veda; specifically, in the Yajurveda, [the phrase] "standing in the midst of the day" occurs by way of association (*sahayoga*).
(1) G. [This is] distinct.

The meaning is that this word *ṛk* refers exclusively to the Veda. Furthermore, the instruction regarding the *sāmans*—specifically the instruction that a *sāman* is to be chanted loudly—is only thus justified; otherwise, if one were to hold the position that the properties belong to the *mantras*, then because of the injunction for the *ṛc*, the word *ṛk* would [by extension] imply loudness.

A separate injunction would be purposeless because [the application] is already established by the general injunction. Furthermore, an injunction for the *prajāpati-hṛdaya* and other *sāmans* that do not depend on Ṛg-verses would not be meaningful in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, as they are absent there. For if the view is that these are properties of the mantras, their placement would necessarily be within the Jyotiṣṭoma itself; yet it is impossible for the *prajāpati-hṛdaya* and the others to exist therein.

And the term *trayīvidyā* refers to one who knows that. The word *trayīvidya* applies to one who knows that—that is, to one who knows the three Vedas. What follows from this? This follows: since the use of the words *Ṛk* and so forth is observed in the Veda, he who knows the three Vedas is called *trayīvidya*; and the word *Ṛk* and so forth is applied to the *Trayī*, as in "the three are the *Ṛk*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*. Therefore—

The word *dṛk* and so forth is observed in the Veda. As for the objection that there is a fault because a different accent would result for what is enjoined as stated in another Veda—the meaning is that there is no fault, because the option (*vikalpa*) arrived at by the force of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) does not constitute a defect. Furthermore, the sublation of context (*prakaraṇa*) by syntactical connection (*vākya*) and so forth is indeed accepted. Therefore, having sublated the status of being an auxiliary to the Jyotiṣṭoma—which arises from the consideration of context—by means of syntactical connection, [the injunction applies] to all...

Regarding the phrase "being a subsidiary part of the ritual" (*kratvaṅgatā*): what, then, is the reason that even when there is a connection with the Veda, the *prakaraṇa* (context) is not taken into account, as is the case in the injunction of the properties of the *ṛc*? One might ask: "Just as there is an acceptance of the *prakaraṇa* in the injunction of the properties of the *ṛc*, why should it not be the same here? It is replied: Because the *ṛcs* are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), it is logical that their property is grasped by the *prakaraṇa*. For it is logical that a property resting upon a subsidiary part is grasped by the governing injunction (*adhikāravidhi*).

Furthermore, when it pertains to the nature of the Veda (*vedadharman*), the re-enactment (*punarvidhāna*) is merely indicative; since it is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that [re-enactment], the injunction of dharma (*dharmavidhi*) extends as far as the re-enactment itself.

In the view that *dharma* consists of the injunctions regarding eligibility (*adhikāravidhi*) whose objects of knowledge are the Vedas, the injunction of eligibility is merely an indirect indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), because a connection with *dharma* is impossible therein. Rather, *dharma* resides in the connections among its constituent parts (*aṅga*). And since the injunction of eligibility is not itself a constituent part, the connection with *dharma* extends only as far as the injunction of eligibility.
This is according to the principle of "the displacement of the subordinate by the principal" (*guṇamukhyavyatikrama*): "He who, knowing thus, establishes the sacred fires."
Thus, the rule belonging to the Yajurveda— “He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāravantīya”—
is considered as if it were a rule belonging to the Sāmaveda within the context of the fire-consecration (ādhāna), by way of a hypothetical deliberation (kṛtvācintyate).
This is a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*) based on the premise that the Sāmavedic [element] is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the Yajurvedic primary (*pradhāna*). What is being considered here?

It might be argued that let there be whispering (*upāṃśutva*) for the Yajurvedic primary and loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*) for the Sāmavedic subsidiary; and even if they belong to different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇatva*), there would be no contradiction between whispering and loudness.

To this, the resolution is: it is indeed true that if the injunctions for the subsidiary and the primary were distinct, then, due to the difference in injunctions, the rule regarding the property (*dharma*) would be dependent upon that distinction.

It may be that there is a difference [between the two Vedic texts]; however, as will be stated later regarding the principle that "that which is without fruit when in proximity to something with fruit is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of it," a doubt arises because both Vedas enjoin [the same rite] without distinction. The objector says: "Even so, there is no doubt; since both Vedas enjoin it, let there be an option (*vikalpa*).
He refutes this: "An option is not possible. If that were the case, the injunction of the subsidiary would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*)."

This demonstrates that the injunction regarding the subsidiary depends upon the injunction regarding the primary. The meaning of this is: there would be an option only if both properties were applicable.

It may be so. And when there is a difference in injunctions (*vidhi*), there is the attainment of both properties. However, there is no difference between the injunctions for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the injunction for the principal (*pradhāna*).
Therefore, it must be by the very property of the single injunction of the principal; thus, there is no option (*vikalpa*). The objector says: "Even so, what is the doubt?

The property of the principal injunction is indeed certain. The defender states the doubt: "Is this subsidiary injunction one whose own thing to be enjoined (*svavidheya*) is implied [by the principal], or..."

Does it exist as an independent primary element, or does it enjoin the thing to be enjoined having become one with the primary? If, after enjoining its own thing to be enjoined, it subsequently attains unity [with the primary], then, because the *Vāravantīya* has already been enjoined in the first stage, it must possess the accent belonging to the Sāmaveda. On the other hand, if its status as the thing to be enjoined belongs only to that which has already become one with the primary, then it must possess the low-voiced (*upāṃśu*) quality belonging to the Yajurveda.

There is a doubt as to whether [the *vāravantīya*] must necessarily be performed. In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that, having established its own meaning, the *vāravantīya* "sings the *vāravantīya*" becomes unified with the primary act by virtue of its purpose. Therefore, it possesses the status of an auxiliary only when endowed with the Vedic accents of the *Sāman*. The meaning of this is as follows: its own meaning is made known by its own sentence alone, independently of other sentences; however, for that [sentence] which lacks a specific qualification...

Because it lacks application and is therefore ineffective, the statement would result in a shift to a different meaning. Consequently, since the subsidiary (aṅga) is enjoined by the subsidiary injunction itself—which does not enter into the primary injunction—the subsidiary status in the primary injunction belongs only to that which is joined with the accent based upon that [subsidiary]. Thus, the Vāravantīya must possess the Vedic accent. To this, it is replied: True; it is indeed established that the accent is enjoined for its own specific purpose.

The primary [act] unites with its own purpose alone; it does not do so even by establishing subsidiary status (*aṅgatā*). Therefore, because subsidiary status is not made known by a subsidiary injunction (*aṅgavidhi*), that [status] is not brought about merely by the knowledge of one's own purpose; rather, the performance of the subsidiary depends upon the knowledge of its subsidiary status. Consequently, the accentuation is not based on that [mere purpose]. This would be the case if the subsidiary injunction did not make known the subsidiary status.

To the question, "What then makes it known? he says: it will be stated in the first section of the seventh book that the primary injunction prescribes subsidiary status (*aṅgatā*); for that very [subsidiary status] has already been expressed [by the word].

An injunction (*kāravidhi*) makes known a proximate object as being for its own sake; however, intermediate injunctions do not make known that their respective objects are auxiliary (*aṅga*) to something else—this will be explained in the seventh chapter, first section (*saptamādya*), through the analysis of the "grasper" (*grāhaka*). Furthermore, the performance of the *vāravantīya* chant occurs by virtue of its being an auxiliary, and not because it is the object of the injunction "he sings the *vāravantīya*. For the performance of ritual acts does not proceed from the mere knowledge of their essential form (*svarūpa*) alone, without [the knowledge of] their utility (*upayoga*).

[This is] because of knowledge [of their nature], and because actions consist of suffering. He concludes: Therefore, an injunction for one's own purpose (svārtha-vidhi) cannot sublate an injunction of performance (prayoga-vidhi), since the former exists for the sake of the performance. An injunction regarding the subsidiaries (aṅga-vidhi)—which is dependent upon the injunction of performance—cannot sublate the primary duty (dharma), because it exists for that purpose; that is, because the injunction of subsidiaries exists for the sake of the injunction of performance. By this, the following is stated: even though the injunction of subsidiaries...

Even though it is engaged in its own purpose, it must nevertheless be characterized by the very dharma that is bound to the primary injunction, because it is subordinate to that primary. This pair of points was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya with the following passage: "How might the primary become endowed with qualities through the performance of the subordinate?"—by which he means that one proceeds to perform the subordinate because of the performance of the subordinate; thus it is not said that the injunction of the subordinate functions for its own sake, [as expressed in the phrase] "if [it were] by the performance of the subordinate."

By such commentary as this, and because the injunction of a subordinate element (guṇa) is an auxiliary to the performance, it has been stated that it must conform to the quality of the primary element; "performance" here refers to the injunction of the primary act. [The sūtra states: "On account of the greater number, when both are heard. It has been established, therefore, that a subordinate element is dependent upon the injunction of the primary act. The injunction of the subordinate element—

The meaning is that there is no deliberation regarding the purpose of the *niyoga* (injunction). Now this is also considered: where there is a scriptural mention (*śruti*) of the primary element in both [the Veda and the Smṛti], in which case does the injunction of the primary element apply?

Where there is an injunction of the primary element in the Veda, it must be accompanied by the accent based on that; this deliberation is for the sake of establishing that. This has been explained [in the previous section]. Both of these points are incorrect; neither plurality is the reason, nor is the fly-whisk and so forth an appropriate illustration.
He states the defect in the reason: where has it ever been observed that the principal action is obstructed by the performance of its numerous constituent parts?

In some cases, multiplicity is not the cause for the designation of a formal application (*prayoga*); nor does the yak-tail fan and the white umbrella lead to the cognition [of a king] because of their multiplicity.

What then? It is designated as "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) because it is unique—since it does not exist elsewhere apart from the king—and because it is excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). However, if it were equivalent to "possessing fragrance" (*gandhavattva*) and so forth, it would simply be non-cognizant. Therefore, this [argument] is irrelevant.

We consider this to be the commentary: here it is stated. This is not incoherent; for by "abundance" (*bhūyastvena*), the understanding of the performance (*prayoga*) is indicated, meaning that the entire performance is understood. Where there is an abundance of constituent parts (*aṅga*), there the entire performance is known. [Where] there are few parts—(1) P. 810.

Furthermore, when there is a statement [of the application], there is no comprehension of the entire application; and when the entire application is being comprehended, there arises the cognition of the statement of the application.

For it is established that the comprehension of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) arises from the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Indeed, the application is the object of knowledge, as is the rule for the application.

The means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is understood only when the object of knowledge (*prameya*) has been understood in every respect; therefore, since the object of knowledge is understood upon the understanding of the entire performance (*prayoga*), the comprehension of the means of knowledge occurs only then. Consequently, the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*) applies precisely there. However, it is established that if even a few auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are not understood, the performance itself is not understood, and thus the injunction regarding performance is not understood; hence, the knowledge of the injunction regarding performance arises through the majority [of the auxiliaries]. As for the example of the yak-tail fan (*vālavyajana*) that was proposed—

It is well said that this [the *prayogavākya*] exists as a general indicator (*gamaka*) by way of being an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), since such a thing indeed exists. Just as a king is understood through [signs] such as a yak-tail whisk (*vālavyajana*), so too is the understanding of the injunction for performance (*prayogavidhi*) through its abundance; thus there is a similarity between the illustration and the illustrated. However, what is intended is not that the mode of indication (*gamakatva*) is of one and the same kind in both cases.

[This is] unconnected [to the context]. The *Bhāṣya* states: "Are there only this many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? It raises an objection to that: "What is the meaning of this question, 'Are there only this many means of valid cognition'? If it does not even refer to the subject matter of the *sūtra*..."

The intention [of the opponent] is that [the meaning] can be explained even without a question; however, that is incorrect. What is the use of a question here, since that which is not connected by way of syntactical connection (*saṃyoga*) is applied by way of context (*prakaraṇa*)? The meaning of the Sūtra can indeed be explained.

[Page 756] But surely we do not know with what it is not conjoined? If that is so, then this very point should be asked: with what is it not conjoined? What is the use of this [discussion]?

Is it merely to establish that there are only these many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Or is the intention this: why [should one rely] on direct audition (*śruti*) rather than on indicative mark (*liṅga*)?

"Or rather, that which is not connected by means of a direct statement (vākya) is applied [to a purpose] by means of the context (prakaraṇa). Are there only these four means of proof? How is it irrelevant? If there is indeed another...

Why is it said that what is not connected by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), or syntactic connection (*vākya*) is applied by means of context (*prakaraṇa*)? For application must indeed be stated even beyond these four. This is said while accepting the validity of the question; however, in ultimate reality, the question itself is not even tenable. Therefore, [the objection] that "what is not connected by direct statement, indicative mark, or syntactic connection is applied by context" [is based on] another authority...

Because [the opponent's position] has been refuted, even the question itself is not tenable. This is understood from the use of the word "even so" (*tathāpi*) in the passage beginning with "nevertheless, first the answer... Furthermore, ignorance itself is not known as a means of valid cognition other than those derived from scripture (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*).

Thus, for one who does not know another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), this question—"Is it only this much?"—arises; nevertheless, even when explained in this way, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) must be stated, for it is not appropriate [to say] "it is not unconnected" merely because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). It should be stated as will be said later: "of that which is to be performed and which requires a manner of performance (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣin*).
Just as he will state the nature of the context with the words "of that which is to be performed," so too should it be stated, and not [merely] "unconnected."
It is appropriate to say that this is because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, the purpose of the question appears to be somewhat irrelevant. To this it is replied:

This is the intention of the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*): the definition of the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) was stated in the section on definitions (*lakṣaṇa*), and the means of application (*viniyoga*), such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest, were also discussed there.

And regarding the "causes" (kāraṇāni): therein, first of all, the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) to be applied by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) has been explained. But what will be the application here by means of context (*prakaraṇa*)? Now, one might ask: since the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are indeed things to be applied by context, why is this question asked? Certainly, the purpose of the question exists; for the *prayāja* offerings and the rest are characterized by a single injunction (*ekaniyoga*).
He will explain the connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites in the fourth [book]; what other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is to be sought here? The meaning of this is:

he will explain in the fourth [book] that the connection of all—the Prayājas, the Āgneya, and so forth—is established by a single authoritative injunction (adhikāraniyoga); and thus, "he offers the Samidh-oblation."

Thus, by means of these [words] conjoined through their function as auxiliaries to the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is stated that they are conjoined with the supreme *apūrva*; this application (*viniyoga*) is indeed based on direct scriptural authority (*śruti*). What need is there here for any other means of proof? And in this way, the very relationship described in the *tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*—that words denoting conjoined meanings are the cause for understanding the meaning of words everywhere—becomes a universal principle. This is what was stated in the *tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*.

Thus, this relationship—attained through words that convey the connection with the *apūrva* by means of the theory of "expression of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*)—is the cause for the comprehension of word-meaning everywhere;

it is therefore all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*). And this being the case, when another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is further sought, [the relationship] is not based on the "expression of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*).
(Bhāṣya 652)
The connection can be demonstrated. Why? To this he says: "The understanding of the connection between the meanings of sentences occurs through context and other such means;

that is, the connection between the meanings of sentences—such as the injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings—and the injunctive mandate of entitlement (*adhikāraniyoga*), which constitutes the meaning of the sentence."

This is understood through context and other such means. Furthermore, there is no relationship characterized by the denotation of words between one sentence-meaning and another sentence-meaning. Why? He says: a word denotes its own meaning as already connected with other meanings. Therefore, the relationship among word-meanings is characterized by the denotation of what is already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*); however, a sentence does not denote a sentence-meaning as being connected with another sentence-meaning.

Because an indivisible sentence is not expressive [of meaning], for it has been stated in various places that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs through its parts. He concludes: "Therefore, the question arises for one who considers the connection of the meanings of sentences such as those concerning the *prayāja* offerings with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice to be non-verbal (*aśābda*). He considers the connection of the sentence-meanings to be non-verbal; however, the connection of the word-meanings (*padārtha*) is verbal (*śābda*). But according to that view, there is nothing other than direct assertion (*śruti*) and so forth—

This question arises for one who considers that the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [is being discussed]. Now, it might be argued that the question ought to have been, "Are there only these many means of valid cognition? by someone who considers the relationship between the sentence and its meaning to be non-verbal; it should not, however, be, "Are there only these many means of valid cognition? To this it is replied:

this very point has already been stated—that if something is not connected by direct assertion (*śruti*) and so forth, then it cannot be applied either, because the relationship between the sentence and its meaning is non-verbal.

This [statement] "of the relation" is indeed an implication of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because you, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*), by stating that [the object] is "unconnected," have asserted that there are only this many means of valid cognition. [Page 759] "Are there only this many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? The meaning of this is as follows: when the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) has indeed accepted the inclusion of those not connected by explicit statement (*śruti*), the opponent (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) says: "Is it also your view that there are only this many means of valid cognition, such that you say 'unconnected' refers to that which is not connected by *śruti* and so forth?"

Otherwise, one might ask: "Why would even that which is not connected by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and so forth remain unconnected? To this, the opponent—the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*)—replied, "No. His thought was: "Verbal meaning is not necessarily only that which is connected with the meanings of words; for a word conveys a relationship even through the sense of being for the sake of something else (*aidamarthyena*). This has been stated. for it is not necessarily the case that only what is already connected with word-meanings is verbal or a proven object of words. Rather, even that which is understood through the necessity of explaining the purpose (*aidamarthya*) otherwise would be verbal.

the supreme *apūrva* is not denoted as being first of all connected with the meanings of the words through the relation of *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance); rather, it is [denoted] as being connected merely by way of *aidamarthya*.
