It is replied: the relationship characterized by a single injunction is not tenable if there were no relationship characterized by the procedure. Its meaning is as follows: one...

Even when the subservience (*aidamarthya*) toward the application of the qualification (*sādhikāraniyoga*) is understood, as long as the relationship characterized by the *itikartavyatā* (the "how-to") is not apprehended, that subservience—which has an undifferentiated object—cannot be established otherwise; furthermore, because it is already occupied by the instrument (*karaṇa*), a relationship characterized solely by a single application (*ekaniyoga*) is not possible. To the question, "Why is it not possible?", he says: "For a single injunction (*ekavidhānatā*) of that which is to be enjoined is not possible if there is no [prior] relationship."

That injunction for which there is no connection with the thing enjoined—that injunction does not attain the state of being a single injunction together with that [other] injunction, because of the plurality of the things enjoined. For two injunctions that are distinct by their very nature, when combined with a plurality of things enjoined—and regarding those two injunctions whose enjoined objects are distinct—this state of being a single injunction is not possible without a mutual connection between the things enjoined. Therefore, regarding the meanings of the subordinate injunctions...

For those things enjoined by their own injunctions, there is a relationship characterized as that between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), established through the *prakaraṇa*— which is defined by the primary injunction’s requirement for a procedure— and with the instrument enjoined by that primary injunction; furthermore, there is a relationship characterized as "being for the sake of this" (*aidamarthya*) with the primary mandate, which is based upon the theory of the expression of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*).

Thus it is. Furthermore, the relationship characterized as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), which is implied by that [primary injunction], is also indeed verbal (*śābda*). And in this regard, the following is the methodological process (*prakriyā*):

the subordinate injunctions (*avāntaravidhi*) are to be enjoined because they are employed for the sake of the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*); for it is the established usage in the *Tantra* that "whatever is employed for the sake of establishing something else is enjoined by the injunction of that thing. However, the primary injunction itself is not something to be enjoined. Now, [one might object: "But how can there be an entry into the primary injunction..."
How can there be a relation with the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), given that it terminates in the instrument (*karaṇa*) alone? To this he says:

"And the connection of the instrument with the *itikartavyatā* is established. The connection of the instrument with the *itikartavyatā*—that is, the connection of the mandate (*niyoga*) [with the manner of performance]—is observed elsewhere even in worldly things to be accomplished. For even a worldly object to be accomplished is connected with the *itikartavyatā*, while the instrument is merely the means.

This is well-known in the world; moreover, this meaning of the *niyoga* (injunction) is that which is to be accomplished. He concludes: "Therefore, it is established that because there is a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it is the cause of the connection with the thing to be enjoined.
That is to say, it is the cause of the connection between two things to be enjoined. And this has been explained:
if the connection even between two sentence-meanings were verbal (*śābda*), then why would there be an innate (*autpattika*) connection of the sentence itself with its meaning?

To the extent that it has been shown for the collection of sentences as a whole, it must also be demonstrated. It is said: by stating "not [in the sense] of an action" (*kriyārthena*), you—who do not understand the meaning of the sūtra—have actually demonstrated the authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*) of this entire [Vedic corpus]. For, insofar as anything is presented as having an action as its purpose or as having an injunction (*niyoga*) as its purpose, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of all that is purely verbal and not merely imagined through intuition; thus, this entire [body of scripture], characterized by the syntactic connection of word-meanings—

And the validity of that which is characterized by the connection with the meaning of the sentence has been demonstrated. Now, one might object: "By saying this, you have stated that the verbal relationship is only that characterized by *aidamarthya* (subservience to a single purpose) with the meaning of the *niyoga*, and not the mutual connection among the things to be enjoined (*vidheya*) themselves. To this he replies: "Those who know the Veda consider the relationship to be precisely that characterized by *aidamarthya*; however, for the sake of establishing that [relationship], the denotation of words as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*) is observed even among the meanings of the individual words."

The meaning of this is as follows: even the mutual relationship between the meanings of words exists solely for the sake of establishing the relationship characterized by "being for this purpose" (*aidamarthya*). This is the cause of everything here.

The relationship [of words] is defined solely as their subservience to the *niyoga* (the mandate). Therefore, here too, the relationship among the meanings of the sentence is characterized by their subservience to the *niyoga*.

However, the connection with the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) exists for the sake of establishing that [subservience]. Furthermore, this very subservience to the *niyoga* is the reason why the word is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is not apprehended through any other means of knowledge. On the other hand, the denotation of a related meaning is equally present in common worldly usage, as in the case of "Devadatta..."

Even in common worldly expressions such as "one does not cook the fragrance with wood" or "in a pot," [the locative sense is understood]. He concludes the discussion on the meaning of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*):

therefore, it is established that subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) exists even for that which is assigned by context (*prakaraṇa*). As for the practical application, however, it has been explained according to the logic of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the seventh book and need not be explained here.

And sequence [is established] from similarity of location. Now, what is the meaning of this question? For in the preceding section, the question was appropriate with the intention that there is no other means of proof (pramāṇa) called "context" (prakaraṇa). But here again, what is the meaning of the question? The answer is:

it has been stated that those who know the Veda consider the relationship in the Veda to be characterized solely by "subservience to a purpose" (aidamarthya). And that [subservience] is merely a relationship—

It is capable of establishing [the sequence] by that much alone, for it is sufficient; it does not, however, require even a connection with a specific instrument. Furthermore, there is no connection other than this purposefulness (*aidamarthya*)—namely, a mere commonality of place—which, being otherwise inexplicable, would necessitate the assumption of a connection with a specific instrument. Thus, the question consists in the implication of a sequence as a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might object: "But are there not only these many means of knowledge?"—this is the objection.
It must be so. What is the meaning of this question, "Are there only these many means of valid cognition?
To this it is replied: here too, [the author] intends to exclude what is not connected [to the definition].
The mention [of *grahaṇa*] recurs for the purpose of indicating another object; since that exists, this question is as before, and thus it is faultless.

The other says: "It is true that there is no relation apart from *aidamarthya* (the state of being for the sake of that); nevertheless, there certainly is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for *aidamarthya*."

In the case of understanding a specific detail, there is what is called "commonality of position" (*sthāna-sāmānya*). This is what was stated [in the sūtra]: "And the sequence [is determined] from commonality of place" (*kramaś ca deśasāmānyāt*). Its meaning is as follows: the consecratory mantra (*anumantraṇa-mantra*) beginning with "Thou art *Dabdhi*" requires syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with some object to be consecrated; therefore, it enters into syntactic unity with that which is proximate. Wherever the status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) is preceded by syntactic unity through position, there it is by position alone [that the application is determined].
"The connection for the purpose of making a distinction. The purpose has indeed already been shown.

And the designation (*ākhyā*) is likewise [determined] because it serves that purpose. Now, in this case, the sense of a question is not appropriate, because when there is such a purpose, the designation—like the position (*sthāna*)—serves as the cause for the comprehension of the specific [function]. The meaning of this is as follows: the *adhvaryu* and others [are established] in the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Regarding those [mantras] recited by way of a fixed rule (*niyoga*) which have attained a specific purpose (*aidamarthya*), how do they come to possess that purpose? Through titles (*samākhyā*) such as "the office of the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*), which denote specific ritual acts, one understands their connection to particular functions; thus, subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) is established precisely through that medium.
Since this is the authority of the title, the question raised to challenge it is not tenable. It is replied: there is indeed a distinction here between position (*sthāna*) and title (*samākhyā*).

It is indeed appropriate that the location serves as the cause for understanding a specific detail, because it is Vedic; for in the sequence of the *upāṃśuyāja*, the mantra for the consecratory recitation (*anumantraṇa*), "Thou art named Adabdhi," is recited in the Veda itself. In that context, the denotation of a word as connected with what is proximate is a linguistic convention established in common worldly usage.
The word contained in the mantra "asī" is connected with the deity of the *upāṃśuyāja* itself, which is present there. Therefore, it is appropriate that the place possesses this distinction.

[The name] is not a cause for understanding the meaning of the Veda. Furthermore, a worldly designation, such as "the office of the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*) and so forth, is not a means for comprehending the meaning of the Veda, just as in cases such as "he cooks" (*pacati*). The meaning of this is as follows:

a worldly designation that has not entered into the Veda is not a cause for understanding the meaning of the word, just as "he cooks" and the like [are not]. Otherwise, even [expressions] such as "he cooks" would [be causes for such understanding].

It might be argued that [the *samākhyā*] would serve as an injunction for cooking that is a subsidiary part of the Vedic meaning; however, since the *samākhyā* does not possess the quality of being a cause for understanding the Vedic meaning, it lacks authority (*apramāṇatva*). Therefore, it was asked: "Are these the only means of knowledge? To this it is replied: although the *samākhyā* is worldly in nature, it is nonetheless a cause for understanding a Vedic matter. This is the case with *samākhyās* such as *ādhvaryava*, which pertain to specific ritual actions.

It serves as the cause for understanding a specific agent. Why? Because the designation of primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds is well-established in relation to a related entity; and although this designation—namely, the titles such as *hautra* and so forth—is itself worldly, it is a designation of a Vedic matter because its subject matter consists of Vedic rituals. This is the meaning: just as a worldly expression such as "he cooks" is not connected to a Vedic matter, so too [one might think] the titles like *hautra* are not, yet they are, because they pertain to Vedic rites.

Furthermore, a name ending in a *taddhita* suffix is observed to denote a connection with the meaning of its base through other words ending in *taddhita* suffixes. Since no specific agent is heard mentioned in relation to the ritual acts (*karmasu*), when there is a requirement for a specific agent, it is understood that the *hotṛ* and others—who are already known as connected to the acts by virtue of their names—are the agents.
Therefore, the name conveys a specific distinction. Because the name is present in the mind, these acts are designated by means of that specific agent.

This is the meaning. Now, one might object: this designation is worldly (*laukika*), and that [worldly usage] is preceded by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, having understood the connection with a specific person through that other means of valid cognition, the worldly designation should be employed. Furthermore, since the connection is not understood prior to the name (*samākhyā*), how can there be a restrictive rule (*niyama*) based on the name? To this, he replies: "And this does not depend upon another means of valid cognition like a traditional scripture (*smṛti*), because the relationship between word and meaning is innate (*autpattika*)."

(1) G. These are the specific characteristics of the author of the relationship. The meaning of this is as follows: for in the case of Smṛti, the sentence is composed by a person; and that sentence is said to be "composed by a person."

That which is employed by a person after having cognized an object through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the purpose of communicating it—regarding this, it has been said: "And here, 'composition' (*kṛti*) consists in the communication of an object perceived through another means of valid cognition; nor is there the state of being an effect of phonemes and so forth.
Therefore, in that case, there is a dependence upon another means of valid cognition.

In this context, however, there is the term "ādhvaryava" and so forth; nor is such a term of human origin, because it is beginningless (*anādi*). Therefore, there is no dependence here upon other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Consequently, it is logical that "the designation (*ākhyā*) is also [determinative] because it serves that purpose. Why is it logical? Because it is the cause for the comprehension of a specific detail:

when the agent in general has been understood through the implication of an action, and a requirement for a specific detail arises, the designation (*samākhyā*) is the cause for the comprehension of that specific detail.

Therefore, the meaning is that even *samākhyā* (name/designation) is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it brings to mind a specific agent in order to establish the expression of a qualified [action].
The purpose has been stated.
[Regarding] *śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, *prakaraṇa*, *sthāna*—here the *Bhāṣya* begins with "But what [is *samākhyā*]? and so forth; he raises an objection to that.

But what, then, is *śruti* here? What is this *liṅga*? Now, this question is not appropriate. Why is it not appropriate? Because it was stated by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) in this very context that "the means for application (*viniyoga*) have been explained. And it is not possible for that which is not yet known to be something already explained. Therefore, the statement "the means for application have been explained" is contradictory. What, then, is *śruti* here? What...

And regarding the phrase "the indicative mark" (*liṅga*): the word "stated" (*uktāni*) expresses that [the meaning] is already known; whereas the questions "What is the scripture? (*kā punaḥ śrutiḥ*) and "What is the indicative mark? (*kiṃ liṅgam*) express that [the meaning] is not yet known. Furthermore, it is impossible for a single object to be both known and unknown simultaneously.
(1) *Bhāṣya* 824.

Now, if this is the intention— that it is only the application (*viniyoga*) that is stated by means of direct assertion (*śruti*) and the rest, and not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of direct assertion and the others—

then both the statement of what was said and the question are justified; for even though only the application is stated and not the essential nature of direct assertion and the rest, such being the case...

In that case, it should be stated simply that "the application has been declared by the Śruti and other means," and not that "the causes for the application have been declared. Furthermore, even by stating the application itself, the causes for the application are indeed stated.
Why? Because the cause is understood through its effect; the application is the effect, and the Śruti and other means are the causes for the application.

When the effect is understood, the cause is understood. That whose effect is the application (*viniyoga*) through direct assertion (*śruti*) is the means of knowledge called *śruti*. He states that this is the distinction of verbal [knowledge] from other means of knowledge: "For verbal [knowledge] is specifically that which is delimited by an object; it does not arise merely from the cognition of the phonemes themselves as to their own nature. This division—that 'this is a word' or 'this is a sentence'—is a division based on function (*kārya*)."

It is indeed a restrictive rule (*nibandhana*). Nor is there a difference in the verbal [means of knowledge] by its very nature apart from the comprehension of the meaning as an effect, because [it would otherwise follow that] there is comprehension of the mere phonemes by their very nature. Therefore, even when the application (*viniyoga*) has been stated, since the knowledge of the cause has already arisen, the question is not justified.

And he states another objection: "Having stated the distinction between direct assertion (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), what is the intention behind the subsequent question regarding syntactical connection (*vākya*)? It is not so.

We understand this. For when there is a deliberation regarding the relative strength or weakness of two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to a particular object, it is only appropriate to inquire into the essential nature of those two, and not of any other. Now, if this is the intention of the questioner—namely, that after the nature of the sentence (*vākya*) has been asked about and the answer given that "a sentence consists of words expressing a meaning through their combination"—it would follow that no distinction between *śruti* (direct statement) and *liṅga* (indicative mark) from the sentence could be established. Therefore, [the nature] of the sentence...

And this deliberation regarding the sentence must be formulated as an objection: for the purpose of establishing that "this must be performed," there is this question-and-answer concerning the sentence;
and indeed, without a statement of application (*viniyoga*), the question does not arise.

The answer to the question: That too is not tenable, because the mention of the *gārhapatya* fire is *śruti* (direct scriptural statement), while the expressive power of the word "Indra" is *liṅga* (indicative mark); and since words express a meaning when combined, we clearly perceive the mutual distinctness of these three. Now, one might object that by saying "when combined," the text seems to suggest that the collection of words expresses a new, unprecedented meaning (*apūrva*). This...

And this [position] is untenable, because the denotative capacity of a collection [of words] has been refuted. For it has been stated in various places that each individual word denotes its own meaning as already connected [with others]. It is replied: by the use of the plural form "denote" (*abhidadhati*), it is stated that the denotation occurs individually.
However, since each single word denotes its own meaning as connected [with others], it requires another word to present that with which it is connected.
[The word] is exhausted [in its own meaning]. Therefore, it is said "by combining" because it requires another word to bring about the presentation of a different object.

This has been stated by us in the *Vākyārthamātṛkā* and in the section on *tadbhūta*. Consequently, those who pride themselves on their knowledge of the texts consider this commentary to be nothing but a string of blind words. To this, we reply: It is true that the comprehension of the means of proof arises from the sense; nevertheless...

The question "What then is the *śruti* here? is indeed appropriate. The underlying intention here is as follows: by the mention of application (*viniyoga*), the very nature of the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) is also stated; it is with this in mind that it was said, "the causes of application have been stated. Nor is there any lack of occasion for the question regarding *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth once the nature [of the means] is known; thus the question is justified. How is it justified? The answer:

It is true that the direct statement (*śruti*) regarding the Gārhapatya fire is authoritative, and it is also true that the indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting in the capacity of the name "Indra" is authoritative; nevertheless, [the meaning] cannot be understood independently of other words. That the mantra is to be applied to the Gārhapatya fire by means of direct statement (*śruti*)—namely, "one should worship the Gārhapatya with the *aindrī* [mantra]"—is not established, nor is the mantra’s orientation toward Indra established by indicative power (*liṅga*) independently of other words. Therefore, since both are equally dependent upon other words, [there is no difference between them].
Not knowing the distinction between *śruti* and *liṅga*, both of which are to be understood through their effects, he asks: "What, then, is *śruti* here, and what is *liṅga*?
Now, why was this not determined at the beginning of the chapter, given that the very commentary states that *śruti* and the other means are the causes for application (*viniyoga*)?

To this it is replied: even in that case, this must be stated as being *utsūtra* (not based on a sūtra). For if this were indeed stated in a sūtra there, then the author of the Bhāṣya, while explaining that sūtra, would have said, "In that case too, this is *utsūtra*," since there would be no distinction [between the two cases]. However, the specific difference here is that this statement is connected as an incidental (*aupoddhātika*) discussion because the sūtra beginning with "śruti-liṅga" is yet to be explained.

It occurs as follows: for when the distinct natures of two things are known, there arises the occasion for discerning their relative strength and weakness; thus, the knowledge of the intrinsic nature [of the words] is an incidental introduction. But how is it now that the word *gārhapatya* is said to possess direct denotation (*śruti*) despite its equal connection with another word, since both of these are merely syntactical connection (*vākya*)? This is explained: the connection with another word refers to the application (*viniyoga*) residing in the mantra.

And this [linguistic capacity] residing in the sentence is the same whether it denotes Indra or the Gārhapatya fire. However, it is only the hearing of the word "gārhapatya" that functions toward denoting the Gārhapatya. Thus, by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it is the hearing of the word "gārhapatya" alone that functions toward denoting the Gārhapatya.
But was it not said that the accusative case-ending indicates pervasion? For even when Indra is to be approached, the word "gārhapatya" [is used].

It indeed enters into syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by virtue of its being in the locative case-ending; it does not, however, do so as a second [accusative] object, and thus that very [locative form] serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire.

This is true provided that the word "Gārhapatya" is heard [in the text]. Even that [locative form], however, is not capable of effecting the application (*viniyoga*) to the Gārhapatya fire independently of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*);
[rather, it connects] through a sentence (*vākya*).

Since the meaning of the accusative case is also applicable to *indra*, it follows that what has been shown belongs to the word (*pada*) itself and not to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone. Thus, even though the accusative is not explicitly mentioned, it is implied; and even when the accusative is employed, the nominal stem is also included—therefore, it is the word itself that denotes the Gārhapatya fire.

It functions [in this way]. Thus, even when there is an application (*viniyoga*) for addressing Indra or for standing near Indra, another word in the mantra remains indifferent (*udāste*), because the same applies even when addressing the Gārhapatya fire. Therefore, since the other words remain indifferent, there is a distinction between *śruti* (direct statement) and *liṅga* (indicative power) from *vākya* (syntactical connection).

And this being so, while it might be suspected that there is *vākya*-hood due to the dependence on other words, it is precisely for the sake of discerning this [distinction] that [the definition] is applied even to *vākya*.

The question and answer are thus entirely appropriate. He concludes: "Therefore, because it is the cause of an uncommon cognition, even though it denotes the meaning through a combination [of words], *śruti* (direct assertion) is also called *liṅga* (indicative mark). This is because there is a distinction between *śruti* and *liṅga*. Consequently, it is logical to ask: when there is a conflict between *śruti* and *liṅga*, does both serve as the means of application (*viniyojaka*), or is it *śruti* alone? However, the intention of the question regarding the *prakaraṇa* (context) is as follows:

We shall explain—meaning we shall analyze—in its proper place, namely in the section concerning the conflict between sentence and context (*vākya-prakaraṇa-virodha-adhikaraṇa*), within the discussion on the inquiry [into the relative strength of the means of proof]. The phrase "we shall explain" is to be supplied also to the discussion on the conflict between position and name (*sthāna-samākhyā*). Now, if this is so, when there is a difference between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), the deliberation should be stated as follows: "Are both direct statement and indicative mark authoritative, or is direct statement the stronger? Here...
Furthermore, it is not appropriate [to ask] in the Bhāṣya whether between *śruti* and *liṅga*, which is stronger—is it *śruti* or is it *liṅga*? Why?

Because he will state that this is a cause, and that this is also a cause—namely, that both *śruti* is a cause and *liṅga* is also a cause—by virtue of their dependence upon the meaning of the words (*padārtha*).

Therefore, it is appropriate that there be a doubt as to whether both [direct statement and indicative mark] possess the power of application by virtue of following from that [context], or whether direct statement alone does so. Consequently, one must present the matter exactly as we previously proposed; one should not instead inquire whether direct statement is stronger or whether the indicative mark is stronger.

If these two reasons are of equal strength—this being the view of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on the observation of reasons—then there must be a corresponding reason that serves as the applicator for both. Having raised this objection, he concludes: "Therefore, the introduction is of one kind, while the conclusion is of another. In this very same way, even the contradictory results of the *pūrvapakṣa* and the final position (*siddhānta*) have been set forth: "Is it Indra's..."?

One must perform the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire, or is it only the *gārhapatya*? Therefore, the consistency between the opening and the conclusion must be stated. He states another objection: "Furthermore, if that were so, then it is *liṅga* and *vākya* that are being deliberated here as being in conflict, not *śruti* and *liṅga*; that too is incorrect, for [the relationship] is seen everywhere both as inherent and as distinct."

Because of this statement regarding discrimination (*viveka*). He states another objection: "But the scriptural text (*śruti*) here is contradicted by the indicative mark (*liṅga*); whereas the syntactical connection (*vākya*), moreover, is indeed possible even through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Having said this, he introduces another scriptural text with the words "or rather" (*athavā*). It is not known whether this is done because of dissatisfaction [with the previous position] or for the sake of providing an alternative (*vikalpa*). Previously, having stated that the mention of the *gārhapatya* fire was based on direct scriptural text (*śruti*), he then says "or rather."

He shows the second scriptural citation (*dvitīyāśruti*). It is not known whether this is stated because of dissatisfaction with that [first position], or rather by way of the possibility of an alternative view (*pakṣāntara*).
(1) G. dvitīyām [p. 771]

It is said: regarding this presentation—namely, whether the *śruti* (direct statement) is more powerful or the *liṅga* (indicative mark)—the intended meaning here is this: just as the *śruti* is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) precisely by subverting the *liṅga*, so too is the *liṅga* a means of valid cognition precisely by subverting the *śruti*.
And when both are means of valid cognition only through the mutual subversion of each other, then this presentation—"Is the *śruti* more powerful?"—is indeed appropriate.

Or rather, [is it] indicative power (*liṅga*)? How is this justified? He says: "This is what is meant—we do not know which is stronger. Therefore, this is the meaning of the Bhāṣya: Is it that *śruti* alone is stronger than *liṅga*, or is it that *śruti* is indeed strong? Likewise, is *liṅga* also stronger than *śruti*? Consequently, both are means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And when both are means of valid knowledge, both—

[This is] the designation. For this very reason, it was stated that there is no fixed rule (*aniyama*). And as for the statement "if these two causes are of equal strength," the phrase "because no distinction is perceived" is to be supplied as a continuation. Having restated the *bhāṣya*, he raises an objection: "From that, there is an option (*vikalpa*). What is this option?
Is it not the case that, under this view, there is actually a combination (*samuccaya*), since the mantra is applied both to Indra and to the Gārhapatya fire?

He provides the justification: "This was stated by accepting the alternative regarding the designation (*abhidhāna*), not the alternative regarding the application (*prayoga*). The meaning of this is as follows: when [the mantra] is employed for the purpose of designating the Gārhapatya fire, then Indra is not designated by the mantra; when it is for the purpose of worshipping Indra, then it is not for the Gārhapatya. Thus, there is a fixed alternative (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) regarding the designation. However, regarding the application of the mantra, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) with respect to both Agni and Indra.
"Precisely because of the repetition of the subordinate element for each principal element according to the distinction of the principals; however, if the indicative mark (*liṅga*) were stronger..."

This commentary (*bhāṣya*) should also be regarded as being like an introductory statement (*upanyāsa*). And "superiority" (*balīyastva*) means, like direct assertion (*śruti*), the capacity for independent application (*viniyojakatva*) within its own domain.

Even though *śruti* and *liṅga* have already been discussed, the distinction among *vākya*s (syntactical connections) is stated. Thus, the question "In that case... is not [intended] merely regarding the *gārhapatya* fire.

From hearing [the word], there arises the understanding of its presence, because a mere word is not expressive. It has been shown that such a [mere] portion constitutes a *śruti*, and that is non-expressive. And that which is expressive is a *vākya* (sentence). When this has been urged, the author now explains the intention of the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādin*), thereby showing that this is an elaboration of what was previously stated: "True, without a sentence, this comprehension does not occur."

The understanding that the *gārhapatya* fire is to be worshipped follows from the mention of the *gārhapatya*; this has been stated in the passage beginning with "But as for the scriptural statement here," because the same logic applies even when Indra is being denoted, since the other words [of the mantra] remain identical. How is there equality? For even though the indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger, if Indra were the one to be worshipped, the phrase "one worships with the *aindrī*" would have to be accepted as forming a single syntactical unit with the word *gārhapatya*.

For if it were not to be approached, then the sentence (*vākya*) would be contradicted by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), and here there would be a contradiction between sentence and indicative mark, not a contradiction between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark. Here, the meaning understood immediately after the hearing of the word *gārhapatya*—which consists of a specific fire—is contradicted by the indicative mark. Therefore, this is indeed a contradiction between direct statement and indicative mark. Alternatively, [the phrase] "not because of being a single sentence" (*naikavākyatvāt*) does not apply here.

(1) Or how has it been explained that the presentation of an alternative position is for the purpose of demonstrating all the words? It is not due to dissatisfaction, nor is it because of another position—

By this, another scriptural passage (*śruti*) is introduced. However, previously only the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) was mentioned, whereas now it is presented together with its case-ending (*vibhakti*).

And it has been shown earlier that it is the word accompanied by the case-ending that possesses the power of application (*viniyojakatva*). What, then, is appropriate here? Since the own-meaning is understood in both cases. He explains: even from the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the meaning indicated by that mark—consisting of the worship of Indra—is understood. From the scriptural statement (*śruti*)—

Furthermore, the meaning of the Śruti is understood to consist in the worship of the Gārhapatya fire. Since the syntactical connection (vākya) is indifferent, the very act of denotation occurs in both cases; thus, the application of the mantra to both is established by the word alone, and no contradiction arises. Moreover, no distinction is perceived regarding the act of denotation itself; therefore, it has been stated that these two grounds possess equal force. And so, in formulating the prima facie view here, [the sūtra states] "But because of the direct statement... (*vacanāt tu*).

There is no clear tautology with the phrase "according to the actual fact" (*yathārtham*). For in that [preceding] case, having stated in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone is the applicator, it was stated in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the direct statement (*śruti*) is indeed capable of being the applicator. Now, here, since the applicatory power of the direct statement is established...

It has been stated that even the indicative power (*liṅga*) is suspected of being a factor of application. On this point, the Bhāṣya says: "But surely the form of indicative power is as if fragile, for the conviction arising from indicative power is indeed accompanied by doubt.
This [objection] is raised: what is this so-called "doubt"? The answer follows:

—This is an incorrect cognition (*asamyak-pratyaya*). What is the incorrectness here? The answer is: it is not the case that from the mention of "Indra," there arises the cognition that "Indra is to be addressed. Nor does the mere capacity [of a word] produce the knowledge of what ought to be done, namely, "this is to be performed by this means.

However, from the hearing of the term *gārhapatya*, there arises the knowledge of what ought to be done, namely, "by this [means], the *gārhapatya* fire is to be attended," as established by the injunctive sentence.
Because the word *gārhapatya* has already been used [elsewhere]. But surely, since an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not injunctive, it lacks authority altogether; how then [can it be authoritative]?
(1) Bhāṣya 842 (2) G. adds *evameva* [p. 774].

There is a contradiction; the meaning is that there is no contradiction of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by that which is not a valid means of knowledge. He refutes [this objection]: True, the mere capacity for expression is not itself a valid means of knowledge; rather, it becomes a valid means of knowledge when, upon the understanding of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), a specific detail is understood from another source. By what is the understanding of the procedure obtained? By context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth. When it is generally understood through these that "one must assist here," and there arises an expectancy for a specific detail as to "by doing what?"—[the capacity for expression then functions].

Whatever one is able to perform, by performing that very thing, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) indeed becomes the applicator for a specific task; and regarding the comprehension of what is to be done, it remains nothing more than the verbal expression itself—so it is stated in the Bhāṣya. This very point has been established and clarified in the section on Indicative Mark and Order (*Liṅgakramādhikaraṇa*). He concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Therefore, these two causes are of equal strength. Here follows another passage from the Bhāṣya.

Regarding the statement, “Even a stronger [means of proof]...,” he explains it as follows: It is not stronger at all; for, by the reasoning already stated, the *śruti* and the *liṅga* possess equal force. He considers that even if one were to proceed by way of concession (*anvāruhya*), there is no contradiction. [Objection: “But surely this very thing is the contradiction!”

"Is it not the case that while the attendance (*upasthāna*) is enjoined once, it is performed repeatedly? No, this is not so. Because of the difference in those to whom one attends (*upastheya*), the principle that 'subsidiary elements (*guṇa*) repeat with each principal element (*pradhāna*)' applies; thus there is no contradiction.
Having restated this from the *Bhāṣya*, he raises an objection: "But surely this..."

The objection based on contradiction is not tenable, for here two objects of worship are not heard; in the injunction "one worships the Gārhapatya," only the Gārhapatya is heard as the object of worship, not Indra either. Nor is there an understanding that it must be performed on the basis of indicative power (liṅga). Therefore, this statement in the Bhāṣya is no answer at all.
(1) Bh, p. 844; (2) G. *avagamaḥ*; (3) G. *kartavyatvānavagame* [p.
775]. It is said: because the necessity of performance (*kartavyatā*) is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*), the denotation of Indra is also cognized from the word "Indra."

Thinking that the comprehension of the necessity for performance (*kartavyatā*) arises even from an indicative mark (*liṅga*) when it is dependent upon the context (*prakaraṇa*), [the author] stated, "due to the difference in the object of worship" (*upastheyabheda*).

Or, it is due to the similarity of the sentence (*vākya*). The meaning of this is as follows: even among the factors that effect application (*viniyojaka*), the word *gārhapatyam* alone is the factor of application because the other words are indifferent; likewise, in the mantra as well, the word *indra* is no different [from the others], and thus it too can be a factor of application.

"Because of the commonality of the sentence" means because it is shared; it has already been stated previously that this is equal in both cases. If that is so, then the status of being secondary (*gauṇa*) and primary (*mukhya*) is not tenable—thus the contradiction is raised once again. Now, one might object: "But surely, when there is a repetition of subordinate elements (*guṇa*) for each principal element (*pradhāna*), this contradiction does not arise. The meaning of this is as follows: since there is a contradiction in both cases due to two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there must be a repetition of the subordinate elements for each principal element.

This mantra is to be employed twice; in one application it has a primary sense, and in the other a secondary sense, so there is no contradiction. For if a primary and secondary meaning were asserted within a single application, then indeed there would be a contradiction. He resolves this: "This contradiction is contingent upon the mantra being unassigned. This [alleged] contradiction arises through the imposition of primary and secondary meanings only with respect to a mantra that has not yet been assigned its specific function.

There is a contradiction. What is meant is this: at the time of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), since a mantra has only a single application, it is not appropriate for it to have both a secondary (*gauṇa*) and a primary (*mukhya*) meaning.

How then is there no contradiction? To this he says: "But there is no contradiction in the case of ritual application (*viniyoga*). Because the application differs according to the difference in the principal acts (*pradhāna*). And when that [application] differs, since there is a distinct application for each principal act, there is no contradiction; thus the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established here.

He begins the final conclusion: Here it is said that between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), the direct statement is more powerful. Why? Because of the remoteness of the meaning (*arthaviprakarṣāt*).

What is this "remoteness of the meaning"? The remoteness of the meaning is *arthaviprakarṣa*. But what is the "meaning" here? It is the meaning of the direct statement (*śrutyartha*), namely, that Indra is to be invoked (*indropastheya*).

[The injunction] takes the form: "By this, this must be done. In this context, the meaning of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)—namely, "one should stand near the *gārhapatya* fire"—is proximate because the Vedic word does not depend on any other means of knowledge. On the other hand, the idea that "Indra should be worshipped" is remote. Why? The answer follows: "Never... [p. r776]

Having restated the Bhāṣya—"It is not heard in scripture that Indra is to be worshipped with the mantra 'starīrasi,' even though he possesses the capacity to be denoted by it, because there is no such injunction;
thus it is understood that Indra is not to be worshipped"—the author raises an objection: "But was it not already stated previously that..."?
That indicative mark (*liṅga*) by which Indra is denoted in the sense of "that which is to be performed"—characterized as it is by capacity (*sāmarthya*)—is the authority for the denotation of Indra.

Consequently, there would be an absolute equality between the two, namely Indra and Gārhapatya, in their being denoted. Therefore, both *śruti* (direct statement) and *liṅga* (indicative mark) possess authority. But what is this that has been raised [as an objection]? It is the authority of *liṅga* that was previously challenged, and now its justification is being stated.

“Since Dharma has sound as its source, that which is not based on sound should be disregarded. This statement refers to both the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*); both of these are non-verbal. Furthermore, in a matter characterized in this way—which transcends the domain of direct perception—determination is not possible without verbal testimony.
Therefore, we consider the indicative mark to be more remote than the meaning of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).

It is said: by this commentary, in order to demonstrate the distinction that "this is not based on verbal testimony" (*aśābda*), the validity of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) which had been raised again as an objection is now established. It is further stated: the word "and" (*ca*) should be applied to the preceding [sentence]. But if this is so, then if it is not based on verbal testimony, the validity of the inferential mark itself would be lost.
(1) G. Regarding the distinction:
from what does the contradiction arise? For contradiction occurs only with respect to validity (*prāmāṇya*), because it presents mutually opposed objects. Now, this is the intended meaning:

"In the absence of contradiction, the authority of *liṅga* (indicative power) is like that of *smṛti* (tradition); just as *smṛti* possesses authority in a domain where it does not contradict *śruti* (direct Vedic statement), so too does *liṅga*. This is incorrect. Why? Because in the case of *smṛti*, having first understood its meaning, a reversal [of that meaning] is postulated due to contradiction—as when one understands from *smṛti* that "the entire *audumbarī* post must be covered," and then, due to contradiction with *śruti*, a reversal of that meaning is established. However, in the case of *liṅga*, there is no such process of first understanding a meaning and then subsequently postulating a reversal. Therefore, the analogy is invalid. Furthermore, since the *liṅga* is weaker than *śruti*, its authority is sublated by the stronger *śruti*. Thus, the *liṅga* is set aside. It is postulated [in other cases]. But here, it has been stated that no *upasthāna* (proximity/establishment) is perceived at all. How can inference be possible regarding a matter that is not perceived?

Therefore, this appears incoherent, like the speech of a thief who has been poorly apprehended. The meaning is: "This commentary is incoherent, like the speech of a thief by whom a crime (*durācarita*) was poorly committed (*durgṛhīta*). Furthermore, the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*)—from the context—...

He demonstrates that the understanding of the meaning arises from the *liṅga* itself, even when there is an expectation of further duties to be performed: "And since direct statement (*śruti*) is possible, and since the understanding is common to both [the *liṅga* and the] sentence, it must be explained how this distinction [of the *liṅga* alone] occurs. The sense is that because the sentence is indifferent—being common to both the *śruti* and the *liṅga*—it is logical that the understanding arises from both.

To this it is replied: the definition of *prakaraṇa* (context) is "the statement of that which is to be performed and which requires a knowledge of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). By means of that [definition], the relationship characterized by *aidamarthya*—specifically the *aidamarthya* of the instrument—is understood through *prakaraṇa*, and not, however, the relationship characterized by the mutual connection of word-meanings;
for that [relationship] would have as its definition or means of proof (*lakṣaṇa/pramāṇa*) the word-meanings already connected.

It has been stated in the section on Context (*prakaraṇa*) that [the meaning] is not understood from context alone. What follows from that? This follows from that: there is a contradiction with the opposite of the connected word-meanings (*anvitapadārthaviparyaya*).

The relationship characterized by definition is understood from the word-meanings themselves. However, the relationship characterized by being for the sake of this (aidamarthya) is understood solely from the task (kārya), and not from the connection of word-meanings. For it is through the task that the state of being for the sake of the instrument is understood within the context (prakaraṇa);
it is not the connection of word-meanings. The task itself, which requires the "how-to" (itikartavyatā), constitutes the context. Therefore, [this is] from the context.

Since it is understood that the purpose of the instrument is solely [to bring about the result], the syntactic connection (*padārthānvaya*) is not yet apprehended. Even so, what is the distinction? This is the distinction: the definition consists in the connection with word-meanings. When there exists that relationship characterized by the connection of word-meanings—namely, the sentence-meaning which is connected with word-meanings through a mere relation—only then does the subsequent connection with the action (*kāryayoga*) arise, characterized as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) together with the action.

The connection characterized by the syntactical relation of word-meanings (*padārthānvaya*) occurs first of all. However, when there is a context (*prakaraṇa*) regarding an action (*kārya*), the syntactical relation of word-meanings occurs later by the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the form of semantic competency (*sāmarthya*); this is what constitutes the remoteness of meaning (*arthaviprakarṣa*). In the case of direct statement (*śruti*), the syntactical relation of word-meanings occurs first, whereas in the case of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it occurs later. [Objection: Granted that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has this remoteness of the syntactical relation of word-meanings, how then is direct statement (*śruti*) more powerful? To this he says: "And for the purpose of demonstrating the syntactical relation..."

Those who know the relationship between the subordinate and the principal consider this a third among the six means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nevertheless, [the author] asks "why? and replies: "And this syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is understood first of all from the Vedic text (*śruti*). For by that much alone, the purpose of the apprehender and the recitation of the mantra is fulfilled. There is no evidence for understanding the syntactic connection of word-meanings at a later stage through functional necessity (*kāryataḥ*). Why? Because the connection of what is already connected is not observed.

For this reason, it is logical that direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is stronger than indicative mark (*liṅga*). In this section, the mention of "inference" (*ānumānika*) in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) refers to the requirement for the syntactic connection of word-meanings (*padārthānvaya*). For the syntactic connection of word-meanings occurs subsequent to both context (*prakaraṇa*) and indicative mark; thus, [it is stronger] than (1) the subsequent [context], (2) the word-meanings themselves, and so forth.

Because it functions like inference (*anumāna*), it is called "inferential" (*ānumānika*). And it is said to be non-verbal (*aśābda*) because it lacks the character of directly indicating the related word-meanings.

Now, one might object: "In this context, how can the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) be stated by way of conjunction (*samuccaya*), given that an alternative (*vikalpa*) is improper?"—thus it is stated in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).

Regarding the phrase "because of the impropriety of optionality" (*vikalpasya cānyāyyatvāt*), he says that this refers to the mantra-text. He explains this very point: the intention is that it is not logical for the word "Indra" to have two denotations. For it would be improper for the word "Indra" at one time to denote the Āhavanīya fire and at another time to denote Indra. Therefore, because optionality is improper, [the mantra] belongs only to that which has been specifically enjoined.

The reason why the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra is not possible has been shown to consist in the fact that an alternative interpretation (*vikalpa*) is improper. As for what was stated—that there is no contradiction—this is a restatement of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). This very contradiction is as follows: it is not possible for the word "Indra" to have two denotations in relation to the mantra-sentence; for a mantra-sentence is uttered only once, and by it only a single meaning [can be conveyed].

It must be stated that there cannot, however, be two meanings [for a single word], because it is impossible for that which is uttered once to have multiple meanings. Now, one might argue that there is no contradiction because the two applications (viniyoga) result in two separate performances; to this, he replies: since the purposefulness (aidamarthya) is obtained through syntactic connection (anvaya), the requirement for the "thing-to-be-done" (kartavyatā) is already satisfied by the direct audition (śruti);

thus, two simultaneous requirements (ākāṅkṣā) are not possible, and so there is a contradiction. The meaning of this is as follows: from the first understanding of the connection between word-meanings derived from the direct audition...

Since the suitability for the instrument (*karaṇaidamarthya*) is obtainable through the specific ritual purpose (*kāryaviśeṣa*) understood first from the direct Vedic statement (*śrauta*), the requirement for a specific purpose is already satisfied;

thus, two simultaneous requirements do not arise. Consequently, because there is an application (*viniyoga*) in both cases, there is a contradiction between the mantra-text and [the general requirement]. This state of the mantra and the "grasper" (*grāhaka-grahaṇa*)—namely, their dependence on a purpose prior to the application based on the direct Vedic statement—is what constitutes their lack of established capacity (*akṛtasāmarthyatva*).

The application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra-sentence has been explained by the two terms *vākya* and *prakaraṇa* as they appear in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*). By the word *vākya*, the mantra-sentence is meant; by the word *prakaraṇa*, the meaning is the enjoining injunction (*grāhakaniyoga*) [of that sentence]. These two possess the capacity (*sāmarthya*) [to effect application]. (1) Bh. P. 846.

The two applications of the mantra are either those whose efficacy has been established (*kṛtasāmarthya*) or those whose efficacy has not been established (*akṛtasāmarthya*); the state of being such is their "reality" (*tattva*). Therefore, the remoteness of the object is logically established.

In this regard, the essence of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and final (siddhānta) positions is as follows: First, by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the mantra dedicated to Indra is enjoined for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire.

Likewise, by means of indicative power (*liṅga*), which has acquired authoritative status as a regulator of the specific application within the general task established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is also enjoined for the worship of Indra. Nor is there any contradiction, because by virtue of the force of these two separate injunctions, the denotation [of the mantra] is justified in both cases through two distinct performances.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): But the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows. A mantra recited in proximity to an injunction regarding a specific qualification (*adhikāraniyoga*), once grasped by the "grasper" (the injunction) and having its status as a subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*) understood from the outset through direct statement (*śruti*), subsequently has its fitness for being an instrument (*karaṇaidamarthya*) understood through its inclusion [in the ritual]. Since it lacks any further expectancy for another function, an application (*viniyoga*) is impossible; therefore, application even by means of indicative power (*liṅga*) is not tenable. Moreover, there is no simultaneity between application by direct statement and application by indicative power.

Because the application of direct statement (*śruti*) is more rapid than the application of context (*prakaraṇa*), and because the application of indicative power (*liṅga*) depends upon the application of context, [direct statement prevails].

What is the example for a conflict between indicative power and syntactical connection (*vākya*)? "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee, for the ghee... (*syonaṃ te sadanaṃ karomi ghṛtasya...*)... [and so forth].

[The opponent attempts to challenge the commentary] with the mantra: "I fashion a comfortable seat; sit upon it, O immortal one, and take your stand in it, O essence of rice, being well-disposed. Now, has it not been stated that the reason [for the subordination of *liṅga* to *vākya*] is the remoteness of the meaning (*arthaviprakarṣa*), and that the dependence and independence of *liṅga* and *vākya* are as follows: namely, *liṅga* is independent of *vākya* regarding the making of the seat and the establishing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)?

A *mantra* is capable of being applied after it has been analyzed [into its constituent parts]. A sentence (*vākya*), however, is capable of applying [a mantra] only with reference to the application based on indicative power (*liṅga*).
For when one part has been applied by the indicative power acting as the applicator, the inclusion of another part within that same [application] is then postulated by means of the sentence.
Therefore, the remoteness of the meaning is indeed manifest. Why then is another section (*adhikaraṇa*) commenced? Not merely—

This very section is the subject at hand. This is indeed a critique of all the preceding sections. For the remoteness of meaning is easy to understand everywhere. How so? First, it was stated that *liṅga* (indicative power) is stronger because of its independence; it was also stated that *vākya* (syntactical connection), which has a relationship understood through the mutual connection of word-meanings, is stronger than the relationship of *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting), which is characterized by the purposefulness (*aidamarthya*) [of the whole]. For the syntactical connection of the sentence-meaning is understood through the meanings of the words already being mutually connected.

Through context (*prakaraṇa*), the relationship between the sentence and its meaning is understood as one characterized by the purposefulness of the instrument (*karaṇaidamarthya*), not as one characterized by the syntactic connection of word-meanings (*padārthānvaya*). Therefore, it was shown in the investigation of Direct Assertion (*śruti*) and Indicative Power (*liṅga*) that context requires Indicative Power for the relationship characterized by the syntactic connection of word-meanings. Furthermore, since Order (*krama*) depends upon that [context], Context is stronger than Order; for once a general relationship has been established by Context, Order effects the specific [application].

The connection with the instrument [of action] is as follows: since even sequence (krama) establishes a specific connection with the instrument and is understood from the Veda itself, it is indeed stronger than name (samākhyā). For proximity (sannidhāna)—which is accepted as a condition in the acquisition of the knowledge that words denote connected meanings—is the cause of the connection; since that is understood directly from the Veda, it establishes the connection more swiftly and is therefore stronger than name.
Therefore, those who pride themselves on their knowledge of the remoteness of the meaning [of the Vedic text] maintain that these legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) need not be undertaken.
To this, it is replied: as for what was stated—that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger because it is independent—that is incorrect. Why?
Because the understanding of what is to be done arises from the entire mantra; the understanding of what is to be done does not arise from a single word alone.
(1) G. However, elsewhere [p. 782] this is the intention: for as many words as are employed, so many, when combined, convey a single meaning; they are capable [of doing so].

First, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is determined on the basis that these words intend to convey a single meaning; subsequently, such a unified unit is applied to a specific ritual act by means of its indicative power (*liṅga*). As for the literal sense: since the entire mantra sentence conveys what is to be done and thereby brings about the knowledge of performance, the knowledge of performance does not arise from a single word alone. Therefore, it is the sentence itself that first establishes the mutual relationship between the words.

The cause is the sentence (*vākya*). Because it conveys the meaning of a single sentence, the understanding of the function (*kārya*) of the collection of words and their mutual relation is subsequently derived from the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, the view arises that the sentence alone is more powerful. Furthermore, this must necessarily be accepted:
that the relation of words exists first of all by their own nature through their capacity to convey a single meaning; for otherwise—

Furthermore, there would be no connection with other words such as *sadanam* (seat) that are not in conflict; only the single word *sadanam* would be employed. Why? Because the indicative power (*liṅga*) is independent of other words in its application (*viniyoga*). Therefore, this distinction between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and indicative power (*liṅga*) is difficult to discern, and thus this section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been commenced. Now, [one might object]: in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) [claims] that by means of syntactical connection, the whole...

He states that there is an application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra, and not by means of *liṅga* (indicative power); regarding this, he says: "And this is precisely the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*)—that *liṅga* is the applicator only when it depends upon a connection with another word. The meaning of this is as follows: that applicability of the sentence (*vākya*) which was asserted by the proponent of the prima facie view does not exist independently of *liṅga*; rather, it is *liṅga* alone that is the applicator. However, that...

"Of the group of words mutually connected"—thus, in both cases, namely in the making of the seat and in the establishing of the *puroḍāśa* cake, there is the application of the entire mantra. As for what was stated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*)—that "because the indicative power (*liṅga*) is sublated even by direct statement (*śruti*)"—what is this reason for the sublation of indicative power by syntactical connection (*vākya*)? For it is not logical that what has been sublated by direct statement should be further sublated by something else.
(1) Bhāṣya p. 849 (2) G. *svavirodhi* [p. 783].
Therefore, this appears to be merely written by a fool. This is not written by a fool; another intention has been expressed.

Of what? Just as *liṅga* (indicative power) is sublated by *śruti* (direct statement) because it serves as the cause for knowing the connection between word-meanings through syntactic relation—and because [the mantra] is to be employed in a single action due to the unity of the purpose—so too is it sublated by *vākya* (syntactical connection), since the mantra is to be employed in a single action that requires an expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this, it is replied: "The application of the *yajus* (prose formula), however, is word by word. The meaning of this is: [in the case of] a continuous [text]...

There is no division of the recited *yajus* mantras from any other source. As many as constitute a collection of letters that convey a single meaning, so many form a single word. The understanding of the meaning, however, arises from the application (*viniyoga*). And application consists in the illumination of a ritual performance; thus, that by which a performance is illuminated is its object of application. Since a ritual performance is illuminated by a single word, the application belongs to that much alone. Now, regarding the view that words denote [their meanings] as already related (*anvitābhidhāyitva*)...

Even so, let there be an application of both [the primary and secondary elements] with respect to the second word. How, then, can other non-contradictory words be included? To this he says: "Furthermore, by virtue of the purpose (*kāryataḥ*), there is unity among the words; as long as there is a single purpose, the connection with other words is not contradictory.

The meaning of this is as follows: when the question arises as to how other words also—studied within the context (*prakaraṇa*)—are to be included, [the answer is that] they are included through whatever means of connection they possess.

To the extent that they are understood as being connected to a single purpose, they enter [into the ritual] despite the contradiction of their gender. However, when another function is already established through gender, and there is an opposing factor, it is not possible to understand a connection with yet another function. For it is not logical for something to depend on another when it has already obtained its own function inherently. To the question "How is its function obtained inherently?", he says: "Precisely because the *yajus* formulas are prescribed for each individual word."

But why is there a prescription of the *yajus* formulas for every step? To this he says: "For here, the status of being a mantra is determined by its function (*kārya*). The classification of mantras depends upon the function; the function does not depend upon the mantra. Since the status of being a single mantra is understood prior to the function, the function does not [determine it] afterwards. (1) G. liṅgetā vi.

Since there is no evidence for the unity of the mantra prior to its function—just as in the case of the *ṛks* and *sāmans*—the proposed construction is reversed; for the measure of the *ṛks* and *sāmans* is known from other sources alone. Therefore, [one must consider] the relationship with the mere connection of word-meanings, independent of the ritual function.

Indicative power (*liṅga*) subverts what is based on syntactical connection (*vākya*). The meaning is that indicative power subverts that mutual relationship of words which is based on syntax—that is, the connection of words through the mere mutual relation of word-meanings when they are devoid of a specific function (*kārya*). But surely, this same [principle] would apply even in the case of direct statement (*śruti*), such as "With the *aindrī* [verse], one worships the Gārhapatya fire"? In that case too, it would follow that the word "Indra" should be applied separately for the worship of Indra.
He refutes this: It is true that [the mantra] would attain the status of a *yajus* if it were such; however, its application (*viniyojyatva*) has been shown to belong to the *ṛks*.

Furthermore, the function of the *ṛks* is established by their nature as mantras; it was stated in the section on "Oneness of Purpose" (*Arthaikatvāt*) that the function of the *ṛks* occurs through their application only when they are understood as being endowed with meter (*chandas*). As for the *yajus*, even where there is an application such as "To the wood (*iṣe tvā*"), there too [it is determined] by the act of taking up (*upādāna*).

There is a separation [of sentences]. To the extent that something is taken up for a purpose, to that extent it is a single *yajus* (sacrificial formula); thus, separation arises from the act of taking up [the words]. Furthermore, there is no cause for being a *yajus* other than the purpose and the taking up [of the words]. As for the word "purpose" (*kārya*), its inclusion occurs solely through the purpose itself; while others, which lack a specific purpose, are included by virtue of their syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with that [purposeful part]. Therefore, a division of sentences is logical due to the difference in purpose.

Furthermore, as for that which has been shown by the author of the Bhāṣya—"But surely, even when there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*) operates"—that appears to be improper. Why? The answer is: "In this case, the determination of the meaning is based on the purpose (*kārya*). Why? [As stated in] the Bhāṣya, p. 824.

Because of the difference in their effects, there are two distinct meanings; the determination of meaning does not arise from capacity alone, such that there would be a single meaning by virtue of its own capacity.
For it has been established that capacity is a logical mark (*liṅga*) only when it is dependent upon an effect, not when it is independent of an effect. And as for what was [previously] refuted—

"For in this case, remoteness from the purpose (*arthaviprakarṣa*) is the cause of sublation; and since there is a verbal expression of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) as part of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyabhūta*), there is a remoteness from the indicative mark.

This seems incorrect. It has been stated that the indicative mark which serves as the cause for syntactical unity is not [itself] an indicative mark. For that which is devoid of an effect is not an indicative mark, and the consideration of sublation is inappropriate for what is not an indicative mark. To this it is replied: because of the application (*viniyoga*) to each individual word.

Furthermore, since the accomplishment of the ritual purpose (*kārya*) is possible through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the suspicion that [the word *syona*] functions as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is justified. Even in the case of syntactic unity, there is no total absence of a ritual purpose; for, by serving as a qualifier of the purpose—as in the case of words such as *syona*—it obtains its own purpose. Thus, the suspicion regarding its status as an indicative mark is indeed justified. However, the refutation is also appropriate because of the remoteness of the meaning (*arthaviprakarṣāt*), since direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than even an indicative mark, and an indicative mark is stronger than syntactic connection (*vākya*). Therefore, in this instance, there is neither direct statement nor an indicative mark or syntactic connection.

The *tantra* (the common application) is intended exclusively [for the primary purpose]. However, that which is remote from the direct meaning of the Vedic text (*śruti*) or from the syntactic connection of word-meanings (*padārthānvaya*), being non-obtaining and non-instructive, is the meaning of the Sūtra. Therefore, it is established that there is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to the difference in the functions to be performed. If there is a split of the sentence, then what is the basis for the pronoun "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "sit upon that"? The answer is: we say that its basis is the previously mentioned subject matter.

The meaning is that whatever was introduced in the preceding sentence is denoted by the word *tat* (that). Now, an objection is raised: "If this is the case, then the former [sentence] would necessarily result in being for the sake of another (*parārthatā*), and consequently, it would follow that the sentence is more powerful. He refutes this: "It is not necessarily the case that in a reference (*parāmarśa*) there must be a state of being for the sake of that (*tādarthyam*).
[Page 786]

It occurs; because even when one thing is intended for another purpose, it may indeed be referred to by a pronoun intended for yet another purpose, so there is no fault. Just as the rule "the independent agent is the *kartṛ*" is referred to by the word "that" in the rule "and its instigator is the *hetu*," and just as in the Veda, in the passage "of this very [sacrifice] among the *revatī*s," it is established that the denotation of the word is more powerful than the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Now, how is it with regard to sentence (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*)?
An indication of the topic (*adhikaraṇa*). Here, the Bhāṣya asks, "What, then, is context (*prakaraṇa*)? and this [commentator] raises an objection to that: "What is this question?

The meaning is that this question is not tenable. How so? It has been stated that context is the application (*viniyoga*) [of a subsidiary] due to the requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). That by which something is applied is "application"; that by which one is applied because of the requirement for the procedure is what is called "context."

Since the context (*prakaraṇa*) has been thus determined on the grounds that it requires a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), we do not know for what purpose this question is asked. He provides the justification: "It is said here that [the context] requires a procedure; yet we do not know whose requirement for a procedure this is. That to which this requirement for a procedure belongs is stated here as "of the thing to be done" (*kartavyasya*), meaning the object of the mandate (*niyoga*).

This is the meaning: here, regarding that which is to be performed—which possesses a threefold expectancy as to "what," "by what," and "how"—there is this third expectancy in the form of "how" (katham), namely the expectancy for the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) characterized by the qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). That is *prakaraṇa*; by means of that, there is the application (*viniyoga*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. This application is caused by that [expectancy], not merely by the state of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā-mātra*), nor by anything else devoid of the expectancy for the *itikartavyatā*.

Therefore, the meaning of the question is appropriate, because there is ignorance regarding the specific requirement [of the context], namely, the very nature of the *prakaraṇa* characterized by the desire for the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*). And the answer is also appropriate; this was asked as being useful for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), given the expectancy for application (*viniyoga*).

[Page 787] When the response "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is given, it will result in the attainment of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). The meaning of the *Bhāṣya*, however, is as follows: "Context is that statement or exposition which pertains to what is to be performed—the meaning of the injunction—which is characterized by a requirement for the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*)."
When the question arises as to what that section is, he says:
“For that is the commencement of the act of speaking—that is, the act of exposition—of that which is to be done; the task to be performed is thus fulfilled.”

That which is to be accomplished must reach completion, and this cannot occur without the constituent part consisting of the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*). Therefore, the statement that expresses those [details] constitutes the "commencement" (*prārambha*), as there is an expectancy for them. To explain how that very expectancy arises, he says: "This [injunction], beginning with the injunction and ending with the injunction, is dependent upon the subsequent injunction.
It is that.

Thus, the injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth, which consist of the form of "what is to be done," requires the "manner of performance" (*itikartavyatā*) up to the end of the injunction; for without that, it is impossible to comprehend or to carry out [the action]. Now, an objection may be raised: in the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated that the "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is the presentation of the injunction as requiring the manner of performance, and not that the injunction itself possesses a requirement for the manner of performance. Therefore, how can context be said to be characterized by the "desire for the manner of performance"? How [is this so]?

It is said that the *prakaraṇa* (context) will explain that the very action (*kārya*) requires a procedure (*itikartavyatā*). The author of the Bhāṣya stated that "the *prakaraṇa* is the exposition" in order to show that the injunction (*vidhi*), which consists of the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatārūpa*), requires a procedure precisely while it is in the state of being expounded. Therefore, it is the *niyoga* (obligation) itself that requires a procedure while it is being expounded; and its third requirement is the *prakaraṇa*.

Thus, there is no contradiction. Now, regarding the statement that when there is a conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and physical proximity (*prakaraṇa*), these two causes are of equal strength—what is the intention here? The questioner’s underlying thought is this: "Syntactical connection alone is stronger, because it is the cause for establishing the relationship between the meanings of the words.
[The author] explains the questioner’s intention: "Because the relationship exists for the sake of the ritual action (*kārya*), both are employed by means of that action. This is the meaning.

The syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of all constituent elements is for the sake of the action (*kārya*); therefore, even that which is assigned by means of a sentence (*vākya*) is assigned by the action alone, and likewise, that which is assigned by means of context (*prakaraṇa*) is also assigned by the action alone. Thus, when there is a conflict between these two, the assignment is equal. Alternatively, since syntactic connection is sublated in the absence of an action, on the contrary, context itself is stronger, because a sentence is dependent upon it. Thus...
The Commentator has stated that the sentence is sublated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*). The meaning of this is as follows:

for the context (*prakaraṇa*) is indeed the task itself, which consists in the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). And when there is a conflict with that [task], the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is sublated. For example, [as in the case of] the *prayāja*...
(1) Bh. P. 853 (2) R. prapṛṣṭamabhi...

In the cases of *jaśeṣeṇa* and *saktūn*, it is the context (*prakaraṇa*) that is stronger than the sentence (*vākya*). This is because a sentence is a means of cognition (*pratyaya*) regarding the action (*kārya*). A "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is so called because one cognizes by means of it; thus, it is precisely the action that is communicated by the sentence.

In the case of a conflict with a *liṅga*, a sentence (*vākya*) is weak, because subordinate elements (*guṇa*) are weaker when they conflict with a principal element (*pradhāna*). With this intention, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: “Since the sentence is sublated by the *liṅga*, it is also proper that it be sublated by the context (*prakaraṇa*).
