To this it is replied: here too, the reason stated is "due to remoteness of meaning" (*arthaviprakarṣāt*). How is remoteness of meaning stated? [Because] for the sake of the task...

The connection [of the mantra] must be postulated by her [the injunction]. This has been stated in the section on Direct Assertion and Indicative Power (*śrutiliṅgādhikaraṇa*): "Since it is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) that [the mantra] expresses what is connected [to the action], its connection must be postulated as being for the sake of the task (*kārya*), in the capacity of a procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
And once the connection of that which has been postulated is established as being for the sake of the task, there is no further connection.
Because of the contradiction between what has already been enjoined and further enjoinment, just as in the case of *liṅga* (indicative power), it is possible to postulate [an application];

however, for that which has already established a connection or has been enjoined, it is not possible to postulate another connection through the context (*prakaraṇa*) by means of the sentence (*vākya*), because of the contradiction between what has been enjoined and further enjoinment.

This is just as when *liṅga* contradicts *śruti* (direct statement). If, in accordance with the connection to the meaning of the sentence, there were no purposefulness toward the injunction (*niyoga*), then...

In another case, a different syntactic connection might indeed be postulated on the basis of context (*prakaraṇa*). However, in the present instance, since the acceptance of the connection understood through the sentence (*vākya*) does not cause the status of being for the sake of an action (*kāryārthatā*) to disappear, the connection apprehended by the sentence is stronger because it is apprehended first. Therefore, the sentence is more powerful. Now, if the sublation of context occurs solely due to the remoteness of the purpose (*arthaviprakarṣa*), then this matter would already have been settled by the section concerning Direct Assertion and Indicative Power (*śrutiliṅgādhikaraṇa*); for in that very place, its [sublation] was stated on account of such remoteness of purpose.

To this he says: "This elaboration of the *adhikaraṇa* (topic-section) is to be viewed like a logical mark (*liṅga*), for the purpose of making known the difficulty of comprehension regarding remoteness. Its meaning is as follows: it is true that weakness arises from remoteness, but that very remoteness is difficult to comprehend; therefore, this elaboration of the *adhikaraṇa* is for the sake of fully understanding that.
An example is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: the recitation of the *sūktavāka*. Now, what is the example when there is a conflict between *prakaraṇa* (context) and *krama* (order)?

Regarding the term "taking away" (*haraṇa*): here too, it serves merely as an indication of the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*). The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the order (*krama*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be of equal strength.
(1) Bh. P. 853 (2) G. *kāryārthatā’nveti* [p. 789].

How so? The author of the Bhāṣya provides an answer that constitutes a partial justification: he points out that ignorance itself is the proof for their being of equal strength, stating, "We do not perceive any distinction.
The objector refutes this: "Is their equality due to ignorance?"

It is established; the sense is that it is not established at all. For whether knowledge possesses equal or unequal strength, its object is that which is to be known (*jñeya*); such is not the case for non-knowledge (*ajñāna*). An adherent of a particular school (*ekadeśin*) says: "But surely even non-knowledge has indeed been presented as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*. The objector himself replies: "That was stated in the first chapter (*pāda*) to be merely a matter of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-mātra*). Furthermore, those [properties] of non-existence...

Even those who maintain that [non-existence] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) hold, in their own view, that the object of cognition (*prameya*) is merely the absence of another means of valid cognition and its corresponding object. That which is perceived by another means of valid cognition, such as a jar, has as its object of cognition merely the absence of that [perception]; there is nothing else. Therefore, in this context—namely, the state of being equal in strength or unequal in strength—it is impossible to say that it is merely the absence of the object of another means of valid cognition; hence, non-existence [is not the object].

The object of knowledge (*prameya*). Now, a certain partisan (*ekadeśin*), having been refuted, asks: "How then is this Bhāṣya [to be understood], namely: 'We do not perceive any particularity'? The objector says:
"The author of the Bhāṣya himself should be questioned on this point. The proponent of the defense says: "To this it is replied:
this is merely the talk of one who is pretentiously learned; [it is not that] 'the author of the Bhāṣya himself should be questioned here.'"

Thus [it is said]. For this is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya: that no distinction between these two is known here—that is, no distinction is known between these two, namely *krama* (sequence) and *prakaraṇa* (context), regarding their application (*viniyojakatva*) to the acts such as gambling (*videvana*). If a distinction were known, then only one would be the applicator.

It might be so; we do not perceive any distinction. Therefore, both are the means of application (*viniyojaka*). But is it not the case that context (*prakaraṇa*) alone is the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)?
The distinction is that the *anvaya* (syntactic connection) makes known the relationship of all the instruments (*karaṇa*) with the acts such as gambling; this is understood. To this he says:

"In every case, because of the continuity of the context (*prakaraṇa*), even the sequence (*krama*) is understood as having a function. Because the context—the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-niyoga*)—is continuous throughout, the sequence also possesses a function; through sequence, too, there is application (*viniyoga*) precisely by virtue of its function. And from the function...

Proximity (*sannidhi*) makes known that which is connected [with it]. For if there were no connection with a purpose (*kārya*), then proximity would certainly not make known the connection. But since proximity possesses a purpose, it therefore indeed makes known the connection. On the contrary, it is the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself that is understood here as being sublated by proximity, because proximity effects a restriction to a particular [instance]. For by means of context, [the injunction applies] generally to everything—

The connection with the instruments (*karaṇa*) is to be understood. In that regard, the application (*upasaṃhāra*) is made specifically to the particular instrument by means of the sequence characterized by proximity (*sannidhi*).
Why, then, is the application made specifically? To this he says: "For it is not possible to speak of a postulation (*kalpanā*) of proximity when [proximity] has already been established.
The meaning of this is: when the connection with all instruments must be effected by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*) as the authority (*pramāṇa*), proximity necessarily exists with all of them.

It must be inferred [as present], because a relationship with that which is not proximate is untenable; for expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatva*) are the causes of a relationship. Nor is it proper to disregard an established proximity and instead infer a further proximity, just as one does not infer a further syntactic connection once it is established. Just as when a syntactic connection is established, no further relationship is inferred, so it is here as well. Therefore, it is held that order (*krama*) alone is more powerful. But even if proximity exists, there is still expectancy—

Since there is no distinction [between them], it cannot be that [the connection] exists merely by virtue of being related; thus, even *krama* (order) has a dependence on *prakaraṇa* (context). Likewise, expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is not a cause for connection without proximity (*sannidhi*). Therefore, because the two are mutually dependent, it is logical that they possess equal strength, and not that *krama* is stronger. Regarding this, he says: "That, moreover, was stated in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) as a statement made by way of concession (*anvāruhyavacana*); this is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhavāda*)."

But this is not so from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Thus, it has been demonstrated in the section on *śruti* and *liṅga* that this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is based on an equality of strength;
and this should be understood to apply everywhere.

To this it is replied: Context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger than Order (*krama*). Why? Because Order is not a cause for connection with respect to that which has no expectancy; there can be no connection by way of Order with that which lacks expectancy, for Order is merely proximity (*sannidhāna*). And a connection is not understood from mere proximity alone, as in the case of "The king’s wife, Devadatta’s man. Just as the word *bhāryā*— [the sentence remains incomplete in the source].

The meaning is that, because the connection with the word "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*) is already satisfied by its own relation [to the sacrifice], there is no further connection with the person (*puruṣa*). Even though the connection arises precisely from expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), he asks "why is that so? and replies: "And since expectancy is equal for those things situated within the same context (*prakaraṇa*), there is a connection of the gambling and other acts with all the primary elements. Now, one might ask: why does a connection not arise through expectancy even for those things situated in a specific order (*krama*)? To this he says:

From sequence arises expectancy; from expectancy arises syntactic connection (*anvaya*); and from syntactic connection arises subordination (*tādarthya*). This is what is meant by "remoteness of purpose" (*arthaviprakarṣa*).

Its meaning is as follows: because the sentence-meaning of the *abhiṣecanīya* rite—already rendered free of expectancy through its own constituent words and word-meanings by virtue of being uttered in proximity—is nonetheless present, one must first postulate an expectancy for other word-meanings such as the gambling (*videvana*) and so forth; and only after having postulated that expectancy does the syntactic connection occur.

[The relationship] must be inferred. Once the connection (*anvaya*) has been inferred, its subservience to that purpose (*tādarthya*) must be inferred. Thus, this subservience based on sequence is delayed.

However, for those things possessing a context (*prakaraṇa*), the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) arises immediately because they are incomplete; and by means of that [expectancy], the subservience to the purpose of the instrument (*karaṇaidamarthya*) is inferred. Therefore, subservience through context is more rapid.

As for what was stated—that there is a sequential withdrawal [of the procedure] due to expectancy—that is incorrect. Even if it pertains to all [the rites], the proximity of something must necessarily occur; therefore, that [proximity] is merely for the sake of the textual recitation (*pāṭha*). Its meaning is as follows: if there were an expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) regarding the intermediate injunctions contained therein, then the status of being the procedure would be restricted only to that in whose proximity it is recited. But here, [there is only] one [such instance].

Since the injunction governing the *rājasūya* constitutes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), its inclusion [in the context of other rites] is not possible. Therefore, those [elements] which have been excluded by those connected with the single injunction governing the *rājasūya*...

The instruments (karaṇas) are connected with the ritual procedures (itikartavyatā), such as the gambling and so forth. However, their proximity is necessarily incidental, since they could not otherwise be recited; thus, their proximity serves solely for the purpose of recitation, and not for the purpose of bringing about a connection. For it has been stated that it is proper to favor what has been set aside.
On this point, the Bhāṣya states: “There is syntactic unity with that which is recited in proximity to what possesses the context, even if it is complete.

Now, one might object: “Even without the phrase ‘even if it is complete,’ the intended meaning is indeed established; why then say ‘even if it is complete’? He provides the answer: This is what is meant—it is not that sequence (*krama*) is a means of valid cognition [for establishing syntactic unity], for if it were, there would be no syntactic unity at all. Now, as for expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)—

"Proximity" (*sannidhi*) means "fitness" (*yogyatva*); this is the reason for syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). It is true that these three alone are the causes for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; however, in this case, there is a relationship between the [sentence-meaning] and the [action-meaning]. And it has been stated that this [relationship] is connected precisely through the requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Furthermore, "sequence" (*krama*) has been stated as the proximity of the [sentence-meaning] and the [action-meaning].

This has been demonstrated in the examples "the king’s wife" and "Devadatta’s man. The intended meaning is as follows: this was stated—"even by that which is complete"—for the purpose of refuting an objection. For the opponent objects thus: "In the section concerning *krama* (order), both [order and context] are of equal strength due to their mutual dependence. Indeed, even when a connection is being established by means of *prakaraṇa* (context) as a form of procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it cannot be established without the presence of *sannidhi* (proximity). This is because—

The cause for the comprehension of a relationship is the conjunction of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatva*). Therefore, sequence (*krama*) must be considered in relation to the context (*prakaraṇa*). To this, the following refutation is offered: this syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is established through completion. For the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), which constitutes the sentence-meaning and consists of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is connected only with the subsidiary injunction (*aṅgavidhi*) that constitutes the sentence-meaning and is situated within the portion concerning the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

And that which constitutes a complete syntactical unity is due to the requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*); and since the requirement for a procedure belongs to a single primary injunction (*adhikāravidhi*) and not to the subsidiary injunctions (*aṅgavidhi*), there is a connection of the dice-playing (*videvana*) and other such acts with all the constituent parts (*karaṇa*). As for the literal meaning: if there is a sequence...

If authority were not accepted, there would be no single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) between all the ritual instruments and the *videvana* (shaking the dice) and so forth. The three factors—expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatva*)—combined together are the cause for syntactical unity. Therefore, even sequence (*krama*) must be respected.
When there is mutual dependence, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is equal; thus, both proximity characterized by expectancy and sequence serve as means of application (*viniyoga*).
Regarding the objection "this is not logical," the reply is as follows: It is true that these three alone are the causes for the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence.

However, in this case, the relationship between one sentence-meaning and another is connected solely through the requirement of the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), and not through the requirement of the relationship between action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*), as stated in the *Prakaraṇādhikaraṇa*. Furthermore, since a single injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) possesses the requirement of the *itikartavyatā*, it is by virtue of that [injunction] alone [that the connection is established].

In all cases, a connection based on context (*prakaraṇa*) is logical. Sequence (*krama*), however, is merely proximity (*sannidhāna*), as there is no intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) due to the absence of any expectancy for a procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*). Furthermore, a connection does not arise from mere proximity alone, as has been shown by the examples: "the wife of the king" and "the servant of Devadatta."

Now, it is considered which is stronger when there is a conflict between *krama* (order) and *samākhyā* (name): for *krama* arises from proximity to that which has a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) and is the cause for understanding a specific application; whereas *samākhyā* is itself a cause for a specific application. Thus, these two causes are of equal strength. Therefore, both are applicatory. The meaning of this is: "Be purified... (*śundhadhvam*).

Thus, the mantra reveals purification (*śundhana*). In that context, those things which are to be purified are required, because the sentence remains incomplete without them. Therefore, by virtue of proximity, the vessels for the *sānnāyya* offering are connected [to the mantra]. Consequently, since it reveals their purification, the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra is to the *sānnāyya* vessels.

By virtue of the name (*samākhyā*), [the mantra] applies to the *puroḍāśa* vessels; for the name functions as a specific indicator. Furthermore, since the *sānnāyya* vessels are recited in proximity to the *śundhana* mantra—which itself possesses the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) "because the name functions as a specific indicator"—sequence (*krama*) also serves as a cause for understanding a specific application.

Moreover, the name "Pauroḍāśika" is itself based on a specific factor, according to the rule: "The suffix *ṭhak* is applied to a word ending in *adhi*, when the sense is 'a work composed concerning that'."
In this context,
according to the rule "from *pauroḍāśa* and *puroḍāśa*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* [is applied]," the word *pauroḍāśa* is used in the sense of a treatise composed concerning the *puroḍāśa*.
It is prescribed as being located there. By the term *pauraudāśa*, those things related to the *puroḍāśa* cake are denoted;

thus, it is understood that the mantra has a connection specifically with the vessel containing that [cake], namely the section (*kāṇḍa*) that sets it forth. Therefore, both sequence (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*) are means of application (*viniyojaka*).

This being the case, it is replied: "The order is stronger, for that is Vedic; whereas the name, on the other hand, is worldly. Not understanding the meaning of this from the perspective of the three [means of proof], the opponent objects: "But surely, by saying this, you have stated that the name is not a means of valid knowledge at all. The meaning of this is: you, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*), indeed say that the name is merely worldly. By saying this, because of its worldly nature— *Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument as presented.*

It has been accepted that *samākhyā* (name/designation) is not a cause for determining the meaning of the Vedas; and thus, one might object that the authority of *samākhyā* would be destroyed everywhere. To this, he replies: "Do not say so. By this method, it is merely stated that there is a remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) of the meaning. But how is there a remoteness of meaning simply because it is worldly? It is said: For *samākhyā*, being based on a relationship, brings about the understanding of proximity (*sannidhāna*) and so forth. [This applies to] the worldly...

To begin with, a name (*samākhyā*) does not directly establish a connection regarding the meaning of the Veda; rather, being based on a connection, it postulates expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*) for the sake of establishing that connection. Order (*krama*), on the other hand, is itself proximity. Furthermore, it is not possible to postulate another proximity when proximity is already directly perceived. Thus, regarding direct proximity—

The genitive case is not used here in the sense of "regard" (nādara). The meaning is that it is not proper to assume another form of proximity while disregarding the direct proximity [of the name to its object]. This, then, is what is meant by "remoteness of meaning" (arthaviprakarṣa). How, then, is there a designation (samākhyā)? The meaning is: how can there be a designation without a relationship? It is established through inherence (samavāya) and other such relations, as in the expression "the Brahmin village. In that section (kāṇḍa), because of the inherence of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), due to its abundance or its priority, it is called *pauroḍāśika*.
The designation "Kāvya" is like the term "Brāhmaṇagrāma.
Now, as for what is stated here and there, namely, "this is sublated by that," [it refers to the following].

Regarding the statement, "This is sublated by that," one must consider whether that which is sublated has reached the object of the sublater or has not reached it; of what [interpretation] is this the commentary?

When the Bhāṣya was challenged, a partisan (ekadeśin) said: "We say that it does not explain anything at all. No part of the [sūtra] *śrutiliṅga* etc. is explained by this; therefore, this is not an explanation of anything. The challenger asked: "Then what is done here by this? Having been refuted, the partisan said: "The author of the Bhāṣya himself must be questioned regarding this, since he stated this."

The proponent of the ultimate argument says: To this it is replied—this commentary is supplementary to the investigation into the relative strength and weakness of direct assertion (*śruti*) and the other means of proof. How so? The answer follows: for the investigation of relative strength and weakness depends upon that which is to be sublated; indeed, that which is weak is what is sublated, and that which is strong is the sublater. Therefore, there can be no investigation of relative strength and weakness without something to be sublated. What, then, is that which is to be sublated now?

When a sublater reaches its object, is it sublated or is it sublated even without reaching it? In both cases, the fault has already been stated. If it has reached [the object], how can it be sublated? Because it is impossible. If it has not reached it, what is there to be sublated? Because that which is to be sublated would be non-existent. But surely, "sublation upon reaching" was demonstrated in the tenth [book]. Why, then, is "contradiction" shown when there is reaching? For that indeed is called "contradictory."

That which is not seen anywhere—attainment (*prāpti*) and sublation (*bādha*)—is indeed observed. How, then, can there be a contradiction between these two? For in the tenth [book], the sublation of the collection of archetypal items already attained is demonstrated. He provides the resolution: there is no fault if attainment occurs through functional necessity (*kāryataḥ*). There is no fault even in the sublation of what has been attained. For when something is attained through functional necessity, another function need not be postulated for it; therefore, that which is postulated...

r796] Since attainment is preceded by the task to be accomplished, sublation is logical either through the omission of the task or by having already fulfilled one's duty; it consists in the sublation of performance.

"But here, the instruction (upadeśa) is being considered. Nevertheless, why is that so? He says: "And by means of an instruction, an attainment is difficult to sublate. Why? We shall demonstrate that very point in the tenth [book]. For when there is an instruction, the action must be performed according to the instruction; thus, it is impossible to sublate it even through the requirements of the ritual act.
Why is this not demonstrated right here? It has indeed already been shown: "The subordinate elements (guṇas) repeat themselves for each primary element (pradhāna)."

By this commentary, it has already been shown that attainment through direct instruction (*upadeśa*) is difficult to refute. How is its unrefuted status demonstrated by the statement regarding the repetition [of the procedure] for each primary element? The answer is: by the admission of the authority of both, the demonstration is made through the statement regarding each primary element. When the authority of both—direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*)—is admitted, it follows that the subordinate elements (*guṇas*) are repeated for each primary element.

Since it has been stated thus, it has been shown that sublation (bādha) is impossible. For by speaking in this way, one accepts that the action must be performed according to the instruction (upadeśa). Therefore, what is obtained through an instruction cannot be sublated by another instruction. Furthermore, because there is no distinction in the manner of attainment, there can be no sublation of what is obtained from an instruction by something else obtained from an instruction. However, in the case of what is obtained through the requirement of the ritual action (kāryataḥ), since it is obtained through extension (atideśataḥ), it may be sublated by what is obtained from an instruction.
Sublation is logical. Therefore, it is improper to say that "this is to be sublated by that. It is not only improper when [the rule] has already been reached;
it is also improper when it has not yet been reached, because there is no possibility of its application. Indeed, only that which has become applicable deserves to be sublated, and nothing else.
At this point, those who know the sublation of instruction state: "Considering the application to be general, they disregard the particular..."
Those who are confused designate the cognition of what has been attained as being caused by a lapse of memory, just like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

However, because of the subsequent realization of the specific nature [of the object], that cognition ceases for them; this is the reason for the use of the term "sublation" (*bādha*). Its meaning is as follows: *barhir dārveṣadanam*...

In cases such as "dāmī," the application of a word's indicative power (*liṅga*) toward its own specific function is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the similarity between the indicative powers of both the applicator and the non-applicator, those who— considering that general application to be a valid cognition even in the case of the non-applicator,

and recollecting it— fail to perceive any distinction between that recollection of application and the actual knowledge of application, [conclude] that the knowledge of application is caused by a lapse of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*).

The phrase "the cause of which designation is the loss of the element 'I remember'" is an adverbial modifier of the action. Those who are deluded designate it as "we know [it] to be present. Just as in the case of mother-of-pearl, there is a cognition of silver; for when the mother-of-pearl is perceived merely through that form which is common to silver, a recollective cognition of silver arises, because its nature as a memory is not grasped.
Not perceiving any distinction, they designate the very recollection of silver arising from the cognition of silver as the "cognition of silver," saying, "We know the silver.

Likewise here too, they designate the recollection of attainment as the "cognition of attainment. However, through the perception of a distinction, that [designation] is set aside for them, [realizing]: "This is the recollection of attainment, not the cognition of attainment.
For, upon the perception of the distinction, it is understood that in reality no attainment is known here, due to the absence of the causal complex for attainment.

Due to separation, there is a lack of the causal totality (sāmagrī), which is shown to result from the remoteness of the object. Consequently, this "attainment" (prāpti) is remembered rather than known;

thus, even the linguistic usage based on attainment through knowledge is suspended, which is why the term "sublation" (bādha) is employed. In ultimate reality, however, this is simply the knowledge of the true nature (svarūpa-jñāna) itself—this has been determined in detail in the very first pāda. This, then, is the summary of the meaning here.

There is a common form shared by both the non-applicatory (*aviniyojaka*) and the applicatory (*viniyojaka*) [indicators such as *liṅga*]; when one recalls the status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) residing in the applicatory *liṅga* on the basis of that [common form] belonging to the non-applicatory *liṅga* and so forth, and because that recollection apprehends [the object] without grasping its specific distinction—thus failing to connect with the specific [differentiation]—both the designation and the practical usage occur that even the non-applicatory *liṅga* and so forth are "applicatory means of valid cognition. In that regard, the purpose—

Due to remoteness, when there is a conflict with direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and so forth, inferential signs (*liṅga*) and the like possess no authority; since they lack authority, their status as a means of valid cognition cannot be apprehended. Rather, because it is observed elsewhere and then remembered, the linguistic usage and designation [of these signs] cease upon the discernment of this distinction. Thus, the very authority of inferential signs and the like—which was previously established by a trustworthy person—is, though being remembered, set in motion as if it were being apprehended through linguistic usage due to the non-perception of the distinction; and by the removal of such linguistic usage, [the error is corrected].
It is designated as "being sublated.

But surely this type of sublation, characterized by non-attainment (*aprāptabādhalakṣaṇa*), was already stated in the very first pāda in the passage beginning with "for one whose instrument is defective" (*yasya ca duṣṭaṃ karaṇam*).

Why, then, has this been restated? The meaning is that this section (adhikaraṇa) need not have been commenced for the purpose of establishing a sublation of what has not yet been reached. The resolution [is as follows]:

There is a distinction here: in that case, because the object "mother-of-pearl" is not apprehended, and because there is a "loss" (pramoṣa) of the thought "I am remembering silver," the conventional designation [of the error] is established.
The meaning of this is as follows: the mother-of-pearl is perceived through a form common to silver;

and although it is distinct from silver, it is not understood to be distinct, because no other form—which would serve as the cause for the cognition of difference—is perceived. As it has been said: "another form..."

For the cognition of difference is based on [the perception of] another entity, not on the basis of a distinct object. And when that [cognition] occurs in such a manner, there arises a memory of silver. Furthermore, that silver is not perceived as distinct from the mother-of-pearl; therefore, the distinction between the mother-of-pearl being perceived and the silver being remembered is not apprehended. Likewise, even that memory of silver—

It is not determined as distinct from the act of perception because it lacks the conceptual construction that "this is memory. Therefore, memory—which is not determined as distinct from the perception whose object is the mother-of-pearl—induces both designation and linguistic usage based solely on that perception regarding the mother-of-pearl.

Consequently, since the establishment of the designation occurs through the mere recollection of that [perception], even a non-apprehended sublation (*aprāptabādha*) would be possible. However, in this case, by virtue of its being innate...

Since the consequence of equality indeed arises for both [means of proof], the discussion is commenced once again. Its meaning is as follows: because both *śruti* (direct statement) and *liṅga* (indicative mark) are means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the consequence of their equality arises. Therefore, one cannot say that the application (*viniyoga*) is merely remembered; rather, there is the doubt: "Why should this not also be the case that it is cognized by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) as a means of valid cognition? It is for the purpose of removing that doubt that this [section] has been commenced.

But what is the reason that, when both [the word and the indicative mark] are non-originative (*āgamika*), there occurs an equality [of authority]? And when there is an equality [of authority], by what further reason does sublation (*bādhaka*) occur through the word (*śruti*) even over the two, namely the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth? When there is an equality [of authority], by what reason is there sublation? To this it is said: because there is no contradiction (*viparyaya*) [of the cognition] by itself. For if, in this case, by itself—

If the misconception that "this indicative mark (liṅga) is [merely] a prompter" were to arise, then the cognition of equality would not occur. Furthermore, in this case, a misconception does not arise spontaneously as it does in instances such as mother-of-pearl; for while a person who has not examined the nature of the cause may spontaneously develop a misconception regarding mother-of-pearl and the like—thinking, for example, "this is not silver"—such is not the case here. How then [does it occur]?
He says:

"It exists. Furthermore, in this case, there is a reversal of application (*viniyoga-viparyaya*) brought about by the examination of the cause; therefore, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) must be commenced.

Here, the reversal is based on the examination of the nature of the cause of application regarding the two—the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grahaṇa*)—which have not yet accomplished their purpose within the context of the treatise.

Regarding the two types of *samāmnāna* (recitation): since the means of application (*viniyojaka*) consist of direct assertion (*śruti*) and the rest, while *samāmnāna* and its like have no power of application because their purpose is already fulfilled, it is established—upon examining the nature of the means of application—that only *śruti* and the others possess the power of application due to their proximity (*sannikarṣa*), whereas *liṅga* and the rest do so due to remoteness (*arthaviprakarṣa*).

On that basis alone, since the requirements of the "grasper" (*grāhaka*), the "taking up" (*grahaṇa*), and the recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa-samāmnāna*) are already satisfied, one might erroneously conclude the opposite: that *liṅga* and the rest lack the power of application.
This section must be commenced for the purpose of examining the nature of the applicator [of a rule]—namely, that "a person knows"—and for the purpose of making known the remoteness of the meaning.
And this commentary is intended for the sake of clarifying that [point]: this commentary is for the sake of clarifying that sublation (*bādha*) which was mentioned by means of that section.

But what kind of purification of sublation has been effected by this? He says: "This is a case of sublation of what has not yet attained [application]. And as to how there is sublation of what has not yet attained [application]...
This has indeed been shown. Therefore, this is the meaning of the Bhāṣya: "We say that the prior cognition has reached the object of the sublater.

We say that the prior cognition—the cognition of an inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth—has reached that which is the object of the sublater, such as direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*). It is not [sublated] in an ultimate sense.

It has been attained; however, we say that even though it is not actually attained, it is attained from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because there is no discernment of the distinction between attainment and recollection.
He asks, "How is there recollection of what has been attained? and replies: "Because the cause, which is the universal (*sāmānya*), exists.
This refers to [the universal] residing in the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, which have become means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Because a common form exists even in the absence of a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa). [Question: "Then how does it cease? It does not cease at all. [Answer: It is rather a recollection of what was attained;
however, there arises another cognition to the effect that "this is indeed a false cognition."
Recollection itself, which initiates the conventional usage of grasping [an object], is called false cognition;

and thus, the knowledge of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) alone becomes the sublater (*bādhaka*). For when that [true nature] is understood, the conventional usage based upon the former ceases. Thus, the purification by sublation is established.
Or rather, because of the context, it is secondary (*gauṇa*). Now this is considered: which is stronger—the proximity of the injunction (*niyoga*)—(1) Bh.

Or rather, is it proximity to the injunction (*niyoga*)? Since it has been established that when there is a conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), syntactical connection is stronger, the question is now considered whether or not there is such a conflict regarding the twelve *upasads* mentioned within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma. To establish that, this is considered: is the proximity of the Jyotiṣṭoma-related injunction stronger, and by virtue of that proximity?

Should the twelve-fold number of *upasads* be understood as being for the purpose of the *jyotiṣṭoma* injunction? Or rather, by virtue of its application (*viniyoga*), is there proximity (*sannidhi*)—proximity meaning a connection between ritual elements—and since that proximity belongs to the *ahīna* injunction, it is stronger; therefore, it serves the purpose of the *ahīna* injunction. For by the word *ahīna*, a sacrifice lasting twelve days, consisting of twelve nights, is denoted, since the word *ahīna* is the name of that [sacrifice].

However, there is no application [of the property] to that which lacks an entitlement (*ahīna*). Therefore, it is understood that the twelve-fold attendance (*upasattā*) belongs to the *ahīna* sacrifice;

and by virtue of that connection, the proximity of the injunction regarding its entitlement is understood. On the basis of that, the connection [to the sacrifice] is established. This is what is meant:

because of the proximity of the new-acquisition (*apūrva*) belonging to the entitlement of the Jyotiṣṭoma, does this [attendance], preceded by that connection, become a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the Soma-sacrifice through the context (*prakaraṇa*), or...?

"By virtue of the connection between the word-meanings, there is the grasping of what is not deficient and what is unprecedented (*apūrva*). In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers that because application (*viniyoga*) has a purposeful action as its object, when a connection with the action under discussion is possible, a connection with that very action is logical. The meaning of this is as follows: every application is a word-meaning, a relationship whose purpose is the application of the qualification (*adhikāra-niyoga*). Therefore, because it is primary, a connection with the application under discussion alone is proper.

How, then, is there application (*viniyoga*)? It is the connection between word-meanings. The answer is: because application has the purpose of accomplishing an action, it is explained through a figurative sense (*gauṇī vṛtti*) as being consistent with that—namely, consistent with the connection to the primary action. By this, the Soma sacrifice itself is expressed. If this is so, then it follows that syntactical connection (*vākya*) is weaker than context (*prakaraṇa*). He refutes this, saying: "No. Why?

When there is no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*)—that is, when there is no distinction in proximity (*sannidhāna*)—the sentence (*vākya*) is more powerful. For when a connection within a single context is established, if there is an application (*viniyoga*) in that very same context by means of both sentence and context, then the sentence is more powerful, as in the case of the *sūktavāka*.
However, where there is not even the proximity of the function (*kārya*), what will the sentence do there? And here, there is no proximity to the function of the *ahīna* sacrifice.

(1) There exists a single-contextual connection (*ekaprakaraṇa*) for the *ahīnayāga* sacrifice. Therefore, it is logical that the explanation of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) must conform to the purpose (*kārya*), and not that the purpose conforms to the constituent elements; this is correct.
"It is called *ahīna* because of its being diminished (*hīyamāna*);
however, for the primary [sacrifice], it is so because of the absence of connection."

To this it is replied: We have already stated that the connection between word-meanings is the cause of the relationship [between words]; we have said that whatever is the connection between two word-meanings is the cause of the relationship of "being for the sake of this" (*aidamarthya*). Furthermore, the very connection is understood through the effect (*kārya*). For as long as the connection between word-meanings is not apprehended, the connection with the effect cannot be established. Therefore, the connection is understood even through the effect. Nor is there a [lack of] connection...

In the case of comprehension, it is logical to abandon the established positive concomitance (*anvaya*); for when an elephant is already perceived, an inference based on the word "elephant" is not possible.

Therefore, it is proper to explain the meaning of a word as being without a counter-instance (*apratipakṣa*). Now, one might ask: if there is a counter-instance in the form of an effect (*kārya*), how can there be a lack of counter-instances? To this he says: indeed, only the word-meaning itself becomes a counter-instance to another word-meaning, but not the effect. For otherwise, if even the effect were [to serve as a counter-instance]...
If that were the case, then even the words of the *arthavāda* (eulogistic passages) would have to denote something to be performed (*kartavyatā*).

Consequently, all *arthavāda* words would possess a connection solely with an action to be accomplished (*kāryānvayitā*), rather than merely a connection with what is understood (*pratītyanvayitāmātra*). For their utility in providing praise depends upon their relationship with the connection between word-meanings; however, by the force of a connection with an action to be accomplished, all such words would instead become instructions for performance (*anuṣṭhānopadeśataiva*). This is because of the term "something to be performed" (*kartavyatā*).
The performance is thus described. Therefore, by virtue of the syntactical connection of the words "of the Ahīna," it is logical that this refers exclusively to another sacrifice.

But is not the status of being based on direct Vedic statement (*śrautatva*) exactly the same here? In one case, *ahīna* means "that which is not diminished" (*na hīyate*) in a Soma sacrifice; in the other, it means "a collection of days" (*ahnāṃ samūhaḥ*) in the context of an *ahīna* [rite].

In one instance there is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), while in the other there is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), namely the suffix *kha* according to the rule "the suffix *kha* is added to *ahan* when referring to a sacrificial rite.
But surely...

A negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is untenable due to a contradiction with the accentuation; for in a *nañ*-compound, by the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its original accent] when it signifies similarity, or ends in the third, seventh, or second case, or is an upamāna, an indeclinable, or a *kṛtya* suffix," the final acute of the compound is barred and the first member retains its original accent, resulting in an initial acute (*ādyudātta*) for the word *ahīna*.

This word is transmitted as having its middle syllable accented (madhyodātta). Since the status of being middle-accented is established when the suffix is treated as a secondary derivative (taddhita)—given that the accent of a suffix begins with the first syllable—it follows that this word ends in a taddhita suffix. Furthermore, since it does not apply to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice in its primary sense, how can it be said to be Vedicly authoritative (śrauta) in both cases? Even granting, for the sake of argument, its authority in both instances, this is a deliberation based on a hypothetical concession (kṛtvācintā).

This was stated in order to demonstrate that even by means of logic (*nyāya*), there is an understanding of logic; as he says: "What is the use of this deliberation of ours, considering that in one case [the term] is primary (*śrauta*) and in another it is secondary (*gauṇa*)? If a primary or secondary sense is not possible here, then there will be another example. Or rather, the Commentator considers [the word] to be conventional (*rūḍhi*); therefore, because it is etymological (*yaugika*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma—

According to the maxim that "conventional usage (rūḍhi) supersedes etymological derivation (yoga)," this [term] must be understood as conventional. And since it is established that it is primary in Soma sacrifices, it follows that its status is Vedic (śrauta) in one instance and secondary (gauṇa) in the other. But why does the Commentator consider it to be conventional? To this he says: "Because of the non-observation of its usage in Sattra sacrifices. Now, this is incorrect, because it would result in [terms like] *paṅkaja* ("born in mud") also being considered conventional; for they too [denote] lotuses...

Even in other cases, such as with the word *paṅkaja* (mud-born), they are not applied [as a whole]. It is said: it is appropriate that words like *paṅkaja* possess a derivative (*yaugika*) meaning, because the words *paṅka* and *ja* have established capacities through their separate usage. However, in this case, the word *ahīna* is not observed to be used for a collection (*samūha*). Therefore, since its application would otherwise be untenable according to any established capacity, a [new] capacity must be postulated. In that regard, the twelvefold [set] belongs to the collection itself.

In the case of sacrifices such as the *śāha* and others, which are enjoined by the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) and whose performers are not fixed, a [conventional] power (*śakti*) is postulated because they are observed in usage. However, this does not mean that the word *ahīna* is etymological (*yaugika*). For if its usage were also observed in the context of a *satra*, then—out of fear of postulating multiple powers—one would have to postulate the power for the word *ahīna* itself. But this is not the case. Therefore, this word *ahīna* functions solely through a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*).

Thus, this is merely conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Why, then, is there a rule for secondary derivation (*taddhita-vidhi*)? The rule for secondary derivation serves only to provide an etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*), just as the rule for compound formation (*samāsa-vidhi*) does in the case of *śunaḥśepa* and similar words. For instance, in the word *śunaḥśepa*, by means of the collective power of the whole, even though its constituent parts lack case-endings, [the compound is formed].

Even in the case of a present compound, there is a rule for its formation: "There is an optional non-elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case-ending, as an addition to the rule, in the words *śunaḥ-śepa*, *puccha*, and *lāṅgūla*.
Furthermore, the purpose of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is the prescription of specific accents. Therefore, this example is indeed appropriate.

"Or rather, it is connected with duality and plurality because there is no injunction for that [singular number]. But is this not already covered by the previous section? For it is not proper to abandon a perceived syntactic connection merely out of regard for the ritual purpose; thus, the abandonment of the perceived connection with duality and plurality is not proper out of regard for the ritual purpose at hand. He provides the resolution: "True, but here there is an additional doubt. Even in the present case..."

Because the possibility of duality and plurality exists, there is the further objection that there is no contradiction between the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*). But how is it possible even in the case under discussion? To this he says: "In the performance of obligatory rites according to one's capacity, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the inclusion of another sacrificer, or else the expression using a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) refers to the wife. The meaning of this is: for one who is entitled to the obligatory rite, according to his...

The performance according to capacity: in that case, when a single sacrificer is unable to carry out the entire procedure, he shall perform it in conjunction with another sacrificer. In that situation, the requirement of having only a single agent—which is merely a subsidiary element—will be waived. In such a state, even in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the possibility of multiple sacrificers arises. Likewise, by including the wife as well, there is the designation of "the two sacrificers" (*yajamānayoh*) based on the principle of singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*).
It is inferred that [the rule applies] "to those who are sacrificing. Therefore, there is no displacement of the injunction regarding the *pratipad* verses.

"Not due to the connection with the original nature. To this it is replied: First of all, the entry of another sacrificer is not possible. Why? Because it is said that the sacrificer [is like] "barley-meal" (*śaktu*). In that case, for that which is impossible, there is either a figurative interpretation (*gauṇārthatā*) or its abandonment; however, there is no application by means of taking up another sacrificer. The meaning of this is: the entitlement (*adhikāra*) belongs to only one person.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, because there is a single agent for the subject matter, when there is a distinction of entitlement (*adhikāra*), there is a distinction of agents for each entitlement; thus, the performances (*prayoga*) are distinct for each sacrificer (*yajamāna*). In that case, if several sacrificers were to perform the sacrifice together, since the performance is one and the entitlement of one alone would be established due to its unity, there would be only one sacrificer and not many. Therefore, even in the performance according to one's capacity (*yathāśakty-anuṣṭhāna*), [the rule applies].

It is stated that the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) preceded by the right of entitlement (*adhikāra*) belongs to a single sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and not to two sacrificers acting in conjunction; thus, in a performance involving a single sacrificer, that which is impossible [in that context] is either treated figuratively (*gauṇatā*) or abandoned, but there is no inclusion of another person as a sacrificer. At most, if one person is unable to perform the rite, another person may be included during the stage of agency (*kartravasthā*), yet the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is not denotative of such a person.

And there is an injunction for a specific *pratipad* with reference to the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*). Now, one might object: if the *pratipad* is enjoined with reference to the sacrificer, then—since the qualification of that which is being referred to is not intended to be significant—and since even in the present context a mere sacrificer can possess the entitlement (*adhikāra*), an "exaltation" (*utkarṣa*) [of the rule] would be untenable. To this we reply: the words "for two" and "for many" are terms referring to the person to be designated; and that refers specifically to the subject of the sacrificer.

It is stated [in the text] "with reference to the sacrificer" (*yajamānoddeśena*). Therefore, the displacement (*utkarṣa*) is logical. And when the sacrificer is being led in here, the fulfillment of the ritual performance (*prayogasampat*) does not occur through the inclusion of another sacrificer; rather, it occurs through the inclusion of the agent (*kartṛ*) in general. This being the case, neither duality nor plurality of the sacrificer is possible in the archetype (*prakṛti*), namely the Jyotiṣṭoma—this is the meaning. As for what was also said regarding the wife (*patnī*)—

It might be argued that the designation "of two sacrificers" or "of many" is also logically consistent [if it referred to the wife]. That too is incorrect. Therefore, the mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) does not apply with reference to the wife, because in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical retention of one), there is no mention of the woman alone, since she is singular.

Because a mere woman has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) anywhere, when there is a *ekaśeṣa* (a grammatical formation where only one of two similar words remains), the second [referent] necessarily understood must also be a male.
Therefore, the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) does not intend the wife; rather, what is intended is two males. But surely, even the intention regarding the wife—[is that not also possible]?
[The opponent argues: "The conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) certainly exists [in the case of the *ādhāna*], just as in the case of the statement ‘wearing linen garments’;

the same will apply here as well. To this, he says: "But in the *ādhāna*, [the conjunction] refers to the wife by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because of the impossibility of the literal sense (*śrauta*). The meaning of this is as follows: in the *ādhāna*, the mutual conjunction refers to the wife through indication, because the literal sense is impossible.

Because mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is impossible with the intention of referring to two males, and because there are no two males in the present context of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*), [the dual number cannot apply]. Now, one might argue: "Even here in the present ritual, since there is no plurality of males, let figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) be resorted to. That is not so; for the cognition of plurality of males derived from the syntactical statement (*vākya*) cannot be sublated by the context (*prakaraṇa*). In the case of the fire-laying, however, the hearing of the word "fire-laying" itself occurs through the syntactical statement, and that refers to the subject at hand; thus, it does not denote any other thing.

Because it serves as an antidote (*pratipakṣatvāt*), figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is appropriate. He states another argument: "Just as a mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) with the wife is not possible in the sacrifice, so we shall explain in the sixth [book]. Entering by way of coexistence, the wife is not eligible for mutual conjunction; and for that very reason, there is no contradiction with the singular number in the word 'yajeta' (he should sacrifice), as we shall explain in the sixth [book]. Because of the mention of 'sacrifice,' there is no mutual conjunction with the wife in the sacrifice."

It is possible [to apply the dual number]. However, it has been stated that it is possible only in the act of denotation (*abhidhāna*). Furthermore, in cases such as "the king and the domestic priest" (*rājapurohita*), where there is a possibility of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) dependent on external action, it is not logical to rely on the act of denotation [as the basis for the dual]. For that mutual conjunction belongs only to those performing a sacrificial session (*sattrin*), and not to the wife and the sacrificer. Therefore, because the dual or plural number is absent here as well, as in the previous case, [the dual ending] must be applied in accordance with the syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
"Because of the sublation of the context, there is a displacement (utkarṣa).

And the tail (jāghanī) [is displaced] because it is a single part. Although this is relevant to the chapter because it consists of an inquiry into application (viniyoga), he asks with the intention of addressing the intermediate connection: "By what occasion has this section arrived? The answer is: by this [following].

This has come about as a consequence. It is established, therefore, that syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), whether the effect is in close proximity or not. Here, this is doubted: is this the meaning of the sentence, or is that the meaning of the sentence?

There is a doubt: are the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings enjoined with reference to the tail (*jāghanī*), or is it the reverse? The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are enjoined with reference to the tail. Why? Because in this way, the meaning is established by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). The injunction is made through the direct hearing of the word "they perform the *saṃyāja*" (*saṃyājayanti*); otherwise, there would be an injunction based on the meaning of a syntactical connection (*vākya*). [The tail—]

Because of the injunction. But even in this view, it is indeed the meaning of the sentence that is enjoined. Another action is stated in relation to this substance—the meaning is that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are stated to be performed with the tail (*jāghanī*). It is replied: you are ignorant of the modes of verbal expression (*vacanavyakti*). We do not say that there is no connection with an injunction for the meaning of the sentence; rather, [we mean] by way of the relationship between the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) and the subject of the injunction (*uddeśya*).

However, it is not the meaning of the sentence that is to be enjoined; rather, it is the case that the meaning of the sentence is not being enjoined. This very point is explained as follows: "It is said that it is not proper to enjoin a remote object by abandoning a proximate object. That is to say, it is not proper to abandon the action denoted by the word within the same syntactical unit (*pada*) and instead enjoin a remote substance denoted by another word. Furthermore, there is this other [objection] against this position:

There would be the gain [of the tail], yet the conceptualization of the tail as something to be taken up from the animal would not have been established. For under this view, the injunction for the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings would serve merely as a disposal (*pratipatti*) of that very tail which is already obtained in the animal sacrifice; thus, because it is a disposal, it would lack causal efficacy (*aprayojakatva*).

However, if the tail were enjoined within the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings themselves, it would be included precisely within that context; consequently, the tail would be something to be procured (*upādeya*) for the sake of accomplishing the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Therefore, there is also an elevation here.
[Page r807] The proponent of the injunction (codanāvādī) says: To this it is replied—here, the tail (jāghanī) itself is enjoined in connection with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. Why?

For in the injunction for the sacrifice, another [injunction] for the sake of the wives would have to be formulated, namely: "They join the wives with the tail" (*jāghanyā patnīḥ saṃyājayanti*). If this sacrifice were enjoined in the animal sacrifice as a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the tail, then another [injunction] for the sake of the wives would have to be prescribed as their agency. However, in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), since the wives' performance of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is already established, the word "wives" (*patnīḥ*) is merely restated when the tail is enjoined.

In the other case, by resorting to a qualified injunction, there would be the prescription of the sentence-meaning as a whole and a resulting complexity of injunction (*vidhigaurava*); therefore, since only the tail-tendon (*jāghanī*) is to be enjoined, there is no displacement [of the action]. The opponent objects: "But even here, the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are indeed present through the force of the extended application (*codaka*); thus, since they are already established as having the wives as their agents, an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) will be possible even under this view. The author replies: "True, they are present."

However, because it is being enjoined within a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), there is a difference in purpose, which results in the status of a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*). He objects again: "But surely, non-proximity (*asannidhāna*) is the cause for a ritual act being distinct, not the fact of being enjoined; and since there is proximity here, the status of a distinct ritual act is untenable. Furthermore, if there were no injunction here other than that which enjoins the very nature of the ritual act itself..."

In that case, there would be a split of the ritual action (*karmabheda*) according to the principle of repetition (*abhyāsanyāya*). However, here, because the purpose is to establish a connection with the tail (*jāghanī*), it does not serve to enjoin the essential nature of the ritual action itself. As it has been said: "And here, the act of killing (*vāvadha*) does not have the status of being for no other purpose, since its purpose is to connect it with the tail. Therefore, this avoidance of the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) based on the injunction of the wives (*patnī*) is not tenable for the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*). It is replied:

The "beloved of the gods" (devānāṃ priyaḥ) is ignorant of the distinction between scriptural injunctions (*śāstrabheda*). For the proximity of an injunction (*vidhānasannidhi*) indeed prevents a distinction within an enjoined injunction. The meaning of this is as follows: where that which has already been enjoined is enjoined again, there the very proximity of the injunction prevents—that is, wards off—a distinction.

There is no proximity of a distinct entity (*padārtha*). The intention here is as follows: since in the present injunction (*vidhi*) there is recognized an absence of scriptural authority (*śruti-pramāṇa*) for another injunction, it is not possible to postulate another thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*). However, when only the general category of an entity (*padārtha-mātra*) is present, because the absence of authority is not recognized and because it presents another thing to be enjoined, there indeed exists a separate scriptural teaching (*śāstra-antara*). And in this case, the things to be enjoined are those belonging to the archetype (*prākṛta*).

Although [the details] are brought near by the *codaka* (the extended application rule), they are not so by way of being things to be enjoined (*vidheya*), but rather as mere constituent elements (*padārtha*). For when something is the object of reference (*uddeśya*), even the proximity of constituent elements becomes a cause for comprehension; since the status of being an object of reference depends solely upon the constituent element itself, the reference requires only the constituent element and nothing more, as there is no lack of authoritative means [to establish it]. Therefore, that which is proximate in its mere form as a constituent element becomes the object of reference, just as in the case of the nine *prayāja* offerings and so forth.

Therefore, because a separate action is enjoined, the avoidance of the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is appropriate when enjoining an object not previously established, such as the wife. And since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) are established by this much alone, for what purpose did the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) set forth two methods for the sake of enjoining a relationship, beginning with "where the relationship is enjoined," and so on? [The answer is: In one case, there is the injunction of the relationship of one thing to another, and of the relationship itself...

He states that [this] is a direct injunction (*sākṣādvidhāna*): "Furthermore, as for this presentation by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*)—the injunction of the connection of both, the injunction of both in one of the two, and the direct injunction of the connection—for what purpose is this? It is said: it is for the sake of demonstrating the distinction between the indirect (*nāntarīyaka*) and the direct injunction. Where a factor connected to either one is enjoined because it was not previously established, there it is indirect."

The prescription of a relationship (*saṃbandhavidhāna*). However, where both relata are already established and a relationship is prescribed for them by their own words, the meaning is that this is to demonstrate the distinction that "therein, the prescription of the relationship is self-evident. For what purpose is this demonstration of the distinction made now? It is for the sake of showing the non-establishment of either one [of the two relata]. That is, it is to show the non-establishment of one or the other. In this context, the establishment of both is not possible; therefore—

One or the other must be enjoined. And since the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings themselves are already established, it is the *jāghanī* (the tail) alone that should be enjoined. Therefore, there is no displacement (*anutkarṣa*).
(1) G. *sya pratya* (2) R. & G. *nāntarīyakavidhiviveka* [p. 809]

Furthermore, as for what was stated in the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument—"it does not employ the animal"—that is equally applicable to our own position, because while the ordinary *jāghanī* (tail-end of the animal) is indeed available, its employment specifically for the sake of the animal is impossible.

Regarding *santardana* (the joining together), it belongs to the archetype (*prakṛti*). Here too, there is a suspicion of displacement (*utkarṣa*), because the word "long" (*dīrgha*) would otherwise be inapplicable. [The purpose is] "for support" (*dhṛtyai*).

And because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would otherwise be untenable. For if the insertion were indeed into the very *soma* sacrifice under discussion, then the word "long" (*dīrgha*) would be incoherent [with the purpose expressed as] "for support" (*dhṛtyai*).

Thus, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would not be tenable; for it is only when there is a fear of splitting that one ought to pray for support. Moreover, there is no such fear of splitting in the *soma* itself at that stage. However, the proponent of non-transference (*anutkarṣavādī*), considering the statement "of the long *soma*" to be a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the length of the creeper, believes this injunction applies to the archetype (*prakṛti*) alone. This word "long" (*dīrgha*) refers to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

Because it is understood as referring to the *latā* (the creeper), its placement is within the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself in order to favor the context (*prakaraṇa*). However, an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not capable of subverting the connection with the context. The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*), however, maintains that in this case, "length" must be understood in relation to the Soma, not in relation to the creeper; and this is merely an illustration, for it is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) who is indicated by the term "long. Thus, the word "long" is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with Soma.
It exists and brings about a specific modification in the ritual procedure. Furthermore, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) stating "for stability" would not be tenable without the excess [of Soma].

Since there is no possibility of the vessel splitting without an excess of Soma, the explanatory passage is not otherwise possible. Therefore, [this applies] to those ritual terminuses (saṃsthās) involving additional offerings.

He said, "It is an insertion. But even in this view, there is indeed an extraction from the context; for there is an extraction from the permanent (*nitya*) application because the insertion occurs in the optional (*kāmya*) terminuses (*saṃsthā*). For it will be stated in the section on the Terminuses (*saṃsthādhikaraṇa*) that the terminuses are also modifications (*vikāra*). [End of] (1) P. 871 (2) the discussion concerning the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).

[The opponent] objects: "This displacement (*utkarṣa*) is intended for the sacrifice; since the sacrifice is one even in the *saṃsthās*, there is no fault, for the displacement applies with respect to the effect—that is, with respect to the mandate of entitlement (*adhikāra-niyoga*). As for what was said—that this is an option (*vikalpa*), like the case of 'he buys with lead'—" [the reply follows].

The commentary has been restated. He states the refutation: "But surely, in that case, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) and not an option (*vikalpa*), because [the text says] 'he purchases with ten alone'.

And this was stated in the twelfth [book]. The reply is: "This was shown by accepting an option regarding the injunction (*vidhāna-vikalpa*), not an option regarding the performance (*prayoga-vikalpa*). The meaning of this is: if the rule "he purchases with lead" is the injunction for the purchase itself, then [rules such as] "with cloth" and so forth are injunctions regarding accessories (*guṇa-vidhi*).

If the injunction is "one purchases with cloth" (*vāsasā*) alone, while the others are injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*), then there is an option (*vikalpa*) in the formulation of the rule, but in practice there is indeed a combination (*samuccaya*). [Objection: But when the rite has been enjoined by one [injunction], how can another enjoin an accessory? For, due to the obstruction by an accessory enjoined at the time of origin (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇa*), it would result in the rite being a different action (*karmāntara*). [Reply: This is not so; for in the case of directly contributing auxiliaries (*sannipatyopakāraka*), since their purpose is understood to be one, there is no distinction [between them].

[The number] associated with the sacrifice should [belong] to the context, because of the context. He states the intermediate connection: "The consideration of displacement from the context, which depends upon the integration of the sentence-meaning, has been concluded. The integration (*samavāya*) of the sentence-meaning—that is, its being inherent within the context—depends upon that; thus, the consideration of displacement from the context has been concluded, because the sentence-meaning is inherently present in another context. In that regard:

It has been stated that the meaning of the sentence is being elevated. Now, a dispute regarding the denotation within the sentence itself is considered: does this word *prathama* (first) refer to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice alone, or to the first performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma? The meaning of this is as follows: "One should not perform the *pravargya* at the first sacrifice."
Thus, the prohibition of the *pravargya* rite in the first sacrifice is understood. In that regard, what is signified by the word "first"?

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated as follows: Is it said that the Jyotiṣṭoma alone [is meant] in comparison with other sacrifices such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa? Consequently, one should not perform the Pravargya rite in any performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma whatsoever; or is it said that the first performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself [is meant] in comparison with its other performances? Therefore, one should not perform the Pravargya in that [first performance] alone, while it should be performed in the other performances. This is the prima facie view.
Because of the scriptural statement, “In this very way, indeed, is the first among sacrifices,” it is clearly understood that [the word ‘first’] has the meaning of a sacrifice.

Its meaning is as follows: by virtue of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word ‘sacrifice,’ it is clearly understood that the word ‘first’ denotes the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

And because that [injunction] has the status of being a statement regarding what is to be performed; for the Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed the first sacrifice, as it is heard in scripture: "This, verily, is the first of sacrifices, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Therefore, one must not renounce the world during any part of the Jyotiṣṭoma. In this regard—

The commentary states: "And in this way, the context will be upheld. In that regard, perhaps what is called "upholding the context" refers to the intention behind the injunction for the *pravargya* rite for one who is prone to error; and that [intention] is indeed consistent even with a prohibition concerning the first performance. Therefore—
There might be the misconception that this is a proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*); in order to dispel that, he says: "That [statement] intends a prohibition.
If the prohibition were restricted to the Jyotiṣṭoma alone, then the context (*prakaraṇa*) would be respected, since the prohibition would be established for the entire Jyotiṣṭoma.
Or [it might be] based on an indicative mark (*naimittika*). To this it is replied: It is true that from this usage it is understood;
from the usage, "This indeed is the first of sacrifices, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma," it is indeed true that the Jyotiṣṭoma alone is understood to be the first.

That is not its application; rather, primacy is understood even from the application [of the text]: "He who, having not sacrificed with this, should then sacrifice with another. The meaning of this is as follows: just as from the application of the words "eṣa vāva" (this indeed), the primacy of the Jyotiṣṭoma alone is understood.
Likewise, by considering the phrase "ya etena," it follows from its usage that the first [element] is [the agent], and not by its own form. How so? "ya etena" — [etc.]

Is primacy [of the agent] due to its being employed through consideration of that [action]? The answer is: because it is heard as connected with the agent, and because it is heard as connected with the sacrifice denoted by the word *yaḥ* (who). Even so, why is this? He says: and the connection of the agent is with the performance (*prayoga*), not with the person to be prompted (*prayojya*).

For the agent is a constituent of the performance, whereas the person to be prompted is not, since [the action] is accomplished merely by means of the substance and the deity. This is everywhere the case.

It should be understood that the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth are accompanied by the action precisely because they are internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the agent (*kartṛ*), on the other hand, enters into the action only while being active through the instrument and so forth. Consequently, due to its connection with the performance (*prayoga*), the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice takes precedence. For the word "first" (*prathama*) is used in its primary sense (*śrauta*) with respect to the performance itself, while it is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) with respect to the object to be performed. And when there is a conflict between direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the direct scriptural statement is to be respected. Therefore, [the result accrues] specifically at the first performance.

This is a negation. He states another argument: it is heard in scripture that "In the context of the performance [of rituals], this indeed is the first of sacrifices. The meaning of this is: this sentence is concerned with the performance; it enjoins that the first performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma must be carried out, and therein [it says] "this indeed..."

Thus, it is understood that what has been heard refers specifically to the performance (*prayoga*). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: this indeed is the first among the performances of sacrifices, namely the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma; for one who, having not sacrificed with this performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma, should sacrifice with another performance, there is certainly a transgression (*āpatti*), he suffers loss (*antaḥ-jyāni*), he goes to ruin, or he perishes—that is, he dies.

Therefore, this priority belongs to the performance (*prayoga*) itself, not to that which is to be performed (*prayojya*). Thus he says: "But it does not reside in that which is to be performed. In some instances, the use of this word "first" (*prathama*) is found in reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice itself. Consequently, this word "first" refers exclusively to the act of performance. By this, the meaning becomes: "One should not perform the *pravargya* at the first performance of a sacrifice. Now, one might object that the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) denotes that which is to be performed.

How will it be applied in practice? To this he says: because the word *yajña* refers to the object to be employed (*prayojya*), it is indeed applicable even in the sense of "practice" (*prayoga*). For practice itself consists in that which is to be employed. Therefore, its designation by the term "that which is to be employed" is not untenable. Thus, by means of this action—(1) R.
The meaning is that it is to be employed first among sacrifices. And in this way, the injunction for the *pravargya* becomes appropriate within the very context (*prakaraṇa*).
The sense of this is as follows: in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, within the section on the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is stated: "They proceed with the *pravargya* prior to the *upasads*."

Thus the rule for the *pravargya* is heard in scripture. In that regard, if the prohibition were to apply to the performance of the *jyotiṣṭoma* alone, then, in order to avoid an option (*vikalpa*), it would have to be transferred to another context; consequently, there would be a sublation of the context (*prakaraṇabādha*). Alternatively, if [the prohibition] is to remain within that very context in order not to contradict the context—
From that, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would arise. In our view, however, because the prohibition is conditional (*naimittika*), there is no distinction whatsoever.
