The grinding for Pūṣan (*pauṣṇaṃ peṣaṇam*) occurs in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). It has been stated that "the grinding for Pūṣan" is mentioned with the intention of what follows. By this, the section—
The purpose has been stated;

it applies to all matters because there is no distinction. Now this is considered: should everything up to the offering to Pūṣan be ground, or only the *caru*? In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that it applies to all matters because no specific distinction is perceived.

The grinding [of the grain] is for the sake of the *caru* and the *paśupuroḍāśa*, because there is no distinction in their being dedicated to Pūṣan (*pauṣṇatva*). Now, an objection is raised: since grinding is already established in the case of the *puroḍāśa*, it cannot be the object of an injunction. The reply is: No, because it is not established by way of its dedication to Pūṣan (*pauṣṇatayā*). The meaning of this is: True, [grinding is established] in its own form...

The grinding is already established by virtue of being dedicated to Pūṣan, yet it is not [otherwise] established. Now, that which is established in its entirety cannot be the object of an injunction; however, that which is not established in some respect is certainly subject to an injunction. Therefore, it pertains to all [the gods]. But surely, when the grinding is performed...

In the case of the animal victim (*paśu*), there is the destruction of the heart and other organs; therefore, because of the consequence that the generic form (*ākṛti*) would be destroyed, there should be no grinding (*peṣaṇa*). The reply is: Let there be the destruction of the generic form, since there is a scriptural injunction for grinding; why should the scripture not be followed? The meaning is that one should do everything [it prescribes]. To this it is said: In the case of the *puroḍāśa* cake, since grinding is already established by general rule, it is not a new injunction (*vidhi*). But [one might object] on account of its being dedicated to Pūṣan...

It was stated that there is "attainment" (*prāpti*). The reply is: attainment is intended only by way of the effect (*kārya*), not by way of a relationship (*saṃbandhitva*). The meaning of this is: the attainment of things is intended for the sake of the effect, and not for the sake of establishing a relationship. And here, since the grinding of the *puroḍāśa* which was attained [from the model sacrifice] has already accomplished its purpose, there is no further purpose for the grinding. Consequently, in the absence of an effect—

Since there is no performance of another grinding when [the first] exists, a re-enjoining is not possible, because an injunction culminates in performance. Otherwise, it has been stated that even the words of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would have to serve a purposeful function. If that which lacks a purpose were also something to be performed, then the meaning of the explanatory passages—though not included within the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—would have to be performed as well.

But surely, if this is the case, it has been stated that syntactical connection (*vākya*) is weaker than context (*prakaraṇa*). The meaning of this is as follows: since grinding would apply to the *puroḍāśa* cake by virtue of syntactical connection, if the grinding were not enjoined for the *puroḍāśa* because there is no purpose to be served, then it would be said that syntactical connection is weaker than context. If one were to assume a connection even by abandoning the perceived connection, then [the rule regarding] the twelve *upasads* would [apply].

The sense [of the objection] is: why is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) not also postulated here in the case of the word *ahīnasya*? The answer is: the postulation of a syntactic connection occurs when there is a purpose (*kārya*); therefore, the superior force of the sentence has been stated. For where the attainment of a purpose follows from a syntactic connection understood through the sentence, there the sentence itself is that which must be enjoined by its name.

[The opponent replies: It is stronger. One does not accept the connection understood from the sentence when there is no connection with the purposeful action (*kārya*). What then? There is the postulation of another connection.
Therefore, due to the absence of a purposeful action, the injunction of grinding for the *puroḍāśa* is not possible. In that case, it is possible for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).

No, for even in that case, there would be the consequence of the scripture being dependent; for the injunction regarding the animal sacrifice is indeed dependent on the sublation of the generic form (*ākṛti*).
And it has been stated by those learned in the science of words that when a non-dependent application to the *caru* is possible, it is not proper to resort to a dependent one.
Therefore, we understand from the word itself that the grinding must be performed only upon the *caru*. Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "Even if at that time—"
"Even if the form were perceived, they would nevertheless be confused regarding the place of its removal"—this has been stated.

That is untenable. To dispel the doubt that "once the heart and other organs have been ground, their original form can no longer be produced because that form is subject to transformation," he says: "As for what was further stated..."
The intention of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with "even though" (*yadyapi ca*) is that even in this case, the state of being dependent (*sāpekṣatva*) cannot be avoided.

The meaning of this is as follows: even if the generic form (*ākṛti*) is established, it has been stated that the dependence upon the displacement of the location for extracting the first half and so forth cannot be removed. This is merely a concession (*anvāroha*); in ultimate reality, however, the generic form is indeed destroyed once the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) is performed.

The meaning is that the reason has already been stated previously. [Objection: But even in the case of *caru*, the nature of being *caru* would be lost, because the word *caru* is used for well-cooked rice (*odana*), and rice made of flour does not exist. [Response: The answer is—“the nature of being *caru* would not be lost, because even in the case of *caru* made of flour, there is the commonality of cooking. Thus it was stated, because the word *caru* denotes the act of cooking; and this remains true even when grinding takes place.
The term *caru* is employed. He concludes: "Therefore, it is established that the grinding applies only to the *caru*.

Because of the connection with one [deity] in one [case]. But surely, a ritual rule prescribed for that which has a single deity cannot apply to that which has two deities, just as in the case of the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*) or the mantra "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*). To this, he says: here the author of the Bhāṣya has shown the distinction by means of the words *indrapīta* and *āgneya*; just as in the statement "Pūṣan has a portion of ground flour," the statement of a reason—"for he is toothless"—[applies] to the *somāpauṣṇa* [offering], so too [here]... the half-portion (*nema-*)...

"Ground rice-offering" (*piṣṭaścaruḥ*). Its meaning is as follows: Pūṣan is called "the partaker of the ground [grain]" (*prapiṣṭabhāk*) because he partakes of what is thoroughly ground (*prapiṣṭam bhajati*). If there were grinding even in a rite for two deities, then he would be a partaker of the ground; otherwise, he would not be a partaker of the ground.

Thus, the statement of a reason—"for he is toothless" (*adantako hi*)—shows that the grinding is caused by Pūṣan. This is seen in the case of the "rice-offering half-ground for Soma and Pūṣan" (*somāpauṣṇo nemapiṣṭaścaruḥ*), where there is partial grinding (*nemapiṣṭatā*).

It is restated. And that [restatement] is appropriate for the grinding which has *pūṣan* alone as its cause; thus, in the injunction of the *caru* offering to Soma-Pūṣan, the phrase "half-ground" (*nemapiṣṭa*) is properly understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*). For if "half-ground" were being enjoined, then by implication (*lakṣaṇāt*), the *caru* would be intended for that [grinding], and the reference to the Soma-Pūṣan offering would become unintended. This section (*adhikaraṇa*) is for the purpose of refuting such additional doubts. To this, it is said: How are these doubts [to be resolved]?

What is the refutation? The answer is: the reason has already been stated—that "dharmas are prompted by the ritual act" (*kāryaprayuktatvāt*). The meaning of this is as follows: dharmas are prompted by the ritual act; therefore, those dharmas which are impossible in the ritual act itself become applicable to the sacrifice connected with that act. Consequently, from the statement "Pūṣan has the ground portion" (*pūṣā prapiṣṭabhāgaḥ*), it is determined that there is an injunction regarding the deity for the sacrifice characterized by Pūṣan. For it is by virtue of being the deity that Pūṣan is able to characterize the sacrifice.
Because the connection serves as the indicator [of the deity]. Furthermore, in a rite dedicated to two deities, it is impossible for there to be an absence of Pūṣan as a deity;

therefore, the injunction of ritual properties (*dharma*) therein would be improper. But how can there be a connection with the ritual action for those words associated with the term "deity"? The answer is:

[This is] because the deity has no purpose [in itself]. Now, one might object that in this case there would likewise be no connection in the sacrifice; to this he says: "And because the sacrifice is for the sake of an effect, the [offering] to Pūṣan is brought about by the effect. By means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the sacrifice is indicated by the deity. And if the deity is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), [then...]

In a rite dedicated to two deities, Pūṣan is capable of being characterized [as the recipient of the grinding]. For in that dual-deity ritual, Pūṣan is indeed not a deity [in the sense of being the primary recipient].

However, the statements regarding his "lack of teeth" and so forth have been declared to be *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) functioning as *hetuvannigadas* (statements resembling reasons). And such *arthavādas* are explained through figurative speech (*guṇavāda*).

Furthermore, because the grinding of what is already ground is contrary to logic—and since it is not established by any other rule—there is a specific injunction for grinding in the case of a dual-deity offering.
It will be so. Therefore, it is established that grinding applies to *caru* offerings dedicated to a single deity.
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*.
In the *Ṛjuvimalā*,
the fourth quarter of the third chapter.

Regarding the *nivīta*: how, then, can there be a suspicion of a further injunction (*vidhāna*) once it has been established that [the passage] is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), because it forms a single syntactical unit with an injunction for the purpose of praise? For if there is a single syntactical unit, two separate injunctions are not possible;

thus, an injunction for the *nivīta* state and so forth is not feasible. If it is argued that one considers it an injunction because one assumes an optional (*pākṣikī*) application, [we reply: the meaning—

For a statement is indeed a restatement (*anuvāda*) [only] when it refers to something already established. Now, the *nivīta* and so forth are not invariably established [prior to the injunction]. Therefore, since even a partial restatement is untenable, one must resort to the view that this is an injunction (*vidhi*). That too is incorrect, because it has already been refuted by the phrase "on account of the majority" (*prāyāt*), even though [the practice] is merely prevalent (*prāyikī*).

It has been stated by the sūtra beginning with "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) that a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) occurs based on something already established. For example, the injunction "the speech is one that speaks the truth" [is an arthavāda] because the rule regarding "the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (*prācīnāvīta*) was not previously established. If it is argued that this [latter] is also enjoined because of its connection with that [former], [we reply: "The *prācīnāvīta* is for the ancestors."

Thus, even in this view, [the *nivīta*] is not obtained [by implication]. Therefore, it must be enjoined. If that is enjoined, then a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is necessarily admitted; and consequently, since the *nivīta* would also be enjoined, that is improper—because it is already obtained through another statement, and thus the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is perfectly justified. When [the objection] has been thus raised, he defends [his position]: "This section [is begun] by one who considers that there is no [prior] obtainment because [the *nivīta*] is not a subordinate element of the context (*prakaraṇa*)."

The discussion is commenced. Since there is no possibility of its application even as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the context (*prakaraṇa*)—because it would not be obtained as such even in the alternative view—the present section is begun by one who considers that *nivīta* is being enjoined, on the grounds that it cannot be a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) according to the principle of *prāya*. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*):

Even if it were an injunction, its status as a subordinate element of the context is not possible; thus, its status as an explanatory passage remains established. Even though it is enjoined, nevertheless...

Because of the mention of "of men," there arises the implication that it pertains to independent authority; therefore, it cannot be a subordinate member of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Rather, it is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*).

If it were a property of man (*puruṣadharma*), then the statement "he would depart" would indeed be appropriate as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). But one might object: since there is no prior application (*aprāpti*) in the case of hospitality and so forth, an injunction is proper for men;

for even though there is the scriptural hearing of "of men," why should an injunction not be possible when the rite of hospitality has man as its primary element, given that [the act] is absolutely unestablished (*ekāntato’prāptatvāt*)? No, because their connection is not understood. The connection with the rite of hospitality is not perceived.

Rather, [the connection] is with human beings alone. And since that is established through the *prāya* (preponderance) and other criteria as being an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), its status as a restatement (*anuvāda*) is proven.
Thus he says: "But when there is a connection with human beings alone, it is established as an *arthavāda* because it is justified by the *prāya* and so forth.

This concludes the section on the division of directions. Regarding the passage concerning the "mutilated" (*paruṣidita*): what does the rule of extension (*atideśa*)—"it is like that"—add for one who perceives [the similarity]?

The answer is as follows: For the application [of the rule] regarding the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is one way, that regarding the directions is another, and that regarding the days of the waxing and waning moon (*parvadin*) and so forth is yet another;

thus, this extended application (*atideśa*) is for the purpose of establishing these specific distinctions. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) remain the same. However, for the sake of describing the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the basis for the application must be stated.
And since that basis occurs in various ways and in different contexts, there is a distinction between the respective topics (*adhikaraṇa*).
Not connected with ritual action. It was stated in the section on the *nivīta* that practices such as the *nivīta* are understood to be properties of the sacrifice (*kratudharma*).

Because [the term] "human" and so forth is heard, it is generally understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) since [the practice] is already established. Now, regarding the rule "one should not speak untruth," the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this too is a restatement, just like the former case. By this, he states the contextual connection (*avasara-saṅgati*) and the prima facie position. As for the meaning: because of the scriptural statement "the *nivīta* is for humans," the *nivīta* and other such practices are not perceived as being duties of the sacrifice (*kratu-dharma*), but rather as duties of the person (*puruṣa-dharma*).

If it were a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*), then because it would generally apply for the sake of the person, the rule regarding *nivīta* and so forth would be a restatement (*anuvāda*)—this was stated in the section on *nivīta*.
Now, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) belongs to one who considers the prohibition "one should not speak untruth" to be a restatement. He objects:

"But surely, since the word 'man' (*manuṣya*) is heard there, it is understood that the connection is with human beings in general; and since no connection with the ritual (*kratu*) is understood, a restatement is appropriate."

And this is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) based on what is generally the case. However, in this instance, since the word "man" (puruṣa) is not heard, it is not understood that [the prohibition] has man as its purpose;

rather, by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa), it is understood that it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (kratvartha). Furthermore, since there is no prior attainment [of the act] in connection with the sacrifice, a restatement (anuvāda) is not possible. He refutes this: here too, because it is a restatement of a previously established prohibition, it is indeed understood that the man is the one to whom that prohibition applies. In this case as well—

"One should not speak untruth. That man for whom this Smṛti-based prohibition exists is indeed understood to be the qualified agent. Why? Because it is a restatement (anuvāda) of a prohibition that was already established [by natural law], and because the Smṛti specifically records the person as the qualified agent therein. Now, one might object: "This cannot be a restatement of a prohibition, because in that case [the prohibition against lying] the qualification belongs to one who desires to avoid the resulting sin (pratyavāya), whereas here [in the context of the ritual], since it is a subordinate element of the ritual procedure (prakaraṇāṅga), there can be no such qualification. To this, he replies:
For in every prohibitory scripture, the entitlement belongs only to the agent of the action being prohibited; this is the meaning of the passage at Bh.

In the case of a prohibition based on Smṛti, there is no entitlement for one who seeks to avoid the sin (pratyavāya) resulting from the performance of the prohibited action, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence. For there is no evidence whatsoever that a prohibited action produces sin. If it is argued, "But surely the scripture of prohibition itself is the authority; how so? Because renunciation would otherwise be inexplicable in the absence of sin," we say: no.

For the cessation [of activity] is logically established only upon the understanding of the qualification (*adhikāra*). Now, one might object: "But no qualification is explicitly stated. True; it will be understood by implication, just as in the case of the rules for acquiring wealth. For he who is engaged in a certain action is the one who must be turned away from it, and not anyone else; thus, by implication alone, the qualified person who possesses the engagement is obtained. Therefore, it was rightly said: "In every prohibitive scripture, it is precisely the agent of the prohibited action who is [the subject]."

Regarding the term *adhikāra*: here too, the prohibition of false speech applies to the agent of the action being prohibited, because a prohibition for anyone else would be untenable; thus, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a prohibition already established previously. Now, one might object: since the performance of false speech is obtained only as part of the ritual purpose, it is logical that the prohibition also serves that same purpose. For one who is engaged in one thing cannot be enjoined to another.

To this he says: "And attainment exists by way of implication. There is indeed an attainment of false speech by way of implication; for since the prohibition of a person is justified both as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and as being a mere attainment for the person (*puruṣaprāptimātra*), it does not have the context of the sacrifice (*prakaraṇa*) as its sole purpose. And if a prohibition were only possible when the attainment is for the sake of the sacrifice and not when it is for the sake of the person, then [the following would apply].

The prohibition [of what] is already established as being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) would itself be for the sake of the ritual. But this is not so, because a prohibition is logically possible even from the mere fact of its being established.
Now, of which injunction is this a restatement (*anuvāda*)? This is the intention: it has been stated that the authority [of a Vedic text] consists in its being directed toward an injunction.

In that context, the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*) possesses the character of being directed toward an injunction by virtue of its connection with the task to be performed. However, the words of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) possess the character of being directed toward praise, as they are connected with the cognition [of the purpose].

[Objection: But a restatement (anuvāda) is not directly intended as an injunction; therefore, it must be stated of which injunction this is a supplement (śeṣa), otherwise it would lack the status of being subservient to an injunction. [Reply: We say that it is not a supplement to any [injunction]. Because it lacks syntactic unity (ekavākyatva) with any other injunction, this is not a supplement to any injunction whatsoever. If it does not enter into another injunction, it is like the *nivīta* [which is meaningless without reference to a specific act].

In that case, how can it be a restatement (*anuvāda*)? The answer is: priority (*prāpti*) is the cause for being a restatement, not the status of being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). For if it were an explanatory passage—(1) G.
because of non-adherence; (2) R. because of prohibition—[p. 822].

If being a restatement (*anuvāda*) were the reason [for its status], then, since an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would be untenable without entering into another injunction (*vidhi*), the restatement would be a subordinate element of that other injunction. However, what is the cause for being a restatement is the fact of prior attainment (*prāpti*), not the state of being an explanatory passage. If this [passage] refers only to what is already attained, why then does it not become an explanatory passage just like the *nivīta* [passage]? To this, he says: "For it becomes an explanatory passage by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), not by virtue of the prior attainment."
It depends [on another], as in the case of the statement, "One should offer oblation with wild sesame gruel.
For although the offering of wild sesame gruel is not [otherwise] established, nevertheless, there is the rule: "One offers the Agnihotra with milk."

Because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with this [preceding injunction], it is explained as being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Therefore, a restatement (*anuvāda*) depends merely upon [the existence of] something already established; whereas an explanatory passage depends merely upon forming a single syntactical unit—this is the distinction. Since the restatements are touched by the injunction by virtue of being subordinate to the injunction that is being restated, there is nothing deficient whatsoever. Therefore, it is a restatement.

[Objection: But surely this Vedic statement will be the source (*mūla*) for that Smṛti. If it is said that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) because the Vedic statement and the Smṛti statement have the same meaning, then, since that Smṛti requires a source, this very Vedic statement will be its source; how then can it be a restatement? [Response: It cannot be so, because here the meaning being heard...

It is understood that this pertains to the context (*prakaraṇa*) and not to the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). On the other hand, in the case of it being a restatement (*anuvāda*), since [the prohibition] is already established as serving the human purpose, its status as a human purpose is proven. The meaning of this is as follows: if this sentence were the original source (*mūla*), then even for a prohibition related to a person engaged in speaking untruth, an eligible agent (*adhikārī*) would have to be postulated. Consequently, by means of that very injunctive rule of eligibility (*adhikāravidhi*) which has had an eligibility postulated, [the prohibition would be established].

It would be grasped by the injunction itself due to proximity; consequently, this prohibition would have the character of *prakaraṇa* (context), meaning it would serve the purpose of the *niyoga* (obligatory mandate) pertaining to the subject matter at hand.

Furthermore, since the Smṛti serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), the injunction of the prohibition cannot be its source. However, when a prohibition related to the person is understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*), because its scope is already established, there is no room for the postulation of another scope. Therefore...

It is not grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*). For when the assumption of a governing topic (*adhikāra*) has already proceeded, a rule of context that possesses an established governing topic takes hold; it does not [apply] to a prohibition that is already established as having a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) through its own force, because [the context] aims at an independent governing topic—this is the meaning. But is it not understood [otherwise]?

How can it be appropriate to assume that what is understood solely as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is restated (*anuvāda*) as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)? The meaning of this is as follows:
you have stated that if this were the foundational basis, then it would be for the sake of the sacrifice; and by speaking in this manner—

It has been stated that the engagement in speaking untruth for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is prohibited. Otherwise, how indeed could there be "sacrificial purpose" (*kratvarthatā*) in that which is injunctive?
And since this is so, how can this prohibition of engagement for the sake of the sacrifice be restated as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)? It is replied:
the sacrifice itself is indeed for the sake of the person; therefore, by virtue of its connection with that [sacrifice], speaking untruth would certainly result from the person's own desire.

"There is no fault in saying 'the face' (or 'speaking'), because its connection [to the person] is understood. This is the meaning: even that activity of a person which is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is indeed connected to the person. Therefore, the prohibition of that [activity] is also rightly for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Since the sacrifice itself is indeed for the sake of the person, for this reason, even for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice, speaking untruth (*anṛtavadana*) necessarily accrues to the person due to natural inclination (*rāga*); thus, there is no fault regarding the sacrifice.

Because the connection [of the prohibition] is understood through that [context], the meaning becomes this: "One should not speak untruth for the sake of accomplishing the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. And since all speaking of untruth for the sake of human ends is prohibited, its status as a restatement (anuvāda) is established. Furthermore, because sacrifices occur after the time of initiation (upanayana), the restatement is proven; for if sacrifices did not occur after the time of initiation, then [the prohibition would apply to] even those [acts] prescribed by the Smṛtis.

Since ritual acts (*padārtha*) are Vedic in nature and occur subsequent to initiation (*upanayana*), there is no prohibition regarding eligibility for these Vedic acts prior to initiation; therefore, this [textual passage] would not be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Consequently, it is established that the sacrifices (*kratu*) occur subsequent to initiation, and thus the text is indeed a restatement.

"Or rather, it is an injunction because of a different connection. To this it is replied: You yourself have stated that this does not establish itself as the source for the words of the Smṛti. If that is so, then you yourself have stated this "different connection.
[End of section] (1) P. 911.

And if there were a separation [of this statement from the context], it could not be called a restatement (*anuvāda*). The meaning of this is as follows: first of all, this sentence by its very nature provides a prohibition that is an integral part of the ritual context (*prakaraṇa*). For this very reason, it has not become a lack of basis for the Smṛti. If this is so, then [the Smṛti] cannot abandon its status as being for the sake of the internal constituent of the sacrifice (*antaraṅga-kratvarthatā*).

Through the consideration of other sentences, the prohibition remains as something being restated (*anūdyatayā*). But is it not said that in every case of a prohibition, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) belongs only to the agent of the action being prohibited? The meaning of this is: for a lack of entitlement enters into that which possesses an entitlement; and this prohibition possesses an entitlement, because the entitlement is understood to belong only to the agent of the action being prohibited. True, this has been stated, but not within that specific context (*prakaraṇa*).

It can be said that the agent of the action being prohibited is not heard of as having an entitlement (*adhikāra*) by direct scriptural statement; rather, it is inferred from the sense of the context. And when an established entitlement is possible and present, it is not appropriate to postulate another entitlement. Why, then, does the context not also establish an entitlement for the very agent of the prohibited action? The answer is: because [the prohibition] pertains merely to the object of the act itself.

Because it is logically consistent; for even in the case of speaking untruth, the prohibition is established even with respect to the mere act itself, regardless of whether its performance depends on the person's desire.

This is what is meant: in a ritual context (*prakaraṇa*), the activity is understood as being connected to that very context. Therefore, since the entry into the governing injunction (*adhikāra*) has already been established by way of that [contextual connection], it is not logical to assume a separate governing injunction based merely on the sense of the matter. In worldly activities, however, activity proceeds solely from the person's own desire.

Since the object of the prohibition is understood [to apply] to that very person who is the agent of the action, it is logical that the entitlement (adhikāra) belongs to that agent alone. However, in this case, the engagement with the ritual element is understood as being solely for the sake of the sacrifice; therefore, it cannot be said that the entitlement belongs to that agent.
But surely, in verbal suffixes (ākhyāta), the agent is understood as the primary factor. By this, he says the following: even within its own sentence, the restriction regarding the subject matter—

Because it establishes an injunction endowed with an agent (*jyānvita-niyoga*), it is not logical for it to enter into the sphere of qualification (*adhikāra*). To explain: the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is the object of the injunction, while the speaker of untruth (*anṛtavādaka*) is the qualified person (*adhikārī*). Furthermore, the suspicion that verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) denote the agent is based on the literal understanding of the words of Pāṇini and others. [Objection: If this were so, then even the *prayāja* offerings and other such subsidiaries would lack the status of being auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), since an agent is also heard mentioned in their case.

Regarding the point that there would be the consequence of [the injunctions] being independent (svatantra), he says: "But because there is no difference in the mandate (niyoga), the status of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is understood; for all of them are connected to a single result. The meaning of this is as follows: in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, only the agent is heard in the scripture, not any qualification of that agent.

If the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are indeed qualifiers of the agent, then they cannot be the subject matter (*viṣaya*) [of the injunction]; if, on the other hand, they are the subject matter, then the agent is not qualified by them. Consequently, how could there be an unqualified person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārī*)? Therefore, since there is no separate injunctive application (*niyoga*) for those [subsidiaries], their status as auxiliaries (*aṅgatva*) is established through their inclusion within a single injunctive application. As for the purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarmāṇi*), their status as auxiliaries is likewise appropriate, because it is understood that they serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) by way of being the objects to be refined (*saṃskārya*).

Even in those cases, since there is no understanding of a connection with specific objects or persons to be enjoined, there is no occurrence of an independent entitlement (*adhikāra*). There is no contradiction in their being subsidiary to a sacrifice (*kratuśeṣatva*) by way of the substances to be consecrated and so forth. However, in the case of a prohibition, because that which is prohibited is not for the sake of the sacrifice and because the agent is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), it is understood that the entitlement belongs to the agent alone. The meaning of this is as follows: although indeed [in the rule] "one should not speak untruth," untruth—

Only the act of speaking is understood from the word; nevertheless, if no qualification (*adhikāra*) is heard within the sentence, then the prohibition against speaking untruth (*anṛtavadana*) is understood as pertaining to the context (*prakaraṇa*). However, when both the qualification and the subject matter are obtained within its own sentence, then the speaking of untruth is understood as entirely independent. Since the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes the agent and the prohibition does not pertain to the ritual (*akratvartha*), the qualification belongs to the agent alone.

Because there is no reason for it to enter into another context, and because its own context is heard [in the text], it has thus been shown that the injunction is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Now, even while assuming the perception of untruthful speech as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), he shows that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*): "And there is no comprehension of that connection"—that is, no comprehension of a connection with untruthful speech for the sake of the sacrifice.

It is also contradictory in the context of independent injunctions (*svatantrādhikāra*). Since even a sacrifice has the person as its ultimate purpose, and because activity directed toward it occurs subsequent to initiation (*upanayana*), it has been stated that this is established as a restatement (*anuvāda*). What is meant is this: the prohibition against speaking untruth for the sake of a sacrifice is merely a restatement of the Smṛti-based prohibition against all untruthful speech, which pertains to the person in the context of independent injunctions.

To this it is replied: This might be so if the agent were the expressed meaning of finite verbs (*ākhyāta*); however, it is not possible to postulate that finite verbs possess the power to express the agent, because all case-factors (*kāraka*) are understood simply from the expression of the action itself.

The meaning of this is as follows: for in that context, the expressive power (*śakti*) of a word is postulated only for that which cannot be understood from any other source. Furthermore, all factors of action (*kāraka*) are implied by the action itself, since an action is impossible without them. How then is Pāṇini’s rule—"*laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*"—to be understood? Likewise, how is this commentary [to be understood] regarding the word "ca" (and)?

Regarding the phrase "kartari ca": from the statement of the author of the Sūtra and the author of the Vṛtti, it is understood that the *lakāras* denote the *kārakas*. He refutes this by showing: "This is for the purpose of prescribing number. The meaning is that the number of the object (*karman*) and the number of the agent (*kartṛ*) are prescribed as being denotable (*vācya*), not the object and the agent themselves. However, the object and the agent are indicated (*lakṣyate*) by their respective numbers. How, then, [is this so]?

The authors of the *Vṛtti* recite [the rules]: "When a *sārvadhātuka* suffix expressing the action occurs, *yak* is added" and "when the agent is expressed, *śap* is added"; regarding this, he says—[concerning] number—

And [the rules] "yak" and "śap" depend upon specific prescriptions. Here too, the grammatical rule regarding "yak" and "śap" is based on the expression of specific numbers for the object and the agent; therefore, even here, verbal suffixes do not denote *kārakas*. If it is argued that the number of the object and agent is expressed as implied by the action (*kriyākṣipta*), then why is the number of other *kārakas* not also expressed?

The meaning is: since the state of being understood (*gamyamānatva*) is equal [in both cases], why is the number of instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth not expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)? He provides the answer: "The world cannot be questioned. He asks, "Why? and says: "For the great multitude (*mahājana*) is invincible. The meaning of this is:
what can we do if the world expresses only the number of objects (*karman*) and agents (*kartṛ*), and not the number of instruments and so forth? [Objection: Let the world be so; however...
Pāṇini might ask why he does not record this; to that he replies: "And this treatise of the venerable Pāṇini is rooted in common usage" (1).
The meaning is that the *kartṛ* (agent) is prescribed as being denotable (*vācyatvena vidhīyate*) for the purpose of prescribing specific rules regarding the object, the agent, and number.

He asks "Why? and replies: For it is the rule that prescribes a restriction for what has been employed, not for the mere mention of what has not been employed. Therefore, this is not a subject for censure. He concludes: Consequently, this prohibitory scripture is based solely upon the engagement in the performance of those ritual elements that serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). This prohibition is based precisely on that engagement which occurs toward the mere utterance of untruth (*anṛtavādana*) regarding all ritual elements serving the purpose of the sacrifice, by virtue of its connection with the meaning of the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*).

The treatise [states]: Now, it has been argued that the activity residing in the person who is prohibited does not have the sacrifice as its purpose, because it is not enjoined. For speaking untruth is not enjoined as being for the sake of the sacrifice; and what is not enjoined cannot be an auxiliary (aṅga) of the sacrifice. Thus, the activity toward speaking untruth does not have the sacrifice as its purpose. The reply is: being enjoined for the sake of that [the sacrifice] is not the sole cause of the relationship; rather, the status of being related is indeed established even by way of providing assistance.
Even though there is no injunction for that purpose [directly], nevertheless, there is indeed a connection between false speech and the sacrifice by way of being an auxiliary.

And it has been stated that when there is an injunction regarding something connected [to the rite], it serves the purpose of the sacrifice—as in such cases as "milk is the vow of the Brāhmaṇa. Even though eating is not enjoined as being for the sake of the sacrifice, nevertheless, because it is an auxiliary to that sacrifice, the milk which depends upon it (eating) certainly becomes for the sake of the sacrifice.

In this way, even the prohibition against speaking untruth for the sake of assistance will serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Now, one might object: since the prohibition concerns that which assists [the sacrifice], there is no distinction between its being for the purpose of the sacrifice and its being for the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). The meaning of this is as follows: if, first of all, the speaking of untruth were a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, then because it could not be prohibited by a prohibition intended for the person, the prohibition would indeed be purposeful as something serving the purpose of the sacrifice.

This is for the purpose of providing an alternative view (*vikalpārtha*). When there is a prohibition regarding that which has already been attained as an object, since the prohibition is established by the prohibition aimed at the person’s welfare (*puruṣārtha*), what is the use of a prohibition aimed at the ritual’s purpose (*kratvartha*)? The answer is: it has already been stated how there is a distinction. In the case of a prohibition aimed at the ritual, if it is transgressed, the ritual becomes defective; therefore, an expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed by the Veda is required to remove that defect. However, in the case of a prohibition aimed at the person, if it is transgressed, [the penalty falls upon] the person.
The distinction is that because of a deficiency, a Smṛti-based expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed for its removal.
828] Like the *ahīna* sacrifice, it is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*), because it is for his sake. But what, then, is the distinction from the rule "the *nivīta* mode is for men"?

Regarding the phrase "of one yawning": by this, he introduces the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Although the recitation of the mantra—"When yawning, one should say: 'In me [are] strength and will' (*mayi dakṣakratū*)"—is heard as being connected to the act of yawning, nevertheless, why [should it not apply to all men], just as in the case of the rule "the *nivīta* [wearing mode] is for men"?

The *nivīta* does not pertain solely to the context [of the sacrifice]. Since it is heard as being connected with humans in the statement, "The *nivīta* is for humans," yet it nevertheless pertains to the context itself, why should this [other case] not be the same? This is the distinction: a resolution based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not possible here, because it is not a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). For example, [in the case of]: "The *nivīta* is for humans."

Thus, because it is a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the sentence "he wears the sacred thread over the left shoulder," it is connected to the context as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); however, the connection of the phrase "one who is yawning should speak" is not like that, because it lacks the status of being a single syntactical unit with another injunction. [Objection: But surely, since it is not a supplementary part, let it not be an explanatory passage.

Let it be a restatement (*anuvāda*), as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the previous section, like the injunction "one should not speak untruth. To this he says: nor is it a restatement, because the recitation of the mantra is connected with the act of yawning (*jañjabhyamāna*) and is not established from any other source—unlike the case of "one should not speak untruth," where there is no possibility of the subject matter being established by the sense of the context. If the state of yawning were already established within the sacrifice itself, then it would indeed be the subject matter of the mantra-injunction.

It might be that, just as the non-speaking of falsehood is implied by the injunction "one should not speak falsely," so too this injunction for the mantra would be for the sake of the sacrifice, since its connection to the sacrifice is understood through the yawning that pertains to the sacrifice. But this is not the case. Why? Because the state of being one who is yawning never attains the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice, unlike the non-speaking of falsehood. Therefore, this injunction of the mantra for the person yawning does not belong within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the sacrifice.
It can be established that, within one's own statement itself, there is a mantra-utterance characterized by the yawning of what is not to be accepted for the qualified practitioner.

Furthermore, there is no reason for the inclusion [of the act] within the context (prakaraṇa) upon the acquisition of its object. But surely, if this were the case, there would be the assumption of a result;

that is to say, there would be the assumption of a separate qualification (adhikāra). Let it be so on account of the explicit statement (vacana); what is the fault? The fault lies in assuming a separate qualification based solely on the verbal text. Therefore, the sublation of the context by the sentence is established, just as the number twelve of the *upasads* belongs to the *ahīna* sacrifice.

To this it is replied: this sentence does not deserve to have a separate fruit (phala) postulated for it. This is the underlying intention here: the recitation of the mantra is perceived as being connected with the act of yawning (*jañjabhyamāna*). In this regard, is this a separate injunction (*adhikāra*), and should the word *jañjabhyamāna* serve to designate a specific qualified performer?
Or rather, should the very same agent under discussion be indicated by the word *jañjabhyamāna*, [the latter] merely referring to the deficiency (*vyalīka*) produced by the occasion of yawning?

When a doubt arises that the recitation of the mantra is a purificatory act (*saṃskāraka*) by way of pacifying the hair, since the function [of the mantra] is already established in its original context, such a new assumption is not tenable;

thus, it is not right to assume a different governing purpose (*adhikāra*), and the one who is stretching his limbs enters into the connection solely as the object of the purification. Wishing to explain this intention, he asks: "Why? The answer is: "For a sentence is capable only of establishing the relation between word-meanings."

Not as an action (*kārya*). For from the sentence itself, there is only the comprehension of the relationship between word-meanings; there is no connection with the person performing the *jañjabhyamāna* (the one who is yawning) even as something to be refined (*saṃskārya*). By being merely the agent, he who is already the agent is refined by this recitation of the mantra. To the question, "Whence then is the comprehension of the action?", he says: for the action is indeed to be understood only through the mandate (*niyoga*). For everything is for the sake of the mandate; therefore, it is accepted as having the mandate as its purpose.

That which is the effect (*kārya*). For this very reason, there is a transposition of case-endings in the case of *saktu* and so forth. Let it be that the effect is necessarily [the object]; nevertheless, he asks "why?"—[the answer being] "this injunction (*niyoga*) pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapūrṇamāsika*) is the subject under discussion. Since it is grasped by means of that subject under discussion, one must postulate an effect conducive to its grasping; thus, this [act of grinding] is solely a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent (*kartṛ*) involved in the subject matter. Even if it were [connected] with the subject matter...

If [the injunction] were not apprehended by way of a mandate (*niyoga*), then the sentence would not terminate in the mere relationship between word-meanings, but rather would terminate only in an action (*kārya*).

Indeed, all this is a cause for application (*viniyoga*). Now, one might object: "Granted that there is a mandate in the context, nevertheless there is no proof that that very mandate is itself the action (*kārya*), by virtue of which one could postulate an action conforming to it. To this he says: "And there is no postulation of another action."

Since it is possible for [the injunction] to be established, its placement occurs within the very context [of the sacrifice]. But it has been argued that the state of being "one who is yawning" cannot be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), just like the speaking of untruth; therefore, how can there be entry into the sacrifice? The answer is: let it not be so.

The state of being yawned (*jañjabhyamānatā*) is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). However, the fact that it pertains to the agent will serve as the reason for its connection with the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, it is established that this is a duty (*dharma*) of the agent of the sacrifice. In the case of the *ahīna* [sacrifice], however, because it is something to be performed (*kārya*), its displacement (*utkarṣa*) is appropriate.

For in the *ahīna*, the injunction of entitlement (*adhikāraniyoga*) which is perceived as connected to that [yawning] is understood to be the thing to be accomplished (*kāryabhūta*); thus, since the status of being a task is understood from its own sentence, its displacement is justified.

The excellence [of the former case] lies in the existence of twelve [repetitions]. Here, however, since no connection with a ritual act (*kārya*) is understood through the mere connection with one who is gargling (*jañjabhyamāna*), it is more logical to resort to an established substratum when a ritual act must be inferred; this is the distinction. And in the case of the *Śaṃyu* [verse], because of the surrender of everything: "One should not threaten a Brāhmaṇa."

Thus, the prohibition applies only to the specific context, because it is taught within that context and because, by its very meaning, it does not apply to the ritual as a whole—just like the prohibition against speaking untruths; such is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

He states the final conclusion (rāddhānta): "But in the case of the Śaṃyu-rite, because of the scriptural mention of a result—'one would be punished with a hundred [cows]'—it is not logical to assume a connection with the general context."

For the comprehension of the purpose (kārya) residing within its own sentence is more powerful. If no result were understood from its own sentence, then, since the performance would be established through entry into the modification of the archetype (prakṛti), no further purpose would be postulated; it would merely be a subsidiary (aṅga). But here, a result is understood from its own sentence: the avoidance of a hundred torments (śatayātanā) and so forth. Indeed, the comprehension of the purpose residing within its own sentence is superior because it is internal (antaraṅga).
r831] Therefore, this is a duty pertaining to human beings in general: "One should not threaten a Brahmin."

Thus [it is said]. But surely, even in the case of the *jañjabhyamāna* (one who yawns), there is indeed the hearing of a fruit in the statement, "He places the prāṇa and apāna within himself. He refutes this: No, because the word "places" (*dhatte*) is a teaching in the present tense.

The fruit is not understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*); therefore, because it is already present, it cannot serve as a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Indeed, that fruit which is yet to come (*bhāvi*) connects with the injunction as its result by virtue of being fit to be accomplished by it; it is not, however, as has been shown, connected as a result simply because "this is not to be accomplished by an injunction. In this case, however, regarding the *Śaṃyu*, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the word *yātayet* expresses a future sense.

It causes one to understand [the meaning] through the verbal root *yātayati*. From this, it is understood that there will be torment (*yātanā*); therefore, the distinction is that there will also be its avoidance. By the word *liṅ*, the fifth mood (*leṭ*) is denoted in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*), whereas this word *yātayāt* is a different form of the fifth mood. Here, however, it must be explained: how, in this case, are the hundredfold torments and the threatening (*apagoraṇa*) related as the means and the end to be accomplished?
The existence [of the result] is understood. And how can a momentary threatening become the cause of torment at a later time? To this it is said:

this is stated with reference to Śamyu—"He who should threaten a Brāhmaṇa, him one should torment with a hundred [blows]. In that case, it is understood that the threatening of a Brāhmaṇa is the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), and the torment by a hundred [blows] is the occasional effect (*naimittikī*). Nor is there a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) immediately—

Because it is not perceived as something already cultivated (*bhāvita*). Nor is the torment perceived as the fruit of an action such that it would occur immediately thereafter. In this regard, in accordance with the perceived relationship between cause and effect, some intermediate effect is postulated, by performing which the torment is brought about through the threatening gesture (*avagoraṇa*). [As in the rule: "One should not threaten a Brāhmaṇa."
Thus, this meaning is understood in accordance with the prohibition;

it is not possible to maintain that the "torment" (yātanā) is not intended to be expressed. For here, the qualification of the person entitled to perform the act (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇatā*) belongs specifically to the agency in the action being prohibited. The avoidance of torment, however, serves as a qualification for the cessation of the threatening act (*vagoraṇa*), which is denoted by the negative particle (*nañ*) that constitutes the scope of the prohibitive injunction.

Because it enters into the scope of the [prohibited] object, it is not a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), since it is not the fruit of the injunction. For when the goal to be accomplished is the torment [of hell], the avoidance of that torment occurs through the mere cessation of threatening (*avagoraṇa*) itself, independent of the injunction; thus, this is merely the fruit of the [prohibited] object, not [the fruit of the injunction]. (1) G. *viṣayāṅgānu* (2) G. *sanniyoga* (3) G. *svādhyāyāntaranivṛttau*

It should be understood that the fruit belongs to the *niyoga* (the injunction). For this very reason it has been stated that, in every prohibitory scripture (*pratiṣedha-śāstra*), the entitlement (*adhikāra*) belongs solely to the agent of the action being prohibited. And thus, since the performance of the act is obtained through the object and the fruit themselves, there is no entry into the sphere of entitlement; therefore, this is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*).
This is the prohibition against threatening.

Prior to the exclusion of the woman in her menses (*malavadvāsas*). On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya raises a doubt: "Is there a prohibition of conversing with one who is in her menses as part of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, or is it a rule prohibiting such conversation for a person in all circumstances? He...

This is improper because the explicit statement lacks a counter-position. For it would have been more appropriate to state: "Is this a prohibition of conversation with one who is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, or a prohibition of conversation in general? Or, if it is indeed a prohibition, is it for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)?
He removes this inconsistency in the Bhāṣya as follows: "There is doubt regarding the prohibition of conversation with a woman in her menses; [is it] conversation for the sake of the ritual..."

Is it established as a ritual act (*kratvartha*) or as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*)? In the Bhāṣya, however, this result is proclaimed for the position that prohibits the recitation of the *saṃvāda* [mantra] for the sake of a human goal:
"The injunction pertains to the person. What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? That the *saṃvāda*—such as "O wife, this is your world"—pertains to the sacrifice (*kratu*).

Since it is possible [for conversation to occur], the conversation for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is prohibited, just as "one should not speak untruth" prohibits untruthful speech for the sake of the sacrifice.

When it is thus argued that, just as untruthful speech for the sake of the sacrifice is prohibited, so too is conversation for the sake of the sacrifice prohibited—the reply is given: this is not for the sake of the sacrifice.

The prohibition [of non-conciliation] is because non-conciliation is already established in the ritual; therefore, since there is an absence of conciliation for the sake of the ritual, this prohibition of conciliation for the sake of the person is itself for the sake of the person. For, by way of being for the sake of the ritual, non-conciliation is indeed established by the rule: "One should sacrifice after having excluded her. Indeed, not...

A conversation with one who is under restraint is possible; "restraint" (*aparodhana*) consists in causing indifference toward the performance of a ritual act. Therefore, what is prohibited is that which serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and the prohibition itself likewise serves the purpose of the person alone. And it has already been stated that the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than the context (*prakaraṇa*). In this regard:

And regarding the locative case, having accepted that this is merely a prohibition of conversation— as in the rule "one should not converse with a woman wearing soiled clothes"— this investigation proceeds.

The opening of this *kṛtācintā* (examination of a settled matter) is based on the premise that "this is a prohibition against approaching [the teacher]. For if one were to accept the prohibition against approaching as absolute, there would be no room for the doubt raised by the *pūrvapakṣa*, since there is no approaching [of the teacher] during a *kratu* (sacrificial rite). However, since conversation does exist during a *kratu*, the doubt regarding its prohibition is justified. Furthermore, the mention of "seclusion" (*aparodha*) is for the purpose of directly prohibiting the act of acting as an agent [in sexual intercourse]; it is not with the intention that she should not be conversed with even by another person. Thus, the *pūrva-* [pakṣa]...

It has been argued that, in the event of an obstruction, one should not converse with her because of the prohibition against all forms of association with a sacrifice; this is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*). Now, taking up the objection raised by way of a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*), he challenges [the position]: "But surely this non-conversation is already established even as a duty pertaining to the person (*puruṣārtha*), for it is said:
'One should not take pleasure with an unattractive woman, nor with one who is menstruating.'"

Thus, since this non-conformity in the form of a prohibition of approaching [the mother] is already established through implication (*lakṣaṇā*), how can it be a prohibition even with respect to a human goal (*puruṣārtha*)? The answer is: this very [Smṛti] will be the source (root) for that [Vedic text]. Therefore, since the act of approaching [the mother] would indeed have been obtained through passion (*rāga*) prior [to the Smṛti], the prohibition is justified; or else, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

[This refers] to one who has attained the object through the recollection of that [prohibition]. Now, if it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), why does it not pertain to the sacrifice itself? To this he says: "In any case, there is no status as a constituent of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*). Since the prohibition is perceived as being connected to the person, how could it be a constituent of the sacrifice? This is because approaching [the wife] is not enjoined as a subordinate element of the sacrifice. If it is a restatement, why would it transcend its connection to the person? Thus, even in the case of a restatement, [there is no such transcendence].

[The opponent asserts] that it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*). To refute this hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*), he says: "But surely this is merely a prohibition of conversation; how can it be the source for this Smṛti, or a restatement (*anuvāda*) of it? It is replied: "One should not eat its food" [and] "Indeed, with ointments for a woman... [etc.].

Regarding the statement "food," since "approaching [the wife] is indeed the food of a woman," this very prohibition of approaching is established along with its reasoning; thus, the meaning of the Vedic sentence—which consists of a prohibition of the agreement that takes the form of a prohibition of approaching—is explained by the Veda itself as a prohibition of approaching. This is the "removal of doubt. Prohibition of approaching.
This is so. Therefore, either there is a root for the Smṛti, or it is a restatement (anuvāda) of what has already been established. The mention of "restatement" is a bold assertion (prauḍhavāda);
in ultimate reality, however, the Smṛti itself is the root.

"But in the absence of a specific context, that property belongs to the person because of its distinction [from the ritual]; for the injunction 'gold is to be worn' is a rule for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) due to being an *anārabhyavāda* (a statement not introduced by a specific ritual context), since no ritual is perceived as being proximate here. Therefore, it is for the sake of the person"—having thus begun with the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).

He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But surely, refinement (*saṃskāra*) belongs to that which has a purpose, not to that which is purposeless; and because of the use of the accusative case, it is proper that this is a refinement of gold, [thinking] 'the refined [gold] will assist the sacrifice'. The meaning of this is: "because of the use of the accusative" means that by virtue of being the object (*karma*) of the action, it is the object itself that is expressed by the word in the accusative case. Therefore, [the text says] *suvarṇam*.

Because the suffix *kṛtya* (in the word *bhāryam*) indicates a purpose for an action, this "wearing" (*dhāraṇa*) is indeed a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the gold. Furthermore, a consecration cannot be without a purpose; therefore, since it will assist the sacrifice once consecrated, the gold is consecrated by means of wearing for that very purpose. Thus, this consecration serves the purpose of the sacrifice. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): To this, it is replied—it might be so.

If the consecration of refined gold were applicable for the sake of a ritual action (*karman*), it would not be so here, for there is no purpose for the gold in a ritual action in this context. He demonstrates this: first of all, no ritual action under discussion exists; nor is there an injunction for a ritual action here, because of the absence of a connection between a material substance and a deity.
Therefore, since the consecration of a substance would be purposeless, this is a duty pertaining to the person (*puruṣadharma*). [Objection: But even in this case, a result must be postulated.

Since no qualified person (*adhikārin*) is heard mentioned, one must postulate a qualification for the qualified person. The reply is: because injunctions (*niyoga*) have action as their purpose, and since there is no action under discussion here, there is no fault in postulating a qualified person. [End of section on] the qualified person.

Since the connection between the mutual word-meanings is for the purpose of an injunction (*niyoga*), and because there is no absence of the relevant injunctive mandate of qualification (*adhikāra-niyoga*), it is not a fault to forcibly postulate another qualification, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice. Therefore, the wearing of gold is enjoined as a duty for the agent of the ritual action. Furthermore...

The opponent says: "If the result is postulated as being for the sake of purifying the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*), why is it not also postulated as being for the sake of purifying the substance (*dravya-saṃskāra*) as a benefit to the sacrifice?
Since the postulation is equal [in both cases], what is the distinction? The sense is this: there is indeed a distinction;

for when a connection with the agent is understood through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) within the same sentence, the postulation of a result is justified because of its internal proximity (*antaraṅgatvāt*).

Furthermore, there is no assumption of a connection with the sacrifice (*kratu*) as something extraneous, because such a connection with the sacrifice would involve a remoteness of meaning (*arthaviprakarṣa*) and would thus be an external factor (*bahiraṅga*). This [previous argument] is merely supplementary, as it is not universally applicable. Now, he states the fundamental reasoning which is universally applicable—this other distinction should be observed everywhere: for the establishment of entitlement (*adhikāra*) occurs through the connection with an agent (*kartṛ*), and for one who is entitled, the fruit [accrues].
The assumption of a purpose is logical; however, it is not the case that one assumes a purpose for the connection with a substance, as was demonstrated in the case of the *saktu* (barley meal).

The meaning of this is as follows: agency (*kartṛtva*) is indeed an effect of the entitlement (*adhikāra*); therefore, once the connection with the agent is understood, the establishment of the entitlement—which serves as the cause—is appropriate. Furthermore, since an unqualified person cannot be entitled, one must also assume a specific result (*phala*).
When, however, the connection with a substance is understood through the action, it is not logical to assume a purpose for the substance, as there is a lack of evidence.
Nor is the very fact that the action is for the sake of the substance (*tādarthya*) the evidence [for its purpose], because purposefulness would be untenable if the substance itself were purposeless;
for that very purposefulness toward the substance is not yet understood. Furthermore, it has been stated in various places that this purposefulness is not expressed by the accusative case.

(1) G. It is logical that the remainder [of the offering] applies to all rites when no specific context is mentioned, because there is no distinction; for it is said: "With whatever rite one seeks success, in that one should offer the *jayā* oblations."

Thus, it remains established for now that the *jaya* and other offerings (*āhoma*) are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the ritual action, because they are connected with actions that achieve prosperity (*ṛddhi*) and because no other fruit is heard of [for them].

Now, a doubt arises regarding these [offerings]: are they subsidiary parts of ritual action in general, or only of Vedic ritual action? By the term "ritual action in general" (*karmamātra*), both Smārta and Vedic rituals are intended here, but not agriculture and the like; for since the subsidiariness of those [latter] is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), their being subsidiary parts of Vedic rituals is untenable.

In the Bhāṣya, however, the mention of agriculture and so forth is merely for the sake of raising an objection and not in an absolute sense. The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) considers that [the rite] applies to all purposes because there is no distinction. Now, one might object: since one who has not maintained the sacred fires lacks the Āhavanīya fire, this oblation (homa) is not possible. The meaning of this is as follows:
regarding the Jaya-oblations, it is stated, "One offers them in the Āhavanīya."

Because of this statement, [the offerings] must be performed in the *āhavanīya* fire. In that case, if they were to be subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of worldly (*laukika*) or Smārta rites, then since those rites are possible even for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the *jayahoma* would follow as a requirement.

However, one who has not established the sacred fires is not able to offer oblations in the *āhavanīya*. Nor can it be argued that "one who has established the sacred fires will offer in the *āhavanīya*."

"But it is not so for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)," [some might argue]. This is because it would entail the sublation of the *āhavanīya* fire, which is enjoined as a constant requirement. Nor is this position tenable—that the rites such as the *Aṣṭakā* performed by one who has not maintained the fires will be devoid of the *jaya-homa*, while those performed by one who has maintained them will not. For it is impossible for a single injunction to simultaneously involve both being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) and not being an auxiliary. Therefore, the established conclusion is that it is better to have the omission of the *jaya-homa* from the Vedic rites of those possessing the three fires (*tretāvat*), rather than having it apply inconsistently.

He refutes [the objection]: "This will simply not be an *āhavanīya* fire, because it must conform to the primary act (*pradhāna*). It is not proper to abandon the primary act for the sake of conforming to a subordinate element (*guṇa*); rather, it is the subordinate element itself that must be abandoned in order to conform to the primary—so the experts in ritual limbs (*aṅga*) maintain. The meaning of this is as follows: since it is established that the *jayā-homa* is for the purpose of all rites based on the general scriptural statement, "Whatever rite one should desire to perform," [it follows that] in whatever primary act...

In rites such as the Aṣṭakā, because one has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the Āhavanīya fire is absent. Regarding this, a doubt arises: "Since the primary rite exists, should the Jaya-homa be performed?

Or, since the Āhavanīya fire is absent, should it not be performed? In this doubt, because the primary rite must be favored, the Āhavanīya fire—which is merely a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the oblation—[is disregarded].

Having abandoned [the primary], the *jayā-homa* must be performed; however, it is not proper to abandon the *jayā-homa*, which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the primary rites such as the *aṣṭakā*, merely for the sake of the *āhavanīya* fire, which is itself a subsidiary of that subsidiary *jayā-homa*. The *āhavanīya* is merely a subordinate factor (*guṇa*).

Those who know the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) maintain that it is proper to abandon [the primary] in accordance with the principal (*pradhāna*). He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "What you have said is true; indeed, this is so. However, this principle does not apply here. For, 'in the case of a conflict between the quality of an auxiliary and the purpose [of the principal], [the former prevails] because it exists for that purpose.
Why? Because, first of all, the sublation of the *āhavanīya* fire is not possible in the Vedic context, nor [is it possible] for that which is merely worldly."

It can be said that it is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Smārta [rite], as you yourself have stated on the grounds of non-distinction. This is the underlying intention: where the status of being an auxiliary is certain, there the principle of the conflict between the auxiliary and its quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*) applies. But here, the status of the *jayā-homa* as an auxiliary is not even certain. In that case, it is proper that the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*) belongs to that which, when adopted as the principal, does not subvert the essential nature of the thing to be enjoined (*viniyojyasvarūpa*). And the principal is that which is connected with the *āhavanīya* fire.

Because [the text] states "its own form" (*svarūpam*), the application (*viniyoga*) is restricted to Vedic rites alone, since the *āhavanīya* fire is possible therein; whereas in the case of Smārta rites, the *āhavanīya* is absent for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). Thus, the application is concluded in a manner that does not conflict with the subsidiary status of the *āhavanīya*. Nor is there a contradiction with the rule "by whatever rite one desires [to perform]," because that refers to rites in general without distinction. Therefore, due to the mutual exclusion between existence and non-existence—that is, the mutual exclusion between the presence and absence of the *āhavanīya*—[the application is so restricted].

It is logical that the determination of the specific [deity] occurs precisely through the existence of the Āhavanīya fire, and not through its absence; for this [absence] is a cause of non-comprehension—it is a cause for the lack of comprehension itself, and not a cause for the comprehension of a specific [deity]. Therefore, it is established that the *jayā-homa* is indeed Vedic.
r838] There would be a desire for the removal of faults in the worldly case. In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, it is heard: "As many horses as one might receive..."

Regarding the injunction, "One should offer oblations on four potsherds to Varuṇa," there exists the horse-donation sacrifice (*aśvapratigraheṣṭi*). In that context, a doubt arises as to whether this sacrifice pertains to the worldly acceptance of horses—as expressed in the phrase "as many horses as one might accept"—or to the Vedic [acceptance]. Regarding this, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): it pertains to the worldly [acceptance].

Because a fault arises from accepting [a gift] from a Śūdra or from another who has committed a sinful act; for this sacrifice is heard of in scripture as being for the acceptance of a horse that possesses a fault, and such faulty nature exists in the worldly acceptance of a horse, since a fault arises when there is acceptance from a Śūdra or from another who has committed a sinful act. Therefore, the worldly acceptance of a gift is faulty, and thus this sacrifice applies precisely to that case. Here...
The commentary states: "The enumeration of faults is not a qualification of the subject matter of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), but rather serves the purpose of praising expiation.
He begins to explain that:
"Is this a qualification of the subject matter of expiation, or is it for the purpose of praise? This is as follows: of this...

When the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is for the purpose of removing the matter known as the "Varuṇa-graha," then the Varuṇa-graha is a qualification of the object of that expiation. However, that which is indeed for the purpose of purifying a fault must be performed only where the fault exists; thus, by implication, the Varuṇa-graha is a qualification of the acceptance (*pratigraha*) that constitutes the object of the expiation. And since the Varuṇa-graha occurs only where there is such acceptance, the horse-donation sacrifice (*aśvapratigraheṣṭi*) is for the removal of that [fault] only in that specific case. But when it is to be performed...

In that case, it is for the sake of praise; however, by examining the sequence of the preceding and following statements, this is understood to be for the purpose of removing a fault, and thus it is recognized as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Therefore, it ought to apply to the worldly case. On this point, the *Bhāṣya* states: "But surely, even in the Vedic case, there is sin for one who accepts a gift from someone who should not be accepted; therefore, an expiation must exist [there too]. It is replied:"
r839] This would be so if there were a desire on the part of the agent of the acceptance; however, that indeed is just as it is for the causal agent, as will be explained in the subsequent section.
"We shall explain [this] later.
Anticipating this, he says—(here he raises an objection)—"This commentary is incoherent.
If there is no sacrifice for the recipient in the worldly case, then why should there not be one for the recipient in the Vedic case as well?"

And therefore, even in the case of Vedic [practice], since there is a fault for one who accepts a horse from an improper donor, why is there a suspicion of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the recipient alone in the worldly case, even though there exists an expiation intended to remove that fault? If it is argued that the sacrifice belongs to the giver because of the observation of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) understood from the introduction (*upakrama*), then this is equally applicable to the worldly case; for even in that view, by considering the introduction, [it would follow] that the sacrifice belongs to the giver alone.

And there is no fault in that [act], because giving is not prohibited. Therefore, since its purpose is the removal of a fault, there is no application to worldly cases. Now, even regarding the worldly position of acceptance (*pratigraha*), the intention is that it pertains only to the giver; thus, the commentary stating "from a Śūdra or from another" would be incoherent, for the fault must be shown to belong to the giver, not the recipient. By asserting that the sacrifice is for the giver to remove his fault, the fault is indeed attributed to the giver.

It must be explained [as follows]: In the case of receiving a gift from a Śūdra or anyone else, the fault lies not with the giver, but rather with the recipient alone. Furthermore, this sacrifice does not belong to him (the giver), because that would contradict the introductory statement. How so? Because in the subsequent section, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that "this sacrifice belongs to the recipient," since the conclusion is determined by the introductory statement: "Or rather, it belongs to the Veda, because it is seen in the majority of cases" (*vedo vā prāyadarśanāt*). Thus, the conclusion is fixed by the introduction: "Or rather, it belongs to the Veda, because it is seen in the majority of cases."
