It has been stated that the conclusion must follow the beginning; therefore, here too, by considering the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) situated at the beginning, it is understood that the sacrifice is for the giver.
To this, it is replied: this commentary is not incoherent; rather, this is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).

The mention of a fault (*doṣa*) in the case of receiving a horse in a worldly context is appropriate only as a qualification of the object; when a sacrifice is undertaken with the worldly reception of a horse as its subject, the mention of the fault is appropriate only as a qualification of the object—characterized by the act of receiving—insofar as it serves to present the result. On that view, this sacrifice, being for the purpose of purifying the fault, belongs only to the recipient who is susceptible to the fault. It is the recipient alone who...

[The word] "adhikārī" means "the entitled person. But how can the recipient alone be the entitled person, given that by virtue of the introductory context it is more appropriate for the giver alone to be the entitled person? The answer is: because in this view—namely, the view that relies upon worldly acceptance—if, even in that view, this sacrifice were to belong only to the giver, then one would have to assume that this sacrifice is a subsidiary (aṅga) of the worldly, Smṛti-based act of giving.

The form (*rūpa*) is either a different fruit or a different governing context (*adhikārāntara*). First of all, its status as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of giving is not possible, because it is exhausted by being the objective cause (*nimitta*); since it is already spent, it is untenable for it to be the remainder (*śeṣin*) of the act of giving. If, on the contrary, the status of giving as the principal (*aṅgin*) is postulated through a reversal [of roles], then this itself is improper: namely, the postulation of something that has been exhausted as a cause as again being the principal, for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [to support such a claim]. Now, one might object:

This alone is the proof: that the mention of a defect residing in the giver is [merely] an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). He says this because it is possible for an explanatory passage to be justified even by way of figurative praise (*guṇavāda*). Thus, the acceptance of a horse is the cause of the defect. Since a defect occurs even for the giver, how much more so for the recipient?

Because it is possible for the explanatory passage to be intended as demonstrating the defect of receiving, it cannot be established that the gift is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice by postulating a defect in the giver and then seeking its removal through that means.

Regarding the phrase "to imagine": one might object that this must indeed be a separate entitlement (adhikāra) based solely on the act of giving. To this he says: because it is understood from the sentence that the result is the liberation from sin. Therefore, its connection must be described in such a way that it becomes logically consistent. And since the person to be enjoined (niyojya) is the recipient, its connection is appropriate with him, not with the giver; thus he says: "And it is not possible to imagine sin on the part of the giver."
(1) Because giving is enjoined in exactly the same way both in the world and in the Veda, therefore, according to the worldly view, this sacrifice belongs to the recipient alone.

In the Vedic view, however, because it is inserted within the very context (*prakaraṇa*) and its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is determined by that context, there is no need to postulate a separate result; thus, this sacrifice would belong to the donor alone. In that case, the mention of "liberation from fault" would be unintended, since the donor has no fault. Therefore, this sacrifice pertains only to the worldly acceptance of gifts. For in that case, according to the aforementioned reasoning, the sacrifice belongs to the recipient.

And since there is a fault for the recipient, it would be intended that the hearing of the release from that fault applies to him. Consequently, this is the point of doubt here: does this sacrifice belong to the recipient in the case of a worldly (*laukika*) acceptance, or rather to the giver in the case of a Vedic (*vaidika*) one? In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because of the hearing of the release from sin, it belongs to the recipient in a worldly acceptance. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) [states] that the acceptance of a horse does not [remove] the sin as it is heard in the text.

The acceptance of a horse as the cause of dropsy is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as its cause; nor is it established by verbal testimony (*vacana*). For that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). If this statement were intended to inform us that "dropsy arises from the acceptance of a horse and that it is removed by this sacrifice," then there would be a split in the sentence due to the difference in meaning. And yet, this [text] is a single [statement].

This is the statement. Therefore, it is not on the basis of the verbal testimony that the acceptance of a horse (*aśvapratigraha*) is the cause of dropsy (*jalodara*). Consequently, the mere mention of sin and the mention of dropsy are entirely consistent even in the Vedic context, because the recipient of the gift experiences suffering through the necessity of guarding, nourishing, and so forth [the animal]. Now, one might object: "In the Vedic view, there ought to be a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) for the giver; thus, the fault should be shown to belong to the giver alone. Why then is this presented as a fault of the recipient?"
The mention [of the recipient] is because the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*) has not yet been established. It is appropriate to observe the fault in the recipient;

in this present section, it is established that the entitlement to the sacrifice belongs to the giver alone by virtue of being an auxiliary to the ritual (*kratvaṅga*). However, in the subsequent section, there will be an investigation into the agent—whether the giver or the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) [performs the sacrifice]. Therefore, the observation of the fault of officiating (*ārtvijadoṣa*) is logically applicable when the recipient is the agent.

Furthermore, in the case of the view that this is an *iṣṭi* (sacrificial rite) regarding the acceptance of Vedic gifts, a fruit must also be postulated, since it is logically established as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action. Whether it is enjoined by the context (*prakaraṇa*) as belonging to the agent—be it the giver or the receiver—if this *iṣṭi* has the giver as its agent;
or even if it has the receiver as its agent, the meaning is that it is a subordinate part of that [Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice] because of the context of the Pauṇḍarīka.

"And it is not enjoined because of the difference in action. Here, he raises an objection: "It is indeed reasonable that when [the gift] belongs to the giver, it is a constituent part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*), due to the connection with a single entitlement (*ekādhikāra*); but when it belongs to the recipient, how is that so? For the recipient..."

This objection—that there is no connection because it belongs to a different section—is raised by one who is mistaken. The answer is: it is inferred through grammatical modification (*vipariṇāma*), on the strength of the opening and the conclusion, just as in the case of the phrase "one should cause [the pupil] to accept" (*pratigrāhayet*). The meaning of this is: just as in the final established doctrine (*rāddhānta*) there is a modification of the word *pratigrāhayet* due to the force of the opening statement, so too, through the modification from the form *kṛta*, even though the agent is the recipient (*pratigrahītṛ*), there is a single substratum (*ekādhiṣṭhāna*).

Subservience (*aṅgatā*) is postulated through the connection with the person performing the action. He demonstrates that very modification: "The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are to be made to sacrifice, as in the case of fasting.

Just as the priests are made to fast, so too are they to be made to sacrifice; the meaning is that they are to be caused to sacrifice by means of the four-cup vessel dedicated to Varuṇa. Therefore, it is rightly said: "It may belong either to the giver or to the receiver. As for what was further stated...

Or rather, he considers that [the Veda] is so because of the observation of the majority of cases. Now, it was stated that this fault does not exist in reality; to that, he says: "For even a fault that has become a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda) applies directly to the recipient alone, as we observe the suffering involved in protecting, nourishing, and so forth.
But how will the mention of the giver found in the opening passage be consistent with this? To this, he says: "The opening passage also, like the worldly position, pertains to the giver as well."
To that extent there is a fault; how much more so for the recipient? This has already been stated by us. But the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) says:
In any case, one must necessarily assume the meaning "he should cause [them] to be extinguished.
Therefore, it is considered better to take it as "he should cause [him] to accept," in accordance with the introductory context;
for since a modification of the word is inevitably required, it is preferable to effect that modification in conformity with the opening statement.

It is logical that [the Veda] should be considered [authoritative]. Since the commentary has already explained that the *arthavāda* is intended to establish the necessity of performing the ritual action, there is no tautology with the section beginning with "Or the Veda" (*vedo vā*). However, for one who explains these two sections as a single unit, this is the underlying intention:

In the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) must be refuted by demonstrating that the purpose of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is consistent with the true meaning. Furthermore, the description of the ultimate purpose of the *arthavāda*—which consists in its being necessarily to be performed—is dependent upon the subsequent section. "And the mishap from drinking is like that. Is the phrase "like that" an extended application (*atideśika*) intended to indicate a distinction? For [a distinction] cannot be established without a specific difference.

"In that case, it would be exactly the same. This is the distinction: because a fault is heard in the scripture—namely, "He who vomits Soma is deprived either of his sense-organ or of his vigor"—because this fault is heard, there must be an expiation for the vomiting of Soma in the worldly context.

The distinction [is as follows]: Now, it might be argued that in the previous section it was stated that [the practice] is worldly precisely because a fault was observed; here too, if it is stated that it is worldly precisely because a fault is observed, there is no distinction. He provides the rebuttal: True, the inconsistency was stated there regarding the fault characterized by dropsy (*jalodara*). But here, exhaustion (*glāni*) resulting from vomiting is indeed consistent with the sense organs; thus—

What doubt could there be? The increase of the sense faculties is indeed supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Precisely because this [increase] is supported by valid means of knowledge, the fault [of the objection] that it is for the purpose of vomiting has been removed. Otherwise, the rebuttal should have been given that there is no exhaustion at all.

It might be asked: how, moreover, is the fault avoided by stating that it is for the purpose of inducing vomiting? To this he says: "For that which is intended solely for the purpose of alleviating illness, its resulting illness cannot be conceived as a fault. For that which is for the purpose of vomiting is inseparable from the illness of the one who vomits.

Because it has been cultivated for the sake of illness itself, and since it can be said that there is no fault in the illness that serves the purpose of illness, the status of being a fault is already refuted. Since there is no fault, this *Soma-indra* rite does not have the purpose of removing that [fault], as before; rather, this rite is enjoined on account of the vomiting of Soma-drinking, out of fear of the assumption of a [specific] result.

The meaning is "what? This rite is caused by the vomiting of that Soma-drinking which was enjoined. Therefore, since it is caused by the vomiting of Soma-drinking connected to the sacrifice (*kratu*), it is established that this rite is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice.
This applies everywhere without distinction. Does this expiation apply whenever there is vomiting by as many persons as there are Soma-vomiters?

Although the author of the Bhāṣya has not explicitly stated it, he expresses the doubt that is understood by implication: "Or rather, [the expiation belongs] to the master alone. When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached—that because there is no distinction, the vomiting belongs to everyone—it is said in reply: "This expiation belongs to the master alone. Why? The answer is: "A single injunction cannot apply both to the sacrificer and the officiating priests. For in one case, the injunction is "he should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).

The injunction "one should cause another to sacrifice" [applies] elsewhere. Its meaning is this: if there were a single injunction for both the vomiting of the sacrificer and the vomiting of the officiating priest, then there would be no distinction. However, such a single injunction is not possible, because in one case—namely, the position regarding the vomiting of the sacrificer—[the result differs].
The injunction "one should sacrifice" would, in that case, have as its sentence-meaning: "He who vomits the *soma* should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma-Indra.

However, in other instances—specifically regarding the alternative where the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) vomits—the injunction is "he should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice. For it has been established that this is an act for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), as previously stated.

Therefore, this is not the meaning: that "whosoever vomits Soma, that officiating priest (ṛtvij) should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma-Indra. Nor is it possible for both [the general rule and the specific restriction] to exist within a single sentence. Consequently, because there is no distinction, the rite dedicated to Soma-Indra applies to the vomiting of all [officiating priests].

[Objection: Even so, let it apply only to the vomiting by an officiating priest. To this, he says: Why? Because this injunction (*codanā*) remains unaltered. [The text specifies] "the officiating priest" (*ṛtvij*).

For even in the case of one who causes pleasure (*manapa*), since the entitlement belongs solely to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), a modification (*vipariṇāma*) must necessarily be assumed; yet this injunction remains unmodified. And that [injunction] is understood to apply specifically to the vomiting by oneself, because this rite has as its cause the vomiting of the sacrificer; therefore, according to the principle that "that which is without a fruit in proximity to something with a fruit is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to it," it becomes so. Otherwise, if the vomiting of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) were the cause, then—[the injunction would remain] unmodified—

This injunction would enjoin an independent rite for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) themselves as its qualified performers (*adhikārin*). Therefore, because of the difference in the qualified performers, it would not be an auxiliary (*anaṅga*) at all; thus, the principle that "that which lacks a fruit in proximity to that which possesses a fruit is an auxiliary to it" is not established. This non-auxiliary status was stated on the basis of the original injunction (*codanā*)—without modification—in the case of the view that the vomiting pertains to the officiating priests, because a sacrifice belonging to one person cannot benefit another. Therefore, [it does not apply] to the officiating priest...
This is for the purpose of the owner's vomiting. The meaning is that what is enjoined for one does not benefit another. He concludes:
"Therefore, it is established that this is indeed caused by the owner's vomiting.
Regarding the offering of the entire oblation because the sacrificial material is intended for that [deity], the Bhāṣya here asks: "Is the whole oblation to be given to Agni?"
That is untenable, because there is no act of giving toward a deity; likewise, it would follow that one must leave some portion remaining and give away only a portion.

He explains this as follows: Here now a doubt arises regarding the injunction "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*): Is there a renunciation of the entire offering, or is it only that much [of it] according to the statement, "he cuts off twice from the oblation, he offers the fourfold portion" (*dvir haviṣo ’vadyati, caturavattaṃ juhoti*)? Thus, by the word "giving" (*dāna*), "renunciation" (*tyāga*) is expressed through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). But surely, a doubt of this kind is not even possible here; for [the text simply says], "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni."

The injunction for the sacrifice has been concluded. Therefore, since there is no definitive statement of the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) that "there is a relinquishment of the whole," doubt itself is untenable. But [it may be argued]: "He cuts twice from the oblation" and "He offers the fourfold portion."

From this hearing [of the text], it appears that there is a relinquishment of the mere purification of the two [portions]; to this he says: "He cuts off twice from the oblation"—this is an injunction for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the oblation, just as in the case of "he sweeps away the grasses from the fire."

[Objection: But surely it is not only the cutting out (*avadāna*) that is heard; "he offers" (*juhoti*) is also heard. Therefore, it is understood that the sacrifice must be performed with exactly two cuttings. [Response: The answer is—there will be a disposal (*pratipatti*) of what has been removed from the oblation. Just as in the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), after the sacrifice, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other rites are performed from the remnant (*śeṣa*).

The *sviṣṭakṛt* and other such offerings constitute the performance [of the sacrifice]. To this, it is replied: it cannot be thus that there is a relinquishment of the whole, because the *juhoti* and the sacrifices (*yāga*) are accomplished by means of the substance connected to them; the *homa* and *yāga*, being essentially the relinquishment of a substance, are accomplished only by means of one's own substance. And if there were a relinquishment of everything, then the *homa*, the *yāga*, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* and others—

They are not tenable. The meaning of this is as follows: under the view that the whole [of the sacrificial cake] is to be given away, the *puroḍāśa* would have to be abandoned even without performing the double-portioning (*dvayavadāna*), because otherwise its status as "the whole" would be untenable. Consequently, having performed only the double-portioning from the *puroḍāśa*, one would have to offer it and perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other sacrifices; these, however, are not tenable, because the substance that has been abandoned is no longer one's own property. Therefore, the whole is not to be abandoned.
There is a doubt as to whether [the offering] should be performed. Now, one might argue that the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other offerings will be made from a different substance; to this he replies:

"The injunction concerns the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*). This is because that alone constitutes the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), and because the word "remnant" (*śeṣa*) refers specifically to the substance under discussion.

Therefore, a doubt arises. And regarding this doubt, which side’s conclusion is appropriate? The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that because the injunction for the *āgneya* offering is not counterbalanced by another, and because the other offerings depend upon it, the former alone is stronger.
This has been stated: "The entire oblation is to be offered, because it is for that purpose. How then is the rule "he offers the fourfold portion" to be understood?
Thus,
regarding the oblation: from the usage of the dative case in the injunction "he cuts off [the portion] for Sviṣṭakṛt," it is determined that Sviṣṭakṛt is the deity.
By that [act], the substance and the deity are determined; from that connection between substance and deity, the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice arises.

And those two—oblation (*homa*) and sacrifice (*yāga*)—are not possible when the substance has been discarded. [Objection: Then the meaning of the root *yaj* and the root *hu* must be understood figuratively as consisting merely of the act of throwing [into the fire]. Or else, another substance possessing those characteristics must be produced. He explains this very point: "twice from the sacrificial oblation..."
"He cuts" means he cuts according to the nature of the sacrificial offering (*haviḥ*).

However, because the action has already been performed, it should occur only once, since the substance is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the action. To this, it is replied: It is indeed true as you have said, provided that [the injunction] were "an eight-potherd cake for Agni."
Thus, that secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would have renunciation as its limit; it would be—(1) G.
omits "tena...yete" [p.

Thus, since it is understood that "this deity belongs to this [sacrifice]" merely by way of a general relationship, the status of being related remains entirely valid even when only a portion of that [deity] is relinquished. This is what was stated: "Even when the relationship is not complete, the application of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is possible; therefore, it will be accepted from that. Now, one might ask: "How can there be 'belonging to Agni' (*āgneyatā*) for the whole, if a portion is not being offered and thus lacks that relationship? The answer is: it has been shown from that [very point].

The connection is with the phrase "of that which has been taken," namely, of the two portions. And this being the case, when the injunction regarding the offering to Agni is established, [the texts] "he offers the fourfold portion" and "he cuts off for the *sviṣṭakṛt*" become logically consistent.
Thus, a figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) cannot be postulated;

rather, it is the production of a substance possessing the characteristics of an oblation, and by the very offering of the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*), the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled, as in the case of "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*).

Thus, the observation of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and subsequent rites becomes logically consistent, as seen in the injunctions: “He cuts off the *iḍā* from the remnant” and “He cuts off for the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the remnant.”

Thus, the observation of a remainder is also logically consistent; otherwise, the word "remainder" would apply to that which is not a remainder at all. Furthermore, as for this objection raised—that because the two portions are *saṃskāra* (preparatory rites), there is no contradiction in discarding the whole—it is merely a mere suspicion. It has already been stated that the oblation (*havis*) exists for the sake of the sacrifice. The meaning of this is as follows: as for this further suspicion raised regarding the two portions...

The refinement of the substance consisting of its constituent parts has been accepted; that very [substance] is offered by means of the *homa*, and even when that has been offered, the *āgneya* (oblation for Agni) will be performed with the entire remaining *puroḍāśa*. Therefore, there is no contradiction. To this it is replied:
this would be so if the sacrifice were for that purpose, or if the sacrificial material (*havis*) were to be connected with the sacrifice. However, the sacrificial material...

It is stated in the Bhāṣya that once two portions have been cut off for the sake of the sacrifice by him, since the sacrifice has already been accomplished, no further sacrifice need be performed even though the substance remains.

Because it lacks a specific purpose, the subsidiary rites should be performed from a single remnant, since the remnant is a subordinate element. Here, the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakāryāṇi*) serve as the example. Should one stop after performing them once, or should there be repetition as long as there is remnant? The meaning of this is: should one stop after performing the subsidiary rite from only a single remnant, or should the subsidiary rites be performed individually from all the remnants?

Regarding the phrase "the ritual acts are to be performed": therein, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that because the act has already been accomplished, it need only be performed once; for even from a single remnant, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by performing the subsidiary acts (*śeṣakārya*) once, just as in the case of the *Āgneya* sacrifice. But is it not the case that since subordinate elements (*guṇa*) repeat with each primary element (*pradhāna*), repetition is indeed understood for the remnant due to its lack of primacy? To resolve this, he says:

This is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*): since the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) is for the sake of benefiting the primary (*pradhāna*), and because the task is accomplished by performing it once, he does not consider repetition necessary. Because the object to be benefited is one and the same, the function of the subsidiary should be performed only once.

It is not because of its status as a subsidiary that it is to be refined, but rather for the sake of benefiting the primary. [Objection: But would this same principle not apply even in the case of the cups (*graha*) and so forth?

In that case as well, only a single ladle would have to be cleansed. To this, the reply is: it would indeed follow [so] if this were not settled here. If it is established right here that many [ladles] are to be cleansed, then what concern is there regarding the non-intentionality of singularity? This is stated: repetition continues until the remainder [is exhausted], even though it is for the sake of assisting the primary rite.

Nevertheless, even regarding the remaining rites, a distinction is indeed appropriate due to the difference between the principal acts (*śeṣin*). But is it not the case that it was stated that [the rite] should be performed only once because the purpose of the scripture has been accomplished?
(1) G. omits *na* [p. 850].

It is said: For it has been stated that the status of being assisted by the primary act (*pradhāna*) occurs through the medium of the remaining subsidiary acts (*śeṣa*). And no distinction is perceived among these subsidiaries as to which one is "this," "that," or "the other. Therefore, because no such distinction is apprehended, there must be a repetition for each primary act. Since there is no difference in their status as media, the effects (or results) accrue to all of them. Furthermore, indicative marks (*liṅga*) have been shown in the Bhāṣya. As for the argument that the subsidiaries lack a motive force (*aprayojakatva*)—

This is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). As for what we have stated—that "this very thing [is the object], because it is not a subordinate element (*śeṣa*)," and therefore it is that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*)—there is no contradiction with the Bhāṣya on that account. However, the author of the Bhāṣya does not consider the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of the subordinate element (*śeṣa*). The meaning is that the author of the Bhāṣya does not raise the prima facie argument with the intention of asserting subordinate status. Why? He says: "For there is neither the state of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*) nor the state of not being an instigator (*aprayojakatva*) in the case of a subordinate element."

This is appropriate. Its meaning is as follows: if the status of being a subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) were to belong to the remainder (*śeṣa*), then—due to [the rules regarding] destruction, defects, and removal—in the absence of a remainder of the substance already taken, and because the remainder would lack the capacity to motivate (*prayojakatā*) the substance, it would be "non-motivating" (*aprayojaka*). But this is not tenable.
Therefore, that very prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) which was shown by us remains; it is not [established] merely by the occurrence of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in the Bhāṣya.
As it appears:

if [the action arises] from one [source], this is a consideration regarding the performance in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the preceding section. For if the prima facie argument is that [it comes] from one, then this consideration applies. Even there, since no specific distinction is perceived, the prima facie view is that it may come from any [source whatsoever].
r851] The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that as long as the primary cause itself exists, it cannot be asserted that there is an impairment of the effect produced by that cause.

Since the occurrence of the remaining causes—the characteristics of the remainder—is possible when they first present themselves, it cannot be said that there is an obstruction of the contingent subsidiary rites (*naimittika-śeṣa-kārya*). In that case, the contingent rite is performed; however, because the subsequent subsidiary rites (*jaghanya-śeṣa*) have already been accomplished, the requirement for the contingent rite is fulfilled by its very first occurrence. Thus, the non-performance of the remaining subsidiary rites is indeed logical.

[The opponent says: "Because there is no mention of eating [the remnant]. But how can there be a suspicion of purchasing [the priests] with the remnant here, given the contradiction between what has already been employed and what is being employed?

To this, he says: because of the conclusion regarding the two portions with the words "This for the Brahman," the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view considers the purchase to be by means of the remnant of the sacrifice.

The proponent [says]: That purposefulness (*tādarthya*) of the substance toward the sacrifice which was intended is fulfilled by the mere two-fold portioning; therefore, because the remainder has no purpose elsewhere, and because there is no contradiction between what has already been employed and what is to be employed—given that the dative case is not heard in the formula "This for Brahman"—the remainder belongs to Brahman and the others.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers this to be a purchase (*parikraya*). However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) maintains that since even that [substance] is produced for the purpose of being offered, it serves solely the purpose of the sacrifice and thus cannot be employed for any other purpose. Since even the remaining substance is produced for the purpose of the two-fold portioning (*dvayavadāna*), it has the nature of being for the sacrifice; therefore, it cannot be employed elsewhere, and by this [principle], there is no purchase. If [the substance] were indeed the whole...

How then can the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other such sacrifices be for the purpose of the [main] sacrifice? It is not logical that they be employed in another sacrifice. The point here is that the learned do not deal with what has been dedicated to a deity as if it were their own property. The answer is: "It is logical because the remnant has not been relinquished and because of a scriptural injunction. The meaning of this is: since the remnant has not been relinquished, ownership over it has indeed not departed; however, even while [that ownership remains]...

[Page r852] "If ownership were established by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), there would be no legal transaction regarding ownership. Since the conduct of the learned is sublated by its contradiction with the Vedic injunctions, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
[The opponent objects: "But surely even the act of giving will occur on account of the scriptural statement, for giving is indeed perceived [in the texts]. He refutes this:

If it is true that there is a statement [to this effect], yet no gift is heard of here—surely a gift is understood because of the hearing of the phrase "this is for Brahman," which indicates purpose (*tādarthya*)? To this he replies: the scriptural mention of purpose is indeed consistent even with the sense of being beneficial; thus, the benefit has been demonstrated.

For indeed, a substance being consumed necessarily produces pleasure; however, even in that case, the status of being a "remainder" (śeṣabhāva) is exactly the reverse. It is the substance alone that is primary as the object to be conveyed, while the person is merely subordinate as the conveyor; thus, there is no fault.
Thus ends the third [section] in the *Ṛjuvimalā*.
The Fourth Chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā* [p. 853]
The fifth section of the third chapter:

"And from the clarified butter, because of its connection with everything. It has been established that one takes portions from the remnant of whatever principal oblation (*pradhāna*) is enjoined. Regarding the *upāṃśuyāja*, there is a doubt: is it [to be taken] from the *dhruvā* vessel because there is no distinction, or from the subsidiary and the principal—?

Is the portion for Sviṣṭakṛt not to be cut because it is common to both [the subsidiary and the primary], or is it to be cut as a remnant of the primary, even though it is also a remnant of the subsidiary? Or is it to be cut from the *jauhava* (clarified butter) already taken, just as it is done with the *camasa* (cup)? Is it to be cut in the same manner as the *camasa*, or is it not to be cut because there is no remnant? When the prima facie view is reached that it should be cut because there is no distinction, [the conclusion is: although it is common to both the subsidiary and the primary, it should nevertheless be cut from the *āghāra* (clarified butter), because there is no difference in its status as a remnant.

Since there is no distinction regarding the *camasa* cup, it follows that one should take the portion from the *jauhava* [oblation] alone; this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: one should not take the portion from what is common, because it lacks the status of being a remnant of the primary sacrifice alone. Even the remaining portion is indeed common. Granting that it is common, he asks "What then? and replies: the taking of the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* is from the remnant of the primary sacrifice alone; for it is only from that which is the exclusive remnant of the primary sacrifice [that the portion is taken].

The *sviṣṭakṛt* portioning is from the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and other such materials, but not from that which remains as a remnant of both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) rites. For where the portioning is from a remnant of the principal alone, there the purpose of the sacrificial cake and so forth pertains solely to the principal; whereas where it is from a remnant of both the subsidiary and the principal, there the purpose pertains to both the subsidiary and the principal. It is not right to resort to such an asymmetry when symmetry is possible. Nor can it be said that the very same [remnant] is exclusively a remnant of the principal.
(1) P. 989 (2) G. api śeṣāt [p. r854]:
Precisely because it is common to all. As for the argument that there is an understanding of only what has been grasped, as in the case of the *camasa* cups—that is incorrect. Why?

The answer is: because of the scriptural injunction, "He offers with four portions. Since the entire four-portioned oblation is connected to the act of offering, there is no basis for leaving a remnant. If it is argued that the very injunction regarding the cutting of the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion serves as the authority [for a remnant], we reply: no; for the cutting of the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion is not possible without a remnant. Therefore, if it is claimed that the injunction for the *sviṣṭakṛt* cutting itself is the authority for the fact that a remnant must be left over—

It is not an authoritative means [of proof], because it serves a purpose when the remnant of the *puroḍāśa* and so forth is employed by another and not employed by oneself. As for what was said regarding the analogy with the *camasa*, that is not so; for the scriptural injunction for the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* has no other scope, whereas the *camasa* is mentioned merely as a vessel for taking up [the soma], as in: "O Agni, eat the soma; he performs the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*."

Thus, this scriptural injunction regarding the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* has no other scope; therefore, it serves as the authority for what must be left over. Furthermore, only the taking up of the cup (*camasa*) is heard in the scripture, not its offering. Consequently, since there is no contradiction with the teaching even by the falling of the first drop, the possibility of a remnant exists; thus, it is proper that the ritual action pertaining to the remnant should be performed in the cup. As for the [alleged] observation, it has been refuted.

Regarding the *sākaṃprasthāyya* sacrifice: by what distinction is this extended application (*atideśa*) made, given that here too there is simply an absence of a remnant (*śeṣa*)? The answer is as follows: since the rule "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*) applies, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers there to be a remnant for the sake of performing the ritual functions. It is correct that there is no remnant in the *upāṃśuyāja*, because the connection of the various functions of the remnant with that [sacrifice] is not established due to its being an archetype (*prakṛti*).

In that case, because it has undergone modification (*vikṛti*), the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakārya*) are obtained for the *prasthāyya* sacrifice by virtue of its being like the archetype (*prakṛti*). When those [rites] have been obtained—

The substance is made subordinate because it exists for the sake of that [action]; thus, there is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*). No; the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that the purpose (*kārya*) is more powerful because of the scriptural injunction (*vacana*).
For by the injunction, "He approaches while carrying the water-pots and offers the oblation," the approaching together with the water-pots serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

The entire oblation is understood [to be offered]. Even though the status of being a remnant (*śeṣatva*) might be possible through the application of rules for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth, since a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*) is stronger than the functional requirement (*kārya*), it is logical that the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other such rites—which would otherwise be required by function—are set aside. Thus, because there is no remnant, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other rites are not to be performed in the *sākaṃprasthāyya* sacrifice; this is the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).

And [it applies] in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice as well. Now, one might object: since it is heard in the scripture that "one offers the milk-draughts (payograhān) in the northern fire and the liquor-draughts (surāgrahān) in the southern fire," there is no remnant (śeṣa) because the substance has already been offered; therefore, there should be no expectation of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other rites from the archetype (*prakṛti*). To this, he replies: in the Sautrāmaṇī—

Regarding the statement, "He leaves a remnant in the ladle; he does not offer it as a *sarvahuta*," there arises again the suspicion that a remnant remains, leading one to consider the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* offerings [as applicable].
The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that this is not so, because that remnant is employed elsewhere—that is, because of its connection through being utilized for another purpose.

The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because it is to be disposed of by means of consumption purchased from a Brāhmaṇa, there is no *sviṣṭakṛt* or *iḍā* offering. Regarding the unity of the substance: however, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that in the *sarvapṛṣṭha* sacrifice, because the purificatory rites for the remnant apply to each primary act, there should be a repetition [of the offerings]. Since there is a plurality of primary acts and the duties regarding the remnant accrue to each primary act, and because the substance is abundant, there must indeed be [an offering] for each primary act.

r856] The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the meaning of the scripture is determined by the remaining ritual elements (*śeṣasaṃskāra*), because no specific distinction is perceived. For it is precisely those which are the remainder—

It appears that the consecration (saṃskāra) performed for one applies to all the remaining [portions] because no distinction is perceived. Therefore, since the purpose of the scriptural injunction has been fulfilled, there is no authority for repetition; this is the established conclusion (rāddhānta). [Objection: But it was stated regarding the clarified butter (ājya) that there is no Sviṣṭakṛt offering at all when [the substance] is common to all.
How then can there be even a single Sviṣṭakṛt offering here when the substance is common? [Response: True—but because the task has not yet been completed, [the offering must be made].

And there is a distinction because of the predominance or subordination of the constituent parts (*guṇa*). It is true that the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering does not exist in the case of the clarified butter (*ājya*). For in that case, this is the reasoning:

immediately after the *upāṃśuyāja* has been performed, the disposal of the remnant (*śeṣakārya*) should not take place, because as long as other rites have not been completed, the remnant is unfit for disposal. Once the other rites have been performed, due to the predominance of the constituent parts, there exists a commonality of being a remnant among the sacrifices which stand in a relationship of primary and subordinate elements (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) with respect to those principal acts.
Diti says: "The argument that 'the substance is not common' is merely this much; however, here this remnant also belongs only to the principal [offerings].
Therefore, the ritual act pertaining to the remnant must be performed."

Regarding the cup for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*): [the opponent asks], "But surely there is no prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here at all, because of the scriptural statement? For there is the statement: 'He consumes the cup for Indra and Vāyu twice. Indeed, on the prima facie view, it is impossible to claim that this statement has any other purpose. To this it is replied: This is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view; since the act of consuming is for the purpose of consecrating the Soma, the word "twice" refers to another performance (*prayoga*).

It will be a restatement (*anuvāda*). Its meaning is as follows: Soma is consecrated by the act of consumption, and it is consecrated by that single act of consumption alone for the sake of its primary status.

Thus, a second consumption is not logically established. Therefore, the statement "twice" is a restatement intended with reference to a different performance. However, the proponent of the final view (rāddhāntavādī) stated, "The determination of the action follows from the scriptural injunction," because of the word [in the text]. It is true that the Soma is consecrated by the act of consuming; nevertheless, because of the scriptural injunction—the specific mention of "twice"—and because the twice-consuming is thus prescribed, the determination of the action must indeed conform to the scriptural injunction, namely, that there is twice-consuming.

This is logical. Regarding the Soma, there is no consumption because it has not been so prescribed. There is a doubt as to whether or not there is a consumption of the remnants of the Soma. But is this doubt not improper, given that the Soma is a remnant? It is appropriate [to raise such a doubt] in the case of the sacrificial cakes and the like, because of the scriptural statement: "He cuts off twice from the oblation."

In that case, because of the scriptural statement and the inclusion of the sacrifice, there is the status of being a remnant, and consequently, its consumption [is prescribed]. Here, however, due to the absence of those factors, there is no suspicion of consumption at all. How then are these scriptural statements to be understood: "He drinks twice of the Aindravāyava," and "He carries the Āśvina around on all sides"?
And regarding the phrase "he performs the *anuṣaṭ*," the objector says: "For here, you yourself are striving to support the Bhāṣya."

This must be asked: Alternatively, let them be *arthakarman* (primary acts), because since there is no remainder [of the substance] to be consumed, it is not possible for them to be *pratipatti* (disposal acts). However, since an *arthakarman* is capable of employing the substance, let that alone be the case. If the entire Soma that was taken up is offered, how then [is the expression] "of the Aindravāyava" [to be understood]?
And regarding the term "belonging to the Aśvins": even when it is employed with the consumption of a different substance, it does not [become] the Aindravāyava [cup].
And it can also be said that it refers to the Āśvina cup. The answer is: it will have the meaning of indicating its *dharma* (characteristic ritual procedure).

That is to say, it means "of the Aindravāyava cup" or "possessing the *dharma* of the Aindravāyava. Therefore, this question—whether or not such a thing exists in the Soma sacrifice—is indeed untenable. Now, if—
From those statements based on the remnants, it is inferred that the remnants must be disposed of. No;

because the remnants lack a purposeful function, the ritual acts do not employ the substance for the sake of the subsidiary rites. Why? Because a purificatory act has that which is to be purified as its primary object.
The substance is said to be that which is to be purified; thus, while the substances are the primary objects, the purificatory acts are subordinate. And—

The principal [substance] employs the principal [rite]; therefore, the substance is not employed by means of the subsidiary rites. Therefore, the principle regarding this matter must be stated when a remnant exists. It is said: there is no authority here for the offering of the whole [substance], because in the case of the cups for Indra-Vāyu and others, the drawing [of the soma] is for that specific purpose. And once it has been drawn, even if the rite for Indra-Vāyu is performed with only a portion of what was drawn, the requirement for Indra-Vāyu is indeed fulfilled. Why, then, would there be a remnant of the whole?

This is the intended meaning: Soma, having become a liquid, is accepted for the sake of a deity. And the dedication of that substance to a deity becomes meaningful only if it is relinquished specifically for that very deity. Regarding that which is being relinquished, [the text says]: "He offers with a fine stream."

Thus, by this rule, there is a sequential abandonment [of the substance]. In that case, however, since the taking [of the portion] for the sake of the deity is purposeful by means of the falling of the first drop, there is no authority for an offering of the whole; therefore, because the sacrifice is concluded with only the first drop, a remnant remains. But surely, it is heard in scripture that the entirety [of the substance] is subordinate to the sacrifice: "One should sacrifice with Soma."
Thus, it follows that the sacrifice must be performed with the entire [Soma], and therefore there is an offering of the whole.
He refutes this: the sacrifice is not performed with the entire [Soma]; for even in that case, it is established that it is performed with only a portion of the Soma. [p. 859] Fragment—

Since the connection with the instrument is established even by means of a portion, there is no authority for an offering of the whole. Thus, the taking of this juice and the discarding of the *ṛjīṣa* and so forth [are justified]; for if the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled even when performed with a single part, why then does the text say, "he cuts off twice from the sacrificial oblation"?

From this very point, the conclusion follows: just as in the case of Soma the sacrifice is performed even with a single part, so too in the case of the cake (*puroḍāśa*), the sacrifice is performed even with a single part.

Thus, even without the statement "he cuts twice from the oblation," the completion of the sacrifice by means of even a single portion would already be established. Why, then, has this presentation of the completion been made? Because the establishment of the completion occurs there in some way or another;
for there too, in the case of the *puroḍāśa*, the completion would occur by means of whichever part whatsoever. [The author] raises an objection against the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).

If it is argued that this [mention of the two-fold cutting] is for the purpose of restriction—that is, if it is claimed that the statement regarding the two-fold cutting is for the purpose of restriction because the offering of the whole would otherwise be applicable—[the author] refutes this: "In that case, the offering of the whole is not tenable for the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin); for when the restriction to the two-fold cutting is heard in scripture, a doubt regarding the offering of the whole is not appropriate. Furthermore, since it is possible even by means of a single part, one cannot conclude that the whole [is to be offered] on that account alone."
It should not be offered. Even by means of a complete oblation (*sarvahoma*), it is indeed possible; therefore, the existence of a remnant of Soma does not at all occur as if it were obligatory.

Consequently, a distinction must be stated regarding the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the Soma. In the case of the sacrificial cake, even without a statement concerning the two portions (*dvayavadāna*), the offering of the whole would result; however, in the case of Soma, even without such a statement, the offering is by means of only a single portion. This is now explained.

This is the distinction: when the purpose of the scriptural injunction has already been fulfilled by the falling of the first drop of Soma, a further performance is not justified; for it has been demonstrated that the purpose of the scriptural injunction is accomplished even by a single part. If the purpose of the scriptural injunction were accomplished by a single part even without an explicit statement, then how could there be any suspicion of "offering the whole" (*sarvapradāna*) based merely on the falling of the first drop of Soma? [The answer is: because the offering of the two portions (*dvayavadāna*) is established only by an explicit scriptural statement.

(1) [Objection: Because it is heard from only one [source]. [Response: Even though the statement is heard [only once], it must be given by breaking it down piece by piece, because the meaning of the statement is understood in that way.

Thinking that "one should offer by cutting off [portions] repeatedly," one might suspect that the entire substance is to be offered; however, the conclusion is that there is no offering of the whole, because the substance exists for the sake of the sacrifice.
For the substance is intended for the sacrifice; therefore, once the sacrifice has been performed with it, it should not be repeated merely out of regard for the subordinate details (guṇas).

Thus, the conclusion is that the sacrifice is accomplished by means of two cuttings-off (dvayavadāna). Therefore, this rule regarding the portioning is restricted to a single part: "one cuts off twice from the oblation."

When the sacrifice is applicable either in part or in its entirety, this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the partial portion, and not an injunction for an offering of a partial portion that was previously unestablished; for it is precisely because the fulfillment of the scriptural purpose is achieved even by means of a single component. For this very reason, worldly people, having prepared milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like dedicated to a deity, set aside a portion from it and offer a small amount to the deity; and when the act of taking [the portion] is rendered meaningful by being dedicated to the deity, the remainder [is consumed].

They employ [the remnants] as they desire; otherwise, they would have to give the entirety to the deity. Therefore, since a remnant exists, the doubt arises: is the disposal of the remnant accomplished solely by eating it, or not? In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because there is no scriptural injunction, it is not accomplished by eating; the second view is that because there is a specific injunction regarding eating, eating does indeed take place. Otherwise, if eating did not exist—

The specific injunction, such as "twice for the Aindravāyava," and so forth, would not be tenable. Even if it were not tenable, one could not determine the consumption [of the cup] without an explicit statement. Nor is this untenable, because the specific injunction is logically consistent in the sense that when one consumes it, then [it is done] twice. In that case, if the consumption were not established as a constant rule, then by means of these very [injunctions], it would be qualified.
The established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that these [passages] are injunctions for consumption.

Regarding the cups (camasa), because of their designation (samākhyāna), there is no consumption in the case of the *camasa* cups due to the absence of a scriptural statement; such was the previous [view].
This is the position: that very fact of being a *camasa* would not otherwise be possible if there were no sipping (*camana*) therein. Therefore, "this is his *camasa*, this is his *camasa*."
Thus, let these statements, such as "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward," and so forth, be the very injunctions for consumption (bhakṣa),

just as in the previous case the statement was [understood] because otherwise a specific injunction would be inexplicable; likewise here too, because the status of being a cup (camasa) would otherwise be inexplicable.

Regarding the phrase "the rule for rinsing" (*camanavidhāna*): [The opponent objects] that the status of being a *camasa* (sipping vessel) is possible even by means of prescribing a different substance; to this, he replies: "Rinsing with another substance, as well as carving and so forth, would not be established. First of all, a different substance must be imagined as the object of rinsing, because the already-established substance, Soma, is available, and furthermore, because that [Soma] is not a remnant of the sacrifice. For its purification, carving and so forth would have to be imagined. But in the case of Soma..."

In that regard, even when drinking [other substances], one does not become defiled by the *soma*, according to the scriptural statement; therefore, there is no assumption of [the cup] being for the purpose of carving. Consequently, the status of being a *camasa* (cup) is based solely on the occasion of sipping *soma*; and since that status would not be possible without a scriptural injunction, these statements—such as "Let the *hotṛ*'s cup go forward"—are [the necessary injunctions].
Regarding the cup of the Udgātṛ, because of its connection with the Vedic text, there are four possible positions here: (1) is the consumption for the Udgātṛ alone?

(2) or for all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)? (3) or for the three *chandoga* priests excluding the Subrahmaṇya? (4) or for all four *chandoga* priests—the Udgātṛ, Prastotṛ, Pratihartṛ, and Subrahmaṇya? In this regard, the status of it being "his cup" (*taccamasatā*) would otherwise be untenable.
It is established that these are words of permission;
(1) P. 999 (2) P. 1001 (3) G. eating and so forth [p. r862].

In this regard, the proponent of the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that because the nominal stem *udgātṛ-pratipadika* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as denoting a specific officiant (*ṛtvij-viśeṣa*), and because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is primary, the plurality (*bahutva*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*) in accordance with that [stem], just as in the case of the word "ropes" (*pāśān*). The proponent of the second prima facie view...

However, since the literal meaning of the statement is not intended to be expressed, it is more logical to describe the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as being figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). In this way, both the case-ending and the nominal stem will possess meaningfulness. In the case of the *pāśa* (noose), however, because there is no object to be indicated by the nominal stem, a description based on figurative indication is impossible; therefore, as a last resort, the literal meaning of the statement is disregarded, and the consumption [of the soma] belongs to all the priests indicated by the term *udgātṛ*.

Thus he says: one who maintains that there is no *subrahmaṇya* priest has stated that the *bhakṣa* (the portion) belongs to the three chanters—the *udgātṛ*, *prastotṛ*, and *pratihartr̥*—on the basis of the word *udgātṛ* being used in its etymological sense (*yaugika*) as "one who performs the act of chanting. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*), rejecting the etymological sense on the principle that "conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) sets aside etymology," holds that because they are all students of the recitation designated as belonging to the single *udgātṛ*, the word *udgātṛ* applies to all of them by the maxim of the "umbrella-bearer" (*chatrinyāya*).

For the Chandogas, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And therefore, he says that the consumption belongs to them alone: "Of the Udgātṛs. Here, what is the reason that [the word] does not indicate the performers of the act of singing?
Why does the designation (*samākhyā*) itself indicate it? The meaning of this is:
for what reason does it not indicate the agents of the act of singing? What is the reason that the word *udgātṛ* is not etymological (*yaugika*)? It is the designation itself.

"What does it indicate? means by what reason does the word *udgātṛ* function through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). An exponent of a partial conclusion (*rāddhāntaikadeśin*), providing an argument, says: "If those who perform the singing are indicated [by the term], then the word 'ut' (in *udgātṛ*) would become unintended. If one who sings is called an *udgātṛ*, then there would be only one singer of the *udgītha*, and not all three; for if all three are singers..."

If they were understood by the word *udgātṛ*, then it would follow that the syllable *ut-* is not intended to be significant; and this has already been demonstrated: "The singing (*gāna*) is one thing, and the *udgāna* is another. However, in the case of the technical designation (*samākhyāna*), this fault does not apply. For there, without relying on etymological derivation, the word *udgātṛ*—as a term denoting a specific officiant (*ṛtvij*)—indicates other chanters (*chandoga*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, there is no error.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) further objects that there is the fault of the prefix *ud-* being unintended in meaning: "But surely, what is called 'singing upwards' (*udgāna*) is not singing at all;

therefore, because it does not bring to mind a different meaning—just like [the expression] 'it hangs down' (*pralambate*) and so forth—the word *udgātṛ* refers to one who performs the act of singing.
[To this, the author replies: This is not a fault.

Thus, there is no fault of not intending to express the word *ut*. For the fault of non-intention applies only to that which has meaning, not to that which is meaningless. A *bhakti* is indeed a portion of the *sāman*; a *bhakti* is a segment of the *sāman*. That which is the second *bhakti*, which the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) called the Udgātṛ sings, is the *udgītha*.

The word is denoted by convention alone; however, the root *gā* (to sing) does not occur there accompanied by the prefix *ud*. But is it not said that "one who sings the *udgītha* is an *udgātṛ*"? Therefore, [the opponent] argues that the root *gā* occurs there indeed accompanied by the prefix *ud*. To this, he replies: as for the usage in such expressions as "one should *udgāyet*," meaning "one should sing the *udgītha*," the prefix *ud* there has the sense of indicating a specific part (*bhakti*). [It refers to] the singing.

But it is singing itself. Even there, the root *gā* denotes mere singing; the prefix *ut-* alone serves to indicate the whole of which it is a part—that is, the word *udgītha*. Thus, a collective power for the root *gā* joined with the prefix *ut-* is not postulated. Since singing itself is what constitutes "high-singing" (*udgāna*), therefore *udgātṛ* is simply the name of a specific officiant (*ṛtvij*); it does not mean "the performer of high-singing."

This word *udgātṛ* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) for a specific type of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), and it is not etymological (*yaugika*); for if it were based on the act of singing, it would apply everywhere to anyone who performs singing.

If indeed "singing" (*udgāna*) were a specific kind of chant, then the application of the word to a specific priest could be established by virtue of performing that act; but this is not the case. Therefore, this word is purely conventional. However, the proponent of the final view (*paramasiddhāntin*) says: precisely because this word *udgātṛ* is conventional...

For this very reason, it has been established as the final conclusion (*rāddhāntita*) that the conventional name (*samākhyā*) alone is capable of indicating [the meaning], and not the act of singing (*gānakriyā*). This is because if the act of singing were the indicator, it would result in the term being etymological (*yaugika*). Furthermore, when a conventional sense (*rūḍhi*) exists, it is not proper to resort to an etymological interpretation. [Objection: But if one resorts to a conventional sense, the plural number (*bahutva*) would not be justified. [Reply: If you say it is justified through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), we say no; for indication itself is the fault. To this, it is replied: by way of convention (*rūḍhyā*)...

When the possibility of an etymological (yaugika) sense has been set aside, a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) consistent with that [etymological meaning] follows from the scriptural statement; it is not the case that, having perceived the statement, one turns back and resorts to an etymological sense. For this very reason, since the name indicates [the connection], even those who argue against the *subrahmaṇyā* are indeed arguing against the correct principle (*nyāya*). Since the secondary indication occurs through inclusion within a single recensional tradition (*pravacana*), all those who perform that recitation are indicated by it.
Thus, it is not possible to exclude the Subrahmaṇya priest. But is it not the case that, according to the rule "the Udgātṛs chant after sitting down," the Subrahmaṇya is excluded?
One might think that here too it should be so; to this he says: "And here there is no authority for a restriction, as there is in the case of hearing praise and so forth.

For in that case, because of the connection with praise, only the three chanters of the *stotra* are included. But here, however, such is not the case; this is the distinction. Now, one might object: since the plural number in "of the *udgātṛ*s" (*prodgātṝṇām*) is applicable to exactly three—just as in the case of the *kapiñjala* birds—why [should it not be restricted]?

The consumption [of the Soma] is prescribed for those devoted to Brahman. To this, the following reply is given: if, for the sake of justifying the plural number, it is indeed true that only three are meant to be included—wherein it has been stated that the word *udgātṛ* here refers to those who perform the functions of that [priest]—then the plural number here is the reason for the word-base (*prātipadika*) functioning with a different meaning; it is not merely occupied with its own primary sense. Thus, by means of the plural number, a figurative application (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*) is resorted to.

And because the indicative mark (lakṣaṇā) is connected with a single recensional text, all the Chāndogas are to be understood [as included]. Therefore, it is rightly said that there is a consumption [of the Soma] for those including the Subrahmaṇya priest. There is no consumption for the Grāvastut priest, because it is not mentioned [in the text]. It has been stated that the consumption occurs by virtue of a direct injunction and from the designation (samākhyāna).

Now, these sections (adhikaraṇas) are commenced for the purpose of reaching a consensus regarding a disagreement over the meaning of the scriptural statement. By this, he states the intermediate connection (avāntara-saṅgati). [Objection: But surely, because of the statement, "All desire to obtain a share of the Hāriyojana," there is a consumption (bhakṣa) of the Hāriyojana by all.

Regarding the statement "there is also a consumption for the Grāvastut," he says: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because [the text] says "all desire the Hāriyojana," it refers only to those who possess cups (*camasins*).
(1) P. 1004 (2) R. & G. [p. 865] *hāriyojanaṃ* [p.

The proponent has raised an objection based on the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣāt*). Its meaning is as follows: “Just as the other cup-bearers (*camasinaḥ*) consume their respective cups, so too do all [the priests] desire to partake of this *hāriyojana* cup.
Thus, in the remainder of the sentence, the cup-bearers...

Because of the mention of "all" (*sarva*), the term refers only to those who possess cups (*camasin*); thus, the consumption at the *hāriyojana* offering belongs only to the cup-holders. Since the *grāvastut* is not a cup-holder, he has no share in the consumption. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that it is not appropriate to restrict the scope of the word "all"—which refers to the subject under discussion—on the basis of the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*). The meaning of this is as follows: "All [of the priests] [partake] of the *hāriyojana*" is an unambiguous totality.

The term "ṛtvij" (priest) is the basis for the cognition [of the referent]. Furthermore, sixteen priests are the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), and the word "all" (*sarva*) refers to those who are under discussion. If it were restricted solely to the *camasins* (cup-bearers), then the meaning of the word "all" would be contradicted. Therefore, a restriction based on the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) is not tenable.
Even if the word "camasin" in the supplementary statement were to function with an indirect (*parokṣa*) sense, then let there be a restriction; however, this is not the case for the word "camasin."

The cups are consumed by the cup-holders because their purpose is indirect; however, in the case of the *hāriyojana* cup, all consume it. Thus, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that the *hāriyojana* is praised for its great significance. Furthermore, one should consume [the soma] following the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call, for here it is said: "The first consumption belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*."

Having raised the objection that, because of the hearing of these qualities (*guṇa*), there is no injunction for eating, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) was established on the grounds that it is an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*). By this, the author of the commentary has restated the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) exactly as heard in order to refute it. He states the refutation: "But surely, in this case, there is no injunction of a qualified entity."

For "primacy" (*prāthamya*) is not a factor (*kāraka*) of the act of eating, by which a qualified action could be enjoined. The meaning of this is as follows: in that case, there is no *ācamana* for the *grāvastut*.

For a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) occurs only where the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is possible. However, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not possible between "firstness" (*prāthamya*) and "eating" (*bhakṣaṇa*), because firstness is not a factor of action (*kāraka*). Indeed, a factor of action is employed as a qualifier toward an action by means of a case-ending denoting a *kāraka*. Therefore, a qualified injunction is appropriate in that case. But where, on the other hand, [the relationship is impossible] due to the lack of being a *kāraka*...

Since it is indicated by a case-ending denoting a *kāraka*, there is no connection with an action therein; so how could there be an injunction of something qualified? Nor is priority (*prāthamya*) a *kāraka*, for that is a sequence. And since that [sequence] depends on the word-meanings, it is a quality of the word-meanings and not a *kāraka*, because it has no operation when the word-meaning has ceased. Therefore, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) itself is untenable. The respondent says: "Precisely because it is qualified—"

There is no suspicion of a [separate] injunction. For this very reason, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) suspected that a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhāna) is not possible. The objector says: "Let the prima facie view stand; how then is the final conclusion (rāddhānta) reached? The respondent says: "Because the two words 'first' and 'consumption' (prathamabhakṣa) denote a single meaning, and because it is an enjoined statement, he considers it an injunction of a single entity. This is the meaning.

If the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) did not exist, then there would be no injunction of a single object. However, when there is a compound such as *prathamabhakṣa* (the first eating), the two words together denote a single object consisting of the act of eating as qualified by "firstness. And that which is denoted is precisely what is enjoined; thus, the injunction of a single object follows from the very act of denotation. The opponent says: "That is incorrect."

For even in a compound (*samāsa*), there is no departure from the principle of *tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*; since you assert that a single meaning is expressed by two words, you have effectively accepted the *sphoṭa* theory itself by not admitting a meaning for each individual word (*pratipadam*). And that is incorrect. For in a compound, there is indeed no departure from the principle of *tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*, which establishes expression for each constituent word (*pratipadābhidhāna*). Therefore, how could there be a single meaning—?

[Question: What is the designation? [The author] provides the answer: "It is true that this is so; nevertheless, in a compound (*samāsa*), the connection with another word-meaning depends upon the relationship between the preceding and following words. The meaning of this is as follows: I do not assert the expression of a single meaning in a compound by accepting the theory of *sphoṭa*; rather, (1) G. [it is] comprehension (*avagati*).

By means of two words denoting two meanings standing in the relation of qualifier and qualified, a single qualified meaning is conveyed; and its subsequent connection with other word-meanings occurs. In a sentence, however, there is a mutual connection among those word-meanings that are connected to other word-meanings. [The word] *nīla*—

In the case of "Bring the blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam ānaya*), there is first a connection between the two [words] with the verb "bring," and subsequently a connection between the quality (*guṇa*) and the qualified (*guṇin*). But in a compound, as in "Bring the blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam ānaya*), the connection with "bringing" occurs only between those two which are already mutually connected by way of the relation of quality and qualified. Therefore, it is the same here as well.

In the expression *prathamabhakṣaḥ* ("first-eating"), there is a connection between "firstness" (*prāthamya*) and "eating" (*bhakṣa*), which are related as quality and qualified, with the injunction conveyed by the verb root *karoti*. This is not the case, however, for two things that are unrelated to one another; for in that latter case, there would be the enjoining of multiple distinct objects. Since a mutual relationship is understood in a compound, it is rightly said that for one who enjoins by means of a compound, the enjoining of multiple qualities is not difficult. Therefore:

In this matter, there is a specific injunction established. For one who speaks thus—the author of the commentary—the sequence already stated is both the means of application (*viniyojya*) and that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). On the other hand, it is observed as a principle that that which is understood through the "power of hearing" (*śruti*) and so forth belonging to the fifth book (the *Pañcamaka*), known as the "expanse of injunctions" (*vidhivitāna*) and devoid of the application of expression (*abhidhānaviniyoga*), is not what is being enjoined. For in every case, this meaning of the scripture is [determined] by the force of the word's own power.

[The author] describes [this]. However, the commentator (Vivaraṇakāra) does so by determining the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing itself. Therefore, it is stated in that very work that, according to his view, sequence is never something to be enjoined (*avidheya*).
And [it is said]: "By means of the oblation (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*)," as in: "Having pressed [the Soma] and having offered the oblation, he consumes [it]."
Thus, there is also an injunction for consumption (*bhakṣa*).

Why, then, is consumption enjoined? Is it not observed that, since it is said "having pressed" and "having offered," why are only the offering (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*) not enjoined, while consumption is merely restated as something already established by the sense of the matter? To this he replies: because the offering and the pressing are already established therein. But surely—
Why are the *homa* and the *abhiṣava* not enjoined as being subordinate to the *bhakṣaṇa* (eating)? Or why is the *bhakṣaṇa* not [enjoined] as being subordinate to them?

Regarding the statement "it is enjoined," he says: "because its injunction as a subordinate member (aṅga) is untenable. Since there is no other mode of injunction, the *bhakṣa* (eating) itself must be what is enjoined.
This is because of direct instruction (*pratyakṣopadeśa*) through such designations (*samākhyā*) as "the Hotṛ’s cup" (*hotṛcamasa*), which apply to all the cups.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that because the connection [of the act] is understood through the words "having pressed" and "having offered," the consumption (*bhakṣa*) occurs elsewhere than in the cups (*camasa*).
The meaning is that since the entire cup is connected with the Hotṛ and others, the consumption occasioned by the pressing and the offering will take place apart from the cups.
This being the position reached, it is replied: even the consumption occasioned by the pressing certainly occurs in the cups. [Objection: But the Hotṛ’s cup...
Thus it was stated that there is no comprehension of all the cups; this is true as stated, yet it cannot negate the fact that eating is occasioned by the pressing [of the Soma].
And since the eating is not negated when its being occasioned by the offering and the pressing remains intact, the eating occasioned by those factors certainly applies to the *camasa*s as well.
For these statements are prescriptive (*prāpaka*), not restrictive (*parisaṅkhyāpaka*). Why? He says: "The *hotṛ*-cup... [and so forth].

In this understanding of the relationship, the exclusion of other relationships cannot be understood, because only the attainment [of the relationship] is apprehended. For when there is attainment, upon the inquiry "To whom does this belong?", the exclusion of others is perceived. When there is attainment in a general sense, upon the inquiry for a specific [relation] as to "Whose is this?", the exclusion of others is perceived through the specification of the particular—just as in the case of "belonging to Agni" (*āgneya*).
When this had been said, (1) P. 1009 [p.
There is no comprehension of [the exclusion] of the cup for Indra-Agni. Here, however, because the sentence has attainment as its result, the exclusion of anything else cannot be understood;
by the phrase "the Hotṛ’s cup," the act of drinking qualified by a specific agent is enjoined, but another act of drinking caused by something else is not thereby set aside.
But surely, even when there is attainment—or rather, even when sentences have the function of making something known—there exists a contradiction with the comprehension of the whole. The whole—

For it is understood from the comprehension of the relationship that the entire [cup] is to be consumed by the cup-bearers (*camasin*); therefore, when there is another consumption [by the Hotṛ], a contradiction certainly exists. He refutes this: "True, there would be a contradiction—if the acquisition were by means of the name (*samākhyā*). But here, the acquisition is by virtue of the statement, 'Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward'. The meaning of this is: truly, if the connection of the Hotṛ were with the entire cup...

It is understood through the name (samākhyā). And there is no attainment [of the specific application] from the name; rather, it is from the direct statement (vacana). Now, one might object: since the name itself is untenable, even the direct statement that must be inferred would be inferred as having a universal scope, just like the name. To this he replies: That [statement] is to be inferred; however, it is inferred in a manner that does not contradict other statements, such as "having pressed [the Soma] and offered [the libation]," because it is something to be inferred. Therefore, by way of a single part [of the whole],...
The establishment of all relationships and designations [is as follows]:
"In a single vessel, according to the sequence, the Adhvaryu, the Camasins, the pressers, and the Hotṛs drink.
