Here, it is now deliberated: who should drink first? By this, he states the intermediate connection. He states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
The *adhvaryu* drinks first because it is in his hand, according to the maxim: "He whose hand holds [the object], he wins. For indeed, that which is in one's hand—(1) P.

The substance exists; first he consumes what is present, and afterwards the others. [Objection: But since there is the statement, "The first consumption belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer," how can there be a consumption for the *adhvaryu*? [Response: The sense is that it is not right to oppose a scriptural statement with logic. The answer is: this section is intended for one who, even though there is a rule for mere consumption, thinks that the first consumption belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer alone. This is its meaning.
Although the statement prescribes only the act of eating, nevertheless, one might think that priority is obtained through logic alone;
thus, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) would not have been commenced. This means that the present inquiry proceeds by accepting the prescription of priority.

Furthermore, it has been shown that [the priority belongs] to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance because of its precedence; therefore, this section was begun as a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvā-cintā*). And this priority has already been demonstrated.

Because it is the *vaṣaṭkāra*, it is logical that even the consumption [of the soma] caused by it should occur first; this is because of the statement of this principle (*nyāya*). Otherwise, the statement of the principle would be useless. [Objection: In that case, the citation of the scriptural text (*vacana*) would not be appropriate. To this he says: "And because of the scriptural text" (*vacanācca*), which concludes [the discussion]. The meaning is that this is the opening of a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*).

The eating [of food] is permitted by verbal authorization. This section is intended to demonstrate the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as to whether one should eat what has been authorized or what has not been authorized. Furthermore, this section is for the purpose of the subsequent inquiry, in order to show that the acquisition of authorization is based on a scriptural statement (*vacana*). In the absence of such a statement, there would be no restriction; however, because of the scriptural statement, there is indeed a restriction regarding the request for authorization. Regarding that restriction:

r871] When this is the case, there arises the consideration: is the request for permission to be made with a worldly word or with a Vedic one? Because of the traditional recitation of mantras, it is to be done with a Vedic word.

The rule is that the request for permission is made with a mantra; this too is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the attainment of the mantra. These two sections of the discussion (*adhikaraṇa*) are indeed supplementary to the subsequent deliberation. For this very reason, having written down the preceding section, the [next] sūtra was not written again.
In that case, the response follows by implication. Now, there is a doubt regarding the response: is the response to be given with a mantra, or...

"By means of a worldly word. With this, he restates the doubt in order to raise an objection. He states the objection because there is no prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But how can there be a doubt when the mantra 'upahūta' is recited? The meaning is that since this mantra, which is capable of being an answer, has been applied by its indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is proper for the answer to be given with this very mantra. He provides the resolution: [it belongs] to "upahvayasva" itself.

There is doubt for one who considers the remainder [of the mantra]. Since it is part of the mantra intended for requesting permission (*anujñāpana*), it serves only that purpose. Why? The intention is this: for that which is recited prior to the request for permission is not fit for the response, even if it were capable of being a response. That which is recited before the request for permission must be employed first; and permission (*anujñāna*) is not employed until the request for permission has been made.

Thus, by implication, this mantra is intended solely for the purpose of requesting permission (*anujñāpana*). However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*) has established the conclusion that in this case, it is the "priority" (*pūrvatā*) itself that is sublated. The meaning of this is as follows: since the application (*viniyoga*) is established through indicative power (*liṅga*) according to the rule "the order [of performance] follows the application," it is the priority of the mantra's employment that is sublated, and not the application based on indicative power.
(1) P.1012 (2) G. Because of its capacity [p.
872], due to the association with those who share a single vessel; for when the request for permission and the response are established, what [is the purpose] for those who share a single vessel?

The consideration is whether this request for permission (*anujñāpana*) and the response (*prativacana*) apply only in specific cases or without distinction. By this, he states the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*).

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers them to apply without distinction because no such rule is prescribed; for here, no distinction is heard in the scripture as to whether it concerns a single vessel or separate vessels.

Therefore, [the opponent concludes] they apply everywhere. However, the final established view (*siddhānta*) is that they serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*); for the request for permission and the response when using a single vessel serve a visible purpose.

"Not elsewhere" means that it occurs only in that very case; for it is impossible to postulate another effect when the effect has already been perceived. By the removal of the *yājyā*, the consumption (*bhakṣa*) is removed. The intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), who considers that only the *yājyā* is being removed, is that the consumption belongs to the *hotṛ* alone. [As it is said: "Or he himself, sitting down, performs the sacrifice."

By this [statement], only the *ājyā* (the offering of clarified butter) is removed from the presence of the *hotṛ*, but not the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance. Therefore, the consumption [of the remnant] occasioned by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance belongs to the *hotṛ* alone. Here, an objection is raised: "Do you not see the scriptural injunction, 'He sacrifices while sitting without breathing' (*anavānam*)? For he who sees [this]...

How could one say this? By the injunction "one should sacrifice without pausing," non-interruption (*avicchedakatā*) is taught as the function of the *hotṛ* priest regarding both the *homa* and the *yāga*.

In that case, even the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), while performing the function of the *hotṛ*, must accept non-interruption. In that context, if the sacrificer were to perform only the *yājyā* mantra while the *hotṛ* alone performed the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, then the sacrificer would be interrupting [the flow] by means of the *yājyā* alone.
The sense is: since a sacrifice cannot be accomplished without the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, how could the sacrificer’s desired result be achieved through the employment of the *yājyā* alone?
It is not that he does not see [the result]; he certainly sees it, but only in the case of the *yājyā* alone. Thus, both of these points are established.
This is the intended meaning. This state of being without pause (*anavāna*), which consists of non-interruption, is appropriate only in the performance of the *yājyā*;

likewise, since the *yājyā* also serves the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice (*yāga*), the agentship toward the sacrifice indeed exists even during its recitation. Thus, the *yājyā* possesses two forms: that of being without pause and that of being the agent of the sacrifice.

Since it is possible even in the mere performance of the ritual application (*prayoga*), there is no evidence whatsoever for the removal of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance. He explains this very point: the meaning is that even when the *yājyā* is being recited, the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) remains entirely possible. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) considers: "True, it is logically possible; yet, there is still no evidence for the removal of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance. Thus, even in the mere performance of the *yājyā*, [the sacrifice] must indeed be accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*.

"It is appropriate" means that agency is logical only by accepting the performance of an action (*vyāpāra*). The meaning of this is as follows: wherever the Hotṛ priest is established, there the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is also enjoined; and since the Hotṛ is established at the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, he is established at the performance of the *yājyā* recitation along with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance.
Therefore, the injunction for the sacrificer applies only to the performance of the *yājyā* together with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, and not when the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is removed.
There is some evidence for this. Consequently, when the *vaṣaṭ*-call is removed, the Hotṛ priest has no consumption [of the portion] caused by that *vaṣaṭ*-call.

As for the fact that the *pravara* (the ancestral invocation) is not removed, it is because it is based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*); it has been shown how the *pravara* is not removed precisely because it is based on direct instruction.
The meaning of this is as follows: the *pravara* is indeed based on direct instruction; therefore, wherever it can be performed with its full qualities, [it remains].

In that very case, it should be performed by the *hotṛ*, for it can be performed with its full qualities (*saguṇa*) by him, whereas it cannot be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) because his opportunity has passed. For it has been shown in the *Bhāṣya* that in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), even a rite is performed despite being deficient (*viguṇa*) due to sublation (*bādha*), but not so in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*). The fruit-cup (*phalacamas*) is an occasional modification of the consumption (*bhakṣavikāra*). Is the fruit-cup a modification of the sacrificial offering (*ijyāvikāra*) or a modification of the consumption?

Regarding this doubt, we say: there is no doubt at all here, because of the statement, "one should offer that portion to him for consumption" (*tam asmai bhakṣam prayacchet*), which establishes a connection with the act of consuming (*bhakṣa*).

Because it is enjoined as being for the purpose of consumption (*bhakṣa*), it modifies the *soma* in the act of eating, not in the sacrifice (*yāga*). For that which is enjoined only where it is heard applies only to that context and sets aside only what serves as its means. Indeed, the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is heard of as an instrumental factor (*kāraka*) in the act of eating, not in the sacrifice;

for the scripture says, "One should make this his food," but not, "One should sacrifice with it. Thus far, it has been stated on the grounds that it is not heard of as being connected to the sacrifice.

Now, even though a connection [with another substance] is heard, he states its impossibility: "And it cannot be said that this is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyāvikāra*), because *soma* is enjoined as the primary material at the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭatvāt*). At the very moment of the originative injunction, "One should sacrifice with *soma*," the sacrifice is perceived as being conjoined with *soma*; it cannot be perceived as conjoined with anything else. And when another substance is being enjoined, [the principle applies]: "An accessory (*guṇa*) [is subordinate] when there is a connection with something new (*apūrvasaṃyoga*)."

By this reasoning, there would be the consequence of it being a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*). And consequently, even a modification of the consumption (*bhakṣavikāra*) would not occur, let alone a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyāvikāra*). To this, it is replied: the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is not capable of modifying the consumption without a modification of the sacrifice. Why? Because of the sacrifice—

For the consumption [of the Soma] pertains to what remains; and when that which has not become "remainder" is being consumed, it does not become a modification of that [consumption]. The meaning of this is as follows:

if the sacrifice is performed with Soma alone, then it cannot be said that the fruit-cup (*phalacamas*) is a modification of the consumption that serves as the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the sacrificial remnants. For if one sacrifices with Soma, that very [Soma] must be consumed; and the consumption of that [Soma] is not accomplished by means of the fruit-cup.

It cannot be prevented. For when one thing is established, another is not thereby established. Therefore, since a connection with eating as a form of performance is untenable, it must be understood that even the *phalacamas* (the fruit-cup) is merely a remnant of a sacrifice (*ijyāśeṣa*). To establish the connection with eating mentioned in the scripture, its connection with the sacrifice—which is not explicitly stated—must be inferred. But surely, because Soma is enjoined as the primary material for the sacrifice by its originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*)...

It was stated that such an injunction is not possible. He refutes this: "For it was said that there is no recognition [of the sacrifice] when there is an injunction by way of restating the sacrifice (*yāga-anuvāda*), but this is not so even when there is a connection with the action (*kārya*). The meaning of this is: if, having restated the sacrifice by means of the word *yaji*, the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*)...

If it were enjoined [as an independent act], then it would be a different sacrifice distinct from the [original] quality. However, when this connection is established through the purpose (*kārya*), then there is no difference;

for if one accepts that the [act] enters into the sacrifice by way of its connection with the *bhakṣa* (consuming) related to that sacrifice, not even a suspicion of a different sacrifice arises. Furthermore, this connection is established through the purpose, as it is heard in the scripture: "One should perform the *bhakṣa*. It must be performed in such a way that the *bhakṣa* comes to be. If...

And when that [fruit-cup] becomes a remnant of the sacrifice (*yāgaśeṣa*), then it becomes something to be consumed (*bhakṣa*). Thus, this relationship exists solely through the function (*kāryataḥ*). Now, an objection is raised: the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), having raised the issue of the absence of a connection with the sacrifice, stated the connection as "one should cause [him] to sacrifice" (*yājayet*). Therefore, the Commentator stated the connection of the fruit-cup by way of a reference back to the sacrifice (*yāgānuvādena*), not through its functional role. He provides the resolution: that was stated for the purpose of demonstrating the connection with the sacrifice, but not [as a statement of its primary function].

There is no fault in [interpreting] this as a restatement for the purpose of an injunction. Since the opening passage mentions a sacrifice (*yāga*), this consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) is indeed connected to that sacrifice. By that, it is demonstrated that when [the consumption] is joined with that [sacrifice], there is no lack of connection to the sacrifice; however, it is not a case of enjoining a substance (*dravya*) by way of a restatement of the sacrifice.

Furthermore, the concluding statement, "one should perform the consumption," clarifies this very same meaning—namely, its form as being connected to the sacrifice—by means of its connection to the consumption.

Therefore, it is established that the fruit-cup (*phalacamas*) is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyāvikāra*). Furthermore, the injunctions regarding secondary qualities (*guṇavidhāna*) have been demonstrated; specifically, the injunctions regarding secondary qualities such as the young *darbha* grass and so forth have been shown. This is because of the commonality among those who follow in procession (*anuprasarpiṣu*), based on the injunction: "Ten by ten, they follow in procession toward each cup."
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that for one who considers the statement "a hundred Brahmins consume the Soma" to be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), the King is not one who consumes it.

In the Rājasūya sacrifice, since the king holds the primary entitlement, [the rule] regarding the drinking from the sacrificer’s cup would apply to the king alone; however, if the injunction were "one hundred Brāhmaṇas drink the Soma," then, because it is an injunction concerning Brāhmaṇas, the exclusion of a non-Brāhmaṇa king would follow. But when the injunction is simply "ten [persons] each approach one cup," then the number "one hundred" is merely restated as a consequence of the total sum, referring to "one hundred Brāhmaṇas."

Furthermore, the word *brāhmaṇa* applies to actual Brāhmaṇas by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to its predominance; therefore, it is appropriate for the King as well. Moreover, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*), which is logical; otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) resulting from the injunction of multiple qualities while restating the consumption already obtained through the general rule (*codaka*). This is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that it is indeed true that it would be a restatement if such were the case. But since the King is not included in the [preceding] recitation, a restatement is not possible.

Because it would follow that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of something not in accordance with reality. The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "na ca" has the sense of the word "but" (*tu*). If it were a restatement, then the king’s eating would indeed be established; however, this is not a restatement, because if the exclusion of the *rājanya* were [already] established, the term "Brāhmaṇa" would result in a restatement of something not in accordance with reality. But in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), there is no lack of correspondence to reality. Therefore, "one hundred Brāhmaṇas" is indeed an injunction. Now, as for the objection that it is a restatement—

In this discussion, the status of being a non-literal restatement (*ayathārthānuvādatva*) is not a defect, for there will be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by way of predominance. In a restatement, that which is already established is restated; thus, just as Brāhmaṇas and non-Brāhmaṇas are established [in the world], so too their restatement occurs through indication. The reply: True, if it were exclusively a restatement.
But here, since its status as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is also possible, one cannot resort to the charge of non-literality. Therefore, both of these are enjoined.

"One hundred Brahmins, ten for each cup, and one for the *camasa*. Now, by the principle that "it should be equal, since there is no scriptural statement to the contrary," when the hundred are divided, ten are obtained for each [cup]; thus, it follows that "ten [Brahmins] approach each *camasa*."

This is a discussion (*vāda*). The objection, "How is this injunction stated? is merely a formal challenge (*codya*) and not a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). For even if it were a restatement (*anuvāda*), since [the prohibition] has not ceased and the *rājanya* has not been excluded [from the scope of the rule], [the objection remains].

This restatement alone is appropriate because it conforms to the actual state of affairs; it is not the case that "a hundred Brahmins" [should be assigned], as that would lead to an inconsistency with reality. Therefore, this is merely an objection. He refutes it: "No, because a hundred is obtained for each individual, since the completion of the sentence occurs with respect to each specific instance. [The author explains: The number ten is prescribed so that there may not be a hundred in each cup (*camasa*). He concludes the section on the subject matter:

Therefore, the king is not entitled to consume [the Soma], because of the injunction for Brāhmaṇas. As for the view held here—that the statement "a hundred Brāhmaṇas [drink] Somas" constitutes an injunction of multiple things—that is incorrect; for we shall explain in the tenth [book] that even by means of an injunction for a different ritual act, there can be a purpose for the original function.

The meaning of this is as follows: let this very different consumption (bhakṣa), characterized by multiple qualities, be enjoined; thus, by virtue of having a visible purpose, it supersedes the original consumption.
"He will cause [them] to turn back"—this is merely a concession, as indicated by the word "also" (*api*), which shows that this could also be accomplished by the injunction of other ritual acts.

In reality, however, the injunction is "ten for each one," while the statement "a hundred Brahmins" is a subsequent injunction regarding the Brahmins alone; thus, the term "a hundred" is a restatement (*anuvāda*). In this way, everything is consistent.
Thus ends the fifth quarter of the third chapter in the ŚrīṚjuvimalā.
Now begins the sixth quarter of the third chapter:

"It is for all purposes, because it is not restricted by context. What, then, is the reason for presenting these two alternative views? To which [objection] does the presentation of the two views respond? The answer is: "The injunction that is not introduced by a specific context is stronger than the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), because it is based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*)."

First, regarding the first position—that the general rule (*anārabhyavidhi*) is stronger than the specific injunction (*codaka*)—the purpose of this [argument] is to support the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). How so? To that he says: "In this case, there is no such thing as 'double-stating' (*dviruktatā*), because the *sruk* ladle exists in both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*). The meaning of this is: if, in the case of the general rule being for the sake of the ectype, there were the defect characterized by "double-stating," then indeed [that defect] would exist.

It has the status of being for the sake of the archetype alone. For even if it were for the sake of the ectype, there would be no fault of tautology; rather, having referred to the *sruk* ladle—which is not obtained through direct instruction in the archetype but is obtained in the ectype by the force of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer)—the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood is enjoined. Therefore, that quality is directly taught (*aupadeśika*) in both cases. Consequently, it does not need to be obtained again in the ectype through the *codaka*, because the application of the *codaka* occurs at a time subsequent to this [injunction]. This is what was said.

It occurs as follows: first, setting aside the *anārabhyavidhi* (unattached injunction), the benefit (*upakāra*) is described by taking only those constituent elements (*padārtha*) prescribed in connection with the archetype (*prakṛti*). Subsequently, there is the extension (*atideśa*) to the modified forms (*vikṛti*). Thus, in both the archetypes and the modifications, once the ladles (*srucaḥ*) have been obtained through the common injunction, properties such as being made of *parṇa*-wood are enjoined by means of the *anārabhyavidhi*. This is the presentation of the second position.
He states the justification: "In that case, then, by means of a general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), it refers to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). This is the presentation of another position;
[thus ends] the first of the two positions.

Like the observation [of a general rule]. If there is no distinction between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*) because of the occurrence of the *sruk* ladle, then, in that case, just as a determination is made by observing what is generally seen (*prāyadarśana*), so too here it is possible to determine that [the mantra] is for the sake of the archetype through what is observed in common (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). In the archetype, there is an instruction both in brief and in detail;

this [mantra] also consists of brevity and expansion, and thus its being for the sake of the archetype appears evident. This, first of all, is the immediate position (*anantarapakṣa*) regarding the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).

The view that [the Veda] has a manifest form is refuted. First, inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*) is not the cause for the comprehension of the meaning of words. This is the underlying intention:

since the status of being a "subsidiary" (*śeṣatva*) is Vedic, there is no occasion here for inference based on general observation. Because perception and the other means of knowledge have as their object established facts (*siddha-artha*), they lack the capacity to grasp the nature of what is to be accomplished (*kārya*). However, observation of common usage (*prāyadarśanam*) is indeed a cause for the comprehension of the meaning of words.

Because it is observed in the world that [a rule] serves as a supplement to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), by that fact, the word itself is presented as referring to a specific case through the observation of a general rule (*prāyadarśana*). However, it is not an independent means of valid cognition like inference (*anumāna*). And such an observation of a general rule does not exist here either, because even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), an instruction of that same kind is observed. Thus he says: "Nor is there an observation of a general rule in the modified sacrifice as there is in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*); for both brevity and detail [are found]."

Because of the observation of the instruction. Now follows the refutation of the other position: If the injunction not connected to a specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*) depends upon the extended application (*codaka*), then the prior instruction in the archetype (*prakṛti*) must be expected; for extension depends upon the instruction. The meaning of this is as follows: if the injunction not connected to a specific context depends upon the extended application for the sake of the possibility of the *sruk* ladle in the ectype (*vikṛti*), then the prior instruction in the archetype must be expected. Why? Because it depends upon the instruction.

This is because of the extension (*atideśa*) [of details] from that [archetype]. For it is by virtue of the direct instruction (*upadeśa*) that an auxiliary benefit (*upakāra*) is established in the archetype; through that medium, the extension of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) occurs in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). Therefore, one must accept that the *anārabhyavidhi* (independent injunction) first applies to the archetype for the sake of completing the direct instruction.

Nor is the postulation of the auxiliary benefit in the archetype independent of the *anārabhyavidhi*, since the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is to be accomplished by the performance of all its constituent parts.

If, by means of the direct instruction (*upadeśa*), the injunction not stated in a specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*) is subsumed within the archetype (*prakṛti*) and accepted as serving its own purpose, then it does not depend upon extension (*atideśa*) for entry into the ectype (*vikṛti*) in order to obtain the ladle (*sruk*). Even in the ectype, it does not [require the extension] with respect to the ladle obtained through the rule of transfer (*codaka*), because of the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood. (1) G. sa.

That is to say, it enacts [the injunction] and so forth. Why? Because the *parṇatā* (being made of *parṇa-wood*) and other such qualities are already obtained in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by virtue of the effect alone.

Furthermore, there is no room for a re-enactment (*punarvidhi*) of what has already been obtained. Therefore, since a double statement (*dvirukti*) is impossible, it is established that there is no "double-statement" (*adviruktatvāt*).

The reason is stated in the Sūtra. Here, the author of the Bhāṣya states that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is connected with the sacrifice; as to what the utility of this is, he says: "As for the mention of the connection with the sacrifice, it is intended to show that the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) necessarily applies. And since its application is necessary, the establishment of the principle of non-redundancy (*adviruktatva*) is stated. The meaning of this is: in order to support the reason characterized by non-redundancy, [it must be] necessarily...

The connection with the sacrifice is introduced as the *itikartavyatā* (procedure) in order to demonstrate that the *codaka* (transfer rule) applies to the cultivated [elements]. For if the modified sacrifices were independent of the [archetype] and thus lacked expectancy, the *codaka* would not operate; and in the absence of the *codaka*, the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood (*parṇatā*) would not be obtained, and thus it is enjoined. However, when the procedure is connected with the sacrifice and not with the vessels, then even though the vessels are mentioned without reference to a specific context (*anārabhya*), [the *parṇatā* applies].

Although they become complete through the primary injunction alone, nevertheless, because there is still an expectancy regarding the sacrifice, the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) must necessarily be produced.

If that *codaka* is to be produced, then the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood (*parṇatā*) is also obtained. And since that which has been obtained cannot be sublated, it is established that the impossibility of "double mention" (*dvirukti*) is the reason for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

But because there is no distinction in context, it would be contradictory in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Now, both the *sāptadaśya* (seventeen-foldness) studied as an isolated injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*) and the *pāñcadaśya* (fifteen-foldness) studied within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) are, by the very force of the scriptural statement (*śruti*), connected with the *sāmidhenī* verses.

It is questioned and applied. What is this introduction of the context (*prakaraṇa*)? He says in a single passage: "In this case, the context is not the applicator, such that the injunction of the context would be stronger. The meaning of this is: [regarding] the seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses—

Regarding the statement “one should recite,” both the *sāptadaśya* (the number seventeen) taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*)— namely, “one should recite fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses”—

and the *pāñcadaśya* (the number fifteen) taught within the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), are enjoined and applied by the Vedic text itself (*śruti*) as being connected with the *sāmidhenī* verses. It is not [the case that they are applied] otherwise.

"By context" (*prakaraṇena*). If application were determined by context, then only that which is studied within a specific context would be applied, and nothing else. However, context is not the means of application here; therefore, there is application for both. He raises an objection: "Now, the intention might be that it is *śruti* and the others themselves, when dependent upon context, that are the means of application," as established in the first section of the seventh book (*saptamādye*).

[The opponent] says: "Therefore, only that for which there is a recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa*) is applied by direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, and not anything else. [The author] refutes this: "True, [the subsidiaries] depend upon the context characterized as the 'grasper' (*grāhaka*), but they do not depend on [that context] as the actual applicator (*viniyojaka*). And the dependence on the grasper is exactly the same even for a rule not stated in a specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*). The number fifteen (*pāñcadaśya*) is also grasped precisely through its connection with the *sāmidhenī* verses."

Furthermore, the connection with the *sāmidhenī* verses is equal for that which is taught as unattached (*anārabhyadhīta*), because there is no distinction in the way both are grasped by the "grasper" (*grāhaka*). Therefore, since a double-statement (*dvirukti*) is impossible here as well, it is logical that the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*) applies only to the contextually relevant [sacrifice]. The author states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): There is a distinction here.

For when the fifteen-fold number (*pāñcadaśya*) is the subject of the context, its recognition by the "grasper" is possible due to the lack of intervention; however, this is not the case for the unattached injunction.

The reflective awareness of the apprehender arises from the effect (*kāryataḥ*). Its meaning is as follows: indeed, that which is heard in proximity to the application of the state of the apprehender possessing its specific function is understood by the very act of hearing to be for that purpose; whereas, however, that which is heard at a distance, its necessity of connection with the meaning of those words [is established].

The relationship that grasps [the meaning] is established through the principle of "otherwise it would be impossible" (*anyathānupapatti*). Therefore, whatever is grasped more quickly is applied first, due to the swiftness of the causal complex for application (*viniyoga-sāmagrī*). On the other hand, that which is grasped slowly is not assigned to the subordinate element (*śeṣin*) because it is overtaken by its opposite;
thus, it is applied elsewhere. As it has been said: "And this being so, when the established fifteen-foldness (*pāñcadaśya*) is possible as a counter-position..."

Since the assumption of the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*) is possible [only there], it does not find a place in the archetype (*prakṛti*). For an assumption follows the requirements of the ritual performance (*pratipatti*), and does not subvert what has already been established. Therefore, it is logical that the number seventeen belongs to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). In this section, the following is demonstrated: is the archetypal subsidiary (*aṅga*) grasped by way of its connection with the ritual act (*padārtha*), or merely by virtue of its proximity (*sannidhi*)? In that regard, the grasping occurs by way of the connection with the ritual act.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that otherwise it would follow that even the twelve-fold number of *upasads* should be taken as belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*), however, asserts that its inclusion [in the Jyotiṣṭoma] occurs merely by virtue of proximity (*sannidhāna*). But because the proximity of the injunction (*niyoga-sannidhi*) is set aside by the stronger proximity of the application (*viniyoga-sannidhi*) regarding the twelve-fold *upasads*, they are not included by the Jyotiṣṭoma. Nor does there arise an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if inclusion is based on mere proximity, for such is the very nature of proximity itself.

"In every way because of its existence. But the occasional [element] belongs to the archetype (*prakṛti*). How, then, is there a doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here? The intention is as follows: just as the cup (*camasa*) is heard of in the archetype, so too is it extended by implication (*atideśa*) to the ectype (*vikṛti*); therefore, since there is no contradiction with the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) in either case, by what distinction [is the conclusion reached]?

Is it suspected that [the rule] applies to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)? The answer is: such is the suspicion. If the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) were sublated, the direct instruction (*upadeśa*) would be violated. And without the direct instruction, there can be no understanding of the ritual integrity (*sāḍguṇya*). Therefore, the performance must be according to the instruction in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).

Therefore, if the *camasa* were set aside, there would be a deficiency in the sacrifice (*kratu*) in its archetypal form (*prakṛti*); however, in the modified form (*vikṛti*), the understanding of its completeness arises precisely from the performance of the task itself.

Thus, because they share a single purpose, it can be said that the completeness of the sacrifice is achieved even through that which serves the person’s purpose, owing to the distinction in the tasks performed.

For it is through their function (*kārya*) that constituent elements (*padārtha*) are obtained in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). In that case, if the purpose is accomplished by means of even a single element that performs the same function as the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), then there is no perception of deficiency at all, because the emphasis lies on the constituent element itself. Therefore, the application of those elements serving the human goal occurs only in the modified sacrifice. This is true provided that there were no specific function even in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*); however, here, because they have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*)—

The specific function of the secondary instruction regarding the *camasa* and other vessels is the same. When that purpose for the person has been accomplished, the *camasa* is set aside; and when it is set aside and not employed, there is no deficiency in the sacrifice. Now, by what distinction is the *camasa* set aside by the *godohana*?
If you say it is because of its being optional (*kāmyatva*), then what is the status of the *phalacamasa*? Therefore, it must be explained regarding the *phalacamasa*. That is now stated:
Furthermore, because a specific rule is understood in the case of the *phalacamasa*, the general rule is superseded by the specific instruction, just as in the case of the word *pada* and so forth.

Since the specific instruction—concerning those who desire cattle (*paśukāma*) or the *rājanya* caste, which are specific subjects—is more powerful than the general instruction concerning all those entitled to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifices, it is like the instruction regarding the *āhavanīya* fire; thus, its application is within the context of the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself.
Regarding the phrase "of those who perform occasional rites":

the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) is for the sake of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Here, the author of the Bhāṣya advances the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the establishment of the fires is for the sake of the *iṣṭi* due to the context. He challenges this: "But how can there be a context for the *iṣṭi* here? For even in the case of the *iṣṭi*, there is no scriptural injunction regarding entitlement (*adhikāraśruti*)."

r884] For the context belongs specifically to the injunction of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) which possesses its own governing authority (*adhikāra*). As it has been said: “Because that [context] proceeds from the two-fold expectancy.”

Thus [it is argued]. Nor is there an injunction regarding eligibility (*adhikāra-śruti*) for the Pavamāna-iṣṭi; therefore, it cannot be said that the context (*prakaraṇa*) belongs to the iṣṭi. When this objection has been raised, the partisan of a single view (*ekadeśin*) asks the respondent: "How then is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? The respondent asks the partisan of a single view in return with a touch of irony: "And what is your intention? The partisan of a single view replies:

Nothing appears [to be the answer]. The supreme synthesizer says: "In this regard, it is stated that both of these examples are [applicable]. Is the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the fires) primary, or is it the *iṣṭi* (the sacrifice)? The meaning of this is as follows: first of all, neither of the two is for the sake of the fire (*agni*). For instance, are the fires already employed as the subordinate elements (*śeṣin*) of the two, or are they not yet employed? If they were for the sake of fires already employed, then [the rule regarding] the *parṇatā* (being made of *parṇa*-wood) and so forth—"

There would be the undesirable consequence [of the fire-installation] being merely a subordinate part (*aṅga*). However, since it has been established that those things not enjoined for a purpose—being devoid of a function like flour-meal (*saktu*)—do not deserve to be treated as subordinate (*śeṣita*), an entitlement (*adhikāra*) must be postulated. In that regard, there are two possibilities: either the entitlement is postulated with respect to the *pavamāneṣṭis*, such that they themselves become the primary act (*pradhāna*), or the postulation of entitlement is with respect to the fire-installation (*ādhāna*), such that that alone is the primary act. Both of these cases, consisting of the fire-installation and the *pavamāneṣṭis*, constitute the examples.

Regarding this: the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that it is improper for both [the fire and the sacrifice] to be primary; rather, since the sacrifice possesses a greater number of constituent parts (aṅgas), the prima facie view attributes primacy to it. By the maxim "the mention of both occurs because of their plurality" (*bhūyastvena ubhaya-śrutiḥ*), primacy is inferred from the abundance of parts, and thus it is logical that the establishment of the fire (*ādhāna*) is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that [sacrifice]. However, in ultimate reality, neither of the two has the fire as its purpose; such is the prima facie view. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Because there is no authoritative basis for both [the sacrificer and the wife] being the primary objects, and because their application is logically established as being for the sake of the fire, both have the status of being for the sake of the fire.

Even though there is no actual application [of the two] at present, nevertheless, since the status of the fires as the primary objects (śeṣitva) is established by means of a future application, these two are indeed for the sake of the fire. And thus, there is the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).

(1) G. By necessity, it serves the purpose of that primary element (*prakṛti*), as others hold; for when its status as being for the sake of fire (*agni*) is established, is the installation (*ādhāna*) now for the sake of the primary element alone, or for the sake of everything?
[The word] "iti" indicates that the doubt of the author of the Bhāṣya has been restated. Here, he states the doubt which serves as the cause:

this is what is meant—does the establishment (*ādhāna*) belong to the rites for the sake of the fire, or do the fires, once established, exist for the sake of the rites? If the establishment belongs to the fires for the sake of the rites, then, like the *parṇa*-twig and so forth, it would be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the rite; and consequently, like those very things, it would serve the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

But if the consecrated fires (*āhitāgni*) were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), then, because they are connected to independent fires, they would not be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice. Therefore, since [the fires] are connected solely with the *āhavanīya* and others, and since the *āhavanīya* and others serve the purpose of all sacrifices, it is said that the consecration (*ādhāna*) is for the sake of everything by way of those [fires];
however, in the ultimate sense, it is not an auxiliary of anything. He clarifies this point by means of a question: "What is the distinction here?"

This is the distinction: if the establishment (*ādhāna*) of the fires is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), then, like the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood, the injunction for the establishment would apply only to the archetype (*prakṛti*).

But if the fires, once established, are for the sake of the sacrifice, then the establishment of the fires is said to be for all purposes, since the fires are merely subsidiary to the oblations and so forth.

He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "What, then, is appropriate here? He thinks as follows: like the *parṇa*-quality and other such features, it is only the fires that are connected to the sacrifice [that are intended].

Regarding the term "laying of the fires" (*ādhāna*): he states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*)—because the qualification belongs to one who has laid the fires, it is logical that the fires, once laid, exist for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*). The meaning of this is as follows: just as acts such as threshing are performed only by one who is qualified [for the ritual], so too is the laying of the fires. However, the qualification for the injunctions of the rituals belongs to one who already possesses the laid fires; this is because the fires are a necessary means (*niyatopāya*) and because they cannot be produced at the time of performance. Therefore, by the person...

Just as with iron, gold, and so forth, fires are acquired through ritual application (*prayoga*). Since one who has acquired the fires possesses the capacity for ritual action, he holds the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform it.

Consequently, because there is no entitlement prior to that, the grasping by the "grasper" (*grāhaka*) is not established; and since there is no application of the fires [to the sacrifice], they cannot, by way of those fires, be like the purchased [Soma].

[The fire-installation] is a constituent part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅgabhāva*). Or rather, just as there is an entitlement (*adhikāra*) for one who has already kindled the fires (*āhitāgni*), so too, as we shall explain in the sixth [book], there is an entitlement according to the specific application (*yathāviniyogamadhikāra*). When the installation of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not a constituent part [of the sacrifice], then the injunction regarding the seasons such as spring becomes more appropriate.
Otherwise, if it were a constituent part, [the rule] "because the time of the subsidiaries is that of the principal" would apply.

Thus, when the primary time has been established, the injunction regarding spring in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Since the primary time alone is already established, in the case of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices which are performed at different times, it is an injunction for a previously unestablished time for the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*). When these are performed in spring, it is a restatement of an already established time for the fire-consecration. Moreover, there is not just one single injunction.

It would be logical that one [passage] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) and another an injunction (*vidhi*), as otherwise there would be the consequence of inconsistency. However, in this view, it is more appropriately established, because in every case there is an injunction for its own time, and thus it serves as the injunction for the establishment of the fires (*adhāna*) which are its constituent parts.
Regarding the fire for those [offerings]: how, then, could it be suspected that the fires in the *pavamāneṣṭis* have not been consecrated by the *pavamāneṣṭis*?
Those sacrifices intended for the sake of the fire-altar (*agni*) are indeed the *pavamāna-iṣṭis* themselves. Therefore, this doubt that has been raised is not even worth considering.

The meaning of this is as follows: whatever is the effect of something cannot be its own cause; and since the *pavamāna-iṣṭis* are not the cause of the *āhavanīya* and other fires, how could they possibly be the things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by those very fires? Because this matter is impossible, this doubt should not be entertained.

It is stated: here it is argued that this very point is to be considered—does this extended application (*atideśa*) extend as much of the assistance as exists in the archetype (*prakṛti*), or does the extended application follow the specific purpose (*kārya*)? It is not the attainment of the Pavamāna-iṣṭis within the Pavamāna-iṣṭis that is being considered here; rather, [the question is as follows]...

[Page r887] Here it is considered: regarding this extension (*atideśa*) which applies everywhere, does it extend to whatever constitutes an auxiliary (*aṅga*) or non-auxiliary (*anaṅga*) to the archetype (*prakṛti*) as long as it is beneficial? In that case, there would be an extension even for the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices, which are not auxiliaries. Or rather, is it according to the function (*kārya*), only as far as...

An auxiliary (*aṅga*) is extended [to the modified sacrifice] only so far as it produces a benefit; however, that which does not produce a benefit is not an auxiliary. Therefore, the meaning is that only that which is an auxiliary is extended. Consequently, there is no extension of the *pavamāneṣṭi* offerings to the modified sacrifices, because they are not auxiliaries. In this regard, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) is that the extension occurs according to the extent of the benefit produced; for the collection of ritual items is extended based on their connection with the benefit.

It is indicated that even for that which is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*) but is nevertheless beneficial, there exists a connection with the benefit; therefore, its extension (*atideśa*) is also logical. The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*), however, says: "Extension is according to the effect. Only so much is extended as is a constituent part that produces a benefit. For that without which the benefit cannot be realized is precisely what is required for the realization of the benefit and for the realization of the effect.

In the cognition of a genus (*jāti*), that which is perceived as being invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyakatayā*)—just like the individual instance (*vyakti*)—is extended by analogy (*atidiśyate*) to the modified forms (*vikṛti*). Furthermore, that which produces the benefit (*upakāra*) cannot be defined without it. However, that which produces the substance (*padārtha*) which itself produces the benefit does not enter into the benefit and is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*); even without that, the benefit can indeed be cognized as delimited by the class of producing substances.

Because it is not so, that [principle] is not extended by analogy (*atideśa*). In the case of direct instruction (*upadeśa*), however, the opposite is true. For in direct instruction, even that which is merely auxiliary is indeed subject to instruction;

for example, the *pavamāneṣṭis* serve as auxiliaries to the sacrifice. Even though the *pavamāneṣṭis* themselves are not constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, they are nonetheless directly instructed.

Therefore, this means of establishing the elements of ritual action known as extension by analogy should not be regarded as being like direct instruction. Now, suppose it is argued that it may not be auxiliary—

Let it be granted that there is an extension (*atideśa*). Nevertheless, since that [extension] brings about the constituent elements (*padārtha*) as its subordinate parts (*aṅga*), there is indeed an implication (*ākṣepa*). What is the point of explaining a meaning that is not extended? It is said: if there were an extension, then the very set of constituent elements that is extended would be intended as the subordinate part;

consequently, because the *Pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices are subordinate parts in the modified rites (*vikṛti*), the modified rites would take place only upon fires consecrated by their own subordinate parts. For by the modified rite...
The fires should be extinguished at the conclusion of the *vikṛti* sacrifice. Therefore, this demonstration of the lack of extended application (*anatideśa*) is purposeful.

Furthermore, this was deliberated upon in the section defining direct instruction (*upadeśa-lakṣaṇa*) for the sake of showing a specific type of instruction. For one who thinks that, just as in the case of extended application (*atideśa*), [this] is also purposeful for you—[the author] says "extended application" (to address that).

As far as there is an extension of the ritual function (*kāryātideśa*), so too must there be an extension by way of instruction (*upadeśa*). Consequently, the instruction regarding the *ādhāna* and *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices would not be possible. Now, if the instruction extends as far as the beneficial auxiliaries (*upakāraka*), then the extension (*atideśa*) should likewise be so. This is the [objection].

A distinction has been stated [in the previous section] in order to remove doubt regarding the *upadeśa* (direct injunction). It was deliberated upon under the definition of *upadeśa* in order to show that in an *upadeśa*, even that which is merely auxiliary (*upakāraka*) is enjoined, whereas in an *atideśa* (extended application), only that which is actually required for the purpose (*kārya*) is included. Otherwise, if this section were not the locus for distinguishing between *atideśa* and *upadeśa*, it would instead be intended solely for the purpose of investigating whether the *pavamāneṣṭis* are obtained through *atideśa* or not.

It might be so; however, in that case, the matter would have been already resolved by the section concerning the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice. For there, the attainment [of the rite] through implication (*ākṣepa*) was considered. Here, however, that is not considered; rather, the distinction is that it is simply a case of extension (*atideśa*). Furthermore, effort is made regarding the difference in the direct injunction (*upadeśa*) of the *pavamāneṣṭis* because they serve the purpose of the fires (*agni*), and because the *pavamāneṣṭis* are the producers of the fires. Thus, regarding the *pavamāneṣṭis*:

The author of the Bhāṣya has made an effort to show that fire consecrated by the Pavamāneṣṭi does not [automatically] obtain [the status of being fit for sacrifice], and thus, regarding the scope of the Pavamāneṣṭi, he has exerted himself to demonstrate that when there is a difference in instruction through this additional factor, it brings about as much assistance as is possible. For that very purpose, the Pavamāneṣṭi is cited as an example. [Objection: It is equal for all; how then has this section (adhikaraṇa) been commenced? The respondent says:

Just as the author of the Bhāṣya [has stated], the objector says: "It cannot be understood in that way. He asks: "Therefore... The objector says: "Therefore, if this is indeed the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, then [it would apply] to the animal sacrifices (*paśuyāga*).

Because there is no *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting), the acts such as slaughter (*viśasana*) are connected with the animal sacrifice by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and the other criteria alone. Why is it said that these serve all purposes because there is no distinction of *prakaraṇa*? The phrase "because there is no distinction of *prakaraṇa*" can be understood in two ways: either as "because there is no distinction in the *prakaraṇa*," or as "in the *prakaraṇa*..."
Or [it may be argued] "because there is no distinction. In that regard, first of all, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is not possible because there is no context (*prakaraṇa*) for the animals.
If it is argued that there is no distinction here regarding all animals within the *Jyotiṣṭoma* context, and thus it is called "without distinction," [the author] refutes this:
"How then [is it said in the Sūtra]: 'But there is a distinction in the context'?"

Thus [it is argued]: there is no specific distinction among all the animals within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma. Now, if it is claimed that there is indeed an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) for the animals themselves, while the Jyotiṣṭoma constitutes the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), and that for the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites contained therein there is an intermediate context—then this [distinction] is certainly possible; yet, there is indeed a distinction within the context. To this, he says:

Furthermore, there is no such thing as an "intermediate context" (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*). Within the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is a requirement for both the *karaṇa* (the means) and the *itikartavyatā* (the procedure) for a single injunction that possesses a specific objective (*sādhikāra*), but not for intermediate injunctions that lack such an objective. Since the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) itself constitutes the procedure, it is the end that requires a procedure, not the means. And this requirement for a procedure—

[This concerns] the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, within a single injunctive rule of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), there can be no occurrence of two distinct contexts. Furthermore, if a separate context were admitted, then the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and others would not fulfill the requirement of "how-to" (*itthambhāva*), that is, they would not supply the constituent part of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Why? He says: because in that case, the connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma would have to be accepted as being merely "for what purpose? (*kim iti*). And thus, [the same would apply to] the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites.

Indeed, the very absence of *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) would be lost; there would be nothing but causality (*kāraṇatā*). The meaning of this is as follows: for a proponent who desires a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) and, wishing to establish the status of being an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*) for the injunctions (*niyoga*) such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, desires them to possess a primary purpose (*sādhikāratva*), must state that the person engaged in the *jyotiṣṭoma-apūrva* of the primary context itself is the qualified agent (*adhikārī*). And this being the case, [the subordinate acts] would indeed be merely qualifiers of the qualified agent.

The *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma is like heaven; and as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the *apūrva* serves as a qualification for the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*). Since that which is to be accomplished functions as a qualification for the person entitled, the verbal root’s meaning (*bhāvārtha*), which constitutes the object of the injunction, possesses instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) only up to that point. For that alone is the instrument in the mandate (*niyoga*).

That very [action] is the instrument even with respect to the fruit, and nothing else; for that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) becomes fully realized. Here, however, there is no other thing to be accomplished as the fruit, nor is there any further conceptualization of another object to be accomplished. Consequently, since the action such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*—which serves as the instrument within its own specific application—is itself the instrument even with regard to the *apūrva* that functions as a qualification of the entitlement (*adhikāra*), the status of being a "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*) is lost.

Nor is there the fault of being obstructed by a quality prescribed for the origin [of the rite], because its status as an instrument is established through its function, as in the case of the *phalacamas* (the fruit-cup). For this instrumentality is directed toward that which serves as a qualification for the entitlement (*adhikāra*), and not as a presentation of an instrument to be accomplished as a goal. Now, if it be argued that in this case the primary injunction’s expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) would remain unfulfilled; true, yet even so, the status of being a procedure cannot exist without a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It cannot be determined [by that alone]. If it is argued that the very expectancy for the *itikartavyatā* (the "how-to" procedure) arising from the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) is itself the authority, we say no;

for it is only when the connection with the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*) is understood that the expectancy for the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*), postulating the form of the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*) as its means, becomes the authority designated by the term "context" (*prakaraṇa*). And in this view, the connection with the injunction of qualification has not been accepted prior [to that]. If [that connection] were understood beforehand—[then the injunction of qualification would be redundant].

If a connection with the injunction (*vidhi*) is admitted, there is no room at all for the postulation of a qualified agent (*adhikāra*). Once that connection is understood and the application (*viniyoga*) is established through the context (*prakaraṇa*), the performance of the rite is accomplished by virtue of its being prompted by the primary injunction. For it is observed in the world that an injunction (*niyoga*) is expressed as being conjoined with a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) for the sake of securing its performance; it does not, however, serve the purpose of expressing the conjoining of the agent in some unseen form.

For this very reason, even in the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), there is no assumption of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), since the performance of the act is established solely through the impulsion of the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*). Consequently, in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites whose connection to an injunction specifying the qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*) was previously unknown, a qualified person is postulated only upon their mere proximity to that which is directed toward the supreme transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*). And in that context, whatever meaning is understood through the natural sense (*svarasa*) must be accepted; and by the natural sense, [the word] "instrument" (*karaṇa*)—

We understand it to be precisely that; thus, its status as a *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is not established. Furthermore, if there were an expectancy for an *adhikāra* (qualification/entitlement) in the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), then why would the very things heard within their own sentences—such as the *varmā* [observances] and so forth—not stand as qualifiers of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), as in the case of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice?

And why would the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), which is directly heard [in the primary injunction], not be supplied (*anuṣajyate*) as the provider of the qualification? The same applies to the milk-vow (*payovrata*) and other such observances.

Why should the person engaged in eating not be considered qualified [for the rite], just as there is a rule regarding facing the east? Furthermore, the qualification is postulated for the sake of accomplishing the performance. In that regard, it is better [to hold] that, with reference to the sacrifice for which one possesses qualification—as in the statement "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—the injunction "He offers the Samidhs" [is prescribed].
Thus, the injunction regarding the *samit* and other materials, along with the sequence of performance (*itikartavyatā*), serves to establish their status as instruments (*karaṇatva*).

It should be accepted that when one performs the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices desiring heaven, [the injunction] is "one should sacrifice the *samidh*s," and so forth. Consequently, because the qualification of that which is being pointed out (*uddiśyamāna*) is not intended to be significant, the *samidh* and other [subsidiary acts] would have a connection only with the sacrifice in general, just like the entitlement (*adhikāra*).

Thus, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) would be obtained for the *aindrāgna* and other [principal sacrifices] through direct instruction (*upadeśa*) alone. Furthermore, even if [the procedure] were initiated by the supreme transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*)...

Even though the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is connected as the objective of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites by way of being the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), nevertheless, it does not follow that he is the procedure for all [of them] collectively. Rather, since he is connected as a qualification of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) for each individual rite, he must be considered the procedure for each one individually, just like heaven (*svarga*). To illustrate: in the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other sacrifices, heaven is indeed the objective for each one individually.

[In the case of the word "sacrificer" (*adhikārin*),] it is construed as a qualification of the [agent]; it is connected with each [element] independently. The same would apply here as well. Even when [the goal] functions as a qualification of the qualified agent, its connection does not reach completion without the relationship of means and end (*upāyopeyabhāva*); therefore, the state of being means and end must be postulated.

Furthermore, the means (*upāya*) is twofold, characterized as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). In that context, since there is no connection as an instrument, there is a connection as a procedure.

Furthermore, since the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are understood from each individual sentence as being independent, their status as the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) would likewise be independent. However, for one who holds the view that the connection with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others occurs through mere proximity to the *paramāpūrva* residing solely within its own sentence,

then— in that very conceptualization of the qualified injunction (*adhikāravidhi*)— since all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) fall together like pigeons upon a single [target], there would be only a single benefit to the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*) corresponding to that [injunction].

It has rightly been stated by all [the commentators] that the door of characteristics (*lakṣaṇadvāra*) should be postulated, and that this constitutes the entire procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Furthermore, it is not the case that a connection is never observed in the world based on mere proximity (*sannidhāna*) alone. For even in the case of unseen effects (*adṛṣṭa*), we observe that a connection is established and an injunction is carried out based on mere proximity, just as it is seen in the case of visible effects and the like. Nor does the doctrine of connection through mere proximity lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because such proximity is not present in every instance.
If proximity were ineffective, why would the qualified person (adhikārī) be restricted only to those subsidiaries (aṅga) that are present at the time of the primary apūrva? If, however,

the connection with the qualified person occurs everywhere only through the mediation of the syntactical relation of the constituent elements (padārtha-anvaya), and not merely by virtue of proximity, then there would be equality between the fifteen-fold and seventeen-fold recitations (pāñcadaśya-sāptadaśya) which are connected via the Sāmidhenī verses— those studied within the context and those outside the context— and thus [the distinction] would be rendered useless.

Enough of this verbosity; let us return to the subject at hand. He states another objection: "And [there would be] the consequence that the *prayāja* and other [subsidiary rites] belong to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices"—that is, they would be enjoined by the context (*prakaraṇa*).

The meaning of this is as follows: the *prayāja* and other rites are also enjoined by the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; consequently, the person entitled to perform them (*adhikārī*) would be the same one who is engaged in the production of the ultimate transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*). Therefore, because they would possess such an entitlement...

In that case as well, a specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*) would necessarily follow. For if the *prayāja* and other such rites were to be applied solely by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest, then there would be no room for the postulation of a governing context (*adhikāra*), just as in the case of the *parṇatā* (being made of *parṇa*-wood). However, those [rites] which are unconnected [to a specific result] and thus find no basis for performance—

Considering that the assumption of a specific qualification (*adhikāra*) is superior, it was stated [above] that [the procedure] is to be applied by virtue of its belonging to the context (*prakaraṇa*). Now, one might object: "Let it be that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is worldly (*laukika*). To this he replies: "And therefore, according to the rule ‘But in the case of unmanifest [rites], [the procedure] belongs to the Soma sacrifice’ (*avyaktāsu tu somasya*), the procedure is that of the Soma sacrifice."

[The sacrifice] obtains the procedure belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa, just as [the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites obtain theirs]. The meaning of this is as follows: when there is a requirement for a procedure (itikartavyatākāṅkṣā), because of its unmanifest nature, the procedure belonging to the Soma-sacrifice is obtained through extended application (atideśa) to the Prayāja and other rites by means of the indicative mark (liṅga) of the injunction; yet this is not desired.
Now, if it be asked, "How can the procedure of the primary rite apply to its subsidiaries?", he says: "Just as in the case of the Dīkṣaṇīyā and so forth, [it applies] to the Darśa..."

[The sacrifice] is the Full Moon [sacrifice]. There is no distinction between primary and subordinate status when both are equally things to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Thus, even for the two primary sacrifices, the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa, an *itikartavyatā* (procedural detail) is observed in their subsidiaries, such as the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and others. Regarding this, a certain person who considers himself a scholar says:

"If there is an acceptance of the extension of the Soma ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) to the *Prayāja* and other [Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa subsidiaries], then, without postulating a benefit to the Soma [from those subsidiaries], the Darśa..."

There is no postulation of assistance for the two [Darśapūrṇamāsa] months. Without the postulation of assistance for the Darśapūrṇamāsa, there is likewise no postulation of assistance for the Soma sacrifice; thus, through the mutual postulation of assistance, a circularity (itaretarāśrayatā) results. This too is like the crushing of one’s own head by a falling rock and the resulting fear of the mountain splitting—[the error of] one who is ignorant of his own means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). For instance, assistance is postulated by means of its own constituent parts (aṅgas), not...

Furthermore, this applies even to the relationship between primary and subsidiary parts (*aṅga-aṅgin*). It was stated in the ninth [book] that the subsidiaries such as the *prayāja* offerings do not become subsidiaries of the injunction for the primary sacrifice, because they are established in relation to their own intermediate apūrva. Consequently, even in the absence of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) derived by extension (*atideśika*) from the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries, the assumption of benefit (*upakāra*) for the New and Full Moon sacrifices is possible.

Likewise, in the case of the Soma sacrifice as well, it is indeed consistent that there is an extension of the procedure even without the specific injunctions for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites; thus, mutual [benefit] is established.

There is an extension (*atideśa*) to the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). It has been stated that as many subsidiaries as are extended, so it applies; therefore, only those subsidiaries belonging to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*), such as the *prayāja* offerings and others, are extended to them, but not the subsidiaries of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites. Likewise, even in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, the extension applies only to those subsidiaries belonging to the model sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), and not even to subsidiaries such as the *prayāja*. At most, once the extension is completed, the subsidiaries [of the subsequent rite] are implied by necessity.
"That very attainment [of the result] is self-sublated either through mutual dependence or circularity; this is a matter for those of subtle vision.

He asks: "Why does it not occur? He thinks thus: since the *prayāja* and other rites also possess an entitlement by virtue of being subordinate to the primary entitlement, let there be the *saumika* procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for those things that are to be accomplished, because they are brought about precisely through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

(1) Regarding "by means of the injunction" (*vidhinā*), he provides the answer: "It has been stated that there is no intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*). If there were an intermediate context, then it might indeed be so.

But that [separate] locus does not exist. Why does it not exist? He says: for in a single injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), a manifold expectation of "what? is not possible. In a single injunction of performance, an expectation of "what? in both forms is not possible, because the performance—characterized by its execution—is already stated by the single governing injunction (*adhikāravidhi*). For [the injunction] exists for the sake of obtaining the performance.

There is no requirement for a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) when [the performance] is already established from another source. But if you think that the performance is not implied by anything else, to that he says: "And this is a single injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), because there is a single word for the performance together with its procedure (*itikartavyatā*)," as he will state later. The injunctive rule regarding entitlement (*adhikāravidhi*) is indeed one alone for everything.

It has been shown by the principle of *ekaśabdāt* (from a single word) that [the injunction], having grasped what is proximate as being for its own sake even though it lacks a specific qualification (*niradhikāra*), employs it and thereby implies its performance;

therefore, there is no requirement for various specific qualifications of an agent (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Since the *prayāja* and other such elements lack a qualification, their status as things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is not understood, and thus they have no requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*); consequently, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the characteristics belonging to the Soma sacrifice. How then is it so in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others?

Furthermore, there is a requirement for the "how-to" (kartavyatākāṅkṣā), and without such a requirement, there can be no extension of ritual properties (dharmas). And this has been accepted by you yourself when you stated that the procedure (itikartavyatā) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices applies to the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites, using them as an illustration. The reply is: Let it be that there are no extended ritual properties;

however, two requirements—namely, "what [is to be done]" and "how [it is to be done]"—cannot coexist within a single context (prakaraṇa). The meaning of this is not merely a matter of formal acceptance.

The entity is established as follows: if, this logic being established, your acceptance [of the position] does not hold, let it not hold; for this is a statement made by way of concession (*anvāruhya-vacana*). However, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), the attainment of ritual properties (*dharma*) certainly occurs in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites.

This is because, even in the case of those things that are merely auxiliary members (*aṅga*), transcendental potencies (*apūrva*) must be admitted; otherwise, as has been stated in the eleventh book, the status of being an auxiliary member would be impossible for things that are momentary.

By the Commentator: it is inferred from the observation of the *prayāja* offerings and other such elements that those *apūrva*s (transcendental potencies) depend upon the archetypal (*prakṛta*) assistance. As it has been stated:

"But in the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), the established rule is that there is only an indicative mark (*liṅga*). And this we shall explain in the section concerning the complete prescription (*kṛtsnavidhāna*).

This being the case, since there is no intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), that which is stated—namely, "by virtue of the context [it belongs] to the *savanīya*" and "by virtue of the position [it belongs] to the *agnīṣomīya*"—is all of this mere gibberish (*andhapada*). This is because it proceeds without due consideration. Therefore, the objection is: "The Bhāṣya must be explained with great effort. The resolution, however, is stated here: First of all, this is indeed the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

[This concerns] the *ṣṭoma*. On the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*), the ritual rules (*dharmas*) are enjoined; yet, not all animals are present on that day. A word that denotes presence is a term that functions as a reference (*uddeśaka*). Therefore, it must be considered in the injunctions for slaughter and so forth: "To what does this refer? What is being said here is this: the inquiry is not conducted by accepting the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the animals; rather, [it concerns] the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—

This is precisely the context [of the discussion]. Furthermore, acts such as slaughter (*viśasana*) are enjoined by the Vedic text itself as being connected with the animal. In that regard, the word "animal" (*paśu*) is the indicator (*uddeśaka*); and an indicator-word refers to what is proximate (*sannihita*). Thus, it is considered: among the injunctions of ritual duties (*dharma-vidhi*), which animal is proximate that is taken up by the words acting as indicators? In that case, because there is no distinction of context (*prakaraṇa*), all animals [are included].

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that because these [rites] are introduced as being for the sake of the Jyotiṣṭoma, they serve all purposes. However, another proponent of the prima facie view maintains that since the Savanīya [offering] and its ritual details (dharmas) are prescribed on a single day characterized by fasting (aupavasthya), there exists a specific proximity (sannidhi-viśeṣa) of the Savanīya; thus, there is indeed a context (prakaraṇa).
It has been stated that this refers to a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). But surely, here we observe the acceptance of a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) alone, since he says:

"The characteristics of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*) are recited in the context of the *Savanīya*.
