To this, he replies: what is intended here by "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is the characteristic of the subject matter at hand (*prakṛtalakṣaṇa*), which is characterized by proximity (*sannidhāna*).

It does not, however, have the characteristic of being defined by a requirement for the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance). Therefore, there is no contradiction. Precisely because *prakaraṇa* (context) is intended there as having the characteristic of proximity (*sannidhāna*), it is correct that the *agnīṣomīya* [rite] [is connected] by virtue of *sthāna* (position). Otherwise, since *sthāna* is weaker than *prakaraṇa* when the latter is defined by the *itikartavyatā*, *sthāna* would not even possess the capacity to enjoin. Proximity—

In this view, however, it is logical that both possess equal strength. For the *savanīya* offerings are present there by virtue of their injunction (*vidhāna*), while the *agnīṣomīya* is present by virtue of its position (*sthāna*); thus, it is logical that both serve as subsidiaries. Furthermore, the statement that the *savanīya* is enjoined on the day of the Soma pressing (*sautye ’hani*) for the sake of accomplishing what is not part of the original model sacrifice (*aprakṛta*) becomes meaningful; otherwise, even if there were an injunction on another day, [the result] would not be the *jyoti-* [sacrifice].

It cannot be said that there is an absence of context (*prakaraṇa*) as in the case of the *ṣṭoma*. But how is it that, once it is established that [the rite] is for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice due to its specific proximity (*sannidhāna*), and that its recitation within the context of the *jyotiṣṭoma* is purposeful, an extension (*atideśa*) of two animals is made into that very same context? For a single injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) does not take up those same ritual details (*dharma*) both by way of direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and by way of extension (*atideśa*). [The injunction of performance...]

This objection belongs to one who is confused by the idea that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) is grasped solely through the verbal injunctions. He states the reply: "We shall provide the resolution to this objection in the section on extended application (*atideśa*), under the rule ‘The Soma sacrifice is new because its entire procedure is prescribed. This formal objection regarding the injunction arises from a failure to understand the distinction between obtaining [the rite] and undertaking [its performance]."

By this [statement], that very injunction regarding the subsidiaries (aṅgavidhi) is the bringer of the primary subsidiaries, which is raised by the observation of indicative marks (liṅga) and possesses a requirement for the archetypal assistance (prākṛtopakāra). That very same sacrifice which has all the cups as its consecrated materials is also present in the *ukthya* and other rites; it is the Soma juice itself that is to be consecrated by all the cups.

The analysis of the compound is: "that very [Soma] is the substance (dravya) belonging to which. What is meant by this is as follows: whatever portions of juice are prepared by means of the various cuppings (grahaṇa) performed for the sake of specific deities, it is by means of those that this Soma-sacrifice (somayāga) is accomplished. Even in the Ukthya and other such rites, there is likewise only the taking of the Soma that remains from the sacrifice; therefore, in those cases as well, that same sacrifice must be performed. This sacrifice [does not cease] in the Ukthya and other rites.

There is no other originative injunction; rather, the originative injunction is simply "one should sacrifice with Soma. If that sacrifice [is the same], then even in the case of other extractions such as the *ukthya* and so forth, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is exactly the same as that which is performed during the sacrifice through the extractions of the *aindravāyava* and others—meaning, as long as the sacrifice is being performed.

If every specific extraction up to the end of the *agniṣṭoma* were the cause for the application of the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the sacrifice, then [the properties] would not apply to the other extractions.

The *itikartavyatā* (procedural details) would not apply to the *ukthya* and other [soma-offerings]. But this is not the case. Thus he says: "And the specific nature of the drawing (*grahaṇa*) is not the cause for obtaining the *itikartavyatā* of the sacrifice; rather, it is the injunction of performance itself—the injunction alone as that which is to be executed—that is the cause for obtaining the *dharma*. Furthermore, there is no separate injunction of performance for the sacrifice in the case of other drawings; even in the *ukthya* and others, there are [only] drawings..."

In other [subsidiary] rites, there is no injunction for a different performance of the sacrifice. What then? That very performance which was enjoined by the statement "one should sacrifice with Soma" is the same one that applies to the Ukthya and other rites as well. For, just as in the case of the Aindravāyava and other cups, it is only the specific extractions (grahaṇa) characterized by their accessory qualities that are enjoined there in the Ukthya and others for the sake of the result, not the sacrifice itself. This is just as in the case of the injunction, "For one desiring cattle, one should lead forward [the water] with a cow-milking vessel," which does not apply to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves.

(1) R. Thus, up to this point—[p. 907] no formal argument (*prayoga*) has been urged. Therefore, let them be like the *phalacamasa* (the fruit-cup), being devoid of the instruction regarding the properties of grasping. Not so.

It can also be said that the *punaryāga* (re-sacrifice) is not connected with the ritual properties (*yāgadharma*) [of the original sacrifice]. For it has been stated previously that among all consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*), a single performance—that is, a single execution—is enjoined, since the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is grasped by the performance itself. Precisely because all the forms (*saṃsthā*) have identical injunctions, the term "Agniṣṭoma" is employed [in the rule]: "If he performs the Agniṣṭoma, he offers [the oblation]."
Thus, if the ritual properties were taught as belonging exclusively to that which ends with the Agniṣṭoma, then even without the mention of "Agniṣṭoma," they would belong to the Agniṣṭoma alone;

in that case, the mention of "Agniṣṭoma" would be redundant. However, if there is a common application (*samānavidhāna*), the mention of "Agniṣṭoma" is for the purpose of connecting it with specific preparatory rites (*viśeṣasaṃskāra*).

And the combination is demonstrated. For, since the animal sacrifice for Agni (Āgneya) is directly enjoined (aupadeśika) in all sacrificial terminuses (saṃsthās) by means of a common injunction, its combination with the specific animals associated with the Ukthya and other terminuses is logically established. Consequently, when that [combination] exists, the observation of a second and a third [animal] is justified; otherwise, [if it were not so], the Āgneya animal, being merely extended by analogy (ātideśika), would not coexist with those belonging to the Ukthya and other terminuses.

"If there is sublation by those [rites] based on direct instruction, there could be no combination. To this, an objection is raised: "Since the animals serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), their combination alone is logical; as it will be stated later: 'And because they are prescribed in the case of the *prājāpatya* offerings'. To this it is replied:
"Because the common designation *savanīya* indicates that all the animals have an identical function, sublation is indeed appropriate. Therefore, [the conclusion] is established."

The observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). To this it is replied: This would indeed be so, if the obligation to perform the sacrifice were obtained through the injunction of performance itself in other forms such as the *ukthya* and others, just as it is in the case of the *godohana* vessel in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. But here, in the *agniṣṭoma*...

The injunction for the performance of the sacrifice extends only as far as the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). In this context, however, the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice—namely, "one should sacrifice with Soma"—extends only as far as those purificatory rites called *grahaṇa* (the drawing of cups), which are occasional and for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), ending with the *agniṣṭoma*. Beyond this, the *grahas* such as the *ukthya* and others are enjoined in connection with specific desires; these alone constitute the injunctions for the sacrifice.

They do not imply [the permanent application]. Just as the *aindravāyava* and other cups (*graha*) are permanent, so too would there be repetition. If this were the case, the ritual properties (*dharma*) could not be grasped by the injunction for the sacrifice (*yāga-codanā*) in the *ukthya* and other rites. Therefore, like the *phalacamas*, the contradiction between the permanent and the non-permanent (*nityānitya-saṃyoga-virodha*) is appropriate. In the *ukthya* and other rites, the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice is occasional (*naimittikī*), [as it is] by means of the optional cups (*kāmya-graha*).
Because they are drawn [to the sacrifice]; and since the ritual properties (*dharma*) are connected with the permanent sacrifice, they ought to be grasped through its permanent performance.

For if they were grasped through an occasional performance, there would be a contradiction between the permanent and the occasional. Thus it is established here as well—just as in the case of the *phalacamas*—that even a single sacrifice drawn by the [act of] drawing [the cup] possesses these properties, such as those belonging to the *ukthya* and other rites. Furthermore, the acquisition of properties occurs through the [specific] function. Therefore...

The inclusion [of the *agniṣṭoma*] will occur by virtue of the scriptural statement (*vacana*). When this prescriptive injunction (*adhikāravidhi*)—which has as its object the sacrifices implied by the mention of the *ukthya* and other forms—requires assistance, it accepts the assistance provided by the prescriptive injunction regarding the permanent forms (*nityasaṃsthā*) mentioned in proximity; thus, the acquisition of the ritual properties (*dharma*) occurs through functional necessity (*kāryataḥ*).

Consequently, when an exclusion by means of a direct instruction (*aupadeśika*) would otherwise have occurred, there shall be a combination (*samuccaya*) due to the scriptural statement. Furthermore, the word *agniṣṭoma* will function as a restatement (*anuvāda*).

By the statement, "If it is an Agniṣṭoma, he offers oblations," [the injunction is established]. It is not a fault for this to be a restatement (anuvāda), for even statements that are restatements are observed, such as: "They lead [the fire] around in two cases."
Thus, the observation of the absence of the *homā* (oblations) and so forth will be logically consistent.

As it is said: "If he anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) for the *ukthya* sacrifice, he does not offer an oblation. This is the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remnant of the *pracaraṇī-homa*. In that case—

In the view that the procedure is identical, it would follow that the Agniṣṭoma oblation applies because of the rule "if it is an Agniṣṭoma, he offers"; likewise, the smearing of the enclosing sticks (paridhi) would apply in the Ukthya sacrifice. That is not so, because of the text: "he does not offer."

Thus, the restatement of the absence of the oblation (*homābhāvānuvāda*) would not be tenable, for this [passage] has the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*), as it is an expression in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*). Furthermore, because [the act of smearing] is sublated by the smearing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhyañjana*)—which is directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) and serves the same purpose in the relationship between the archetype and the ectype—the restatement of the absence of the oblation is appropriate. Since [the action] is obtained through direct injunction, it must be performed according to that injunction; therefore, by the force of the two injunctions, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of both.

It is to be inferred. However, since the requirement is already established by the purpose, the injunction applies to that which is already established for the purpose; thus, the cessation of the original *pratipatti*-type oblation is indeed logical.
Thus, in the *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā*.
The sixth quarter of the third chapter.
Now, in the *Ṛjuvimalā*:
The seventh section (pāda) of the third chapter:

"That which is unconnected [to a specific rite] belongs to all because there is no distinction of context. Regarding the doubt as to whether the properties of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) are for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice, or for the sake of the primary alone, it is first stated that they are for the sake of the primary due to the context (*prakaraṇa*); then, on the grounds of being a source of assistance (*upakāraka*), it is declared that they are for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the primary. By this, just as—

The previously heard topic has been restated in order to raise an objection. He raises the objection: "That is incorrect. For it is through direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means [of proof] that the fact of being for the sake of that [the primary] is understood, not by way of assistance (*upakāra*).

That which appears to be for the sake of the primary cannot be otherwise established by means of assistance, because there is no absence of the authority of application (*viniyoga-pramāṇa*) characterized by assistance. He provides the reply: "It is said: Direct statement and the others, which were indeed presented, [establish] the fact of being for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary..."

For the sake of accomplishment: since the word "oblation" (*havis*) in the injunction "he places the oblations on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)" denotes all oblations whatsoever, the fact that the *barhis* serves both the subsidiary and the primary rites is established by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) itself. If subordination (*śeṣatva*) is [determined] through scripture, then what is the purpose of mentioning "benefit" (*upakāra*)? The answer is: because that [benefit] might sometimes be absent, there would be a restriction of the scriptural statement; however, since such a uniform benefit does exist, it is mentioned.

The meaning of this is as follows: this mention of "benefit" (*upakāra*) is for the purpose of removing doubt. Subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) does not exist anywhere apart from benefit. Therefore, the benefit that serves the purpose of both the subsidiary and the primary oblations must be investigated. In that regard, if a benefit observed in one case were of an unobserved nature in another, then subsidiarity would exist only where the benefit is perceived; thus, so that such a doubt may not arise, [the author states] "everywhere."

r911] The mention of "assistance" (*upakāra*) is intended to show that assistance is observed to have a single form; if, however, it were for the sake of both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*), then it would be by means of the sentence (*vākya*) alone.

The connection [of the *barhis*] is with the properties (*dharma*) of the remainder (*śeṣa*). If the connection were by means of the sentence (*vākya*), why would it not apply even to mere *barhis* used in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*? For if the connection were by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*), then the properties would belong only to that which has that specific context. He resolves the objection: subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) is stated to exist when there is the status of being an apprehender (*grāhakatva*). [As stated: "Due to the specificity of the context, there would be a contradiction in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)."

In this regard, it was stated in the first section of the seventh book that what is grasped by the grasper (*grāhaka*) is then applied (*viniyujyate*). And here, the grasper is the procedural injunction (*prayogavidhi*) for the New and Full Moon sacrifices;

because the ritual details (*dharmas*) are in proximity to that, there is no application of the details belonging to other [sacrifices]. Thus, the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅgadarśana*) has been explained.

"But because of the connection with the result. Here, the Bhāṣyakāra examines whether acts such as shaving the hair and beard are for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary rites, or whether they are for the sake of the primary alone. To state the doubt that serves as the reason for this inquiry, he first clarifies the subject of the example, saying: "In this context, the purificatory acts (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) are the examples. Although there is no mention of them in the accusative case here, nevertheless, from common worldly usage itself, [the purpose of] shaving and so forth is understood.
Since they are observed to be for the purpose of purifying the person (*puruṣa-saṃskāra*), these are indeed purifications of the person. Now, he states a doubt regarding their cause:

"Are they for the person in the state of being an agent (*kartṛ-bhūta*) or for the person in the state of being authorized (*adhikṛta*)? For there are two states of the person in ritual action: first, the state of being authorized, characterized by sovereignty; second, the state of being an agent. If, therefore, this is a purification of the person in the state of being an agent, then because the auxiliaries and the primary rite are for the sake of the agent, that purification—

The meaning is that [the rites] are for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice. Thus, even in the *paśubandha*, which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *agnīṣomīya-paśu*, acts such as shaving (*vapanādi*) would apply by virtue of the extended injunction (*codaka*). Now, if it is argued that these are purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) belonging to one who stands in the position of the agent (*kartṛ*), then, since the person’s qualification (*adhikāra*) pertains only to the primary sacrifice, acts such as shaving would be for the sake of that primary sacrifice.

In this way, the status of being a subsidiary to the ritual action is established for the one who has become the agent; such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). Its meaning is as follows: the agent is indeed a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the ritual action. If...

r912] If those formative forces (*saṃskāra*) were to belong to that [very person], then even the factors (*dharma*) would possess the status of being limbs of karma. However, it is the one situated in the state under discussion who is the primary factor.

His *saṃskāras* (purificatory rites) are not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the ritual action (*karman*), because they belong to a state that is not an auxiliary. Furthermore, for that which has not become an auxiliary of the ritual action, its very connection with the injunction (*niyoga*) is lost. Therefore, [the view] that they belong to the agent constitutes the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*). He states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): we shall explain in the first section of the seventh book that the "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*) falls under the category of "what" (*kimiti-aṃśa*), because it arises from two types of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

The meaning of this is as follows: whatever *itikartavyatā* (procedural requirement) there may be, it falls within the scope of the *sādhya* (the goal to be accomplished), not within the scope of the *sādhana* (the means). Why? Because the two requirements—namely, "by what" (*kena*) and "how" (*katham*)—have that [goal] as their agent. It has been demonstrated in the first section of the seventh book (*Saptamādya*) that it is the *sādhya* itself, together with its *itikartavyatā*, that requires an instrument (*karaṇa*), and not that the instrument necessitates an *itikartavyatā*. This being the case, what [is the status of the agent] in the state of being the agent (*kartṛbhāve*)?

It is considered whether this refinement (*saṃskāra*) brings about fitness (*yogyatā*) or pertains to the state of being authorized (*adhikṛtabhāva*). In that regard, it is logical that the refinement should serve the same purpose for which the status of being an agent (*kartṛbhāva*) exists; for the agency [of the person] is for the sake of the state of being authorized. A person assumes the role of an agent for the sake of accomplishing the authorization characterized by sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Thus, the refinement belongs only to the person who is in the primary state of being authorized.

It is appropriate [to consider them as purificatory rites], because the purpose of the scripture is the accomplishment of the qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, it is logical that they are purificatory rites for one who is qualified. Furthermore, the Bhāṣya states that when the qualification—which is the result—is brought to completion, those purificatory rites for the qualified person also become auxiliary factors (*itikartavyatā*) of the sacrifice, as they desire to provide assistance in the fulfillment of that result.

And because of the connection with the desire to perform [the sacrifice]. Regarding the section on the properties of the *barhis* grass, what is the difference here that this new section is commenced? Just as in that case the *barhis* and so forth serve both the subsidiaries and the primary rite, so too here it is logical that the altar (*vedi*) serves both the subsidiaries and the primary rite, since it is produced for that purpose.
(1) P. 1078 (2) R. Because it is made for that.

[Page r913] For what purpose is this section commenced? The answer is: the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) belongs to the primary cause alone (*pradhāna*). The meaning of this is:

the proponent of the prima facie view maintains that the desire to act belongs to the primary cause itself. Nevertheless, he asks: "What is the purpose of that desire?"—to which it is replied: "Whatever is the object of that desire, for that very purpose do the others [act]."

The intended meaning is "the subsidiary parts" (*vāṅgāni*). For it is logical that the subsidiary parts are precisely those intended for the sake of whatever is to be accomplished. By this very principle, it should be understood that this applies everywhere—even that which is taught in general terms, such as "he places the sacrificial offerings upon the *barhis* grass," is to be taken as an illustration here.
For this very reason, the plural number is used in the phrase "the subsidiary parts are for its sake."

It is so by virtue of that designation. However, regarding the touching (*abhimarśana*), the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) holds because of the direct connection with the word denoting the primary [sacrifice].
Since, in the phrase "with the *Caturhotṛ* [formula], [one touches] the *Paurṇamāsī*," the word *Paurṇamāsī* denotes the primary [sacrifice], the touching applies only to the primary oblations;
it is only the oblations related to the primary [sacrifice] that are presented by the word denoting the primary in relation to the touching, and not the subsidiary oblations as well. Thus—

Having established the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) through both reasoning and scriptural statement in these two examples, he now states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "It is true that the primary act (*pradhāna*) is intended to be performed, but it is performed together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*) for the sake of accomplishing the qualification (*adhikāra-nirvṛtti*); this is the conclusion. Who says that the primary act is not intended to be performed? Rather, it is precisely that which is intended to be performed; however, one cannot say that it is intended to be performed for its own sake alone. Its intention to be performed is for the purpose of accomplishing the qualification.

The primary act, together with its subsidiaries, accomplishes the qualification; it does not do so when devoid of its subsidiaries. Therefore, it is the primary act along with its subsidiaries that is intended to be performed.

In the same way, the touching (*abhimarśana*) also pertains only to the means for accomplishing the qualification. For there too, because the accusative case is observed, it is understood to be the most desired object (*īpsitatama*).

And this state of being the most desired belongs only to the means, not merely to the instrument (*karaṇa*) alone. Furthermore, the means is the instrument accompanied by the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Thus, both types of touching the sacrificial altar (*vedyabhimarśana*) serve the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal acts. Having formulated two prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on this common established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the final conclusion (*siddhāntita*) was reached.

[Page r914] But the initiation-fee (*dīkṣā-dakṣiṇā*) belongs to the principal [rite] because of a direct scriptural statement. Even though the initiation-fee is for the completion of the entitlement (*adhikāra-nirvṛtti*) of the [rite] together with its subsidiaries, having raised the doubt that it belongs to the [rite] together with its subsidiaries, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that it belongs to the principal because of the scriptural statement. Why? Because by this [statement], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion are [established].

Both [the views] have been stated. This inquiry is undertaken by accepting that initiation (*dīkṣā*) serves as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent. In that regard, since the qualification for the rite is accomplished only when it is performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), it must be executed precisely with its parts. The agent is a constituent part of that [rite]; therefore, the refinement of the agent is likewise necessarily a constituent part of it—this is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*). However, the scriptural statement should be explained as intending the primary rite together with its constituent parts. There is no evidence for the statement having any other purpose.

"It exists"—this has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Now, an objection is raised: "It is indeed appropriate that initiation (*dīkṣā*) belongs to the principal sacrifice; but when the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is the principal element, how then can the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) be performed by those who have not been hired? For these [subsidiaries] consist of the priestly functions (*ārtrijya*) and so forth. To this it is replied: Who said that the subsidiary rites are performed by those who have not been hired? There will certainly be a means of measurement (*māna*) derived from the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛta*), such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering].

In the *diṣṭaiṣṭika* sacrifices, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) will be obtained through the force of the extended injunction (*codaka*). If the archetypal fee were present there, then there would be no case of "incidental application" (*prasaṅga*) regarding the fee. We shall explain the definition of incidental application exactly as it occurs. The observation has been stated. Likewise, regarding the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the altar (*vedi*): since it is heard in scripture that "half [of the post] is within the altar," there arises a doubt: is the altar an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the post, or not?

(1) P. 1081 (2) P. 1082 (3) He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "For what reason is it a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *śruti*? Because of the statement, "Half within the altar," the altar is a subsidiary of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); this is the prima facie view.

The prima facie view (*pakṣa*) is as follows: [The word *antarvedi* denotes a location]. However, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is this: because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the word *bahirvedi*, it is not possible for it to enjoin the literal meaning [of "inside the altar"]; rather, it indicates a location (*deśalakṣaṇā*). This is because if both [the inside and outside] were enjoined, there would be the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). The meaning of this is as follows: "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*). If one were to fix it inside the altar, it would burn [the sacrificer]; if outside the altar, it would not be secured. One fixes it half inside the altar and half outside; thus it is secured and does not burn."

Thus, because the opening and the conclusion form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), it is determined that this is one sentence. If the literal meaning of the scriptural statement (*śruti*) "within the altar" (*antarvedi*) were accepted, then its syntactic unity with the word "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*) would not be possible; therefore, for the sake of establishing this syntactic unity, it is logical that the term refers to a location by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

"One recites the *śāmidhenī* verses there. But what is the distinction of this [passage] from the previous one? Just as in the previous case there was an indication by way of location (*deśa-lakṣaṇā*), so too here let the location be indicated by means of the *havirdhāna*. The answer is: this is the distinction; for here the *havirdhāna* is heard mentioned independently of other words. It is not connected with the word "within the altar" (*antarvedi*) as it was [in the previous case], nor is it connected with the word "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*). Therefore, there is a relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgi-bhāva*).

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers this alone to be logical on account of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). For in that case, the reason for abandoning the literal meaning of the scriptural statement was its syntactic unity with the word "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*); here, however, since that is absent, the literal meaning of the scripture itself must be accepted. Therefore, it is appropriate that either the *sāmidhenī* verses are subordinate to the *havirdhāna* cart, or the *havirdhāna* cart is subordinate to the *sāmidhenī* verses. There is no such thing as a contradiction consisting in the application of what has already been applied.

There is no contradiction whatsoever. For instance, the single genus *dadhi* (curd) is employed both in the ritual (*kratu*) and with respect to the person (*puruṣa*). Indeed, that which is not—(1) P.
r916]—[is not so employed].

"It is said that what is perceived as such is contradictory; therefore he says: 'Indeed, that which is contrary to cognition is called contradictory; on the other hand, that alone is non-contradictory which is known exactly as it is. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*) considers that, because both [terms] have different referents, a relationship characterized by spatial location (*deśalakṣaṇa*) alone is logical. This is the intention: although there is no contradiction in the thing itself, nevertheless, that which [is perceived] as being connected to something else..."

It is simply not possible to understand [the connection] in the way one understands "this belongs to Devadatta" or "this belongs to Yajñadatta. Here, in the term *havirdhānam*, a connection with the oblation (*havis*) is perceived; likewise, in the term *samidhenīḥ*, a connection with kindling (*samindhana*) is perceived. Therefore, since a syntactic connection with the literal meaning of the Vedic word (*śrautārtha*) is untenable, the connection is determined through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of location. Thus, regarding the term *havirdhānam*...

Thus, the designation "Sāmidhenīs" is not contradicted; for otherwise, if the literal sense of the Vedic text were accepted, it would follow that either the Havirdhāna shed is the Sāmidhenīs, or the Sāmidhenīs are the Havirdhāna shed.

Just as [the statement] "This is Havirdhāna's" or "This is Devadatta's" or "This is Yajñadatta's" would be incoherent, so too might this [present case] be; therefore, here also, as before, it is logical that it is merely a definition of place (*deśalakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, as in the *Āgneyī* section, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the relationship between the general and the particular.
The meaning of this is as follows: just as in the *Āgneyī* section, if non-contextual [verses] were to be grasped, there would be a general connection with them.

Furthermore, in the case of a connection with a specific [quality], there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); so it would be here as well. Here too, there would be a syntactical split: first a connection with the *havirdhāna* in general, and then again a connection with that specific *havirdhāna* in which they press the Soma. "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer. But how can there be a doubt here when hiring (*parikraya*) and other such acts are being heard?

The meaning of this is as follows: when both hiring (*varaṇa*) and purchasing (*parikraya*) are heard in the scripture, since these two serve a visible purpose and thus function as causes for the performance of the ritual, they apply to those who have been purchased (*parikrīta*).

The ritual acts must be performed by those very [persons] [indicated by the titles]. Likewise, in the statement "the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the directions and recites the responses," another person is explicitly heard.

Furthermore, there exist designations such as "the office of the Adhvaryu" (ādhvaryava) and so forth; how, then, can there be doubt in this matter? [This is because] there is no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
He provides the justification—the intention is this: here, the fruit of the action is heard to accrue to the agent. This is the entitlement (adhikāra)—

By the force of the injunction, the agency of the qualified person (adhikārin) is heard here. In that case, if another were to perform the ritual acts, his very agency would be subverted. Therefore, to avoid that contradiction—and because it does not contradict the agency understood through the force of the qualification—one considers the hiring (parikraya) to be figurative. Thus, this is not a literal hiring; it will be "like hiring," or it will be a hiring for an invisible (transcendental) purpose. As he says:

Alternatively, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers [the injunction] to have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Furthermore, words such as "Maitrāvaruṇa" and so forth must somehow be explained as referring to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). How then are the designations (*samākhyā*) such as "pertaining to the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*) possible, given that there is no direct connection between the actions and the Adhvaryu? They will be justified through their connection with the texts; for the texts themselves are "pertaining to the Adhvaryu," and the action prescribed therein is "pertaining to the Adhvaryu."

"It shall be so. Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that it is only logical for the agent to perform the action himself. However, the proponent of non-restriction (aniyamavādī) maintains that only the relinquishment of the substance must be performed by oneself, because its defining characteristic is the renunciation of ownership; as for the remainder, another may perform it or one may do it oneself.
He who asserts non-restriction believes that even when performed by those hired for the purpose, it is considered done by that very person [who engaged them]. Why? Because it is done.

For he is their instigator (*prayoktṛ*), and there is a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) regarding the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the instigator; thus, by the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule "the instigator is the cause," his agency is established through that traditional teaching. Furthermore, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) implies the accomplishment based on the injunction (*niyoga*), but it does not directly constitute agency itself; therefore, there is no contradiction with that [agency]. However, the primary act (*utsarga*), characterized by the relinquishing of one's own property, must be performed by the sacrificer himself.

Thus, since agency is established, it is not possible to assume that the act of hiring is secondary or that it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Furthermore, designations such as "the office of the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*) and so forth will apply to the rituals in their primary sense, rather than being based on the texts. But surely—

Regarding the point that designations such as *adhvaryava* refer to the texts and not to the ritual actions themselves, he says: "For students are not denoted by the word *adhvaryu* at the time of study. If students were denoted by the word *adhvaryu*, then the designation would apply to the text because of that connection. But this is not the case. Since that designation occurs only at the time of the ritual action, the words *adhvaryu* and so forth denote only those who perform the ritual actions."

Because of that connection, the designation "agent" applies primarily only to the action. But how, then, is it considered non-obligatory? Because the acts of hiring and so forth are heard of as being mandatory. And it is logical that agency can be established even by means of relinquishing [one's own performance], such that the auxiliary role must always be performed by others. This is the intended meaning: when one lacks the inclination to perform it oneself, then there is hiring; and when there is hiring, then it is indeed by others.
He thinks thus: the meaning of this is that, upon considering the visible purpose, if there is a dependence on another person, then hiring and so forth apply only in the case of incapacity;

however, one who is capable must perform it himself. But the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*) thinks: because hiring is enjoined as something permanent (*nityavat*), it cannot be assumed that one may hire when one is personally unable; therefore, [hiring] is [required] always.

The remaining duties must be performed by those who have been hired. [Objection: But surely this will happen by virtue of their capacity; when one is unable, it will happen by virtue of capacity, as is seen in the world. [Response: He refutes this: for capacity does not prevail when there is a direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) as an opponent. And here, the scripture enjoins hiring as an obligatory rule. As for the statement "when," that is because it is not heard [in the text]. But in the world, however—

Since its purpose is perceptible, it is logical that it should be performed according to the actual facts. However, since the *niyoga* (the ritual injunction) here is of an imperceptible nature and must be accomplished by means of a hired person, the hiring of such a person must invariably be undertaken.

In that context, the number of agents is determined by implication. Such being the case, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that, since the rule of hiring agents is set aside in other instances, there is no restriction on the number of others [to be hired]. For men are employed for the sake of the task; therefore, as many as are required for the task should be employed. But [one might object]: if only a few are employed, how will the designation (samākhyā) be consistent?

And how is the distinction of the enclosure (*varaṇabheda*) established? [The opponent says: "Because it is enclosed. To this, he replies: Because both designation (*samākhyā*) and enclosure are possible even for a single entity. Just as in the case of the maxim regarding the tree and the sapling, the application of designations is possible for one and the same thing. Likewise, the distinction of enclosures is established because that very same entity serves the purpose of various respective actions. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*), considering the distinction based on designation at the stage of origin (*utpatti*), [states] in the Śruti:

To that extent, designations such as "Adhvaryava" and so forth are perceived. In that regard, because of the difference between those [designations], a difference among the things designated (saṃjñin) also appears.

However, they are not one and the same, for the designations are understood from the injunctions (codanā). Indeed, these designations are understood solely from the injunctions, not from common worldly usage. If they were understood from worldly usage, then non-difference or difference would follow accordingly.

Regarding that which is to be understood through injunction (*codanā*), there is a distinction between the designations (*saṃjñā*) according to the injunction; thus, as long as there is an injunction, so many are the persons. He stated that "as many as are the originative injunctions (*utpatti-codanā*), so many are the persons. This was likewise stated regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices.

In this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*), the formulation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: because one observes a plurality of designations even for a single [entity], there is no distinction among the designated things (*saṃjñin*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows. The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that these designations for persons are to be understood through injunctions (*codanā*). In that regard, because of the difference in words, it is logical that each has a distinct meaning; it is not possible for a single word-meaning to be justified by having multiple words [for it]. But where there is perception through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), what can be done?

and because they are designated by those [terms], there are the *camasādhvaryu*s. Are the *camasādhvaryu*s to be counted within the number of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)?
The doubt has been restated in order to raise the objection: "Are they to be delimited by a different number? He states the objection:

"But surely, because of the designation 'the Camasādhvaryus of the Hotṛs,' there must be Camasādhvaryus distinct from [the others]. Consequently, since there would be no prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the doubt itself does not exist. That designation [of one priest by another] is made in relation to other priests; thus, the *camasādhvaryus* are not in addition to the number of *ṛtviks*.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) considers them distinct, on the grounds that there is no mutual relationship among those [priests] denoted by the genitive case. The meaning is this:
all the *ṛtviks* are indeed indicated by the genitive, as in the term "of the *hotrakās*."
In such sentences as "of those who act with moderation" (*madhyataḥ kāriṇām*) and so forth,
there is no mutual understanding of a relationship between two words ending in the genitive case, as in the case of "Devadatta’s brother is Yajñadatta’s brother."
A third [class] is understood from those two, but there is no mutual relationship between them; thus, the *camasādhvaryus* are distinct from the *ṛtviks*.

Furthermore, because there is a difference in designation (*saṃjñābheda*) at the time of their origin, if there were no difference in designation at the time of origin, then this would be a worldly title and would function according to common usage; consequently, there would be no distinction [between the classes]. Since there is a difference in designation at the time of origin, a difference in function is appropriate. Therefore, they are distinct.
"O Camasādhvaryus! Because the plural number is heard in the original injunction, this is now doubted: are they indefinite in number, or must there be many?

The plural number is not restricted because it is established by the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Even when there is only one, it is not restricted because it is established by the meaning of the nominal stem. Now, how can there be a plural form in the statement "one should choose the *camasādhvaryus*"? To this he replies: because the plural number is appropriate even under the alternative of non-restriction.

He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): No, because the plural number is heard as being permanent (*nityavat*), it is impossible for it to be merely optional. To the objection that—since the *camasādhvaryus* are the objects of reference (*uddeśya*)—the number, like that of the *grahas*, is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*)—he replies: "And because the plural number is intended to be significant in the original injunction (*utpatti*). The meaning of this is as follows: although the *camasādhvaryus* are indeed the objects of reference in this sentence, nevertheless, their...

Since the number is not understood, there is an expectation for a number, namely, "how many are to be produced? Because this is expected, the number is intended to be expressed. In the case of the *graha* (cup), however, because the number is already known, there is no expectation at all; therefore, the non-intentionality [of expressing it] is logical. Thus he says: "A nominal stem (*prātipadika*) whose meaning is not yet established does not require a verbal suffix (*vacana*), nor a suffix that produces [the meaning]; therefore, there are many."

It is precisely this that is being established here: that even when it is the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), the number residing in the thing to be produced (*utpādya*) is intended to be significant.

That the number is "ten" is due to the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*). Once plurality is established, there arises a doubt: is there no restriction, or is there some specific number denoted by the plural that is fixed, or is it specifically the number three? By this, he states the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*).

When it is argued that—just as in the case of the *kapiñjala* birds—there is no fixed rule because the number is simply three, we reply: since ten *camasādhvaryu* priests are observed as established facts in the *daśapeya*, which is a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is a restrictive rule that the number must be ten; this is also because of the [required] tenfold nature of the patron (*svāmin*). And here, the position of no fixed rule...

This is merely a preliminary objection. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there should be exactly three, according to the principle of the *kapiñjala* (partridge) rule. But how can it be said that because ten are seen in the *daśapeya* sacrifice, there should be ten here?
To this, he says: even in other cases, a fixed number is capable of restricting the instruction, provided there is no contradiction.

If there were only three [deities] here, then a vision as if they were established would not be possible; however, in the case of ten, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the plural number, because even ten constitute a plurality. And thus it has been said: "there is a transgression of the cause. But is this not already covered by that very [previous argument]? No, because the number ten belongs to another context, and the opponent’s doubt concerns something additional.

And the *śamitṛ* (the slaughterer) is distinct because of the difference in designation. Just as the *camasādhvaryus* are distinguished from the *ṛtvij*s due to the difference in their titles, so too the *śamitṛ* is distinguished because of the difference in his designation. By this, the intermediate connection has been stated. He states the reasoning: "The difference in designation is also logically established; otherwise, it would be improper to assume that a single entity possesses multiple names."

He states the final conclusion: "There is no difference here," for it was stated that difference is based on origination (*utpatti*). And this [word] has no origination. The meaning of this is: difference was not stated merely because of a difference in words; rather, it is due to a difference in the injunction of origination (*utpatti-codanā*). For in an injunction of origination, there occurs a non-worldly (*alaukika*) designation. Otherwise, however, since there would be no other non-worldly object, [the word would refer to] those already under discussion.
It is determined that this word applies to that [object]. If its production does not exist, how then can there be a difference in designation?

The general rule is that a difference in designation is not possible without a difference in the object. The reply is: this is not a [proper] name; rather, it is an etymological designation. One who pacifies (*śamayati*) is a "pacifier" (*śamitṛ*). Therefore, whoever pacifies the animal will be one among those mentioned in the context. In this way, the technical designation (*samākhyā*) "Adhvaryava" will be justified. [Regarding] the *śāmitra*—

It is designated by the technical name *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu). If the *śamitṛ* (the slaughterer) were indeed the Adhvaryu himself, then this designation would be appropriate. Furthermore, there are the *upagās* (accompanying singers), as seen from the indicative mark (*liṅga*). By what distinction is this an extension (*atideśa*) of the present topic? For the word *upagā* is also etymological (*yaugika*), and it has no separate origin [as a distinct office]. This is the distinction: "upagās" refers to those who perform the singing.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that they belong to the *hotraka* priests, just like the *camasādhvaryu* priests. The meaning of this is as follows: the *upagā*s (accompanying singers) are related to the chanters (*gātṛ*s), and yet the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*s) do not have a relationship with other officiating priests.
Therefore, just as the *camasādhvaryu*s are distinct from the *hotraka* priests and from the other officiating priests, so too are the *upagā*s; thus says the proponent of the prima facie view.

[The opponent] thinks: "Because no origination is heard," thus the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is extended [to this case]. Since no origination is heard and there is no other entity [present], the word *upagā* is etymological (*yaugika*) with respect to those very [singers]. Furthermore, the connection with the singers is based on their performing the augmentation of the singing, not on their performing the work of a master. The indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been stated.

r924] vikrayī tv anyaḥ | Is the Soma-seller, moreover, indeed one of those very officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), or is he someone else? Regarding these officiating priests—

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that [the selling] is one of these [other duties]. He states the objection: "But surely the selling is not enjoined, whereas those who are enjoined—the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—are taken as the agents. The meaning of this is as follows: that which is enjoined is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice;

and that which is a constituent part must be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Since persons are appointed only to perform that [which is enjoined], how could the selling be the duty of the officiating priests?

He refutes this: the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) belongs to one who considers that selling is the remainder of the acquisition through purchase. Purchase, indeed, has been enjoined, and it is not accomplished without selling. Since no one engages in the selling of Soma of their own accord—because the selling of Soma is prohibited—there is no prohibition against selling when it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*). Thus, as a subordinate part of the acquisition through purchase, selling is also an auxiliary (*aṅga*).

Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this must be performed by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) alone, just like the other subsidiary parts of the ritual. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) does not consider it a subsidiary part, because the purchase of the Soma from the seller is established simply through greed, much like the acquisition of wealth. Even though there is a prohibition, some individuals—having transgressed that prohibition out of greed—are naturally inclined toward the sale of Soma; it is with reference to such persons that the injunction for performance (*prayogavidhi*) does not [apply] to the sale of Soma.
It does not imply [the same] as the acquisition of wealth. Furthermore, since the sale of all goods is permitted for Śūdras and others, there is no transgression of prohibitions;
thus, they are indeed non-officiating priests (*anārtvij*). Therefore, it is established that the Soma-seller is someone other [than the officiating priests].
[This applies] to all because of their functional role (*karmakārya*). But surely, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) here is not tenable? How is it not tenable? The objector [asks]:

r925] He says: Even in the case of origination, there would result only a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*) if the very act of origination were the cause for the application of the word "officiant" (*ṛtvij*).

Nevertheless, it follows that there must be an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) that "there are seventeen priests. Why? Because the *camasādhvaryus* (cup-priests) are also heard of in the originative injunctions. If their application of the term "priest" (*ṛtvij*) were based on those originative injunctions, the number seventeen would be untenable; thus, an exclusive specification must be resorted to. Now, if an exclusive specification is indeed desired, then the refutation of the view that the designation [of "priest"] is based on performing sacrifices at the seasonal rites (*ṛtu-yajana*) becomes purposeless.

It might be argued that even if the designation "officiant" (*ṛtvij*) were based on the performance of seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtuyajana*), this would still result in a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*), namely, "there are seventeen officiants.

To this, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) connects [the following]: it is said here that if the [seasonal sacrifice] is accepted as the basis for the origin [of the term], such a restrictive enumeration does not follow; because the word *ṛtvij* is identical in its application to each individual [priest] like the words *udgātṛ* and so forth, there is nothing here to be excluded.

Something exists. The meaning of this is as follows: there is a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*) in a case where something is to be excluded; for when the origin of a word is accepted as being based on its literal etymology—just as words such as *udgātṛ* (chanter) each have a unique, non-worldly referent—so too this word *ṛtvij* (priest) has a denotative relationship that is to be understood solely through the injunction regarding sixteen [specific individuals]. Therefore, it applies only to those for whom it is employed by the Veda.

It is determined that [the term] "officiant" (*ṛtvij*) applies to these [specific persons] and not to others; thus, there is no exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*). However, regarding the word "officiant" when its application is based on the occasion of performing a sacrifice (*ṛtuyajana*), there is a denial of its primary meaning, because everyone performs sacrifices during their season. To the question, "Let it be so; what is the harm?", he says: "And this [denial] cannot be accomplished even by a hundred statements. This is because, once the occasion exists, the application of the word is unavoidable. Precisely because [the application] arises from an originative occasion (*utpattinimitta*), [it cannot be set aside].
Thus, this is a worldly designation. For this very reason, the subsequent discussion becomes logical.

When the meaning of the word *ṛtvij* is determined through Vedic usage, it is concluded that the word denotes [the officiant] only where it is actually employed; by this, the status of being an *ṛtvij* is established for exactly sixteen persons. Otherwise, if the basis were the performance of the sacrifice (*ṛtuyajana*), everyone would be denotable by the word *ṛtvij*.

The rule, however, concerns the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). The doubt arises as to which [priests] they are. Having begun with the statement, "He gives the sacrificial fee to the officiating priests," the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that those who are mentioned as the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) in the subsequent sentences—which are intent on prescribing specific details regarding the fees—are the ones intended.

Likewise, it has been shown that "those who are the sacrificers (yajamāna) are the officiating priests (ṛtvij). The master is the seventeenth. It is heard in scripture: "There are seventeen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

In this regard, there arises a doubt: are there seventeen including the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), or are there seventeen others distinct from the sacrificer? And by speaking thus, the term *gṛhapati* [is explained].

It has been explained in the Bhāṣya that [the term] refers to those other than the sacrificer. What is the prima facie view? There are seventeen others than the sacrificer, because this is a number of ritual performers (*karmakara*). The word has been etymologically derived; [it follows that] a master does not perform the work of a servant. Thus, it is logical that [the master] is indeed distinct [from the others]. For if the connection with a single property were not accepted...

[The opponent] raises an objection regarding the number [of priests]. [The author] refutes it: "By whom was it said that [the sacrificer] is not employed as a common laborer (*karmakara*)? If so, how is it that the master is the seventeenth? The answer is: the sacrificer is not the seventeenth by virtue of being the master (*svāmin*); rather, he is so by virtue of being the agent (*kartṛ*) alone. The phrase "let him choose" (vṛṇīta) establishes this number by accepting the production of the choosing itself; however, the sacrificer (yajamāna) is not produced [by it]. The meaning of this is as follows:

this number exists because of its connection with the single property characterized by being produced by the sacrificer. And there is indeed another [element] that is to be produced by the sacrificer.
The seventeenth is named the *sadasya*. For indeed, they prescribe his selection [with the words]: "He chooses the *sadasya*.
And here too, the word *ṛtvij* is purely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), because even when there is another person, the *sadasya*, the word *ṛtvij* [is applied to him].

Because of the application [of the number]. For this very reason, the author of the commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) having set aside his doubt, the author of the treatise (Nibandhanakāra) has presented the doubt differently. Furthermore, the mention of the "Sadasya" (the assistant priest) in the Bhāṣya is merely illustrative. What is meant is this: does this number refer to anyone other than the sacrificer, or does it refer to the sacrificer himself? He resolves the objection: It is said—[it refers] to the sixteen alone.

[Their] production is by means of selection (*varaṇa*). But surely, since it is said, "he selects the *sadasya*," the *sadasya* will be the seventeenth, provided that this word *sadasya* applies to the Brahman priest. The meaning of this is as follows: we shall explain that the acquisition of persons is by means of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). [This refers to] the selection (*varaṇa*).

This [verse] is supportive of that [conclusion]. Therefore, although the selection (*varaṇa*) of a *sadasya* is heard of in the scripture, nevertheless, because of the mention of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), it is not possible for there to be some other person named *sadasya*. And in that context, the word *sadasya* (member of the assembly) applies by way of its etymological function (*yogika-vṛtti*), for it is "one who exists in the assembly" (*sadas-bhava*). Therefore, seventeen [such persons] are accepted. Now, why is one *camasādhvaryu* (cup-officiant) not accepted? Is the number seventeen intended to refer to persons produced [by creation]? He answers: It has been stated that they are not to be chosen by the sacrificer; therefore, their production [is established].
The meaning is that their form is not uniform. Therefore, because of the commonality or equality with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who perform the ritual actions,

and because the sacrificer himself performs the obligatory rites, it is the sacrificer alone who constitutes the seventeenth, and not the *camasādhvaryu*, since the latter pertains to cases of incapacity.

do the priests perform as much of the sacrificer's work as is possible for a person to do, or only that which is expressly stated? "That very [result] has been obtained. And [the statement], "The fires, because they have their own time,"—what is this? Why then is this 'being for all purposes' stated again? This is the meaning: (1) P. 1102.

If it is argued that the fires are for all purposes by virtue of being things yet to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*), that is incorrect, because they have already been established as such. If, on the other hand, it is argued that they are for all purposes by virtue of not being excluded from any purpose, that is also not the case, because there is no overturning of the established principle. And it is said: "The fires are for all purposes because they belong to their own time. This has been understood.

The phrase "metad" (this) indicates that the very same point already established is being shown. Therefore, [the objection] "this is improper" is raised. He provides the resolution: "This very quality of having all things as its object is here further established because it belongs to its own time. The meaning of this is as follows: what is being said is that this constitutes a different section (adhikaraṇa) by means of a distinct sūtra.

This is stated in order to refute and establish the view that [the fires] serve all purposes (*sarvārthatā*). In this regard, the following objection was previously raised: since the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is heard to belong to one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*), the fires are for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*); therefore, the production of those fires already employed [in rituals] occurs through the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), and thus the *ādhāna* is said to serve all purposes.
To this, it is replied: But this very point—that the entitlement belongs to the *āhitāgni*—is itself improper, just as one who is entitled produces the *puroḍāśa* cake and so forth.

"In the same way, [the view] that 'one should maintain the fires' is indeed the correct one. To this, the following resolution is offered: because the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) has its own specific time, and since it is impossible to perform it at the very end [of life], the qualification for rites belongs only to one who has already established the fires (*āhitāgni*). Here, an objection is raised: "But surely, because the establishment has its own time, it is said that all duties pertaining to the fire are to be performed with those fires—just as all duties pertaining to a person are to be performed by means of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The meaning of this is as follows: one—

Because they are mentioned in the Sūtra, such a statement regarding the universal purpose (*sarvārthatā*) of both the fires and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is made. Furthermore, the universal purpose of the priests is stated on the basis of their performing the work for all persons. Therefore, since the fires also have their own specific times, it is stated that they perform the entire range of functions pertaining to the fires.
The proponent of a partial view (*ekadeśin*) asks: "What follows from that? The objector replies: "This is not tenable; this has already been established."

"And the fires [are for all rites] because they have their own specific time. Why? Because it is not the case that, merely by virtue of having their own specific time, the fact that the fires serve the purpose of every fire-rite is established; for in that regard, having their own specific time is not the reason. What then? The principle stated is that by virtue of having their own specific time, it is established that the fires serve the purpose of all rites. For there is no separate production of the fires for each individual rite; rather, the fires are [produced] by the installation (ādhāna) at its own specific time.
It is shown that they are acquired like iron and gold, and not through repeated action. He provides the resolution: if it is established by virtue of its own time...
The efficacy for all ritual actions (*sarvakarmārthatā*) is established. If that is so, then what you have stated is precisely our own intended position. Why?
Because whatever is the reason (*hetu*) is itself the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñātārtha*). Therefore, the efficacy for all ritual actions is asserted, since the reason conforms to it.
Consequently, these constitute two sūtras; and because there are two sūtras, [it serves as the basis] for the preceding sūtra.
The rebuttal is stated as follows: however, this universal applicability (*sarvārthatva*) remains established even now. Now he states the rebuttal:

for in this case, the scriptural statements are not assumed to be mere restatements of what is already established (*nityānuvāda*). If indeed these statements were assumed to be restatements, then the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) would have to serve the purpose of every person's ritual activity; but this is not the case, as [the application] belongs to other persons as well in that instance.
Because it has already been established [that the priests perform their duties]. Therefore, the duty of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) consists precisely in what is stated [in the texts].

Its specification is made through direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and traditional designation (*samākhyāna*). Now this is being considered: must that which is designated by a particular name be performed by that person alone, or may some of it also be performed by another? Thus is shown the doubt expressed in the *Bhāṣya*.

This, first of all, is the general rule: that whatever is designated by a certain name must be performed by that [person]. It is said in response: in that case, it is because of a specific scriptural statement (vacana).

And because of the designation of the specific, there is an exception [to the general rule]. How, then, is there a designation of the general? The answer is: it is like the term "Brāhmaṇa village," so there is no fault. Furthermore, the designation of the general is weak because it can be accounted for otherwise; whereas the designation of the specific is stronger because it cannot be accounted for otherwise. However, since a direct statement (vacana) leads to an understanding of application more swiftly, the conclusion is that the direct statement is stronger.
The *darśana* (textual indication) has been stated.
The recitation of the *praiṣas* (directions) belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa; for it is said, "The Maitrāvaruṇa gives directions and recites after.
Does this refer to the mere giving of directions?

Having raised the doubt as to whether all that is connected with the *anuvacana* (recitation), as well as that which is unconnected, and likewise all that is merely *anuvacana*, whether connected or unconnected with the *praiṣa* (direction), must be performed by the Maitrāvaruṇa—or whether only that which is connected [with the *praiṣa*]—the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Because that which is connected exists, the unconnected is not accepted. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not stated here because it is obvious; for the completion of the sentence occurs at each specific reference (*pratyuddeśa*), and thus it applies to the *praiṣa* alone.

The application (*viniyoga*) of the Maitrāvaruṇa is thus merely the recitation (*anuvacana*). However, the meaning of the concluding section (*rāddhānta-grantha*) is as follows: it is well known to all people that when there is a relationship between two things that are associated and those that are not, the suffix [denoting agency] applies to the one that is associated. Now, the recitation is accompanied by the command (*praiṣa*), and the command is accompanied by the recitation; therefore, this word *preṣyati* (he commands) refers to the command precisely as it is accompanied by the recitation.

It occurs thus: the word *anuvāha* denotes an *anuvacana* (recitation) that is indeed accompanied by a *praiṣa* (directive). And both of these [the recitation and the directive] exist in such a manner.

Furthermore, the word *ca* (and) is justified in this way as indicating a state of conjunction (*samuccaya*), because we observe the application (*viniyoga*) of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest only when the two are conjoined. This observation has already been stated.
Regarding the cup-bearers (*camasādhvaryu*), there arises the doubt: do the cup-bearers offer with the cups, or does the *adhvaryu* alone offer?

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that the designation [“camasādhvaryu”] would otherwise be inexplicable. If the *camasādhvaryus* offer with the *camasa* cups, how could they obtain the designation “camasādhvaryus”? They are called *camasādhvaryus* because they are *adhvaryus* in relation to the *camasa*.

Furthermore, it is understood that the office of the *adhvaryu* elsewhere consists in performing the oblation; thus, the prima facie view is that those persons possess a similarity to him. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows:

Since the word *adhvaryu* functions as a term denoting its origin (*utpatti-nimitta*), it is not logical for it to denote multiple referents; thus, those who act like the *adhvaryu* with respect to the cups (*camasa*) are called *camasādhvaryus*. Therefore, [the rule] "the *adhvaryu* offers the oblation" applies. The meaning of this is as follows: the word *adhvaryu* is not polysemous; rather, it denotes a specific officiant (*ṛtvij*), while its application to other persons is figurative (*gauṇa*). In that regard, if...

If there were no oblation by the Adhvaryu in the *camasa*, how then could there be the status of being "like the Adhvaryu" (*adhvaryuvat*) in the *camasa*? Therefore, the oblation by the Adhvaryu in the *camasa* must necessarily be admitted; thus, he himself offers it. How then is there the status of being "like the Adhvaryu"?

[It is because] such similarity to him is untenable without the performance of the action. The answer is: when that primary Adhvaryu is occupied elsewhere, [the one in the *camasa*] is the secondary (substitute) Adhvaryu.
Because its performance is observed; "observation" has already been mentioned.

Because of the instruction in the Veda. The *Śyena* and *Vājapeya* are the examples. There arises a doubt: is the *Śyena*, being designated by the name "Udgātṛ," to be performed by the Udgātṛ together with all its subsidiaries because of that designation, while the *Vājapeya* is to be performed by the Adhvaryu? Or is it to be performed by all sixteen priests as well?

r933] Since it is established that [the offering] is performed by the Udgātṛ and the Adhvaryu based on their specific designations, it follows from the observation of the benefit that it may also be performed by all sixteen priests.

We say this. The meaning is as follows: Are the constituent elements (*padārtha*) that were performed by a certain agent in the archetype (*prakṛti*) to be performed by that very same agent in the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well? For those constituent elements are obtained there [in the ectype] from the archetype. Now, one might object that a specific name (*samākhyā*) pertaining to the ectype postulates a different agent; to this he says: "Between that which is already established (*klṛpta*) and that which is to be postulated (*kalpya*), the established is stronger"—this is the reason stated. From this, the following is meant: in the archetype, a person is already established...

The connection must be postulated for the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). And it has been stated in various places that when a [connection] is already established, a further postulation does not find room for itself.
Thus, in the *Ṛjuvimalā-pañcikā*, [the discussion] of the third...
The Seventh Chapter [p.
934] Now, in the *Ṛjuvimalā*:

The eighth quarter (pāda) of the third chapter concerns the purchase [of services] as the duty of the master. While it might initially appear that this is the duty of the Adhvaryu priest based on its designation (*samākhyā*), the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that it is the duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), because that would contradict the scriptural injunction regarding entitlement (*adhikāra-śruti*). The meaning of this is as follows: in the section designated as "Adhvaryava," the purchase—

Since [the act of] purchasing is prescribed [in the text], it follows that it must be performed by the Adhvaryu priest alone. Nor should this objection be raised: "Why would one person hire other individuals to perform work for which they themselves are not the agent? For such a practice is observed in the world, driven by the desire for greater profit. This being the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because it would contradict the primary injunction regarding the entitlement (*adhikāra-śruti*) which establishes the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) as the performer in all instances.

By the sublation of the designation (*samākhyā*), the purchase (*parikraya*) belongs to the sacrificer alone. Ritual acts performed by persons other than the sacrificer—specifically those performed by persons purchased by the Adhvaryu priest—are neither performed by the sacrificer nor caused to be performed by him. [Objection: But surely, by resorting to the worldly practice of the Adhvaryu, these will be considered as performed by the sacrificer. [Reply: No, it is said in response. It is proper to describe the meaning of the scripture only by resorting to exactly what is heard therein; and there is no [scriptural basis for] purchase—

Immediately following this, it is heard in the case of the Adhvaryu: "Whatever sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed for the Adhvaryu, [the sacrificer] does not have the capacity to act as an employer toward the Adhvaryu for the purpose of hiring other persons with that same amount. Therefore, if the hiring were part of the Adhvaryu’s own duties, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding eligibility (*adhikāra*). On the other hand, the hiring of the priests may occur by virtue of a specific scriptural statement; in that case, it is untenable to assume a separate act of hiring.

The preparatory rites (*saṃskārāḥ*), however, depend on the capacity of the person; thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is that the eligibility for acts such as shaving is not contradicted by their technical designation (*samākhyayā*). By this, he states the distinction from the preceding section: whereas in the previous case there was a contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding eligibility for the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijatve*), [here there is none].

Likewise, in this case, the acts such as shaving (*vapanādi*) performed by the priests (*ṛtvij*) do not exist [for them], because they have been performed by the sacrificer himself. Therefore, acts such as shaving are designated as *ādhvaryava* (belonging to the Adhvaryu) by virtue of their technical name (*samākhyā*). This being the established position in this section (*adhikaraṇa*), regarding the point that [these acts] are purificatory rites for the sacrificer because of their connection with the fruit (*phalasaṃyogāt*), [the following applies].

(3-7-2) It has been stated that [the *adhvaryu*] is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the status of the qualified person (*adhikṛta*). However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*), considering it to be a refinement of the person (*puruṣa-saṃskāra*), maintains that persons are not hired for the purpose of being refined, but rather for the purpose of having [the ritual] performed. Therefore, he considers that the etymological designation (*samākhyā*) is set aside by the force of the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).
The meaning of this is as follows: if this were not a refinement of the person, then, like the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and other such acts, it would certainly belong to the *Adhvaryu* priest.

(Thus ends the consecration of the person. These consecrations of the person are like those in common worldly practice. In that regard, if they were consecrations of the Adhvaryu priest, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding eligibility (*adhikāra-śruti*), because it would be impossible for the sacrificer to be the agent in those rites. Indeed, the sacrificer’s agency in those rites occurs only through the medium of hiring (*parikraya*). However, hiring is not for the purpose of performing a consecration; for one takes up a substance that is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) for another action, but not a substance that is itself the principal (*śeṣin*).

Furthermore, the purchase [of the officiants] is for the purpose of securing the person; therefore, that person is intended to perform the ritual action, not to undergo a preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*). Since the purchase lacks the purpose of being a refinement for him, it is not possible—on the basis of the purchase—to establish the sacrificer’s status as the agent in acts such as shaving, by treating them as refinements of the officiant. Consequently, because this would contradict the scriptural injunction regarding eligibility (*adhikāraśruti*), the conventional designation (*samākhyā*) is set aside.

Furthermore, where the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is enjoined by the direct Vedic text itself, there the exclusion of the priests does not occur by the force of the injunction regarding entitlement (*adhikāra-śruti*), as [the author] will later explain regarding the fast (*upavāsa*). But how, then, can the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) be the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to those [refinements]? It is said: the purchase (*parikraya*) is for the purpose of the refinement, because the ritual act is to be performed by an officiating priest who has been refined by that [purchase]. In this regard, it is stated: here [the matter] is doubtful.

The distinction is that [the *saṃskāras*] belong to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
