Now, if it is asked: "Why is there not a common injunction (*samānavidhāna*) applicable to both the priest and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), so as to favor both and to conform to the force of the name (*samākhyā*), the qualification (*adhikāra*), and the direct statement (*śruti*)? The answer is: because an act performed upon the priests is neither performed by the sacrificer nor caused to be performed by him; therefore, it is not common to both.
(1) G. omits *vidhānam* [p. 936]:

"Why was it not performed, or why was it not caused to be performed? The answer is: precisely because of its commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) between the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

Precisely because it is common [to both]. Now, one might object: "As in the case of the eating of the *iḍā*, he performs it himself and causes it to be performed by others; just as the sacrificer performs the eating of the *iḍā* himself and causes the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to perform it, so too with the shaving and other rites. He refutes this: "No, because in that case there is no distinction regarding agency. But here, because there is no distinction regarding primacy, it is untenable. The meaning of this is: eating is a [consumption of] substance—

Because it is a *saṃskāra* (consecratory rite), in that case there is a connection between the sacrificer and the priests by virtue of their being agents; therefore, since the hiring (*parikraya*) is for the sake of that [rite], its being caused [to be performed] is appropriate. But here, since [the rite] is primary, a lack of distinction is suspected, and thus its being caused [to be performed] is untenable.

Therefore, it is established that [the eating of the *iḍā*] belongs to the sacrificer. Regarding the eating of the *iḍā*, he states another resolution: "Or rather, because of a scriptural statement, the sacrificer is the fifth."
"Or rather, because of the statement 'they consume the *iḍā*,' the refinement will be common [to all].
And austerity [is a means] because it results in the attainment of fruit, as in the world. What is being extended here? The answer is: the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is being extended.
But what is the doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here? This [doubt] exists because austerity consists of hardship; [it is] hardship—

It is well known in the world that austerity consists of bodily mortification. Nevertheless, what [is the purpose]? Furthermore, the hiring of laborers (*parikraya*) will have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), namely, the removal of fatigue; for when it serves the purpose of removing fatigue, the hiring of laborers has a visible purpose. Therefore, because the hiring of laborers is for the sake of austerity, [the result follows]—(1) P.
1115 (2) simply from the general designation—[as stated in the] *Mūla*.

[Page r937] "The sacrificer’s status as agent is established through the medium of hiring [the officiants]; thus, there is no contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding eligibility. To this, he states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*):

"Not so, because of the commonality of being a refinement (*saṃskāra*). This is the conclusion. Even though austerity (*tapas*) consists of suffering, it is nevertheless a refinement of the person (*puruṣa-saṃskāra*). And...

The hiring [of priests] is for the purpose of consecration; because it is identical to the consecrations such as shaving and so forth, that too belongs solely to the sacrificer. Furthermore, it has been stated that fasting also [belongs to the sacrificer] because of a direct scriptural statement: "The officiating priest fasts.
This is because of the explicit hearing of the word.

And because it is a subordinate element (*guṇatva*), according to the Veda; however, in the case of items such as golden garlands, since they are subordinate elements, the agency of the ritual act is not restricted by the name (*samākhyā*). Therefore, the subordinate element may belong to all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) through repetition for each primary act (*pratipradhānāvṛtti*). For this has been stated regarding the Vājapeya sacrifice: "Those ritual acts which are directly enjoined must be performed by the Adhvaryu alone," and these [golden garlands] are indeed directly enjoined.

Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) objection that the golden garland and other such items must be performed by that very Adhvaryu priest, this final conclusion (rāddhānta) is stated: this designation of the rites as "Adhvaryava" is based on the person being subordinate (guṇabhūta), not on the person being primary (pradhānabhūta). Therefore, it does not establish a restrictive rule regarding the primary status. Since the instruction for the golden garland and so forth is given with respect to the person as a subordinate factor, the subordinate elements repeat themselves for each primary element.

According to this principle, since the wearing of golden garlands and other such honors belongs to all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as their primary status, and their agency (*kartṛtva*) is likewise preceded by that primary status, the designation (*samākhyā*) cannot be restrictive, for that would entail the sublation of their primary status. However, where the connection of a person is established solely through their agency— as in the case of the *ukthya* and other sacrifices— the aforementioned restriction by designation applies.
(1) P. 1116 (2) G. Regarding the case of *upagava* and others [p.
r938], desire arises from the connection with an object. Now, when this connection with desire is heard, should it pertain to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)?

There arises a doubt: are the connections between the qualities and their results related to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)? What is appropriate? [They belong to] the officiating priest. Why? Because the connection between the quality and the result is dependent upon the ritual acts (*padārtha*) performed by the officiating priest; thus, even the conjunction with the desire for a specific result belongs to the officiating priests alone. The meaning of this is as follows: first of all, the measuring of the *sadas* is indeed the duty of the officiating priest, because he is the agent therein. In that context, it is said: "If he should desire, 'May Parjanya be rainy... [and so forth].

When it is stated, "One should measure the sacrificial hall (sadas) low," it is understood that this desire belongs to the very person who is the sacrificer (mātr̥). Therefore, in the case of desires for specific qualities (guṇakāmas), the entitlement belongs only to the officiating priests (r̥tvij). To this, it is replied: the sacrificer alone is entitled to the ritual action along with its constituent parts (sāṅga-karma).

Because it has been performed [by the priest]. Whatever predominance exists here, that—by way of general rule (utsarga)—belongs to the sacrificer alone who is authorized for the ritual together with its subsidiaries as the principal agent. Therefore, the fruit of the subsidiary [act] also belongs to the sacrificer. But [an objection is raised]: this [subsidiary act] is a matter pertaining to the officiating priests; the substratum, such as the measuring and so forth, has no connection with the sacrificer. How then can that which depends on it belong to the sacrificer? He answers:

We say: it is performed by him [the officiant], but it does not belong to him; it is not a service to the officiant, but rather to the sacrificer alone. Therefore, the officiant—who is connected to that [act] as a subordinate factor—does not possess primacy; rather, primacy belongs only to the sacrificer, who is connected to it as the principal factor. Thus it is said: "That action, even though it rests upon him..."

The phrase "of that very person" indicates that the sacrificer alone is entitled [to perform the rite]; in this way, the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) becomes justified. Regarding the *jyotiṣṭoma*—(1) P. 1117 [p.

"One should sacrifice. Otherwise, if the fruit were produced by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would be justified with reference to the intention of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), whereas it would be unjustified with reference to the intention of the officiating priest. For even though this is a fruit of a subsidiary (*guṇa*), it nonetheless arises from the primary act itself. Therefore, the statement "because of the prior accomplishment of the *apūrva*" is well-said. However, where there is an entitlement for the officiating priest due to a specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*), even in that case, although the ritual element depends on something belonging to another [the sacrificer], [the fruit accrues to the priest].
It is postulated that a result accrues to one who is engaged in a subordinate act (*guṇa*), for there is no excessive burden for a scriptural injunction.

Mantras that do not perform an action are likewise [to be understood]. Now, the benedictory mantras (*āśīrmantra*) serve as the example. Are they *yājamāna*, to be performed by the sacrificer? And thus: "O Agni, giver of life, grant me life."

Thus, it must be considered whether the fruit is prayed for by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) or by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Since the priests are the ones employed, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the fruit belongs to the priests alone, because of the designation (*samākhyā*) "pertaining to the priests" (*ārtvijya*). To this, it is replied: "By the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, they belong to the sacrificer," because these [priests] are those who pray for the fruit; and the fruit belongs to the sacrificer.

One must remain seated. For it has been stated that indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than name (*samākhyā*). Furthermore, the observation of the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) by one who is away on a journey is an indicative mark. It is shown in the Bhāṣya that "one who is away on a journey does not become a priest (*ṛtvij*); rather, it is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) who becomes one while away. Now, an objection is raised: "But [indicative marks] such as 'of me, the sacrificer' are appropriate. The meaning of this is that the word "sacrificer" itself will be supplied [as the subject].

Let the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) be the performer. By this, the meaning becomes: "Grant long life to my sacrificer. Therefore, even that which concerns the arrangements for one who has gone abroad [is included].

The justification for both the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the name (*samākhyā*) is as follows. He refutes this: "This very thing is the fault, namely, what is called *adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis). Therefore, it is logically consistent that "mine" refers to the speaker alone in the case where the mantra is employed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Regarding those mantras recited in both [sections], some mantras are recorded in both the *Yājamāna-kāṇḍa* and the *Ādhvaryava-kāṇḍa*.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: are these [mantras] to be performed by both [the Adhvaryu and the Yajamāna], or by the Adhvaryu alone? How, then, does it appear to the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) that because they are recorded in two places—namely, being recorded in two sections (*kāṇḍa*) and being designated for both the Adhvaryu and the Yajamāna—they must be recited by one or the other? He provides the resolution: "Because the mantras have a single function," meaning they perform the single function of illuminating a single purpose.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that there is a single employment—that is, employment by the Adhvaryu alone—on the grounds that since the Adhvaryu is the sole performer of the ritual action, the mantras must be employed by him alone for the purpose of recollection. The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*), however, holds that because one person, the Adhvaryu, performs the ritual acts while another, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), supervises them, both recensions of the texts are meaningful; therefore, they should be employed by both.
He thinks thus: it will be supported by both designations.
And when [the person] is known, there is no injunction for one who is ignorant; for it is said, "He makes the sacrificer recite the *klṛpti* formulas."

Thus it is heard: "Should only one who knows [the ritual] be made to recite, or even one who does not know? This doubt, stated in the Bhāṣya, is restated here in order to be refuted. He raises the objection: "But how can there be a suspicion regarding one who does not know, when the qualification belongs only to one who knows? For if..."

If there were eligibility for the ignorant person, then there would be the act of making him recite. But he has no eligibility. [The author] answers: precisely because of the word "makes recite" (vācayati). For in the case of one who is already learned, the purpose of the act of making recite cannot be a visible one; thus, when the eligible person is himself learned and speaks [the text], "making recite" serves an invisible (transcendental) purpose. In the case of the ignorant person, it serves a visible purpose. Therefore, [there is eligibility] for the ignorant person.

[The opponent] says: But surely, if the purpose is seen [as practical] for one who is ignorant, then the recitation (*vācana*) should belong to the ignorant alone. The respondent says: Let it be so; what is the fault? The objector says: It follows that there is a loss of qualification (*adhikāra-hāni*) for the learned person. According to that view, because the recitation is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*), the injunction regarding performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), which requires the inclusion of all auxiliaries, applies only to him for whom such a [complete set of auxiliaries] is possible; therefore, only he has the qualification.

The respondent says: We do not deny the eligibility [of the ignorant]; even for the ignorant, there is eligibility in the stage of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), with the understanding that "this is the fruit" and "this is the locus. The meaning of this is: there is eligibility for both parties, and in the case of the ignorant, the recitation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) because its purpose is perceptible. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): This [recitation] is not capable of negating the eligibility of the ignorant, nor is it capable of establishing it through implication.

[This refers to] the word *vacana*. Why? Because the verbal root *brū* expresses "he causes [another] to speak," meaning "he speaks"; it does not denote the activity of one who is not speaking. The causative suffix (*ṇic*) arises only when there is the state of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*) with respect to one who is already engaged in the action expressed by the base verb (*prakṛtyartha*), and not otherwise. And for one who knows... (1) P. 1121.

The application [of the rule] pertains to the primary meaning and not to one who is ignorant. The visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) of what has been stated is accomplished even by its mere utterance. Therefore, since this recitation also has the learned person as its subject, there is no entitlement for one who is ignorant. Thus, it is established that the recitation is according to one's entitlement.

The meaning is that the recitation belongs to that very learned person who possesses the qualification [for the sacrifice], because of the designation (*samākhyāna*) in the *Yājamāna* section. Here, the dual compounds (*dvandva*) serve as the examples. The doubt is: "Are these to be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), or by the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*)? How does the doubt arise? Because in one place the ritual acts (*padārtha*) are prescribed in the *Adhvaryava* section, while in another...

Regarding the *yājamāna* (the section pertaining to the sacrificer), because of the requirement for proximity (*samabhyāśīkaraṇa*), and since this proximity is accomplished through the performance of ritual acts (*padārtha*), there arises the question: should proximity also be performed wherever the ritual acts are located, or should the ritual acts also be performed wherever proximity is required? In that regard, by virtue of a specific designation (*viśeṣa-samākhyā*), these acts belong to the sacrificer; whereas, although they would generally fall under the *ādhvaryava* (the section pertaining to the Adhvaryu priest), they are assigned to the specific [category] by the specific designation.

By the designation *yājamāna* (pertaining to the sacrificer), the *yājamāna* duals [of actions] prevail over the designation *adhvaryu* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu priest). Now, let it be granted that the act of bringing things close together (*samabhyāśīkaraṇa*) belongs to the sacrificer; but how is it so with respect to the constituent acts (*padārtha*)? To this he says: because the proximity (*samabhyāśa*) is preceded by the constituent acts. Since the proximity of the constituent acts to be performed is accomplished only through the performance of those constituent acts, the constituent acts themselves must also belong to the sacrificer. To this, it is replied:
To begin with, since the ritual items (*padārtha*) are prescribed specifically for the Adhvaryu, and because no contradiction has yet arisen, they must be performed by the Adhvaryu alone.

For ritual acts (*padārtha*) are those that exist prior [to the sacrifice]. To begin with, these belong exclusively to the Adhvaryu as their performer. Since it is not possible for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) to maintain proximity to a ritual act while it is being performed, that [act] also belongs to the Adhvaryu alone. The application of specific designations (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*) has already been shown;
this is because of the instruction by the sacrificer, "Do this and that," and because of the employment of certain consecratory formulas (*anumantraṇa*).

In case of conflict, the instrumental [act] prevails. When there is an instruction regarding a duty belonging to another officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a doubt arises as to whether, in the event of a contradiction, he should perform his own specific task or that which is extended by analogy (*atideśa*). It is established that it is the extended duty, because of its direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhāna*). Since this is clear, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not recorded. There is a sublation of the extended duty by that which is directly enjoined and performs the same function; and here, there is not one...

There is no contradiction in the sense that "there is a task to be performed. At most, there may be an inability to perform both due to conflict; in that case, one will be performed. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows:

even in the absence of a single common purpose, a conflict nonetheless exists. In that situation, that which is directly enjoined (*pratyakṣavihita*) possesses greater force because it has no other recourse, whereas the other is meaningful only in its original context (*prakṛtau*).

Regarding the *praiṣas* (directions), because they pertain to another's authority: when there arises a doubt as to whether both the direction and the object of the direction are to be performed by one person or by two, [the conclusion is that they are performed by two].

How is the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) formulated? Regarding the point that [the injunction] is impossible, he says: "The prima facie position is that [it is enjoined] by one person due to a confusion regarding the time [for performance].

In the command "O Agnīdh, spread the fires," the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) will signify that the time has arrived. Thus, the performer speaks in this way: "O Agnīdh, the time for spreading the fires has arrived. Therefore, there is no impossibility; and because of the designation (*samākhyāna*), both [acts] belong exclusively to the Adhvaryu—this is the prima facie position.

The position [of the opponent] is as follows: since there is no reason for not accepting the referent of "you" (yuṣmad), this *loṭ* suffix is indeed an injunction (*praiṣa*); such is the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).

Because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of not intending the second person, the *loṭ* does not signify "the time has arrived" (*prāptakāla*), but rather an injunction. Since it is impossible for both [the agent and the object] to perform the act of commanding and being commanded, the injunction and the object of the injunction must be performed by two different parties.

But the Adhvaryu [is the agent], because it is so seen. Now that the two agents have been established, there arises a doubt: should the Adhvaryu himself perform the purpose of the *praiṣa* (the call)—that is, the act consisting of the form of the *praiṣa*—or should another do so? Regarding this doubt, [the text says]: "If he were to hold the wooden sword (*sphya*) behind him, the wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt; thus the Adhvaryu would strike with the thunderbolt."

Thus, from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it follows that another person performs the command (*praiṣa*). This is because the wooden sword (*sphya*) is seen elsewhere; and he who holds the *sphya* in his hand is the commander. Therefore, the *āgnīdhra* is the commander and the *adhvaryu* is the one commanded. Even the technical designation (*samākhyā*) is set aside in accordance with the words of the explanatory passage. Such being the case, based on the indicative power of the mantra (*mantra-liṅga*), the *adhvaryu* performs the command: "O *āgnīdhra*, spread the fires! (*agnīdagnīn vihara*).

Thus, because the meaning of the *praiṣa* (direction) is understood from the mantra "agnīd agnīn... and because the mantra is stronger than the *arthavāda* due to its capacity to convey the performance [of the rite] and because the designation (*samākhyāna*) is possible in terms of its purpose, the *adhvaryu* alone is the one who gives the direction. As for the *arthavāda*, it is resolved through figurative speech (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) by way of praising a quality (*guṇavāda*).
In the Bhāṣya, it is stated that "by the word *adhvaryu*, the *agnīdh* alone is expressed through a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*).
(1) 1129 (2) G. [p. 945] Regarding the difference in agents.

The fruit belongs to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) because it serves a purpose within the ritual instruments. But what is the distinction between this [fruit] and the benedictory mantras (*āśīr-mantra*)? It has been determined that benedictory mantras belong exclusively to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Likewise, why should these mantras not also belong to the sacrificer? Thus, there is no basis for the inquiry at all. For this deliberation—whether they reveal the fruit of the sacrificer or the fruit of the officiating priest—is only appropriate if the mantras belong to the Adhvaryu priest.

The term "illumination" (prakāśa) does not imply that it belongs to the sacrificer. The answer is as follows: since the designation (samākhyā) establishes that the Adhvaryu is the performer, the injunction of the mantra for the *agnyanvādhāna* is by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Furthermore, it is not possible to set aside the primary element on account of a subordinate quality. Therefore, the mantra belongs to the Adhvaryu. To begin with, the *agnyanvādhāna* itself is exclusively the duty of the Adhvaryu; consequently, the mantra which is its constituent part also belongs to him alone. Not [the sacrificer].

Furthermore, by examining the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, since the mantra applies to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), who is the performer (*prayoktṛ*), the *agnyanvādhāna* (the placing of fuel on the fire) is also indeed to be performed by the sacrificer.

This is because, regarding the principal act of *agnyanvādhāna*, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of displacing the agent. Thus, it being established that the mantra belongs to the Adhvaryu priest due to the displacement of the agent within the mantra itself, the question arises: whose is the benediction (*āśis*)? Based on the indicative mark, it belongs to the Adhvaryu; for the speaker is connected with the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*).

For in all cases, the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*) occurs according to the intention of the speaker, as in "I do" (*karomi*). Just as the word "we" (*asmad*) and the first person have the same referent, so too this word "we" [is used] in the mantra "O Agni, may there be splendor for me" (*mama agne varcaḥ*). In that context, the officiant (*adhvaryu*), acting as the agent—

"It is precisely the object [of the action]. An objection is raised: "But surely, because of the mention of a fruit connected with the ritual act (*karman*), the mantras must have the ritual act as their purpose. And since fame is not understood from the injunction (*codanā*) to be the fruit of the ritual act, how can they have the ritual act as their purpose by virtue of manifesting that [fame]? The reply is: "The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) considers that for one who manifests the fame prompted by the ritual act, it is indeed appropriate that they have the ritual act as their purpose. [This concludes the] established conclusion (*rāddhānta*).

But the proponent of the [Vedic] view, considering that what is derived from a meaning is not itself the meaning of the injunction (*codanā*), maintains that the mantra reveals only a fruit connected with ritual action.

He considers that it has the sense of "action" (*karman*). The meaning of this is as follows: fame is not understood from the injunction (*codanā*) as being the fruit of the action; rather, it is understood by implication (*arthatas*). And that which is obtained by implication is not the enjoined purpose of the injunction, nor is the enjoined fruit to be manifested by the mantra even as a secondary consequence (*anuṣaṅgika*). Therefore, it is only the fruit connected with the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) that is manifested by the word *varcas* (splendor). [The mantra says: "May splendor be mine, the sacrificer..."
Such is the meaning of the mantra. By the word "us" (asmad), it is the sacrificer himself who is denoted through the force of devotion (*bhakti*).

However, the fruit for the sake of the ritual is for the master of those [priests], because it serves a purpose directed toward him. But where the fruit is indeed of a perceptible nature, characterized by freedom from distress (*asantāpa*), does that belong only to the priests, or even here is it the fruit of the ritual itself? Is it the absence of distress belonging to the priests?

When there is a doubt as to whether it is being wished that "may I not suffer" or whether the fruit of the sacrifice itself, produced by the ritual act, is being proclaimed, we state the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) that, according to the reasoning already stated, it is indeed the fruit of the ritual act. To this, it is replied: "And that purpose which follows from the purpose... (*yaścārthādarthaḥ*).

The statement "that is not the purpose of the injunction" was made with the intention that the fruit does not assist the ritual action, having accepted a fruit that provides no assistance. However, that which does assist the ritual action—such as freedom from distress—is such that an Adhvaryu priest who is free from distress is able to perform the ritual action. Therefore, whatever assists the ritual action becomes subordinate to it by way of being an instrument for its performance; thus, this applies even to those [mantras] that illuminate that [action].

"The fact that mantras do not lose their status as instruments for ritual action is stated here; thus, what is being proclaimed is precisely the lack of distress on the part of the officiating priest.
And because of the designation. Where the fruit is indeed designated for the priests, that has been shown in the passage, "That [fruit] is ours together.
And this is merely an exception; since there is no reason to disregard the dual number in the phrase "that is ours together," the fruit belongs to the priests as well.
The preparation of the substance [is for both] because there is no distinction in the context. It was stated that "the altar and the properties of the altar" was said with a subsequent intention;

that is, it was already stated that the altar and the properties of the altar are for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the primary rite. That very point is recalled for the sake of the subsequent deliberation.

However, because of the specific instruction, it remains established that in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the primary rite. Now, this is considered in the modified rite (*vikṛti*).

—In this case as well, do the ritual duties (*dharma*) apply to the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the sake of both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rite (*pradhāna*), that is, for as many subsidiaries as there are, whether archetypal (*prākṛta*) or non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*)? Or do the duties of the sacrificial grass apply only for its own sake? Or rather, are they applied only to that which takes over the function of the archetypal [grass], just as in the archetype the duties of the sacrificial grass were observed to apply only to that which had assumed its function; and likewise in the modification (*vikṛti*), they apply only to that which has assumed that same function? In this regard, by virtue of the commonality of being connected to the subsidiaries and the primary rite...

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that "as in the archetype, so also in the ectype. The meaning of this is as follows: the ritual properties (*dharmas*) which serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*) serve that same purpose in the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well. Otherwise, the ectype would not be "like the archetype. And in the archetype, they serve the purpose of all the subsidiaries and the principal.

"All ritual elements (dharmas) serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the primary act, even in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti). However, the proponent of the final view (rāddhāntavādī) maintains that the determination of ritual elements in the modified sacrifice occurs by way of their function (kārya), not by way of their connection with the original model (prakṛti). The meaning of this is as follows: when there is a requirement for a function characterized by benefit (upakāra) in the modified sacrifice, the benefit belonging to the original model is obtained. Since that benefit cannot be realized without the constituent items (padārthas), [the items are brought in] by means of those items.

[The object] is perceived as delimited by that [function]. Thus, the determination of the ritual elements (*padārtha*) in the modification (*vikṛti*) occurs by way of their function (*kārya*). It is not the case, however, that the connection which exists in the archetype (*prakṛti*) must likewise be established in the modification; for if it were so, the instruction (*upadeśa*) would apply everywhere merely by virtue of the general nature of the connection.
Indeed, the distinction is this: extension (*atideśa*) is the attainment of ritual elements by way of their function, whereas instruction (*upadeśa*) is the attainment of independent ritual elements.

If, even in the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), the connection between ritual items were independent of the purpose (*kārya*), then it would be a matter of direct instruction (*upadeśa*) alone. Consequently, the observation of *ūha* (modification of mantras) would not be possible; for if it were a matter of instruction, the performance would have to occur exactly as instructed, without any alteration. Therefore, it is established that when the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), which is an accessory of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), has been transformed into something other than its original form due to a different purpose, the properties of the sacrificial grass (*barhirdharma*) should not be performed upon it, because it is no longer in its original state (*aprākṛtatvāt*). [This applies to] the anointing—...

And [the rule] "and in the *jya* [there are no properties of the *ājya*]" applies because of the contradiction due to the specific scriptural statement (*śruti-viśeṣāt*). Since it is not logical for something to function as a subordinate element (*śeṣa-bhāva*) in multiple places, something other than the *paribhojanīya* [grass] must be employed.
Because this is clear, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) has not been recorded here. For instance: two *darbha* blades with uncut tips...
(1) Regarding the statement,
"One makes the two strainers a span in length," since there is an application based on their mere physical form, there is no contradiction with what has already been applied.

The meaning of the concluding (rāddhānta) section is as follows: since there is no agency elsewhere for that which has already been employed as a subordinate element (śeṣa) in another context, one should take two blades of *darbha* from the *paribhojanīya* grass and fashion the two strainers (*pavitra*). Specifically, the two *darbha* blades included within the act of spreading [the sacrificial grass] are what should be taken.

The removal (apanaya), however, pertains to only one part. According to the principle of the preceding section, the previous position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is not logical for there to be a state of being a remnant (*śeṣa-bhāva*) when the offering is made at multiple sacrifices and the Aindravāyava vessel is set aside. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is reached through the restriction to two portions and the act of disposal (*pratipatti*). Its meaning is as follows: first of all, there is no contradiction in the status of the constituent factor (*kāraka-bhāva*) existing in multiple places, because the sacrifice is completed by means of the mere two portions; as for the remainder—

Because it is not occupied elsewhere and because another function is possible, there is no contradiction in enjoining what has already been enjoined, since this is a case of formal recognition (*pratipatti*). In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) serves all purposes. Now, the properties such as low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) in the modified sacrifice are considered: here too, as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), do these properties serve both the subsidiaries and the primary, or not? This is the doubt. The meaning of this is: in the modified sacrifices such as the *yajñātharvaṇa* and others...

In the case of those [Vedic texts] that teach only the primary (pradhāna) rites, it is considered whether the properties such as *upāṃśutva* (whispering tone) and so forth are taught for the sake of both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary, or whether they are for the sake of the primary alone. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that, as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), these properties serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the primary. Whispersing tone is a subsidiary by way of the agent; for through the state of whispering, the agent is able to perform the rite without becoming fatigued. [The subsidiary...]

r950] And the agent is for the sake of the primary purpose. Therefore, just as when the primary ritual is directly taught, there is a state of being for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary, so it is in the case of such [an agent].

2. "And likewise even in the case of modification (vikṛti)," thus the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that the direct instruction (upadeśa) does not connect with the extended application (atideśika).

The meaning is that because of the inequality between the primary act (pradhāna) which is directly instructed and the auxiliary acts (aṅga) which are subject to extended application, the instruction regarding low-voiced recitation (upāṃśutva) does not connect [with the latter].
What, then, is the reason why it does not connect? The answer is: because extended application depends upon the direct instruction, [it follows] the direct instruction of the primary act—

The extension (*atideśa*) of the quality arises with reference to the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*). Therefore, the connection of the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) is with the primary element that occurs first, and not with the subsequent subsidiary elements that are subject to extension. Those learned in the principles of logic maintain that between the dependent and the independent, the independent is stronger.

This is due to a distinction in proximity. In the case of the Śyena sacrifice, however, because there is no directly taught (aupadeśika) connection, the connection is established solely through extension (ātideśika); this is the distinction. Here, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is based on the specific point of the preceding section. Therefore, in the primary rite—the Śyena itself—it is stated:
"The clarified butter (ājya) is fresh butter from a living cow (dṛtinavanīta)."

Thus, *navanīta* (fresh butter) is enjoined. The mention of *ājya* (clarified butter), however, is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), because *navanīta* is itself a form of *ājya*. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: since it is possible for the word *ājya* to be connected with the ritual action (*kārya*), its connection through a mere restatement is not logical;

therefore, there is an injunction of *navanīta* with reference to *ājya*. Furthermore, since there is no *ājya* in the primary sacrifice, the *Śyena*, this refers to the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) obtained by extension (*atideśika*).
Such is this instruction: (1) P. 1136 (2) G. of the Dharma [p. r951].

Or [it may be] at that time. The prima facie (pūrva) position is that, due to the delusion caused by observing the indicative mark (liṅga), the injunction here pertains only to the times of the Soma-pressing (sutyā).

The meaning of this is as follows: in the Sādyaska sacrifice, "he immolates the animals together"—thus "togetherness" (sahatva) is heard in the scripture. That [togetherness] occurs only at the time of the Soma-pressing.

From this we understand that whatever is prescribed in general applies only at the time of the *sutyā* (the soma-pressing). Based on this misconception, the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) position is that the rule regarding the leather bag and fresh butter applies only to those auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) that occur at the time of the *sutyā*. The fundamental reasoning for the prima facie position is the proximity to the principal rite (*pradhāna*).
The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that because there is no distinction, it applies to all; for both those proximate and those not proximate to the principal rite—[it applies].

The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that because there is no distinction in the relationship [to the sacrifice], it is an injunction regarding butter (*navanīta*); thus, the logical consistency of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been stated. It is stated in the *Bhāṣya* that the simultaneous immolation of the animals at the very time of the Soma-pressing belongs to both the Agniṣomīya and the Anubandhya, as there is no difference between them;
however, the meat belongs to the Savanīya [animals]. "The Savanīya cakes consist of *tarasa* (meat)."
Thus it is heard in scripture.

In that context, since there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) if both the *savanīya* and the *puroḍāśa* were intended [to be modified], a discussion arose as to which of the two is more reasonable to regard as non-literal. It was concluded (*rāddhāntita*) that the *puroḍāśa* is the non-literal one, because its deviation from the literal sense is observed. The meaning of this is as follows: *tarasāḥ*...

Regarding the phrase "the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes" (*puroḍāśāḥ*), here the *savanīyas* are enjoined either with reference to the *savana* [pressings] or with reference to the *puroḍāśas*. In that case, it is not logical to intend the *puroḍāśa* as a qualifier for the *savanīyas* being referred to, because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Nor... [P.

The *savanīya* is a qualification of the *puroḍāśa* being intended as the subject, precisely because it would otherwise result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, one is described as a restatement of what is already established (*nityānuvāda*). Nor is it the case that all *savanīyas* are exclusively *puroḍāśas*; thus, by the logic of the "man with a staff" (*daṇḍin-yāya*), [the term applies] to both *puroḍāśas* and non-*puroḍāśas*.

The word *puroḍāśa* must be explained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Likewise, since not all *puroḍāśas* are *savanīya*, the word *savanīya* applies to both those that are *savanīya* and those that are not. In considering which term should be explained through secondary indication, it is appropriate that the word *savanīya*—which occurs first—be taken in its primary sense. This is because the word *puroḍāśa* is subordinate and because its deviation from its primary meaning is observed. It is observed...

For indeed, just as the word *puroḍāśa* is used for the *puroḍāśas* in the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too here it should be understood that the word *puroḍāśa* itself must be explained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because it is extended [from the archetype] according to the principle "as in the archetype. In this regard, the Bhāṣya states: "The *tarasa* cakes become the *savanīya* offerings."

Thus it has been stated. Regarding that, the author of the *Nibandhana*, considering that the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) cannot be asserted—that the term *puroḍāśa* alone is justified as being used according to its literal meaning because it occurs earlier [in the text]—states: "The *savanīya* sacrificial cakes are made of meat."
Thus it has been illustrated by way of reversal.
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Ṛjuvimalā*, the commentary (*pañcikā*) composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra.
The Eighth Chapter [p.
953] Now, in the *Ṛjuvimalā*:

The First Pāda of the Fourth Adhyāya: Now, therefore. In this section (*adhikaraṇa*), it is established that the operation of injunction characterized as *upādāna* (appropriation) constitutes a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which exists in some cases regarding purpose (*aidamarthya*), in some regarding performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), in some regarding qualification (*adhikāra*), and in some regarding origin (*utpatti*). For example, [this applies] to sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth—

For those things whose purposefulness (*idamarthya*) toward the injunction (*niyoga*) has been understood through their designated names—such as *vrīhi* grains and the like, whose purposefulness toward the injunction is established by direct statement (*śruti*) and other means—the "purposefulness of the instrument" (*karaṇaidamarthya*) arises subsequently. This instrument-purposefulness is the means for accomplishing both types of purposefulness (the purposefulness of the door and the purposefulness of the end) and is established by the purposefulness of the door (*dvāraidamarthya*), which serves as the basis for the understanding of both. Likewise, in the case of a qualification (*adhikāra*) that culminates in a specific occasion (*nimitta*), the performance of the primary rites along with their subsidiaries occurs solely through the act of undertaking (*upādāna*). Similarly, in sacrifices such as the *Viśvajit*, a qualification is postulated [even in the absence of an explicit statement].

[The injunction] is based on inclusion (*aupādānikī*). In cases such as "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," where there is an injunction regarding a mere qualification (*kevalādhikāra-codanā*), the implication of the origin-injunction (*utpatti-niyoga*) occurs precisely through inclusion. Indeed, without the origin-injunction, the establishment of the qualification-injunction (*adhikāra-niyoga*) from the primary act as embellished by its subsidiaries would not be possible; for it has been shown that because ritual acts are momentary, they lack the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakārakatva*).

In the eleventh [chapter], the Commentator [states]: "And this operation of injunction characterized as *upādāna* (appropriation) is distinct from the six means of knowledge such as direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth; it depends upon the application (*viniyoga*) discussed in the third [book]. We shall explain this in various places. Thus, there is a relationship of cause and effect even between these two definitions. Regarding the phrase "kratvarthā" (for the sake of the sacrifice) in the *Ṭīkā*, the meaning is as follows: why is the inquiry into what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) proposed separately? [Is it not already covered by] "Now, therefore, the definition of the subordinate (*śeṣa*)"?...

This is not so, because it has already been asserted. Nor should it be said that "subsidiarity" (*śeṣatva*) was asserted therein, but not "subservience to this purpose" (*aidamarthya*). For it has been stated that subsidiarity is defined precisely as subservience to this purpose, since "the subsidiary exists because it is for the sake of another. This is because there would otherwise be no distinct subject matter for the chapter; [thus concludes] the Adhyāya...
(1) P. Bhāṣya 1193.
The objection that [the previous argument] is illogical also remains in mind. Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha matam" (if it is thought): therein, this is the intended meaning.

The status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) based on injunction (*viniyoga*) has been examined; now, however, that which is based on adoption (*aupādānika*) is proposed separately. For instance, [it concerns] the state of being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatā*).

The fact that sacrifice is the means for attaining heaven, and that heaven is to be enjoyed by the qualified person, is not understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof. As it has been said: "The desire for that [heaven] is characterized as a purpose. To this, he replies: "In that case, the inclusion of 'for the sake of the rite' (*kratvartha*) is refuted;

because every instance of being for the sake of the rite is understood through *śruti* and the rest, and it cannot be claimed that this [desire for heaven] is also characterized as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)."

Because, in the absence of the word, the cognition that "sacrifice is for the sake of heaven" is not possible; nor does the cognition arise that "heaven, which is to be accomplished by that [sacrifice], is a human goal (puruṣārtha) and an object of qualification," since it occurs only when the word is present. The point is that the knowledge of the human goal arises from the word alone, produced specifically by the direct statement (śruti) and so forth. Furthermore, the mention of "śruti and so forth" in the phrase "yadapi ca" is also meaningless—this is the sense. And as for [the claim regarding] that which is for the sake of the ritual (kratvartha)—

Regarding the phrase "of the two human goals": the author of the *Bhāṣya* includes [the categories of] the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the non-instigator (*aprayojaka*) within these. His purpose for doing so is this:

how indeed might the subsequent investigation have as its object the matter already proposed? However, this inclusion is not tenable. For if there were an inclusion, it would have to occur either by way of essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), as in the case of "subservience" (*śeṣatva*) and "being for that purpose" (*tādarthya*), or by way of function (*kāryataḥ*).

Or [is it] that all have a single effect? For example, just as the fulfillment of the modified injunction (*vaikṛta-codanā*) is the effect of the specific marks (*viśeṣa-liṅga*) and so forth, and thus it is postulated as their cause, so too there is the inclusion of all the objects of the subsequent six chapters. This occurs either by way of definition (*lakṣaṇataḥ*), or because all have a single—(1) G. omits *na*.

If that alone were the defining characteristic—just as it is for the various injunctions (*codanā*) and so forth—then all Vedic meanings would be included within what is asserted to have that characteristic.
However, none of these three is present here; for first of all, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is distinct precisely because it is denoted separately.

If these [categories] were to possess only a single essential nature (*svarūpa*), then their distinct mention and exposition in various respective contexts would not be possible. Furthermore, the definition (*lakṣaṇa*)—by which logical principle the essential nature of these is characterized—is itself distinct precisely because of the difference in their essential natures. For a difference in essential nature does not arise from a single definition, since the establishment of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is precisely because of that [difference in the means] that there is a difference in the object of knowledge.

Furthermore, the Bhāṣyakāra has shown that even those [passages] which primarily enjoin the fruit of the prompter (*prayojaka*) are included within the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), thereby constituting a benefit to the person; likewise, those primarily consisting of non-prompting explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are included within the ritual purpose (*kratvartha*), thereby constituting a benefit to the sacrifice. This is incorrect, because it contradicts logic, contradicts other sections [of the work], and contradicts what was stated in the *Arthavādādhikaraṇa*. [End of section on] Arthavāda.

For it has already been stated that the purpose [of the action] is for the sake of praise (*stuti*). Furthermore, primacy (*prādhānya*) is based upon the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor. That which is the beneficiary of the benefactor is primary with respect to it; however, this primacy does not arise from being the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), but rather from being the beneficiary. Moreover, the instigator (*prayojaka*) establishes its own primacy in relation to the one to be instigated (*prayojya*), but it does not thereby establish its own subservience to another.

For being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) is the primary factor, and not merely being a benefactor to a person. Therefore, there is no inclusion [of the *pradhāna*] even from the perspective of its function (*kāryataḥ*). This commentary is like a "night-journey" (*rātriprayāṇaka*); a night-journey is one that occurs at night and, because it lacks a person to describe the path and because of the absence of such a person, it produces confusion due to the lack of one's own reliable cognition regarding its nighttime nature.

Because he is free from dependence on others, he is called a "teacher" (*deśin*), meaning one who points out the path. [He is so called] because he teaches the path for the sake of the highest human goals.
(1) G. *katvam* [p. 956]

Thus it is said: "Without rest, without support, without provisions for the journey, and without a guide. To this it is replied: Both of these—the presentation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) and others as distinct entities, and the statement regarding their subsumption—are incorrect; therefore, nothing need be said there.

Furthermore, as for the fact that being for the sake of another (*tādarthya*) is the reason for being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*), since one asserts both subordination and being for the sake of another, [there is no contradiction].

The proposition regarding what serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) has also indeed been made. In that regard as well, the Commentator stated "that" by means of citing the direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, thereby indicating that those [criteria] depend upon the direct statement and other means of proof. By this, it is said that this proposition is based solely on the operation of the injunction (*niyoga*). But if this is so, it was also said that the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice is refuted; for that [status] is based on the direct statement and other such means. This would indeed be so.

If it is said that "that which arises from application" (*vainiyogika*) refers to what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), then here, however, it is asserted that everything based on inclusion (*upādāna*)—comprising all that pertains to the purpose of the sacrifice and the purpose of the person, whether it be motivators or non-motivators, injunctions regarding results, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), subsidiaries, or primary acts—is "based on inclusion" (*aupādānika*) and thus exists as being for the sake of the sacrifice. This is the intended meaning.

As for the status of being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatā*), although it is verbal (*śābdī*), it is not "arising from application"; this he will explain in the section concerning desire (*lipsādhikaraṇa*).

He raises the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*): "What, then, is meant here by 'appropriation' (*upādāna*)? The underlying point here is this: in common worldly usage, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized as "appropriation"—which is distinct from direct audition (*śruti*) and the other [means of knowledge] and consists in the operation of an injunction (*vidhi*)—is established. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "Appropriation is the implication (*ākṣepa*) of the mandate (*niyoga*). It is true that it is not established in common worldly usage; nevertheless, when a meaning is conveyed by a word, it cannot exist without another meaning [that serves as its basis].

In common worldly usage, it is well known in general that something "accomplishes" (nirvahati) means it "implies" (ākṣipati), as seen in cases such as a door becoming the instrument of an action. In the Veda as well, there is no inconsistency in the fact that an injunction (niyoga), once communicated by the word, implies another element for its own fulfillment. But what is the object of knowledge regarding the material cause (upādāna)? To this he says: "And by that [implication], the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvarthatva) and the status of being for the sake of the instrument (karaṇārthatva) of acts such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) are established."

It has already been stated that, due to the application (*viniyoga*), it serves the purpose of the rice (*vrīhi*) itself; for the application possesses the capacity to establish the *aim-for-ness* (*aidamarthya*) toward the rice and so forth as required by the injunction (*naiyogika*), and not the *aim-for-ness* toward the instrument (*karaṇa*). Now, if this is being considered because it is implied by the injunction, then the extended application (*atideśa*) must also be considered.

It might be so; [but] no. Here, it is the completion of a single *upadeśa* (direct instruction) that is being considered. And an *atideśa* (extended application) is completed by means of reflecting upon the purpose of another *upadeśa*. Therefore, it is not considered here. [Question: "Then why is there a declaration regarding the distinction of the meaning? [Answer: Why is there a declaration regarding the distinction of the meaning—that which is to be conveyed—as well as the motivating and non-motivating factors, the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), the primary elements (*pradhāna*), and so forth? Or rather, why [is this asked], and by whom?

Inclusion is by way of category. The separate presentation is due to the difference in the causes of comprehension; that is, because the logical principles (*nyāya*) which are the causes of comprehension differ, the subjects to be established—such as those pertaining to the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and so forth—are presented separately. Inclusion, however, occurs on account of the commonality of their contribution (*upakāra*).

Thus, the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning non-productive subsidiaries (*aprayojakāṅga*) are included within the "purpose of the sacrifice" because they contribute to the sacrifice. This is what is meant: by the term "purpose of the sacrifice," [these are included].

The inclusion of that which assists the sacrifice (*kratūpakāraka*) is also established; for even an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), though it culminates in the category of authoritative testimony (*pramāṇa*), assists in the performance [of the rite] and thus serves the sacrifice.

Furthermore, the injunctions regarding the primary results—which are the motivators (*prayojaka*) for assisting the sacrifice—are included within the ends of man (*puruṣārtha*) because they share the commonality of assisting the person. Thus it is proven that "there is some motivating factor that is an end of man."

Thus, someone [objects] that the mention [of the injunction] is for the purpose of making known that even the motivator (*prayojaka*) does not have a human goal (*apuruṣārthatā*). Immediately at the beginning of the statement "just as," the question "of what? is asked. The answer given is "of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), which is the motivator for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*). The meaning of this is: of the injunction for becoming a teacher, the study of one's own Veda—

Furthermore, even for the instigator (*prayojaka*), there is an absence of being for the sake of the person (*apuruṣārthatva*), because the boy (*māṇavaka*)—who is denoted by the word "person" (*puruṣa*) as an independent agent—is not the intended purpose.

For whatever injunction (*vidhi*) impels a particular action, that action is indeed for the sake of that person; as, for example, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and so forth. However, it is established that the injunction regarding the role of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) impels the student's study (*adhyayana*), but it is not for the sake of the student.

"It is contradictory to say that 'whatever a person finds pleasure in, the desire for that arises solely from the object itself and not from the scripture,' for by this very commentary, it is [implied] that the sacrifice possesses a human purpose consisting in its being a means to heaven, and that heaven [is likewise a human purpose]."

(1) P. 1193 (2) R. Because it is an object (*arthatvāt*), it has been stated that [the state of being] the object of enjoyment for those entitled to it (*adhikāribhogyatātmikā*) is not understood through the scripture; and that is contradictory, because both—

That [relationship] is not understood apart from scripture. This was stated with reference to the scripture concerning the relationship (*saṃbandha-śāstra*) having been accepted; it was said with the scripture concerning application (*viniyoga-śāstra*) in mind, not the scripture concerning entitlement (*adhikāra-śāstra*). For both of these are understood precisely through the force of the inclusion [of the agent] in the scripture concerning entitlement. Therefore it was said: "It comes about by the purpose alone" (*arthenaiva bhavati*). And the purpose is the accomplishment of the mandate (*niyoga*), because that alone constitutes the meaning of the sentence.

And that has been called "appropriation" (upādāna). In this section, the definition of what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), which are to be established, is stated. For instance: being for the sake of the person does not consist in the production of pleasure, because it would fail to apply to obligatory rites (*nitya*) and restrictive injunctions (*niyamaniyoga*). Nor does it consist in having a qualified agent (*sādhikāritva*), because that is impossible in the case of Vedic study and the like. Nor does it consist in the purposefulness derived from appropriation (*aupādānika-aidamarthya*).

[Otherwise, there would be] the over-extension [of the definition] to number and other factors that are subsidiary to the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*) by virtue of being included in the [general] inclusion (*aupādānika*). And if that [distinction between human ends and ritual ends] were not discerned, then even the status of being a ritual end (*kratvarthatā*) would be difficult to establish because it is distinguished from that [status of being a human end]. Therefore, the definition is undertaken for the sake of such discernment. Among these, the definition of what is a human end is precisely that which is included: "That whose purpose is this [human aim] is a human end," as in the case of the sacrifice and heaven. But is it not the case that the status of being a ritual end is also stated by means of inclusion?

With the words "of number and so forth," he raises the objection of the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). The rebuttal is stated as: "when there is an application (*viniyoga*). The meaning of this is as follows: when there is an application, number and so forth possess a subsidiarity (*śeṣatā*) based on their inclusion (*aupādānikī*). To explain: since the application of gender (*liṅga*) occurs by virtue of its inherent nature through its location in the object, we shall state that number and so forth possess subsidiarity based on that inclusion. By means of that application...

That which possesses "remainder-ness" (*śeṣatva*) independently of being a means to an end (*aupādānika*) is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*); thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For it is precisely from the [context of] purpose (*artha*) that it is distinguished as a human goal. What is this "due to non-separation" (*avibhāgāt*)? The author of the Bhāṣya states that non-separation consists in pleasure (*prīti*). That is incorrect, because it is impossible in the case of entitlements (*adhikāra*) that terminate with a causal motive (*nimitta*). With this doubt in mind, he asks: "What is this? To that, the answer is given:

"—because of the inseparable connection of the person with the sacrifice. By this it is stated that since the person exists as the performer within sacrifices, and having distinguished [the person] therein— [p.

Therefore, the injunction, being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is capable of implying the subservience (*aidamarthya*) of the sacrifice. We shall establish this more precisely in the sixth [book]. Now, if it is argued that in this way only the status of being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*) has been stated, he says: "When there is application (*viniyoga*) by way of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*)," whereby its status as being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvarthatā*) is stated. Therefore, both are indicated here.

Or rather, [one might object]: "Has it not already been stated that these are injunctions of results for subordinate elements (*guṇaphalacodanā*)? What, then, is this further deliberation? For in the second and third [books], it was stated that these are injunctions of subordinate elements such as the milking of cows (*godohana*) for the sake of a result; and since their status as subsidiaries with respect to the result is understood solely through the mention [of the result] itself, once their being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*) is established, this further deliberation is redundant. It is replied: We have already demonstrated this.

"Because it was stated on account of application (*viniyoga*). This means that for the reason that the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) is not possible upon a thorough consideration of the application, its status as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*) was stated. However, in this case, since a visible purpose can be established through the act of taking [the water] (*upādāna*), an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*) is not possible; such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). For the *godohana* vessel and so forth, the accomplishment of the act of carrying water (*praṇayana*) is the visible purpose, while the attainment of cattle and so forth is the invisible purpose. In that regard:

In considering whether an injunction (niyoga) adopts [an accessory] through a visible means (dṛṣṭa-dvāra) or through an invisible means (adṛṣṭa-dvāra), it adopts it through that very visible means because the visible effect occurs more rapidly. Consequently, since the application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of adoption, the application itself is likewise [based on the visible].

And the word "desiring cattle" (paśukāma) is an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for anyone who is entitled [to perform the rite]. Furthermore, by the sentence "one should carry forth [the water] with the godohana vessel," [the vessel is applied] to the act of carrying forth (praṇayana).

[Objection: "The *godohana* vessel serves the purpose of the sacrifice because of its specific application (*viniyoga*). [Reply: No, because the function is understood according to the application. For it is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) that the postulation of a function applies only to that which has been specifically enjoined, not to that which has not been so enjoined. The meaning of this is as follows: according to the application—[p. 960]—the application...

The connection is as follows: "In accordance with the application (*viniyoga*); because the purpose is understood through the understanding of the instrumental purpose (*dvārakārya*), it is the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*). He asks, "Why is it so? and replies:

"For the postulation of a purpose (*kāryakalpanā*) applies only to that which has been applied (*viniyukta*), not to that which has not been applied. Thus, even for that which subserves the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), the application to the sacrifice is established.

The purpose must be postulated as something to be accomplished (*kāryabhūtā*). And in that postulation, the application (*viniyoga*) is the basis. Furthermore, by the force of the application, the instrumental purpose—"

[This is] appropriation (*parigraha*). Furthermore, there is no application (*viniyoga*) here even for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Therefore, although this effect is perceptible, it does not depend on application. Consequently, it is established that in injunctions regarding qualities and fruits (*guṇaphalacodanā*), the result belongs solely to the person (*puruṣārthatā*)—both by way of application through the consideration of application, and by way of necessity (*niyoga*) through the consideration of undertaking (*upādāna*). The mention of Bādari, moreover, [is for the sake of indicating] the assistance (*upakāra*)...

This is for the sake of illustration, and not for the purpose of excluding other reasons—such as the fact that [the subsidiary] exists for the sake of another (*parārthatva*). Now, one might object: "The author of the *Bhāṣya* states that subsidiariness (*śeṣatā*) arises from utility (*upakāra*), and not from being taken up (*upādāna*), since he introduced the view of Bādari. And that is untenable, because this [view] has been refuted. To this, he says: "The mention of Bādari is intended to demonstrate that utility is indeed observed in the case of substances (*dravya*) and so forth."

And therefore, it is a subsidiary by way of being taken up (*upādāna*) as a means (*karaṇa*). This is for the purpose of negating that reason for subsidiarity which is "being for the sake of another" (*parārthatva*). Why? Because in the context of application (*viniyoga*), that reason—namely, "because it is for the sake of another"—was stated. Now, one might object: Bādari also presented this very application, where the reason is "beneficiality" (*upakāra*); however, he did not present the taking up (*upādāna*) by way of that [beneficiality].

For this reason, because Bādari’s view was presented, it appears that the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatā*) was stated solely on the basis of utility (*upakāra*). Therefore, the resolution is that he [Bādari] was refuted for that very reason. Since Bādari stated that the status of being a subordinate element is based on utility, for that same reason Bādari was refuted. Consequently, a further objection is not tenable. Why, then, was his view presented? To this, he says: "But here, however, [the status of being a subordinate element is established] precisely by way of function (*kārya*)."
Bādari was not cited again on the grounds that appropriation occurs solely through benefit, for no such benefit is observed here;
and thus, (1) G. omits *na* [p. 961].

This is stated in order to show that Bādari, by virtue of that [authority], asserts [the status of] being a subordinate (*śeṣatā*). How, then, is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)? It is refuted by the aforementioned reasoning because it does not conform to the application (*viniyoga*); such is the contradiction. Or rather: here, the restrictive rules regarding the acquisition of wealth (*dravyārjananiyama*) are the examples. This has been introduced as the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In this case, it is not appropriate to hold that one who desires wealth is the qualified agent based on a consideration of the result of the object [of the ritual]. For if that were so, the injunction would be rendered purposeless, and a restriction (niyama) would also be impossible; because when activity proceeds out of passion due to the desire for a specific result, there is no room for questioning why one engages elsewhere rather than here, and thus the scriptural performance would not be established. On the other hand, if [the knowledge] serves the purpose of the sacrifice (kratvartha), then because it is understood as being accomplished by that [knowledge], the person engages in that [sacrifice] alone; thus, by implication, a restriction is established.

"It is established. Regarding this, the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: Since injunctions of restrictive rules (*niyamaniyoga*) would lack a qualified subject (*adhikāra*) if they were independent, and since such independence is not explicitly heard in the text, it is inferred by observing the result of their specific domain. Furthermore, because it is improper for that [result] to be rendered purposeless by the injunction, and because if the restrictive rule produces the material substance required by the injunction for a specific desire (*kāma-śruti*), the qualification for the rite is thereby established—thus avoiding contradiction with the principle of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice.

And thus, since the acceptance [of gifts] and so forth are for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), the substance acquired thereby is also for the sake of the sacrifice; consequently, one who undergoes its loss is indeed not entitled to the sacrifice. This is because it is understood that there is a single entitlement (*ekādhikāra*). Furthermore, the fact that the *kṣāmavati* offerings and others are for the sake of the ritual action becomes clearly established. Otherwise, if one who has suffered the loss of a substance unrelated to the sacrifice were to have entitlement, there would be independence (*svātantrya*) itself.

He concludes: Therefore, for one who lacks the qualification (*anadhikārī*), the injunction (*vidhi*) is purposeless; it is devoid of meaning. Even when words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) that convey an obligation (*niyoga*) are present, the expression of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) cannot be established without a qualified person. Thus, "being devoid of meaning" means precisely being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvarthatā*). Now, if it is for the sake of the ritual, then ownership—characterized by the power to dispose of things as one pleases—does not exist at all; consequently, [the act] consisting of the renunciation of one's own property...
"The claim that it would not even constitute a sacrifice—and thus, due to contradiction with the primary rite, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is improper—is a mere prattle by someone. Why?
Because (1) [it is so] due to the experience of questioning; (2) because, being a single producer, it possesses the exclusion of those [other things]."

Regarding the statement "it is mere idle chatter," he says: "That acquisition does not produce ownership is a contradiction. The point here is this: ownership is not based on the power of disposal at will, because that would lead to the over-extension [of the definition] to things taken by force, and because it would fail to apply to the wealth of children and others. What then?

What is the definition of ownership (*svatva*)? It is said: for the venerable author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) has stated, "That which a person is entitled to employ according to his own intention is his property.
Therefore, ownership consists in the fitness for disposal according to one's will; and that fitness exists in a thing with respect to a person wherever [the latter's] entitlement to it resides.

In the world, means such as acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*) and so forth are well-known and in operation. Consequently, it is contradictory to claim that ownership (*svatva*), which is based on acceptance and the like, does not exist even when those means are present. Furthermore, acquisition (*arjana*) takes various forms: in some cases it is birth, as in the case of paternal property; in other cases it is marriage, as in the case of the wealth of a husband and wife; and so on, as should be inferred from similar instances. Moreover, the authors of the *Smṛtis* employ precisely those means that are well-known in the world.

[This is] for the purpose of removing delusion, like grammar and other sciences. How, then, is there subservience to the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*)? If one has the misconception that "if it is the sacrificer's own property, then it does not belong to the sacrifice," [the answer is: the intention is that ownership (*svatva*) exists for the sake of that [sacrifice], as in the case of *vani-vanana*. *Vani* means wages; *vanana* means begging. Just as in the act of begging for wages, ownership is for the sake of the sacrifice and not for the sake of personal pleasure—such is the meaning. One thing is the state of being for the sake of that (*aidamarthyam*), and another is ownership.

This is the intended meaning. To this, it is replied: these restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) cannot be said to be devoid of an *adhikāra* (qualification for performance). Why? Because they are undertaken for the sake of living; those who are engaged in that by which one lives—that is, wealth—will become the qualified performers (*adhikārin*).
By this, the desire for wealth is not a qualification for the performer; rather, it is the inclination toward the acquisition of wealth whenever there is a need for the acquisition of wealth.

In that case, because one is enjoined by the rule regarding acceptance and so forth, anyone who proceeds by other means commits a transgression of what is prescribed; thus, it is established that the restriction (niyama) is effective in terms of its result. Furthermore, for one who proceeds for the sake of wealth, there is no qualification as a performer of a desire-based rite (kāmyādhikāra), such that his engagement therein would be rooted solely in passion; for if that were so, a transgression of the prescribed rule would not occur upon his failure to follow it. Moreover, by the word "livelihood" (jīvana), wealth is denoted—

The intended meaning here is this: while there is an invariable engagement in action for one who desires to live, life associated with a ritual sacrifice is variable; therefore, entry into the ritual does not occur by way of that [mere desire to live]. Now, it may be objected that no person qualified for the ritual is heard of as being engaged in living; to this he says:

Nor is there entitlement solely from the word; nor is there entitlement merely from the title itself. The meaning of this is as follows: the intention of one who speaks is that "this person possesses the [necessary] word. Such is not the case with the title. Rather, the title belongs to one for whom the matter consisting of the title is understood. This is what is meant: the word does not become a qualifying attribute (upādhi) for the essential nature of the entitled person.

This object, which consists in entitlement (*adhikāra*), is sometimes understood through verbal testimony and sometimes through other means of knowledge; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever. Furthermore, by observing the nature of accepting gifts and so forth, the entitlement of one who has engaged in action for the sake of livelihood is understood here. For no prudent person, even when engaged in acquiring wealth, fails to perform acts such as accepting gifts. Therefore, since ownership (*svatva*) is common to all, [the entitlement follows].

Since [the injunction] is not specified by way of *aidamarthya* (subservience to a specific purpose), and because there is no distinction that can be determined regarding the accomplishment of all human goals—which consist in the fulfillment of the sacrifice for living—it follows that it must be performed by everyone. Having restated the commentary beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*), [the question is asked]: "What is the meaning of this?"

Thus he objects: "What is this *tantra*? If you say it is 'living,' then one will live regardless of any restriction (*aniyamāt*). Since a restriction is a subsidiary element of the ritual (*kratvaṅga*), the restriction is not for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*); just as, even due to the restriction of threshing (*avaghāta*) within the ritual, pounding and so forth may also occur for the sake of the person. Alternatively, if other rituals are intended by the term *tantra*, then there would be their total omission."

Even so, because there is a rule for each individual sacrifice (*kratu*), one might argue that by earning wealth through unrestricted means, the performance [of the sacrifice] will still take place, and thus there would be no omission. To this it is replied: what is intended by the term *tantra* are indeed other sacrifices themselves.
Furthermore, there is no evidence for the claim that acquisition (*arjana*) involves the inclusion of a specific [qualification]. The meaning of this is as follows:

when acquisition by way of property is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), then, because sacrifices are accomplished through property, this acquisition would pertain to all sacrifices; however, there is no evidence for its involving a specific qualification.

[Objection: There is [a distinction], for there is no specific indication such as, "this cleansing is intended for this [deity]," or "it is not for this [one]. [Response: Let it be so; nevertheless, why [is it not possible]?
