He says: Furthermore, it is not possible to perform the entire rite with every substance, because once something has been relinquished, its relinquishment again is impossible.
In that case, if a particular sacrifice were performed with a certain substance, then its purposefulness (*tādarthya*) toward another sacrifice would be subverted;
thus, there would be a collapse of the *tantra* (the common ritual framework), because all rites are commenced by means of the subsidiary act of acquiring the substance. This is another defect:

the established view—that "when the *tantra* of one [rite] has been set in motion, the *tantra* of another is not set in motion"—would not be tenable. [This is known] through direct perception regarding other sacrifices...
Because another rite is seen within the tantra, starting with the words "Now, if it is thought...

and so forth. Thus, he begins to explain the commentary beginning with "And this being the case," etc.: "Now, this is not an auxiliary (aṅga) of even a single one of the rites, but rather an auxiliary of all of them combined, as for example..."

The intention is that because the *aikādaśina* animals are distributed between the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* sacrifices, there will be no loss of the *tantra* (the common ritual procedure) due to their connection therein.

[Objection: In that case, this is certainly not grasped by the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance), because there is no *prayogavacana* that applies to all sacrifices, as is the case with the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice; for a subsidiary (*aṅga*) status does not exist for that which lacks an adopted *prayogavacana*. [Response: For one who... through study...

The statement regarding the performance (*prayoga-vacana*) has not been mentioned, nor has it been accepted; for that whose statement of performance is not recited, there is no status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) at all. Consequently, this is the meaning of the Bhāṣya: even if something is intended to be a subsidiary to a single [rite], if it exists outside the time of its performance, it would indeed be a non-subordinate (*anaṅga*). Now, [an objection is raised]: "But the Bhāṣya says it is 'non-beneficial' (*anupakāraka*), not that it is 'not a subsidiary' (*nānaṅga*). To this he replies: "If the status of being a subsidiary does not exist, then for that which indeed possesses the nature of a subsidiary..."
It is not the case that there is no assistance rendered by its non-application; rather, this very absence of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatābhāva*) has been shown through the lack of assistance.

Nor can it be like the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires). This act of acquisition (*ārjana*) cannot be for the sake of the substance alone, nor can it be for the sake of the fire alone, just as the *ādhāna* is.
The meaning is this: just as the *ādhāna* is for the sake of the fire and not for the sake of the person, so too the rule of acquisition must be for the sake of wealth alone.

And by means of the substance, it will enter into another sphere of entitlement (*adhikāra*). Nor will there be a loss of the ritual framework (*tantra*), because there is no contradiction, just as in the case of the fire.
Because [it would follow from] existence. This also is not the case, because it is understood that one who is engaged for the sake of living has the qualification [for the rite].
For he who lacks qualification enters into the qualification of another. However, by virtue of being for the sake of the substance [of the fire], qualification is understood as inherent.

But in the case of the *ādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires), there is no qualification even by implication, because the fires—being independent of any other qualification—are not themselves human goals (*puruṣārtha*). [Therefore,] they serve the purpose of living.

However, since the substance exists by its own nature, there is authority for it therein; therefore, this [acquisition] serves only the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), unlike the act of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*).

Consequently, if the acquisition of the substance were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), the established defect would be the loss of the ritual procedure (*tantra-parilopa*). This is because the *kṣāmavatyā* and other rites are heard as having authority for one who has established the fires, and such a person is fit for connection with the sacrifice. Let there be connection with the sacrifice; even so, the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*) is not established merely by the result.

[It is] to be imagined. And these two [points] have been stated as a concessionary argument (*abhyupagamya-vāda*). Let this occasional [act] be for the sake of the person alone; there is no harm whatsoever. Therefore, it is established that the rules regarding the acquisition of property are for the sake of the person. He states the purpose of the inquiry: "Hence, there is a transgression of the rule"; the transgression belongs to the person, not to the sacrifice. Therefore, the transgression of the rule—

The accomplishment of a sacrifice (*kratusiddhi*) occurs even through wealth acquired gradually. Nor should it be argued here that, in that case, the accomplishment of a sacrifice would also occur through wealth acquired by theft;
for in the world, theft is not recognized as a means of producing ownership (*svatva*).
(1) G. *anyārthameva* (2) G. *kratvarthadravyā*

Regarding the rule for the renunciation of that [act], it has been stated that when the prefix *prati* denotes a person, there is a desire for its acquisition as characterized by the purpose [of the act]. However, in this case,
since the prefix *prati* is not directly heard as a qualification of the qualified agent— as in the injunction, "One should not look at the rising sun"— [the rule does not apply].

Because only this much is heard [in the text] and because the qualification of the eligible person is not understood from the meaning— as in the case of "One should not eat *kalañja*," which [only serves to restrain] the inclination toward eating— so too [is it here].

Therefore, because this injunction [of non-injury] is devoid of a qualified person (*adhikārin*), it does not result in a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) that lacks qualification; thus, this is a prohibition of looking that pertains to the ritual purpose (*kratvartha*).

[Objection: If this is indeed a prohibition of looking, then a qualified person who is engaged in looking must necessarily be understood. Moreover, such engagement in looking does not occur solely within the context of the ritual, since it can also occur by chance. [Reply: To this it is said: True, there is looking even outside of the ritual.

Nevertheless, due to the parsimony of application (*prayukti-lāghava*), this is understood to be a prohibition specifically regarding looking at [the sacrificer] during the sacrifice. But if that is so, why is the restriction (*niyama*) regarding the acquisition of wealth not also for the sake of the sacrifice? Let that too be cited here as an example. Where the thing to be prohibited does not exist within the sacrifice, its prohibition is not suspected of being for the sake of the sacrifice, as is the case with the eating of *kalañja*. Or rather, let it be a restriction (*niyama*), since the context begins with the discussion of vows (*vrata*).

Or rather, even so, this [prohibition] is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Now, under the view of a restrictive rule (*niyamapakṣa*), by what connection does it enter into the sacrifice? For a prohibition would enter into the sacrifice by way of the object to be prohibited. It is said: even if the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the restriction of not looking were independent, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a separate application (*prayukti*); therefore, it enters into the sacrifice itself. But if this is so, then the Viśvajit and other such [rites] would also [apply here].

Let there be examples; let there be no fault whatsoever. To this it is replied: even when there is a renunciation of pleasure, this is what is being said—that even when no qualification (*adhikāra*) is explicitly heard, it is proper to assume a qualification; however, one should not assume a connection with a ritual sacrifice (*kratu*).
But what is the difference between these two? This is the difference: just as when a qualification is heard, the agency of that [qualification] is understood.

It is logical. For one whose entitlement (*adhikāra*) is heard in scripture, their status as the agent of that action is inferred because that entitlement would otherwise be inexplicable. Indeed, he who understands the injunction (*niyoga*) as something to be accomplished is the entitled person; and the injunction has its object as its goal. If that [injunction] does not [accomplish] the object...
The injunction regarding it must indeed be carried out; for [the agent] is understood to be the doer by virtue of being the accomplisher of the object.

And although that agency may be established in both ways—either directly or through the instigation of another person—nevertheless, since a direct relationship is possible, an indirect succession is untenable; therefore, its own agency alone is logical. One should not, however, assume the agency of another person in the absence of a scriptural statement.

[The agency] belongs only to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Thus, since the agent is understood through the implication of the action (*kriyākṣepa*), it is logical to postulate a specific qualification (*adhikāra*) [for that agent].

For without a qualification, agency is untenable. Nor can agency be established elsewhere by means of a qualification belonging to one thing through its entry into the qualification of another as a subordinate part (*aṅga*); for when a qualification is possible directly in this very case, a mediated succession is untenable. And thus, according to reason...

When an *adhikārin* (the person qualified for the rite) is established, even the postulation of an *prayukti* (an impelling force) is not a fault. How then is the *Kartradhikaraṇa* [to be explained]? Even in the case of "one should not speak untruth," since the agency (*kartṛtva*) is understood, why is there a need to postulate a direct *adhikāra* (qualification) for the sake of establishing that agency, rather than accepting that the agent (*kartṛ*) is directly expressed?

[Objection: Is it not a rejection? For even if "being denotable" (*vācyatva*) is rejected, and even if the agent is understood [from the verb], that agent would incur the status of being an independent authority (*svatantra-adhikāra*).

[Response: The answer is: for in that case (the prohibition of lying), the application (*viniyoga*) is the counter-agent to the assumption of an authority; but here, the assumption of an authority is without such a counter-agent. This is because, in the prohibition of speaking untruth (*anṛta-vadana-pratiṣedha*), [the prohibition] is already grasped due to its proximity to an enjoined authority (*sādhikāra-niyoga*).

And because it has been assigned by the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no room for the postulation of a separate qualification (*adhikāra*). Here, however, since it is recited as an unattached injunction (*anārabhyāmnāna*), there is no grasping of a qualification; thus, a connection with another qualification is not possible. Therefore, when the postulation of a qualification proceeds, it is faultless that there is only the postulation of an independent qualification. Thus, this section has first been resolved. Now, in the spirit of a friend—
He defines the qualification of the eligible person: "Furthermore, what kind of person is authorized here?

Since it is heard [in scripture] that "by this much he becomes free from sin," the eligibility belongs to one who is still alive; for in this example, [the text speaks of being freed] from this much sin (enas).

"He becomes separated" is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). In that regard, if the qualified performer is one who possesses life, then because [the rite] is obligatory (*nitya*), the connection with sin (*enoyoga*)—which is precisely the fault of transgressing what is enjoined upon non-performance—serves as the basis for this explanatory statement. However, unlike the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and others, where heaven is the qualification, [here it is not so]. (1) G. *vikalpa* (2) G. *prakṛtāyām*

If it were assumed that this is a qualification [of the person], then there would be no fault even in the non-performance of the desired act; in that case, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would have to function in an extremely remote manner. Therefore, this is a compulsory rule (*niyama*) to be observed as long as one lives, by virtue of being one's own duty (*svadharma*).

But is it not the case that a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is more logical? Its meaning is this: "Is this not indeed a simple negation? In that case, the person qualified [for the rite] would be one who performs the very action being prohibited. Why, then, is it said that he must be "living"? True; from the perspective of considering his own sentence alone, it would be so. However, because of the understood connection with the words "his vow" (*tasya vratam*), figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is indeed more logical. What is indicated is the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) of non-looking, which takes the form of a vow.

Therefore, this is not a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). [Objection: In that case, why should the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) not also have the substance as its purpose, just like the act of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*)?

To this he replies: Even in this case, having the substance as its purpose is not possible, because there is no direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Since there is no connection with a substance that has been specifically enjoined, and since there is no visible refinement (*saṃskāra*), it certainly does not have the substance as its purpose. However, if a visible [result]...

It would be a *saṃskāra* (a preparatory rite). Can it be said that it has a visible purpose? The meaning of this is as follows: it is established that everything cognizable through words pertains to the *codanās* (Vedic injunctions). Even though a visible effect (*dṛṣṭa*) exists in the form of a *saṃskāra*, nevertheless, its being for that [visible] purpose alone is not logical. Certainly, it can be so, because its utility is seen even in common worldly practice, like the polishing of a mirror. The intention here is this: when a purpose must be inferred, even a perceptible one—

Since a purpose that is capable of being fulfilled by removing a deficiency cannot be abandoned, it is therefore logical that this restriction (niyama) is a human goal (puruṣārtha) consisting of a mental resolve (saṃkalpa). Furthermore, because a visible purpose is impossible, it has been stated that even the *karkarī* and *karṇa* [vessels] serve human goals.

Even the characteristics of the *gokarṇa*—such as "the *karkarī* and *karṇa* vessels should be made with cow-ear-shaped handles"—are visible purificatory acts (*dṛṣṭasaṃskāra*) performed upon substances connected to the sacrifice.
It is established that, by virtue of his nature, only one who seeks the human goals (*puruṣārtha*) and only a cowherd (*gomān*) is entitled [to the ritual].
(1) G. *nāprasajya* (2) G. *kartṛkaraṇādayo’pi* (3) G. *kartarīkarṇyaḥ* [p. 969]

Regarding the substances: [An objection is raised]—"But was it not stated in the third [chapter] that the application of the wooden sword (sphya) and other implements is restricted solely to the acts of digging (uddhanana) and so forth?

How then can it be suspected here that they might apply elsewhere? To this, he says: "It has been stated," and so on. What is meant is this: the investigation into the application of the sentences concerning digging and so forth was conducted together with the passage beginning with "And the wooden sword" (*sphyaśca*). In that context, the sentences regarding digging and so forth were established as the means of application (*viniyojaka*).

[The topic] is established. Now this is being considered: regarding the statement, "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements," is this a separate scripture [independent] from such texts as "One digs with the wooden sword" (*sphya*), or is it a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those very same things? Thus he shows another point of consideration. [Objection: But surely this consideration belongs to the second chapter, concerning the distinction or non-distinction of scriptures. Why is it being considered here in the fourth chapter? It is said: for the purpose of establishing separate performance (*pṛthak-prayukti*).

A reflection on the meaning of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is now made. If this were a separate scripture (*śāstrāntara*), then it would have to be employed independently as a direct means for accomplishing the sacrifice; however, under the view of non-difference (*abheda*), because there is no distinction between the scriptures, there is no separate employment. To the question, "What kind of reflection on the meaning of the second case is intended? he says: Is this sentence characterized by difference (*bheda-lakṣaṇa*) due to the difference in the goal (*sādhya-bheda*) in the view that it prescribes another accessory (*guṇāntara-vidhāna*)?

If, however, there is the injunction of another action possessing specific qualities, then because of the difference in the subordinate elements (*anubandha*), it constitutes a distinct act; whereas if it is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), there is no difference in the subordinate elements of the goal to be accomplished, and thus it is characterized by non-difference. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers that in sentences such as "he digs with a wooden sword" (*sphya*), since a direct connection with the sacrifice is not perceived, this must be a separate injunction [of sacrificial implements], as in the statement "these are the sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhāni*). The intention is this: the term *yajñāyudhāni* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*)...

This is as follows: although the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs when there is a mere relationship, nevertheless, since a direct relationship is possible, it is not proper to resort to an indirect one; thus, only a direct connection with the sacrifice is understood. And this [connection] is not already established such that it would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, "the statements are indeed [injunctions], because they convey what is unprecedented" (*ato vacanāni tvapūrvatvāt*).

Thus, this is also an injunction (*vidhi*). And that [injunction] prescribes a substance only for the *āgneya* and other offerings. For those [offerings] are already occupied by another quality; therefore, [this injunction establishes] a different ritual action (*karmāntara*) endowed with a different quality. Now, one might object: "An indirect connection is also possible, just as in the case of 'the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of the *vājapeya*'. This is appropriate in that case because of the absence of a sacrificial post for the sacrifice. But it is not so here.

(1) Nor should it be said that [the seventeen-ell measure] will be enjoined; for the sentence is intent upon enjoining the seventeen-ell measure, and in the case of a restatement (anuvāda), it follows whatever has been previously established.

Even through an indirect means (*praṇāḍyā*), [the primary sense] is resorted to. But here, since even a direct injunction (*vidhāna*) is possible, what is not tenable? This is the intended meaning. To this, it is replied: first of all, the term "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhāni*) involves figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And if there is figurative indication, there is no difference whether it is direct or mediated. The meaning of this is as follows: by the word "sacrificial implement," the means of accomplishing that [sacrifice] is not denoted directly; rather, [it is denoted] through figurative indication.

That which is related to it is indicated [by implication]. If this is indication based on a relationship (*saṃbandhilakṣaṇā*), then there is no distinction between direct connection and indirect mediation, because the nature of being related remains the same in both cases. Therefore, since the word *yajñāyudha* (sacrificial implements) conveys a direct relationship, one cannot claim that its meaning is already established (*prāptārthatā*). [Objection: But in that case, it would also not be possible to claim with certainty that its meaning is already established. [Reply: True—but [this applies] only where there is an absence of an injunction (*vidhi*).

This statement is one that assumes a ritual injunction (*kalpyavidhika*). Such an assumption is only made when there is an inconsistency (*anupapatti*); however, here there is no inconsistency, because the meaning is established by resorting to a mediated relationship through the act of stirring (*uddhanana*). Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) and not an injunction (*vidhi*). On this very point, he states another argument: "Metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) follows another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And when another means of knowledge already exists, it is impossible to postulate yet another. [In the case of] the *sphya*...

It does not mean "one should not dig," because that is established for both parties. Furthermore, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is well-known in common usage, as in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā.

In that case, when [the word "Gaṅgā"] indicates the bank of the Gaṅgā, it is because the presence of the hamlet on the bank is known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, here too, since it is established by another means of valid cognition, it is proper to rely on a relationship mediated precisely by digging and so forth. Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

And in this way, the dilemma is resolved. If there is an injunction of material in the *āgneya* and other sacrifices, then the dilemma regarding [the choice between] the *puroḍāśa* and so forth is resolved. Furthermore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) becomes consistent. If it were an injunction of a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*), then, because it would be unmanifest due to the absence of a deity, the application of the procedure (*vidhyanta*) pertaining to the Soma sacrifice would follow; consequently, the observation of the number of offerings (*āhuti*) would not be possible. Likewise...
By virtue of occupying the place of Soma, the wooden sword (sphya) and other implements pressed [for the sacrifice] would not be seen at the concluding rite (paridhānīya-karma).
(1) G. dvārakasya [p. 971]

And in that context, oneness (*ekatva*) is not a constituent part of the sacrifice. [Objection: But surely oneness and so forth are expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*) as being connected to the task (*kārya*); therefore, because it is a constituent of the task, if it were not employed, the task itself would not be accomplished. To this, he says: "Oneness is not a constituent of the sacrifice due to the absence of application (*viniyoga*). This is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*). The meaning of this is as follows: although oneness is grasped by the "grasper" (*grāhaka*), nevertheless...

Because there is no application (*viniyoga*), because there is no connection with a door (*dvāra*), and because in the absence of that [connection], a general relationship (*sāmānyasaṃbandha*) cannot be established, it is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice. But how is it that oneness (*ekatva*) is not applied? For case-endings (*vibhakti*) express the relationship of their own meaning (*svārtha*) with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), since their own meaning—such as instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and so forth—is related to the meaning of the nominal stem; however, they do not [express] those things which constitute their own meaning...
The case endings express relations such as "having made" (kṛtvā) and so forth. Therefore, both oneness and instrumentality belong to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself;

it is not that oneness possesses the state of being an instrument. And since, in the absence of instrumentality, there would be no connection with the action, [oneness] would not be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice. For if there were a connection with the instrument, then through that instrumentality, there would be a connection with the action, and thus no connection with the meaning of the nominal stem. As in the case of "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*), [the connection is with the action].

In the case of a relation, there is no relation between substance and quality; therefore, even though it is perceived, this [gender] is not connected with the action, just as in the expression "the eastern one runs," there is the cognition of "the other. By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even though it is perceived," he says this: because of the absence of connection with the action, it is simply not denotable as being integrated into the function (*kāryānvayi*). Even if it were denoted, it would still be non-essential (*anaṅga*). These are the observations of the indicative marks (*liṅgadarśanāni*).

And thus they become established. This being the case, it is said: the status of being an auxiliary to an action does not arise from application (*viniyoga*) alone; rather, it is by virtue of [the agent's] intention (*bhāva*). What then? It is that which is not to be performed [by that intention].

Remainderhood (*śeṣatā*) also arises from being an object of appropriation (*upādāna*). Just as there is appropriation only of that which has become an instrument (*karaṇa*), so too there is [appropriation] of that which is connected with singularity. For just as there is no appropriation of that which has not become an instrument, so too there is none of that which is not connected with a number. The intention is that the appropriation of something that is not an instrument is not possible even for that which is connected with a non-number. First of all, the animal is enjoined and must be appropriated; and it...

Without number, it is impossible to grasp [the object]; and that oneness residing therein is what is heard [in the text]. Moreover, that [oneness] is heard as being connected with the ritual action (*kārya*). For its inclusion [in the action], it necessarily requires a substratum. Therefore, just like that [action], it is accepted as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

And once accepted, being situated within that which is employed [in the rite], it attains the status of a subsidiary (*aṅga*) by virtue of its location therein. For number, by its own inherent capacity, [establishes] its own countable object as subordinate—

It has come into being; for that [word], having previously resided in the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), has now, in its state of being employed, become assigned to a specific function. Its status as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*), however, follows from the mark (*liṅga*) characterized by the very nature of the thing itself; thus there is no fault. And so, worldly people understand it in exactly that way in expressions such as "bring the cow. But surely the author of the Bhāṣya states, on the strength of the sentence (*vākya*), that [the word] is subordinate to the action?

Regarding the point that [the meaning] is not obtained through *upādāna* (inclusion), he says here: "That which has been stated by us has also been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya with these words: 'The Śruti does not declare that there is no sentence-meaning.
To the question "How was this stated?", he replies: "Inclusion (*viniyoga*) does not declare the *upādāna*."

The meaning is that [the action] does not exist. Now, an entirely different meaning is perceived; there is no contradiction with the direct statement (*śruti*) of the sentence, because from the sentence the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*) is understood without abandoning the meaning of the *śruti*. It has been stated that in case of contradiction, there is weakness [of the sentence]. (1) P. 1205 (2) G. tadaivāva (3) G. śrutyaparityāgena.

To this, the reply is as follows: We have already stated that no application (*viniyoga*) is possible; even by means of a sentence (*vākya*), there is no application because there is no comprehension of a connection with an action. Therefore, this Bhāṣya is not to be explained according to its literal reading. How, then, is the sentence—?

The word "śabdaḥ" (the verbal expression) is a synonym for "samabhivyāhāra" (co-utterance), not a synonym for "viniyojaka" (that which enjoins). In a single sentence, both the action and its singularity are co-uttered; by virtue of that [co-utterance], there is the status of being a subordinate element through the act of taking up [the object]. Therefore, the meaning is that the status of being a subsidiary to the action is stated precisely because of this. Consequently, it is established that number and gender possess the status of being subordinate elements through the act of taking up [the object]. Now, [one might object]: "In the spring..."

In the case of the injunction, "In the morning, one should sacrifice a black-necked animal dedicated to Agni," how can the gender (liṅga) be considered subordinate to the act of procurement (upādānaśeṣa), given that it is expressed by the nominal stem portion and assigned its function by the case-ending, just like the meaning denoted by the nominal stem itself? It is replied: the meaning which is conveyed as the primary element by the nominal stem...

In that very case, the gender expressed by the feminine suffix, as well as the case-role (kārakatva) and number, are understood as the meaning of the inflectional ending (*vibhakti*). However, this is not because the gender is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) dependent solely on its primary substratum (*pradhāna*). Since the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) alone—devoid of gender—is already understood by the initial utterance of the nominal stem portion, the meaning of the inflectional ending is connected with that [stem-meaning] alone; thus, the principle is the same.

By way of number: thus the views are established. And the view of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Or rather: what is the intention of one who says that the section concerning the indicative mark (*liṅga-adhikaraṇa*) is "again thus" (*punarevam vā*)? Its meaning is this: for it was stated in the preceding section that even the indicative mark is subsidiary to the act of taking up (*upādāna-śeṣa*). What else, then, is being considered here once again?

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) lacks definitiveness. For number, being determinative, expresses the measure (*parimāṇa*) of a substance. The meaning of this is as follows: when other numbers are employed, because there is a difference in the measure of the factors of action (*kāraka*), the performance [of the ritual] would become manifold.

Because it is expressed by word, when there is a requirement for a specific number, that [number] is subsidiary to the act of taking up (*upādāna*). However, in the case of gender (*liṅga*), since there is no taking up of another substance, it does not bring about a specific performance; therefore, a requirement for a specific [gender] is not justified, and thus it is not subsidiary to the act of taking up. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that gender is also taken up because there is no difference in its being heard [in the text]. Just as the number is heard, so too is the gender. But [an objection]:

This is a reminder of what was stated previously: that because it does not bring about a specific measure (*aparimāṇāpādakatvāt*), the gender (*liṅga*) need not be taken into account. To refute this, [the author] states:

"In this case, the measure (*parimāṇa*) is not required for the taking [of the material], because the taking is directed toward a specific [object]. Just as there is an expectation for a specific mode of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-viśeṣa*), so too is there an expectation for a specific grammatical factor (*kāraka-viśeṣa*). Therefore, the gender (*liṅga*) which brings about a specific grammatical factor must also be taken into account. Consequently, the number (*saṅkhyā*)..."
Thus, it is established that [the term] refers to the taking up (*upādāna*). The remainder is as before.

This applies without distinction to those things which have a substratum (*āśrayiṣu*). Here, the categories of things possessing a substratum are the examples (*udāharaṇa*). An example has been presented in order to raise a doubt. Now, is the Bhāṣya incorrect when it asks: "Is the sacrifice itself merely a purification (*saṃskāra*) of the deity, or is an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the sacrifice?"
Since it would be purposeless for that which does not produce an unseen effect (*adṛṣṭa*) to be performed as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the deity; and because even in cases such as threshing,

the restrictive unseen effect (*niyamādṛṣṭa*) must be accepted— otherwise the restriction would be entirely meaningless— therefore, even in the view that it is a refinement (*saṃskārapakṣe*), [the same applies].

1207 (2) Regarding the statement that "there exists a seen [result] for that," he says: it has been declared to be of two kinds. That which restates an injunction already attained by another is, for example, "he threshes" in the case of the Āgneya [offering].

[The sentence] "He offers the *samit* oblation" (*samidho yajati*) is a restatement of an injunction (*niyoga*) understood through the original injunction (*codanā*), and it serves as a means for qualification (*adhikāra*) by virtue of its connection to its own injunction, because one accepts that there is a distinct originating injunction (*utpatti-niyoga*) for each [such sentence]. Now, a doubt arises here: is this verb a restatement of an injunction already obtained elsewhere, or does it serve as a means for qualification by virtue of its connection to its own injunction? This is what is meant: [regarding] the refinement (*saṃskāra*)—

In the view that [the sacrifice] pertains only to the material (*mātra*), there is no further injunction; thus, it is held that an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) is produced in the deity. Here, "unseen" refers to the *apūrva*. Therefore, this is the meaning of the Bhāṣya: when the deity is being consecrated, the supreme *apūrva* is produced by the act of sacrificing (*yajati*). Consequently, this is a doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of another *apūrva*. Why is there such a doubt? Because, in one part, the action culminates in the oblation (*homa*), while in the other part, it consists in the casting of the material (*dravyaprakṣepa*).

Since the visible [result]— namely, the purgative effect of the substance as well as the recollection of the deity through the mantra which constitutes its subordinate part— is possible, and since the invisible [result] is possible through the sacrificial part, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that, because no other visible result is possible through that [sacrificial] part, it is not logical to postulate an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) or to postulate another *apūrva* when the visible benefit residing in the substance and the deity already exists. By means of that [benefit], [the sacrifice serves]...

Because it is assumed to be an integral part of the ritual action (*kārāṅga*). Now, an objection is raised: "In this case, the purpose of the sacrifice (*yajyartha*) is not accomplished; since there is no visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāra*) in that respect, it does not enter into the sphere of the qualified person’s obligation (*adhikāra*), and thus, due to the absence of its being prompted by that qualification, the purpose of the sacrifice would not be accomplished. The intention [of the objector] is that it will serve the purpose of fulfilling a visible result through performance, just as the mantras and so forth do in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*) and other such acts. To this, it is replied: "The visible..."

Why is it that the very purpose of origination (*utpatti*) is not tenable? Because the accomplishment of the injunction (*niyoga*) is not intended [as its primary meaning]. This is because the accomplishment of the injunction for origination is [established] by way of what has already been explained.

Because it is intended [to be expressed]. Nevertheless, he asks "Why so? and replies: "For activity proceeds from an injunction (niyoga) toward the object of that injunction. The intention here is this: if the injunction were not intended to be expressed, the mere sacrifice (*yajati*), being momentary, would not serve the purpose of the injunction regarding the qualification (*adhikāra*). And if it did not serve that purpose, there would be no activity directed toward it; for since activity arises from an injunction, it is directed toward the object of the injunction, and not toward something that is not the object of an injunction. [Objection: But what of the subsidiary part of the sacrifice?

It has been stated that there is subsidiarity (*aṅgatā*) by way of the substance and the deity. It is replied: first of all, the sacrifice does not have the substance and the deity as its purpose directly;

rather, it does so through the mantra which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*). And if that [subsidiarity] occurs by means of the subsidiary, there is a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatā*): once the status of being the object of the injunction (*niyoga*) is established, there is a connection with the subsidiary; and when there is a connection with the subsidiary, there is the status of being the object of the injunction by way of the substance and the deity. For there is no connection with the dharma in that which is merely the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and lacks a connection to a injunction.

Regarding the word "ghaṭate" (it fits): if, for that purpose—that is, for the sake of the *adhikāra* (qualification/entitlement)—the *utpatti-niyoga* (origination-injunction) is intended, then the fact that [the sacrifice] has the *apūrva* as its purpose is established.

Subsequently, once it is determined that the sacrifice serves the *adhikāra-niyoga* and its connection with the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is settled, it is indeed accepted that [the sacrifice] exists for the sake of accomplishing visible purificatory effects (*dṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) pertaining to the substance and the deity by means of those subsidiaries. Therefore, this is a third mode of restating the *niyoga*.
The phrase "by means of its own [obligation] and that which is connected to it" is concluded according to the view of others.

He states his own view: "Nor is this a third category, because the accomplishment of the obligation is identical, and thus the connection to its own obligation already exists, as in the case of the *samidh* and other [subsidiary offerings]. [Objection: But if this is so, then even in the absence of the substance, there would be no [need for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering].

Regarding that, he says: "There is an omission. Whether the purpose be visible (*dṛṣṭa*) or invisible (*adṛṣṭa*), and whether there be performance or non-performance based on that purpose—this is the meaning:

even though the fulfillment of the injunction (*niyoga*) exists, nevertheless, because it is visible, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the substance and so forth alone is the motivator (*prayojaka*). The purpose of the injunction, however, is not the motivator at all. Therefore, in the absence of the substance, there is an omission of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; for this reason.
The status of being the object of its own injunction is established:
(1) the origin [of the rite], (2) the injunction for production, and (3) subsequently, the qualification [to perform it].

"Thus, there is equality or inequality in the purpose of substances and actions; the third subject matter has been transcended. What is this "third subject matter"? This question is asked with the intention: "If this is the third subject matter, why is it being considered in the fourth [chapter]?
The answer here is: "The realization of subservience to another (pārārthya). That has been transcended. The intention is as follows: although this realization of subservience to another...

That has been transcended. This is the intended meaning: although this comprehension of being for the sake of another exists, it is nevertheless not established here by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth; rather, it is considered here as being based solely on the operation of the injunction (*niyoga*). Now, however, since being for the sake of another is established, only "appropriation" (*upādāna*) is considered. Appropriation is "impulsion" (*prayukti*); that is what is being considered: for what purpose is the appropriation of the *āmikṣā* and other such things?

"By what means? [The opponent asks: "But surely even prior to this, the consideration of the material cause (*upādāna*) was already based on the purpose (*prayojana*). Since the material cause of number and the other categories is likewise produced by the material cause itself, by what distinction is it said that 'this [is the case] now'? [The author replies: "True.

However, even that state of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) is caused by that [material cause] alone, and not caused by a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*). Therefore, this was stated as referring to the third subject matter."

This is the subject matter of the third [section], yet it cannot be understood by means of the third types of evidence (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it was deliberated upon in the fourth [section] that its subservience to another (*pārārthya*) is caused solely by an injunction (*vidhi*). And this has been explained [in the passage]: "Not by direct assertion (*śruti*) and so forth is everything... (P.
"It is possible to establish that [the sacrifice] is for the sake of another.
This very point is stated here; and thus, regarding the sacrifice and its fruit:

On the basis of the context (*adhikāra*), he will explain in the first section of the sixth book that [the sacrifice] exists for the sake of another (*pārārthya*). By the force of understanding the relationship characterized by the *niyoga* (injunction) and the *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined), he will explain that the sacrifice is subordinate (*śeṣatva*) to heaven as its fruit, and that the fruit is subordinate to the person. Precisely because the subordination of the sacrifice and the fruit is not understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof, Bādari held this misconception that subordination exists only in the case of substances, qualities, and preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*). [This is so despite] the existence of direct statements and the rest [of the proofs].

In this regard, because [subsidiariness] is possible in respect to substances and so forth, it is determined by one who does not perceive the capacity for either material cause (*upādāna*) or qualification (*adhikāra*). And by saying this, it has been stated that although the *Bādari-adhikaraṇa* belongs in the fourth chapter, it was placed in the third precisely to remove the intervening distance.
Precisely because this subsidiariness (*śeṣatva*) is not based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the like, it is said to be a different definition.

Even though the understanding of the remainder is equal [to that of the primary], because of the accomplishment of one [act], from this point forward only the operation of the material cause (*upādāna*) and only its application (*prayukti*) are considered. However, the status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣatā*) arises solely from the application (*viniyoga*), not from the material cause. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), however, [argues] based on the observation of the mere benefit...

He states that it is the deity that is the material cause (*upādāna*), and he considers that nothing else remains to be expected; just as in the case of the animal, its singularity, and so forth, which are subordinate to the material cause.
(1) By means of direct statement (*śruti*) and the other criteria, the fact that everything is for the sake of another is (2) capable of being understood and (3) is definitively established.

The meaning of this is as follows: the bringing of the curd is beneficial to both the *āmikṣā* (coagulated milk) and the *vājina* (whey). Even if, at most, it is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) with respect to the *āmikṣā*, the impelling force (*prayukti*) is based on its utility (*upakāra*) and not on its status as a subordinate element; for even in the case of singularity and other such qualities, which were previously not subordinate elements, they are nevertheless taken up simply by virtue of being employed.

Since it is a subordinate element (*śeṣatā*), therefore both [the curd and the whey] are motivators (*prayojaka*). To this, it is replied: here the whey (*vājina*) is not a motivator. Why? Because only that which is a subordinate element has a requirement for a purpose (*prayojanākāṅkṣā*). And since that requirement is satisfied by the very purpose belonging to that of which it is subordinate, it is impossible to conceive another purpose as being a motivator. The meaning of this is: the bringing of curd (*dadhyānayana*) is a subordinate element.

The inquiry "by what purpose should it be employed? constitutes the expectation for a specific motivator (*prayojaka*). In that regard, it is logical that the very milk of which the [curd] is a remnant (*śeṣa*) is the motivator; for it is understood from the words as being connected to that [milk]. And curd (*āmikṣā*) is indeed milk, because its flavor is recognized within that very [curd]. We shall explain this in the *Vivaraṇapañcikā*. Therefore, that [curd] alone is the motivator, and not [the other].

The term *vājinam* is established [as the object]. But how can that which is not a subordinate element (*aśeṣabhūta*)—such as singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth—be subordinate to the material cause (*upādānaśeṣatva*)? For that which is not a subordinate element has no requirement for a purpose (*prayojanākāṅkṣā*). How can singularity and the like, being non-subordinate, be subordinate to the material cause? Because if they were non-subordinate, the very notion of a "material cause" would be untenable. To this it is replied: because a subordinate element is understood; for that which is subordinate, such as the animal (*paśu*) and so forth, its singularity— [...is subordinate to the material cause. (Note: The provided fragment ends here.)

It is not the case that what is empty is not apprehended, for it is not accepted as being devoid of that [apprehension]; otherwise, there would be no apprehension, since acceptance is preceded by apprehension. Furthermore, because it is impossible for that which has become a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to be employed otherwise than through its subordinate status—for indeed, the employment of the animal, which has become a subordinate element, is not possible otherwise. Why? Because it is not possible to accept something that is not delimited.

Thus it has been said. For it is not possible to take up [a portion] that is not delimited by number; therefore, for the sake of taking up the remainder, there must be the taking up of the entirety as well, because of the requirements of the remaining ritual acts.
(1) G. From the perspective of the remaining rites [p. 980].

Furthermore, that which is understood to be neither a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) nor situated within a subsidiary, because the status of being a subsidiary is understood even without it, and because it does not depend upon the employment of a subsidiary—since the employment of a subsidiary is established even without it—that cannot be something to be employed (*prayojya*). This is just as the bringing of curd (*dadhyānayana*) is not a subsidiary of the whey (*vājina*), as demonstrated in the Bhāṣya. And thus the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been shown.
The act of placing the foot is not the motivator [of the action]. What, then, is the distinction between this and the preceding section?

For just as the bringing of the curd is motivated by that very thing which is a remnant of the *āmikṣā* and not by the *vājina*, so too the one-year-old cow is a remnant of the purchase; therefore, its bringing is also a remnant of the purchase through that very means, and thus it must be motivated by the purchase itself, not by the dust of the footprint. This is the distinction.

For in that case, the bringing of the curd produces the *vājina* at the very same time as the production of the *āmikṣā*. Therefore, it is logical that the production of the *vājina* does not depend on any other cause. The meaning of this is as follows: although the bringing of the curd is subsidiary to the *āmikṣā*, nevertheless, if the *vājina* were also produced separately [from it], then, in view of the need for a cause, the aforementioned bringing of the curd would apply there as well.

It would be employed as a cause. And since that [seventh step] is produced solely by the *āmikṣā*, it is not logical to employ the curd under discussion there by depending on another cause. Here, however, when it is said "the seventh step," an expectancy arises as to "whose? and because of the context, it is understood to belong to the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*). Since they have different modes of production, when there is an expectancy for another cause here, it is only the one-year-old cow that—

[Page r981] Since that which is expected is connected, one considers the word "purchase" (kraya) to have a dual purpose: it serves both its own meaning and the meaning of the "one-year-old cow" (ekahāyanī). This being the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the following is stated: It is true that if an expectation of "whose? were logically possible, then, in the presence of that expectancy, the one-year-old cow would be connected [to the purchase] by its mere form alone.
It is not by way of being a remnant of the purchase that the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) would serve both purposes; for here there is no expectancy at all as to "for whom?
because when a related entity is taught while another related entity remains unknown, cognition arises preceded by expectancy.
In a case where another related entity has not been previously perceived, the understanding of the related entity manifests with expectancy as its precursor.

Furthermore, where the instruction is preceded by another related entity, there the relationship is understood according to that comprehension; as was established in the case of the "receiving of horses" (*aśvapratigraha*), the instruction is indeed preceded by a known related entity. Therefore, the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) connected to the seventh step is for the purpose of purchase alone, and is not [used] otherwise, because it is the very one intended for purchase that is the subject under discussion, and such is its relationship.

[This is] because it has already been understood [by that]. Here, the objection raised by one who is confused due to hearing the word "prasaṅga" in the Bhāṣya—namely, “by one who relies upon a *prasaṅga*”—is as follows:
"But surely this is the definition of the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the non-instigator (*aprayojaka*); what occasion is there for a *prasaṅga*? For when [the definition] exists..."

Regarding the state of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*), the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) was stated: "In this very way, the same consequence would apply if one's own rule were already present.

Here, it is argued that there is no such thing as an instigator at all. To this it is replied: This was stated by accepting the consequence regarding the *śāstra* (the grammatical treatise), not the consequence regarding actual usage (*prayoga*).
This is not a fault. The meaning is as follows: by the scriptural injunction, "One purchases Soma with a one-year-old tawny-eyed cow," the one-year-old cow is prescribed.

That very same cow is connected to another scriptural rule, "He takes the seventh step," and thus there is no occasion for a separate performance; this is what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya, and therefore there is no fault.

And the function of denoting the object will be performed by that which is yet to come. Regarding the statement, "He winnows the husks with the cake-potsherd," the opponent in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that there is no possibility of the scriptural injunction applying here; thus, he considers that the potsherd also possesses the status of an instrument (*prayoktṛtva*) for the winnowing of husks. Nor is it the case that...
The addition [of the husks] cannot be said to be invariably concomitant [with the purpose], like the *bājina* [offering]. Therefore, both are motivators (*prayojaka*).

The meaning of this is as follows: in the statement, “He scatters the husks with the cake-pan (*puroḍāśakapāla*),” there is no direct mention of the cake-pan itself [as being for the sake of scattering].

Furthermore, there is a re-grasping [of the term] by virtue of its being the subject under discussion, as in the case of the *ekahāyanī* cow. Therefore, the *puroḍāśakapāla* (the cake-pan) mentioned in its own sentence is enjoined by that very sentence even for the purpose of scattering [the grains]. Now, an objection is raised: the term *puroḍāśakapāla* refers to a pan related to the *puroḍāśa* cake, specifically one that remains as a residue from the cooking (*śrapaṇa*). It is not possible for that which is a residue of one thing to become a residue of another; it is like something already engaged elsewhere being engaged elsewhere. How, then, can it be used for scattering?

The application [of the mantra] is by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*). It is said in reply: for syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) cannot be established without a relationship of subordinate and principal.

In this case, the husks (*tuṣa*), which serve the purpose of igniting the fire, do not have a subordinate relationship toward the potsherds (*kapāla*); rather, it is the potsherd itself that has a subordinate relationship toward them. Nor is there a contradiction between what has already been applied and what is being applied, because the application is justified through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the substratum.

For a contradiction regarding the application of what has already been applied is indeed a contradiction regarding the performance [of the rite]. And that would occur only if the application were accepted in the very form of that which has already been applied. However, when the substance itself, as characterized by its prior application, is applied, then there is no contradiction. Nor is the scattering of husks an indispensable factor, such that there would be no dependence on other causes.

There would be no application [of the rule]. Therefore, since there is no distinction in the application, both are the motivators; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this, it is replied: It is true that there is no occasion for the scripture regarding the application, nor is there any contradiction with the necessary implication (*nāntarīyakapratīti*).
[This is] the state of being.
However, this application of what has been taken up does not extend to the assumption of its acquisition. The meaning of this is as follows:

in the expression "the *kapāla* for the *puroḍāśa*," the *kapāla* is indicated by virtue of its connection with the *puroḍāśa*; it is that very [vessel] which is indicated because of its connection with the *puroḍāśa*.

It is the state of being a substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatā*), just as the bank of the Gaṅgā, though being perceived, is perceived precisely as something related to itself. And since that potsherd has been taken up for the purpose of cooking, this application (*viniyoga*) concerns an object already appropriated. Therefore, he says: "The postulation of appropriation does not follow. This is what will be stated by the future [author]: "This is a connection with the future, not with the past or the present. For when there is a connection with the future...

It is simply the state of having an object that has been grasped (*upāttaviṣayatā*). There is no room for appropriation (*upādāna*). If, moreover, there is a connection with the past and the present, what would constitute appropriation?
This is merely a question. "It is said" is the answer:
[it is] not that which is a relation belonging to the past.
Since that which is for a future purpose is not yet appropriated, its protection will indeed come later; for appropriation itself is essentially a form of protection.
Furthermore, even regarding that which belongs to something present, because it is occupied elsewhere, its application to another purpose is impossible;

thus, by implication, something else must be appropriated. However, in the case of being for a future purpose, [the appropriation] concerns that which was already taken up, accepted, and maintained for the sake of another.

It is established that the application (*viniyoga*) is possible, and thus [the opponent's argument] lacks a proving motive (*aprayojakatva*). Now, if this is so, one might ask: "In a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) where there is no baking of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), how can the scattering of husks (*upavāpa*) be performed without the cake-pan (*kapāla*)? To this he replies: whether the scattering of husks should be performed or not performed is not the subject matter of this section (*adhikaraṇa*). This is because the conclusion of the section is established in every respect through the *agnihotra*— [The text continues: ...the *agnihotra*... [The text appears to be truncated here].
It is understood that it must indeed be performed according to the principle of the *havani* (the sacrificial ladle);

for there is no mention of the immolation (*ālambha*) in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). In this section, there is the statement regarding the cutting out of the heart and other organs, as well as the statement regarding the simultaneous striking (*saṃpravyādha*).

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that both [the injunctions] are motivators (*prayojaka*), because both are understood as referring to the subject at hand (*prakṛta*)—namely, the animal sacrifice—by virtue of their equal application to the topic under discussion, as in the statement: "One should immolate the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma" (*agnīṣomīyaṃ paśumālabheta*). The meaning of this is as follows: although [the specific rule] "One should immolate the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma" applies...

At first glance, it may appear that the animal itself is dedicated to Agni and Soma; nevertheless, because the animal is destroyed upon hearing the command for its slaughter, the sacrificial materials belonging to the animal possess the status of being dedicated to Agni and Soma. The white and the red [blood] likewise belong specifically to the animal; therefore, they too are connected to the deities. Furthermore, the animal's dedication to Agni and Soma is established by its being the source-material (*prakṛti-dravya*) for the substance intended for the sacrifice. Nor should it be argued as follows:

The animal itself is the object [of the sacrifice] for the sake of the heart and so forth; for in both cases, the animal is grasped as the material cause (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, there is no direct scriptural mention (*sākṣāt-śravaṇa*) of it in the sentence concerning the heart and other parts. Moreover, because of their connection with the deities, the discarding (*nirāsana*) and the striking (*saṃpravyādha*) will serve as the disposal of the remnants (*śeṣa-pratipatti*) for the blood and the dung, which have already become subsidiary elements of the sacrifice. How, then, can there be a suspicion that these two [blood and dung] are the motivators (*prayojaka*)? It is said: not the discarding...

The status of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) is stated for the two things possessing the wound (*sapravyādha*), namely blood and excrement alone. And since these two are intended for the sacrifice, it is logical that they motivate the animal, which is the primary substance for the sacrifice; thus there is no fault.
To this, it is replied: "He cuts off first from the heart"—this is a summary of the sacrifice. This is the intended meaning here.

It is true that the animal itself does not directly serve the purpose of the sacrifice; rather, it is only the substances connected to the animal that directly serve the purpose of the sacrifice by way of assisting the substances related to it. That [direct sacrificial purpose], however, is restricted to the heart and other such parts, because of the scriptural statement: "With the limbs, at the third pressing. What is meant is this: since there is the scriptural mention of "with the limbs," the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatā*) belongs first and foremost to the limbs.

It is determined as follows: even in that case, since the heart and other parts are seen to undergo the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of cutting out (*avadāna*) for their natural functions, and since this is logically consistent with their being employed for the purpose of the sacrifice, it is those alone—and not others—that have the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*yāgārthatā*). This is because blood, dung, and so forth, which belong to the animal, are not constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the ritual.

And because [the acts] begin with the heart and so forth. However, the single piercing (*saṃpravyādha*) terminates at that point alone, because both the throwing away (*nirasana*) and the piercing are of a stationary nature and do not enter into any other action. It is a disposal (*pratipatti*), because it serves as a substratum for a substance that has arrived by way of association with the animal under discussion for the sake of the sacrifice, and which is fit for disposal. Now, one might object: "That very [piercing] shall employ the substance. Anticipating this, [the author states: "The well-known [nature] of disposal..."

He has demonstrated the impossibility of the substance being the motivator (*prayojaka*). Furthermore, the disposal (*pratipatti*) is not a motivator, according to the maxim: "That which is to be disposed of is not taken up for the sake of the disposal. Therefore, the dung of the animal and so forth are not motivators; this is the summary of the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇa*).

And [the rule] regarding a substance consisting of a single part applies at the time of its production. Now, one might object that the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself is untenable here, because the scriptural statement, "He cuts off for the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the northern half," refers to a substance already appropriated; that is, it concerns the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) which has already been taken up.

Thus the latter half [of the verse] is understood. And since that [object] is a specific substance (*dravya*) whose purpose has already been fulfilled, this is a cognition of a substance. Furthermore, cognition itself is not the motivating factor [for action]. Anticipating the question, "How then can it have as its object a substance already employed? he says: "Because the remainder is understood, like a piece of sugarcane.
For example: "Give him a piece of sugarcane."
Thus, in that case, a fragment of the *ikṣu* (sugarcane) that is present is understood, not one that is absent;
likewise here as well, because of the understanding that it is the remnant of the offering of the *puroḍāśa* which is present, the [act] has as its object a substance already employed. This is true.

However, in this case, because the *puroḍāśa* serves another purpose—namely, for the sake of the *Āgneya* sacrifice—it should not be used elsewhere for another function, such as the *Sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice.

The application (*viniyoga*) is thus established; for if it were used to perform another function than that of sacrifice, it would contradict the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). This is prohibited by virtue of its being the subject under discussion (*prakṛtatva*).
[p. 986] (1) G. pratiṣiddham.

Even in the case of the taking [of the portion], because it is untenable to apply the substance merely as a substrate—according to the logic of the *puroḍāśa*-cake and the *kapāla*-pot—the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that another substance must be procured. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) has argued that the completion of the *Āgneya* sacrifice is achieved by the mere two-fold cutting (*dvayavadāna*) alone; he has presented this for the purpose of making the application elsewhere possible after the completion of the sacrifice. In this regard:

What is the intention? This is the intention: it is true that the sacrifice is accomplished by the mere offering of the two portions (*dvayavadāna*), but the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) itself is not thereby established as being for that purpose [of the recipient]. Because even the two portions intended for the recipient are in fact for the sake of the sacrifice; therefore, he gave this answer: "True. There would be a contradiction with the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) if it were given to another, for in that case, what is being given would be for the sake of the recipient."

That is not tenable. Therefore, its application cannot possibly be for anything other than the purpose of the sacrifice. Furthermore, it cannot be said that it serves another purpose by virtue of being the effect of the sacrifice. That which has the Āgneya and other sacrifices as its effect—that state of being such—cannot be said to serve another purpose; rather, the disposal (*pratipatti*) is for the sake of the sacrifice, by means of the offering of the substance belonging to it, [just as] the head of Devadatta is [disposed of].

Like a garland, its placement in a pure location is for the sake of Devadatta; therefore, there is no contradiction with the injunctions regarding the Agneya and other offerings. Consequently, it is established that there is no taking [of the portion] according to the maxim of the unopposed sugarcane-cube. This is because we see the remainder [in the rule]: "From the remainder, he cuts off for the Sviṣṭakṛt. Thus, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that there is a scriptural injunction for equal cutting-off (*samavadāna*).
Regarding the pouring over (*abhidhāraṇa*): what, then, is distinguished here by the *puroḍāśa*-potsherd? The meaning of this is: let it be—(1) G.

The pouring of the clarified butter (ājya) is a purposeful act (*arthakarma*) for the sake of the principal oblations (*havir*). Nevertheless, because there is a scriptural injunction regarding the remnant (*śeṣa*) taken up for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings, another substance need not be procured. This is just as, although it is a purposeful act, another potsherd is not procured when one hears the scriptural statement, "with the cake-potsherd" (*puroḍāśakapālena*). Therefore, since there is no difference in the result, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) should not be commenced. [The author] refutes this:

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is as follows: it is already established that there is no taking up of the substance [the grains] in that manner; however, the taking up of the vessel for holding is not contradicted because the oblation (havis) is primary and not for any other purpose. The meaning of this is: since the earthen shards (kapāla) have a future purpose, one should not employ their taking up or their holding for the scattering of the grains (upavāpa); but as for the remnant of the Prayāja offerings, although it is connected to a past purpose, even so—

The substance of the *kapāla* (potsherd) is not something to be taken up [as a primary object]; nevertheless, because the act of holding is not prompted by the *prayāja* offerings—which have already been completed—and because even in the view that the action is for the sake of another purpose (*arthakarma*), the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) possess primacy, the prompting of the act of holding is not contradicted. For if the oblation possesses primacy, then whichever oblation is not sprinkled with clarified butter (*abhighārita*) would suffer a loss of its consecration (*saṃskāra*); thus, holding [the butter] is indeed proper. And for the sake of accomplishing that [holding]:
"A different vessel should be used.

But how is it that the oblation (*havis*) has primacy? Because the accusative case is heard [in the scriptural injunction], and because the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) is for its sake, and because the remnant of the *prayāja* offering is for its sake as well—just like the potsherds of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśakapāla*). Nor is there a contradiction between what has already been assigned and what is being assigned, because of the [role of the] *prayāja* remnant.

Since it is logical that the substance already established—which serves as a substratum—is employed [for the purpose of sprinkling], just like the *kapāla* used for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

it is proper that the clarified butter (*ājya*) alone is primary, because the oblations (*havir*) serve a visible purpose. The meaning of this is: although it is heard in scripture that "one sprinkles the oblations," nevertheless, it is not proper for the oblations to be primary; for if they were the purpose of the sprinkling, it would result in the sprinkling having an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose. [This applies to] the *prayāja*— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly.]

However, the remnant alone possesses primacy because it serves a visible purpose; when the vessel is emptied, a visible purpose is observed: namely, that there is no contact with the *ājyabhāga* portions.
