Therefore, this [sprinkling] is indeed the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings. How then is the plural form "he sprinkles the oblations" (*havīṃṣy abhighārayati*) justified, given that the act of sprinkling is accomplished with a single oblation? The meaning is as follows: if this disposal of the clarified butter were for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*), then since it would be accomplished by even a single oblation, how could the plural number be logically sustained?

If one were poured over in one place, everything would be considered poured over; for in that case, the act of pouring would not need to be applied to each individual substance, and once a substance has been poured over, it cannot be poured over again with another oblation.
To this, the reply is: because no distinction is perceived, the plural number is not contradictory. It is true that even with a single oblation...
The disposal (*pratipatti*) is established; however, it is not known what that [disposal] is. Furthermore, there are many oblations (*havīṃṣi*) here.
Therefore, the use of the plural in the act of sprinkling (*abhidhāraṇa*) is not contradictory. Since the disposal will be performed here and there in turn, therefore—[regarding] the substance—

The conclusion of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that, just like the act of giving away (*pādāna*), the act of holding (*dhāraṇā*) and taking up (*upādāna*) are also not logical, because the final disposal (*pratipatti*) is accomplished with the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) as soon as it is present.

Now, one might object that it is impossible to understand the second and third case endings as having any other meaning than their literal sense, since the scriptural statement is according to its actual meaning.

Because of contradiction. The meaning of this is as follows: it is not possible to assume that the two case-endings (*vibhakti*) are non-representative of reality merely on the strength of their having a visible purpose, because the purpose follows from the application (*viniyoga*). In that regard, if a visible purpose is not possible, let it be; it is proper to resort to an invisible purpose alone by virtue of the force of the application. This would be true if there were no contradiction with the scriptural statement; however, in this case...

(1) Therefore, it contradicts the term *prayājaśeṣa*. The meaning of this is as follows: for it is not possible for something to be a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) of one thing while being intended for another purpose, because that which has already been assigned (*viniyukta*) cannot be further assigned (*viniyoga*).

Because of contradiction. Now, if it is argued that the contradiction between what has already been enjoined and what is being enjoined must not arise, and therefore only the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is indicated, even so, the *prayāja* offerings would be merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*), like the cake-pan (*puroḍāśakapāla*). Just as the cake is merely indicative with respect to the cake-pan, so too would the *prayājas* be here. But this is not tenable, because when it is possible for them to serve as non-indicative purposes, it is illogical for them to be merely indicative.

In the case of the *puroḍāśa* cake, however, it is appropriate because there is no other possible course; here, however, another course is possible since one does not abandon the primary connection with the nominal stem. Thus he says: "But in the case of a secondary act of disposal (*pratipatti*), this contradiction does not exist. It is logical that the case-ending, which expresses a subordinate meaning in accordance with the meaning of the nominal stem, should have a different purpose—namely, that the third case is used by way of substitution for the second case. And this being established here...

In the *pāśādhikaraṇa*, when the meaning of the case-ending was observed in accordance with the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), a displacement (*utkarṣa*) was suspected in order to favor both meanings; however, this was refuted on the grounds that the gender and number inherent in the nominal stem are more powerful. Since the meaning of the instrumental case is not understood here, even the word "oblations" (*havīṃṣi*) cannot be taken as its direct meaning. In this case too, it is logical that it serves another purpose, because two actions are connected within a single sentence.
The locative sense should be understood as being consistent with the relationship [of the action]. This has been explained.
However, the *samānayana* (the act of bringing together) should be primary. Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya asks: "Is the *samānayana* of the *āmikṣā* non-causative of the ritual duties?"

Thus he reflects. Regarding this, the commentator demonstrates the doubt concerning the cause: "In the passage, 'Having passed over the iḍā, he pours [the butter] together toward the barhis,' there is a doubt: Is this pouring together intended solely for the sake of the two subsequent prayāja offerings?"

1216 (2) Therefore, the *utmiśrī* is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the *prayāja* [offering], as well as of the clarified butter (*ājya*) held in the *aupabhṛta* ladle for the sake of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s, and of their respective ritual properties (*dharma*).

This [pouring] is for the purpose of the act itself, namely for the sake of consecrating the *jauhava* (the butter in the *juhū* ladle). Consequently, because it is accomplished by means of a substance employed for another purpose, it is not the motivator (*aprayojaka*) of the properties (*dharma*) of the other [butter]. In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers it to be merely a mixing, based on the scriptural mention of "bringing together" (*samānayana*) alone.
Furthermore, he considers that the injunction "he takes eight portions in the *upabhṛt*" serves the purpose of all the *prayāja* offerings. Why? Because no specific distinction is heard; therefore—

"This bringing together (samānayana) is for the sake of what is already seen (dṛṣṭārtha). The meaning of this is as follows: it is not heard [in the scripture] that "the two subsequent prayājas are to be sacrificed"; therefore, it cannot be said that its purpose is solely for their sake. And if the purpose of the drawing from the upabhṛt vessel were understood to be for the sake of the two subsequent prayājas, then, while those [sacrifices] are about to be performed, this bringing together might also be understood as being for that purpose. But such is not the case.

It is heard [in the scripture]; however, [the pouring] serves the purpose of all *prayāja* offerings. And that is possible only if the pouring is for an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose; for by means of mixing, the substance from the *jauhava* ladle is consecrated. And since that [consecration] pertains to all [offerings] both those already performed and those yet to be performed, its being for the sake of all is logical because it serves as their consecration. Otherwise, it would serve only two purposes, and that is not logical. Therefore, the pouring is for an invisible purpose.
This being the case, it is replied: this bringing together (*samānayana*) is for the purpose of accomplishing the two *prayāja* offerings. Why?
Because in this way, the bringing together has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*), as does the drawing [of butter] into the *upabhṛt* vessel for the sake of the *prayājas*. The meaning is this:

although only the mere act of bringing together is heard in the text, nevertheless, when there is a requirement for a purpose, it is logical that the accomplishment of the two *prayājas* intended to be performed is indeed the purpose.

Because it serves a visible purpose, there is no further unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭasaṃskāra*), as there is a lack of evidence for such a thing; for by means of the visible purpose alone, the requirement is satisfied. Likewise, the taking up [of the butter] in the *upabhṛt* ladle will serve a visible purpose; otherwise, if it were for the sake of the *praṇītā* water by way of an unseen refinement, it would result in serving an unseen purpose.

But surely, that *aupabhṛta* [butter] is heard of as being for all purposes without distinction, and it is logical that even an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*) follows from what is heard. To this, the answer is: a general scriptural statement (*aviśeṣa-śruti*), when established in a specific instance by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), does not abandon its status as the meaning of the word. If, while being established in a specific instance, the general scriptural statement regarding the two subsequent *prayāja* offerings were to abandon its status as the meaning of the word, then—

An unseen [result] might be postulated; however, it is not so, for even the two subsequent *prayāja*s are indeed denotable by the word *prayāja*. Therefore, since the word is not obstructed and an unseen result can be postulated only when a seen one is possible, this is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*). This has been stated because of observation.

In that case, the origin [of the substance] would be undifferentiated. Now, one might object: "If it is heard that the *jauhava* (the butter in the *juhū* ladle) is intended solely for the *prayāja* offerings, then its being intended for both purposes is not logical. To this he says: "What, then, is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) who asserts that 'both [substances] are for both purposes'? His intention is as follows: because it is heard without distinction that "one takes four [spoonfuls] in the *juhū*," and because the accomplishment of the ritual action occurs specifically [through that means].

The Jaiminiyas consider the mention of the *prayāja*s to be a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*), just as the mention of the *anūyāja*s in the *upabhṛt* vessel is seen to be a permanent restatement for a visible purpose.

In that case, there would also be the taking of the *prayāja* offerings at the *jauha* [ladle]. Now, if it is argued that because only the *prayāja*s are heard of, they are for the sake of the *prayāja*s alone, then by parity of reasoning, because only the *anūyāja*s are heard of in the case of the *aupabhṛta* [ladle], it would follow that it is for the sake of the *anūyāja*s alone; such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) based on this objection.
To this it is replied: if the application were established solely through the act of taking [the butter], then this might be so; however, from the mere act of taking, there is no dual purpose.

Because it is understood. For it has been stated that the material to be taken is determined according to the application (*viniyoga*), and the application of the *jauhava* [clarified butter] is solely for the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings. Now, he reveals the underlying intention of the aforementioned objection: "If that is so, then let the *aupabhṛta* [butter] be for the sake of the *anūyāja* offerings alone, since there is a scriptural statement regarding it as being exclusively for the *anūyāja*s. It is replied: because this applicatory injunction already serves its purpose, [it does not apply] to the exclusive *anūyāja*s—

He considers this to be a restatement of the relationship. From what source is its application obtained? The answer is: because it is for the purpose of both, as it is said, "he takes that [clarified butter] from the *prayāja*s and the *anuyāja*s. But surely, since the section on the *samānayana* (the pouring together) has already been established, how can this doubt now be raised? For in that [section], by stating that the butter in the *aupabhṛta* ladle is poured together for the sake of the subsequent *prayāja*s, its dual-purpose nature was already declared. How then could it be for the *anuyāja*s alone?

The possibility that it serves the purpose of the *anuyāja*s is raised. It is said in reply: this [conclusion] occurs once this [principle] is established. Otherwise, the pouring together (*samānayana*) would be merely a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*) with an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). The meaning of this is as follows: when the dual-purpose nature [of the butter] is established in this section (*adhikaraṇa*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is attained;

otherwise, if it served solely the purpose of the *anuyāja*s, there would be no understanding of the butter held in the *aupabhṛta* ladle being poured together for the sake of the *prayāja*s, and thus only the butter in the *jauhava* ladle [would be used].

It would serve the purpose of all the *prayāja* offerings; consequently, by implication, the act of bringing together (*samānayana*) would be for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), being merely a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*). For this very reason... [G. 1993, p.

When the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) has been established, there is the attainment of a *siddhānta* (conclusive doctrine) regarding that very subject; for this reason, the presentation here is that "in this way, the bringing together [of the butter] serves a visible purpose. That [quantity] is eightfold because of the scriptural mention [of the number eight]. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya asks: "Is the butter in the *aupabhṛta* [ladle] consecrated by the taking [of it] in the number eight, or..."
There is a doubt regarding the number four being subordinate to two acts of drawing [the offering]. In that regard, the author of the *Ṭīkā* raises a doubt concerning the result:

it is heard in scripture, "He draws eight times in the *upabhṛt* vessel. Here the doubt is: are these two [acts] each consisting of four drawings, or is this one single act consisting of eight drawings? [Objection: But was it not stated in the section on the *samānayana* (bringing together) that, in order to perform two *prayāja* offerings, this single four-drawing [portion] is used?
"It is brought together. By what reasoning? The meaning is: by the reasoning that "in this way, there will be a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*).

This very point is being challenged because of the hearing of the number eight. Its meaning is as follows: if there were two *caturgṛhīta* portions in the *upabhṛt* for the sake of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s, then if the bringing together (*samānayana*) pertains only to that which is here for the sake of the *prayāja*s, then there would be a visible purpose.

Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the act of pouring together (*samānayana*) is that it serves a visible purpose. However, when this single [portion] is taken eight times (*aṣṭagṛhīta*), then the fact that what is poured together is intended solely for the *prayāja* offerings is not understood; and since as much as is taken eight times is already understood [to serve that purpose], one does not pour together more than that. Therefore, this pouring together could not be for the sake of the subsequent *prayāja* offerings. To the objection that, in this case, the pouring together would be for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), he says:

Moreover, the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) of the act of bringing together (*samānayana*) is indeed established. For the sake of favoring the *jauhava* clarified butter—which is occupied with the three *prayāja* offerings in the eastern *āghāra* and is thus incapable of performing its own function—it is brought together. Therefore, in this case...

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that the taking up of the portions must be exactly eightfold because it is so stated in the scripture. However, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that since the numbers four and eight refer to different objects, one cannot claim that either of them fails to apply. The meaning of this is as follows: the fourfold portion...

In the case of the oblation (*homa*), the number four is heard in the injunction "he offers"; and in the case of the taking [of the ladle], the number eight is heard in the injunction "he takes eight times in the *upabhṛt*.

Therefore, because their spheres of application are distinct, there is no contradiction, and both [injunctions] are applied. Nor is it the case that the taking [of the substance] is for the sake of the oblation.

Contradiction can only be asserted when there is an equality of purpose; since the number eight is heard in the context of taking up the material (*grahaṇa*), and the number four can be asserted as being produced in the context of the oblation (*homa*), there is no contradiction, and thus neither [number] need be abandoned. But how does the number eight produce the number four? The answer is: because in the oblation these two [sets of] four-fold takings (*caturgṛhīta*) are conjoined.

Because of the application [of the formula] "for the *prayājas* and *anuyājas*" as serving both purposes, the requirement of both is fulfilled by the taking of eight portions (*aṣṭagrahaṇa*) through two four-portioned (*caturgṛhīta*) ladlings. This is supported by the scriptural statement, "He takes eight in the *upabhṛt*," and the observation that these two constitute two four-portioned ladlings is established as before. Thus, that observation regarding the plurality of four-portioned ladlings is likewise validated.
And thus, the previously stated purpose of the *samānayana* becomes established; consequently, its purpose would directly be one that serves a visible (empirical) end.

The *svaru*, however, is produced from multiple [materials]. Now, one might object: "In both these sections (*adhikaraṇa*), the subject matter, the doubt, the deliberation, the conclusion, and the purpose appear to be identical; how then can there be a distinction between the sections? To this he replies: "In this case, one section is described with reference to a different sentence, while the second is based on accepting a single sentence. However, the arguments [used] in the deliberation of a single sentence [apply] to the other sentence..."

And it has been demonstrated in the *Pekṣiṇī-mīmāṃsā* that these two are equal. The meaning of this is as follows: in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), there are the [scriptural] statements, "He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya svaruṃ karoti*) and "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*" (*svaruṇā paśumanakti*).

Having cited these two sentences, it is considered: "Which [sentence] comes first? Does the sentence "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*" presuppose the sentence "He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)", or is it the reverse? In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) asserts that the sentence "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*" presupposes the sentence "He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post."

And there is the principle that when there is an injunction by direct statement (*śruti*), it is an injunction by direct statement; otherwise, it would be an injunction by syntactical connection (*vākya*). For if the application (*viniyoga*)—namely, "he anoints the animal with the *svaru*"—were to occur first, then the word *svaru* would function solely on the basis of its performing the act of anointing; and in that case, the meaning of the statement "he makes the *svaru* of the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya svarum karoti*) would be as follows:

It is established as follows: that which has been obtained for the purpose of performing the function of the *añjana* (anointing) is to be taken as the *svaru* for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). And thus, because the sentence is intent upon enjoining a connection with the sacrificial post, there would be an injunction by means of a syntactical connection (*vākya*). Since direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical connection, it is therefore the very performance of the *svaru* that is enjoined. The term "of the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya*) means of the wood of the post, such as *khadira* and so forth. And thus, [the functions of] cutting and so on—

It is connected as something that brings about its own production. But is this not improper? Because [of the statements]: "He chooses the sacrificial post" (yūpaṃ joṣayati) and "He cuts the sacrificial post" (yūpaṃ chinatti).

From the statement "he fashions the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ takṣati*), it is understood that the act of selecting (*joṣaṇa*) and so forth relates specifically to the sacrificial post, not to the *svaru* chip. It is replied:

the meaning of "he selects the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ joṣayati*) and similar expressions is that he selects *khadira* wood and other such materials in order to make the sacrificial post; it does not mean that he selects a sacrificial post that already exists as a finished object.

And in that case, it is not proper to intend the qualification "and no other sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is to be made," because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Rather, since the consecration (*saṃskāra*) exists for the sake of a function, and because each of the two functions—namely, the sacrificial post and the *svaru*—serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for its respective purpose, the selection (*joṣaṇa*) and so forth of the *khadira* wood and others are understood to be for that very purpose. Consequently, the word *yūpa* must serve only to indicate the archetypal function. By this, the following meaning is established:

Through acts such as selection (*joṣaṇa*), the *khadira* and other woods become sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and also become the *svaru*. On this view, the word *svaru* is based on its specific production; therefore, it is considered that the *svaru* necessitates a separate act of production. In this way alone is the statement regarding the suspicion of it being a different genus (*jātyantara*) justified. Consequently, the word *yūpa* would serve solely to indicate the function of the archetype (*prakṛta-kārya*), and not otherwise.

The Siddhāntin, however, considers this statement, "He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya svaruṃ karoti*), to be preceded by the injunction, "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*.

This is because the *svaru* is heard in scripture as being connected to the sacrificial post in the phrase "he makes the *svaru* of the sacrificial post. Furthermore, a relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) between the sacrificial post and the *svaru* is not tenable, as it would entail the destruction of the sacrificial post. Nor can the wood such as *khadira*, which serves as the material for the post, be indicated by the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) [and thus serve as the material cause] for the *svaru*.

It cannot be said that [the word *yūpa*] will refer to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) [in the sense of its wood], because that would entail a figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, by considering the direct syntactic connection (*śrautānvaya*) of the word *yūpa*, this statement—"one makes the *svaru* of the sacrificial post"—is preceded by an application (*viniyoga*), namely: "one anoints the animal with the *svaru*. In that case, since the status of being a *svaru* is established precisely through its function of performing the anointing, the *svaru* itself need not be produced; rather, when there arises the requirement as to what [substance] is used for the anointing, [the answer follows].

It is prescribed that [the *svaru*] belongs to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). How does it belong to the sacrificial post? It is produced as a by-product (*anuniṣpadyate*) of the sacrificial post. Consequently, since the act of fashioning the *svaru* is not independently enjoined, and since its connection with *khadira* wood and so forth—as well as its selection (*joṣaṇa*) and other requirements—constitutes a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) of the sacrificial post itself, the sacrificial post alone is the motivator (*prayojaka*), while the *svaru* is not a motivator. Furthermore, because of the scriptural mention of a "chip" (*śakala*), the *svaru* is a part; and when the whole exists, a part does not motivate the whole. And in this view:

The root *kṛ* (to do/make) functions in the sense of "appropriating" (*upādāna*), and in this sense, it possesses its primary meaning, as in the example "make [something] out of wood. Thus, the following is investigated here: should there be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by virtue of the injunction of the literal sense of the word (*śruti*), or should the injunction of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) be accepted in order to avoid such indication?

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that the injunction of the word is indeed stronger because it is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the sentence, involving a mediated connection, is indirect and must be inferred (*kalpanīya*).

Thus he says. But the proponent [of the final view] thinks: this would indeed be so if there were a mediated connection; however, since the injunction itself pertains to the verbal root (bhāvārtha), it is called a "quality-injunction" (guṇavidhi) through the distinction between what is already established and what is not. Therefore, even when the sentence-meaning is being enjoined, there is no mediated connection, and thus he considers that metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is not logical. As for the suspicion regarding another class [of entities], it was previously [addressed] by the mention of "that which is produced subsequently."

(1) R. [the object] to be refined; (2) G. the essential nature of the material cause; (3) G. adds: "How is it prescribed by that as being prior? (4) G. there is no production of effects such as approval (*joṣaṇa*).

For the purpose of praising the injunction, the observation of the *svaru* at each sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has been stated as an indicative mark (*liṅga*). In the second section (*adhikaraṇa*), however, having cited this very same sentence—"He anoints the animal with the *svaru*"—the inquiry is considered:

Is this *svaru* which is employed for the anointing something to be produced (*utpādya*), or is it something to be taken up (*upādeya*)? In that regard, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is to be produced, precisely because of the force of the scriptural injunction (*śruti*). In the same way...

Since it is impossible for [the term] to produce a connection with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and since there would be the fault of *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) if one were to indicate the wood for the post, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that only what is produced as a byproduct of the post (*yūpānuniṣpanna*) is to be taken. The supporting arguments for both the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final position (*uttara-pakṣa*) are exactly those same ones. Furthermore, since the root *kṛ* (to take) also applies to the act of taking up, it is logical that the established conclusion is precisely as stated. The arguments are identical in both these sections.

The distinction between the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) arises from the difference in subject matter and the difference in the types of doubt. This is what is meant: even if an investigation into the sequence [of the texts] is conducted by accepting two separate sentences, the *svaru* chip remains irrelevant; and even if an investigation into the inclusion [of the chip] is conducted by resorting to a single sentence, the *svaru* chip remains irrelevant nonetheless.

"Because that [branch] is the primary meaning in the word *śākhā*. Why is this section included here, in this definition of what is primary (*prayojaka*) and what is secondary (*aprayojaka*)? For neither the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) nor the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is understood here from the perspective of an injunction (*vidhi*). Its meaning is as follows: whether the word *prācī* denotes the direction or denotes the branch, in either case, no consideration regarding its material cause (*upādānika*) is being deliberated here; rather, it is the denotation [that is the issue], and thus it is irrelevant.

It is said: This reflection arises precisely from the injunction (*vidhi*). The meaning is that this is a reflection concerning the specific performance of the material cause (*upādāna*). What kind of reflection is it? He says:

"Is the taking up of the branch from the eastern side of the tree? For according to the Siddhānta—the doctrine of the branch—the taking up of the branch must be performed with reference to the eastern side of the tree, because the eastern branch is what is to be brought. In the expression "from the eastern side of the tree" (*vṛkṣaprāgdeśāt*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap*.

Or rather, it is the taking up [of the branch] from the eastern part of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*). For according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is not said that the branch itself is "eastern," but rather that the eastern direction belongs to the location of the *vihāra*. And since that [direction] must be brought [to the altar] by means of the location, it follows that it is the bringing of the branch itself [that is intended].

That which is qualified by its location (*deśa*) is what should be adopted. The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the act of adoption follows the same principle as the act of application (*viniyoga*); just as only that which has been applied is adopted and nothing else, so too only that which has been denoted (*abhihita*) is to be adopted, because it alone has been applied. Furthermore, the denotation occurs through the primary function (*mukhyā vṛtti*) and refers only to the eastern direction, not to the branch. However, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this [denotation] necessarily involves secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The meaning of this is as follows: the branch alone is to be taken up; "bringing from the east" means bringing it to a specific location.
To say that "the east" refers to the direction itself is not possible, because a direction cannot be physically brought. However, something must be brought toward the direction.
Nor is it possible to regard "the east" as an "unexpressed object" (*akathita-karman*), for nothing is directly brought toward the direction itself; rather, [something else is brought].

Regarding that location: since the instruction for bringing about the direction (*digānayana*) is intended for the performance of bringing about the place (*deśānayana*), figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is necessary. However, the bringing about of the direction itself, being the resulting fruit, is not something to be instructed. Therefore, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), by virtue of the function of implied intention (*tātparyavṛtti*), this is indeed a figurative indication; thus, the word "eastern" (*prācī*) indicates the branch itself, which is the direct object of the action. Furthermore, there is this additional distinction: the branch must necessarily be indicated.
Regarding the two alternatives, this very position is logical: for it is not possible to understand the instrument (*karaṇa*) without the primary action (*pradhānakarman*);

thus, the primary action must necessarily be specified. The word "eastern" (*prācī*) is capable of bringing to mind the eastern branch under discussion through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, this word "eastern" refers precisely to that [branch]. As for the location, it pertains to the sacrificer situated at the *devayajana*.
Because it has already been performed, it is "obtained" and thus not even to be characterized; this is faultless.
Because that [branch] is the primary element in the branch [of the ritual], the Bhāṣya here considers only the taking up of the parivāsana-vessel.
It shows that this is merely an illustration—here, either the taking up of the parivāsana or the taking up of the branch is being considered.

(1) G. There is no bringing [of the branch] because of its antiquity; (2) G. because the place for sacrifice (*devayajana*) is the subject under discussion, it follows from the remainder. For if the trimming (*parivāsana*) is performed with both ends—the root and the tip—then the fetching of the branch (*śākhāharaṇa*) would also [be required].
It is indeed employed by both. Now, if the taking up of the branch (*śākhā*) is employed by both [the root and the tip], then the setting aside (*parivāsana*) is also employed by both.
What, then, is the correct view here? Both are the motivators (*prayojaka*) for the setting aside, because both the root and the tip are designated as "branch" (*śākhā*).
This is the intended meaning: when it says "he brings the eastern [branch]," that branch which has been brought from the tree is already possessed of its root portion.

The word "branch" (*śākhā*) is used [here]. And its cutting is heard in the scripture: "Having trimmed the branch from the root, he makes the *upaveṣa*. By means of this cutting, the branch is not being consecrated; rather, it is brought forth after having been split in two. Therefore, the cutting is not for the sake of the branch itself, but for the sake of separating the root and tip portions. Nor is there no purpose even for those two: with the root, the placing of the potsherds (*kapāla-upadhāna*) will be performed.

"By the 'front' (agra) [is meant] the driving away of the calves and so forth. Therefore, because it serves both purposes, both [the root and the tip] are motivators (*prayojaka*), just as in the case of the cutting (*parivāsana*), so too in the case of the fetching of the branch (*śākhāharaṇa*). The meaning of the *Ṭīkā* is as follows: for the cutting or for the branch, both the root and the tip are motivators; and since both exist as motivators, they reside together in the branch as a whole (*avayavin*) by virtue of being its parts (*avayava*)."

To this, it is replied: This would be so if the connection were "he makes the root into an *upaveṣa*. How, then, is the connection? It is "he makes an *upaveṣa* from the root. By this—

Thus it says: "He trims the branch from the root. The root is taken up solely for the purpose of trimming the branch, because of its immediate proximity; however, the connection is not "he makes the *upaveṣa* from the root," as that would entail a disjointed syntactical relation (*vyavahitānvaya*). Furthermore, when the question arises—"What is that which he makes into the *upaveṣa*?"—the root is connected [as the answer], even though it was already taken up for another purpose, just like the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).
What follows from this if it is so? This is what follows: [the rule] "the *upaveṣa* is made from a root produced elsewhere. Herein lies the doubt:

when the *upaveṣa* is to be accomplished by means of a root that is a by-product (*anuniṣpanna*), then the root itself is not employed, because it has already been obtained elsewhere, just like the *svaru*. And since the root is not employed, the cutting for its sake and the fetching of the branch are likewise not employed. He concludes:

Therefore, although the word *śākhā* (branch) denotes both the root and the tip, it is nonetheless established that the paring (*parivāsana*) is not for the sake of the *upaveṣa*. Rather, it is solely for the sake of the tip, because it is accomplished by means of a substance produced as a byproduct of the action performed on the tip.

Furthermore, the designation "branch" is employed specifically for the tip in other ritual functions, such as in the injunction: "One drives away the calves with the branch" (*śākhayā vatsānapākaroti*). Thus...

This word "branch" (*śākhā*) is employed hereafter for the purpose of purifying the root through its application; moreover, if it were produced as a secondary result from the taking up of the branch—(1) R.
*śākhopādānānuniṣpanna* [p.

If the word "branch" (śākhā) were to denote both the root and the tip, then the ritual acts enjoined by the word "branch" would not take place [at the tip]. Likewise, in the injunction "he drives away the calves with the branch at the tip," the word "branch" would not have its primary meaning; furthermore, the cutting would result in the destruction of the branch.
But this is not the case. Therefore, this word "branch" refers only to the tip, and it is that very [tip] which [is affected] by the cutting of the root.

The ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*) consists precisely in bringing that very [branch] from the tree as the "top" (*agra*), whereas the root is obtained from the fallen portion. Furthermore, it is separated from the root-section by means of cutting;

therefore, the fetching of the branch and its trimming (*parivāsana*) are for that purpose alone. Consequently, the *upaveṣa* (the wooden chip) is not a motive [for the action], as the purpose has already been stated:
namely, the absence of the *upaveṣa* at the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).

"But the act of carrying [the branch] is a *homa* (an oblation). Now, this objection challenges the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this carrying is solely for the purpose of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the grass-bundle (*prastara*).

In that context, the meaning is as follows: the carrying is a disposal; how then could the branch be a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*) therein? Here the underlying intention (*ākūtam*) is this: this carrying is indeed for the purpose of the disposal of the grass-bundle, and since the branch is connected with the grass-bundle in an identical manner, it is not proper for it to be a subordinate element either.

But has it not already been stated that this carrying (*dharaṇa*) is indeed a sacrifice (*yāga*)? How then can it be accepted as a disposal (*pratipatti*)? To this he replies with "even though" (*yadyapi*).

Even while accepting its status as a sacrifice, he declares it to be a disposal: "Even though the root *harati* (to carry) is a sacrifice, and the deity is prescribed by the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*), nevertheless this is merely a disposal-rite, just like the final *prayāja* [in the injunction] 'he sacrifices the *svāhākāra*. The word "final" (*uttama*) refers to the third—

He states the last of the *bhṛti*s: "And in the case of disposal (*pratipatti*), there is no subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) for the substance. Now, if it is argued: "Just as in the final *prayāja* offering the clarified butter (*ājya*) is subordinate even in its disposal, so too shall the branch (*śākhā*) be subordinate here," the point here is this:
this instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) of yours is not based on concomitance (*sahayoga*). For the branch is not already known to have a connection with the act of throwing away (*praharaṇa*).

"It must certainly be resorted to in this way.
