However, in that case, since the sacrifice is for the purpose of recollecting the deity, the subordinate status of the substance is logical; "therein" means in the final *prayāja* offering. Regarding this, [the following was said] by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*).

It has been stated: "Now, just as in the case of the final *prayāja*, the clarified butter (*ājya*) is subordinate even in its disposal (*pratipatti*)," and someone objects there, thinking that because the word "disposal" is heard, the nature of the substance's disposal is indeed intended. [The objection is: "But surely the final *prayāja* is not a disposal at all;
for a ritual act is a 'disposal' only where a substance is being disposed of, and therefore it does not have the form of a disposal. To this, the reply is:

—By whom was this "nature of disposal" (pratipattitva) stated? The nature of disposal is not intended here; rather, the status of being a *kāraka* (a factor of action) is intended, and not the form of a disposal (*pratipatti*). A sacrifice whose purpose is to serve as a *kāraka* is called a "disposal rite" (*pratipattikarma*). Regarding its status as a *kāraka*, in some cases it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) through the clearing of a location, as in the case of the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle; in other cases it is a recollection, as in the case of the final *prayāja* offering. This is the purpose.

For these are indeed distinctions; therefore, there is no fault. He concludes the objection regarding the subject at hand: "Therefore, it cannot be argued as a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the branch is subordinate. It is replied: The proponent of the prima facie position considers it to be subordinate because the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is heard precisely in the context of disposal (*pratipatti*). Not everything is necessarily primary even in the context of disposal; rather, it is exactly as it is heard [in the scripture].

It must be so, just as in the case of "he offers with the *juhū* ladle," where the *juhū* is merely a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*). Here, the intended meaning is this: first of all, the act of carrying away (*haraṇa*)—(1) R.
adds *ātmagamana*; (2) G. states it is precisely of the nature of its disposal (*tatpratipattirūpa*)—is thus [subordinate].

It is understood that the branch is intended solely for the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the grass-bundle (*prastara*). In that context, because the hearing of the word "with" (*saha*) [in the phrase *śākhayā saha*] is otherwise untenable due to the lack of prior established connection, the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), which indicates a grammatical factor (*kāraka*), expresses the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of the branch. Furthermore, since the word "with" (*saha*) is a particle (*nipāta*), its syntactic connection must be explained in some way. It should be understood that the branch is subordinate in some manner, whether as an auxiliary to the *juhū* ladle or otherwise.

To this it is replied: this would indeed be so if the word "saha" (together) were not heard here. But since the word "saha" is heard, the fact that the branch possesses an equal connection with the grass-bundle (*prastara*) is certainly understood. Therefore, the branch is also indeed to be disposed of. Otherwise, there would be no equal connection. Consequently, in the case of the branch as well, the accusative sense alone must be understood, just as in the case of the grass-bundle.

The meaning of this is as follows: the word *saha* (together) expresses the equal conjunction (*tulyayogitā*) of two meanings that are mentioned in close proximity (*samabhivyāhriyamāṇa*). Since the sacrificial branch (*śākhā*) and the *prastara* bundle are mentioned here in close proximity, there is equal conjunction regarding their disposal (*praharaṇa*). But surely, the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is not justified? If it is not justified, let it not be justified; for we also observe the transposition (*vyatyaya*) of case endings. Such a context is precisely the domain for such transposition.

However, since the word *saha* is not seen to have any other meaning [than accompaniment], it possesses greater force. If, even in the case of the branch (*śākhā*) and the bundle of grass (*prastara*), the accusative case applies because they are the objects of the act of carrying (*haraṇa*), then the accusative would indeed result; therefore he asks: "How then is there the instrumental case? This [instrumental] does not have the characteristic of a *kāraka* (grammatical participant); what then? Its purpose is to indicate connection with the word *saha*. The meaning of this is: this case-ending does not depend upon an action.
What then? It is the requirement of association with something else. How then did the author of the Bhāṣya speak of a change of case-endings? To this he says:

"Because association is indicated by what is well-known, a change of case-ending was stated. This should be understood in the same way as the throwing of the *prastara* [grass-bundle], because that is well-known; whereas the branch (*śākhā*) is not so well-known. Therefore, the formulation of the statement is as follows:
"One strikes the branch together with the prastara-bunch. The remainder has been stated; and the purpose is the distinction from the case of the flour-meal (saktu). (1) As heard in the text [p.
Because of the lack of connection at the time of origination. The carrying forth of water (*apaḥ praṇayati*) originates as unconnected with two distinct purposes.

Since the two purposes are heard of only later, one considers both to be the motivators (*prayoktṛ*) without distinction. The meaning of this is as follows: at the time of the origination of the carrying forth of water, neither the kneading (*saṃyavana*) nor the pouring out (*ninayana*) is heard as its purpose; however, since both are heard of subsequently, both are considered to have the status of being motivators.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) thinks: "But surely, the accusative case is heard in the text 'he pours out water' (apo ninayati). Its meaning is this:

because the accusative is heard, water is the primary object; and the pouring out is solely for the purpose of its disposal (pratipatti). This is because the instrumental case is heard in the context of mixing (saṃyavana)."

The intention is that since it is indeed a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*), that alone is the motivator (*prayojaka*). To this, the reply is: "Because it is not what is intended to be attained (*anīpsita*), it will apply to the mere *kāraka*"; the meaning is that the accusative case applies to the "unintended object" (*anīpsitakarma*) according to the rule *tathā yuktam cānīpsitam*. But how can it be said that it is not intended? All the cognitions (*pratipatti*) mentioned here are examples. In this regard, the following is considered: what is it...?

Is it possible for even a substance that is already employed to be something intended to be produced (*cikīrṣitatva*), or not? Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that a substance is indeed intended to be produced because it assists the ritual action. However, as for that which has already fulfilled its purpose, what need is there for it to be intended to be produced?

Therefore, this pouring out (*ninayana*) is merely a primary act (*arthakarma*). In that case, even though water functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*), it still possesses a share in the fruit produced by the action.
"It is joined with the second [case-ending] because it is an object not intended [by the agent]," so it is said. To this, it is replied: there is no reason for its being unintended;

for even though its purpose has been accomplished, it is still indeed desired as something to be communicated. The intention here is this: although the substance has its purpose fulfilled in the cognitions [of it], nevertheless, the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) is still possible—[namely,] "What should be done with this now? Should it be neglected, or rather..."
"Should it, therefore, be discarded in another location? This is indeed well-known even in common worldly practice. Likewise, the procedure in the Veda follows that of the world;

in that regard, whatever is heard concerning a particular act is accepted as being dependent upon that [context]. And here, the pouring of water into the interior of the altar (*antarvedi*) is indeed heard.
(1) p. 1235 (2) G. *tasyāpekṣitam* (that which is required by it).

Nor does it fail to function because of its lack of utility, for in the world, we observe that even a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) whose purpose has already been fulfilled persists; just as, for example, a garland removed from Devadatta’s head is placed in a clean location. And in that case, worldly people regard it as being merely the impression of Devadatta.

They think: "In this case as well, it is postulated that there will be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the subordinate element (*śeṣin*). But surely, even in the case of what is not intended (*anīpsita*), since the connection with the fruit produced by the action is never absent, it is only that much—the mere [connection]—that is logically the meaning of the accusative, and not "the state of being intended" (*īpsitatva*), because that is subject to deviation. And if [the accusative] were used in its primary sense, how would one understand that "this accusative does not apply to an object that is not intended"? To this, he says: "Nor [is it restricted] to what is intended."

Resorting to an unintended substratum is possible, because that [substratum] is understood as preceding it. Although the accusative case is primary in meaning in both instances, nevertheless, since an action everywhere requires a purpose, its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) must be stated in some way.
In that regard, whatever is seen to be produced by it appears first; thus, that very thing manifests as the purpose. And that which is the purpose is precisely what is [denoted] by that [accusative].

Regarding the rule *kriyayepsitam* (Pāṇini 1.4.49), it is precisely the state of being desired (*īpsitatva*) as previously understood that attains the status of being required; therefore, nothing else is postulated by abandoning that [status]. Thus, the meaning is: "because of such an understanding which is preceded by and primary to that [state]. Consequently, since the water has already fulfilled its purpose in the act of mixing (*saṃyavana*), pouring it out (*ninayana*) is merely a disposal (*pratipatti*); hence, it is established that it does not constitute a motive for performance (*aprayoktṛtva*).

Regarding the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, it is like the throwing [of the grass-bundle]. The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that the statement, “He hands over the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa,” constitutes a disposal (pratipatti), because the staff has already served its purpose in supporting the sacrificer; thus, the holding of the staff by the Maitrāvaruṇa is merely a disposal of the staff.

Because of the second [rule]’s specification. But is it not the case that the subordinate status [of the recipient] is already established by the rule: "That person whom one intends through an action is the *saṃpradāna*"? No; for by that [rule], the purposefulness (*tādarthya*) of the action is understood.

"In the case of an action accompanied by a recipient (*saṃpradāna*). The meaning of this is as follows: because of the traditional rule that "by means of the object" (*karmaṇā*) indicates the instrumental case, wherever there is a recipient, the object (*karman*) is subordinate. Therefore, since the staff does not possess primacy, this is not a [valid] cognition. To this, the reply is: "The recipient..."

The status of the action (*karman*) is due solely to its being the producer of pleasure for the recipient; it is not, however, because it is to be accomplished by another action, for in that case its status as an action would be untenable.

The meaning of this is as follows: with respect to the act of giving, this [gift] is not the instrument (*karaṇa*), but rather the means for the production of pleasure in the recipient. For if it were also the instrument with respect to the act of giving, then its status as the object (*karman*) would not occur. Therefore, because it is the object with respect to the act of giving, it possesses primacy with respect to that.

Giving alone is appropriate as the performance (*pratipatti*); thus, because of the maintenance [of the staff] by the initiated one, it is called "that which has giving as its means" (*tatsādhya*), and by that state (*tattā*), it does not again become a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*). While the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) stands, he raises an objection: "How then is there the observation such as 'the holder of the staff (*daṇḍin*) recites the *praiṣa* formulas'? Here, the intention is this: if this were the giving of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa, then...

The gift must indeed be for that purpose [of holding the staff]. And that "being for that purpose" occurs only if the staff being given assists one who is performing the ritual action, so that the holding of the primary object [the staff] may be rendered possible. However, if the gift were merely for the sake of the staff itself, then the purpose of the scripture would be fulfilled simply by the Maitrāvaruṇa going [to receive it], and the staff would not be held; in that case, the mention of the staff in the *praisha* (directions) would be inexplicable. The answer is as follows:

This is a restatement of what occurs by chance; for in the world, one frequently observes mere action performed by chance, independent of any other purpose. Thus, this will be the observation regarding the staff held [by the Maitrāvaruṇa]: it refers to the state when the performance according to the rule is established.
To this, it is replied: because of the designation "the staff for the Maitrāvaruṇa," and because of the observation that "the bearer of the staff recites the *praiṣas*."

This is indeed an act for a purpose (*arthakarma*), not a preparatory rite (*pratipatti*). The intention here is as follows: first of all, from the accusative case-ending, it is not understood that [the object] exists for the sake of the word-meaning; rather, it is understood as being the recipient of the fruit produced by the action. And this is not incompatible with the giving of the staff to Maitrāvaruṇa. (1) R. *tatpratyayaḥ*—therefore, there is no state of being a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*). (2) G. *yāvatprāsanaṃ*. (3) G. *tadvadetasyedaṃ*.

It has been stated that because the staff (*daṇḍa*) is first perceived, its purpose is accepted; and that applies when the verbal expression is not contradicted. But here, in the case of the Maitrāvaruṇa—
The designation "this is the staff" would be contradicted; for in this designation, the predominance of the Maitrāvaruṇa is perceived.

And such predominance occurs only if the gift is for his sake. Furthermore, according to the principle stated previously, and because of the observation that "the staff-bearer [utters] the *praiṣas*," it is determined that this is an act for a purpose (*arthakarma*). Therefore, it is correct that this is an accusative case expressing something not intended as the primary object (*anīpsita-dvitīyā*). But surely, what is obtained by chance—

It has been stated that this might be a restatement (*anuvāda*). This very point is a defect, because it would result in the contingency of being optional (*pākṣikatva*), which would contradict its being heard as an obligatory rule (*nityavacchravaṇa*). How then is the accusative case [to be explained]? It has been said that it is used according to the rule "and that which is not desired [by the agent] when so connected" (*tathā yuktam cānīpsitam*). That appears incorrect. For in that context, what is cited as an example is something not to be adopted (*anupādeya*), such as "he leaps over the snake" (*ahiṃ laṅghayati*) or "he tramples the thorns" (*kaṇṭakān mṛdnāti*). And yet, [the object in question here] is something to be adopted (*upādeya*).

The meaning is that the staff (*daṇḍa*) is fit for the second case ending because it is to be held by the sacrificer himself; since it is not something to be taken up (*anupādeya*) in the act of disposal (*pratipatti*), the use of the accusative is justified.

Thus, regarding the groats (*saktu*), it was stated that there is a transposition of case endings; because they are things to be taken up (*upādeya*), they do not lack the quality of being desired (*anīpsitatva*).

For that which is to be taken up is indeed desired for the sake of accomplishing the action. It is replied: Well said regarding the groats; for their taking up there is for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*).

In this case, however, the object of acquisition (*upādāna*) does not bestow its own substance; rather, it bestows only that which has already been acquired. Therefore, such an action is indeed neither "desired" (*īpsita*) nor capable of being construed with another case-ending. For the staff is understood to have been acquired solely for the purpose of supporting the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); thus, it lacks the status of being an object of acquisition (*anupādeyatā*). And this has been stated merely as a possible way of resolving the objection. In reality, however, where in the Sūtra there is the term *anīpsita*—

By the word, that which is to be accomplished by the action is intended; however, it is not something unintended because it is not included as being for the sake of that action. Furthermore, this is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of the action here, because it is something to be prescribed (*upādeya*); thus, it is logical.

The staff (*daṇḍa*) is desired because it is the object of the act of giving (*prayacchati*). For this very reason, in the expression "he gives a cow" (*gāṃ dadāti*), the dative case is justified even though the cow is presented as the object of the act of giving. Here too, although the taking up of the staff is not explicitly mentioned, its holding must necessarily be performed; thus, its status as something to be taken up (*upādeyatva*) is unavoidable. However, in the case of the groats (*saktu*), such a state of being "thus connected" (*tathā-yuktatā*) does not exist; therefore, a reversal [of the rule] has been stated. Because it is not...

In that case, the reduction to ashes occurs through the oblation (*homa*), whereas [the state of being] a substrate occurs through the pouring of the liquid; this is shown in the second [section]. Furthermore, there is another point of inquiry: is it only the maintenance (*dhāraṇa*) that is enjoined, or is the production (*utpatti*) also [enjoined]? The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that there is indeed the status of being an agent of performance (*prayoktṛtva*).

"At the time of its production, it is connected by that [which is the cause]; another topic (adhikaraṇa) has been stated. This is the meaning: this topic was indeed mentioned in the Bhāṣya itself. And since, in the final position (siddhānta), it is stated that the purpose is accomplished, it is understood that in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the purpose is considered not yet accomplished. The proponent of the prima facie view thinks thus: "The fulfillment of the purpose for the horn occurs only at the end of the entire performance; however, in the middle of the performance..."

Because scratching is possible [before the end of the sacrifice], the act of throwing [the horn] is not a *pratipatti* (disposal) because its purpose has not yet been fulfilled. Therefore, the throwing of the horn into the *cātvāla* pit is not a disposal, but rather a primary ritual act (*arthakarma*). It is replied: It is heard in the scripture, "When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been led forth, he throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla*. Therefore, the settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the scratching with the black antelope horn must be performed even earlier. But how can this be, given that it is heard without qualification?

It abides in the specific [context]. If it is argued that this is because of the injunction for performance (*pratipatti-vidhāna*), we say no, because that would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). It is not so; for the performance is established from another source due to the non-hearing of the accusative case-ending, and because it has already served its purpose in the Soma sacrifice. He raises an objection against the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But what is the specific distinction here regarding the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings?"

Just as in the case of "with the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings," even though there is no accusative case ending, the remnant of the *prayāja* is treated as a disposal (*pratipatti*), so too here, in the statement "whatever is smeared with Soma, with that they go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*)," it is logical that this is indeed a disposal. He provides the resolution: "But surely, in the case of 'with the remnant of the *prayāja*,' [the word] is heard as a syntactically connected remainder (*ananvayaśeṣaḥ śrutaḥ*), even when only the *godāna* [rite] is being understood. (1) P. 1238 (2) G. even in the cognition of the *godāna* alone (3) G. a syntactically connected remainder is heard.

The fact that it serves the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings is understood from the term "smeared with soma," which indicates its status as a ritual substance (*karmārthatā*). Why is there no distinction?

The so-called "remnant of the *prayāja*" is the residue of the clarified butter (*ājya*) employed during the *prayāja*. Since it was not employed there for any other purpose, its subservience to that specific purpose (*tādarthya*) is understood therein.

However, the fact that [the vessel] is merely smeared with *soma* does not imply its purpose is for that [specific act]; thus, it further reinforces the objection. It is replied: even in the expression "by that which is smeared with *soma*," the connection with *soma* is solely for the sake of the *soma*-sacrifice. For whatever has the status of being for the *soma*-sacrifice, when it is necessarily employed therein, it becomes "smeared with *soma*"; it is nothing other than that, and thus it is equivalent to the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings. If this is so, then regarding the *avabhṛtha*—
Considering that the scriptural text connects the *somalipta* (the Soma-smeared [ladle]) with another ritual act, one regards it as being subsidiary (*śeṣatā*). The meaning of this is as follows:

first of all, because of the context, the word *avabhṛtha* refers to the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) itself and does not apply elsewhere. And since that [act] is a primary ritual (*pradhānakarma*), it cannot have the *somalipta* as its purpose—just as the act of sprinkling (*abhidhāraṇa*) [does not serve the ladle]—because there can be no relationship between two things without a relation of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*). Therefore, [it must refer to] the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)...

Just as in the case of the *kapāla*, by virtue of its characteristic as a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-lakṣaṇā*), that which is smeared with Soma is employed as a remnant of the *avabhṛtha* bath; and thus the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in its literal sense. In this way, the meaning of the sentence becomes: "In order to perform the *avabhṛtha*, they enter the water with that which is smeared with Soma. To this it is replied: even when there is a connection with a different ritual act, one thing cannot be understood as a remnant of another simply because it is a remnant [of something else].

As if occupied elsewhere, it is not [available] elsewhere; therefore, the word "karma" (action/rite) must be understood only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The meaning of this is as follows: when the literal sense of the Soma-residue is grasped, it is subordinate to another—that is, subordinate to the Soma-sacrifice—and it cannot be understood as being subordinate to something else, namely, as subordinate to the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). It is as if it were occupied elsewhere; thus, there is a connection with that [other purpose] only through secondary indication. Therein also, an inquiry arises.

Should the word *somalipta* be explained through a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the substratum, or should the word *avabhṛtha* be taken as indicating the location? For the sake of favoring the injunction of the literal meaning of the Vedic text (*śruti*), it is logical that the word *avabhṛtha* itself is intended to indicate the location. Furthermore, the meaning of the verbal root in the word "they go" (*yanti*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]
The sense of the causative (*ṇij*) is thus implicitly included; otherwise, it would be a mere restatement of the root-meaning.

Furthermore, the injunction regarding the *somalipta* (the Soma-soiled items) occurs through syntactical connection (*vākya*). This is what was stated in the Bhāṣya: "Direct assertion (*śruti*) is stronger than syntactical connection. Therefore, the meaning is this: "They lead the *somalipta* to the place of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath)."

There is no injunction regarding the agent, the place, or the time. But surely, on the view that this is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), the sentence would result in being purposeless because it conveys nothing new. On this point, some raise the following prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): Because an efficient [agent] performs the action and an inefficient one does not, efficiency (*śakti*) alone is the cause, not the substance, since the latter is subject to deviation. And that efficiency is to be understood through the effect; even in cases such as "samādiṣu" (in the *samā* etc.)—

It is indeed distinct; and that very [power] must be enjoined as a *kāraka* (participant) in the action. Since that [power] is eternally present, the assignments of *kārakas* are merely restatements (*anuvāda*). With this intention, this passage is directed at refuting the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). For when power (*śakti*) is the *kāraka*, then there is no connection of the *sam-* [prefixes] and so forth with the action. And since that which is not connected cannot be expressive, there would be a lack of expressiveness.

Furthermore, because it would not be expressive [of an injunction], it would be entirely purposeless under the view that it is a mere restatement (anuvāda). To this, the reply is: we do not say that it is purposeless with respect to its application (viniyoga). For in the context of application, the meaning of the sentence is understood precisely in this way [as a restatement]. However, its status as an *injunction to employ* (prayoktṛtva) is not possible. Why is it not possible? Because the collection of factors of action (kāraka-grāma) is eternally established; here, there is a restriction (niyama) regarding the substance.

It is understood that neither for the causal factors (*kāraka*) nor for one who is not a causal factor is agency (*prayoktṛtva*) possible. Therefore, this is merely an application (*viniyoga*), from which a specific object is understood, and not the operation of an agent; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*). Herein lies the intended meaning:

Substance alone is the causal factor (*kāraka*) possessing power, because the effect is observed when it is present and not observed when it is absent; this much is the definition of a causal factor. [Objection: If substance alone is the causal factor, then why does it not produce the effect even when obstructed by mantras, medicines, and the like? An answer must be given to this deviation. [Response: In that case, there exists a certain form (*rūpa*) to be required, which is beyond the reach of the senses and can be removed by mantras, medicines, and so forth.
The capacity (*śakti*) is postulated on the grounds that "some form [of power] exists"; however, it is not itself an agent (*kāraka*). For it merely assists the agent;

it does not act as an agent by itself. Consequently, since only a substance (*dravya*) possessing capacity is the agent, and because agency belongs to the substance alone, it is possible for *sam-* and other prefixes to take the form of action (*kriyā*); thus, the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) is established through this application (*viniyoga*).

It might be argued that [the mention] is redundant; however, it is called a restatement (*anuvādaka*) because, upon considering its inclusion within the agent's activity (*prayoktṛvyāpāra*), it serves as a reiteration. For even when something has already been enjoined (*viniyukta*), its subsequent inclusion occurs precisely by way of being a *kāraka* (participant in the action). And the status of being a *kāraka* is common to all [participants]; at most, there is a distinction between them based on their being merely substances (*dravya*). Yet, a substance is not what is directly included [as a participant], because that form lacks a connection with the action; rather, it is included by way of being a *kāraka*.

"Because there is no restrictive rule (niyama), it is purposeless and is merely a restatement (anuvāda). Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that this specific quality of the sacrifice and so forth—the object of the injunction—is understood precisely at the stage of application (viniyoga), not at the stage of procurement (upādāna). To this, it is replied: if something other than the substance were understood as the factor of action (kāraka), then it would be as you say. But here, it is the substance itself that is understood as the factor of action.

Because of its designation, there is the production of case-endings (*vibhakti*). The meaning of this is as follows: first, *sam* and the others are understood as the factors of action (*kāraka*) of the verbal activity; and since these very distinct entities constitute the factors of action, the injunction (*vidhi*) also takes them up as such. Thus, [the injunction] has a distinct object. (1) G. The state of being employed by the factor of action; (2) G. The pointlessness of the [injunction].

The activity of the agent (*prayoktṛvyāpāra*) is nothing other than the specific distinctions such as *samā* and so forth, because nothing else can be employed [in their stead]. To explain this very point, he raises an objection: "But surely, an instrument (*kāraka*) is employed only through its engagement in an action; and there is no action that is devoid of instruments."

The meaning of this is as follows: the employment of a *kāraka* (participant in action) does not exist independently. Rather, since there is no action devoid of a *kāraka*, it is precisely through the employment of the action that the *kāraka* is employed. And because that form of the *kāraka* is non-distinct [from the action], its application has an unrestricted scope. It is true that an object (*karman*) is not devoid of a *kāraka*; however, there is no such thing as a "kāraka" in general. For whatever indeed...

Either a substance or a quality is presented by a case-ending (vibhakti), and that alone is the *kāraka*. Therefore, although there is agency (*prayoktṛtva*) by virtue of application (*viniyoga*), the *kāraka* is distinct; thus, the restriction of usage is possible. Now, one might object: "Granted that there is a restriction regarding application, but how is it regarding the act of taking up (*upādāna*)? To this he says: "It has been stated, however, that an injunction (*niyoga*) follows the application, provided that it is possible. For whatever [is applied],...

That which is understood through *viniyoga* (application) as the means for accomplishing the *niyoga* (injunction) must itself be adopted for the sake of the fulfillment of that *niyoga*. For if something else were adopted, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-fulfillment of the *niyoga* due to the absence of a proper means. And thus, the injunction is said to be for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), and not otherwise. The same applies to substances (*dravya*). Now, one might object: since even qualities (*guṇa*) and universals (*jāti*) are applied as *kārakas* by means of case-endings, they are just like the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth.

An injunction that is not accompanied by a specific means is not a mere restatement; regarding this, he says: "It is indeed appropriate that a substance is expressed by case-endings because it functions as a *kāraka*, but an injunction is not thereby stated.
[p. r1014] (1) P. 1240 (2) G. na vidhirucyate.

In cases such as "white" (*śveta*) and so forth, the quality (*guṇa*) is merely a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of that [substance]. However, where there is an understanding of the quality as a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) by means of the case-ending itself—as in "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*)—that has already been established by the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*). Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that because the purpose is the procurement of the substance (*dravya*), there is no intention to express either the quality or the genus (*jāti*). The meaning of this is: when not conveyed by a *kāraka*-case ending, it is merely a qualifier of that [substance].

In the Vedic injunction, "A sacrificial pap (*caru*) of white rice grains," the qualities and the genus are the examples here; for in that case, since those two are not heard as being directly subordinate members of the action, they are [to be understood] as being enjoined by virtue of being conveyed by a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*), just like the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) in the application of a substance.

Because [the substance] is already present, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*); and since there is no contact with an injunction (*niyoga*), a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is untenable. Therefore, this is solely for the purpose of taking up the substance, not for the purpose of taking up a quality (*guṇa*) or a genus (*jāti*). To this it is replied: It is true that this is for the purpose of taking up the substance.
For it is impossible to take up that very substance as qualified by those [qualities] while it is devoid of them; thus, even in the case of qualities and genera, [they depend on] the substance.

The establishment of the necessity of taking up [the two]. Its meaning is as follows: first, by virtue of being expressed by distinct words, the substance (*dravya*) is qualified by those two. And that qualified [substance] is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of that ritual action; thus, the injunction (*niyoga*) is to be accomplished by such a substance. If one were to take up other qualities (*guṇa*), there would be an absence of such a substance, and consequently, due to the deficiency of a constituent part, the injunction would not be fulfilled. Therefore, the taking up of those two must necessarily be performed; thus, the injunction is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
And because that [preparation] is the primary factor in the *saṃskāra*. But what is the distinction regarding the *saṃskāra*? This is the distinction here:

for a rule concerning a *saṃskāra* is devoid of a governing context (*adhikāra*), since a *saṃskāra* exists for the sake of that which is to be prepared (*saṃskārya*). Here, the purpose is not that of the subject under discussion; [it is rather] a subordinate element of the sacrifice (*yāgāṅga*).

Action is understood [from it]. Therefore, there is indeed no intention to express [the action] as a primary factor; this is the distinction from the two previous cases. The meaning of this is as follows: that which is the object of a qualified injunction (*adhikāra-niyoga*) is taken up by the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*) because of its contact with that qualified injunction. In that regard, first of all—

The performance of a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakriyā*) is directly the object of the injunction (*vidhi*), because a purificatory rite exists for the sake of that which is to be purified. For those who know the nature of the "object" (*viṣaya*), it is held that the "object" is that for which the accomplishment of the mandate (*niyoga*) itself constitutes the task. Therefore, since they lack the status of being both the qualification (*adhikāra*) and the object (*viṣaya*), purificatory rites do not here serve the purpose of the person entitled to perform them (*adhikṛtapuruṣārtha*). Consequently, because they do not touch upon the mandate (*niyoga*), a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is untenable here as well; thus, [the passage] is a restatement (*anuvāda*). To this, it is replied:

The qualification (*adhikāra*) itself is not understood; rather, the fact that the substance is for the sake of the qualified person (*adhikṛta-dravyārthatā*) is perceived. What follows from this? This results: the substance, as distinguished by its preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), is understood as a qualifier of the object of the qualification. Consequently, like a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), it too is taken up by the injunction of qualification; thus it is said to be "like that" (*tadvat*). The meaning of this is: such a substance—

Since the *niyoga* (the mandate) has the sacrifice as its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), no other substance may be employed. It has been shown that without such a substance, because of the absence of the requisite material, the sacrifice would not exist, and consequently the *niyoga* would not be fulfilled. Furthermore, it has already been demonstrated that injunctions such as "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) function as restatements (*anuvādaka*), because they do not possess a separate objective due to their inclusion within the primary objective of the mandate; thus, being part of the same undivided *niyoga*, they are subordinate injunctions (*aṅgavidhi*). This being the case, the subordinate injunction is a restatement.
Thus [it is said].

The injunction to sacrifice (*yajati-codanā*) consists of substance, deity, and action. Now, one might object: "Is this mere description of the nature of the constituent elements of a ritual act (*padārtha-svarūpa*) not irrelevant to this treatise, let alone to this chapter? Anticipating this doubt, he states the connection: "What, then, are those subjects of qualification (*adhikāra-viṣaya*) which..."

By way of entry, that which effects it is its qualifier; the refinements (*saṃskāra*) of that [agent] enter into the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*). But what are those injunctions of qualification? They are the *niyogas* whose objects are the domains of the injunctions.

"What are the objects?"—this refers to what was previously mentioned by way of context. The answer is: sacrifices, gifts, and oblations, such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," "one desiring long life should give gold," "one desiring good fortune should offer oblations," and so forth. This is merely an illustration; there are others as well, such as fasts, vows, and ascetic penances, which are connected with scriptural injunctions regarding desire (*kāma*). But who [is the agent]?

It is stated that the description of their essential natures (*svarūpavarṇana*) is for the purpose of removing the doubt that there is no mutual distinction between sacrifice (*yāga*), gift (*dāna*), and oblation (*homa*), since they all consist in the relinquishment of one's own ownership (*svatvatyāgātmakatva*). Its meaning is as follows: since sacrifice also consists in the relinquishment of a substance, as do oblation and gift, the doubt arises as to what the distinction between these is. To remove that, the author of the Sūtras describes their essential nature. By means of those three Sūtras—

Thus it has been said: sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity; that same act, when augmented by the pouring of liquid, is an oblation (*homa*); and giving (*dāna*) is relinquishment consisting in the transfer of ownership to another. What is meant by this is as follows: there is a distinction in their status as verbal referents, because words function according to specific limiting conditions (*upādhi*). However, insofar as they consist essentially in relinquishment, there is no distinction whatsoever. But how is this so?

What is the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *yāga* in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*)? It is the determination of the word’s power (*śakti*) with respect to that meaning, having first apprehended the denoted object and ascertained its related referent. Nor can this meaning be attained through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the nature of the deity cannot be understood by any other means of valid cognition; thus, this too must be stated.

What, then, is this so-called "deity" (devatā)? What is the nature of the "designation" (uddeśa), and what is the form of the "renunciation" (tyāga)? To this it is replied: when someone renounces an offering such as a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) while designating Agni and others—whose status as deities is established by injunctions (codanā) such as those concerning the Āgneya sacrifice—then the young and the old say of him in that very context: "He sacrifices to Agni and the others. When he...

When one performs merely the relinquishment of one's own substance, one does not employ the word "yajati" (he sacrifices). Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), the derivation of the meaning of the root *yaji* is as follows:
sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity. This is the method by which even children [understand it];
there is no difference in this regard.
Those elders, too, acquired proficiency during their childhood; thus, because the linguistic usage of elders is beginningless, nothing is amiss. Now, one might ask:
how can there be proficiency regarding the meaning of a deity? It is said in reply: when the oblation for Agni and so forth, as well as the hymn (*sūkta*), have been enjoined, if someone—

When one renounces [an offering] for the sake of Agni, or employs a hymn of praise (*stotra*) or a recitation (*śastra*) characterized by the qualities of Agni, worldly people say in that regard: "Agni is the deity here. Regarding this, the ignorant conceive that he for whose sake the oblation is renounced, who is praised, or who is extolled, is the deity. In this case as well, there is no fault whatsoever, provided one relies on the beginninglessness of the tradition of usage among the elders (*vṛddha*). It is exactly thus.

Those who are learned understand that even in the Veda there exists the status of a deity by hearing words ending in suffixes prescribed according to the governing rules (adhikāra), such as "this is its deity" (*sāsya devatā*).
They maintain that the deity is precisely that which is enjoined there as being the deity; they do not hold that when an oblation is offered to one [deity], another [deity] is the deity.
Thus, following worldly convention, they determine that the state of being enjoined belongs to the deity alone. And it is not thus...

It must be stated that for those who understand the meaning of the deity solely from the Veda and engage in linguistic usage, there would be no acquisition of proficiency (*vyutpatti*); thus, the cognition of the deity's meaning would not be preceded by the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*). For even in the case of earlier individuals, the very cause of their proficiency was the linguistic usage of elders; the comprehension of the Vedic meaning is preceded by that [usage], and linguistic usage is preceded by that [comprehension]. Thus, the proficiency of each subsequent person is likewise preceded by that [usage]. And as for the enunciation (*uddeśa*):
The designation of the recipient (*saṃpradāna-kāraka*) by its own specific term is, for example, as in "to Agni.

Renunciation (*tyāga*), moreover, is the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) of the owner toward indifference, because ownership is a worldly matter. It is precisely when such a resolve occurs in the owner that [he thinks], "This is not mine."

Thus, in that very context, because of worldly convention—namely, that "this belongs to him" and "this ownership does not belong to him"—the cessation of ownership occurs through mere intention alone; this is therefore faultless. Consequently, since the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is possible for the word *yāga* (sacrifice), the derivation of the word *homa* (offering) is also established. For [the root] *yajati*—

In a case where a *homa*—which consists of the throwing of a substance upon a specific location as its substratum—is prompted by an injunction (*codanā*), it can indeed be understood from the use of the word itself that "the *homa* is that which is accompanied by the act of throwing.
Now, for what purpose was the qualification of "giving" (*dāna*) stated as "consisting in the transfer of ownership to another"? It is said: [it is not necessary].

Giving is not merely renunciation; rather, it is also the acceptance by the person who has become the recipient (*saṃpradāna-kāraka*). And such [acceptance] cannot be accomplished by the person who renounces alone; it must also be accomplished by the acceptor. For without an acceptor, there can be no act of accepting. Therefore, renunciation depends upon an acceptor for the sake of the completion of its nature as the acceptance by another. Otherwise, [it would remain incomplete].

For [otherwise] there would be mere abandonment alone. And it is not the case that, when something has been abandoned by a previous owner, if someone were to accept it at the same time or before [the new owner], then it would belong to that person alone. One should not suspect this. For we have already stated that this is a worldly matter; as it says: "for the sake of the deity" (G.), "at the same time or before" (R.), and "there is acceptance" (R.).

Regarding the term "ownership" (*svatva*): in this context, it is a matter of worldly convention that when an owner relinquishes something with the intent of transferring ownership to another, it belongs only to the one who accepts it, and not to anyone else. Now, suppose the person to whom the owner relinquishes it with the intent of transferring ownership does not accept it.
Even then, the fruit would arise from the donor’s act of giving because the mere act of relinquishment constitutes that [act of giving], and it is performed by him.

What kind of dullness is this on your part? We have already stated that giving is not merely the act of relinquishment; rather, it also consists in the form of acceptance. Furthermore, the fruit results from the performance of what is enjoined, and the enjoined matter is the acceptance of that which one has relinquished for its sake.

One must act accordingly; one should strive so that what has been enjoined comes to pass. In this regard, some person desiring to accept [the gift] takes possession of it merely by its relinquishment, while others do so through entreaties and the like; thus, for the sake of attaining the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), such a person should be relied upon.
And at that time, the one who accepts stands in the place of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Enough of this prolixity.

Because the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) concludes with the completion of the action. Here, the *Bhāṣya* considers only the application (*viniyoga*); anticipating the objection that this is irrelevant, [the author] asks:

"What, then, is the connection of this [procedure] with the definition of 'appropriation' (*upādāna*)? Is the connection such that the mere holding of what has been appropriated for the sake of the *Atithyeṣṭi* is employed by both the *Upasad* and the *Agnīṣoma*, or is there a fresh appropriation of what was previously discarded? Or...

The intention is that the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) raised a doubt regarding the cause because he wished to consider this very point: whether this statement indicates that the act of taking (*upādāna*) is distinct from the mere property (*dharma*), or whether the act of taking is indeed common to both. Here, the seed for the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:
one must state the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) only for as many words as are actually heard in the text, and not with reference to words that have not been heard. In that regard—

In the phrase "when [it is] for the *ātithyā*," the word *yat* (which) is heard; and that [word] requires another related element previously mentioned. Here, the *ātithyā* is mentioned in close proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta*). Therefore, it must be described as being dependent precisely upon the *ātithyā*. Consequently, the connection is this: "the *barhis* which is connected to the *ātithyā*. In that regard, if its connection [to the *barhis*] is established solely by virtue of its being employed in the *ātithyā*, then that is the first position (*pakṣa*). Or else...

At that time, the second [alternative] is [rejected] because of being already occupied. On this point, he states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): First of all, there is no application elsewhere of that which is primary and subordinate to another, because it would contradict the established understanding (*pratipatti*), just as the operation of something already engaged elsewhere in one place cannot occur elsewhere due to a contradiction in the nature of things (*vastu-virodha*).

This has been stated in the *Somaliptādhikaraṇa*. Furthermore, it has also been stated in the *Āmikṣādhikaraṇa* that "appropriation follows the application" (*viniyoga*). Therefore, because [the material] has already been applied in the *Ātithyā* sacrifice—as in the phrase "in the *Ātithyā*"—it is not tenable that the mere maintenance of what was appropriated for the *Ātithyā* should be employed for the *Agnīṣomīya* and the *Upasad*s. Moreover, the instruction regarding the "offered-remnant" (*niriṣṭaka*) is consistent with the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

Because of contradiction, it does not occur; for the learned do not perform a sacrifice without bricks. Furthermore, because of the recourse to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since there is no connection with the *ātithyā* at the end of the performance, if there were a connection, its non-connected nature would have to be indicated by that [connection]; thus, it is not tenable that this is merely a figurative indication. Likewise, even the extension of properties (*dharmātideśa*) is abandoned on account of the fear of figurative indication, such that the properties of the *barhis* grass would have to be indicated.

Therefore, it is established that a common understanding alone is supported by the Vedic text; thus, it is proven that the material is indeed common [to all]. Furthermore, the word *yat* (which) should be understood as referring to its connection with the act of cutting, since the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) presupposes such cutting. This should be explained without contradiction as follows: "That which is this sacrificial grass being cut is for the *ātithyā*, that for the *upasads*, and that for the *agnīṣomīya*."
Thus ends the [fourth chapter] in the *Ṛjuvimalā*, the commentary composed by the venerable Śālikanātha Miśra.
The second chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*.
The third quarter of the fourth chapter:

Regarding substances, purificatory acts, and ritual acts. Now, one might raise the objection: "But the author of the Bhāṣya undertakes an investigation into injunctions of results and explanatory passages (arthavādas);
that [investigation] is both irrelevant and redundant, since the fact that they serve as praise has already been stated in the section on arthavādas. To dispel this doubt, he says:

It was stated at the beginning of this chapter that the operation of *niyoga* (the mandate) is considered in all cases. Now, here it is considered whether or not the operation of the injunction (*vidhi*) is possible for a person by way of a connection with a fruit (*phala*). There is no inconsistency in the fact that, having raised the objection regarding the status of the injunction as a mandate of the fruit based on its own operation, its character as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) is now asserted. Nor is there any tautology, because [the previous discussion] established the fruit for the person—

In this section concerning the impossibility of a relationship, it was deliberated upon in the *arthavāda* section of the *pramāṇalakṣaṇa* (the definition of the means of valid knowledge) how the possibility of validity could arise; thus, this present inquiry is preceded by that. Likewise, even the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) presented there in the *audumbara* section of the *pramāṇalakṣaṇa*—which holds that the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*) is perceived [as leading] to the accomplishment of a result—is also [addressed here].

Furthermore, how can the relationship characterized as the means-end relation—consisting in the Audumbara wood being the instrument for making the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—be understood as conveying an injunction (*niyoga*) directed toward another action? The statement "the sacrificial post is to be made with Audumbara wood" conveys an injunction whose object is the instrument for the post;

this is because [the Audumbara wood] is not itself enjoined [by that sentence]. And if it were admitted to be something enjoined, it would necessarily enter into another thing that is to be enjoined, for there cannot be two things to be enjoined within a single [injunction].

(1) P. 1244 (2) G. It is possible for there to be the status of being a single sentence through the application [of the injunction]; and this unity of sentence is understood. And that which is understood ought not to be abandoned. Therefore...

Another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) would have to be required; and since that does not exist, there would be invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). This point has been stated for the purpose of refuting such an objection. Therefore, because another matter was considered through the acceptance of the result (*phala*), there is no tautology. Furthermore, considering that the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is examined as an introduction to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is stated that the prima facie position exists for the purpose of refuting what is to be refuted. However, in this case, [it concerns] its own object.

The consideration is that *niyoga* (the injunctive force) is not possible. How so? Because [terms] such as "of whom" (*yasya*) cannot function as qualifications of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*).

The meaning of this is as follows: here, it is demonstrated that there is no relationship of means and end between the hearing of the "evil verse" (*apāpaśloka*) and so forth, and the *juhū* ladle made of *parṇa* wood and so forth, because of the statement: "He whose *juhū* is made of *parṇa* wood does not hear an evil verse."

Thus, the hearing of the "fame of one free from evil" (*apāpaśloka*) is not heard as a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, in this case, the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇa*) is precisely the denial of the fruit. Consequently, there is no tautology with the *Audumbara* section either. How is it impossible? This is the intention of the objector asking here.

In this way, the relationship between the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is understood from such a statement in the world; the same understanding is obtained in the Veda as well. If it is argued that [the Veda] possesses independence because its own fruitfulness resides solely in the effect of its own statements, [we reply: the relationship between the means and the end is not possible without a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikārin*). Therefore, the status of being a qualification of the eligible person is understood through implication (*aupādānika*). [The opponent states] the answer: "Because of the connection with that..."

"Because an injunction (*niyoga*) is untenable. With that very intention, he asks: "Why? The answer is: "Because the instruction is given as an established fact (*siddhavat*). The meaning is this: just as in the statement "Devadatta cooks rice," one perceives the cooking of rice as a mere description of a person's activity; one does not perceive the cooking of rice as something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), such that "rice must be cooked by Devadatta. Thus, there is no perception of the cooking of rice as a task to be performed.
Likewise here as well, even the hearing of the "sinless verse" (*apāpaśloka*) is expressed in the present tense. Under the guise of a conclusion, he refutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

"Therefore, this is not the meaning of the word: 'He for whom the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood does not hear a sinful verse. [This is because] it arises from another cognition—(1) G. produced by the final position; (2) G. by what? (3) G. through the two qualifications; (4) G. and when understood.

(4) R. Because this meaning is understood from his own statement alone. By this, he states the disparity with common worldly usage; for even in the world, from such a statement, the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)—

That [cognition] is a determination of the [Vedic] entity, because the purport of such a statement has been ascertained by means of another source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor can the purport of a Vedic sentence be understood from anything else; thus he says: "And there exists no other cognition that serves as the cause for determining the purport.
Therefore, it is logical that the meaning stated in the first chapter, in the section concerning the Arthavādas—that it is of the nature of praise—is indeed the correct one.

Thus it stands: when one considers those [passages] which, by their mere appearance, present themselves as if they were results through a commonality with worldly speech, they are seen to be merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) because they lack a causal basis (*nimitta*).

This is because that which depends on a cause (*naimittika*) is subject to modification. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: “In cases such as ‘One desiring cattle should perform the *praṇayana* with a *godohana* vessel,’...”

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position has been advanced on the grounds that sentences convey two types of meanings—those pertaining to the ritual (*kratvartha*) and those pertaining to the person (*puruṣārtha*). He challenges this by asking: "But how can a single sentence here be presented as having a dual purpose? The meaning of this is as follows: it is not logical for a single sentence to have multiple meanings, because the collective function of words is understood from the linguistic usage of elders; furthermore, this sentence consists of three words. In that case, it cannot be [both] by excluding the word *paśukāma*...

The meaning can be understood; and upon accepting that, it possesses the status of being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*) alone, not for the sake of the ritual (*kratvarthatva*). Now, if it should be argued that there are two meanings because no distinction is perceived, that is not so. For a distinction is apprehended through the employment of the word "desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*). And even in cases where no distinction is apprehended due to the absence of contradiction with other words, the sentence still has but a single meaning. As for the apprehension of a distinction, however—

[This is determined] by context and other such factors. He states this very point in the passage beginning with "yatrāpi" and so forth. Now, it might be asked: why should there be a double meaning for the sentence itself, rather than [the ambiguity arising] from the requirement of another word?

To this, he says: "The dual purpose of a single statement has already been refuted in the *pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa* itself, because in the *Vājapeyādhikaraṇa*, neither an injunction (*vidhi*) nor a restatement (*anuvāda*), nor the states of being known or unknown, were heard [as coexisting]. Furthermore, since those two cannot exist simultaneously in one place, here too, in the view that it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), the connection with the leading forth (*praṇayana*) is what is to be enjoined; whereas in the view that it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), it is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, this [position] is indeed an impossible prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)."
The objection appears to be: "In this case, it is stated—this is exactly so; in the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related), there is indeed a single purpose.

At the stage of application (*viniyoga*), it serves only the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatva*), not the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*)—this is the meaning. However, since two purposes are possible here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers it to serve the purpose of the sacrifice as well. This is the sense: even for a single application, there can be a dual purpose.

It has been stated that [the act] can consist of both that which serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and that which serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*); thus, its status as serving the purpose of the sacrifice has also been mentioned. But why is it possible for there to be these two purposes? To this he says:

"And it has been stated that the taking up [of the water] follows from the connection. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason. Because it has been stated that the taking up follows from the connection, and because there is here a connection with the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) as well—by means of which [connection], in the case of its serving the purpose of the sacrifice, [the injunction] "he carries forward the water" and so forth [is established].
When the act of fetching water and so forth has been enjoined by such rules as "He fetches water with a water-jar," and when one is in the state of selecting the means for accomplishing that rite,
it is understood that the *godohana* vessel alone should be used; for no connection with any other [vessel] is perceived, even though the rule is primarily intent upon something else.

It is argued that because there is an understanding of the relationship within the sentence, by virtue of the material being taken up in accordance with that [relationship], it is understood to reside in the *praṇayana* (the act of carrying) as a subsidiary of the sacrifice—just as the number "one" and so forth are. Now, an objection is raised: was it not stated in the *Āmikṣā-adhikaraṇa* that the taking up of material follows the application (*viniyoga*), and not the relationship? This is not so; for it is precisely because application is said to be the cause of the relationship that application [is primary], and not conversely.

(1) Of that which has the characteristic of having two purposes; (2) the meaning is that it is desired solely for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha); (3) because it would result in a state of being [otherwise], that very [purpose] is resorted to, since it has been stated that the adoption [of a rule] follows the connection. Therefore, there are two effects: [the effect] of the sacrifice and [the effect] of the human goal—

The purpose of the *godohana* vessel and other such items is the cause of their employment (*upādānahetu*), because both types of relationship—those with the sacrifice and those with the human agent—are understood [simultaneously]. For, by abandoning the connection with the ritual action, the status of the substance as serving the human purpose is not established;

rather, the result is accomplished precisely through the *godohana* which has become the instrumental cause for the act of carrying water (*praṇayana*). To this, it is replied: what was stated regarding the mere relationship is not tenable.

"Subordinate adoption" (sāryupādāna) means that which is adopted in accordance with the relationship established by the word; it does not follow from the mere relationship. Furthermore, from the word itself, the connection is understood precisely as being for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha). The meaning of this is as follows: an injunction (vidhi) brings about the adoption of only that without which it cannot itself be accomplished. And that without which [the injunction] cannot be accomplished is understood to be its means (sādhana). [The text continues: "means..."

And the verbal expression [of the relationship] occurs through the word alone, not from anything else; nor does the word denote a mere relationship independent of its connection with an injunction (*niyoga*). Therefore, the material is to be taken up in accordance with the relationship established by the word. As for that which is taken up—such as the *ādhāna* (fire-laying) and so forth—which is not itself enjoined, it is solely for the purpose of taking up the fire that has been enjoined. Even here, if the taking up is resorted to only for the sake of accomplishing the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) that is enjoined, then [it is not a separate act].

The restrictive rule (*niyama*) is not established, because it is possible for that [result] to be accomplished by other means as well. However, since sacrificial fires (*agni*) are not worldly [entities], *ādhāna* (the rite of laying the fires) is the sole means [to obtain them].

[Objection: But surely the connection with the action is also understood. [Reply: True, it is understood, but as something subservient to the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), not as something subservient to its own purpose. This is the point here: the connection between the *godohana* vessel and the carrying forward of water (*praṇayana*) is understood from common worldly experience alone, in relation to one who desires cattle.

It is enjoined; however, it is not made known by the word itself in such a way that this relationship would extend to its specific application (*viniyoga*). Therefore, because even that which is understood from the word is of a worldly nature, and because that form is possible in other substances as well, it is not denoted by the word with necessary restriction solely through its application. This is the meaning. Now, an objection is raised: "But has the author of the Bhāṣya not stated that both relations are conveyed by the word itself? To this he replies:

As for what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that because a specific distinction is not understood, the sentence "Go to the Alambusas" must refer to both [the river and the people]—that is intended only for cases where there is no certainty due to the absence of context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth. It is not, however, possible to understand two things from the word alone. But here, since a specific distinction is understood, there is no uncertainty.

This is the meaning. It is true that this was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya during the stage of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*); however, that would not hold during the stage of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). By the statement in the Bhāṣya, "In that case, because no specific distinction is perceived, there is the understanding of both purposes," it is described that since no specific distinction is perceived there through context (*prakaraṇa*) and other means, there would be a lack of determination in common worldly usage; therefore, the understanding of both purposes arises. What is being said is this: when context and the like are absent—

"Let there be no definitive conclusion (anirṇaya) in the world"—this [statement] is intended merely to show that it is not possible to understand both [meanings] from the word alone. However, in this context, because the word *kāmī* is heard, the meaning of that commentary is that there *is* a definitive conclusion. Now, one might object: "This section (*adhikaraṇa*) was commenced as a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*), assuming that nothing exists for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); therefore, the introduction of a rule prescribed in general terms (*sāmānyavihita*) is not appropriate. To this he replies: "But is it not the case that nothing has been prescribed..."
Having raised the objection "it exists," the presentation of a general injunction is not intended to override [the specific], but rather with respect to the praise accomplished by the *sāman*;
thus there is no fault. The meaning of this is as follows: this is not presented as a general injunction, but rather by way of its nature as praise (*stuti*).

That statement is intended to mean that since it is to be accomplished by means of *sāman*, there will be some *sāman* such as the *abhivarta*; it does not, however, intend to describe the specific nature of the *abhivarta* itself.
This is because [the rule] applies when one thing serves two purposes. Now, an objection is raised: "But here there are two distinct sentences: 'He offers with curd' (*dadhnā juhoti*)..."

Thus, one [injunction] prescribes curd for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), while the other, "for one desiring sensory power, [he should offer] with curd," establishes it as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); how then, as in the previous case, can there be only—

The meaning of this is: the *agnihotra*...

Regarding the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt svargakāmaḥ*), although there is a distinction from the original injunction (*utpatti-niyoga*) due to the hearing of the word denoting the qualified person (*adhikāri-pada*), nevertheless, because this [injunction] is connected with the purpose of the oblation (*homa*), and because it is understood to be connected with the oblation mentioned in proximity to the original injunction, and since that oblation is non-different [from the one in the original], and because its performance is prompted by the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*), the original injunction is also established; thus, it does not have a separate status as a prompter (*prayoktṛtva*). Therefore, by means of the [injunction of] qualification—

Just as [the milk] enters into that [act] by virtue of its production being dependent on it, so too here, even though there is a connection with the desire for sense-organs (*indriyakāma*), because of the relationship between the curd and the *homa* to be accomplished, it is logical that it enters into that [act] precisely because it is prompted by it; it does not, however, enter into another prompter connected to the sacrifice (*kratu*). This being the position reached, it is replied: this is not correct, for even the sacrifice is determined to be a prompter here, since the sacrifice also possesses a goal—namely, heaven (*svarga*). Thus, the curd is related to the *homa* which is subordinate to the sacrifice, and therefore it is prompted by the sacrifice. Consequently, the curd is connected to the sacrifice through the *homa*, and thus it is logical that it enters into the sacrifice itself. Therefore, the curd is an integral part of the *homa*, and the *homa* is an integral part of the sacrifice. Hence, the curd is connected to the sacrifice.
