The meaning of this is as follows: because of the phrase "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), [the curd] enters into the sacrifice under discussion; and since that sacrifice possesses its own qualification (*adhikāra*), its performance is established by the very impulsion of that qualification.
Thus, there is no requirement for another impulsion, and consequently, there is no entry into the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, [this is so]...

Regarding the connection between the quality and the fruit: in the case of an offering (*homa*) that has a substratum (*āśraya*), the fact that curd (*dadhi*) and so forth serve the purpose of that substratum is not required [for the connection with the fruit]. And since that which is not required does not enter into a connection, [the offering] does not enter into the jurisdiction of one who desires sense-power (*indriyakāma*). However, the ritual injunction (*kratuniyoga*) does require service to the ritual (*kratudaimarthyam*).

Thus, it is logical that she is included within that specific context. Therefore, the application expressed by "He offers with curd" (dadhnā juhoti) is indeed solely for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*).

The statement "for one desiring sense-power, [one should offer] with curd" is thus for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). As it has been said: "One performs the *agnihotra*," and "One who desires heaven should perform the *agnihotra*."

Thus, it is logical that there is a single performer, because no other qualification is heard; however, in this case, since there are two qualifications—the obligatory (*nitya*) and the occasional (*naimittika*)—the distinction is appropriate. Regarding substances intended for action: how, in this instance, can the vow (*vrata*), though studied within the context (*prakaraṇa*), have the person as its purpose?

Anticipating the objection that the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) might think [otherwise], he says: "But here, because the vow (*vrata*) serves the purpose of sustaining life, the proponent of the prima facie view considers it to be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), just like the rule 'one should eat food facing the east' or the rules regarding acceptance of gifts and so forth.

The meaning of this is: because the vow serves the purpose of sustaining life, the proponent of the prima facie view considers it to be for the sake of the person by means of that very rule (*niyamena*).

Because for one who desires that [result], the engagement in it is possible; and because it is understood that only one who has engaged therein possesses the qualification (*adhikāra*). It is not logical for another qualification to intervene. Just as for a qualified person already engaged in eating, the rule of facing east does not constitute a separate qualification—just like the rules regarding receiving gifts and so forth—for a qualified person engaged in acquiring wealth, the rules regarding receiving gifts and so forth [do not constitute a separate qualification].

Just as the observance of vows does not enter into another sphere of authority once [the state of] attainment has been reached, so too it serves only the purpose of the person. But if this is so, would it not follow that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is sublated? This is not a fault; for by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), the context is indeed weaker. This is because, upon considering the capacity of the vow—(1) P. 1251—[it is seen that the vow applies to all stages].

For one engaged in that [rite], a restriction regarding milk and so forth appears; and through a consideration of the context (*prakaraṇa*), its status as an auxiliary to the sacrifice (*kratvaṅgatā*) is established.

In this regard, it was demonstrated in the third [book of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra] that among these, the capacity (*sāmarthya*) in the form of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), which is the nature of the context, is stronger. To this, it is replied: this is not a restriction—

An injunction (*niyoga*) admits the postulation of an entitlement (*adhikāra*). And the entitlement to the sacrifice is present here. When there is the proximity of an explicitly stated entitlement, that which has no stated entitlement appears as being for the sake of that very [sacrifice] through its denotation. Since the connection with an enjoined person (*niyojya*) is obtained for the injunction precisely by virtue of being for that purpose, there is no need for another entitlement by which an entitlement would have to be postulated through implication. Therefore, the injunction—

This *niyoga* (injunction) is logically valid only as something that enters into the qualification for a ritual (*kratv-adhikāra*). As for what was said—that it ought to be like the rules regarding acceptance (*pratigraha*) and so forth—that is appropriate because no qualification is heard there; the meaning is that no qualification is mentioned in close proximity (*sannihita*) there. [In those cases], one assumes a qualification for the acquirer, the earner, who has set out toward earning. Here, however, the opposite is the case, as it is directly present—

It was shown at the outset that [the restriction is] due to hearing the qualification for the sacrifice (*adhikāra*). Therefore, it is established that the restriction of the substance is indeed prompted by the sacrifice (*kratu*). Now, one might object: "This which has been stated is incorrect, because it would entail the position that [the substance] is prompted by the root *yaj* (the act of sacrificing). To this he says: "It is stated that it is prompted by the qualification for the sacrifice."

"Because no fruit is mentioned in the injunction. Now, one might object that the example of the Viśvajit sacrifice is inappropriate here; for in the sixth book, regarding the *satra* sacrifices, it was stated that [the fruit is] for one who desires [cattle], etc.

Since the topic has been established, he says here: "In this context, injunctions devoid of a governing purpose (*adhikāra*) are the examples. This is the intention: that which is devoid of a governing purpose is the example here; for even though a governing purpose exists there, the logical analysis is conducted as if it did not exist. The doubt is whether one should assume a governing purpose for them, or whether they terminate in themselves alone. [Objection: But surely [an action] must have a fruit...

Regarding the statement "it is fruitless," a doubt is heard in the Bhāṣya. It is replied: "Without a qualification (adhikāra), there is no fruit"—this was demonstrated by the author who stated that the qualification is established in the section concerning those desiring heaven (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*). Otherwise, the concluding summary would have been that "the primacy of heaven is established. Therefore, this is indeed an investigation into whether there is a qualification or no qualification.

The meaning of this is as follows: the doubt regarding the result mentioned by the Bhāṣyakāra concerns the result that serves as the basis for qualification (*adhikāra*), and not the result as such, because the primary meaning of the sentence is the *niyoga* (the injunction), and that *niyoga* is independent of a result. An injunction requires a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), not a result. However, it was shown in the sixth book that when a person desiring [a specific end] hears the injunction, the result is implied. And this has also been shown by the Bhāṣyakāra in the case of heaven.

Because of the concluding statement, "Therefore, having established its primacy, the qualification is proven," for if the fruit were dependent solely upon the qualification, then that very qualification—which serves as the cause—would have to be established first; thus, it would be logical for the conclusion to state directly that heaven, being the fruit thereof, possesses primacy. However, if [the qualification] were independent of that, then the conclusion would simply state that the primacy of heaven is established. Which, then, is the case?

How is this established? Because an injunction (*niyoga*)—as long as it is merely an injunction—must terminate in a specific procedure (*kartavyatā*) and cannot possibly terminate in a qualification (*adhikāra*). He raises an objection against the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But surely an injunction itself cannot be accomplished without a qualification.
(1) G. adds: "We shall explain this in the section concerning the person desiring heaven (*svargakāmādhikāra*)."

For as long as someone does not understand, "This is my duty," so long will they not perform it; and in the absence of performance, the injunction (*niyoga*) is not fulfilled. He resolves this objection: Who has said that an injunction is not fulfilled in the absence of an entitlement (*adhikāra*)?

If it is not accomplished, let it indeed not be accomplished. The injunction belongs to one who is authorized; let there be an injunction for him who is authorized. However, an authorization does not come into being merely by the fact that there is no injunction, even in the absence of a verbal statement. [Objection: But surely, in the absence of an authorization, because [the act] would not be something to be performed, the comprehension of the injunction would be sublated. This is your intention: that the meaning of the injunction consists in the form of a task (*kārya*).

If that [cognition] were performed without an eligible person (*adhikārin*), it would not take the form of an action to be accomplished; thus, because its object would be understood as empty, there would be a sublation (*bādha*) of the cognition itself. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the cognition, we shall postulate an eligible person. The reply is: There is no sublation whatsoever of the cognition; as for those who are not eligible, they simply do not perform it—what does this have to do with the cognition? The meaning of this is: in the world, words are conventionally established (*vyutpanna*) precisely with respect to cognition.

By those [means], the comprehension of meaning has indeed occurred; therefore, there is certainly no sublation of the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). However, while some comprehension is devoid of an object, another is not. What can be done about this? It is certainly not a royal decree that comprehension must possess an object. If, upon investigation, it turns out to be empty of an object, let it be so. If it is argued that [in that case] there would be invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), let it be so. As it was said by the Author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*): [text follows].
"This path is safe; may you proceed"—the meaning is that just as this [statement] is false, so too is this [Vedic statement].

Therefore, we do not perceive the qualification for anyone here. Now, one might object: "In the Veda, the comprehension of meaning from words depends upon worldly linguistic usage, and in the world, comprehension exists even through ellipsis (adhyāhāra), as in the case of [saying] 'the door'..."

In passages such as "the city" (*puraṃ*), and so forth; therefore, here too we shall supply an introductory heading (*adhikāra*). To this, he says: "And when an introductory heading is being supplied, whose authority (*adhikāra*) is supplied? For [it cannot be] from a mandate (*niyoga*)."

(1) It becomes devoid of its effect; (2) it is invalid because it implies two distinct particulars. Furthermore, in common worldly usage, supplementation (*adhyāhāra*) is observed when a sentence is incomplete, and that [sentence] is said to be incomplete.

That which is already associated [with another word], one is unable to express [again]. Furthermore, regarding the necessity of supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), the very impossibility of the theory of "expression of the associated" (*anvitābhidhāna*) is the reason; for if an ellipsis were not supplied, the expression of the associated could not occur. And in this case, we have no evidence that it is incomplete, because the expression of the associated occurs between each pair [of words]; here, however, since that is accomplished by the mention of the object (*viṣaya*), there is indeed no incompleteness.

Just as the utterance of merely "the cloth comes into being" constitutes a complete sentence, when the word "red" is uttered in that very context, then "the red cloth comes into being" also occurs; yet, the two words [alone] do not constitute a sentence. Therefore:

In sentences where the comprehension of a further meaning is established by merely two words, that [comprehension] is based solely on the hearing of another word; therefore, let it be that where a word denoting the qualified person (*adhikārin*) is heard, there is the comprehension of the qualified person. However, its absence does not constitute incompleteness [of the sentence]. Thus he says:
"But when [the word] is not heard at all, there is no authority for the postulation of a further meaning. If the expression of the related meaning were accomplished by two words...

There is no completeness [of the syntactic connection] through mere occurrence; how then [is it explained] in the case of "He sacrifices *kapiñjala* birds for Spring" and "He sacrifices *kalaviṅka* birds for Summer"?

In the latter, the word "sacrifices" (*ālabhate*) is supplied (*anuṣaṅga*), because the expression of the connected meaning is established by the two words "for Summer" (*grīṣmāya*) and "*kalaviṅkān*" [together], as is the case with the meaning of the case-ending.

It is indeed cognizable by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This example is as follows: a word does not become "separated" merely by the intervention of other words;

Even if a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) were imagined, since no specific qualification would be perceived, there would be entitlement for all who possess desires.

Furthermore, it cannot be understood that all people have entitlement from an ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), because the purpose is accomplished by one alone. "Because that very [injunction] is unestablished. Thus it is established that an injunction is not devoid of an entitlement (*adhikāra*). Because it would entail an excessive complexity of application (*prayukti-gaurava*) and because human beings are by nature inclined toward desire, the mere state of desiring (*arthitā*) is the qualification for eligibility (*adhikāri-viśeṣaṇa*). And since no further distinction is perceived therein, all who desire [the result] possess eligibility. The meaning of this is as follows: when a seeker of pleasure (*kāmin*) is postulated as the qualified candidate (*adhikārin*), the desire for the cessation of suffering cannot be accepted as a qualification of that candidate. Furthermore, regarding the mere cessation of suffering...

In the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the experience of pleasure is not necessarily present. Since pleasure exists there as a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikārin*) by virtue of being desired, and because there is no cause for apprehending its specific qualities, nothing remains but unconditioned pleasure-in-general. Therefore, when a general category is postulated, and in the absence of a cause for perceiving a particularity, it is pleasure-in-general alone that constitutes the qualification of the eligible person, namely, heaven (*svarga*).

But surely the author of the Sūtras has stated the reasoning that [the result] is common to all because it is indistinct for everyone—this very point has been expressed [as follows]: "That would be heaven for all" (1 G).

"Because it is non-distinct" (pratyaviśiṣṭatvāt). By this, the meaning is that what we ourselves have stated— that the generality of pleasure (sukha-sāmānya) is non-distinct with respect to every particular pleasure— is indeed stated by the author of the Sūtras as well.

Regarding the statement of the fruit (*phalārthavāda*) in the context of a ritual (*kratu*): it has been established that since no specific qualification (*adhikāra*) is heard [in such cases], heaven (*svarga*) is the cause of qualification because it is common to all. It was stated that certain [passages] are *arthavādas* because they lack the capacity to establish a result. With this doubt in mind, the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*), demonstrating the intention behind the author of the *Bhāṣya*'s uncertainty, says: "But where *arthavādas* are heard that declare a specific result, there a doubt arises:
is heaven alone the cause of entitlement (*adhikāra*) even there, or is it the thing declared by the *arthavāda*? This is the meaning.

The status of [the passage] as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) remains established; nevertheless, it is considered in this way: when a qualification (*adhikāra*) must be postulated for an injunction (*vidhi*) that lacks one, should the person qualified here be one who desires the fruit mentioned in the *arthavāda*, or should it be the "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) even in this case, since there is no specific *arthavāda* stating a particular result? Thus, there is no contradiction. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), because of the [nature of] the mandate (*niyoga*)...

It is considered logical that only that [result] is understood; however, an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is merely an explanatory passage. Its meaning is as follows: it is established that explanatory passages do not, in themselves, establish a result; at most, any such conceptualization occurs solely by virtue of the power of the injunction (*niyoga*), as is the case with the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and others.

Thus, it would be logical that only those desiring heaven (*svarga*) have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for this [rite]. To this, it is replied: it is more reasonable that the fruit is precisely that which is stated in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Why? Because in this way, the purpose of praise is successfully accomplished through the praise of the object itself. The meaning of this is as follows: even when a [result] is being postulated, only that one is appropriate which is consistent with all the words [of the text]. And here, if "heaven" were being postulated, then words such as "firm foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*) found within the explanatory passage—

For the sake of praise, it must be understood that [the result] culminates in heaven; even there, however, an indirect mode of operation (*parokṣārthavṛtti*) regarding the meaning is to be respected. But when "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is postulated as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikārin*), since the ritual action has that as its fruit, the purpose of the praise is fulfilled through the praise of the action's utility itself. Therefore, the qualified person to be postulated is precisely one who desires the "establishment" and so forth denoted by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). [Objection: But surely, from the mandatory injunction (*niyoga*)...

It has been stated that only the fact of heaven being the purpose is understood; and it has also been stated that when there is doubt, a determination is made from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). "Even in the case of a fruit [that is already established], heaven is not postulated; how much less so when it occurs within the statement of the injunction (vidhyuddeśa) as a direct qualification of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa)?"—anticipating this objection, he says: "Now this is being considered: if, moreover, the entitlement to heaven [is derived] from the mandate (niyoga), and the conditions (upādhi) are postulated through the connection with other words—as in the case of 'one should fetch vegetables'—what fault would there be? Now, one might argue that the very fact of the [result] being produced is itself the proof. This would be so if the mandate (*niyoga*) were not defined by its purpose (*artha-lakṣaṇa*).

It may be so; it has been stated more than once that in a sacrifice consisting of momentary factors, the fruit arises at a later time precisely because of the *niyoga*. Furthermore, for each specific desire, there are distinct *adhikāra-niyogas* (obligations pertaining to qualification), because there is a difference in the scriptures (*śāstra*) due to the difference in the goals to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and because there is a difference in the meaning of the scriptures due to the difference in the scriptures themselves.
Therefore, when a particular desire exists, only the *niyoga* connected to that [desire] is established, and not any other; thus, no fruit other than that [specific one] arises.

[Objection: But why are the *niyogas* (ritual injunctions) also not accomplished through the non-difference of their means (*sādhana*)? [Reply: It is not so; for the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is also a means to the accomplishment of the *niyoga*. And since that [qualified person] differs according to each specific desire, the non-difference of the means is untenable.
He clarifies this very intention by means of an objection: "But surely, at the time of performance, the arising of desire is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*)."

It has been stated that [the injunction] is not applicable [in that case]. Therefore, even when desire has not arisen, because there is no deficiency [in the causal factors], the production of the fruit must occur; for [the fruit arises] by virtue of the mandate (*niyoga*).

This is the meaning. Who has said that "origination" is the cause at the time of application? We have already stated that, even when the context is understood, the desire for everything simultaneously is not possible. And since simultaneous desires are impossible, the simultaneous application of all injunctions is untenable. The meaning is that a person does not perceive all injunctions as things to be done simultaneously.

He summarizes: "Therefore, there is entitlement according to each desire. Since the attainment of the fruit extends to the limit of that entitlement, there is a distinction in the performance for those seeking fruits according to each individual desire. On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya states: "Even though the desires may arise simultaneously, nevertheless their conjunction is not intended, because they are [individually] the objects of reference."

Thus it has been stated. In this regard, the following objection arises: "Even though there is a state of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatā*), why is it that the intention to express a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-vivakṣā*) is not possible, given that [the object] is already presented as the thing to be referred to? To this, the author of the *Ṭīkā* first states the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*:
"The injunction is intended for those desires as they were specified," so it was said by the author of the *Bhāṣya*. Those desires which [occur] in each different sacrifice...

Those very [elements] that have been individually specified here are to be designated independently; each one by one. Now, why are they not all expressed by the word "all" (*sarva*) exactly as they were specified? To this he says: the intention is that there is no comprehension of those that have not been specified. Since there is no cognition of what has not been specified, the word "all" depends upon what has been specified, as in the expression "everything has been done."

It is just like that. Since desires, being independent, are the causes for qualification (*adhikāra*), therefore, according to each desire, there is a distinction of qualification; and because of this distinction of qualification, there is a distinction in the application [of the ritual] as long as the qualification lasts. Precisely because the fruit is produced in succession, for this very reason, even in the case of contradictory [desires], there is the fruit of "all one's possessions" (*sarvasva*) at death, and the fruit of longevity associated with Prajāpati, and so forth.
Furthermore, the application of even contradictory [names] is established. For if they were applied simultaneously, death and life would be untenable.
Therefore, it is well said that "the accomplishment of yoga" [occurs];
the intention is that there is no comprehension of those [objects] as they have been specified.

Or rather, it is thus: "But surely there is no connection with the definition here; why is it that in this world there are desires, or in the next? Dispelling such a doubt, he says: "In this section, regarding the fruit of the injunction, is it preceded by the assumption of a body?"

Is there a state of being an instigator (*prayojakabhāva*), or is there the status of being an agent (*prayoktṛtva*) exactly as it is heard in the scripture? This is a supplement [to the argument] by way of supplying an ellipsis. Its meaning is as follows:

those injunctions for the *Citrā* sacrifice and others in this world, which have results consisting of cattle and so forth—do they, being unable to cause one to enjoy the fruit without a body as the locus of experience, imply a body and thereby imply the fruit; or do they imply sons and other such things without implying a body?

Thus it is considered: if there is a restriction regarding the exhaustion of the body [upon death], then the fulfillment of desires occurs in this very world; if not, then there is no such restriction, and they may occur either here or in that world. In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that since no other cause for the assumption of a body is observed, and since the case of animals and others is accounted for by other causes, the projection of results must necessarily be preceded by the assumption of a body.

The meaning of this is as follows: The body is indeed material, produced by the conjunction of the elements; however, not every conjunction of the elements initiates a body, but only a specific one. Therefore, there must be some particular auxiliary cause. Among other things, no such causality is observed. But since the production of results from the injunctions of ritual action would otherwise be inexplicable, it is logical that they possess causality in this regard. Thus, regarding the initiation of the body—

Vedic rituals yield a prior fruit; therefore, their fruit is one pertaining to the next world (*āmuṣmika*). Now, as for the question of what is the cause for cattle and other such things belonging to this world, he says: "The cause of cattle and so forth will be perceived directly [in the form of] receiving gifts and the like. However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*) maintains that the agency [of the ritual] extends only as far as is heard in scripture. This is the supplementation by way of ellipsis. Why? Because of the mere hearing [of the scriptural injunction].

Because the status of the instigator (*prayoktṛbhāva*) is something to be understood; for the instigating power of the *niyoga* is to be known solely through verbal testimony (*śabdaikasamadhigamya*). And that—(1) G. adds: "it is considered"—its meaning is the *saṃskāra*.
It is understood specifically [that there is no fixed rule]. For it is not understood here that the fruit occurs only in this world or only in the next. Why?

Because the scriptural injunction regarding desire is common to both cases, and because desire is possible in both instances. As for the claim that no other cause for the commencement of a body is observed—that is true; this too is not observed. However, the granting of the fruit [occurs] even when the body has been acquired through another cause.

It does not follow as an absolute certainty that [the action] must necessarily produce its result immediately; therefore, it is not untenable that it yields its fruit either in this life or in another birth, depending on specific auxiliary conditions (*sahakāriviśeṣa*). Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya, having set forth the fact that it is not perceived immediately, states:
"We do not apprehend it through perception or inference; it is understood from verbal testimony (*śabda*)."

Thus he spoke. That is incorrect, for it has already been stated that even from the word [itself], immediate succession is not perceived. To this, it is replied: this is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya—[namely,] from the comprehension of the general [meaning], "here" [is understood].

And because there is no comprehension of a specific [object] such as "in that place," the absence of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) does not, by the mere word, destroy the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). The meaning of this is: even if the immediate sequence is not perceived, nevertheless, in an absolute sense—

It cannot be said that there would be no immediate result (*ānantarya*), because even when another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not observed, one understands from the word itself that there is no fixed rule; thus, the result might sometimes be immediate and sometimes non-immediate. The logical mark (*liṅga*) has been stated as formulated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*);
the meaning is that it has been explained in this manner.

[The sūtra states: "There is an injunction regarding the conjunction [of acts]. Now, how can there be a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) here, given that by virtue of the suffix *-ktvā*, this is clearly a connection between a subsidiary act (*aṅga*) and its purpose (*prayojana*)? To this, he says: in the statement "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," the suffix *-ktvā* functions as an indicator (*lakṣaṇa*).
Since the time of occurrence is heard in the sense of "having become" (*bhūtvā*), the prima facie view is that the connection is for the purpose of indicating time (*kālārtha*).

The meaning of this is as follows: First of all, the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is not heard in the definition [of the *ktvā* suffix] as the cause for its production. However, priority in time (*pūrvakālatā*) is indeed heard;

by virtue of that, the state of occurring immediately thereafter is also understood. Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is that this application (*viniyoga*) should be considered entirely new, established for the purpose of prescribing that [relationship].

Since the connection between the meanings of two verbal roots is understood only when they share a common agent, this [relationship] is indeed a connection between roots (*dhātusaṃbandha*). And since that is not possible except through a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that it is precisely a relationship of subordinate and principal.
The meaning of this is as follows: it is true that in the definition [of the *samānakartṛka* rule], "prior" (*pūrva*)—

Nevertheless, that temporality does not reside in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because there is deviation in cases such as "he laughs after closing [his eyes]"; rather, it resides in the cognition (*pratīti*). It is merely an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*). However, the state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛtā*) resides precisely in the meaning of the verbal root. And by virtue of this common agency between the two meanings of the verbal roots—
Since this *ktvā* suffix is prescribed under the heading of "connection between verbal roots" (*dhātusaṃbandha*) because it is understood to convey a sequence of actions,

it denotes a connection between two verbal roots; and since such a connection between two verbal root-meanings is otherwise impossible except through a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), it is indeed a relationship of subordinate and principal.

If it is argued that it serves both purposes, we reply: since the word *saṃsthā* (conclusion) in the expression “having concluded the *Paurṇamāsī*” denotes completion, a relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*) between the *Paurṇamāsī* and [the *Sāṃnāyya*] is not possible; therefore, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is indeed a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that [the Vaimṛdha sacrifice belongs] to the *Vaimṛdha* [rite]. Its meaning is as follows: the word *saṃsthā* denotes completion (*parisamāpti*), and completion is the performance [of the rite] in its entirety. In that case, if the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) has been completed (*saṃsthitā*), then there can be no subsidiary (*aṅga*) to it. On the other hand, if there is another subsidiary called the Vaimṛdha, then the word *saṃsthā* (completion) would not be applicable. Therefore, from this sentence alone, the relationship of primary and subsidiary (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is not understood.

(1) P. 1262 (2) G. This [text] is solely intent upon that injunction; therefore, because it is not connected with the other, it is logical that it belongs as a subsidiary to both by virtue of the context alone—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this, it is replied: if [the text] were for the completion...

Because it is a statement of completion (*saṃsthā*), the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) cannot possess the status of a principal (*aṅgin*); furthermore, its status as a principal cannot arise even from the context (*prakaraṇa*).

This is the meaning: if there were no connection for the *vaimṛdha* offering due to the statement that the full moon sacrifice is completed in its entirety, then it could not have the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) even by virtue of context; for as long as that auxiliary remains unperformed, the completion of the sacrifice in its entirety would be logically untenable. Now, regarding the phrase "having completed" (*saṃsthāpya*), [it refers to] the collection of previously prescribed auxiliaries—

This word "saṃsthā" (completion) has the intention of denoting final conclusion. Now, if it is argued that the word "saṃsthā" is understood as relative for the sake of establishing a connection with the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) of the context (*prakaraṇa*), then in that case, the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice would indeed be a subsidiary of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) by virtue of syntactical connection (*vākya*). Nor should it be said: "Let the *vaimṛdha* not be a subsidiary of the Full Moon sacrifice either through context or through syntactical connection," because there is no evidence for the relativity of the term "completion" (*samāpti*). On the contrary—

Let it be that [the *vaimṛdha*] is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*) because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). For if that were the case, the connection with the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) which is understood would be entirely abandoned; moreover, since subsidiarity (*aṅgatā*) can be established through a relative dependence on the completion [of the rite], there is no distinction whatsoever in the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*).

And as for the unity of the injunction of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-niyogaikya*) which is understood of the *vaimṛdha* due to its connection with the qualification (*adhikāra*), [that too would be lost].

Even if it were intended solely for the Full Moon sacrifice, there would be no contradiction, because it enters into that [Full Moon sacrifice] by way of the Full Moon itself. Therefore, it is established that the Vaimṛdha is an auxiliary (aṅga) of the Full Moon sacrifice. However, in the case of its non-origination, it is a matter of time: "They proceed with the after-offerings (anūyāja) after the Agnimāruta."

Thus, how is there a relationship between the subsidiary (aṅga) and the principal (pradhāna) here? Since the word "ūrdhvam" (afterwards) denotes time, this relationship must be for the purpose of time alone. It is replied: it is logical that this instruction is for the purpose of time, because for those very acts which have attained the status of being performed in a single ritual application, simultaneous performance is impossible; therefore, when there is a requirement for priority and sequence, the teaching serves the purpose of time.

(1) In the case of "striking the enclosing-sticks" (*paridhi*), because of the suffix *-ktvā*, there arises a doubt as to whether these are subsidiary (*aṅga*) or principal (*pradhāna*) acts. But surely, since they are the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), [they must be subsidiaries]?

[Objection: How can this doubt arise regarding those [actions] whose status as subordinate members (*aṅga*) of another has already been fully determined? [Reply: It is said: Precisely because their status as subordinate members is understood, these actions will be distinct acts possessing those specific properties; otherwise, their status as subordinate members would be untenable. To this, the answer is: Even when there is a connection between two things whose status as subordinate members of another has already been fully determined, the injunction (*niyoga*) results only in the prescription of time (*kāla*), because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the action. The meaning of this is as follows: Because [the action] is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*)...

First of all, there is indeed recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the ritual action. And that which is being recognized cannot be understood as a subordinate element (*aṅga*). Furthermore, what is not understood [as such] is not enjoined. Therefore, the connection between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅga-pradhāna-sambandha*) is not what is to be enjoined here. By the principle of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), this statement must be intended solely as an injunction regarding time (*kāla-vidhi*).
Consequently, the injunction has the purpose of specifying time.

Regarding the matter of the time of performance: it has been stated that in the injunction, "Having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma," because no other rite is being enjoined, this is a prescription for the time [of the subsequent rite]. Having restated the meaning of the Bhāṣya by means of this, he states the objection: "But as for this..."
This is incorrect. Why? Because by the statement, "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," there is no distinction;
thus, even from the word *bṛhaspatisava*, only the primary Bṛhaspatisava is understood. Therefore, here too, by means of an injunction for the purpose of [indicating] time—

It must be so. Now, if it is argued that because of the absence [of the original context], there is no recognition here of the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, and therefore this is an injunction for a different ritual, to that he replies:
"In both cases, the purpose of the ritual is the same; the purpose of the injunction is the enjoining of the ritual," because in this case as well, the two rituals are the subject under discussion.

Or rather, a distinction must be stated. In this regard, some have stated that the distinction lies in the *anārabhyavidhāna* (independent injunction), namely: "Having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma. This sentence does not occur within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of any specific ritual. What, then, is the purpose of this independent statement (*anārabhyavāda*) here?

A distinction is understood. This is the distinction: first of all, the injunction of two separate acts is not possible in cases such as "having sacrificed with this, one should sacrifice with that. The intention is as follows: in passages such as "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa," the ritual act is recognized even though it is distant, by virtue of its name; likewise, in "one should sacrifice with Soma," the ritual act is indeed recognized by means of the substance. Therefore, [it is] one [act].

It is not possible to enjoin a ritual action [independently]. Furthermore, in the case of an injunction not connected to a specific context (*anārabhyavidhāna*), not even a single ritual action is under discussion. However, in the context of the *Vājapeya*, because of the proximity to the qualification for the *Vājapeya* under discussion—expressed as "by means of the *Bṛhaspatisava*"—the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is understood as being solely intent upon an injunction regarding a subsidiary (*aṅga*) rite. Moreover, the name [of the rite] cannot produce recognition [of the primary rite] by virtue of being intent upon that [subsidiary]. For where [a rite] is to be enjoined...

The meaning of the verbal root appears distinct there because of the difference in what is to be enjoined; thus, the name applied to it does not produce recognition [of the same action]. From the injunction, the verbal root-meaning appears as a separate context (*prakaraṇāntara*), since the action is being enjoined with respect to a different qualification (*adhikārāntara*).

Likewise, even where two qualities are heard, there too the injunction of an action is stated for the purpose of restricting the factors of action (*kāraka*). Therefore, it is by name [that the distinction is established].

The mention of a well-known ritual action is for the purpose of prescribing a specific time; and it has been stated that even a name is meaningful when connected with a quality or a result. In the case of the *vājapeya*, however, because it is already under discussion (*prakṛtatvāt*), the injunction of a different ritual action is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Furthermore, the name will serve to extend the characteristics (*dharmātideśaka*) of that [original] ritual, according to the principle that "in a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), there is a difference in purpose. In the case of a statement not occurring within a specific context (*anārabhyavāda*), however, due to the difference in context—

Because both exist as such, it is improper to regard them as distinct actions. Even in cases where a distant action is enjoined for the sake of a fruit, since the fruit itself is not what is enjoined, it is the action alone that must be enjoined. In the case of an isolated injunction (*anārabhyavāda*), where there is no injunction of an action with respect to a specific qualification (*adhikāra*), it is for the purpose of restricting the time.

Even when [the rite] has been released, it is improper for it to become a separate action (*karmāntara*). All of this has already been explained. Thus far, it has been stated that where a text is merely an *anārabhyavāda* (unattached statement), there the injunction (*niyoga*) serves the purpose of fixing the time.
But what is the case for those [passages] which are recited within the very context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa? Herein lies the intention: in that case, it is not...

Because the substance is present, recognition is possible; since the action is to be enjoined as the subject matter at hand, it is therefore logical that there is a relationship of subsidiary and principal (*aṅga-prayojana-sambandha*) in that case. To this he says: "Let there be the relationship of subsidiary and principal in that case; what harm is there to us? For the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established by this very section (*adhikaraṇa*), which deals solely with the *anārabhyavāda* (uncontextualized injunction). Or rather, this relationship of subsidiary and principal has already been refuted in the section concerning other recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*).

By one who asserts that "the action is one because it has the branch as its basis," how is this refuted? The sense is this: whatever meaning appears to someone must be for him that very meaning; and since this very scripture is recognized [as the same], it is logical that it is a single scripture and not a different scripture. Here he asks: "Let it be so; nevertheless, we do not understand the *anārabhya*..."

Let the scripture be recognized by means of that which is the meaning of the discussion—the sense of time as an injunction; let that very same [meaning] exist even in another scripture, though studied in a different context. Or, let the scripture be recognized by means of that which is the meaning within the context—the relationship of principal and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin); let that very same [relationship] exist even in an unattached statement (anārabhyavāda) belonging to another branch. The answer is: recognition occurs through the unattached statement because there is no contradiction.

The proponents of difference (bhedavidaḥ) maintain that the meaning of a passage studied independently (*anārabhya-adhīta*) is the same as that of one studied within a specific context (*ārabhya-adhīta*), because there is no contradiction.

When the meaning of an independent passage is accepted everywhere, there is no contradiction with the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) [of the ritual] by means of its name and substance; however, in the case of a passage studied within a specific context, such recognition is contradicted. Therefore, it is well said that the connection is for the purpose of time (*kālārtha*). Thus, the view has been stated.

(1) R. *Saṃyogaḥ* [p. 1051]: "But the connection with the fruit is not enjoined. Here there is a doubt: does the scriptural injunction belong to that father for whom the mandate (*niyoga*) exists? Or [to the son]?

Is the fruit for one person while the injunction is for another—that is, the fruit belongs to someone other than the one who performs the rite? How does this doubt arise? Because in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the word "fruit" is connected with another, namely the son, through terms such as "spiritual luster" (*brahmavarcasa*) and so forth; thus, it is understood that the connection with the fruit pertains to the one who has been born. Furthermore, by the term "eligible person" (*adhikārin*), it is indicated that [the result occurs] "when a son is born."

By this [statement], because of the continuity of another father, [an objection is raised]: "Even so, let the father be the one enjoined, and let the fruit belong to the son; what contradiction is there? To that, he says: "And it is the qualified person who is enjoined. One for whose sake the action is performed is the qualified person (*adhikārī*). And whoever is the qualified person, he alone is enjoined. For in an action performed for the sake of another, the enjoining of that other person is not logical. In that case...

If this rite were for the ultimate welfare of the son, then the father would have no authority (*adhikāra*) therein, because the rite does not have that as its purpose. And if the father lacks authority, he cannot be one who is enjoined (*niyojya*). Therefore, since the father is indeed the one to be enjoined, a doubt certainly arises. What is logical? That the fruit belongs to the father who is enjoined. Why? Because [the injunction] exists for the sake of establishing authority.

Since the connection with the fruit is not understood as a mere relationship, but rather for the purpose that the sovereignty of the person—denoted by the term "eligible" (adhikārin)—may apply to his action, the connection with the fruit is accepted; it is not, however, because the connection with the fruit is merely understood in that way.
Therefore, this fruit belongs to the father. Whether there be a connection through praise of the son's connection with the fruit, even for the son, this [fruit] belongs to him.

Or, by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word "fruit" may be a qualifier of the person entitled [to the rite]. Or, by means of figurative indication, let the word "son" itself qualify the father as the one for whom the fruit belongs; in any case, this ritual act is for the sake of the supreme welfare (*niḥśreyasa*) of the father. And thus, when the occasion connected with the sacrifice has occurred, it does not belong to anyone else.

Because the fruit is seen to belong only to the person enjoined (*niyojya*), it is connected with that ritual act. What is meant is this: even when the occasion (*nimitta*) is not itself directly connected [to the fruit], if the fruit is heard in scripture as belonging only to the person enjoined—just as birth, which is connected to a son, belongs to him alone—then [the fruit belongs to that person].

If that were the case, the fruit would have been stated as being connected solely to the sacrifice; however, it was not stated in that way. To this it is replied: for one to whom the connection with the fruit belongs—namely, the son—it is his fruit [that is intended], because the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is established even through the status of the son being the occasion (*nimitta*). For another person, although the rite serves a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) by fulfilling the injunction regarding the occasion through the occasion of the son's birth, the entitlement is nonetheless established.

[The result] has the characteristic of sovereignty. Therefore, let the scriptural statement regarding the fruit obtained by the son be taken as literal. If the entitlement [to perform the rite] is established even by way of being a cause (*nimitta*), then how is the word for the "fruit" [to be understood]? He says in a single passage: "The fruit is not a qualification of the ritual action; it does not fall within the scope of the factors of action (*kāraka*), nor does it fall within the scope of the entitlement (*adhikāra*), because the entitlement is obtained through the force of the cause. It is said: "It will exist... [as the entitlement].
[This is] a case of superimposition. How so? Because it is heard that one who possesses a son and desires the fruit pertaining to a son is qualified [for the rite].
This is the intention: even in the case of a causal condition (*nimitta*), its status as a direct qualification of the qualified person (*adhikārin*) is not heard in scripture;

rather, it is a condition only with respect to the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). And since performance is invariably dependent upon qualification, the causal condition serves as the cause for qualification.

It must be assumed that [the fruit] is a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikāri-viśeṣaṇa*). Since the fruit mentioned even in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is equally something to be assumed, it is included as a qualification of the person entitled. Under the guise of a concluding summary, he states sovereignty in another manner: "Therefore, for whom there is the injunction, for him there is the fruit.
This, which is assumed by the force of the entitlement (*adhikāra*), is not contradictory, since the entitlement is established even through the joy of having a son.

Because the father’s attainment of sovereignty is achieved through the enjoyment of joy caused by the production of the fruit that goes to the son; this restates what was previously stated in the section on sacrifices—that when a causal condition (*nimitta*) exists, the result belongs only to the person enjoined (*niyojya*). He refutes this: it is logical [only] with respect to the qualification (*adhikāra*)— [p.

We shall explain in the sixth [chapter] that it is "because of the occurrence of the occasion" (*nimitta*); for the occasion is by force a qualification of the entitled person (*adhikārin*). Therefore, what is enjoined in connection with an occasion belongs to the person alone; thus, it is logical that the fruit belongs to the person alone. Or rather: "When a son is born."

Thus it is heard in scripture. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the occasional rite (naimittika) take place immediately after birth, or does it depend upon the inclusion of the auxiliary elements (aṅga), as is obtained by analogy with the archetype (prakṛti)? In this regard, he states the objection: "If such a doubt is raised, why then is the child's capacity to sustain life presented as the reason for its excellence? One—

Let this very topic be considered here: because the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, together with its ancillaries (aṅgas) and including the time for purification as an ancillary, is occasional (naimittika), its performance cannot take place immediately after the occasion—namely, immediately after the birth of a son. Furthermore, since it does not depend on the non-observance of the [specific] time like a compulsory (nitya) rite, there is no requirement to observe purification;
thus, it should be performed at its own proper time, such as the full moon day (paurṇamāsī). This is merely an illustration, for it must be performed by one who is pure.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: This has been stated by accepting the sublation of the occasion (*nimitta*) due to the predominance of the occasional rite (*naimittika*). However, in the absence of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), there is no ultimate contradiction of the occasion, because of its connection with the past participial suffix (*bhūta-pratyaya*) in the word *jāta* ("born"); thus, the occasion is not lost even upon waiting for the time and purity (*kāla-śauca*) to occur. Therefore, the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) appears to be practically useless.

Nor is the requirement for purification after a specific period established by that much alone, because the performance [of the rite] might still be suspected even when a son is born and the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) has been performed. Even in that case, the very same reason must be stated, which consists in the favoring of the auxiliary and occasional rites.

The sense is: "Rather, let that very [time] be presented first. To this it is replied: "The principle that the effect follows immediately after the cause is a general rule (*autsargiko nyāya*); nor is a displacement of time perceived in the absence of a cause. The meaning of this is: that in whose presence something comes to be is called the "cause" (*nimitta*), and if that cause has arrived, the "effect" (*naimittika*) must necessarily follow immediately after it.

It is logical [to conclude this] because there is no cause for delay. But has it not been stated that the rite, along with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*), is occasional (*naimittika*)? He begins to refute this: "We do not know this: should the subsidiary, which is understood through its application (*viniyoga*), be discarded because the injunction (*niyoga*) is understood at the time of the occasion, or should the time of the injunction be postponed? For the injunction is primary, and everything exists for the sake of the injunction."

Those who understand the application (*viniyoga*) maintain that when the application is abandoned, the subsidiary element (*aṅga*) is also abandoned. For example, the morning and other times prescribed as subsidiaries for the ritual bath (*snāna*) are disregarded if one has touched a woman in her menses or similar circumstances. However, "living" (*jīvana*) and so forth are not indicated by the locative case of the occasion (*nimitta-saptamī*).
In this case, however, upon examining its own nature, the sequence immediately following birth appears to be the application. For this indeed is the very nature of being an occasion (*nimittatva*).

Since the injunction (*niyoga*) exists when that [condition] is present, if the condition (*nimitta*) is an accomplished fact (*bhūta*), then the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) necessarily follows, because the purpose of the performance is the fulfillment of the injunction. For this very reason, this application [of the rite] cannot be set aside by the favoring of the occasional (*naimittika*) rule. Therefore, the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to refute this. How would it be refuted? To this he says: for if the performance were carried out at the very time of the injunction itself...

That for whose sake the injunction exists—the fruit residing in the prince—is indeed lost. This is the intended meaning: in the case of optional rites (*kāmyakarma*), the fruit [is not obtained] due to the influence of the occasional rite (*naimittika*).

The injunction (*niyoga*) is not the motivator for performance; therefore, in the absence of a fruit, there is no performance due to the absence of a motivator. But how is there an absence of a fruit? Because it would entail the separation of the child’s life-force. Once the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) has been performed, there is the placing of the breast [to the child]. And the *jātakarman* must be performed by the father. If he were occupied with the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), how could the *jātakarman* be performed? And if it is not performed...

In the *jātakarman* (birth-rite), there is no giving of the breast. How indeed could one sustain life without having drunk from the breast? Therefore, since there is no fruit [of the rite] immediately after the *jātakarman*, the time for the performance of the *iṣṭi* (sacrifice) must be postponed. How then is the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) reached in the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*)? To this he says: "If it is postponed, there is no authority for abandoning its own constituent parts at its proper time"—thus the second section is written.

The meaning of this is as follows: since it is established that there is no immediate performance [of the subsidiary acts] by the force of the subsequent injunction obtained through the nature of the cause (*nimitta*), it follows that the rite must be performed with all its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*) at the proper time and with purity, because of its connection with the principal act (*pradhāna*). Regarding the statement, "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," there arises a doubt: is it one [act], or...
"Is it one injunction (*niyoga*), or rather two injunctions? By this, he explains the doubt held by the author of the *Bhāṣya*.

What is meant is this: is this a single injunction, or is it distinct? If there is oneness, there is a single performance; if there is distinction, there is a division [of performance]. Regarding that, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But surely, if there were two injunctions, because of the connection with distinct injunctions, the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgitva*) would not exist. [If it were] one..."

For the relationship between primary and subsidiary (aṅga-aṅgin) is based on their entry into the performance (prayoga). Since that relationship of primary and subsidiary exists, there is no difference in the performance.
He states the established conclusion (rāddhānta): "Certainly it is appropriate. For the status of primary and subsidiary arises from application (viniyoga), and such application exists here.

Due to the difference in performance (*prayoga*), there is a difference in the injunction (*niyoga*); therefore, let both exist: the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgitva*) as well as the distinction in performance. But surely, if there is a difference in performance due to a difference in the injunction, it would follow that there is a difference in the scripture (*śāstra*). For when the scripture is non-different, a difference in the injunction—which constitutes the meaning of the scripture—is untenable. Let it be so in regard to performance; there is no fault there. However, with respect to application (*viniyoga*), this is indeed one single scripture.

But how can there be a difference in application (*prayogabheda*) for a single treatise? If it were a single treatise with a single purpose, then there would likewise be no difference in application. The answer is: by what is this prevented? It is caused by differences in the "concomitants" (*anubandha*), just as there are differences in the injunctions (*vidhāna*). Just as there are differences in the injunctions, so too, due to the difference in the concomitants—such as time (*kāla*)—which arise from the difference in the rules of application (*prayogavidhi*), the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is performed in whatever manner those concomitants dictate.

It divides. In whatever way time and other factors are connected—that is, become adjuncts—they divide the *tantra* (the ritual procedure) accordingly. And here, when there is a difference in the adjuncts of the performance, there is a difference in the performance itself. Therefore, there is no transition to a different scripture; rather, there is merely a difference in the performance. How there is a difference in the performance has been demonstrated. For instance, the *Bṛhaspatisava*, which is performed after the *Iṣṭi*, is a distinct accomplishment of the *Vājapeya*.

It appears so. Therefore, because they are connected to different modes of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), there is a difference in performance. And it is logical that [the subsidiary] is included within the qualification for the primary desire (*kāmādhikāra*). Likewise, [the phrase] "having piled the fire" (*agniṃ citvā*) is distinct from the completion of the piling (*cayana*), which serves as the consecration of the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*).
It has been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya that because the procedure for the Sautrāmaṇī is understood [from the Vedic text], its performance occurs at the very time of the iṣṭi.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Ṛjuvimalā* Pañjikā composed by the venerable Śālikanātha Miśra.
The third chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*.

The Fourth Pāda of the Fourth Adhyāya: [Concerning] the word *prakaraṇa* (context). Here, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) states that because the word *rājasūya* denotes the origin (*utpatti*) of all the constituent parts of the primary sacrifice, even those acts not involving a sacrifice (*anijyā*) possess primacy (*prādhānya*). He raises an objection to this: "But surely, in the discussion of names (*nāmadheya*), due to the commonality of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice)..."

It has been stated that a name does not arise from its grammatical coreferentiality (*adhikaraṇya*). But how can it be suspected that this [word *rājasūya*] denotes something other than a sacrifice? Therefore, this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself is untenable. The meaning of this is as follows: in the injunction “One desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the *rājasūya*,” a sacrifice is first enjoined. In that context, if the word *rājasūya* were to denote something else, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore—
It is determined that this statement refers exclusively to the sacrifices (*yāga*). And thus, since this is the name of the sacrifices, the sacrifices themselves possess primacy.

How can there be a suspicion of primacy even for non-sacrifices? It is said: True, it is so; however, here, because of the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*), there is a simultaneous denotation of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*); and since this unity of the injunction depends upon the context (*prakaraṇa*), the verbal root denotes everything included in that context.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) thinks as follows: the meaning of this is that when all sacrifices are to be expressed by the root *yaji* through a single mention (*tantra*), the sole cause for that is the unity of the injunction of qualification (*adhikāraniyoga*). For the injunction of qualification, being the primary subject matter (*prakṛta*), encompasses everything. And since those [sacrifices] accepted by the root *yaji* must be presented as the objects of that injunction of qualification, there is a single mention (i.e., unity of the injunction) for all of them.

The basis for this is the state of being "under discussion" (*prakṛtatva*). And since that state of being under discussion is common to both those sacrifices that are well-known (*yajñīna*) and those that are not (*ayajñīna*), it is established that [the mantra] serves to provide the connection with what is under discussion.

The term *yaji* (sacrifice), by virtue of its intended meaning (*tātparya*), applies even to non-sacrifices according to the maxim of the "man with the staff" (*daṇḍinyāya*). Nor should it be argued that there is a unity of injunction (*niyoga*) for non-sacrifices because of their being part of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*); for when a direct relationship is possible, resorting to an indirect one is indeed improper. And since it is understood that all [elements] have the injunction as their purpose directly, the term *yaji*, its intended meaning being known through its role in providing those [elements], applies even to non-sacrifices by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The present [interpretation] is not untenable. And thus, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *yaji* (sacrifice), the word *rājasūya* is also expressive of all [the constituent sacrifices];

this is what was stated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) as the "resultant" [meaning]. Furthermore, the investigation into names (*nāmadheya*) concludes merely with the point that the meaning expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is denoted by the name. Therefore, the doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is justified. This being the case, it is replied: True.

From the context, there is a unity of injunction (*niyoga*), but there is no reason to abandon the subordinate elements (*anubandha*) that are explicitly stated in the text. The meaning of this is as follows: first, an injunction regarding the sacrifice is understood from the statement, "One desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. Subsequently, however, by such [an injunction]...

By necessity, all the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are apprehended as being present. Consequently, when the expectation arises as to how and with what they are connected, the connection of the sacrifices is by way of their being the instrument (*karaṇa*), because the sacrifices constitute the object (*viṣaya*), and that which has become the object possesses the status of an instrument. Therefore, the sacrifices alone possess the status of the instrument, while the non-sacrificial elements possess the status of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). How so? [Regarding] the status of the procedure belonging to the non-sacrificial elements...

He asks with the intention of [addressing] the non-contradiction regarding the unity of the *niyoga*. To this, he states the answer: "For even the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) does not indeed obstruct the unity of the *niyoga*; we shall explain this under the heading 'because of the instruction concerning what has already come into being' (*tathābhūtopadeśāt*). Therefore, it is established that the subsidiary (*aṅga*) is distinct from the sacrifice (*yāga*). This is what is meant: since it is impossible for the *itikartavyatā* to be introduced as the instrument (*karaṇatayā*) within a *niyoga* that is already in conflict with the sacrifice prescribed by the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa-yāga-viruddhe niyoge*)."
The same applies to the *anvaya* (positive concomitance), because it is observed even in other cases where there is a probandum (*sādhya*).

"That which belongs to the middle" means that which is situated in the midst of them. Now, one might object: "In this case too, since context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger than order (*krama*), this very point has already been illustrated. The meaning of this is as follows: in the third section (*adhikaraṇa*) of this very work, under the principle that "context is stronger than order," this same example was already cited.

"If this has been cited here, let it be so; nevertheless, what follows from it? To this he says: "The fact that [the scripture] has all things as its object is already established; therefore, [this statement] is redundant."

He refutes [the objection]: "True, it was established on account of its application (*viniyoga*); however, now, because it must be employed separately, and because of the proximity of that very application of the *abhiṣecanīya*, it is logical that they form a single unit"—thus thinks the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*). The meaning of this is as follows:

since the *abhiṣecanīya* is to be performed separately, a distinction in its performance must indeed be admitted; and acts such as the gambling (*videvana*) fall within the scope of that specific performance.

Because of its proximity, that [king] alone is logically the prompter (*prayojaka*) of this [rite]. And since the application (*viniyoga*) extends as far as the prompting, the opponent in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that the application also belongs to him alone. Nor is there a contradiction with the application based on context (*prakaraṇa-viniyoga*); for even if it were a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, the context remains the cause for establishing a connection with each [individual rite], because it brings about a connection with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for every instance of the context.

Because it is the cause; therefore, the bypassing of the specific proximity [of the subsidiaries] is not tenable. To this it is replied: It is established that there is a single scriptural injunction (*ekaśabdya*) for the governing rule (*adhikāravidhi*). This is because the subordinate and principal elements are taught as the means (*sādhana*) for that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) through the connection with a single governing application (*ekādhikāraniyoga*). Thus, the scripture (*śāstra*) consists of both the subordinate and the principal. What follows from this? This results: for that very [scripture], there is a distinction in the sequence of performance (*prayogānubandhabheda*).

The separate performance of that very [principal action] is determined by its own set of subsidiary procedures (*itikartavyatā*). However, for a subsidiary whose performance is made known solely by the prescriptive injunction (*adhikāravidhi*) of the principal, its inclusion within an intermediate performance cannot be admitted. Therefore, the performance of that [subsidiary] in its specific place according to the sequence is understood precisely through the prescriptive injunction of the qualified person (*adhikāravidhi*). The meaning of this is as follows: first, in accordance with the application (*viniyoga*)...

In the case of application (*prayukti*) and ritual allocation (*viniyoga*), there is indeed a universal purpose (*sarvārthatva*). Therefore, it is only the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) that is its motivator (*prayojaka*), and not a subordinate injunction (*avāntaraniyoga*), because there is no allocation of it for the sake of that [subordinate act]. However, although it is to be performed in that context due to proximity (*sannidhāna*), it is motivated by the injunction of qualification alone.

Thus, due to both the application (viniyoga) and the employment (prayukti), it has universal applicability alone. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that there is no contradiction with the context (prakaraṇa). Indeed, in this very position, you yourself have explained how there is no contradiction with the context by asserting that "context is the cause for connection with each [individual]. And that context is not contradicted precisely when there is a connection with each; however, if there were a fixed connection with only one, then the context—which brings about a connection with all—would be contradicted.

It is indeed contradicted. Therefore, because it does not contradict the context (*prakaraṇa*), it pertains to all [the rites]. Regarding the non-distinction of the context, he raises an objection: "What indeed is the distinction of this [injunction] from the statement, 'They proceed with the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) after the *āgnimāruta* [laud]'? Since the word 'before' (*purastāt*) is heard in the phrase 'before the *upasad*s,' it is more appropriate that the connection be for the purpose of time alone."

Up to the point where it says, "Indeed, no one [is the agent]," and so forth, this is easily understood. However, there is this distinction: according to the context (*prakaraṇa*), everything possesses primacy, or rather, [everything] constitutes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) in the Rājasūya sacrifice. And it has been stated that what is not directly connected [by syntactical connection or direct statement] is [determined] by context. That which was stated regarding the Rājasūya—that everything possesses primacy or constitutes the procedure with respect to all [its parts]—is due to context; and because it is a subordinate element of the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*).

In this context, "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is intended to mean that which consists of grasping what is relevant. In the *Rājasūya*, because the sacrifice that has become the subject matter does not have its form manifested, there arises a requirement for sacrifices that possess a manifest form; likewise, there is a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Among these, those sacrifices (*yajati*) that enter into the subject matter are the primary acts (*pradhāna*), while those that are not sacrifices (*ayajati*) constitute the procedure. And it was stated in the third [book] that what is unconnected is applied through context; and as for those things that are connected...

(1) P. 1272 (2) R. When there is an expectancy for an injunction, [the opponent holds that] the *saumya* and other offerings are connected with the *upasad*s by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*). For the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) thinks as follows: there is a connection between the *upasad*s and the *saumya* offering.

Nor is it the case that the *saumya* and other offerings are connected with the *upasad*s in any other way; thus, there is no relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgitā*). This genitive is properly understood as a "genitive of remainder" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), not as a "co-occurrent genitive" (*upapada-ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, the genitive expresses the predominance of the *upasad*s. Therefore, because they are dependent, the connection is "by means of the *saumya* [offering] through the *upasad*s. As for the word "before" (*purastāt*), it requires a correlative; since the *upasad*s are the subject under discussion, it will refer back to them. Consequently, from the sentence [it follows that the *saumya* is connected with the *upasad*s].

The opponent’s intention is that [the offering] is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the *upasad* rites. Moreover, it is logical that it is indeed a subsidiary of the *upasad*s due to their specific proximity (*sannidhāna-viśeṣa*), because of the restrictive injunction of the context (*adhikāra-niyoga*). The meaning of this is as follows: even if there is a connection [of the offering] with the phrase "prior to the *upasad*s," since the *saumya* and other offerings are linked to the mind through the restrictive injunction of the context and the specific proximity of the *upasad*s, it is logical that they are indeed subsidiaries of those [rites]; such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
To this it is replied: First of all, there is no *prakaraṇa* (context) for the *upasads*. Nor is mere proximity in the mind (*buddhisannidhi*) sufficient to constitute a *prakaraṇa*.

Why? Because a *prakaraṇa* is based upon a governing purpose (*adhikāra*). The meaning of this is as follows: An injunction (*niyoga*) accompanied by a governing purpose is understood as having the form of a task (*kārya*) that effects the expression of syntactic connection; it is not understood when devoid of a governing purpose. Therefore, everything [in the context] is for the sake of that [injunction], and subsequently, that [purpose]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the definition of *prakaraṇa* and the necessity of a governing purpose (*adhikāra*) for the realization of an injunction.*

Because it enters into the ritual procedure (*kārānupraveśāt*), it does not require another governing authority (*adhikāra*) for its entry into that authority, since the expression of the connected meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) is established by that very [procedure]. Even though those things lacking a governing authority (*niradhikārāṇām*) have an understanding of the task (*kārya*), they lack the power to enjoin application (*viniyojakaśakti*); therefore, they do not possess the context (*prakaraṇa*). Now, it was said that [the *upasads*] are subsidiary to [the *sāmnidhya*] by virtue of syntactical connection (*vākya*); however, a syntactical connection is not possible here because there is no connection between both words. This is the meaning.

The meaning of the sentence is not possible [if interpreted otherwise], because when the word *upasat* is uttered once together with the two words *saumya* and *purastāt*, there can be no simultaneous connection [between all three]. Therefore, since the connection must be established with a single word, the connection is only with *purastādupasadām*. Now, why is this connection—*upasadāṃ saumyena*—not accepted? Because it would result in a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the word *purastāt*. The meaning of this is as follows: *purastāt*—

(1) G. "Precisely by way of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal" (śeṣaśeṣitayaiva); (2) R. "In order to obtain the connection with that specific qualification" (tadadhikārānvayalābhāya); (3) G. "Even when the task has ceased" (kāryavigamepi); (4) R. "There is nothing further to be enjoined" (viniyojyaṃ kiñcin nāstīti). [p. 1062]

This word *ca* (and), because it expresses a constant requirement for a correlative, does not convey its meaning when not connected with the *upasad*s. Therefore, as long as there is no connection with the word *purastāt* (before), the sentence would remain unintelligible. Nor should it be argued that it will later connect with the *upasad*s because they are the subject under discussion;
for it is more logical to connect it with that which must necessarily be expected. Otherwise, it would simply fail to convey any meaning at all.

However, in connection with the word "purastāt" (before), since it is impossible for any word to be unaccounted for even in the absence of a governing element (*śeṣin*), and because "purastāt" prescribes a time, the expression "they proceed with the Soma-oblation" is not contradictory. Therefore, this [text] also— namely, "After the Āgnimāruta,
they proceed with the after-offerings (*anūyāja*s)"— [is consistent].
This is not distinct from the previous case;

for [the subsidiary acts] possess a fruit because they have been stated as having that [principal act] as their cause. But how can the status of being equally primary be suspected, given that the Sāṅgrahaṇī sacrifice alone possesses primacy due to its connection with a specific qualification (*adhikāra*), whereas the Vāmana oblations, lacking such a qualification, are merely subsidiaries? To this, he says: "In the Sāṅgrahaṇī..."

Even though it is established that what is fruitless in the proximity of something fruitful is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to it, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to exclude such *anuṣaṅga* (syntactic connection). And it has been shown:

"It is true that what lacks a specific qualification (*niradhikāra*) is an auxiliary to that which possesses a qualification (*sādhikāra*); however, the *āmana*-offerings do indeed possess a qualification, because the word expressing the qualification can be connected (*anuṣaṅga*) even to them.
