Nor are the *paridhi*-mantras interruptive, because they belong to a different class (*asamānajātīyatva*); for only that which belongs to the same class..."

It becomes an interposer (*vyavadhāyaka*), as for example: in the mantra “*saṃ te vāyurvātena gacchatām*,” the word *gacchatām* is [separated] from the [preceding] *saṃyajatrairaṅgāni* by another verbal form, *gacchantām*, [and from the following] “*saṃ yajñapatirāśiṣā*.”
In this case, there is an interruption.
This section is intended to remove the doubt that the mantra words belonging to a subsequent context (*adhikāra*) are not of the same class [as those of the preceding].

The reasoning for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because they are separated by the *paridhi* formulas, there can be no syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*). And the *paridhi* formulas do indeed interrupt the context.
Because it is unfit for connection. To be an obstacle means precisely to interrupt the cognition of eligibility (*adhikāra*). For example, as in the case of that which belongs to the same class;
here too, [it is the same].

Likewise, it applies even to that which is of a different class and unfit for connection with it; for that which is unconnected indeed acts as an intervention, since in that case too the cognition of it does not arise.

The *dadhighraha* (the curd-grasp) is an occasional rite (*naimittika*). Now, one might object: "Since this is enjoined without being connected to a specific occasion (*nimitta*), how can it be considered an occasional rite? Thus is the doubt raised.

As for the statement: "The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers it to be occasional (naimittika) because of the mention of the purpose for removing the defect of impermanence. The meaning of this is as follows:

although no specific occasion (nimitta) is heard in the text, nevertheless, when the *dadhi-graha* requires a means, it is logical that the very rectification of the deficiency caused by another deity—though mentioned merely as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—should be its function.
Consequently, the teacher’s disciple (ācāryadeśīya) maintains that, in effect, it is occasional and serves both purposes, just like the *khadira* wood.

However, one who holds a partial view of the established doctrine (*siddhāntaikadeśin*) considers that the taking of curd (*dadhi-grahaṇa*) serves to benefit the sacrifice by means of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*) for the purpose of removing defects, just like the *khādira* sacrificial post.

He asks: "What is the reasoning? and replies: "He considers that the application of the word 'eldest' (*jyeṣṭha*) is justified because it is permanent. Its status as the "eldest" arises from its being praiseworthy.

And its praiseworthiness results from its possessing both forms [of excellence] and its having a superior meaning compared to the others. But the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is based on the occasion (*nimitta*).

Because there is an absence of conjunction [with a specific occasion], it cannot be postulated that [the rite] is occasional (*naimittika*) for the purpose of removing a defect. Why is it not possible? He states this in a single passage: "By the fact that the removal of an occasional defect would otherwise be inexplicable, that [removal] too ought to be occasional; for it is not the case that an eternal [rite] cannot have the purpose of destroying a non-eternal defect. Therefore, this [removal] is also non-eternal."

Thus it is said. It is true that [a statement] must be accepted as literal if it cannot be explained otherwise; however, since it is indeed consistent when taken as an *arthavāda* (explanatory or commendatory passage), it does not deserve to be so interpreted.
(1) 1273 (2) R. Both are applicable.

The meaning of this is as follows: First of all, it does not appear here as a contingent effect (*naimittika*) because there is no mention of a cause (*nimitta*) for it in its own nature. Nor can impermanence be postulated by the force of an impermanent effect; for it is illogical to postulate an impermanent effect when there is no contradiction in its connection with something permanent. Indeed, it is not reasonable to say that "the permanent must be performed in order to remove an impermanent defect"; nevertheless, one might still suppose that very thing to be the effect.

If the hearing of the removal of defects could not otherwise be logically accounted for, then it would require the postulation of a specific purpose; however, since that is also logically accounted for as being for the sake of praise (*stuti*) or as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it does not merit such a postulation. This has been stated in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) regarding the similarity of forms and so forth. Furthermore, Vaiśvānara would be eternal; thus, even if one were to argue that [the text] is logically accounted for by having the purpose of removing impermanent defects, [it would still be untenable].

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains the conceit that permanence also applies to the Vaiśvānara [fire]. The proponent of the prima facie view holds the mere conceit that the removal of the defect caused by the failure to collect [the materials] for the fire-pot (*ukhā*) is justified as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), just as in the previous case; by using the word "conceit" (*abhimāna*), he expresses the weakness of the prima facie position. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is this: we do not say that its status as contingent (*naimittikatva*) arises from the removal of a defect, but rather from its connection with a specific occasion (*nimitta*).
In this regard, it is heard in scripture: "He who piles the fire-altar (Agni) without having carried the Ukhya fire for a year should offer an oblation to Vaiśvānara.

Since there is a scriptural hearing regarding the qualification of one who has not carried the Ukhya fire, its status as a contingent rite (naimittika) is directly stated here. Therefore, [there is no contradiction] between the connection with the obligatory and the non-obligatory—

Since there is no contradiction, it is not proper to describe [the passage] as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended for the removal of defects. Nor can the scriptural mention of the occasion (*nimittaśruti*) be interpreted as an explanatory statement; for when the literal meaning of the scripture is possible, the postulation of another meaning is not justified. Furthermore, in the case of the *dadhi-graha*, there is no connection with a person; thus, its obligatory nature has been demonstrated.
The sixth layer is for the sake of prior continuity: "The year itself impels him toward stability who, having piled the fire-altar, does not find firm standing;
therefore, he piles the sixth layer."

To the objection—"Since this involves a connection with a person who has not yet established himself [in the higher stages], it is merely occasional (naimittika); how then can its permanence (nityatā) be suspected?"—the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) replies: "Because the suffix '-tama' in the word 'ṣaṣṭhīm' is understood as having the sense of completion (pūraṇa), it is proper to explain the mention of the occasion (nimitta-śruti) as being merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). The word 'ṣaṣṭhī' ends in a suffix denoting completion; by that, [it refers to] six...

That by which a number is completed is a "layer" (*citi*); this is the sixth layer. Nor does this occasional (*naimittikī*) layer complete the number six among the five eternal layers. The production of numbers such as duality and so forth occurs through the entry into a single unitary delimitation (*ekāvaccheda*). Therefore, this [sixth] is also eternal. Furthermore, a scriptural mention of a cause (*nimitta-śruti*) for things that are eternal is not logically consistent; it must somehow be explained as being merely a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*). But surely—

With the intention of asking why the word *ṣaṣṭhī* itself must be explained otherwise by the force of the indicative mark (*nimitta*) and the scriptural statement (*śruti*), he asks: "Why? He considers that the postulation of a governing context (*adhikāra*) is logical in accordance with what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), since it has been established in the section concerning animals (*tiryagadhikaraṇa*) that an injunction (*niyoga*) follows the application (*viniyoga*). However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: this would indeed be true if there were a contradiction, but here there is no contradiction.

Why? Because even with the intention of providing instruction, the meaning of the suffix as "filling" (pūraṇa) is logically consistent; since the number six is possible through the inclusion of a single act of instruction, the venerable Pāṇini’s rule on filling cannot necessarily be explained only with reference to actual performance. For if it were the case that the venerable Pāṇini composed this sūtra with the intention of establishing a number based on actual performance...

If there were such a certainty, then the word "sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would not be applicable in view of the instruction; however, this is not the case. Therefore, it is a part of that which is to be enjoined.

There is a contradiction. Furthermore, as long as there is no contradiction with the injunction (*vidheya*), the scriptural statement regarding the occasion (*nimitta*) cannot be abandoned. Therefore, its status as an occasional rite (*naimittikatva*) is established. The presentation of the [scriptural] observation and the refutation thereof have been stated.
[Topic 2: "The Pitṛyajña, because it has its own time. Now, [one might object]: "They perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña on the afternoon of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*)."

Thus, this is an instruction regarding time. How can the status of being a subordinate member (*aṅgatva*) be asserted for the ritual of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)? Nor should there be a suspicion of subordination based on the understanding of the ritual through the word *amāvāsyā* by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because there is no reason to abandon the directly stated time (*śrauta-kāla*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Secondary indication is better than the postulation of a result"—this is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).

The meaning of this is as follows: Should an implied governing topic (*adhikāra*) be supplied, or should one instead explain the word *amāvāsyā* through a second mode of signification (*vṛtti*), namely the well-known conventional sense (*lakṣaṇā*), and thus accept its entry into the governing context of the *darśa* sacrifice? In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that assuming a different mode of signification is simpler than assuming an unmentioned governing topic.
The proponent’s intention is as follows: it has been stated that once one has entered into the jurisdiction of the *darśa* sacrifice, it is not possible to postulate another independent jurisdiction.

Therefore, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is indeed entered into the same single mandate as the Amāvāsyā rite. To this it is replied: a single mandate is not possible, because, just as in the case of the Amāvāsyā, there is a connection with time [at two different points].

[1067] Because of the distinction [of the term *piṇḍapitṛyajña*]. A distinction is understood from the fact that the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is Vedic (*śrauta*) on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), whereas [the other] is characterized [as smārta];
for the connection with the time [of the new moon] is possible in both cases. The meaning of this is: if the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* were preceded by an instruction regarding the *darśa*...

If it were an instruction regarding the sacrifice (*yajñopadeśa*), then, because the connection with the time of the *darśa* (new moon) or *amāvāsyā* would be understood, the word denoting time would be explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in accordance with that previously understood connection. However, when these two instructions are independent of one another, then, since there is no previously understood connection in either case, it is not proper to explain them through figurative indication. Furthermore, an instruction regarding time is not impossible in the case of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*.

Because it would result in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*): if [the *vaiśvānara* sacrifice] were a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the New Moon (*amāvāsya*) ritual, then since subsidiaries share the time of the principal (*pradhāna*), the time of the New Moon would necessarily apply; thus, there would be no separate scriptural instruction (*upadeśa*). And when the word "New Moon" does not prescribe its own time but serves to designate the primary rite (*śeṣin*), it follows that [the *vaiśvānara*] is a subsidiary of the New Moon. Therefore, the prior and subsequent scriptural statements refer to that time by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and thus there is no contradiction. By means of this conclusion, another objection is raised under the guise of a summary.

He refutes this. For it is objected as follows: "Indeed, the sequence between the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and the Darśa is heard through an explanatory passage (arthavāda). And that [sequence] is based on their entry into a single performance. Furthermore, entry into a single performance occurs when there is a relationship of subsidiary and principal (aṅga-aṅgin). Therefore, it appears that [the Piṇḍapitṛyajña] is indeed a subsidiary. This objection is answered as follows: "When there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that demonstrates subsidiarity, then..."
That scriptural statement regarding the prior and subsequent [acts] refers only to two independent rites: "On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), there is the Piṇḍapitṛyajña for the Darśa;

on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), the Iṣṭi. Therefore, there is no contradiction even with the explanatory passage (arthavāda). The purpose has been stated: because the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices begin with the Full Moon sacrifice, one who has performed the consecration (ādhāna) on the Full Moon day need not perform the Darśa even when the New Moon day arrives. In that case—

According to the Siddhānta, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña takes place; otherwise, in the absence of a primary rite (pradhāna), it would not be performed. Furthermore, in the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is not extended [by analogy] because it is not an auxiliary (anaṅga) to it.
The rope is an auxiliary to the animal sacrifice. But is it not said: "Having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-stranded rope"?

Thus, the act of encircling (*parivyāṇa*) is first an auxiliary to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by virtue of the accusative case-ending; furthermore, by the syntactical statement (*vākya*) "with a threefold [rope]," the rope (*raśanā*) is also an auxiliary to the act of encircling. Consequently, through the medium of the act of encircling—(1) G.
*kālakhaṇḍāva* (2) R. omits *darśasya* (3) G. *yajñasyeti*—[the rope becomes an auxiliary to the sacrifice].

[Page 1068] "But how can there be a suspicion that the girdle (*raśanā*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), when it is like the red color (*aruṇa*) and other such qualities which are auxiliaries of the Soma? To this, he says: 'In this case too, because the suffix *ktvā* requires another action, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers them to belong to a single injunction. This is the meaning."

First, from the statement “he brings near the animal” (*paśum upākaroti*), it is understood that the act of bringing near (*upākaraṇa*) is a subsidiary part of the animal sacrifice. Likewise, the act of encircling (*parivyāṇa*) is also performed by the same agent as the bringing near, as indicated by the suffix *ktvā*. And this common agency is based on a single performance; that is, they constitute a single ritual procedure (*ekaprayoga*).

"By way of the relationship between principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāvena*)," [it is shown that] the *parivyāṇa* (encircling) is indeed a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *upākaraṇa* (dedication). Now, although the relationship of principal and subordinate exists due to the suffix *-ktvā*, why should it not be the reverse? To this he says: "And in that case, the status of being for the sake of the animal (*paśvarthatā*) would result, because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) also has that as its purpose.
The meaning of this is: the *upākaraṇa* is not for the sake of the *parivyāṇa*; for if that were so, everything would have the sacrificial post as its sole purpose, and that is incorrect.

Since the broth (*yūṣa*) is also a part of the animal sacrifice, the rope must therefore be a part of the animal sacrifice itself. However, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) maintained that the conclusion is correct: from the suffix *-ktvā* one understands only common agency (*samānakartṛkatā*), not the unity of the injunction (*niyogaikyam*); thus, it is logical that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) possesses primacy due to the accusative case ending.
The meaning of this is as follows: the understanding of primacy derived from the accusative case is not the same as that derived from the suffix *-ktvā*.

However, because it depends on another deliberation (*vimarśa*), by the force of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*), the rope (*raśanā*)—which enters into the act of encircling for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—is also for the sake of the post.

But is it not the case that without a single injunction (*niyoga*), the state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) is impossible? Even the second case ending can occur when the object is not intended (*anīpsita*). True, it would not be possible; however, the commonality of agent is established through the unity of the governing context (*adhikāra*). Well then, what of the suffix *-ktvā*?
On the basis of this reasoning, let it be stated thus: "He encircles the sacrificial post with the threefold cord.
It is replied: the use of the gerund suffix (*ktvā*) is for the purpose of indicating time;
[moreover], it possesses the sense of the accusative case.

[1069] Here it is objected: But surely, a definition based on time is not possible here at all. For it has been stated that the distinction between times of utterance is the cause for the production of the suffix *ktvā*. The meaning of this is as follows: priority in the time of performance is not the cause for the production of the suffix *ktvā*; rather,

[The suffix -ktvā] denotes priority in time relative to the act of utterance. Therefore, how could there be an instruction regarding priority in time with respect to the performance [of the ritual]? It is true that you have said this; however, that very same time of utterance is also indicated by secondary implication (lakṣaṇā) in relation to the performance. The meaning of this is as follows: because the suffix -ktvā does not have any other purpose, the time pertaining to the utterance is also enjoined for the performance by way of indication. This is the standard principle in every case where time is being enjoined.

In both worldly usage and the Veda, there is this distinction: even the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) is not taken into account there, because the injunction (*niyoga*) is restricted to time. Precisely for this reason, in a sentence whose primary purpose is to enjoin time, the identity of the agent—even if it is understood—is not intended to be significant, just like [the grammatical number] "oneness" (*ekatva*). For this very reason, [in the case of the injunction]: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma."
Thus, the objection regarding the identity of the agent is resolved. The purpose has been stated.
And as for the *svaru*, because it is a part [of the sacrificial post], [the rule applies]: "He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post."

Thus it is heard [in the scripture]. How, then, can the *svaru* be suspected of being for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)? For the genitive case does not express the relation of being "for the sake of" (*tādarthya*). To this, he says: "The *svaru* of the sacrificial post"—meaning that the sacrificial post is possessed of the *svaru*.

The proponent of the prima facie view considers that the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is understood— as in the case of "one who possesses cows" (*gomān*)— and thus maintains it to be for the sake of that [the sacrificial post]. For when something exists for the sake of another, such a purpose is indeed observed.

It has the sense of possession (*matvartha*). The intention here is that it is the same in this case as well. Its meaning is as follows: regarding the injunction "he makes the *svaru* of the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya svaruṃ karoti*), the *svaru* must first be understood as having the purpose of serving that [post] (*tādarthya*). [The phrase is] "the *svaru* of the sacrificial post."

In this context, the sense of possession (*matvartha*)—that "the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) possesses a *svaru*"—is understood. And since the sense of possession is generally observed to exist when there is a relationship of purpose (*tādarthya*), it is logical to assume that very purpose in this case. Therefore, because the purpose is understood from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), the *svaru* exists solely for the sake of the sacrificial post. Furthermore, in the statement "he anoints the sacrificial post with the *svaru*," its disposal (*pratipatti*) occurs through that very act of anointing.

The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*), however, considers that in cases such as "containing barley" (*yavamatī*) and so forth, because there is no inconsistency, and because of the use of the accusative case in "he anoints the animal" (*paśum anakti*), as well as because it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), it is for the sake of the animal alone; this is the connection with the distant [preceding] statement. The meaning of this is as follows: first of all, there is no restriction regarding the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*), because there is deviation in cases such as "containing barley. Furthermore, by the accusative case in "the animal" (*paśum*), [it is shown that] the act of anointing is also [for the sake of the animal].

Because another purpose is heard [in the scripture]; and because, if the *svaru* were for the purpose of anointing (*añjana*), it would have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) through the accomplishment of that action, the *svaru* is indeed for the purpose of anointing. Furthermore, the genitive case is justifiable even when there is a connection with the originative injunction (*utpattisaṃyoga*), so there is no fault. The meaning of this is as follows: although the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is perceived, its subordination (*śeṣatā*) is not inconsistent; thus, it is not untenable even on the basis of what is merely common. This is because the application to anointing is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*). Nor is anointing itself...

The performance [of the action] is directed toward the animal (*paśum*), because even in the case of the ointment (*añjana*), another purpose is heard through the accusative case. Furthermore, if the ointment were the primary purpose, the accomplishment of the ritual act would be the visible purpose of the resin (*svaru*). Nor does the genitive case necessarily indicate a possessive relationship; for it can also be consistent with the substance being for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) due to its connection with its production, and because it is already established as such. The purpose has thus been stated.

The sacrifices in the Darśapūrṇamāsa are distinguished by their primary importance; as stated in the section concerning the Full Moon sacrifice: "He who, knowing thus, performs the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice," and "He who, knowing thus, performs the Amāvāsyā sacrifice."

Thus it is established that these are restatements (*anuvāda*) of the collective whole. Furthermore, even on the view that they are restatements, since they are heard in connection with time, they are restatements only of those [sacrifices] connected to the time of their origin, not of all those possessing a form—(1) G. [the word *utpanna*].

Thus it is established. Now, regarding the word *yaji* (to sacrifice) occurring in the sentence of qualification (*adhikāra*), there arises the consideration: are all sacrifices enjoined in relation to the qualification, or are they merely restated (*anūdita*)? But surely, it is logical that the connection with the qualification occurs precisely at the appropriate time; for [the connection depends on] the accompanying words (*upapada*).

Because of the restriction [of the term *rājasūya*], it is logical that the connection with the qualification (*adhikāra*) belongs to those [sacrifices] alone, since there exists a connection with time, as in the case of a sentence that is a restatement of a collective whole (*samudāyānuvāda*).

Therefore, one asks: how can there be a doubt in this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the equal primacy of all sacrifices? To this he says: It was established in the section on the *Rājasūya* that "the non-sacrifices are excluded because the qualification is heard in connection with the word 'yajati' (he sacrifices); and wherever the verbal root occurs, there alone does the secondary noun (*upapada*) apply."

It is established in the examination of names that [a word] exists by virtue of its name. Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers this root *yaji* to denote sacrifice in general;
thinking that wherever there is the root *yaji*, a qualifying term (*upapada*) must exist, he regards this designation as being of the same form as a dual ending.
The meaning of this is as follows: this root *yaji* denotes sacrifice in general, not a collection of sacrifices connected with specific times. Time—

Furthermore, there are many sacrifices connected [to the context]; among these, a word ending in the dual number cannot appropriately apply [to them]. And since the dual number is not appropriate, the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* does not function as something distinct from the verbal root (*ākhyāta*) with respect to those [sacrifices] associated with the two times; rather, it refers only to the sacrifices denoted by the proximate verbal root. Nor is there a connection for any [single sacrifice] with both parts of the combined time.

Since there exists even a single instance of [the term] "karma," this instruction is sufficient to establish the sacrifice (*yajis*) in its specific sense. Therefore, like the *rājasūya*, it is indeed a primary auxiliary (*paramāṅga*). Consequently, there is a connection with the qualification (*adhikāra*) for all sacrifices under discussion.
And because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with them, the word *darśapūrṇamāsa* is also the name for all of them.

In the expression "darśapūrṇamāsābhyām," it is not a dual number, but rather a form resembling one; or the dual number may be used by transposition of case endings to signify a plural sense. Alternatively, because it denotes a single sacrifice (*ekayajña*), it should be understood as having the sense of a singular number with reference to the aggregate (*samudāya*) implied by that [term]. Furthermore, regarding the statement: "At each *prayāja* offering, he offers a *kṛṣṇala*."
Thus, regarding the observation in the *vikṛtis* (modified sacrifices), how is it that—(1) for some only, (2) only when combined, or (3) there, the *upapada* is not [present]?

In this view, what will happen? If all sacrifices were primary, then because the *prayāja*s would also be primary, and because of the principle that "since the action has not yet commenced" (*karmaṇastvapravṛttatvāt*), there can be no extension (*atideśa*) of details to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*s); and thus, in the absence of the *prayāja*s...

Because it is impossible to enjoin those qualities [there]. As for the subsequent [statement], another means of knowledge must be sought, distinct from the extended application (atideśa), for the purpose of establishing the attainment of the *prayāja*s. This expression "where" (*yatra*) is to be shifted; it should be applied wherever the *prayāja*s occur. Regarding the attainment—

Either the perception of attainment through the nature [of the act] must be considered a delusion, or they must be regarded as distinct rituals. Furthermore, there will be the apprehension of the ritual elements by name. If the *prayājas* were not archetypal (*prākṛta*), why would they not be prescribed as distinct rituals only in the modified form (*vikṛti*)?
Moreover, the word *prayāja* would serve as the indicator for the extension of ritual properties (*dharmātideśaka*). In every respect, this would result in the absence of extension (*atideśābhāva*).
Whatever deficiency may arise, this principle has already been stated: that all sacrifices are primary.
Furthermore, regarding the passages, “He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon” and “He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon,” [the same principle applies].

Thus, why are those two groups under discussion not accepted [as the referents], given their connection with the dual number? To this it has already been stated that the dual number residing in the subordinate element (*upapada*) associated with time does not deviate from its true meaning. The answer is: "And it has been said that the subordinate element follows the meaning of the verbal root. The meaning of this is as follows: this verbal root expresses a sacrifice (*yāga*), not a collection of sacrifices, nor two sacrifices conjoined with two times.
This is the subject at hand. However, many such sacrifices (*yajña*) are under discussion. Since no distinction is perceived among them, the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) applies to all of them;

and since they are many, the dual number is inappropriate. When the dual number is untenable, the verb does not function as a distinct [referent]. Furthermore, there is no sacrifice that conforms to both words [of the compound]; thus, the root *yaji* does not follow the accompanying word (*upapada*). Rather, it is the accompanying word that follows the root *yaji*.

Furthermore, because the word *darśa* conveys a sense of distinctness, this thing denoted by the word *darśa* is not seen in common usage as being denotable by the word *amāvāsyā*. Therefore, it is not understood as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of the time of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Consequently, the distinctness of the subject matter of the injunction is understood. Thus, it is established that here, as in the case of the *rājasūya*, the sacrifice itself is the subsidiary (*aṅga*). To this, it is replied: "True, this is so; the qualifying term (*upapada*) follows the meaning of the verbal root."
(1) Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra 8.1.20; (2) G.: *yāgā*; (3) G.: *kālasamudāyam* [p.
Nevertheless, since two groups are under discussion (*prakṛta*), and because the dual number cannot have any other meaning, it is possible that—

Because the assumption of a form identical to its own meaning is impossible. The meaning of this is as follows: it is true that the subordinate term (*upapada*) follows the meaning of the verbal root;
nevertheless, why should this sacrifice (*yajati*) not apply to both composite groups? For both composite groups are the subject under discussion.

Consequently, the connection with the governing injunction (*adhikāra*) belongs to the two composite groups alone. Why? Because no other meaning for the dual number is possible, and the dual number is indeed applicable here.
Because the assumption that [the suffix] is of the same form as a dual number is untenable. Now, it was argued that this *yajiḥ* does not denote a collective whole;

that is true, indeed. However, it will denote the sacrifices situated in a collective state. And this being so, the dual number will occur naturally. Thus he says: "And when there is conformity with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), there is no contradiction regarding the accompanying word (*upapada*). How so?

Is there a contradiction? Because this prefix (*upapada*) does not function outside the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); rather, it functions within the meaning of the root itself. Furthermore, when it functions within the meaning of the root, it is not logical for the noun (*nāman*) to abandon its own meaning. This prefix is connected with time; therefore, those things associated with time are recognized as nouns in the explanatory statement (*anuvādavākya*), and when they alone are grasped in the governing statement (*adhikāravākya*), that is the intended meaning.
Its meaning is not "renunciation" (tyāga). Since the meaning is already established by the expression of the two groups under discussion, there is no evidence for postulating a different meaning;

thus, one will not have recourse to an extremely indirect function (*atiparokṣavṛtti*) for the accompanying word (*upapada*). And what is its meaning? It is the expression of the two groups under discussion. Thus, since it is established that it follows that [meaning], there is no evidence for postulating a different meaning. But surely—
There is no evidence for the abandonment of the primary sacrifice from the verbal root (*dhātu*). Who has said that there is evidence for its non-abandonment?

Rather, we have stated that there is no evidence for asserting a contradiction with the meaning of the subordinate term (*upapada*). This is what is meant: the primary [sacrifice] is not abandoned; the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) functions precisely in reference to the primary [sacrifice]. However, due to the compatibility with the subordinate terms, it applies to those [sacrifices] associated with time.

It occurs in those things that have attained the state of a composite whole. As for the objection that there is no recognition of the subject matter under discussion because of the hearing of the word *darśa*, that has been refuted by the observation that the remaining parts of the sentences share a single meaning; and it is also possible [to apply] the word *darśa* as well.

Regarding the expression of that meaning: by means of the word *darśa*, through the figure of indirect indication (*viparītalakṣaṇā*) due to the non-appearance of the moon, there is the expression of that same meaning, namely the expression of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Therefore, it is well said: "In proximity to that which possesses a fruit, that which lacks a fruit is its subsidiary. As for the objection raised—namely, "Why should there not be an elliptical extension (*anuṣaṅga*)?"—that has been refuted; rather, it is better [to accept] the elliptical extension.

[The phrase] "the fulfillment of the requirement for the manner of performance (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*)" [is used]. For otherwise, there would indeed be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of requirements. If this is so—if *anuṣaṅga* (supplying a word from a previous context) does not occur when the fulfillment of the requirement for the manner of performance is possible—then why would it not be supplied because of an interruption (*vyavāya*)?
This has been shown in the case of the *Sāṅgrahaṇī* sacrifice; in that case as well, this very principle is appropriate. Or else, a specific distinction must be stated.

This is now explained. It is appropriate that in the case of the Sāṅgrahaṇī sacrifice, since it is a modified rite (*vikṛti*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) remains established as being like that of the archetype (*prakṛti*); thus, because its requirements are satisfied, there is no need for further expectation, and the fulfillment of that expectation is possible through extended application (*atideśa*). Therefore, in that case, the prohibition of *anuṣaṅga* (supplying a missing word from a previous context) is due precisely to the intervention [of other elements]. Here, however, because the requirement for the procedure remains unfulfilled, the expectation for the procedure persists.

Because it is the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is well said that by its very fulfillment there is a single injunction (*ekaniyoga*), and not the postulation of another distinct qualification (*adhikārāntara*). The praises such as "the eyes, indeed," and so forth, are like the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). And the *darśana*s—namely the *prayāja*s and other rites—are stated to belong to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*s).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, they are equal. Now, it might be argued that by the *bahuvrīhi* compound "he whose stomas are lights" (*jyotīṃṣi stomā asya*), it is understood that the Soma sacrifice itself is the primary element. To this, it may be replied: True, the Soma sacrifices possess stomas; however, the term "Jyotiṣṭoma-hood" does not exist [in them], so the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* is not applicable here because its own literal sense would be disconnected. Thus, even the mere act of sacrificing (*yajimātra*) is connected with the grammatical factors (*kāraka*).

That is not so, because in the supplementary portion of that passage, the stotras such as the *trivṛt* are designated by the term "Jyotiṣṭoma. Indeed, designation based on what is mentioned in an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) is observed elsewhere, just as in the case of the statement, "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed *Āgneya*.
Therefore, [the author] asks: how can there be a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in this matter? To this he says: "But here..."
Because there is no dual number and so forth, it is not possible to preclude the application [of the term] to sacrifice in general. The meaning of this is as follows:

just as in the case of "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]," the term does not apply to all sacrifices due to the requirement of the dual number, here there is nothing of the sort. Therefore, its application to sacrifice in general cannot be precluded. [Objection: But surely it can be precluded by the nominal stem *jyotiṣṭoma* itself.

Regarding this, he says: "In the discussion on names (*nāmadheya*), it was stated that because the word *jyotiṣṭoma* is a name, its denoted object—the cause for its application—is not syntactically connected [to the action]. The meaning of this is as follows: the word *jyotiṣṭoma* is not a qualifier of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice); rather, it is merely a name.
For it is not logical to intend a qualification of that which is being enjoined. Nor is the principle of the *aruṇaikahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow) applicable here."

Since there is no other meaning for the word *jyotiṣṭoma*, and because the verbal root alone is directly connected with the injunction (*niyoga*), therefore, in this case, the sacrifice (*yajati*) itself is the primary element without qualification, while the non-sacrifice (*ayajati*) is merely a subordinate part (*aṅga*), just as in the case of the *rājasūya*; the name is likewise [indicative of the whole]. To this it is replied:
(1) the connection of the [root] with its factors (*kāraka*) is grasped; (2) it is apprehended.

1076] —If it were by us that non-concomitance was stated on the grounds of being a name (*nāmatva*), then this would be so; if we had stated that "whatever is a name, that is concomitant with the effect," then this would indeed be the case. However, in that context, non-concomitance was stated precisely because of the lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*). For it is not the case in any way...

Terms such as *udbhid* and others possess a connection with the action (*kārya*). Therefore, those which lack a connection with the action have been declared [to be names]. It is not the case that they lack a connection simply because they are names while a connection actually exists. However, in this instance, the lack of connection being perceived cannot be set aside by treating it as a name, since its function is to bring to mind a specific sacrifice (*yajiviśeṣa*). But surely, here even the status of being a name is abandoned; for it becomes a qualifying word (*viśeṣaṇapada*) at that time. And that is not—
The sense is that this is logical. What is lost to us? Even so, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) remains intact. This, however, is merely a concessionary argument (*abhyupagamyavāda*).

But even this qualifying term is indeed a name (*nāman*), because no other meaning is possible; for it serves only to convey a specific qualification of the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). Therefore, even when conjoined, it resides solely in the qualifier and is thus a name, as it does not denote any other distinct object.

[The word] *nāt*. Its meaning is as follows: this is not a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) like "blue" and so forth; rather, by virtue of its conformity with this name, it is the root *yaj* itself that occurs in reference to a specific sacrifice. For if it were to occur in reference to sacrifice in general, then the connection of the name's meaning would apply to sacrifice in general. And since that [term] denotes the Soma-sacrifice, therefore, in order to conform to this, the root *yaj* itself occurs in reference to that specific sacrifice.
Therefore, one must resort to a mode of operation that is entirely beyond perception; for, due to the contradiction [otherwise], the root *yaj* itself refers to a specific sacrifice.

The word *jyotiṣṭoma* also functions there as its name, because it does not bring to mind any other meaning. But if this is so, why in the case of "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva" (*vaiśvadevena yajeta*) does the root *yaj* not refer only to the sacrifice accomplished by the curd-offering (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to the Viśvedevas, in accordance with the word *vaiśvadeva*?

Consequently, let the term *vaiśvadeva* also be the name of that [single deity] alone, and not of all [the deities]. To this it is replied: A name is indeed of two kinds—some are already established (*pravṛtta*), and some are yet to be established (*pravartya*)—in which case, from another sentence...

The engagement in a sacrifice is determined by the name; that is what is called a "derived name" (*pravṛttanāman*). For example, the terms *darśapūrṇamāsau* (the New and Full Moon sacrifices). Although these two terms denote time, they function as names of sacrifices because no [independent] production of those times is observed, just like the term *āgneya*. Likewise, the word *jyotiṣṭoma* is also a derived name, since the engagement in a sacrifice is understood through the consideration of its explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). And by means of this derived name, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is restricted to a specific [sacrifice] through another sentence.

Because it is understood that the name [of the sacrifice] is independent of that [the word *rājan*]. Although the word *rājasūya*—derived through the etymology "that in which the king (*rājā*), i.e., Soma, is pressed (*sūyate*)"—is a name applied to the Soma-sacrifice due to its connection with the pressing of Soma, it is nevertheless not capable of establishing itself as referring to a specific sacrifice, because the ritual has sovereignty (*svārājya*) as its fruit. This is because another etymology is possible: "that from which the king is pressed. For one who has no other [basis] for applying [the name] to a sacrifice...

It is understood, however, that it must be assumed to be the name of that which is to be prompted [by the injunction], precisely through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) contained within its own sentence.
This is like the word *vaiśvadeva*. For, according to the rule "it applies only to a hymn (*sūkta*) or an oblation (*havis*"), it refers only to a hymn or an oblation, not to the sacrifice itself.

Therefore, in the statement "one should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva*," its status as a name must be assumed on account of its coreferentiality with the root *yaj*. Consequently, [the word *vaiśvadeva*] refers to the sacrifice previously mentioned.

It is thus established that [the word *yaji*] is not capable of being restricted to a specific [sacrifice]. Furthermore, as stated in the *Paurṇamāsyadhikaraṇa*, the very *yaji* occurring in the restating sentence (*anuvādavākya*) applies only to those [sacrifices] associated with their time of origin; for them alone do the words *amāvāsyā* and *paurṇamāsī* serve as names.
Thus ends the analysis of the four names.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth [chapter] in the *Ṛjuvimalā*, a commentary composed by Śālikanātha Miśra.

(1) To this it is replied: The word *vaiśvadeva* is also employed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). And *yaj* applies to all archetypal sacrifices. Furthermore, it cannot be restricted to a specific [sacrifice] by the word *vaiśvadeva*; rather, it applies to all of them because its occurrence is possible therein.

By the term *viśvadeva*, the word *vaiśvadeva* is used in the sacrifice [to mean] "of all the gods" (*viśveṣāṃ devānām*). Nor can there be a connection with either the "all-gods" who have already been enjoined or those who are being enjoined. In that regard, the state of being enjoined is first impossible, because the *āmikṣā* has already been enjoined elsewhere, and it is impossible for it to be enjoined in another place.

However, because they are not being enjoined, the designation of all [of them] is possible, just as in the case of a staff; for example, even though a staff resides in only one person, everyone is designated as "staff-bearers. Therefore, for the sake of establishing a mere designation, an injunction should not be resorted to on the basis of that designation. If the designation is thus established, the sacrifice (*yajati*) is restricted.
It ought to be so understood. [p. 1078] But, one might object, in this case as well, the word *jyotiṣṭoma* would refer to another sacrifice due to its association with the Soma sacrifice.

It is said: in the injunctive statement (*adhikāra-vākya*), the sacrifice together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-yāga*) is enjoined; it is not merely restated. Therefore, the mandate (*niyoga*) is understood as having as its object the sacrifice denoted by the term *jyotiṣṭoma*. Furthermore, it does not include all sacrifices for its own sake. When the consideration arises as to how there might be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) for those [sacrifices] that have been included, it is not all sacrifices [that are connected].

[Otherwise], they would enter into the syntactical connection as instruments, which would result in the name [Vaiśvadeva] functioning in an excessively remote manner. Therefore, all the Soma sacrifices alone enter into the syntactical connection as instruments; thus, there is no contingency of the name functioning in an excessively remote way.

Consequently, the statement "by means of the Vaiśvadeva" is a restatement (anuvāda) of the primacy of the Soma sacrifice itself. And that [restatement] depends upon what has been previously mentioned.

And if there were dependence on the subject matter at hand, there would be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of all [the sacrifices]. But in that case, the statement "He who, knowing thus, performs the *paurṇamāsī*" would be a restatement;
it would not be a restatement based on the connection with a specific time. Thus it has been stated in that very context.

Therefore, it is only those connected with the time that are restated. However, in the case of the word *rājasūya*, because there is no instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) for all the sacrifices [individually], [the name applies to the whole].

There is no harm whatsoever to the name, because the name is indeed bound to its fruit— that action toward which the king feels resentment. Thus, in the *Ṛjuvimalā*, [the commentary] on the fourth [chapter].
The Fourth Chapter [p.
1079] Now, in the *Ṛjuvimalā*:

The first quarter (pāda) of the fifth chapter concerns the sequence [of performance] as characterized by direct scriptural statement (śruti). Regarding this, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) stated that the definition of the "prompter" (prayojaka) and the "non-prompter" (aprayojaka) had already been treated there. He raises an objection to that: "But surely the inquiry into what is for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha) and what is for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha) was also treated there; so why is this now called the 'definition of the prompter and the non-prompter'?"
Regarding the word "vṛtta" (occurrence): its meaning is as follows. If the subject matter of the chapter is stated in brief, then it should be stated thus:

"The occurrence of the subject matter is based on the [acquisition of] materials. If, however, it is stated in detail, then the rules concerning what subserves the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what subserves the person (*puruṣārtha*), as well as the subsidiaries, the primary acts, the results, the injunctions, and the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), must also be stated. Why then is only the instigating and non-instigating [cause] mentioned? For those too are investigated in the fourth [book].

Regarding the phrase "because of its reality," it is said: because this alone is useful in the investigation of sequence (*krama-cintā*). Since only the definition of the "instigator" (*prayojaka*) and the "non-instigator" (*aprayojaka*) is useful in the investigation of sequence, therefore that alone is proclaimed and nothing else, due to the latter's lack of utility. Indeed, only that past event (*vṛtta*) which is conducive to what is about to be explained is proclaimed; for only that which serves as a means (*upāya-bhāva*) toward the meaning that is about to be explained is proclaimed here. Not [anything else].

A *vṛtta* (verse) is not to be designated as such merely by its metrical form (*vṛttatayā*). To the question, "In what way is the consideration of sequence (*krama*) an instrument (*upāya*) characterized by being a motivator (*prayojaka*) or a non-motivator (*aprayojaka*)? he says: "For sequence exists among those things enjoined in a single performance (*ekaprayoga*), not among those that are not so enjoined. Thus, there is a mention of the motivators and non-motivators. For those things to be performed (*prayojya*) by a single performance—that is, by a single injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*)—their execution is implied for the sake of their own accomplishment.
The sequence of these items consists in the performance and expansion of their application; it does not exist for those that are not applied. Therefore, once their status as motivators is known—[P.

Since sequential knowledge arises through the extension of performance, and it fulfills the requirement of being the motivator up to the completion of the ritual application, there exists a relationship based on mutual dependence; thus, it is appropriate to mention both the motivating and non-motivating factors. If the sequence of those things already motivated is being considered, then that sequence is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*). If the sequence is considered at a later time after the things have already been motivated, then that sequence is likewise not something to be enjoined. And therefore—

The point is that if one accepts a sequence based on mere perception, it is not reasonable to have any suspicion regarding those things already perceived. To the question, "How is it that [an action] is not subject to injunction because it occurs after the performance? he says: "For that which is enjoined is performed; there is no injunction for what has not been performed. The meaning of this is: that is called "enjoinable" (vidheya) which is adopted by an injunction for the sake of its own accomplishment. And so it has been stated in the *Śyena* section:
“In the technical terminology of the *tantra*, that which is adopted for the sake of accomplishment is called ‘the object to be enjoined’ (*vidheya*).

Therefore, the state of being an object to be enjoined is pervaded by being put into practice. He demonstrates this: “That which is enjoined is put into practice; however, that which is not put into practice does not even become an object to be enjoined.”

"When the application of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) has ceased, there is the cessation of the pervaded (*vyāpya*), namely *vidheyatva* (the state of being enjoined). He refutes this: "By whom was it said that sequence (*krama*) is enjoined? Now, one might object: "If it is not enjoined, why is it then investigated? For if sequence were enjoined according to the final view (*siddhānta*), then the investigation as to whether sequence is enjoined or not would be appropriate. Anticipating this, [the author] states the nature of the subject of the investigation: [The text continues: ...the nature of the subject of the investigation.

And he says: it is not merely the prescribed extension (*vitāna*) that is being considered here. Rather, the question is whether the performance should be carried out according to the prescribed extension as it has been understood, or without such restriction. That which is the extension of those ritual elements (*padārtha*) at the stage of their performance—that very thing is what is being considered here.
Is the performance to be executed without transgressing this prescribed extension understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means, or is it to be performed without such restriction?

Regarding the term *meneti*: having first formed a *karmadhāraya* compound from *pratipanna* (established) and *vihitavitāna* (provided with a canopy), it is subsequently combined with the word *yathā* to form an *avyayībhāva*.

By stating this, it is demonstrated that in this section (*adhikaraṇa*), the question is being considered whether the entire sequence understood through scripture (*śruti*) and other means is to be respected or not. The sequence of scripture (*śrutikrama*) has been cited merely for the sake of illustration. But how, then—?

In this regard, the intention is as follows: if one respects the sequence merely because it is perceived, then the suspicion that the perception is disregarded is untenable; however, if one accepts them as being objects of injunction (*vidheya*), then—[as stated in the commentary]—of the two things enjoined...

"It is logical that even what is well-known is not subject to injunction. He refutes this: "Because it is devoid of application (*viniyoga*); for there is no comprehension of a prescribed *vitāna* [canopy].

The connection with the preceding is: "Performance is suspected according to how it is understood. The meaning of this is: there is no word whatsoever that denotes a *vitāna*. And that which is not denoted by a word is not applied by the third means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*, i.e., syntactic connection). Nor...

And just as in the case of singularity and so forth, something is made subordinate to the material by means of application (*viniyoga*). Therefore, because it lacks the application belonging to the third and fourth chapters, there is no need to respect the cognition of the *vitāna* (canopy). This same reasoning applies even to the non-prescriptibility of sequence (*krama*), because it is not an auxiliary (*anaṅga*) due to the absence of application—lacking, as it does, any denotation—and because it is not employed by an injunction for the sake of its own accomplishment. It is an invariable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*).

For when the injunction is understood, the notion of "spreading" (*vitāna*) arises; this notion of spreading—occurring when many objects are employed by a single agent—is an inevitable consequence (*nāntarīyaka*), not a direct denotation (*abhidhānika*). He concludes: thinking that "that which is a matter of implication is not the meaning of the injunction," the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains there is no fixed rule (*aniyama*). Therefore, even if sequence were accepted merely on the basis of what is perceived [in practice]...

It has been established that the apprehension of disregard (*anādara*) is indeed justified. Now, however, in the passage “the Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati,” the author of the Bhāṣya has presented this as a prescription of sequence (*krama-vidhāna*). By the statement “because the initiations (*dīkṣā*) are already established,” he [indicates] that there is no other thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

By stating that the scriptural text is intended solely for the prescription of sequence because [the acts] already exist, he asserts that the claim [of the opponent] regarding their non-prescribability contradicts the Bhāṣya. Now he offers a rebuttal: "If this is so"—if the prescription of sequence is improper due to the absence of another thing to be prescribed—then there is indeed another thing to be prescribed here, namely the prescription of a specific agent, as in "these [persons] are to be initiated by him. [This refers to] the Adhvaryu and others...

In this context, the prescription of specific performers such as the Pratiprasthātṛ and others for the *dīkṣās* is also perceived. Now, [one might object]: "But in the case of the passage 'The Adhvaryu [initiates] the Gṛhapati,' even by that..."

There is no other thing to be enjoined, because the office of the *adhvaryu* is already established by the general rule (*codaka*). To this, he says: even regarding the injunction for the *adhvaryu*, there is a restriction;

by the sentence "those who are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*), they are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)," the sacrificers themselves are assigned to the priestly roles. Therefore, as for the *adhvaryu*—
[The objection] has been refuted. However, certain sacrificers (yajamāna) must be initiated by another sacrificer.
In that case, because they perform the duties of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), those very sacrificers are designated by various specific priestly titles such as *adhvaryu* and so forth.

In this regard, there is no rule stating that one who has obtained the designation of *adhvaryu* by performing some portion of the *ādhvaryava* rites must necessarily perform all other *ādhvaryava* duties as well.

Since there must be a restrictive authority (*niyāmaka-pramāṇa*), he says: "Even in the injunction for the Adhvaryu, it is a restriction. By this, it should be understood that the injunctions for the Pratiprasthātṛ and others are also solely for the purpose of restriction. Is this commentary (*bhāṣya*) indeed to be rejected? If one asks whether the scriptural text is intended merely to enjoin the sequence because the initiations (*dīkṣā*) are already established, [he replies: "Is that commentary indeed to be rejected? We say: "No. As for this [use of the suffix] *-ktvā*—

In the case of an injunction regarding the agent, the sequence of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) understood from the verbal expression is useful only for the performance of that [action], not for the injunction of the relationship [between the actions]; thus it is said that "the scriptural statement culminates in that. The meaning of this is as follows: the suffix *-ktvā* does not express a sequence belonging to the performance; rather, it expresses only the identity of the agent. However, the state of being prior in time (*pūrvakālatā*) pertaining to the performance is taken as a qualifying condition (*upādhi*).
[The agent] accepts [the sequence]. Therefore, that which ends in the suffix *ktvā* must be employed first; and that which is employed first, its meaning is understood first.

That which is understood first is performed first, and the other is performed afterwards. Thus, a specific extension of the performance is understood; for, by the force of the hearing of the *ktvā*-suffix, this sequence is understood through the sacrificial arrangement (*vitāna*). Now, why is this rule of sequence not established by the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)?

If it is argued that [the order] does not exist, we say no; for the initiations (*dīkṣā*) are obtained through the force of the archetypal injunction (*codaka*), and the sentence in question is intended to prescribe a specific agent.

If only the initiation were being enjoined, then the performance would also follow the sequence of the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*). For in whatever sequence the originative injunctions are uttered, in that same sequence their meaning is understood; and when the performance follows the sequence of understanding, the sequence [of action] is thereby established. Understanding—

Because the sequence of performance is based on [the order of mention], the initiation (*dīkṣā*) obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) is not understood by means of this specific sentence; thus, in that case, the understanding of sequence does not arise from the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), but rather solely from the hearing of the suffix *-ktvā*. As for the construction of the words: this priority and posteriority, which serves as the condition (*upādhi*) for the suffix *-ktvā* and is understood in the expression or employment of the word during the prescription of the agent—that [priority] pertains to the prescription of the agent for the sake of the performance.

It is utilized for that very purpose, because without understanding the specific details of the expansion, there can be no performance. Since it is the cause for understanding the sequence necessary for performance, the sequential order is what is useful for performance. However, under the view that the agent is enjoined, since the initiations (*dīkṣās*) are not themselves objects of injunction, there is no sequence based on the textual order; rather—

Because of the Vedic text (*śruti*). However, regarding the injunction of the relationship—that is, the injunction of initiation (*dīkṣā*) which is related to the sequence—it serves no purpose for the performance since the sequence is already understood from the very order of the recitation (*pāṭha*); rather, it serves merely to ensure the grammatical correctness of the words. For this reason, the Commentator stated that "the *śruti* is fixed on that," meaning it is fixed on the sequence. Therefore, the words of the Commentary should be construed as follows: "Since initiations have already been established, they [are not mentioned] here in this sentence..."

Because [the order] is subordinate, the sequence is not understood from the textual recitation (*pāṭha*); rather, it is the very hearing of the suffix *-ktvā* that serves to enjoin the sequence—that is to say, it serves to bring about the understanding of the sequence.

The use of the term "injunction" (*vidhāna*) with respect to the sequence is figurative, intended to show that there is a direct scriptural intent (*tātparya*) regarding the sequence just as there is regarding the thing to be enjoined. Therefore, the Sūtrakāra composed the Sūtra *śrutilakṣaṇam ānupūrvyam* (The sequence is characterized by direct scriptural statement) in order to demonstrate that in the passage "The Adhvaryu [instructs] the Brahman," the sequence is indeed scriptural (*śrauta*) and not based on the order of recitation.

The Commentator has shown that [the sequence] is "excellent" (*praṇīta*). Therefore, this investigation arises: Is this sequence in the sentence beginning with "the Adhvaryu" one of *śruti* (direct scriptural statement) or one of *pāṭha* (textual order)? In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) says that, like the sentences concerning the portions of the sacrificial cake (*avadāna*), this is a sequence of textual order. The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*), however, maintains that since the initiations (*dīkṣā*) are already established by the general rule of transfer (*codaka*), there is no sequence of textual order in their original production; therefore, this is not a sequence of textual order.

However, this is merely the sequence of the *śruti* (direct scriptural statement). The purpose of this inquiry is as follows: where the sequence is obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) and there is no direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in a sentence intended for another purpose, there the sequence based on the order of recitation (*pāṭha*) need not be observed. Thus, there are two sections here. In the first section, the discussion concerns whether all sequences are to be observed or not. In the second, however, the discussion is whether this is a sequence based on *śruti* or a sequence based on *pāṭha*. This...

And the third [point] is the avoidance of redundancy. Regarding the second avoidance of the suspicion of redundancy, it should be understood that there is only one interpretation (*varṇaka*), by way of considering whether there is respect for the sequence or disregard for it. The first avoidance, however, was stated according to the opinion of another; for this very reason, another avoidance was stated out of dissatisfaction with it. The third avoidance, moreover, is for the sake of ensuring the pervasion of the subject matter (*viṣaya-vyāpti*). Why, then, [is there mention] of the sequence?

He states here that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the status of being "that which is to be enjoined" (*vidheyatva*) is not admitted at all, such that one could describe a figurative designation of "that which is to be enjoined" based merely on its dependence upon that [enjoined action], as if it were itself enjoined. He says: "The reason stated is simply that what is not employed cannot be that which is to be enjoined. The meaning of this is as follows: for if even that which is not employed were to have the status of being enjoined, then sequence (*krama*) too would be enjoined in an ultimate sense; however, this is not the case. If...

The sequence established by the force of the priority and posteriority understood from the Vedic text (śruti) is indeed "scriptural" (śrauta). If that is so, then the passage, "First he cuts from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest," should also be cited here as an example; for in this case too, the sequence is understood through the force of priority and posteriority expressed by the words "first" (agra) and "then" (atha).

We say: no; we say that this is not the illustrative example. This word *atha* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already understood from the textual recitation (*pāṭha*). This sentence is an injunction for the portions to be cut off (*avadāna*); therefore, the determination of the sequence [of actions] is established by the very order of the recitation of that originative injunction (*utpattivākya*). However, regarding the injunction of a specific agent, the sequence cannot be understood from anything other than the suffix *ktvā*. This is an injunction of the agent, not an injunction of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Therefore...

Since this sequence of initiations (*dīkṣā*) is not characterized by an injunction for its origin, this order cannot be understood from other sources such as textual recitation. Therefore, it is well said that even without the suffix *-ktvā*, another word may function in the sense of "spreading" (*vitāna*); thus, the definition of the instigator and the non-instigator has been proclaimed. Now he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "What, then, is the reason that this necessary rule is observed? For it is not [based on] an injunction..."

The status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatā*) is established for a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) when it is brought about by an injunction characterized by a Vedic mandate (*codanālakṣaṇa-niyoga*). Indeed, that which is not characterized by a Vedic mandate cannot logically have the status of an auxiliary in the accomplishment of an injunction characterized by a Vedic mandate. As it has been said: “And that which is not enjoined does not become an auxiliary. Furthermore, that which is an auxiliary is not necessarily something that must be observed. He states the final conclusion: True, it is not established; true, the status of being an auxiliary is not established.

Precisely because sequence is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*), it is neither performed nor adopted; rather, it is the ritual items (*padārtha*) that are performed, not the sequence. However, when many items are being performed by a single agent, a sequence in the form of an extension (*vitati*) necessarily arises as a matter of course.
If sequence is not an auxiliary, why then is there an observance of its restrictive rule? To this he replies: "But it excludes another sequence that has arisen by implication."

It is said that this [sequence] is not understood through the Śruti and other means; for when one sequence is understood, the understanding of another sequence simply does not arise. And since the performance of those who act with prior reflection follows from such understanding, there is no regard for a fixed order. Therefore, even though independence (*anapekṣatva*) is not being enjoined, it serves a useful purpose and thus there is no fault. The meaning of this is as follows: just as independence is not enjoined...

In that way, it becomes an auxiliary to the performance; thus, even though the sequence is not explicitly enjoined, it nevertheless becomes useful for the performance. Or rather, [the various elements] become auxiliaries to the performance.

There is no fault on the grounds that its performance would be impossible; however, the suspicion of redundancy and so forth has already been raised. First, the suspicion of redundancy was raised; then, once the purpose of the authoritative tradition (āptasmaraṇa) had been demonstrated by the Vṛttikāra, the suspicion that "that [purpose] is its function" was shown and stated in the Bhāṣya. This is also evident from the sense of the matter. Thus, the sequence has first been established as being restricted by the fact that the syllables have no other purpose; now, regarding the function—

The sequence is also regulated by restriction (*rodha*), because the performance of the ritual acts is devoted to that [sequence]. First, the regulation of sequence was described on the basis that the syllables of the *ktvā*-suffix are not intended for anything else, as they are devoted solely to the regulation of sequence. Now, although there are no syllables intended for sequence, nevertheless the sequence is regulated in accordance with the requirement of the action; by whatever temporal connection the action is accomplished, by that much [the sequence is determined].

The sequence of preceding and following must be observed. By virtue of that, the expansion [of the ritual procedure] itself is to be respected, because the performance of ritual elements (padārtha) is for the sake of the task; the ritual elements are performed so that the task may be accomplished. Therefore, it is precisely in accordance with that [task] that the specific time is adopted, and the sequence, which is inseparable from it, must also be observed. Having stated this up to the point of the doubt regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [it is concluded that] the understanding of sequence arises through a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) whose purport is nothing other than that.

Regarding the meaning, however, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its comprehension, because the purpose (*prayojana*) is merely the motive [for action]. The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that even the purpose becomes a cause for the comprehension of sequence by way of making known the difference in the time of performance; and in that regard, examples have already been shown. Is this a sublation of the order of textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)? [As in: "One performs the Agnihotra."

From the reading "he cooks gruel," a different order [of action] results; moreover, it is different according to the sense. In that case, setting aside the order of the text, the order of the sense is accepted.

By saying this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* appears to indicate an objection; however, that is incorrect. The intention [of the objection] is that it is a mere redundancy because it has already been addressed in the section concerning the disruption of the sequence (*kramakopa*). We say: no. This too is presented as a cause for the restriction of sequence, not as something contradictory to anything.
(1) P. 1290 (2) G. *niyamo’vatīrṇaḥ* (3) *kārya*

This too is called "the meaning" (arthākhyam), wherein the cause of the specific time that serves as the reason for the fixed order is demonstrated; it is not [demonstrated] by way of contradiction with anything. However, in the investigation of relative strength and weakness, when there is a contradiction, the greater strength is demonstrated, even if it disrupts the sequence.
Regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*): here, however, this statement is presented solely for the purpose of understanding the nature of the means of knowledge known as "meaning" (*artha*).

Elsewhere there is no fixed rule. Where neither the previously mentioned nor the subsequently mentioned means of knowledge regarding sequence—consisting of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) or "meaning" (*artha*), as well as recitation (*pāṭha*) and so forth—is present, there is indeed no fixed rule, because sequence is understood merely through the inherent nature of the performance. What is an example?

To this he replies: Just as the injunctions regarding auxiliary elements (aṅga) belonging to one Vedic branch (śākhā) are subsumed in another branch—since even in that case there is no restriction of sequence by way of textual recitation (pāṭha)—this [example] is merely a counter-example. Or rather, [the sequence] may be restricted by order, as in cases where the syllables have no intended meaning, such as in "Adhvaryu," and so forth.

Nor is there a contradiction based on the result, as in the case of cooking gruel (*yavāgū*) which is performed according to the sequence [of its ingredients]. In that case, what need is there to mention the restriction of order? For example: "He sacrifices to the *samidhs*, he sacrifices to *tanūnapāt*.
To this, the reply is: even in that case...

1087] There is no fixed rule regarding the order [of recitation]; whatever the sequence of the text, the application [of the ritual] must follow that very same sequence. But is it not the case that the understanding of the sequence depends on the text?

It is rootless; it has no basis whatsoever. Since words are the cause for the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence, if the meaning of a sentence were understood from the sentence alone—wherein the division into words has vanished—then one would conclude that this comprehension of meaning arises from the sentence itself even in the absence of expressive words. But this is not the case. Furthermore, a comprehension that is rootless is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [This is illustrated] in the case of "The front part runs" (*pūrvo dhāvati*).

[Objection: Just as the comprehension of the connection with the *parā* [word] is rooted in a prior relationship, so too would the comprehension of the *aparā* [word] be rooted in a prior relationship; it would not be a comprehension of the related meaning (*anvitāvagati*).

Therefore, one might consider it logical to adopt the sequence here according to one's preference. [Reply: Do not speak thus. Just like the sequence of sentences, the sequence of sentence-meanings is also based solely on the word. Whatever the sequence of the sentence is, such is the sequence of the sentence-meaning; that too is [determined by] the word.

It is indeed the basis. The meaning is that just as the sequence of words is not apprehended without the words themselves, nor is the sequence of *śruti* (Vedic revelation) apprehended without the *śruti*, so too there is no sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) without the meanings themselves. And we maintain that when one thing is apprehended only when another exists—due to their invariable concomitance—the latter is the cause of the former. But [an objection may be raised]: since words are the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, in the absence of the words...

This comprehension of sequence, even as it arises, is intuition (*pratibhā*); it cannot be considered a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It is replied: we shall explain how the word-sound (*śabda*) serves as its instrumental cause. First, that which is recited is first understood; likewise, at the time of performance, it is first remembered, and since performance follows memory, its performance is also first understood.

The performance of that which is understood immediately thereafter (i.e., that which has been remembered) occurs at that very same moment. And in this way, the expansion of the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) is comprehended;
for it is precisely from the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) that the order of performance is understood. And for this very reason, there is study with a fixed order:
(1) [the order] of the constituent elements (*padārtha*), (2) [the order] of the comprehension of sentences (*vākya*).
It serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) except in cases where a specific result (*kāryaviśeṣa*) is perceived; for instance, in the case of cooking porridge,
there the study following a fixed sequence does not serve a visible purpose, since the sequence is understood even from the mere recitation.
For this very reason, when ordinary people have understood the sequence in incense offerings and the like according to the order of recitation, they prohibit any deviation from that sequence.
This has been shown even in the case of rites whose purpose is transcendental (adṛṣṭārtha). For in rites with visible purposes, the sequence is understood through the force of practical necessity;
however, even in rites with transcendental purposes, the reason for the ordinary people’s regard for sequence is that the order of performance is understood by means of the order of recitation.

This has been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya. He concludes: "Therefore, even in this case, it is not logical to assume a different sequence; this is correct. Precisely because the acceptance of a sequence occurs merely through the cognition [of order] based on the mere possibility of a cause for such cognition, for that very reason, in passages such as "the Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati," the establishment of sequence arises from the mere intention (*tātparya*) [of the word], and the establishment of sequence arises from the mere intention of the suffix *-ktvā*. The word *mātra-*...

By the use of the gerund suffix (*ktvā*), both the non-enjoinment and the non-denotation of this sequence are shown. And it is not contradictory for there to be an intended meaning (*tātparya*) even when something is not directly denoted, as is the case with figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). But why, in the absence of being something to be enjoined, is the sequence established by mere intended meaning? To this he says: "For here only the cause is grasped; however, the fact of being denoted as something to be enjoined is not the sole reason for its comprehension.
