That which is accepted through mere understanding [is what is meant].

Only that which serves as a cause for comprehension is accepted here, and not specifically that which is itself enjoined as a cause for comprehension; thus he concludes what was stated regarding the acceptance of sequence by means of mere comprehension:
"Therefore, it was stated in the *Pramāṇaparīkṣā* that a cognition accompanied by a cause (*sanimittā pratipattiḥ*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Consequently, whatever cognition is accompanied by a cause, all of it—whether in determining the sequence or otherwise—is [authoritative] regarding the performance of the Vedic meaning."
It should be understood that the one who has performed the service is the authority. Perception has been explained.
(1) G. Cognition [p.

[This concerns] those [actions] that are simultaneous with the performance. What other cause is there for the determination of sequence? The inquiry begins with this very question. The answer is: we say it is "performance" (*pravṛtti*). For indeed, the cognition of sequence arises through performance as well. Performance is execution; by means of that, the cognition of sequence in the form of what is to be executed arises regarding the subsequent ritual element. Whatever is the sequence of the execution of the preceding ritual element, that same sequence belongs to the execution of the subsequent ritual element.
"Even the order is understood. But how can the order of performance (*pravṛttikrama*) be considered Vedic? The sense is that this [order] is not directly apprehended from the Veda.

The answer is: "Because it relies upon its meaning" (*tadarthāśrayāt*). Since the performance is derived from the Veda by relying on its meaning—the meaning of the Veda—wherein the connection with the first ritual element is first understood, and subsequently the order of the second and subsequent elements follows, there is thus a Vedic character by way of traditional succession (*pāramparyeṇa*).

Therefore, even the *pravṛtti* (the application of a word) serves as a cause for restriction. As for that which was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—namely, "In this way, there is proximity (*pratyāsatti*) to the *pradhāna* (the primary element)"—and likewise, having raised the objection regarding similarity with the *saurya* and other [subsidiary rites], he again stated their dissimilarity; what is the utility of that?

In a single passage, he says: "It is not of much use to determine a strict sequence. For when the order of subsequent items is understood according to the order of prior occurrence, then it is not proper to introduce the proximity of the principal element (*pradhāna-pratyāsatti*). Likewise, as for what was further stated:

"Just as in the case of the *saurya* and other [offerings], the entire section on subsidiary elements (*guṇakāṇḍa*) is distributed to each principal element for the sake of proximity to the principal, so it should be in the case of the *prājāpatya* offerings as well."

Having thus presented a point of similarity, a further point of dissimilarity was stated: "Since the *prājāpatya* offerings are enjoined by a single injunction of performance (*ekaprayogacodanā*), when the simultaneity of subsidiaries and principal acts is established, the sequential entry [of the rites] is appropriate due to human incapacity. However, for the *saurya* and other such offerings, because there is no entry into a single injunction of performance, there is no simultaneous injunction;
therefore, the entire section on qualities (*guṇakāṇḍa*) must be completed for each one individually. This statement of dissimilarity is also not tenable.
There is a utility here: what is called "activity" (*pravṛtti*) is an undertaking that is independent of sequence; and if this undertaking proceeds independently, it is not (1) P.
1293 (2) G. rendered useless by the incapacity of the person (3) G.

For one who thinks that there is a further purpose in [considering] dependence (*apekṣā*), this is the reply: "The proximity to the principal [act], which was understood from the simultaneous injunction (*sahacodanā*), would be impaired by [assuming] inequality; however, in the case of equality, it remains exactly as authorized. The meaning of this is as follows: when it has been demonstrated merely that the understanding of the sequence for performing the second and subsequent items is restricted by the force of the initial commencement, this doubt arises—

It enters [the discussion]: for in the state of active performance (*pravṛttyavasthā*), just as the performance of the first ritual act is understood to be independent of a fixed order, so too is the performance of the second and subsequent acts. And since performance must accord with understanding, it is logical that for all [acts], there is independence from a fixed order.

However, if there were a requirement for a fixed order in the performance of the second and subsequent acts, there would be no purpose [for such a rule], because [the first act] occurs without a fixed order.

Since the sequence of performance is established by the very order of execution, it is not possible to understand the sequence of subsequent items by following the order of engagement with the first item; wishing to dispel this doubt, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has written the following reply: because the injunction for performance prescribes the simultaneous execution of the primary acts along with their subsidiaries, the rule [of sequence] enters only so far as is permitted by human capacity.

It is not considered otherwise. In that regard, if the performance of the subsequent items follows the order of the performance of the first item, then the interval for all of them is indeed equal. Otherwise, if there were a discrepancy—where for one there is excessive proximity and for another excessive distance—then both the proximity and the distance as understood from the injunction for performance (*prayogacodanā*) would be sublated. [This applies when] they are not understood...

For even when proximity (*sannidhāna*) is resorted to, there is indeed a sublation of the proximity as it was previously understood; thus, for the sake of maintaining the injunction regarding performance (*prayoga-codanā*), there is a further requirement for a restriction of order (*krama-niyama*). And since that [injunction] is maintained when the order of procedure (*prāvṛttika-krama*) is accepted, one must admit a restriction of the order of procedure for the purpose of establishing that [maintenance], which in turn serves to establish the proximity of the primary acts (*pradhāna*) as understood from the injunction regarding performance. But if this is so—

Since this fixed order of sequence is based on the proximity to the principal act as understood from the injunction regarding the performance (*prayoga-codanā*), it is not proper to designate it as "pertaining to the commencement" (*prāvṛttika*). To this, he says: "And that rule is preceded by the first commencement," which explains it precisely by that [term]. Now, what is the purpose of the mention of the *Saurya* and other [offerings]? If there were no inclusion within a single performance (*ekaprayoga*), it would not be logical to exclude the entire section on subsidiary elements (*guṇakāṇḍa*) in the case of the *Saurya* and others.

[Page 1091] However, since the *prājāpatya* offerings are enjoined by a single injunction of performance (*ekaprayogacodanā*), it is logical that each individual ritual act (*padārtha*) should be performed separately; thus, the clarity of this distinction is evident. Why, then, is the view of the *saurya* and other sacrifices cited as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? This too has its purpose: it is indeed for the sake of refuting a specific doubt.

"What suspicion, then, is there regarding [the word] *nyasta*? He states that [suspicion]: "If sequence is respected merely by virtue of being understood sequentially, what is the hostility toward the *Saurya* and other [offerings]? The meaning of this is as follows: even in the case of many primary rites such as the *Saurya*, since it is impossible to perform each individual constituent element (*padārtha*) simultaneously due to its connection with all the primary rites, a sequence necessarily arises; and thus, regarding the second and subsequent elements as well...

In that very same way, the sequence is understood; since the sequence is respected merely by virtue of being understood, its sequential order of performance (prāvṛttika-krama) would also follow. Now, because the primary rite together with its subsidiaries is enjoined, in cases such as the Saurya sacrifice, the entire section on subsidiary details (guṇakāṇḍa) would be concluded there, rather than each individual item (padārtha). Thus, it would be the same here as well. Alternatively, if in this case there is the conclusion of each single item, then it would be the same in those cases too; therefore, there is equality with the Saurya and other sacrifices.

Doubt: Now, in order to dispel this doubt, he says—"Indeed, there is no such aversion. Even that which is perceived [in a text] is abandoned because it is not conducive to performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). Although a sequential order (*krama*) belonging to the primary context (*prāvṛttika*) is understood for rites such as the *Saurya* sacrifice—which are enjoined by separate injunctions for performance and thus lack simultaneous execution—nevertheless, since that order does not serve as a means for performance, it is abandoned. [Prājā...]

Among the husbands, however, that which is conducive to the performance [of the rite] is accepted as being in accordance with the primary proximity. He provides an illustration for the abandonment even of what has been understood: "like the phonemic form in words. Just as the phonemic form—the form of each individual phoneme—is abandoned even though it is perceived, because in the state of denotation, the form of each individual phoneme is not a means [to the word-meaning]; or "like unity among the planets. As, for example:
The statement "he cleanses the cup" involves a unity that is not a means [to the end]. For number becomes a means only by way of delimiting the instrument;

and once the instrument called the "cup" has been delimited as the means for accomplishing the goal, there is no further requirement for that number. This is like the case of the two oblations, as in:
"He whose both oblations meet with ruin..."
Thus, that which possesses both [natures] and is not a means is abandoned; yet, by this much alone, the abandonment of what is not a means is not observed.
By this much alone, the abandonment of even that which is suitable—that is, even that which is a means—is logically established. He concludes:
(1) from the perspective of its operation, and (2) from the perspective of being expressive or non-expressive.

Therefore, that which is desired is attended to; even that which has been undertaken is to be disregarded if it is undesired. But if this is so, does it not follow that the undertaking becomes useless and devoid of purpose? He dispels this mere objection, asking: "By whom was it said..."

The meaningfulness of the performance (*pratipatti*) consists in its possessing a purpose (*prayojanavattva*). Meaningful performance itself is the cause of meaningfulness, not mere performance; for performance devoid of that [meaningfulness] is devoid of purpose. Thus it is well said that [performance] culminates in mere performance. In this section, the summary of the meaning is as follows: when the first item has been performed in an indefinite order, then regarding the second item, once again the primary—

The dependence on a sequence exists for the sake of favoring proximity (*pratyāsatti*). In that regard, whatever sequence was employed when the first ritual act was performed, that very same sequence is adopted; for when that [sequence] is adopted, it favors the proximity to the primary act as it has been understood. [This is established] by position (*sthāna*) due to its connection with the origin. Here, the Commentator [Śabara], because the sequence of the recitation (*samāmnāya*) is not observed in cases such as the *triṇava* sacrifices—

Thinking that what exists [in the Veda] is not the actual subject matter [of the discussion], this was cited; that is, thinking it to be beyond the scope [of the inquiry], this was cited: "He sacrifices the animals together.
Here, the construction is as follows: first, the Commentator indeed cited the example, "One desiring vigor should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the Triṇava-stoma.
When the *stoma* is increased, should the verses being brought in be employed in an indefinite order, or according to the order of their recitation (*samāmnāya*)?

Having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that because there is no sequential order in the recitation of the injunctive texts for the *triṇava* and other such chants, there would be no fixed rule regarding their application, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) was established that they must be employed according to the sequence of their position; it was stated therein: "In this case, the rule of sequence is determined by the order of the recitation in the collection of mantras (*mantrasamāmnāya*)."

And considering that this fault—namely, that there is no distinction based on the order of recitation—does not apply to the order of position, [the author states]: "He sacrifices the animals together" (1). P.

Thus another example has been provided. Here, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) has cited this: "He sacrifices the animals together" (*saha paśūn ālabhate*). To the question "Having done what?", he says: "By means of the twenty-seven-fold [stoma] for one desiring vigor" (*triṇavenojaskāmam*), considering that this is not within the scope of the order of position (*sthānakrama*). Why does he consider it outside the scope? He says: because the order of recitation (*pāthakrama*)—which exists according to the deluded others but is not observed in the case of the twenty-seven-fold [stomas] and so forth—is absent from the *samāmnāya* (the traditional liturgical collection).

This was stated by those who consider that [the order of recitation] is not the domain of the mantra, thinking that because the order of recitation is not observed in injunctions such as "triṇava" and so forth, this is not a matter for the order of recitation. In reality, however, this *is* the domain of the order of recitation—whether it be the order of the ritual injunction (*vidhi-pāṭhakrama*) or the order of the mantra (*mantra-pāṭhakrama*); in every respect, this is simply the order of recitation.

Thinking that this is not the subject matter of the sequence of positions (*sthānakrama*), the author of the *Bhāṣya* cited another example. In this example, having taken up a matter established in another section (*adhikaraṇa*), it is settled that by the statement "he sacrifices the animals together" (*saha paśūn ālabhate*), simultaneity is enjoined in place of the *savanīya*. Now, the question is considered: what is the rule for the sequence? Is the very order of performance (*pravṛtti*) the cause here as well?

Since the modifications of Soma are preceded by the Soma sacrifice itself, there is a specific sequence of activity regarding the Soma: first the Agniṣomīya, immediately after that the Savanīya, and immediately after that the Anūbandhya. The inquiry here is whether this very sequence is the cause for determining the order in this case as well, or whether there is another cause known as "position" (sthāna). In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) argues that if one does not accept the sequence of activity when such a sequence is inevitable, [then the rule would fail].

It is thought that because [the order] occurs within another ritual procedure (*prayoga*), the restriction follows from the previously known textual recitation (*pāṭha*) alone. However, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) has stated that since the position (*sthāna*) is not sublated by the statement of simultaneity (*sahavacana*), it is logical that the *savanīya* animal sacrifice be performed first.
The meaning of this is as follows: by the statement "one sacrifices the animals together," the slaughter of all of them is enjoined at the position of the *savanīya*.

The place for the *savanīya* [offering] is not sublated; its timing is subsequent to the drawing of the *āśvina* cup. If the *agnīṣomīya* were performed at that time, there would be a sublation of the scripturally prescribed time. Therefore, the *savanīya* alone should be offered first.
(1) The commencement of the Soma sacrifice.

[Page 1094] If this is so, what is the status of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and the Anubandhya animal sacrifice? How can there be a sequence of earlier and later times? The opponent asks this with the underlying intention of a point that will be stated later. But the proponent, as if not understanding the opponent's intention, says: "What is the use of this introduction?"

By what reasoning? Or rather, it is improper to say that there is a sublation by time as there is by place; for in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the priority of the Agniṣomīya over the Anūbandhyā has already been established. Therefore, to maintain consistency with that, the Agniṣomīya itself must be performed first. If this is so, then it ought to occur even before the Savanīya, because in the archetype, [the Agniṣomīya] is indeed prior even to the Savanīya.

It is argued that the time for the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice] is thus understood. This is not so, because the time for the Savanīya [sacrifice] has been specifically prescribed. By the rule, "Having taken the Āśvina cup," the time for the Savanīya is prescribed; whereas the time for the Agniṣomīya is understood through cumulative observation (*pracaya*). When many animals are prescribed at different times, their relative sequence—whether earlier or later—is understood. He asks: what follows from this? [The answer is: because it serves the purpose of a prescription.

That which is prescribed (*vihita*) is stronger than accumulation (*pracaya*). For accumulation serves the purpose of the prescription; it is not that accumulation itself is being prescribed. Therefore, that which is prescribed is stronger. If the performance were to be determined by the order of position (*sthānakrama*) by overriding the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), then this would merely be a consideration of relative strength (*balābala*) and not the presentation of a different means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is not so; for once the status as a means of valid cognition is established, there is the question of relative strength and weakness.

This is logical: "And the sequence of the subsidiaries follows the sequence of the principals. In this section, the sequence of the subsidiaries is established according to the sequence of the principals. In that regard, as for those modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) which are recited in a specific order, because they are governed by the injunctions of their primary rites (*pradhāna*), [the sequence of] the transferred elements (*ātideśika*)—

1095] Since the sequence of the auxiliary rites follows precisely the sequence of the primary injunctions and their recitation, those [auxiliaries] are not examples here for now. As for those which...

The subsidiaries (aṅgas) are taught in relation to those very [primary rites], or else their sequence is determined solely by the order of recitation (pāṭhakrama). By this same logic, the archetypal rites (prakṛtis) are not examples here. Rather, those very ectype rites (vikṛtis) that are enjoined simultaneously are the examples; because there is no order of recitation for their primary rites, the restriction of the sequence of subsidiaries cannot be established through the order of recitation. Thus he says: "Where there is a simultaneous injunction..."

Regarding the statement "The two Sarasvatīs are [the deities]," what is the authority for a fixed order among the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) therein—is it a mandatory sequence, or may they be employed as one pleases?
The intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) is that because the scripture is recited simultaneously (*tantra*), no sequential order is perceived.
Since there is no sequential order in the primary injunction (*pradhāna-codanā*), no sequential order is perceived even for the subsidiaries included within it. This being the position reached—

It is argued that since the sequence is observed in the primary [acts], it is logical that the sequence is also understood to apply to the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), because the two *yājyā* verses possess a sequence; thus, the sequence of the two primary acts is perceived.

And since the primary acts have a certain order, it is appropriate that their subsidiaries also follow that same order. What will result from this? In this way, there will be only as much separation as is permitted. For if there were no fixed rule, there would be a transgression of what has been permitted.

It may be so; therefore, a restriction is appropriate. The mention of the order of the principal [acts] based on the *yājyā* verses here is merely out of friendliness. Even in the case of the alternative of no restriction, the performance must follow the order of the principal [acts], because in the archetype (*prakṛti*) it is established by its own word. Now, the conflict between the order of recitation (*pāṭha*) and the order of the principal is considered. In that regard, the principal—

Since the subsidiaries are for the sake of the primary, the order of the primary alone is more powerful; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). For the primary is indeed the principal, and [the subsidiaries] must conform to the primary.

This is the non-assumption of auxiliary limbs (*cāṅgākalpanā*). Therefore, whatever sequence follows from the primary act (*pradhāna*) is the stronger one. And thus, there is favor toward the injunction for performance (*prayogacodanā*) due to proximity; for the injunction for performance teaches simultaneous execution. In that regard, it permits only as much intervention as occurs solely due to human incapacity, and nothing else. It permits only such intervention as has been authorized.

In accepting [this], she becomes favored. And in accepting the order of the principal [rites], there is only as much an intervention as is permitted; otherwise, an intervention by the subsidiary parts belonging to another would result. To this it is replied: it is not proper to subvert what has been perceived. Furthermore, since the order of the subsidiaries is understood from the independent textual recitation (pāṭha), it is not proper to subvert it on account of something else. For it is indeed internal (antaraṅga).

The order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is stronger because it is understood independently and because it arises prior to the order of principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), which is extrinsic to it. [Objection: But was it not stated that the order of principal acts is more powerful due to its proximity (*pratyāsatti*) and its predominance (*prādhānya*)? This is a reminder of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). True, it was so stated; however, that statement is incorrect. Why is it incorrect? Because the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) grasps things exactly as they are perceived, and not according to the order of performance.

The understanding of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) arises from the [Vedic] word. And therein, the subsidiaries, whose sequence is already established by their own textual recitation (*pāṭha*), are grasped by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*).

How is this so? It is said: "Being a subsidiary, it is grasped by the injunction of performance. Having perceived those [subsidiaries] as brought forth, the injunction of performance brings them together [into a single performance].

By this passage [it is shown that] proximity is according to comprehension; comprehension of the subsidiaries does not arise from proximity alone. Therefore, it is logical that the textual recitation (*pāṭha*) is more powerful. And it has been stated: "Because it is its own word" (*svaśabdatvāt*). What is meant by this? By being its own word, the internal nature (*antaraṅgatā*) of the textual recitation is asserted.

[Page 1097] "But in case of conflict, it should be by the mantra. When there is a doubt as to which is more authoritative when there is a conflict between the order of recitation of the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa—namely, if the mantra is more authoritative, then the performance follows the order of the mantra; but if the Brāhmaṇa is more authoritative, then the performance follows the order of the Brāhmaṇa.

[The opponent argues: "In that case, there is indeed no fixed rule for both [the mantra and the ritual action], because both consist merely of the nature of recitation. To this, it is replied: The order of the mantra is more authoritative. Why? Because the recitation has no other purpose [than application] and because mantras are intended to be employed. The meaning of this is: mantras are recited solely for the sake of being employed. Therefore, whatever their order of recitation is, that very order is understood to be for the sake of employment. Consequently, those [mantras] which possess such an order...

The mantras are handed down in a specific sequence; therefore, they must be employed in that very order. Since it is traditionally taught that "the ritual action must be performed with the mantras," the actions themselves must also be performed in that same sequence. Now, one might object: even in the Brāhmaṇa portion, the order of recitation is intended solely for the purpose of performance and has no other aim. As for the statement that the purpose [of the Brāhmaṇa] is the origination of the ritual action—that is the purpose of the *vākya* (the explanatory prose passage), not of the *pāṭhakrama* (the order of recitation).

It is said: that sequence of recitation has the purpose of [establishing] the origin [of the mantra], not the purpose of its performance; this is what is meant, because the sentences of the *brāhmaṇa* are not to be performed. In the case of a mantra, however, the sequence is also for the purpose of performance, and thus it possesses greater force. This is what is being stated: the sequence of recitation found in mantras is perceived directly as pertaining to the mantra to be performed; the sequence of the *brāhmaṇa* recitation, on the other hand, does not directly pertain to that which is to be performed.

However, because the sequence is observed in the injunction (*vidhi*), a sequence must also be inferred for that which is enjoined (*vidheya*); yet, this [inferred sequence] finds no footing when it contradicts a sequence already established by the mantras.
(1) P. 1298 (2) Of the sentence (*vākya*).

[Page 1098] Regarding that statement, "in the modification" (*vikṛti*): Is the order in the modification according to the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), or is it according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)—namely, that just as the order of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is determined in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it should be employed in the modification in exactly the same way? What is the correct view? It is the latter, because it serves the purpose of practical performance.

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that since the application of an unextended sequence is untenable, and since the application is understood in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the performance must be according to the modification. Even though another sequence is understood in a different performance within the archetype (prakṛti), nevertheless, here in the performance enjoined by the modification, it is proper to perform according to the modification by means of the primary sequence itself. And it is precisely by this distinction that [the rule applies] to the archetype.

The commencement of a new section [of the discussion] follows from the reason "because it is its own word" (*svaśabdatvāt*). The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: an injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavacana*) belonging to a modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta*) cannot set aside a performance whose sequence is already known. Even if it is a different performance, since there is no difference in the items to be performed (*prayojya*), when there is a requirement for a sequence, that very sequence which was known in the other performance remains present in the mind; thus, there is no room for the postulation of a different sequence.

For the application of a sequence that has already been determined is like that of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). Just as the auxiliaries, having been determined in the archetype (*prakṛti*), are employed in the ectype (*vikṛti*), so too is the sequence. For when a thing is not yet known, one must everywhere postulate further reasons in order to ascertain its essential nature; this is not the case once it is known. Thus says the author of the *Vārttika* (verse): "As long as the object of knowledge is unknown or doubtful, [so long must it be investigated]..."

"It is measured; once it has been cognized, the eagerness of the cognizers to cognize is frustrated. Therefore, just as in the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too in the case of the modification (*vikṛti*), there is the performance of the constituent parts (*aṅga*).
(1) P. 1299 (2) G. *vākyasya*

[Page 1099] *Vikṛti* (the modified sacrifice). There is a deliberation regarding the time of performance being either immediate (*sadyaskāla*) or two days later (*dvayahakāla*). One objects: "What connection does this have with the deliberation on sequence (*krama*)? We reply: It is for the sake of establishing the sequence; otherwise, if the performance were immediate, the sequence would be different.

And otherwise, there would be the state of having two days. Therefore, the investigation is appropriate. In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that there is the state of having two days, as in the case of the archetype (prakṛti), because the scriptural mention of the *savana* (pressing) is without distinction even on another day. For in those cases where two [options] cannot coexist, the rule derived from extended application (*atideśika*) is set aside by the rule derived from direct injunction (*auṣadeśika*). But here, since both are possible, the state of having two days belongs to the archetypal form.

It is accepted that the modified (*vaikṛtī*) time-periods, such as the morning (*prāhṇa*) and so forth, apply even when [the rite] occurs on another day, because the terms "morning" and so on are used without distinction for the morning and other periods. However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) maintains that because another time is heard in the scripture, it does not depend upon the archetypal (*prākṛta*) time, and thus considers it to be of immediate performance (*sadyaskālatā*).
The meaning of this is as follows: everywhere, the modified instruction pertains to the ritual action (*kārya*), and the action is to be inferred from the instruction. In that regard—

Since the temporal requirement established by the instruction of two days (*dvayahā*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*) applies precisely there, in the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well, another time is prescribed rather than a modification of the sub-divisions of the day. This is because the modification of the sub-divisions of the day was not established in the archetype. Consequently, since the archetypal function is accomplished by the ectype’s own time alone, there is no further dependence on the archetypal time; thus, the state of being performed on the same day (*sadyaskālatā*) is indeed appropriate. Now, even so, how is its connection with a single day established?

He says that [the conclusion] is obtained: the *savanas* are understood through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) to be connected exclusively with a single-day sacrifice (*ekāha*); it is not reasonable to assume they depend on other days in the absence of a cause. The meaning of this is as follows: the morning and other parts (*prāhṇa*, etc. are constituent parts of the day; they culminate by implying the day as their whole (*avayavin*). And since that requirement is satisfied by the implication of a single-day sacrifice alone, there is no implication of other days.
By the force of logic, it is stated that when "forenoon" and so forth are heard in sequence, they are understood as occurring on the same day; thus, the observation has been explained.

Because the primary time for the constituent parts [of the ritual] has been established, why would there be displacement (*utkarṣa*) or non-displacement (*apakarṣa*) when neither displacement nor non-displacement is explicitly heard in the scriptural text? With this, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The meaning is: since everything that is understood through words is based on injunctions (*codanā*), why should there be displacement or non-displacement of those things which are not explicitly heard? It is true that the displacement or non-displacement of a scripturally stated element is indeed heard. However...
"Without again making [the subsequent] lower [or the preceding] upper"—if this is not understood, by what could the performance obtained through the sequence be prevented?

This is the meaning: if it were heard that the subsequent performance alone is to be displaced, setting aside the rest, then there would be the displacement of that alone. But when only the displacement itself is heard, then, by the force of the sequence previously understood, the subsequent [elements]—

These [elements] are subject to displacement (*utkarṣa*). For it is understood from the archetype (*prakṛti*) that when they are displaced, they must be performed after having established the intended ritual object; therefore, to preserve the sequence, there must be a displacement of those subsequent elements as well. Likewise, in the case of anticipation (*apakarṣa*), if it were heard that "the ritual object to be anticipated must be performed without even having performed the preceding one," then it could have been anticipated in isolation. But this is not the case.
Therefore, even that which is below must be performed in order to favor the established sequence; having done that, it is considered as having been performed in its original context (*prakṛti*).

Thus, what will the "unheard-of" nature (*aśrutatva*) accomplish here in this statement regarding displacement (*utkarṣa*)? It is incapable of preventing either displacement or downward displacement (*apakarṣa*), because displacement is established from the sequence itself. If it is argued that displacement occurs solely from the explicit mention (*śravaṇa*), then there would indeed be the state of being unheard-of.
Therefore, it is rightly said: "Because of the connection starting from that, there would be an extraction ending with that.
1101] Regarding those whose time is determined by the procedure (*pravṛtti*): should the ritual elements such as the ornaments be performed after the *praiṣa* (direction), or...

"They are understood from the text itself to belong to the Soma sacrifice. This is its meaning: those items belonging to the *pauroḍāśika* (cake-offering) section which follow the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), and those which precede the decoration (*alaṅkaraṇa*)—beginning with the decoration and occurring prior to it—are they to be performed at the time following the command for pouring out, namely, "Pour out the *savanīya* cakes"? For the pouring out must indeed be performed immediately after the command for pouring out. But in that case...

Regarding the *prakṛti* (archetype) sacrifice: should those rites seen as occurring immediately after it—beginning with *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) and ending before *alaṅkaraṇa* (consecration)—also be performed? For while *alaṅkaraṇa* is explicitly enjoined by a scriptural statement to take place at the time following the *bahiṣpavamāna*, should the Soma-related items (*saumika*) such as the *pracaraṇī-homa* and others, which are understood through their textual recitation (*pāṭha*), also be performed? And since the Soma-related items have a fixed sequence established by their textual recitation (*pāṭha*).

In that case, by the force of the scriptural statement (*vacana*), another item enters into the middle. There, as long as it is based on a scriptural statement, it is "stated" (*vācanika*); thus, only the sprinkling (*nirvāpa*) must be performed in the middle. After that, the *pracaraṇī-homa* and so forth [follow]. Thus, in both ways, it is simply the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that there is no fixed rule (*aniyama*), it is said in reply: "The acts preceding the decoration (*alaṅkaraṇa*) must be performed. Why? Because they are not otherwise determined...

For the duty to act is determined by the textual recitation (*pāṭha*). That performance which is not already known is determined by the recitation; however, the recitation does not obstruct that whose duty to act is already known. For it is already known from the archetype (*prakṛti*) that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth must be performed immediately after the pouring out (*nirvāpa*); therefore, that alone is to be done. Thus, from the command (*praiṣa*), the duty to perform the purpose of the command is understood. But when that has been performed, [the duties] occurring immediately thereafter [are likewise established].
These must be performed. From this point onward, however, there is a restriction based on the textual recitation.

But because there is no connection, it remains exactly as it was. Regarding the statement, "During the initiations, one cuts the sacrificial post (yūpa)," an anticipation is heard; this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to remove the doubt that [the entire sequence] ends with that [act]. Since it is understood from the text that the anticipation is restricted to whatever is explicitly stated—due to the absence of a mutual connection—the doubt might arise that when one thing is anticipated, another must also be anticipated by anticipation. This section is for the purpose of removing such a doubt.

This is the topic under consideration. Since the sequence is already established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the principles of "beginning with that" (*tadādi*) and "ending with that" (*tadanta*) apply to the displacement (*utkarṣa*) or non-displacement (*apakarṣa*) of archetypal elements.
However, in this case, the sequence has not yet been determined; therefore, this is not the domain of those principles.
Furthermore, this concerns a secondary application (*prāsaṅgika*). It has been stated that since this same reason applies even to what is secondary, one should not displace what is secondary.

The meaning of this is as follows: This absence of a connection to a sequence, due to the fact that no sequence has been established—which serves as the reason for setting aside the principle of "beginning with that and ending with that"—is equally applicable to the incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) case as well, because it is impossible to establish a sequence between the two *pauroḍāśika* offerings and the *āparāgnika* oblations on the one hand, and the *sānnāyya* after-offerings (*anūyāja*) on the other. By what distinction, then, is a new section (*adhikaraṇa*) commenced? It is said: [the distinction lies in] the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)— [The remainder of the text follows.]

The proponent maintains that there is a connection [of sequence] because the order is determined for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) in their original context and for the two oblations in the western fire (*āparāgnika*). However, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows:
although the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the after-offerings remains the same, there is no determination of sequence based on a difference in the nature of the related elements.

Likewise regarding the *apūrva*: since the connection with the sequence is established by its recitation on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that it must be brought down to the end of that [full moon ritual]. Because the order of recitation is respected on the full moon day, [the altar] whose sequence is already fixed—the *vedi*—[is to be used] on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

Because of this [subsequent] displacement (*pratikarṣa*), one considers there to be a displacement even for those [elements] belonging to the later [period]. However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*), not considering the New Moon sacrifice (*āmāvāsya*) to have the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) as its archetype, stated that the sequence of the remaining elements is restricted only after the displacement has occurred;

thus, he maintained that the displacement extends as far as the scriptural statement [itself] goes. For, only when the relationship of archetype and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) exists, can the meaning of the scripture be determined through prior deliberation.

The determination of the meaning of the scripture is not independent. Therefore, one should not describe the meaning of the scripture for the new-moon sacrifice (amāvāsyā) by depending on the arrangement of the sequence [prescribed] for the full-moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī). Consequently, only as much as the altar (vedi) is deferred is deferred to the new-moon sacrifice; and after that time, there is a fixed rule of sequence therein. Furthermore, the contradiction of purpose here consists in the fact that the oblations (havis) would be reduced to ashes.

[The discussion concerns] the displacement [of the *sāntapanīyā*]. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), thinking that "once the fire has been drawn out for the sake of another [rite], the *agnihotra* should not be offered except by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*)," stated the displacement. In this section (*adhikaraṇa*), regarding the two subsidiary elements—the time and the drawing out of the fire—which [is primary]?

It is considered that renunciation is appropriate. When the fire has been drawn out for the sake of the *sāntapanīyā* sacrifice, if—due to the force of some divine or human obstacle—the *sāntapanīyā* is postponed, the person still possesses the entitlement (*adhikāra*) regarding the evening *agnihotra*, because the condition of being alive, which qualifies the agent, remains present. Now, it may be argued that according to the section concerning animals (*tiryagadhikaraṇa*), entitlement belongs only to one capable of performing all the constituent parts of the rite.

(1) P. 1307 (2) R. It has been stated that this refers to the sequence of ritual activity (*pravṛttikrama*). Furthermore, one who has extracted the fire for the sake of the *Sāntapanīyā* sacrifice, but has not yet performed the *Sāntapanīyā*, does not extract the fire again for the sake of the *Agnihotra*.

[The opponent argues: "One is unable to bring it back [into the Gārhapatya fire]. For when the ritual action has ceased, the Āhavanīya fire enters the Gārhapatya fire by means of its extraordinary (alaukika) nature, and not otherwise. And if it has not entered, how could it be drawn out? Therefore, because of the impossibility of bringing about the drawing out of the fire (agnyuddharaṇa), there is no possibility of eligibility.
[The author] replies: You have spoken the truth, that eligibility belongs only to one who is capable. However, it is precisely this capacity that must be considered here: what is it?

Regarding the word "tat" (that): in this context, apart from the state of having maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgnitva*), there is no other capacity for the extraction and re-establishment of the fires. Since the person here possesses the state of having maintained the sacred fires, there is the capacity for the extraction and re-establishment of the fires; thus, there is no loss of entitlement (*adhikāra*). We shall demonstrate this more precisely in the very section concerning "all capacities" (*sarvaśakti-adhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, even when the entitlement remains intact, performance may take place even with the omission of certain auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).

This being established, it is considered: should the *agnihotra* be offered at that very time, setting aside the extraction of the fire (*uddharaṇa*) for the sake of conforming to the [prescribed] time; or rather, having performed the *sāntapanīyā* on the second day, and having again extracted the fire, should the *agnihotra* be offered while merely abandoning the specific time?

In this deliberation, since time is a subordinate element of the performance (*prayoga*), it stands in the relationship of a subordinate to a subordinate (*aṅgāṅgabhūtatva*). Therefore, it is the extraction itself, as a subordinate element, that must be accommodated here. Not [the time].

And when the fire has been drawn out for the sake of another rite, it is proper to perform the *agnihotra* at that very same time; for the *agnihotra* is not incidental [to the other rite]. If, however, the time were to be accommodated here, then—because of its being prescribed within the framework of the main ritual—the *agnihotra* would become like the *niśīṣṭi* sacrifice, and thus it would have to take place when the fire has already been drawn out for another purpose. But this is not the case. Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that its postponement (*utkarṣa*) alone is logical.

The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin), however, considers that there is no postponement (anutkarṣa) because time is merely a causal condition (nimitta). This is what is meant: time is of the nature of a causal condition;

in its absence, there is no entitlement (adhikāra) at all to perform the rite. Therefore, the Agnihotra should not be offered at another time. But in the case of the non-extraction of the fires (agnyuddharaṇa), since the entitlement does not cease, it is logical that the offering should be made; thus, no postponement is appropriate. How, then, is time a causal condition? For [time] is merely an auxiliary (aṅga).

Time has been mentioned. The answer is: because [the ritual] is performed when that [time] exists, and not because it is a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), since time cannot be brought about by a person. When time itself occurs, then the performance must be carried out;

it is in this sense alone that time is said to be the occasion (*nimitta*), and not as a qualification of the qualified person, as is the case with [conditions such as] "difference" (*bheda*) and so forth. When it occurs of its own accord—

At that time, because at another time the person lacks the capacity to perform the ritual action, there is no entitlement (*anadhikāra*). However, at another time, because he has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), he possesses the capacity for the extraction of the fires; thus, his entitlement is not lost. Therefore, when the occasion arises...
The sense is that it must be contingent; thus, its incidental nature is established. Therefore, there is no displacement (*anutkarṣa*).

Regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* as well: because of the conflict with the time for the subsidiary parts of the *ṣoḍaśin* and because displacement occurs only occasionally, the proponent of the prima facie view maintains that there is no displacement. [As stated: "He draws it after the *ukthya*s."

By this statement, the performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* after the *ukthya*s is enjoined. Even when the *ukthya*s are postponed, there is no loss of the time [for the *ṣoḍaśin*], just as the "conch-hour" remains even in the absence of the conch itself. At most, in the case of non-postponement, that sequence which is perceived between the *ṣoḍaśin* and the *ukthya*s would be abandoned.

And it is indeed proper to abandon [the sequence], because if the *ukthya* were postponed, it would entail the sublation of the time prescribed for the *stotra* which is an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *ṣoḍaśin*. Nor is the injunction regarding the time of the "arrival of the night" (*samayādhyuṣitakāla*) an absolutely impossible matter, since the postponement of the *ukthya* occurs only occasionally. For when there is no postponement of the *ukthya*, everything remains perfectly consistent; and since the sublation of the sequence of a non-integral part (*anaṅga*) is more reasonable than the sublation of the sequence of an integral part (*aṅga*).

The proponent of the final conclusion (rāddhāntavādī), however, has stated that because the transgression of a scriptural injunction is inevitable, it is better to transgress a subsidiary injunction; thus he argued for the displacement (utkarṣa). Even though the sequence is not a primary constituent (anaṅga), nevertheless, the sequence is not thereby rendered non-scriptural. Consequently, since both are indeed scriptural matters, the displacement of the *ṣoḍaśin* is appropriate on the grounds that it is better to transgress a subsidiary scriptural injunction.
Thus ends the first quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*, the commentary composed by Śālikanātha Miśra.
(1) G. *utkṛṣṭa*, that is to say, in the *prāsaṅgika* [texts],
the *Ṛjuvimalā*.

Now begins the second section concerning the combination [of subsidiaries]. But surely, since the sequence is fixed by the order of performance (*pravṛtti*), what is meant by this "the whole for each one"?

By this, he raises an objection regarding the commencement of another topical discussion (*adhikaraṇa*). It was shown that there is no fixed sequence by way of performance when relying upon the method of following the items one by one (*padārthānusamaya*).

"Furthermore, it is not logical to establish the performance according to the sequence of individual items (padārthānusamaya). It is replied: "When this section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] is established, then that [is so]. The meaning is that, having relied upon the performance according to the sequence of individual items—which is already established in this very section—by means of reasoning therein through a forward-looking perspective (*anāgatāvekṣaṇa*), the order of procedure (*pravṛttikrama*) is now considered.
Here, however, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers that even by performing all the items together, simultaneity (*sahatva*) is indeed possible.
"Why is a temporal separation (*kālavyavadhāna*) postulated? It is established that it is authorized in this very way. The meaning of this is as follows:

even if the method of sequential performance (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) is adopted, nevertheless, because the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) that provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*) are performed collectively (*tantra*), the simultaneous performance of all the animals is indeed possible. Therefore, why is a temporal separation postulated? For each individual animal [is connected] with its own respective auxiliaries.

It should be employed. In that regard, due to human incapacity, whatever interval of time occurs is permitted by the injunction for performance (*prayoga-vidhi*). In this context, if each individual ritual act (*padārtha*) is performed even with respect to another animal, then an interval of time occurs that was not permitted.

Therefore, the entire section on qualities (*guṇakāṇḍa*) must be applied to each individual [action]. However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*) maintains that because of the injunction for simultaneity, the simultaneous performance of each ritual act (*padārtha*) is understood; this cannot be abandoned. Therefore, in accordance with that [injunction], [the qualities must be applied to each act].

He stated that there is permission for an interval [between actions], but not by abandoning that [succession]; thus he explained the *padārthānusamaya* (performance according to individual items). The meaning of this is as follows:

since it is enjoined that all the animals, along with their subsidiaries (*aṅga*), must be performed together, each and every subsidiary must be performed in unison. Among those, the subsidiaries that provide immediate assistance (*sannipatyopakāraka*) must be performed separately because their functions are seen to be distinct. In that regard, even with respect to a single item...

When [the performance] is carried out according to all the animal sacrifices (*paśu*), it culminates in the execution of those constituent elements (*padārtha*). In this manner, as long as a temporal interval occurs, the injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) is indeed permitted, and nothing else. Therefore, the sequential performance of the constituent elements (*padārthānusamaya*) alone is logical. Or rather, there is a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇāntara*) intended to demonstrate the abandonment of the understanding of simultaneity—due to the contradiction with the task—just as in the case of the *pātha* (recitation). As for that which...

Thinking that "the ritual action must indeed be performed according to the scriptures, because the establishment of the object of knowledge (prameya) depends upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)," he maintains that there is a sequential performance of the constituent elements (padārtha-anusamaya) based on the force of the scriptural mention of simultaneity; it was stated that another topical section (adhikaraṇa) is introduced to refute this. For when a ritual action has been determined and is subsequently contradicted [by a different order], since the performance is for the sake of accomplishing that action, it is logical that the sequence of the sections (kāṇḍānusamaya) should prevail in accordance with the action. This is just as the sequence of recitation (pāṭhakrama) serves the purpose of the action.

Just as that which is contradictory is abandoned, so too is simultaneity (*sahatva*). Regarding the *muṣṭi-kapāla-avadāna*: in this section, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), considering the purpose of the scripture to have been fulfilled even by means of an unenclosed handful (*muṣṭi*) and so forth, has asserted the sequential performance of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*). For if each individual handful were performed in sequence, then [the rule] "four... [would apply].
He pours out handfuls.

Thus, the purpose of the scripture is indeed fulfilled. By the injunction of performance together (*sahatvacodanā*), it follows that everything must be performed together. And since everything is thus obtained as being to be performed together, it is logical that there should be a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) of all that has been so obtained—namely, the sequential performance of the handfuls (*muṣṭi*) and so forth. However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*) maintains that the determination of ritual elements (*padārtha*) is based on the injunction (*codanā*).

Furthermore, in the case of Vedic matters, [the sequence] is not determined by other means of knowledge as it is in worldly affairs. This single scripture contains both the injunctions, "He offers four handfuls" and "He cuts off twice from the oblation.
Therefore, he considers that following the sequence of the scriptural meaning is the proper course.

The meaning of this is as follows: that which is indeed prescribed in the scripture (*śāstra*) as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) must be performed; and that which is to be performed must be performed together (*saha*); and that which is to be performed together must be followed in sequence (*anusametavya*). Furthermore, the understanding of the auxiliaries in Vedic matters arises from the scripture and not from other means of knowledge. Since the scripture prescribes the offering of four handfuls (*caturmuṣṭi-nirvāpa*), it establishes that only that which is repeated possesses the status of an auxiliary; therefore, there is sequence (*anusamaya*) based on this alone.
He considers it to be logical. "Determination of the meaning of the word" means determination of the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*).

But regarding those things that are conjoined: if the sequential performance (*anusamaya*) is based on the scriptural injunction, then because the scripture states, "he cuts off two portions of the oblation," and because the scripture is singular, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the sequential performance is accomplished by this much alone. The proponent of the prima facie view considers that the act of cutting off is enjoined by the scripture.

Otherwise, there would simply be a "sarvahuti" (an offering of the whole). Now, if it is argued that the action of the whole is performed even through a part, even so, two portions alone are prescribed for the sake of restriction; therefore, because that [portion] is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*), the sequence must apply to that very thing. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is this: this is not a prescription of the ritual act itself (*padārthavidhāna*), but rather a prescription of the number of ritual acts. Herein lies the sense: the disposal of the remains (*śeṣapratipatti*) is as if it were obligatory (*nityavat*).

(1) Since there is no "offering of all" (*sarvahuta*) because of the injunction, when the offering is already established as being performed by means of a portioned-off sample (*avadāna*), the act of portioning itself need not be enjoined; rather, it is for that purpose—

However, since the number is enjoined as being dependent on the portions cut out (*avadāna*) by virtue of being subordinate to them, it is therefore logical that there should be a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) of a single ritual act (*ekapadārtha*) beginning from the cutting out and ending with the offering (*pradāna*), which is already established by other means of knowledge. Consequently, it is established that the sequence must indeed extend up to the offering itself.

"But because of the scriptural statement. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that the holding of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is for the sake of the sacrificer; thus, he advocates for the performance of the ritual acts in their respective order (*padārthānusamaya*).

The meaning of this is as follows: in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the holding of the post was performed by the sacrificer. Since the sacrificer is occupied elsewhere at that time, it is easier to perform the anointing and other rites on the post held by a second person. Therefore, the scriptural statement regarding the sacrificer's holding is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has already been established by practical convenience.

[This is] merely [the case]. Furthermore, that purpose which has arisen from the purpose in the archetype (prakṛti) is not obtained in the ectype (vikṛti) by means of the extended injunction (codaka). Nor can it be said that "this very same purpose will arise from the purpose itself even in the ectype," because there would be a contradiction with the sequence of items (padārthānusamaya) understood through the simultaneous injunctions of the scriptural meanings. Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that the sequence of items alone is logical, on account of the non-difference of the scripture.

Because there is an injunction for the simultaneous performance of the ritual requirements of the various scriptures; for, due to the diversity of the scriptures, those ritual requirements of the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) are distinct, yet they are enjoined by a single injunction for performance, which necessitates their simultaneous execution. However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*), because sequence serves the purpose of making the enjoined elements feasible, has stated that one should follow the order of the sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*). The meaning of this is as follows: it is so that the feasibility of the enjoined constituent parts (*padārtha*) is maintained.

Such a sequence must be respected. In that regard, if the method of following the order of objects (*padārthānusamaya*) were adopted, then the injunction that the sacrificer must not release his hold on the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) from the time of anointing until the end of the encircling with the cord would be contradicted; for it is impossible for a single sacrificer to maintain that hold over a post situated among many. Now, it might be argued that because it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), it can be performed by another as well. The meaning of this [objection] is: by the sacrificer...

The non-release of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has a visible purpose; and since that can indeed be performed by another person as well, there is *padārthānusamaya* (performance of the constituent acts together).

"It does not diminish" means: it is true if there were a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) by way of the sense. The meaning of this is as follows: for a visible purpose is of two kinds—some is obtained from the sense itself, while some is prescribed by the scripture for the sake of restriction (*niyamārthatā*). Among these, that visible purpose which is obtained from the sense itself is performed by whatever means it can be accomplished; however, that which is enjoined by the scripture alone must be performed exactly as enjoined.

The act must be performed, and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is indeed enjoined by the scripture. Since there is the possibility of an unrestricted person acting, the prescription of the sacrificer is indeed appropriate for the purpose of restriction. As it has been said: "But when there is an injunction, even though the purpose is visible, the meaning of the scripture cannot be transgressed. This has already been demonstrated.

Regarding the group of animals (*paśugaṇa*): here too, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), considering it a contradiction of the scriptural injunction (*śāstrabādha*), maintains that there should be a performance according to the sequence of the ritual sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*).

Just as in the previous case, due to the contradiction of the scriptural injunction, there was a performance according to the sequence of the sections, so too here, by the statement—"Having taken the portions for the deities (*daivata*), one should not offer immediately; one takes the portions for *Sviṣṭakṛt*; having taken the portions for *Sviṣṭakṛt*, one should not offer immediately; one takes the portions for the *iḍā*"—the taking of the portions (*avadāna*) [is governed by this sequence].

Because there is an injunction for the three [cuttings] to be performed without interval, and because that [injunction] would be contradicted by performing the sequence of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*), it is proper that the sequence of the three cuttings (*avadāna*) alone should be followed. However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*), considering that even in *padārthānusamaya* there is no contradiction, stated that *padārthānusamaya* alone is logical in order to favor the principle of simultaneity (*sahatva*). The meaning of this is as follows: even when the sequence of the cuttings for the deity has been completed, one who then performs the sequence of the *sauviṣṭakṛta* cuttings...

It does not at all subvert the requirement of continuity. In the archetype (*prakṛti*), however, because the animal is singular, it was performed in that manner with respect to one [animal]. Here, on the other hand, since there is a plurality of animals enjoined together, only a single portion (*avadāna*) must be taken from all of them; thus, there is no subversion of the scriptural injunction (*śāstra*). Therefore, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled through the performance together (*sahaprayoga*), without being subordinate to anything else.

[Page 1111] It is logical that there should be a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) according to the objects (*padārtha*). Furthermore, the dependence on the recitation of the mantra (*mantra-uccāraṇa-tantratā*) is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for simultaneity.

For the *manotā*-mantra reveals the act of cutting out (*avadāna*); in the view that the deities are performed sequentially (*daivata-anusamaya-pakṣe*), it serves as a common procedure (*tantra*). Otherwise, [it would apply only to] the cutting out for the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offering.

Because the manifestation of the *manotā* is separated [from the animal], the *manotā* mantra would have to be employed separately for each other animal, as in the case of various seeds. But what is this distinction made by this section concerning the "simultaneous performance" (*anusamaya*) from the cutting of the portions up to the oblation?
Its meaning is as follows: "But when [the acts] are connected, [the procedure is determined] from the commencement," as in the case of "saṃyukte tu prakramāt."

In this section, it was stated that from the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*) up to the oblation (*homaparyanta*), there is only a single ritual act (*padārtha*), and therefore the performance of those acts must be completed consecutively (*anusamaya*). Similarly, here too, from the spreading of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājināstaraṇa*) up to the husking of the grain (*phalīkaraṇa*), there is only a single ritual act;

thus, it is logical that the consecutive performance should apply to that extent. This constitutes the objection that the present section has already been covered by that [previous] discussion. He provides the following resolution:

Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever. For what purpose, then, is this discussion? He states the distinction: the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) maintains that "the delimitation of ritual acts (*padārtha*) occurs through injunction. The meaning of this is as follows: because the spreading of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and other such acts are enjoined separately, they constitute separate ritual acts (*padārtha*), separate subsidiaries (*aṅga*), and thus their performance must be initiated separately; it is by that much alone that there is *anusamaya* (sequential performance).

However, since the *avadāna* (cutting) has not been prescribed separately, let there be no performance [of it] merely by that much. But the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*) says: because the prescription is established through the distinctness of what is to be enjoined, there is no power [in the injunction] to delimit the ritual acts; therefore, the previously stated position alone is logical. The meaning of this is as follows: by the sentence "He threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), a collection of operations that cause the state of being rice-grains (*taṇḍulībhāva*) is enjoined. All of these...
For verbal roots (dhātu) operate upon a collection of momentary activities delimited by specific results. For example, the root *pac* [refers to Devadatta].

In the case of the word "he cooks" (*pacati*), there is a collection of activities consisting of sweeping the hearth, fetching fuel, placing the pot on the fire, pouring water, kindling the flame, throwing in the wood, pouring in the rice, stirring with a ladle, testing for softness, draining the liquid, and removing [the cooked food]. Therefore,

since the single ritual act (*padārtha*) consists of the threshing process beginning from the spreading of the black antelope skin and ending with the husking of the grain, it is proper that the sequence of performance (*anusamaya*) should be based on that unit alone.

Subordinate injunctions (*avāntaravidhi*), however, are not capable of delimiting the constituent elements (*padārtha*) of a ritual action, since this can be accounted for even by a mere difference in what is enjoined. By this specific distinction, that [case] also serves as an illustration here. Since the act of cutting (*avadāna*) is already included by the very injunction of the *juhoti* offering, it does not constitute a separate constituent element; therefore, there is a simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) from the cutting up to the end of the oblation. In the previous section, let it be granted that [the sequence is determined] precisely because of the difference in the injunctions.

Nevertheless, it has been shown that here there is no difference in the injunction (*vidhāna*) itself; thus, [the argument] is faultless. However, in the case of the modifications (*vikāra*), there are the after-offerings (*anūyāja*s). But what is this introduction of a difference in vessels (*pātrabheda*) in the discussion regarding order (*krama*)? We reply: it is for the sake of establishing the order, because a difference in order is observed when there is a difference [in the vessels]. In the case of a difference in the *upabhṛt* [ladle]...

Taking up one *upabhṛt* vessel, the drawing [of ghee] for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings must be performed; taking up a second, it is for the sake of the *anūyāja* offerings. If there were no distinction [between the vessels], however, one would take up only a single vessel and perform both drawings, which would result in a change in the sequence. Therefore, this deliberation is intended solely for the sake of establishing the proper order.

Here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises from the suspicion that there might be a modification of the substance. [It argues that] if the drawing is performed after mixing [the substances], there would be nothing more than the mere speckled state (*pṛṣattā*) of the substance intended for the *prayāja* and other offerings.

It is a modification (*vikāra*), but not a total alteration (*anyatva*). Furthermore, because there is a concern regarding the modification of the vessel, when the boundary is established, its status as the *upabhṛt* is not destroyed; rather, it is merely a modification of that very same thing. This is also established by the difference in time.
(1) P. 1316 (2) "nāsti" is not present here (3) G. omits this "na".

"One might argue that even the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) will be taken at a later time in the very same *upabhṛt* ladle. However, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: because it would result in a modification of the substance (*dravya-vikāra-āpatti*), and since by the word "substance" both the oblation (*havis*) and the vessel are denoted, a modification of those two would ensue; and that is improper. For if one were to admit a modification of the oblation...

Because it would result in the contradiction of the purpose of purifying [the butter] and so forth; and because, if there were a modification of the vessel, the status of being the *aupabhṛta* (the supporting ladle) would be lost; and because, if there were a difference in time, it would result in the contradiction of the simultaneous understanding of the two acts of taking [the portions]. Therefore, it is established that a distinction of vessels consistent with that—that is, consistent with the simultaneity of the takings—is logical.
As for the original model (*prakṛti*): now, what is being considered here? Is it the modified (*vaikṛta*) first, or the original (*prākṛta*)? For as long as...

Regarding the point that "whenever something is understood to follow immediately after the primary act, that alone should be performed immediately after it," he says: there is a consideration as to whether the sequential order of the modified (*vaikṛta*) acts is interrupted by the archetypal (*prākṛta*) acts or not; the meaning is that the immediate succession to the primary act itself is doubtful. Here he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "It is interrupted" is the prima facie view, because an interruption is perceived through the performance of the constituent elements (*padārtha*). If [it were] immediately after the primary act...

If the archetypal (prakṛta) elements are performed together with the primary (pradhāna), then the sequential order of the modified (vaikṛta) elements that has been understood is set aside; for it is understood from the performance itself that there is an intervention [of the archetypal]. However, the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is that the intervention arises from the injunction of the modified ritual, because the archetypal elements are understood [only] through that. For indeed, the primary rite is recited as being joined with the archetypal subsidiaries precisely for the sake of delimiting the meaning of the modified injunction; thus, according to the sequential order of the text...
Thus, the performance of the modified rites follows after the archetypal ones; therefore it is well said: "But at the end, according to Bādarāyaṇa.

But from the point where it has been performed. Here, the formulation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: It is established that, in all cases, the modified (*vaikṛta*) elements must be performed after the archetypal (*prākṛta*) ones, according to the principle "but at the end, [so says] Bādarāyaṇa. In that regard, it is proper that only as much as is displaced should be displaced, and not the displacement of everything preceding it according to the principle of displacement up to the end; for, being modified, there is no fixed rule regarding their sequence, as in the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

"Like the displacement [of the *pratikarṣa*]. Here he states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): Even in the *Rājasūya*, the acts such as gambling (*videvana*) and so forth—which are contradicted by the modified recension (*vaikṛta-pāṭha*)—do not deserve to be performed at the end. They must occur precisely where they are heard [in the text]. The meaning of this is as follows: first, the sequence between the gambling and so forth and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is understood through the order of the modified recension. In that context, when the consecration is displaced [to the end], [the former acts must likewise be displaced].

It is considered: should the *videvana* and other rites be performed at the end, or prior to the consecration (*abhiṣeka*)? In this matter, that very sequence which is perceived through the force of the modified textual order (*vaikṛta-pāṭha*) is what is adopted. However, performance at the end would contradict the modified textual order itself.
The other [position] is merely based on logic (*nyāyamātra*). What is meant by "merely based on logic"? This is the intention: even if there were performance at the end...

Even that [subsequent recitation] occurs only after the archetypal (prākṛta) and the modified (vaikṛta) elements have been recited, because it is grasped by the primary injunction through the force of its own modified recitation, according to the principle stated previously. Thus, when the opponent objects—given that the modified recitation is equal [to the archetypal one]—why is it said that the other is merely a matter of logic?
To this, the author states the final conclusion (rāddhānta): "This is what is meant: the performance at the end is not understood through any sequential order. What then?"

It is said that the performance [of the modified elements] at the end is merely a logical principle (*nyāyamātra*) because it contradicts the prior understanding. The meaning of this is as follows: the fact that the modified (*vaikṛta*) elements are performed at the end is not understood through any sequence established by direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth. What then? It is the performance at the end due to the contradiction with the prior understanding of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements—which is grasped by the injunction for the primary sacrifice (*pradhānacodanā*)—over those of the modified type.

It is understood that performance follows the understanding; therefore, whatever is first understood must be performed first. Otherwise, there would be a discrepancy between the performance and the understanding.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction; and that is not tenable, because performance depends upon comprehension. That prior comprehension of the archetypal (prakṛta) elements which exists is inferential; therefore, the performance [of those] based on that [inference] is governed solely by logical principle (*nyāya*). On the other hand, the mutual sequence of the modified (vaikṛta) elements, which is based solely on the order of recitation (*pāṭha*), is directly perceivable (*pratyakṣa*). In that case, because direct perception operates more swiftly—

Because that sequence [of the *abhiṣeka*] is stronger on account of its priority—since it was not previously established—for the sake of favoring it, there is a displacement (*apakarṣa*) even of the *videvanā* and other rites recited before the *abhiṣeka*. However, in the case of the displacement of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there is no displacement of the *agnīṣomīya-anuyāja*, the *praṇayana*, and so forth; for with respect to the sacrificial post itself, the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is directly perceived even by those elements that precede it.

"And that which comes before the archetypal [elements]. Here too, because the archetypal sequence is understood, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that the performance occurs at the end precisely according to the injunction for performance. The meaning of this is as follows: since the sequence of the archetypal constituent elements has been established in the archetype itself, it is not logical for an archetypal element to intervene in the middle without a specific scriptural statement; thus, by virtue of the archetypal sequence, the performance [is determined].

Since the injunction makes known the constituent elements (padārthas) such as the Sāvitra-homa and others prior to [the main rite], it is logical that their performance should occur at the end; nor is the mention of the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites sufficient to make known an insertion into the middle, because the sequence is not explicitly stated. However, a repetition of the text, when it serves no other purpose, makes known the sequence itself. Even if the sequence is not explicitly denoted, nevertheless—

The sequence is understood through the power of the textual order (*pāṭha*). Furthermore, since the purport (*tātparya*) of the direct statement (*śruti*) lies in its non-literal sense, by that power there is an insertion into the middle.

If it is argued that this is a case of simultaneous performance (*sannipāta*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that here too the mention of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is for the sake of establishing the sequence, as before. Just as, due to the repeated recitation of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, a sequence is determined with the *sāvitra-homa* and other rites, so it is here as well.

Because they are also performed by means of the release of the golden vessel (*rukmapratimocana*) and other rites, their application is logically appropriate immediately after the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice. In that context, the mention of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* was stated solely for the purpose of establishing the sequence of preceding items.
