The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*) considers what has been stated [regarding the subsequent order] to be correct.
But what is the reason that it applies only to the former and not also to the latter? To this it is replied: because [the sequence] from the latter...

Because of the understanding of difference, and because the prior [element] is understood as different, what was stated is logical. Its meaning is as follows: whichever ritual element (*padārtha*) is recited before the *dīkṣaṇīyā* in the modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta*), in that case, "finality" (*antyatva*) is understood according to the principle of Bādarāyaṇa; for, in accordance with that, the original order of recitation (*pāṭha*) is impossible. Therefore, the Vedic text (*śruti*) has that [the final position] as its primary intent. As for that which is recited later, its "subsequent state" (*parabhāva*) is [understood] by Bādarāyaṇa...

It is also not contradicted by logical reasoning. Even the continuous recitation is justified on the grounds that it must necessarily be performed. Therefore, since even continuity cannot be [the sole] intended meaning, the Vedic revelation does not have that as its primary purpose.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Ṛjuvimalā* composed by the venerable Śālikanātha.
The second quarter of the fifth chapter in the Pañcikā.

The third section, *Ṛjuvimalā*, is the "Increase. Anticipating the objection that this is an inquiry into the "subsidiaries" (*śeṣa*) and is therefore irrelevant, he says: "It is precisely for the sake of the sequence [of the subsidiaries], both individually and collectively..."

The relationship [between the parts] is now considered. For if the connection were made with each individual part, the distance [of the intervening elements] would be great; but if the connection were made with the whole collection, it would be small. "Extension" refers to the sequence [of the parts]; that sequence is large when the connection is with each individual part, but small when the connection is with the whole collection. Therefore, an investigation is appropriate. But what is appropriate? That there is a connection with each individual part, according to the principle that "subordinate elements (guṇas) repeat themselves for each principal element (pradhāna)."

But has it not been stated that number resides in distinctness? The meaning of this is as follows: it was stated in the second [section] that where distinctness inheres, there numbers such as duality and so forth reside; therefore, how can numbers such as six reside in each individual [atom]?

Consequently, let the prescription of number apply only to the aggregate as a whole. True, it has been stated; however, by virtue of the specific rule of application (*vidhāna*), [the number resides in the individuals].

It should be understood in whatever way it logically follows. The meaning of this is as follows: first, if *sāhitya* (conjunction) were a qualifier belonging to the subject (*uddeśya*) because it was intended to be expressed (*vivakṣitatvāt*), then since the expression of such an intention would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), it is certain that when conjunction is not intended to be expressed, the number is prescribed for each individual [subject]. Accordingly, by relying on a distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) based on repetition (*abhyāsa*), the number is rendered consistent.

It must be inferred—just as, for example, in the case of "He recites the first verse thrice and the last verse thrice," the number fifteen of the *sāmidhenī* verses [is established]. Because (1) P. 1320.
Therefore, a connection with each individual is logical; for this very reason, in such cases as "the *ājya* hymns are fifteen," there is a connection with each one individually.

[Otherwise,] for the fifteen [days] and so forth, there would likewise be only a connection with the aggregate. To this it is replied: An injunction is not capable of altering the nature of a word-meaning (*padārtha*). For an injunction conforms to the word-meanings; word-meanings do not conform to the injunction. This has been demonstrated in cases such as "one should sprinkle with fire. The meaning of this is as follows: first, the word-meaning of number consists of duality and so forth.

It resides when there is distinctness (*pṛthaktva*). And the kind of distinctness that exists in a collection (*samudāya*) does not exist in a single instance (*abhyāsa*). Therefore, by considering the nature of the number which is the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*), it is understood that the number is enjoined only in relation to the collection; thus, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is perceived in accordance with the word-meanings (*padārtha*). However, according to the injunction and by the aforementioned reasoning, there is a connection with each individual instance. In that case, the inherent nature of the word-meaning is subverted.
Since it is impossible to alter that [number] otherwise, one must resort to the injunction of number as applying to the aggregate itself, in accordance with the nature of the word-meanings.

Therefore, as long as there is plurality (pṛthaktva), the assumption of repetition is not possible; thus, the connection resides in the aggregate. In the case of *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter), however, the opposite is true. For in that case, there is an injunction of a substance by way of its being a *kāraka* (grammatical factor), and the *kāraka* belongs to the action. And yet, the action—
The collective whole is the action; therefore, since the connection pertains to the collective whole, it is logical that the connection applies to each individual member.

Furthermore, as for what was said regarding "the fifteen *ājya* [verses]," we shall explain that the suffix *ḍa* occurs in the sense of repetition; thus, in that case, the number is not being enjoined. What then? It is a repetition characterized by a specific number, and that remains unimpaired even when the connection applies to each individual member. Therefore, [it is not a flaw].
Since there is no contradiction whatsoever between the injunction and the object [of the injunction], the connection is exactly as prescribed by the injunction.

Regarding the repetition [of the mantras] from their own positions (*svasthāna*): since repetition for the sake of completing the required number has been established, this is now considered—whether the repetition is like the "staff-measuring" (*daṇḍakalitavat*) or according to their own positions. By this, he states the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) for the purpose of establishing the order within a single section (*pāda*). For when the individual connection has been refuted, this deliberation arises; otherwise, there would be an increase only in their own positions. This is because of the collective...

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers this to be a "repetition like a measuring-stick" (*daṇḍakalita*) because of their connection. It has been stated that as long as there is distinctness, one should not practice [the recitation]. However, when repetition must be performed for the sake of establishing the number, it is logical that the repetition be conducted "like a measuring-stick. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that it is proper to place it in its own position in accordance with the sequence previously perceived. The meaning of this is as follows—[regarding] observation—

A person who acts based on prior experience deliberates beforehand; without such practice, there is no security. Therefore, practice must necessarily be resorted to. Now, if it were like the "repetition of the staff" (daṇḍakalitavat), there would be a sublation of the very sequence previously perceived. And that is not logical. Therefore, let there be an expansion [of the sequence] in its own place. However, regarding the connection with the whole, it is both ways—

There is a contradiction. [Regarding] the *samidhyamānavatī* verse: surely, if there is an explicit statement, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself is not possible—namely, that "the *dhāyyā*s are to be inserted in the interval."

When this statement is made, there is no prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), because logic is weaker than a direct scriptural statement. The response is as follows: the proponent of the prima facie position considers that the statement is preceded by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and thus it indeed proceeds even in accordance with logic; such is the meaning [of the text].

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that this statement is preceded by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the *dhāyyā* verses as being "intermediate" (*antarāla*); it is not directly heard in the text itself. Therefore, it is capable of subverting the principle regarding the necessity of supplying missing words (*kalpyavacana*), and thus this explanatory passage must be interpreted according to that logical principle.

[The opponent] thinks thus: "But there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for taking an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) as non-factual; this is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*). Therefore, in accordance with the literal meaning of the *arthavāda*, this statement is exactly as it stands. [The author replies: "Is it not the case that logic (*nyāya*) is the authority for taking the *arthavāda* as non-factual? To this he says: "Logic does not restrict the meaning of a word; it has been stated that it is merely logic [that might suggest otherwise]. Therefore, it is logical that this injunction is precisely according to the literal meaning of the *arthavāda*."

This is not by way of overstepping the nature of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). The definition of the term *dhāyyā*, however, was incidental and has already been shown in the context of the increase of the *stoma*. It was stated that a mere general rule (*nyāya*) is not capable of subverting a specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*). And this injunction is: "The *ṛks* are accompanied by the word *vṛṣan*; the final triplet (*tṛca*) is the *paryāsa*. By this, he restates the meaning of the *ṛk*s.
To object: now he raises an objection—surely this statement applies only to the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice. What grounds are there for such a doubt regarding sacrifices that are not its modifications?

The meaning of this is as follows: since this injunction prescribing the *paryāsa* status for the final *ṛc* is found only in the context of the *dvādaśāha*, because that *ṛc* is recited specifically within that sacrificial framework, how then can there be such a doubt regarding other sacrifices—namely, that it should apply from the final [verse]...?

Since the *tṛca* has become the *paryāsa*, there must necessarily be something that comes as an addition (*āgantuka*), because the ritual properties (*dharma*) are established separately for each section (*pratiprakaraṇam*).
[p. r1121] (1) P. 1323 (2) G. for the sake of straightness (3) G. by means of additions (*āgantubhiḥ*).

Even in other *kratavaḥ* that are modifications (*vikāra*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), such a doubt might indeed arise to the extent that it is obtained through the extended injunction (*codaka*). However, in those which are not its modifications, that [doubt] is utterly inappropriate. He provides the resolution: "Because of the hearing of the word 'last' (*uttama*). What does this mean by "because of the hearing of the word 'last'"?

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that, from the statement "it becomes the last *paryāsa*," the [singing] is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the ritual act (*padārtha*). Upon hearing the word "last," [the status of] the "last" [is established].

The status of being a *paryāsa* is enjoined for the triplet (*tṛca*) in general, not exclusively for that of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers it to be subordinate to the constituent element (*padārtha*) which is the final triplet. Furthermore, since the quality of being "final" is prescribed even in other sacrifices, its status as a *paryāsa* is enjoined there as well. [Objection: But was it not stated that if it were subordinate to the constituent element, it would be purposeless? If the duty (*dharma*) were enjoined merely for the constituent element, then—[the text continues with] the injunction of the duty...

[Otherwise] there would be pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) because of the absence of a connection with the *apūrva* (unseen spiritual merit). Therefore, the injunction is that the rotation (*paryāsa*) is applied to the final triplet (*uttama-tṛca*) specifically in connection with the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). He refutes this: "There is no such pointlessness, because when the rotation is possible, the entire rotation is purposeful.
This very nature of the rotation to be enjoined is such that even when it is enjoined as being connected merely to the constituent elements (*padārtha*), there is no pointlessness."

For the designation "paryāsa" is indeed connected to the sacrifice (*kratu*). The word *paryāsa* is a name for the very end of the sacrifice, just like words such as *nidhana*; this is because the word *paryāsa*, when used without a prefix, conveys the conclusion of the sacrifice. As for the example "kṣetraparyāsa" cited by the author of the Bhāṣya, it should be understood that this was introduced precisely to demonstrate that even when accompanied by a prefix, the word retains its status as a term denoting the end of the sacrifice, based on the observation of such figurative usage. For where...

Let it not be that acts such as threshing, which are connected with the sacrifice (*kratu*) and are themselves the objects of injunction, possess the status of being merely properties of the ritual substance (*padārtha*), for that would lead to the fallacy of purposelessness (*ānarthakya*). Where the object of injunction itself is connected with the sacrifice, there no suspicion of purposelessness arises. Thus far, it has been shown that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) exists even in cases that are not modifications (*vikāra*) of that [archetype]. Now, considering that the example concerns a modification of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice itself, it must be refuted even in those modifications.

"This is the meaning" is the formal presentation (*upanyāsa*). The meaning is that even by means of the extension of the rule (*codaka*) in the modifications of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), a doubt may arise.
(1) This is because of the authority of the direct Vedic statement (*mā. śravaṇaprāmāṇyāt*).

To this it is replied: This is not a property of the ritual constituent (*padārtha*). What then? It is a property of the sacrifice (*kratu*). How so? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the unity of the injunction for the *dvādaśāha* is understood, not the unity of the injunction for another sacrifice. This is understood. What is meant is this: although there is no deviation from the injunction even if it were prescribed as a property of the ritual constituent in general, nevertheless, because it is recited within the context of the *dvādaśāha*, [it applies specifically to that].

Because the injunction is expressed as being conjoined with the twelve-day period itself, the prescription applies only to the constituent elements (*padārtha*) in relation to that [period], not in relation to another sacrifice. Now, one might object: "The injunction follows the constituent elements; otherwise, even the state of having twelve *upasads* would belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma alone. Therefore, it is logical that the connection should be with any sacrifice whatsoever, in accordance with the constituent elements. Thus he raises the objection.

The reply is as follows: Even when following the meaning of the words, there is no contradiction here; for in that [other] case, the term *ahīna* would be contradicted, whereas here there is no contradiction for anything. Thus, by virtue of the context, it refers specifically to the connection with the *dvādaśāha*. Therefore, there is no evidence for assuming a connection with another sacrifice (*kratu*). Consequently, in order to refute this semblance of a final conclusion—which holds that because the injunction would otherwise be purposeless, it must be an injunction regarding things connected to the *apūrva*—[the author proceeds].

This has been stated: that the prescription regarding the nature of the *naiyogika* (that which pertains to the injunction) is solely by virtue of the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*), and not for the purpose of avoiding meaninglessness. This might at most apply to the modifications (*vikāra*) of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, since [the details] are obtained there through the *codaka* (archetypal transfer rule); yet even there it is not so. Or rather, this property does not belong even to the modifications of the *dvādaśāha*; what then? It is the property of those [sacrifices] characterized by the *vṛṣan* verses—namely, that which is the final *ṛc*-triad (*tṛca*) among the *ṛc*-triads characterized by the *vṛṣan* verses.

This quality of being a *paryāsa* (concluding verse) is its specific property (*dharma*). It does not exist in other sacrificial rites (*kratvantara*). Therefore, even in those [other rites], they are merely adventitious (*āgantuka*) and occur only at the end. For since the status of being a *paryāsa* is prescribed for the final [verse] of each round, the adventitious verses would have to occur before that *paryāsa*. That is not the case; thus it has been said. But was it not stated that this is not a property of the constituent elements (*padārtha*)? How then can it be called the property of those [verses] containing the word *vṛṣan*? True, it was stated that it is not a property of the constituent elements.

(1) It becomes the meaning of the verbal root for another ritual act (*kratvantara*), but not even while not abandoning its status as being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*). It has been stated that it does not become a property of the constituent element (*padārthadharma*) by abandoning its status as being for the sake of the ritual.

Nor, however, by not abandoning that [original order]. Therefore, this is the property of the *vṛca* containing the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*) belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice, and not the property of any other *vṛca* belonging to another [sacrifice].
Consequently, it has been stated that it does not occur even in the modifications (*vikāra*) of that [twelve-day sacrifice].

But [it occurs] at the end of the latter two. Now, how can there be a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) here, given that by virtue of the scriptural statement, the additional verses (*āgantu*) apply only to the *gāyatrī* and other meters?

It is logical that it is an insertion (*niveśa*). However, this [argument] that "it is improper because the statement is not seen" is incorrect. For one who has studied the Veda indeed possesses the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*). This, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). This statement also occurs specifically in the context of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice. It is not only in the previous section that there is the statement regarding the *dvādaśāha*: "The *ṛcas* contain the word *vṛṣan*; the final *ṛc* is the *paryāsa*. But rather, there are three... [text fragment]

"Indeed, the Gāyatrī, the Bṛhatī, and the Anuṣṭubh are the bellies of the sacrifice; for here they insert [verses], and from here they take them out"—this too applies specifically to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). Nevertheless, he asks "why? and says: because no specific distinction is mentioned here, let it apply to its modifications (*vikāra*); but not to those that are not its modifications.

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that this should not apply to those [verses] as well, lest there be an error. Because in the previous case, a specific restriction was made—namely, "this is the rule for those containing the word *vṛṣan*"—and because such verses are absent in the modifications (*vikāra*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), the displacement (*paryāsa*) does not occur there. However, in the present case, due to the absence of a specific restriction, both insertion (*āvāpa*) and removal (*udvāpa*) are to be prescribed specifically for the *gāyatrī* and other meters within the modifications of the twelve-day sacrifice. As for those sacrifices which are not modifications of the twelve-day sacrifice...
(1) P. 1326 (2) It has been stated twice [p.

r1124] that this should not apply to them; therefore, only that which is not a modification (*atadvikāra*) is the example here. To this it is replied: this statement is intended as a supplement (*āvāpa*). As long as—
It must be an insertion (*āvāpa*). In this statement, the *gāyatrī* and other meters are praised as being the interior of the sacrifice; to justify this, it is said:
"For here indeed they insert, and from here indeed they take out.
And these insertions and extractions do not belong to the *gāyatrī* [as something already established elsewhere].

"The two have as their object only a small measure [of the mantra]," thus it is said; this is the postulation of a scriptural statement based on the principle "But the statements [are authoritative] because they convey what is not already known. And that scriptural statement, being postulated, must exist for as long as there is an insertion (āvāpa); since the purpose of the reason is established by that much alone, [the argument applies to] the interior of the sacrifice...

The justification for the praise [is as follows]: For here, it is not the *āvr̥tti* (repetition) and *udvāpa* (omission) belonging specifically to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) that are stated as the reason; rather, they are stated in a general sense.
Therefore, even the injunction (*vacana*), if it were to be inferred, would apply generally to all instances of *āvr̥tti*, and not specifically to the *āvr̥tti* of the twelve-day sacrifice.

How, then, is there a unity of the primary injunction (*prakr̥ta-niyoga*)? It is not a case of a single primary injunction, because this injunction is dependent upon the specific function (*kārya*), and the function is the *āvr̥tti*.

This injunction regarding the *gāyatrī* and other [verses] is based on the occasion (*viṣaya*); namely, that this insertion (*āvāpa*) which exists there must be performed in the *gāyatrī* and other [verses]. Therefore, since the insertion is established from elsewhere, this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). Consequently, there is no identity of the original application (*prakṛtaniyoga*). Furthermore, this statement does not concern only the insertion belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), but rather concerns insertion in general. Hence, it applies even to those occurring in other sacrifices.

Since the *gāyatrī* and other meters fall within the scope of insertion (*āvāpa*) and removal (*udvāpa*), there is no identity of the primary injunction (*prakṛtaniyoga*). The distinction is that the basis for the instruction lies in those [verses] containing the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*). Of the *ṛc*s containing "bull" that have been taught, only the last one serves as the filler (*paryāsa*), and no other; therefore, it is established that these [verses] share the same injunction as the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).

[The section on] the *graha-īṣṭaka* (brick of the cup). Anticipating the objection that "this inquiry is irrelevant," he says: "In this case as well, the consideration of the relationship between the primary and the subsidiary is solely for the sake of determining the sequence.

Since [the *graha-īṣṭaka*] is a subsidiary to the *vana-citi*, there would be a difference in sequence: the laying down of each brick would occur at every layer (*citi*), and the taking up [of the cup] would occur at every pressing (*savana*).

How can there be a prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) here, given that because it is taught as being connected to both the sacrifice and the fire-altar, it is logical that the *graha-īṣṭaka* is indeed a subsidiary to those two?
r1125] The reply is: because the purpose of the injunction enters into the effect, and because that entry occurs through the accomplishment of the *citi-savana*. This is its meaning.

Whatever limb there may be, all of that is for the sake of the *niyoga* (the mandate), because it enters into the performance of that [mandate]; either it must be performed by itself, or something must be performed by means of it. For a mandate is not accomplished by means of that which does not enter into the performance of an action and exists as an already-established entity, since a mandate has as its object that which is to be brought about (*saṃpādya*). Therefore, because the purpose of the mandate enters into the performance of an action, this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). But even with this much, the prima facie view is not [established].

It is accomplished because the purpose of the injunction (*niyoga*) is fulfilled by means of entering into the sacrifice and the fire. To this, he says: "And because the entry [into the sacrifice] has its purpose in the accomplishment of the *citi* and the *savana*"; this is the connection with what precedes. Even that entry into the sacrifice and the fire occurs only through the accomplishment of the *citi* and the *savana*, and not otherwise. Therefore, since the entry into the sacrifice and the fire also enters into the purpose by means of the accomplishment of the *citi* and the *savana*, [the result follows from] the *citi* and the *savana*.

The completion of the laying of bricks and the taking up of the cups is indeed the purpose [of the Savanas]. Whatever is to be performed as the purpose of something is the purpose of that thing; thus, the cups and bricks are merely subordinate to the Savanas and the layers (citis). He concludes: "Therefore, this is a remainder of the layers and the Savanas"—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this it is replied: For the purpose is for the sake of establishing the instruction, not the instruction for the sake of establishing the purpose. And this connection between the sacrifice and the fire-altar—

This is the instruction (*upadeśa*). Its meaning is as follows: it is true that the purpose of the injunction (*niyoga*) involves the entry into an action (*kārya*); however, that [involvement] is for the sake of establishing the instruction—namely, so that the purpose of the injunction may indeed belong to that which has been instructed—and not because the instruction itself depends upon an action. Furthermore, this instruction concerns the connection between the sacrifice (*yāga*) and the fire (*agni*).
Therefore, its very establishment is the action, and not the accomplishment of the *citi-savana*. And whatever is an action, that is necessarily subordinate (*śeṣatā*) to something else.

It is logical that the status of being a remnant of the sacrifice belongs only to the fire-altar (*agni*) and the bricks (*iṣṭaka*). But is this not merely a restatement of the established principle regarding the passage "He buys [the Soma] with a red [cow]"?

Its meaning is as follows: even in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, it was stated that by the force of direct injunction (*upadeśa*), the function of redness (*āruṇya*) is precisely the accomplishment of the purchase, even though it does not possess the status of a direct means (*sākṣāt-sādhanatā*). Here too, the same is being said: although it does not have the status of being a direct effect of the sacrifice or the fire-altar.

Nevertheless, by the force of the instruction, that very same thing is the effect; the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that they [the qualities] also come into being there because of impossibility [otherwise].

This [sūtra] is for the purpose of refuting that. The meaning is as follows: the proponent of the prima facie view in this context thinks thus regarding that section concerning the "red" (aruṇādhikaraṇa).

Since there is no way for it to enter into the ritual action (*kārya*) by any other means, it is logical that the redness (*aruṇimnaḥ*) has the purchase (*kraya*) as its ritual function through the force of the direct injunction (*upadeśabala*). In this case, however, because it enters into the ritual function of the altar (*citi*) even through the completion of the *citisavana*, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to refute that very established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) found there. Even in that case, it does not have the purchase as its ritual function due to impossibility, but rather solely from the direct injunction; for even when [the connection] is possible...

Since no other action is heard of by the force of the injunction itself, the injunction alone is the cause for resorting to that action, not the possibility of another action. The purpose has been stated.

[The rule] "They should be at the end because there is no intervention" applies. But [one might object]: "Whatever brick one recognizes as being accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa passage, that one should place in the middle..."

Since there is the statement, "One should place the *māyā* brick upon the altar," the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) position here is simply not tenable. [To this] the reply is: it is not untenable; one considers the statement "all [bricks] possess a Brāhmaṇa description" to be a restatement (*anuvāda*), meaning that all bricks indeed possess Brāhmaṇa descriptions for all of them.

Because it is grasped by the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) stated by the Brāhmaṇa, and because it is already employed (*viniyukta*), it is the injunction of qualification alone that is the allocator (*viniyojaka*) of the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*); the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth are merely its auxiliaries (*sahakārin*). Consequently, if this [specific] injunction were relied upon, then since all [bricks] would have to be laid down in the middle layer (*madhyamā citi*), there would follow the consequence of the absence of any other layers (*cityantara*); thus, the status of being "middle" would be untenable, and this scriptural statement would become devoid of a subject matter (*nirviṣaya*). Therefore—

This discussion refers to the laying down of those bricks which have been obtained as belonging to the middle layer (*madhyamā citiḥ*). There is no other authority [for this], and thus the prima facie view—that the laying down of the *aupānuvākya* bricks occurs in the middle layer—is untenable. This being the case, the observation that "they are different, they are different" becomes logical: "The last layer is indeed a receptacle; in that he lays down different bricks one after another."

(1) P. 1326 (2) R. [The opponent claims that] there is the status of being the meaning of action (*kriyākārthatā*). This being the case, it is replied: those [passages] containing the word *brāhmaṇa* which are enjoined by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) are accepted. Why so?
Because the remaining [mantras] are to be employed through mantras. Furthermore, it has been stated that *samākhyā* (name/designation) is merely worldly. The meaning of this is as follows:
if it is said to be "possessing a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇavatī*) with reference to the [general] recipient, then this statement would be purposeless because it lacks specificity.

If, however, it is intended with reference to the cause of application (*viniyoga*), then the statement possesses purposefulness due to its specificity. And when purposefulness is possible, there can be no pointlessness.

What is appropriate? But how is there the status of being *vaiśeṣika* (specific)? To this, the answer is as follows: because the *śeṣas* (subsidiary elements) are to be applied by means of mantras, and because they are to be applied by means of designation (*samākhyā*), and because designation, being worldly in nature, lacks the status of being Vedic (*brāhmaṇatva*). Therefore, they are to be placed upon the middle layer (*citā*) of the altar. Now, the passage beginning with "by means of the mantra" has already been explained through its own words (*nigadavyākhyāta*); this was stated with the intention of referring to a specific distinction.

There is no fault, because the words must be meaningful. The meaning is that [the text] "possessing a Brāhmaṇa" should be understood with reference to the means of knowledge for specific application (*viniyoga*), namely *śruti* and the rest. However, in the case of the *darśana* (vision/observation), the difference should be described with reference to the mantra; the difference is to be explained as being due to having a different mantra, since a *darśana* is necessarily preceded by [the existence of] something already established.

"Before the *lokapṛṇā*. Here, such a subject is addressed: in the section on the fire-altar (*agniprakaraṇa*), specifically within the section on the piling (*citiprakaraṇa*), without reference to any particular piling, it is recited in general terms: "Fill the space, fill the gap.
[The author] raises an objection against the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But surely, at the end, Bādarāyaṇa..."
Thus, it is not tenable that even the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick must necessarily be accompanied by a *brāhmaṇa* passage. The meaning of this is: "Whichever [brick] it may be" (1) P.
By this [statement], the placement of those bricks recited in the *Aupānuvākyaka* section and the *Lokampṛṇā* bricks occurs in the middle layer (*citau*).

For since the *Lokampṛṇā* is prescribed generally, the injunction that they are to be placed specifically in the middle layer is understood. Consequently, regarding the bricks that are already obtained by a single statement, it is not appropriate to say: "But at the end..."

Regarding the statement "Vādarāyaṇa," [the author] provides the resolution: "But surely that statement is for the purpose of prescribing the mantra; therefore, 'lokampṛṇā' is not accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa passage. The objector replies again: "But surely all [bricks] are enjoined by means of the mantra. Even those which are considered to be accompanied by Brāhmaṇa passages are enjoined by means of the mantra; therefore, 'lokampṛṇā' too is enjoined by means of the mantra."
It is indeed as you say. The synthesizer (Samādhātṛ) says: "True; nevertheless, in such [passages] as 'He lays down the citriṇī bricks,' this designation is primarily intended to denote the bricks.
Therefore, these bricks possess the Brāhmaṇa [explanation]. However, here in the case of the 'loka... [bricks]..."

"This instruction, 'Fill the gap, fill the hole,' has the mantra as its primary element; thus, this is based on indicative marks (*liṅga*). For a mantra, being recited within a specific context, is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) that illuminates a certain meaning. And this mantra is capable of denoting the brick. Thus [it is concluded] regarding the mantra.

By the force of its application (*viniyoga*), the brick also is applied. In this case, this [application] is based solely on indicative mark (*liṅga*). Furthermore, because it is applied as a mantra studied within the context (*prakaraṇa*), it enters [the ritual procedure] first. However, those mantras recited in the *Aupānuvākya-kāṇḍa* enter [later] by virtue of being accompanied by explanatory prose (*brāhmaṇavatī*), and are thus "interpolated" (*āgantuka*). Therefore, it is correct that according to Bādarāyaṇa, they should be placed at the end. Now, even though the *lokaṃ-pṛṇā* brick possesses an indicative mark, [it is not applied here].

It is argued that its placement at the end is appropriate because it serves the purpose of completing [the layer], whereas for those bricks accompanied by Brāhmaṇa texts, it is more appropriate to place them before the *lokaṃ-pṛṇā*. To this it is replied: there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) that the *lokaṃ-pṛṇā* serves the purpose of completion. Even the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) merely praises the mantra itself as serving the purpose of completion, not the brick. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that, because the mantra and the explanatory passage would otherwise be inexplicable, even those [bricks] based on indicative marks (*liṅga*) must be placed earlier.

"It possesses the Brāhmaṇa" is appropriate. Its meaning is as follows: even that explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended for completion which belongs to the mantra, that is the injunction (*vidhāna*) regarding the brick.

It is logical that this [iṣṭakā] serves for the purpose of completing that which is to be illuminated, and not otherwise. Therefore, the iṣṭakā also has only the purpose of completion; hence, it is proper that the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick be placed at the very end. Consequently, it is correct that those [bricks] possessing the Brāhmaṇa texts should be placed earlier. Ritual action is performed upon what has been consecrated, because the entitlement to perform rites is heard to belong to one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*), and because the fires are produced through the act of establishment (*ādhāna*).

The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that the qualification follows immediately [after initiation], because one relies on the well-known consensus of the Mīmāṃsakas that "one who has established the sacred fires" (āhitāgni) is the qualified performer; nor is this consensus baseless, since the fires are produced by the act of establishment (ādhāna), as expressed in the injunction: "One should establish the fires."

Because the scripture prescribes the laying of the fires independently [of other rites], it is logical that once the mere laying of the fires is performed, one possesses the sacred fires (*agnimattva*) and is thus entitled to perform the sacrifices (*kratu*). Now, one might object: "The entitlement (*adhikāra*) itself has been considered in this manner, but that is irrelevant. To this he replies: By this method, the establishment of the sequence immediately following the laying of the fires is stated, as in: "One who has laid the fires (*āhitāgni*) should not place wet wood on the fire."
The sequence for these and other such vows is established immediately after the *ādhāna* (the formal establishment of the sacred fires).

This being the case, the following is stated: it was declared in the third [book] that both [the establishment of the fires and the vows] are for the sake of the fire (*agni*). Therefore, the fires do not arise through the *ādhāna* alone. Furthermore, regarding the qualification of one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*) as asserted by the Mīmāṃsakas, he is considered an *āhitāgni* by way of the *āhavanīya* and other such fires.

One possesses the Āhavanīya and other fires; therefore, it is precisely because of this that one is qualified to perform those rites which require the three sacred fires (tretā). Since the Āhavanīya and other fires do not exist without the Pavamāna offerings, a person who has not performed the Pavamāna offerings lacks the qualification for those rites. Furthermore, the scriptural observation regarding the oblation—namely, "Agni, when created..."—refers specifically to an oblation intended for the fire, and not to the primary fire itself.

The vision concerning the *hotṛ* priest does not apply here, because it is absent according to the logic already stated. Rather, this vision belongs to another [rite] intended for the consecration of the fire; the term *agnihotra* is employed therein merely for the sake of praise. As for the vows (*vratas*), however, they serve the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself.

By that [reasoning], the fires have not been produced as a result of the occasion; and since the primary purpose is already accomplished even without the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices, it is logical that the occasional rite (*naimittika*) applies. However, in the case of the *sañcita* (the piled altar), just as in the rule "one who has established the fires should not place wet wood on them," and so forth, [the rite] occurs immediately after the piling.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that the attainment of the vows occurs immediately after [the respective acts]. Just as the vows of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) are attained immediately after the establishment (*ādhāna*), so too the proponent of the prima facie view maintains that the vows of one who has piled the fire-altar (*agnicit*) are attained immediately after the piling (*cayana*). Why? Because the meaning of the base form serves as the occasion (*nimitta*), and it does so precisely by virtue of being an accomplished fact (*bhūtatā*). For in the word *agnicit*, the suffix *kvip* occurs only when the action is already completed. To this, it is replied: this is not equal to the case of the *āhitāgni*.

For in that case (the *agnihotra*), the establishment (*ādhāna*) is for the sake of the fire itself, and not for the sake of the ritual acts performed with the fire, because there is no application of it within the rituals themselves. Here, however, because it is mentioned within the context (*prakaraṇa*), the piling (*cayana*) is for the sake of the ritual acts involving the fire, just as the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is for the sake of the ritual acts involving the rice-grains (*vrīhi*). And since the "act" here is that which is accomplished through the entire performance of the ritual, one is called an "Agnicit" only upon the completion of the ritual. Therefore, the rule regarding the Agnicit applies at the end of the ritual.

But surely, even the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) is for the sake of the fires, and since the fires are accomplished through the *ādhāna-pavamāneṣṭi*s, one would only be an *āhitāgni* (one who has established the fires) at the conclusion of those sacrifices; therefore, by means of the vows (*vrata*) as well, one ought to remain so only until the end of the sacrifices. To this it is replied: Once the *ādhāna* has been performed, the very function of the *ādhāna*—which consists of an unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) residing in the fire—is already produced. At most, because the *pavamāneṣṭi*s have not yet been performed, the refinement effected by them is absent, and thus the term "Āhavanīya" [would not apply].

The term *āhavanīya* is not applied [to the fire immediately after its establishment], because it is based on the consecration (*saṃskāra*) by both [the *ādhāna* and the *agnihotra*]; since the word is used only when both are performed, one becomes an *āhitāgni* immediately after the *ādhāna*, but not merely by possessing the *āhavanīya* and other fires. Furthermore, these rules are not understood to have the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) as their cause, unlike the oblations for breaking [the ladle] and so forth; for if these were auxiliary parts of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), [they would apply only during the performance of that sacrifice].

(1) If they were restrictive rules (*niyama*), then because the result would not be accomplished without the subsidiaries, there would be no immediate succession to the sacrifice; rather, it would apply only to the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

There would have to be a basis for these [rules], but that does not exist, because the designation "Agnicit" applies only to one who has completed the performance. Therefore, it is established that these are restrictive rules at the conclusion of the sacrifice. [The opponent objects: "But this inquiry is irrelevant," to which he replies: "In this case as well, there is the sequence of the duties of the initiated (dīkṣita)."

For the sake of establishing the meaning, this is considered: by how many [acts] does one become initiated (*dīkṣita*)? The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that one becomes initiated by as many [acts] as there is connection with initiation, because all [acts] serve the purpose of bringing about the state [of initiation], just as the fires [are produced] by the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) and the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices. The meaning of this is: even for such acts as "he initiates him with a staff" (*daṇḍena dīkṣayati*), there exists a connection with initiation, and it is something not found in ordinary worldly experience (*alaukika*).

The constituent element of *dīkṣā* (initiation) is that which is to be accomplished. The relationship with it [the result] is solely by way of being its producer. When the status of being a producer is postulated through the force of such a relationship, then, for the sake of parsimony in postulation (*kalpanālāghava*), it should be postulated that the causal factors (*nimitta*) themselves are the producers. Otherwise, there would be a dilemma (*vikalpa*), since the purpose of initiation would be fulfilled by each factor individually. For if one becomes initiated by the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice alone, then what would be the purpose of the staff (*daṇḍa*) and the other items?

If [the mantras] were to produce [the results] independently, because there would be no distinction regarding their connection to initiation (*dīkṣā*), there would be an option [between them]. And that is improper.

For this very reason, even the designation [of them as "mantras"] occurs only at a later time. To this, it is replied: "One who is about to be initiated" (*dīkṣiṣyamāṇaḥ*) is the term denoting the qualified person (*adhikārin*). (1) P. 1329 (2) G. If the sequence of words is based on the sequence of the word-meanings... (3) G.
That which is to be adopted:
"One who is about to undergo initiation should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu."

This is the qualification of the eligible person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, we shall explain in the sixth [book] that the object of action cannot be established until the eligibility has been fulfilled. Therefore, it is established that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice indeed produces initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Moreover, regarding the staff and other items, only their connection with initiation is perceived; and since that connection is possible even by way of being a purificatory rite (*saṃskāraka*), [they are not the primary means of producing initiation].

The *iṣṭi* (sacrificial rite), however, is the direct producer [of the status of being initiated]. Therefore, the establishment of the state of being initiated (*dīkṣitatva*) results from the *iṣṭi* alone; and in this very way, their combination (*samuccaya*) becomes logical, due to the difference between production and consecration. The *iṣṭi* is productive, whereas the staff (*daṇḍa*) and other items are consecratory for that which has already been produced. Thus, because their functions are distinct, their combination is appropriate. Otherwise, there would be an option (*vikalpa*), since all [the items] would serve the same purpose of production and because they are heard in the scripture as independent [of one another].

How, then, is there a combination (*samuccaya*) of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) and the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices? Because both the installation and the *pavamāneṣṭis* serve the purpose of bringing about the origin [of the fires], and because they are heard in the scripture as independent [injunctions]. The answer is: Since there is no other purpose [for them], there is nothing there that would take hold of those two [as alternatives]. Here, however, regarding the injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between things that have equal purposes. The meaning of this is: if [the fires] were produced by the installation and the *pavamāneṣṭis*—
If there were a single procedure for those things that have become consecrated (*saṃskāra*), then because it would be employed once, there would be only one performance;

and since their purpose would be identical, it would cause only one to be taken up. Consequently, there would be an option (*vikalpa*). But this is not the case. For those [acts] enjoined by desire (*kāmaśruta*), which are to be accomplished by means of the *āhavanīya* and other fires, people employ the *āhavanīya* alone; and the status of being *āhavanīya* is based upon both types of consecration.

For those [substances] employed for that purpose, a combination (samuccaya) is appropriate. However, since there exists an injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma that takes up the staff and so forth, there would be an option (vikalpa) among those things serving a single purpose. Therefore, it is only in our position that the establishment of combination is achieved. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that one cannot claim the non-existence of a thing simply because of the absence of its verbal designation.

(1) G. *adhikārasiddhe* (2) G. adds: "The object is established because the comprehension of the established object results from the qualification of the qualified person; we shall explain this in the sixth [chapter].

[The order of] the constituent parts (*aṅga*) is like that of the sacrifices (*kratu*). Now, it was stated that when a sequence is necessarily present, the order is determined by the textual recitation (*pāṭha*). The meaning of this is as follows:

where several ritual items (*padārtha*) are to be performed by a single agent, since a sequence is necessarily present there, the determination of that order is said to be based on the textual recitation. And for those [items] prompted by a single governing injunction (*adhikāra-vidhi*), performance by a single agent is required, not by multiple agents.

Since they are already established [in their respective places], how can a restriction of order based on the textual sequence (*pāṭha*) be suspected there? Furthermore, regarding the objection raised in the *Pravṛttyadhikaraṇa* under the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "it is like other sacrifices" (*kratvantaravat*), a distinction (*vyatireka*) was also described there—a disparity (*vaiṣamya*) was stated: "Because they have distinct injunctive statements for their performance (*prayogavacana*), an order among them is not tenable. Therefore, by that very same demonstration of disparity, the sequential order of other sacrifices (*kratvantarāṇām pāramparyakrama*)—

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) has already been shown that there is no such restrictive rule (*niyama*). Therefore, how can there be a prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) here? It is replied: this sequence is based upon the performance of multiple acts. The proponent of the prima facie view maintains that for one who performs various optional rites (*kāmya-karmaṇi*), a restrictive rule regarding sequence is indeed appropriate for the seeker of results (*kāmin*). Whether these ritual elements (*padārtha*) are prompted by a single qualification (*adhikāra*) or prompted by multiple qualifications, [the same applies].

In every case where multiple items are to be performed by a single agent, there is a sequence (*krama*). Since many optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) must be performed by a single seeker of results, when such a sequence exists, the restrictive rule of order understood from the textual recitation (*pāṭha*) will be respected. How then is it that in the *Sarvasvāra* sacrifice the order of the text is set aside? The answer is: there will be a sublation (*bādha*) by virtue of the purpose (*artha*). This is because once the sacrificer has reached his destined end (*diṣṭāṃ gatiṃ gatavati*), the performance [of subsequent rites] is no longer possible.

"There will be no fault because there will be a sublation by the means of valid cognition known as *arthāpatti* (presumption based on the fact). To this it is replied: This is an inquiry into the extension (*vitāna*) of injunctions (*vidhi*), not an inquiry into the extension of human desire. "Injunctions" (*vidheya*) refers to those things that are enjoined; their extension is what is being considered in this chapter. It is not an inquiry into the extension of human desire. Why? Because that [desire] is not characterized by scriptural injunction (*acodanā-lakṣaṇatvāt*).
r1134] Regarding the expansion of desire: if there were a fixed order of succession for human desire, then there would likewise be a fixed order of succession for optional rites (*kāmyakarma*).

It would be so, because the qualification [for the rite] also possesses a sequence, following the sequence of the qualifications of the eligible person (*adhikārin*). It is not, however, due to the lack of restriction in desire that the qualification arises without restriction by producing it according to one's whim; nor is the expansion of human desire considered here, because—being characterized by injunction (*codanā*)—it is irrelevant to the investigation of the meaning of the Veda as defined by injunction, and because that [qualification] depends upon desire, it would be non-injunctive like desire itself.

This is the definition. Thus far, by stating that [the order] is inconceivable, it has been shown that there is no fixed rule for the sequence of optional rites (*kāmya*) based on the expansion of a person’s will. Now, he demonstrates directly that the sequence of the rites themselves is not scriptural:
"And for a single injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), its connection with the expansion of subsidiary injunctions (*aṅgavidhi*) does not require another qualification. One—

The meaning is this: for the subsidiaries and the primary rites enjoined by a single qualification (*adhikāra*), which are to be performed simultaneously, there occurs a connection with the ritual expansion (*vitāna*) due to human incapacity; however, they do not require a separate qualification. Therefore, there is no sequential descent (*kramāvatāra*) for those [rites] enjoined by distinct qualifications. Why? Because of non-connection—that is, because there is an absence of mutual connection between the various qualifications. This is the underlying intention here: [in the case of] a single qualification...

The meaning is that for those who have entered [the sacrifice], there is an extension in the form of a row as if they were standing in one place, and not otherwise. Furthermore, it cannot be said that the verbal nature of the canopy—which lacks connection and lacks connection with the thing to be enjoined—is anything other than verbal. Therefore, this mutual sequence of the optional rites is non-verbal (aśābda). And practitioners of what is verbal do not respect what is non-verbal. If, first of all, in one...

If many desires were to arise at once, then, given that there is a simultaneous entitlement to perform many rituals, there would have to be a dependence on sequence. But this is not the case, because desires do not arise simultaneously. Thus it is said: "And there is no entitlement for one who possesses all desires. Why?

Because this has already been refuted in the section concerning the accomplishment of yoga (*yogasiddhi*). Therefore, even by way of desire, and even due to the simultaneity of desires, there is no [simultaneous performance] regarding the ritual acts to be performed.

[This concerns] the connection with sequence. Or, if mere textual order (*pāṭha*) were respected, who could prevent the order of recitation in the *Sarvasvāra* sacrifice? If it is argued that [order is determined] by meaning (*artha*), he says in response: because meaning has as its object only the relationship [between elements]. Since the means of knowledge called "meaning" has as its domain the sequence characterized by the injunction of the relationship between things to be enjoined, it cannot serve as a means of knowledge regarding what is not characterized by an injunction; how then could it be an obstructing factor? Therefore, there is no fixed rule regarding optional rites (*kāmya*).

By this [is meant] the Agniṣṭoma. Anticipating the objection that "this inquiry is irrelevant," he says: [it serves as the basis] for the subsequent section.

This section is intended to demonstrate the subject matter (*viṣaya*). For the subsequent section is for the purpose of considering the sequence (*krama*), and this [present] section serves as its introduction (*aupoddhātika*) in order to establish that subject matter; such is the meaning of the connection. Indeed, once the meaning of the phrase "by this" (*etena*) is known, it is possible to determine the meaning of the word "another" (*anya*)—which depends on that—as being "by another" (*anyena*). [As it is said: "This, indeed, is the first of sacrifices, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma; having sacrificed with this... and so forth.

When it is said, "Then he sacrifices with another," the Jyotiṣṭoma alone is understood, and the Jyotiṣṭoma includes all its ritual forms (saṃsthās). Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that this is a statement concerning all the ritual forms. The established conclusion (rāddhānta), however, is that because the Agniṣṭoma form is obligatory, the context (prakaraṇa) pertains to it alone. In this regard:

Indeed, because the *agniṣṭoma* is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, this sentence expresses that the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself occurs prior to other sacrifices; furthermore, the *agniṣṭoma* configuration (*saṃsthā*) is obligatory (*nitya*). Therefore, it has been stated in the third [book] that the context belongs only to that which possesses this configuration, while the other configurations are modifications (*vikṛti*), lest there arise the contradiction of joining the obligatory with the non-obligatory (*nityānityasaṃyoga-virodha*). Consequently...
"This statement refers only to one who is established in that [Agniṣṭoma] form.

Now, regarding the phrase "by another": because the term "by this" (etena) refers back to the Agniṣṭoma form, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the word "another" to refer to a different sacrificial form (*saṃsthāntara*). This word "another" is relative to things of the same class; for example, as when it is said, "one man has arrived."

When it is said that "it is not another," another person alone is understood; likewise here, when there is difference with respect to the form (*saṃsthā*), another form alone is understood. But the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) [holds] that because of the scriptural mention of "sacrifice" in the passage, "This indeed is the first of sacrifices," the word "another" refers to another sacrifice itself.
(1) P. 1333 (2) G. Anuvādaḥ.

Having stated that it is understood through the mention of the sacrifice (*yajña*), he says that by the word "another" (*anya*), another sacrifice indeed is expressed. If this is so, then by this word as well, let the Jyotiṣṭoma itself be expressed, since it consists of all forms (*sarvasaṃstha*); thus, even the priority would belong to that which consists of all forms. To this, he replies:

Because the *agniṣṭoma* configuration is obligatory (*nitya*), it is said that "one who has performed this [sacrifice]"; due to the contradiction inherent in the conjunction of the obligatory and the non-obligatory (*nityānitya-saṃyoga-virodha*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) belongs to the obligatory configuration. Thus, in the injunction regarding the original form (*pūrvatva-vidhi*), it is specifically the *agniṣṭoma* configuration that is mentioned. In this way, both the occurrence of the original state (*āpatti*) and the modification (*vihāra*) become possible. Occurrence and modification occur when there is a distinction [between configurations], and not otherwise. These two are spoken of in relation to the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and not in relation to the obligatory configuration.

Since the word "yajña" (sacrifice) is heard in the statement regarding the *vihāra* with respect to that [context], and since all *jyotiṣṭoma*s are sacrifices (*yajña*), therefore, by virtue of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*),
the term "other" (*anya*) refers to another sacrifice entirely, which is the subject of the *āpatti-vihāra*. The objections and refutations regarding this *āpatti* are found in the Bhāṣya.
Thus it has been stated.

Or, [it may apply] to those with a single *stoma*. Regarding the "single-*stoma* sacrifices," they are to be understood by the word "other" (*anya*) because of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). Since the sacrifices possessing a single *stoma* are mentioned in the *vākyaśeṣa*, they alone are to be grasped by the word "other. This is not so, however, because the word "other" merely conveys a state of being different from something else.

Nor should the *ekastomas* be accepted [as the subject], because from the word "other" (*anya*) there is the cognition of only that which is other. Now, it was argued that the specific [meaning] is understood from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). For otherwise, the function of the words of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would become excessively remote; such is the meaning. The answer is as follows: (1) P. 1334.

In cases where there is doubt, it has been stated that a determination is reached through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). Here, however, since the understanding [of the term "sacrifice"] applies to others besides the Jyotiṣṭoma without any doubt, this is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). For the function of the words of an explanatory passage does not extend so remotely as to apply to "others" in general.

Even in the case of the mention [of the sacrifice], the reference to a single *stoma* is appropriate. Since the adoption of another *saṃsthā* (concluding form) involves both the attainment (*āpatti*) and the modification (*vihāra*) in relation to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is logical that the term refers to other sacrifices within the scope of attainment and modification.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā*.
The Third Chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā* [p. r1138]

The fourth quarter concerns the disruption of the sequence. By the statement "here there is an inquiry into relative strength," the inquiry into relative strength refers to the section [beginning with] "and because of the sense" (arthāt).

He shows that it is not established as such. The intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the sequence is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*) and because the comprehension is equal, there is an option (*vikalpa*). However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that because of the contradiction with what is enjoined, the comprehension itself is unequal; thus, the strength of the direct statement (*śruti*) and its meaning has been stated. "The Āśvina cup is taken as the tenth, and one offers it third"—thus, the tenth position belongs to the Āśvina at the time of taking (*grahaṇa*).

That which is expressed by the tenth nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is to be understood as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), as it is employed by the sentence (*vākya*) as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the sake of fulfilling the ritual injunction (*niyoga*). When that [tenth position] is accepted, since a specific distinction arises through the force of the sequence of preceding and following elements, whatever extension (*vitati*) is thereby understood is based on the authority of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), because it is rooted in the syllables [of the text]. In this regard, if the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) were respected, the status of being the tenth—which has been enjoined as a subordinate element—would not be logically established.

Therefore, due to the contradiction with the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*), the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is weaker. Similarly, regarding the order of meaning (*arthakrama*), because the gruel (*yavāgū*) is what is to be enjoined, its status as the means for the oblation (*homa*) would be untenable if it were placed after the oblation according to the order of recitation; thus, due to the contradiction with the object to be enjoined, the order of recitation is weak.

Here, how is there a contradiction between direct statement (*śruti*) and meaning (*artha*)? The answer is: there is no such example at all. However, if there were one, then it would be in the case of meaning itself.

Because of that [reason], this is what is meant: the task (kārya) is accessible through direct Vedic statement (śruti); therefore, there is no contradiction between the direct statement and its meaning. Now, if the task is understood from some source independent of the direct statement, then a direct statement contradicting it is not to be respected; for the task is the object of knowledge (prameya), whereas the direct statement is the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), and a means of knowledge exists for the sake of the object of knowledge.

*Avadānābhidhāraṇa*. Here too, there is an investigation into the relative strength (*balābala*) of the order of procedure (*pravṛttikrama*) and the order of the principal elements (*mukhyakrama*). The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that the order of procedure is stronger because it occurs first; for the procedure—the performance—of the properties of the curd took place on the previous day. Since the order of procedure is based precisely upon that, he considers the order of procedure to be stronger.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that because the sequence is for the sake of the ritual action (*kārya*), and because the act of cutting off (*avadāna*) is the commencement of the offering (*pradāna*), the sequence of the primary elements (*mukhyakrama*) is stronger. Just as the ritual action is defined, so too must the sequence be adopted, since it exists for the sake of that action; and since the oblation (*homa*) is the purpose of the acts such as cutting off, the sequence determined by them is what should be respected. Furthermore, because cutting off and the other acts commence with the offering, the sequence must be adopted according to the order of the offering itself.
The vision has been explained.

[The term] *vacana* refers to being preceded by an injunction (*iṣṭi*). Here too, the inquiry is undertaken by accepting the sequence (*krama*) as that which is beyond the syllables (*akṣara-param*). "Beyond the syllables" (*akṣara-param*) means that it is understood by virtue of the syllables; however, the syllables themselves do not have sequence as their primary referent, but rather time (*kāla*) as their referent, because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) has time as its purpose. Therefore, when there is a priority-posteriority relationship consisting of a connection with time, the specific extension (*vitativiśeṣa*) is of the nature of sequence (*krama*).

The phrase "it is settled" (*avasīyate*) refers to the literal meaning of the words. In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), considering that the literal sequence of the words in the expression "one who is about to sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yakṣyamāṇaḥ*) cannot be possible [if taken as a restrictive injunction], asserts that the *iṣṭi* must necessarily come first. But why is it not possible? Because the passage is intended to enjoin the installation of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*).

Regarding the two statements: "One who intends to sacrifice with Soma should establish the sacred fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*), it is the very act of establishing the fires (*ādhāna*) that is enjoined for one intending to sacrifice with Soma;

it is not the immediate succession of the Soma sacrifice to the fire-establishment that is enjoined. For if that were the case, it would have been stated thus: "After the establishment of the fires, one should sacrifice with Soma.
Nor is it so stated. Rather, the sequence is established by the injunction of time: "Having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām iṣṭvā*).

To this it is replied: this present tense suffix cannot occur except immediately after the act of laying the fires; thus, even there, the sequence is established by implication. It is heard in scripture: "One who intends to sacrifice with Soma should lay the fires. In that context, this future-present tense suffix—since it is impossible for it to refer to the immediate present—indicates immediate succession. For if it did not indicate immediate succession, its meaning would be untenable.

Indeed, it would be so. By that, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) between the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) is understood. But where is this not possible? In what state, in which application of authority (*adhikāra*), does this present-tense suffix (*adyatanī vibhakti*) not occur except through immediate sequence? [It is] in the context of authority. The meaning is: if there were no immediate sequence even within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, then this [suffix] would not be possible.

Therefore, the qualification follows immediately after that; and since the performance depends upon qualification, it is understood that the performance of the Soma sacrifice occurs immediately thereafter.

Even in the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the sequence is implied by implication. Although the establishment of the fires is enjoined, nevertheless, because the meaning of the scripture is understood to be "one should establish the fires after having completed the Soma sacrifice through its immediate performance," it is established that the Soma sacrifice follows immediately after the establishment of the fires. Thus, a further supporting argument has been shown.
"Because of the superiority of the Brāhmaṇa. In this section (*adhikaraṇa*), the subject matter of the preceding section is established with respect to a specific scope;

whatever else follows is merely incidental (*prāsaṅgika*). By this, he removes the fault of lack of connection (*asaṅgati*). As for the meaning: that which was established in the preceding section—namely, that the two options, "preceded by an *iṣṭi*" and "preceded by a *soma* sacrifice," are not alternatives—that [rule] applies specifically to the case of the Brāhmaṇa.

The establishment [of the rule] is being made. Therefore, do both options apply to all three castes, or is it that for the Brāhmaṇa alone there is the priority of the Soma sacrifice? This is the fundamental inquiry: what other ritual act follows after the Soma? For instance, is it only the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) that is postponed for the Brāhmaṇa, or are both options available? That is incidental; even without this discussion, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) are already established.

In this regard, after the Commentator has established that for a Brāhmaṇa the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are postponed in their entirety and that the *soma* sacrifice must necessarily precede them, he subsequently considers this question: "Is there a sublation of the time for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), or is there a sublation of the time for the *soma*? He raises an objection to that: "Furthermore, what is the purpose of this intermediate mention of the pregnant woman (*antarā-garbhiṇī*)? The meaning of this is: having accepted the two alternatives already established previously, this section [of the treatise]—

It must be undertaken otherwise, because there would be no commencement of the legal proceedings (*adhikaraṇa*). Therefore, since the two options are established by means of subverting the time for the *Soma* sacrifice, the mention of one who is pregnant during the interval is redundant. The answer is: its purpose is as follows. If the *Soma* sacrifice is to be performed immediately thereafter, then two options are possible for a Brāhmaṇa; however, for others, it is restricted that they must first perform the *Iṣṭi* at their own proper time.

*somādhānam* means both the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*). If these two were immediate and mutually uninterrupted—that is, if the Soma sacrifice followed immediately after the establishment of the fires—[then the rule would apply].

In that case, since two options would have attained their own existence, it would follow that either the Brāhmaṇa or someone else could possess both options; yet at its own time, the Soma sacrifice must indeed be preceded by the Iṣṭi. This is untenable, because if it were stated in this way, the discussion would become a preliminary digression (*aupoddhātikī cintā*) serving as a reason for the commencement of the main topic (*adhikaraṇa*), rather than being an "intermediate pregnant [discussion]" (*antarāgarbhiṇī*). To this we reply: it is indeed an intermediate...

This is the reason for the state of being performed together (*sahabhṛṇītva*). For, once it has been established that there is no separate ritual (*karmāntaratva*) for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) by the same reasoning as the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—since the latter's status as a separate ritual was previously refuted through recognition—and since there is thus no other injunction to be performed, the sequence between the *soma* and the *ādhāna* is established upon the sublation of the time for the *soma*. Otherwise, while the *soma* remains in its own time, [the *ādhāna*] would have to occur immediately prior to it.

It is prescribed immediately after the *dhāna*. Consequently, there would be an absence of the two alternatives (*kalpa*); therefore, for the sake of establishing these two alternatives, this discussion is undertaken in the interval. Now, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the root-section (*mūlādhikaraṇa*): "How, moreover, is it understood that the two alternatives belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone? For even in the two alternatives, there is no mention of the word 'Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, due to the lack of distinction, the two alternatives belong to all [classes]."

[The prima facie view: "Because [the animal sacrifice] is preceded by the *iṣṭi*. However, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is: because of the postponement of the oblation when the sacrifice is preceded by the *iṣṭi*. Since, when the sacrifice is preceded by the *iṣṭi*, there is a postponement of the oblation consisting of the *agnīṣomīya* cake-offering—and that [postponement] applies without doubt only to the Brāhmaṇa—therefore, under the alternative that the sacrifice is preceded by the *iṣṭi*, the following contingency arises for the Brāhmaṇa: that his performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* would lack one primary element. Consequently, this expectation arises: "In what manner can the Brāhmaṇa perform the two [sacrifices] in their entirety from the very beginning?"

"One should perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. In view of that requirement, another alternative—the rule of having Soma first—is taught. By considering this required injunction, it is understood that the rule of having Soma first applies only to the Brāhmaṇa; thus, it is established that the two alternatives apply only to the Brāhmaṇa. Concluding this point, he says: "Therefore, the installation of the fires preceded by Soma belongs to him alone; otherwise, if [the rule] were elevated to apply to the Brāhmaṇa alone, it would be independent [of the context]."

[Otherwise] there would be the prescription of an unintended meaning. If, in the case of the Brāhmaṇa alone, when there is a displacement of the single oblation (*ekahavirutkarṣa*), the state of having Soma as the first (*somapūrvatva*) were prescribed for all [sacrifices], then there would be the prescription of an unintended meaning. The rest has been explained. (1) P. 1325 (2) G. Even without the establishment of the purpose of the two alternatives, this [is the case]: "But the cake (*puroḍāśa*) [is used] when there is no specific instruction. Since it is established that there is a displacement of the single oblation, this [text] is intended to determine its specific details.
The section on the *adhikaraṇa*. By this, the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) has been stated. And this *adhikaraṇa* was mentioned by the author of the Bhāṣya [as follows]:

regarding the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), having previously stated its impossibility according to logical principle (*nyāya*), he demonstrated both the commencement and the completion on that very same day for the sake of establishing its possibility. Herein, this is the intended point: in this *adhikaraṇa*, is it by logical principle alone that the modified sacrifices possess the quality of being performed in a single day (*sadyaskālatā*)? Or...

The question is considered whether there is a two-day duration [for the performance]. This inquiry is conducted by assuming that the statement regarding the "immediate" (sadyaskāla) performance is not authoritative. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), considering the impossibility of a two-day duration for both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*) due to the brevity of the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), asserts that because it is directly heard in scripture, one should favor the two-day duration of the archetype and thus perform both the commencement and the conclusion of the ectypes on the very first day (*pratipad*). The proponent of the final settled view (*rāddhāntin*), however, [holds that] what is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*)...

He stated that for the sake of favoring a two-day duration, the commencement of the *vikṛti* sacrifices should be on the fourteenth day and their conclusion on the fifteenth day. However, in the case of a performance lasting only the *pratipad*, both the connection with the fifteenth day and the two-day duration would be completely contradicted here; for, according to the manner already described, the connection with the *pratipad* alone is what is contradicted. The literal meaning [of the verse] is as follows: by virtue of the previous reasoning, due to its brevity...

The author of the Bhāṣya, from the perspective of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), has stated that because the time of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) lacks a connection to both [the preceding and following days], and because the archetype (*prakṛti*) is explicitly heard in scripture as having a two-day duration, it is impossible for the ectype (*vikṛti*) to have a two-day duration. Consequently, on this very fifteenth day, there would be a commencement of the ectype— which began on the fourteenth day— for the sake of a two-day duration, and a commencement of the archetype, which is to be completed on the first day of the new moon (*pratipad*).

He has shown this for the purpose of demonstrating the impossibility of two [rites] occurring at the same time; thus, since no contradiction with the scriptural injunction is possible, the *sadyaskālatā* (immediacy) follows from the statement.
