He stated, "Of the modifications (*vikṛti*). Having thus investigated according to reasoning (*nyāya*), he now raised the statement that there should be no performance in that manner;

for it is not possible for mere reasoning to be an opponent to a scriptural injunction (*vacana*). Because the rule of immediate performance (*sadyaskālatā*) is prescribed for an action whose time is two days, the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated that the modifications themselves possess the character of immediate performance.

The *sānnāyya* sacrifice; likewise the modifications (*vikāra*) of the Soma sacrifice. By employing the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the author of the Sūtras indicates that the same principle (*nyāya*) applies in both of these sections. To explain how the principle is the same, he says: in both of these sections, the indication of time (*kāla-lakṣaṇā*) is not possible without a governing context (*adhikāra*); therefore, since the sequence (*krama*) belongs only to that which has already been established by a governing context, its [application]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

It is logical that the same applies to the *kāraṇas* (the subsidiary rites). The meaning of this is as follows: if the qualification for the *soma* sacrifice were not established specifically in relation to the *sānnāyya* and the *agnīṣomīya*, then the *soma* sacrifice and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices would not possess their own respective character of occurring at a subsequent time.

Therefore, the one qualified for the *sānnāyya* and the *agnīṣomīya* is precisely the one who has already performed the *soma* sacrifice; likewise, it is precisely the one who has already performed the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

Since time can be restricted only when the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is defined by the qualification "one who has drunk Soma" (*somapīt*), the same logic applies to both sections. If the logic is the same, why then are there two separate sections? To this he says: "For what purpose are there two sections? The answer is: because in the preceding [section], due to the mention of agency (*kartṛtā*), the term "one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice" (*nāsomayājī*) refers to the agent of the Soma sacrifice.

The *sānnāyya* is designated by way of its being the agent [of the sacrifice]. And if the qualification belonged to one who has performed the *soma* sacrifice (*somayājin*), then such an agent would be required, and not otherwise. Since the qualification belongs to one who has already performed the *soma*, the sequence following the *soma* sacrifice follows necessarily; thus it is correct [to say] "one who has sacrificed with *soma*" (*somayājī*).

In that case, there is the state of occurring at a later time. However, in the second section, he raised a further objection, saying "it is not so," on the grounds that one has not performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). This is because there is no mention of the agent. How, then, is the logical consistency maintained in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*)? The answer is as follows:

It has been stated that there can be no indication of time (*kāla-lakṣaṇā*) without an underlying qualification (*adhikāra*); this is what is meant by "equality" (*tulyatā*). The meaning of this is as follows: here too, through the connection with the suffix *-ktvā* and other factors, the fact that Soma has the same agent as the completed Darśapūrṇamāsa is understood; this leads to the understanding that one who has already performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa is the agent for the Soma sacrifice. And it is not possible for such a person to be the agent of something [like Soma] when they do not possess the corresponding qualification (*adhikārin*).
Since the qualified person has been established, it is understood by that very authority that the Soma sacrifice must follow the New and Full Moon sacrifices; thus, their equality is stated.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Ṛjuvimalā* commentary composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha.
